PM Orpo: Finland working on €60m fuel subsidy package
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:19:57 EEST
21:19:57 KST

Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo (NCP) says the government is continuing negotiations on a fuel subsidy for those struggling with high pump prices.
"It's narrowed down to around 60 million euros, which is what's being discussed now."
However, where that sum would come from remains open, according to Orpo. He noted that there's little financial elbow room at the moment.
He said the key priorities are easing commuter travel and supporting professional transport.
Orpo commented on the matter at an event held by the Finnish Association of Political Journalists on Tuesday.
At the end of last month, the PM's National Coalition Party floated a nine-billion-euro savings proposal, among other things it suggested two billion euros in savings by reforming the pension system.
In another savings proposal, finance ministry officials suggested raising the age of retirement to 70. But Orpo has characterised that as unrealistic and reiterated that on Tuesday.
According to Orpo, the National Coalition wants to examine unpaid periods within the pension system — that is, pension accrual during periods when individuals are unemployed or studying, for example.
"Removing those would significantly strengthen the pension system," Orpo said, adding that savings could also be made in pension system administration.
Orpo also said the length of people's working lives should be extended, by enabling young people to begin higher education sooner than they currently do.
Data centre questions
The PM was also asked about suspected illegal logging at Google's Muhos and Kajaani data centre construction sites — and what his role was in that process.
"I haven't been involved in any permit processes whatsoever. I see data centres as a major opportunity for Finland when they're handled properly," Orpo replied.
According to him, not all of the planned data centre projects will move forward, but Google's project has the potential to offer major societal benefits.
Orpo also answered questions about data centre energy demands, and whether there will be enough electricity as more of the power-hungry facilities arrive.
He said the government has taken steps to strengthen the transmission grid so that planned investments in Finland can be accommodated.
According to Orpo, a number of other energy-intensive investments besides data centres are coming to Finland.
As an example, he pointed to a planned aluminium plant in Kokkola.
"There's interest in Finland because we have clean energy," he said, adding that he believes new electricity will be generated as demand for it grows.
Trump's turn against Ukraine
Orpo was also asked about US President Donald Trump positioning himself against Ukraine.
Last Friday, Trump announced that Russia had agreed to supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel to US and world markets. To facilitate that move, the US is temporarily lifting sanctions on Russia for the deliveries.
Trump characterised his conversation with Russian President Vladimir Putin as very successful. Trump has also said that Ukraine should not bomb Russian oil refineries.
According to The Financial Times, Trump is also threatening to halt the supply of US weapons to Ukraine.
Orpo was asked what he thinks of Trump's actions and how Europe should respond.
"It really was a huge disappointment. A direct deal with Putin, which goes against everything we've done together—together with the United States. He's making a deal with Putin which is financing Putin's war."
According to Orpo, Europe must forcefully state its position to Trump. He says Europe needs to continue supporting Ukraine, while ensuring that support from the United States continues.

Spanish crown returns to Ceuta after 19 years amid lingering migration crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:18:26 UTC
21:18:26 KST

King Felipe VI visits Ceuta and Melilla today and tomorrow with Queen Letizia, the first royal trip to both cities since 2007, coming two and a half months after a mass influx of migrants into the Spanish autonomous city of Ceuta.
Felipe VI has taken 12 years on the throne to make it to Ceuta, and he is doing so in the same month, intriguingly, as his great-grandfather. The King and Queen Letizia will enter Ceuta's City Hall, in Plaza de África, launching a two-day trip that continues tomorrow in Melilla. It is the first time they have officially set foot in both cities as monarchs.
The last royal visit was by Juan Carlos I and Queen Sofía, in November 2007, after an 80-year gap. This time the backdrop is very different: around 72,000 people crossed over illegally from Morocco to Ceuta on 30 and 31 July, into a city of just over 80,000 residents.
What does Felipe VI's visit to Ceuta and Melilla involve?
In Ceuta, the president of the Autonomous City, Juan Jesús Vivas, will present them with the keys to the city, a gesture also extended to Juan Carlos I and Sofía in 2007. Afterwards they will visit the Vicente Aleixandre school and end at the Muslim cemetery of Sidi Embarek, where an religious ceremony will be held in tribute to those who died trying to swim across the border. Dozens of them are buried there because Morocco refused to take back the bodies.
The big difference compared with 2007 is that the King and Queen will spend the night in Ceuta. Juan Carlos and Sofía did not.
Tomorrow it is Melilla's turn. The royals will arrive at 11:45am CET at the Assembly Palace; in the afternoon they will visit the Pintor Eduardo Morillas school and meet representatives of Melilla's civil society at the Melilla Puerto hotel. The Royal Household has mirrored the schedule in both cities, in order to give them equal weight even though Melilla did not experience anything comparable to Ceuta's influx.
Pedro Sánchez will not travel with them. The prime minister's office, Moncloa, says the premier does not usually accompany the monarchs on their official trips. The minister on duty is likely to be Ángel Víctor Torres, head of Territorial Policy and in charge of the single command for the crisis.
A migration surge still unresolved in Ceuta
According to the Interior Ministry, more than 70,000 people entered Ceuta from Morocco between 30 and 31 July. Sánchez was in the city on the 31st and described it as an attack on Spain's territorial integrity. On 6 August, Felipe VI received Vivas at the Marivent palace, during his holidays in Mallorca, and the Ceuta leader emerged saying the King wanted to travel when the government considered it appropriate. At the end of August, Sánchez announced that the trip would go ahead once the right conditions were in place.
On 29 September, at the gala dinner during France President Emmanuel Macron's state visit, the King called for greater solidarity from European countries and branded the situation in Ceuta "unacceptable".
Since August, 11,026 people have returned to Morocco, according to Torres: 10,513 voluntarily and 513 expelled.
Juan Carlos I in Ceuta and Melilla, November 2007
Juan Carlos I and Queen Sofía visited Ceuta on 5 November, 18 years ago, and Melilla the following day. They spent around five hours in Ceuta, where the King spoke of an "outstanding commitment" to the city. It was the first visit by a monarch in 80 years.
Rabat reacted before the trip even began. It recalled its ambassador in Madrid for consultations and, according to AFP, Mohammed VI viewed the visit as an offence to the patriotic feelings of Moroccans. Hundreds of people protested in Tetouan and at the border, while in Ceuta thousands of residents cheered the King.
Alfonso XIII in Ceuta in October 1927
Alfonso XIII, Felipe VI's great-grandfather, arrived in Ceuta on the morning of 5 October 1927 aboard the battleship Jaime I, accompanied by Queen Victoria Eugenia and General Primo de Rivera, then head of government. At the Puntilla quay he was received by the high commissioner, General Jose Sanjurjo, and Ceuta's commander-in-chief, General Agustin Gómez Morato.
He inspected the troops and visited the Legion barracks in Dar Riffien, already in Protectorate territory, where the Queen presented a standard to the Tercio regiment. In the afternoon he watched a parade, attended a ceremony at Nuestra Señora de África and ended the day with a reception at the Municipal Palace, which the royal couple inaugurated.
The following day they travelled to Tetouan, capital of the Protectorate, and left 1,000 pesetas (around 6 euros at the time, roughly 2,000 euros in today's money) for Ceuta's poor. The King had already visited Melilla in 1904, to lay the foundation stone of the port, and again in 1911 and 1926, according to El Faro de Melilla.
The timing was significant. It had been six years since the disaster of Annual, near Melilla, where thousands of Spanish soldiers were killed, a blow to the monarchy. Alfonso XIII was accused of having encouraged the advance that ended in catastrophe.
Then came Primo de Rivera's coup, which the King backed, and in 1925 the Alhucemas landing, which paved the way for the end of the Rif War.
The Paramount newsreel preserved by the Ministry of Culture shows Spanish and Rifian troops, enemies until recently, marching together before the King. Four years after that trip, on 14 April 1931, his reign came to an end.
Morocco's reaction
Rabat has spent decades claiming sovereignty over the two cities, which have belonged to Spain since the 17th and 15th centuries respectively. So far it has not responded to enquiries about the trip, and successive Moroccan governments avoid mentioning Ceuta and Melilla in their official statements.
Tomorrow, 14 October, a demonstration has been called in Castillejos to protest against the presence of the King and Queen of Spain in Ceuta and Melilla.
On Saturday, in his opening speech to parliament, Mohammed VI insisted that Morocco's sovereignty does not tolerate pressure, threats or blackmail and described relations with Spain as a "sovereign choice", but he did not mention Ceuta at any point.

U.S. President Donald Trump has stated that the agreements regarding an energy ceasefire are being violated by both sides, yet expressed confidence that the leaders of Ukraine and Russia aim to conclude a peace agreement.
Responding to questions from journalists before departing for a rally in Ohio, Trump commented on overnight strikes and the breakdown of the truce he had announced. Addressing reporters' remarks that Russia had violated the agreement, he noted: "There have been violations on both sides."
Commenting on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's statement regarding support for the energy truce, contrasted with a lack of similar readiness from Vladimir Putin, Trump asserted that both leaders support the initiative.
He believes Putin wants to reach an agreement, and we need to ensure Zelenskyy wants to reach an agreement too. According to him, Putin and Zelenskyy want to reach an agreement, but they don't know how. However, he said, they will make them come to an agreement.
Trump also defended the agreement on Russian diesel fuel exports, which had drawn criticism in Kyiv and the US Congress: "My diesel deal with Russia is actually not a deal for me. It is a deal for the rest of the world."
On October 11, Trump announced that an energy truce had been reached between Ukraine and Russia. At the same time, on the evening of October 12 and into the night of October 13, Russian occupation forces launched massive strikes against Kyiv, Kharkiv, and other Ukrainian cities, attacking civilian and transport infrastructure with ballistic missiles and loitering munitions. President Zelenskyy stated his readiness to refrain from striking Russian energy facilities only on the condition of a genuine, mutual cessation of strikes by Moscow.

Cargo Dragon spacecraft lifts off for ISS from Florida spaceport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:10:23 UTC
21:10:23 KST

NEW YORK, October 13. /TASS/. The US company SpaceX launched a Falcon 9 rocket carrying the Cargo Dragon spacecraft to the International Space Station (ISS) on Tuesday. The launch was streamed on the website of the US National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA).
The spacecraft lifted off from the spaceport at Cape Canaveral, Florida, at 06:33 a.m. local time (1:33 p.m. Moscow time/10:33 a.m. GMT) on the 35th resupply mission to the orbital station.
Cargo Dragon will transport more than 2.8 tons of cargo to the orbiting outpost, including equipment for scientific experiments studying the effects of microgravity on heart tissue, as well as a set of solar arrays for the ISS.
The spacecraft is expected to dock automatically with the ISS on October 15. In mid-November, Cargo Dragon is scheduled to return to Earth carrying the results of scientific experiments and equipment for repair.

MADRID, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Former Real Madrid defender Dani Carvajal has joined Getafe on a free transfer, the La Liga club announced Tuesday.
The 34-year-old right back, who ended a 13-year spell at Real Madrid in June after making 451 appearances for the club, has signed a contract with Getafe until the end of the season.
"The right back begins a new chapter with the Blues, bringing leadership and experience," Getafe said in a statement on its website.
Carvajal was eligible to join Getafe outside the transfer window because he was a free agent, although the club still had to comply with La Liga's financial regulations.
Getafe president Angel Torres said the signing had been straightforward and confirmed that Carvajal would be officially presented Friday.
"Carvajal's signing hasn't been complicated. We have done it and we will present him on Friday," Torres said, adding that the defender had passed his medical examination several days earlier.
However, Carvajal is not expected to make his debut immediately as he works toward regaining match fitness.
"He says he is in good shape, but he will have to speak to coach Jose Bordalas and respect the time frame," Torres said. ■

RIYADH, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Saudi Arabia plans to raise its East-West Pipeline's throughput capacity to around 10 million barrels per day in the coming years, Saudi Minister of Energy, Industry and Mineral Resources Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman bin Abdulaziz said Monday.
Abdulaziz made the remarks during a ministerial dialogue at the 25th World Petroleum Council Energy Congress in Riyadh, the Saudi Press Agency reported.

3 of 4 impeachment articles against Philippine VP Sara Duterte withdrawn
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:07:38 CST
21:07:38 KST

MANILA, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- The prosecution panel for Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial has dropped three out of four articles, the lead public prosecutor and congressman Gerville Luistro said on Tuesday, according to local media reports.
Under the remaining article, Sara is alleged to have unexplained wealth that was not disclosed in the statement from 2022 to 2025. The prosecution stated the adjustments are intended to expedite the impeachment process.
Allowing the withdrawal, Senator Francis Escudero, presiding officer of the Senate impeachment court, ruled that senators would no longer vote on the withdrawn charges and that the defense would no longer be required to present evidence on them.
The two charges dropped on Tuesday alleged that Sara made grave threats against Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos and his family, and misused confidential funds of the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education (DepEd). Last week, the prosecution panel had already announced the withdrawal of the charge that Sara bribed Department of Education officials.
The Senate Impeachment Court will pause its trial from Wednesday and reconvene in November, when the defense is expected to present evidence and call witnesses.
Sara is the daughter of former President Rodrigo Duterte. She announced her candidacy for the 2028 Philippine presidential election in February this year. The Philippine Senate in July commenced the impeachment trial against her.
Under the Philippine Constitution, if two-thirds or more of the senators vote in favor of the impeachment, Sara will be convicted, removed from office, and barred from holding public office for life. The Philippines has 24 senators, four of whom are currently unable to perform their duties due to detention, unknown whereabouts or medical leave abroad.
In September, the Senate impeachment court ruled that the basis for conviction votes shall only cover senators who remain legally and factually capable of taking part in the impeachment proceedings at the time of voting, a move seen as lowering the vote threshold for her impeachment conviction.
Multiple local opinion polls show Sara remains leading in the 2028 Philippine presidential election. ■

Swedish parliament to vote on new PM Thursday amid coalition deadlock
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:07:32 CST
21:07:32 KST

HELSINKI, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- The Swedish parliament is set to vote Thursday on Social Democratic Party leader Magdalena Andersson's nomination as prime minister (PM), parliamentary speaker Andreas Norlen announced Tuesday. Negotiations to form a new government have been deadlocked since last month's general election.
Norlen said at a press conference that he would nominate Andersson to lead a single-party Social Democratic government, despite the lack of an agreement among the four parties that together secured a narrow parliamentary majority in the election.
Earlier Tuesday, Andersson told journalists after meeting Norlen that although progress had been made in coalition negotiations, conditions were still not in place to form a government capable of securing sufficient parliamentary support.
She said she was ready for a parliamentary vote on her nomination as PM, which would concern a government consisting solely of the Social Democratic Party, as no agreement had been reached with other parties.
However, the Left Party and the Green Party, two potential parliamentary allies of the Social Democratic Party, both said Tuesday they would vote against a single-party Social Democratic government. Green Party co-leader Amanda Lind reiterated her preference for a majority government involving all four parties.
According to SVT, coalition talks have been hampered mainly by disagreements between the Center Party and the Left Party. The latter insisted on joining the government and securing cabinet posts, while the Center Party refuses to serve in a government alongside the Left Party.
The Social Democratic Party, Left Party, Green Party and Center Party together won 176 seats in the 349-member parliament in September's election, giving them a narrow majority but leaving them divided over the composition of a new government.
Andersson was first tasked with exploring the formation of a new government on Sept. 18, after outgoing Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson requested to be relieved of his duties following the election.
However, Andersson returned the mandate on Sept. 28 after the Left Party backed the Moderate Party's candidate rather than her Social Democratic Party's candidate in the parliamentary speaker election.
Norlen reassigned Andersson the task on Oct. 2, but negotiations remained inconclusive, prompting her to request a one-day extension before reporting back on Tuesday.
Under Sweden's system of negative parliamentarism, a PM candidate may assume office unless at least 175 of the 349 lawmakers vote against the nomination. If the candidate is rejected, the speaker must then put forward another proposal. ■

China proposes adjustments to export rules for dual-use aviation items
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:07:11 CST
21:07:11 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of Commerce has proposed adjustments to export procedures for dual-use items in the civil aviation sector, allowing eligible enterprises to obtain export certificates through registration rather than applying for individual export licenses.
The ministry recently released a draft regulation on managing export certificates for dual-use civil aviation items, seeking public feedback. The goal is to balance development with security while making it easier to export these items in compliance with regulations.
Under the proposed measures, aviation enterprises exporting items such as aircraft engines and inertial navigation systems for legitimate purposes, including repair, maintenance and leasing, would no longer need to apply for export licenses on a shipment-by-shipment basis, a ministry official explained.
Instead, eligible exporters would automatically obtain export certificates after registering the required information, enabling them to complete customs clearance through paperless procedures.
The new arrangement is expected to shorten supply cycles for passenger and cargo aircraft components, improve aviation safety, support the international development of China's civil aviation industry and boost the competitiveness of related service industries, the official said.
China introduced regulations on the classified management of civil aviation parts exports in 2006, making it easier for aviation companies to send engines, inertial navigation systems and other components abroad for repairs and maintenance. This move helped promote civil aviation safety and support industry development.
Following the entry into force of China's Regulations on Export Control of Dual-Use Items in December 2024, which adjusted the country's export licensing framework, the earlier rules need to be updated accordingly, the official said.
The 22-article draft specifies eligible exporters, applicable export scenarios, registration and customs clearance procedures, compliance obligations and administrative penalties.
The proposed measures would cover exports for overseas repair, maintenance and replacement, the return of damaged items, as well as reasonable quantities of spare parts exported by aircraft manufacturers headquartered in China.
Exports of drones for overseas exhibitions, demonstrations and international emergency rescue operations could also qualify for similar arrangements.
To prevent misuse, the draft sets restrictions on eligible entities and export activities, requires exporters to report certificate usage and unusual circumstances, and authorizes regulators to request additional documentation or revoke certificates under special circumstances.
The ministry will further refine the draft based on public feedback and work toward its early implementation to facilitate compliant exports by aviation enterprises, the official said. ■

Bulgaria PM summons Russian ambassador after merchant ship attacks
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:07:08 CST
21:07:08 KST

SOFIA, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Prime Minister Rumen Radev summoned Russian Ambassador to Bulgaria Eleonora Mitrofanova on Tuesday over a series of drone attacks on merchant ships in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea over the past week.
Radev acknowledged that Bulgaria did not have conclusive evidence regarding the origin of the drones. However, he argued that since one of the vessels targeted was registered in Ukraine and Ukrainian-owned, "it makes no sense for Ukraine to destroy its own ships," according to the Bulgarian Government Information Service (GIS).
Mitrofanova said she understood Radev's reasoning but had received no information from the Russian government related to the recent attacks in the Black Sea, the GIS added.
Meanwhile, Mitrofanova raised the possibility that these attacks on merchant ships near Bulgarian territorial waters could have been a provocation by a third country.
Radev emphasized that attacks on merchant ships were absolutely unacceptable, warning that they risked significantly escalating the conflict. He called for continued investigations with the EU and NATO allies to establish the truth.
Tensions in the Black Sea near Bulgaria have escalated since unidentified drones sank one merchant ship and set another on fire about 70 nautical miles east of Byala on Oct. 6.
Two more merchant ships came under attack early Tuesday.
The "Chelsea 3," flying the Maltese flag, registered in Ukraine, and Ukrainian-owned, was attacked 18 nautical miles east of the town of Byala. Bulgarian authorities rescued all 15 crew members aboard the vessel. The other ship, the Guinea-Bissau-flagged "HS Dignity," sank near Krapets. According to the latest update from Bulgarian authorities, five crew members were rescued, while 11 remained missing. ■

Fleming Philippa Jorissen helps in search for Amelia Earhart’s plane in the Pacific
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:06:39 UTC
21:06:39 KST

American aviation pioneer Amelia Earhart was attempting to fly round the globe, when her plane disappeared. Fleming Philippa Jorissen is part of an international team that believes her craft may well be found on an uninhabited island in the Pacific.
Fleming Philippa Jorissen helps in search for Amelia Earhart’s plane in the Pacific
“I find it very difficult to say how likely it is that we’ll find the aeroplane, but I certainly hope so” says Philippa Jorissen, one of the researchers heading to Nikumaroro Island to search for Amelia Earhart’s missing aeroplane. “In the US, she’s a real heroine; everyone knows her and her story.”
Philippa is part of an international research team from Purdue University in Indiana and the Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) in Oregon. Together, they are searching for aviation pioneer Earhart’s missing aeroplane to determine whether she actually crashed on Nikumaroro Island.
Jorissen completed a master’s degree in archaeology in Leiden and then moved to Oregon to pursue her PhD. “I specialise in island archaeology, mainly on islands in the Caribbean and the Pacific. That’s how I came to be involved in this project.”
After six days at sea, Jorissen finally set foot on Nikumaroro for the first time.
“We took the boat out to the island for the first time today. It was quite an adventure. The sea is quite rough. You have to transfer from the large boat to a smaller one and then navigate that smaller boat through a narrow channel. That’s quite a feat in itself,” laughs Philippa.
“We’ve laid out a path today so that we can carry all our equipment to the other side of the lagoon and then start our fieldwork.”
“The island is completely uninhabited. No one has been here since 2017”.
But is Earhart’s aeroplane really on Nikumaroro?
“We know both a lot and very little about it,” Philippa explains. “There are a huge number of theories about where she crashed. According to some theories, she landed somewhere near Japan or was taken prisoner. But there’s also a theory that she crashed near this island. That has become one of the more widely accepted theories.”
Several expeditions have already been to Nikumaroro. “Her radio signals have also been traced back to this spot,” Philippa says.
“When a hurricane passed through here in 2015, someone started looking at the satellite images. An object appeared in the lagoon that could not be identified. It was a new object, which some people think might well be Amelia’s aeroplane.”
‘I became involved in the project when they showed me the satellite images taken after the hurricane had passed,’ says Philippa.
Earhart a pioneer in many fields
Earhart was a pioneer in the field of aviation, but she was much more than that.
“For example, she was married, but she told her husband she wouldn’t stop flying. From a young age, she stood up for herself and tried to break through gender norms. I think that’s what makes her particularly popular today.”
“At the start of the 20th century, it was absolutely unheard of for women to be in the spotlight like that, certainly not in a male-dominated profession like that of a pilot. She also continued to pursue records: amongst other things, she was the first woman to make a solo flight across the Atlantic and set records for flight distances.”
“Her final attempt was a flight round the world. But sadly, that ended in tragedy.”
Amelia’s aeroplane crashed and has never been recovered.

Iran and Russia ramping up hybrid campaigns in Britain, UK spy chief says
LONDON, Oct 13 - Iran is ramping up attempts to hit harder targets such as military sites in Britain while Russia is escalating its hybrid warfare as it lashes out against Ukraine's allies, the UK's domestic spy chief said on Tuesday.
In his annual speech on wide-ranging threats to Britain, MI5's Director General Ken McCallum also said the greatest concern about the misuse of AI was terrorists being able to develop bioweapons or even create new novel pathogens.
McCallum said state threats had quadrupled over the last decade meaning his organisation now devoted more resources to the issue than during the Cold War.

On Russia, which likewise denies involvement in hostile acts in Britain, the UK spy chief said it remained the "aggressor number one".
He echoed comments from other European spy agencies that Russia was using tactics just short of conventional conflict, citing the attempted drone attack on a cargo plane at a German airport and a cyber attack on Polish energy infrastructure.
"It's no accident that Russian aggressors are trying to unsettle other European homelands at a time when their military progress in Ukraine is minimal and horrifically costly," he said. REUTERS

Critics warn of espionage risks, loss of trust within NATO as Slovakia restores military-diplomatic representation with Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:04:00 UTC
21:04:00 KST

Concern as Slovakia restores military contacts with Russia
October 13, 2026
When Robert Fico sat opposite Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin in May, the Slovak prime minister said relations between their countries should extend beyond energy supplies.
He told the Russian president that steps had already been taken to restore military attaches at their respective embassies.
Five months later, the arrangement is now taking shape.
Slovakia has sent two military officers — Brigadier General Slavomir Staviarsky and his deputy, Colonel Ivo Gahir — to Moscow and is preparing to receive a Russian military attache in Bratislava, restoring military-diplomatic representation for the first time since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
What has Slovakia to gain?
The move has prompted criticism from opposition politicians, who question what Slovakia stands to gain.
They warn that Russia could use the arrangement to strengthen its intelligence operations.
"One additional military attache does not fundamentally change that broader picture; the appointment's main significance is the political signal it sends," Martin Poliacik, a former Slovak MP affiliated with the opposition Progressive Slovakia party, told DW.
"NATO allies should be concerned both about the activities of the incoming officer and about the political environment in which he will operate," he went on.
The appointments were reported by Slovak news website Aktuality.sk on October 8. Both officers appear on the Slovak Defense Ministry's published list of military diplomats serving abroad.
According to public broadcaster STVR, Staviarsky has been in Moscow since the beginning of August.
Meanwhile, opposition defense experts quoted by Aktuality.sk named the incoming Russian officer as Maxim Verezan.
Verezan has received Slovak approval, according to the opposition sources cited by the website, but was not yet listed among accredited military attaches.
Aktuality.sk says that the Defense Ministry has not answered its question as to when Verezan is due to arrive in Bratislava.
Fear of espionage and disinformation
The prospect has revived memories of a Russian espionage scandal involving Sergei Solomasov, the Russian embassy's deputy military attache in Bratislava, a few years ago.
Solomasov was filmed recruiting and handing over money to Bohus Garbar, a contributor to the pro-Russian website Hlavne spravy in 2021.
Solomasov was expelled from Slovakia the following year. Garbar was subsequently convicted of espionage and bribery.
Opposition experts told Aktuality.sk that a Slovak attache in Moscow would be closely watched and obtain little useful information, while the reciprocal Russian posting could facilitate espionage in Slovakia.
They warned that the incoming officer could conduct influence and disinformation operations, questioning what Slovakia would receive in return.
Government defends the move
The government and its supporters have defended the renewal of contacts as a means of gathering information and maintaining diplomatic representation.
In a statement reported by Slovak public broadcaster STVR, Slovak military intelligence said Staviarsky's role was to assess the security and military-political situation and keep the Defense Ministry informed.
Richard Gluck, a member of Fico's Smer party who chairs parliament's defense and security committee, pointed to the presence of American, British and French military diplomats in Moscow.
"We were losing a great deal of information," Gluck told STVR, arguing that ending Slovakia's military diplomatic presence in Moscow had been a mistake.
'A very serious step'
For retired Lieutenant General Pavel Macko, however, the circumstances in which the previous contacts ended are crucial.
"This is a very serious step taken by the Fico government," said Macko, a former Slovak deputy chief of defense and once the highest-ranking Slovak general in NATO's command structures.
"Nothing has changed [since 2022], just the opposite," he went on.
"Russia's adversarial activities continue to grow in Slovakia and in the region. The Russian war of aggression against Ukraine continues with high intensity, so do the hostile hybrid activities against Slovakia and its neighbors," Macko said.
He pointed to a foiled plot to burn down a Ukrainian-owned drone factory in eastern Slovakia and suspicions that incidents in Munich and Leipzig were linked to Russian operations based in Slovakia.
Macko also warned that political influence over Slovakia's intelligence services and the government's pro-Russian policies could further damage intelligence-sharing and trust among allies, despite the presence of "a significant number of very professional and trustworthy officers."
One eye on next year's election?
Martin Poliacik, meanwhile, said he suspected political motives lay behind the decision to restore the military attache posts, which comes as Prime Minister Fico eyes his chances of re-election next year.
"[Fico's] best chance of building a credible narrative for the next election is to claim that everyone else is dragging us into war and he alone wants peace," Poliacik told DW.
"I believe he will argue that he is best placed to talk to Putin about ending the war, and that this requires an exceptionally close relationship with him," he went on, adding that Fico tried to keep quiet about the major role played by Slovak arms manufacturers in supplying Ukraine with ammunition.
The ammunition is supplied under commercial contracts, rather than as military aid from the Slovak government.
Poliacik, too, distinguished between Slovakia's formal commitments and confidence in its political leadership. In his view, Western partners have become accustomed to Fico's behavior.
"Slovakia is formally fulfilling its NATO commitments," he went on.
"Formal compliance does not, by itself, settle the question of political trust," Poliacik added. "Predictability, however, is not the same as reliability."

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Tax revenue totaled NT$3.57 trillion (US$111.9 billion) in the first nine months of the year, up 24.4% from a year earlier, Ministry of Finance data showed Tuesday.
September tax revenue rose 19.6% year on year to NT$496.5 billion, per Tai Sounds. Business tax, corporate income tax, and securities transaction tax recorded the largest increases in September, rising NT$29.7 billion, NT$25.4 billion, and NT$22.2 billion, respectively.
Business tax revenue reached NT$141.4 billion in September, up 26.6% from a year earlier, while the January-to-September total rose 23.9% to NT$623 billion. The ministry attributed the increase to domestic demand and higher taxes on imported electronic components, information and communications technology products, and audiovisual equipment, partly offset by higher tax refunds for exporters, per UDN.
Securities transaction tax revenue totaled NT$53.4 billion in September, up 71.2% from a year earlier. However, it fell for a third consecutive month compared with the previous month.
Average daily trading value on the listed and over-the-counter stock markets reached NT$1.03 trillion in September, up NT$600.6 billion from a year earlier. The nine-month average rose NT$445.1 billion to NT$1.1461 trillion, helping boost securities transaction tax revenue for the period.
For the first nine months, securities transaction tax revenue reached NT$506 billion, up NT$307.7 billion from a year earlier, while corporate income tax revenue increased NT$185.3 billion and business tax revenue rose NT$120.3 billion.

E1 and the fight over Palestinian statehood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:02:36 UTC
21:02:36 KST

Few pieces of land carry as much weight as the 12 square kilometres known as E1. It is an unremarkable stretch of hillside on a map, but for critics of Israel’s settlement policy it is the place where the two-state solution could be decided without negotiation, vote, or treaty.
E1 lies between occupied East Jerusalem and the Ma’ale Adumim settlement bloc. That location is the point. Building there would create a continuous belt of Israeli construction across the central West Bank, cutting the northern part of the territory off from the south and further separating East Jerusalem from the rest of the Palestinian territory.
The plan was originally envisaged at roughly 3,400 housing units and has now reached the tendering stage. Tenders were issued for 1,234 units in August and another 2,167 in September, which means all the planned units are now on the market. Whatever one thinks of the politics, this is no longer a drawing-board proposal.
The legal framework
The legal objection rests on a principle that predates this conflict: territory cannot be acquired by force, and an occupying power may not transfer its civilian population into occupied land. UN Security Council Resolution 2334 applied this to the present case, affirming that Israeli settlements in territory occupied since 1967, including East Jerusalem, have no legal validity and constitute a flagrant violation of international law.
The UN has warned that E1 would undermine the viability of a contiguous Palestinian state because it aims to create irreversible facts on the ground. The argument is practical as much as legal. A state needs connected territory, and a patchwork of enclaves divided by settlement blocs and roads is not a viable state, whatever it is called.
Facts on the ground
Critics describe this as a strategy of faits accomplis: build first, and let the finished buildings make any future negotiation moot. Advocates of the Palestinian position argue that once thousands of homes and the infrastructure serving them exist, reversing them becomes politically and practically close to impossible.
This is why E1 cannot be treated in isolation. It sits alongside the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, displacement in the West Bank, settler violence, and the expansion of Israeli administrative control. Taken together, these developments erode the territorial basis of Palestinian self-determination.
Some critics go further and call the pattern a settler-colonial project that entrenches an apartheid-like reality, a characterisation Israel firmly rejects.
READ: Palestine urges companies to review ties with businesses linked to illegal Israeli settlements
The international response
The diplomatic climate has hardened. Dozens of delegations walked out during Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s address to the UN General Assembly, a moment many observers read as a rare public rebuke on the floor of the world body.
More concrete steps have followed. In September 2026, twelve countries, among them the UK, France, Canada, Spain, Portugal, Norway, and Sweden, announced their intention to introduce or support restrictions on trade in goods from Israeli settlements, explicitly tying the measures to preserving the two-state solution. Trade restrictions are a notable shift from statements of concern to economic consequence.
Voices from the Muslim World
The pressure has not come only from Europe. On 21st August 2026, eight countries, Pakistan, Egypt, Türkiye, Indonesia, Jordan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, jointly rejected the E1 plan and related settlement activity east of occupied East Jerusalem. They argued that E1 undermines the geographic contiguity of the Occupied Palestinian Territory and threatens the realization of an independent, contiguous Palestinian state. They called for immediate action to halt the project, rescind related measures, and allow Palestinians to exercise self-determination.
For Pakistan, the statement was consistent with a long-held position: support for an independent, sovereign, and contiguous Palestinian state on pre-1967 borders with Al-Quds Al-Sharif as its capital, a stance it has repeated at the UN, the OIC, and other forums. Islamabad frames E1 as an attack on the territorial foundation of any future Palestinian state, and its argument is that international law cannot be applied selectively.
Gaza, the Peace Plan, and the Board of Peace
Pakistan also links the E1 question to the broader peace architecture. It supports the Gaza Peace Plan but ties that support to effective implementation, insisting that Gaza remain an integral part of Palestinian territory, reunified with the West Bank and East Jerusalem. In its view, implementation must offer a credible and irreversible pathway to statehood.
It has said it is ready to work with the United States, the Board of Peace, the Palestinian Authority, and other parties to advance the Comprehensive Plan and Road Map. In this vision, the Board of Peace could support the plan, protect Palestinian territorial integrity, oppose annexation and displacement, and facilitate Gaza’s reconstruction and governance. The caveat is that such mechanisms must reinforce, not replace, the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination.
E1 now poses a question larger than one hillside: can international law, UN resolutions, and the right of peoples to self-determination meaningfully constrain attempts to permanently alter territory?
If settlement expansion can quietly erase the map of a future state, the principle that borders cannot be changed by force is weakened everywhere, not just in Palestine.
Supporters of the Palestinian position therefore argue for effective international action: halting E1, protecting civilians, preserving the territorial integrity of the Occupied Palestinian Territory, and advancing a sovereign and contiguous state on pre-1967 lines.
The other side of the argument
Israel and its supporters see it differently. They argue that the area is administered under Israeli control under existing agreements, that Ma’ale Adumim is a major population centre needing room to grow, and that a link to Jerusalem serves legitimate security and housing needs. Some contend that contiguity can be achieved through transportation corridors and that final borders are for negotiation, not for UN resolutions or outside pressure. Israeli officials also reject the labels of apartheid and colonialism, citing historical and legal claims to the land and the security threats they face. These competing claims explain why E1 remains so contested.

Euro introduced smoothly in Bulgaria, citizens struggle with rising prices

Author
Gergana Mancheva
News
Euro introduced smoothly in Bulgaria, citizens struggle with rising prices
Tuesday 13 October 2026 13:28
Tuesday, 13 October 2026, 13:28
PHOTO Pixabay
Font size
Bulgaria joined the eurozone on 1 January 2026, and the technical transition from the lev to the euro was considered smooth and free of disruption. ''Payments continued without interruption, accounts were converted, sufficient cash was made available, and customers received the necessary service. The process was completed without any systemic disruptions. We have every reason to be satisfied, but not complacent'', Bulgarian National Bank Governor Dimitar Radev said.
BNB Governor Dimitar Radev
PHOTO BGNES
Public opinion, however, is more divided. It has been 10 months since we started paying with euro banknotes, and we have almost forgotten the lev-to-euro exchange rate, which was nearly 2:1. Most people say their incomes, now denominated in euros, are proving even less sufficient, forcing them to cut back on everyday spending. Rents and property prices have seen the steepest increases, alongside the cost of services and fuel. Inflation in August 2026 stood at 4.5% compared with the same month last year.
PHOTO Pexels
''We are once again witnessing an external price shock linked to geopolitical tensions and instability in energy markets'', said Bulgarian National Bank Governor Dimitar Radev, comparing the current situation with the inflation peak in 2022, when Bulgaria’s annual inflation rate reached 15.6% in certain months. Inflation in Bulgaria is now significantly lower than in 2022, but remains above the eurozone average of 3%.
Maya Manolova
PHOTO BGNES
Consumers, however, insist that since Bulgaria joined the eurozone, the prices of many goods and services have almost doubled. These observations were also backed by Maya Manolova, Chairperson of the Commission for Consumer Protection, who announced the results of inspections carried out at major retail chains in Bulgaria. Markups on a number of food products at major retail chains exceed 100%, with those on some dairy products reaching more than 140%, Manolova said. According to her, markups of 100% or more have accumulated over the past year, during the period immediately before and throughout the introduction of the euro.
To what extent has the introduction of the euro in Bulgaria contributed to inflation in the country?
According to economist Rumen Galabinov, the euro is likely to account for only a small part of the price increases. This was mainly due to rounding the exchange rate that had been set. Most businesses applied the official exchange rate correctly, but some rounded prices as if one euro were worth two leva. There were also speculators who decided they could simply sell their goods at double the price, which also contributed to inflation”, the analyst told Radio Bulgaria.
Rumen Galabinov
PHOTO BGNES
“A meeting of the European Stability Mechanism was held in Sofia, where it was noted that Bulgaria had successfully adopted the euro on 1 January 2026, that payments and currency exchange had proceeded smoothly, and that only a small part of inflation was attributable to the adoption of the new currency. Of course, the government should have intervened more decisively through the regulatory authorities’ monitoring and supervisory powers, and there is probably still room for improvement in this regard. Meanwhile, the International Monetary Fund forecasts average annual inflation of 3.8% in Bulgaria. This suggests that inflation could ease by the end of the year. We could probably achieve an average annual inflation rate close to 4%.”
PHOTO Pexels
“More importantly, however, our economy is performing well”, Rumen Galabinov adds, referring to IMF projections that Bulgaria could surpass Greece in GDP per capita by 2028. In 2026, Bulgaria has already outpaced several other Balkan economies in terms of economic growth, including Montenegro, Serbia, North Macedonia, Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo.
PHOTO Courtesy of Rumen Galabinov
Economist Rumen Galabinov expects another increase in incomes. He forecasts that the minimum wage will likely rise by around 8% in 2027, from its current gross monthly level of EUR 620.20. “That would mean an increase of about EUR 50”, he says. According to him, however, one of the main reasons for high inflation in the country is the rise in fuel prices, particularly petrol and diesel. ''Diesel is the most widely used fuel in Bulgaria. In addition to freight transport, a large proportion of private cars in the country also run on diesel'', Galabinov notes.
PHOTO BGNES
''Over the past two to three months, rising fuel prices have also driven up prices across the entire value chain. The government should have acted earlier to address high fuel prices. Possible measures include cutting fuel excise duties, temporarily reducing VAT on fuel, or offering state-funded discounts to people filling up their private cars.
PHOTO BGNES
We will see whether the recently introduced EUR 50 assistance payment for people in need will have the desired effect. In my view, the government should continue with a broader support programme to help people cope with rising prices'', said Rumen Galabinov.
Besides fuel prices, there is another issue that should be on the government’s agenda: reducing the size of the shadow economy. Bulgaria has considerable untapped potential to collect more tax and social security revenue, economist Rumen Galabinov pointed out in an interview with Radio Bulgaria.

Investigators hunt French supermarket fridge hackers, no claim of responsibility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:00:57 UTC
21:00:57 KST

Investigators hunt French supermarket fridge hackers, no claim of responsibility
PARIS, Oct 13 - French investigators on Tuesday were hunting the hackers who seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets in a cyberattack that underlined the vulnerabilities of connected systems, with no group publicly claiming responsibility.
The absence of a claim of responsibility by hacktivists or a ransom demand by cybercriminals has puzzled investigators, according to a source with knowledge of the probe. Typically, such groups tend to quickly seek to monetise their hacks or claim credit for them for political ends.
The cyberattack, which manually overrode the temperatures at fridges in supermarket groups including Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarche and Cooperative U, appears to have been easy to pull off, three cyber experts told Reuters.
Staff at some Paris supermarkets threw boxes full of perished meat and frozen goods into giant trash containers on Tuesday. At least 350 supermarkets — a small fraction of the total number in France - were caught up in the strike.
FIRM BLAMES OUTDATED SOFTWARE
The affected fridges relied on software by Danish firm Danfoss.
On Monday, Danfoss said many of the affected units had "reached end of life and no longer receive software or security updates" or were "running outdated firmware". It said it had "advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions".
The company declined further comment on Tuesday.
The serious vulnerabilities present in older versions of Danfoss' firmware have been known for months.
On August 9, cybersecurity firm Claroty detailed weaknesses - since patched - in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A controller that could have allowed intruders to bypass authentication and run code on compromised devices.
'BASIC CYBER HYGIENE'
Although the precise mechanism by which attackers compromised the refrigerators has not been publicly disclosed, cybersecurity experts said all signs pointed to a basic stunt enabled both by the failure to adopt Danfoss' updates and by exposing device interfaces to the internet.
"This is about basic cyber hygiene," said Ken Munro, a partner at the British cybersecurity firm Pen Test Partners. "Get it wrong and you get a smelly mess of defrosted food."
He said the well-known vulnerabilities meant the attackers were essentially pushing at an open door, something that meant the hack could easily be "kids messing around".
"If this was a nation state, why affect only a subset of French fridges? There are plenty of other nations with fridges on the internet," he said. "No ransom or demand suggests a lack of appreciation of the potential commercial losses that the fridge owners may experience."
PROBLEM STILL EXISTS
Plenty of fridges remain reachable via the internet. Using the internet scanning service Shodan, Reuters found at least 4,500 Danfoss interfaces still viewable on Tuesday.
Reuters could not independently establish how many of them were running vulnerable software, but French internet scanning company Onyphe said only a small minority of the devices appeared to be running the latest version of the software.
Outdated and vulnerable versions were "still widely represented among publicly accessible interfaces", Onyphe said. REUTERS

Extremists holding anti-immigration opinions are becoming increasingly likely to consider carrying out terrorist attacks against immigration centres and asylum hotels in the UK, the head of MI5 has warned.

People who ghost tend to feel worse about it than the people they ghost realize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:00:13 UTC
21:00:13 KST

When someone stops responding to your messages, it is easy to assume they simply do not care. But new research suggests that people who leave messages unanswered tend to feel worse about their silence than their conversation partners realize. The findings, published in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, also indicate that even a brief reply can narrow this emotional misunderstanding.
Ghosting occurs when one person abruptly stops responding to another person’s messages without an explanation. In the context of digital communication, it happens when at least one person in the exchange believes the silence might be permanent. Ghosting can range from an intentional decision to end a romantic relationship to a temporary lapse where someone reads a message but gets distracted and forgets to reply. The researchers call the person who stops responding the “ghoster” and the person left waiting the “ghostee.”
Prior studies suggest that cutting someone off emotionally takes a toll on the person doing the rejecting. For example, a 2013 study found that socially excluding someone actually causes emotional distress for the person enforcing the exclusion. Building on this idea, a 2022 study of people who had both ghosted and been ghosted by romantic partners found that ghosters were more likely to describe feeling guilty, but also relieved, while those who were ghosted more often described sadness and hurt.
The research was led by Sophia Li of the Haas School of Business at the University of California, Berkeley, and Coral Zheng, a PhD candidate in organizational behavior at the University of Cambridge’s Judge Business School, who contributed equally to the work. They wanted to expand on this psychological dynamic.
“Ghosting has been a very common, popular, but also annoying phenomenon to many people nowadays. So I think, first of all, we’re definitely motivated to study ghosting as a real-world problem,” Zheng told PsyPost.
“At the same time, the past literature usually defines it as a breakup strategy in the romantic context, while we think there’s more than that,” Zheng explained. “In addition to an intentional strategy that aims to permanently dissolve a relationship, there are situations where people accidentally forget to respond, simply do not see the message, strategically postpone a response (which the other person might already interpret as ghosting), etc. Thus, we want to include a broader definition of ghosting that includes unintentional, temporary ghosting and across different contexts as well.”
To capture this, the researchers designed a series of studies to see if the victims of ghosting actually recognize the internal distress experienced by the people ignoring them. If ghostees fail to notice this guilt, they might falsely assume the other person is entirely cold or hostile.
In the first study, they recruited 195 adults and asked them to recall a specific time they communicated online with someone they knew who wasn’t a close friend or immediate family member. Half of the participants recalled a time they ghosted someone, while the other half recalled a time they were ghosted. The participants then rated how bad they felt about the situation and predicted how bad the other person felt on a scale from 1 to 5, where 1 meant “not bad at all” and 5 meant “extremely bad.”
The researchers found that the people who ghosted others reported feeling worse (an average score of 2.27) than the victims predicted they would feel (an average score of 1.56). The victims underestimated how much guilt and sadness the ghosters felt, but also how relieved they were. The gap was wider when the ghosting was unintentional, such as when someone simply forgot to text back: these ghosters felt particularly bad, but the people they ghosted did not anticipate this. Interestingly, ghosters were accurate in predicting how bad the ghostees felt (averaging 2.11 for both actual and predicted feelings).
In the second study, the researchers tested 601 adults using imagined scenarios. Participants pictured texting back and forth with a friend they did not know very well. Half imagined being the one who stopped replying, and half imagined being the one left waiting. Each participant considered two versions of the scenario: one in which no reply came at all, and one in which the friend sent a short message reading, “Sorry, but I can’t talk right now.”
Once again, those imagining being the ghoster expected to feel worse (an average score of 3.23) than the people imagining being ghosted predicted (1.94). Sending a short reply narrowed this gap: responders expected to feel less bad (2.33), and receivers’ predictions (1.82) came closer to the mark. The brief message also reduced self-blame. When ghosted, about a third of receivers assumed they had been annoying their friend, compared with about one in five after a short reply, with most assuming the friend was simply busy.
For the third study, the researchers paired up adults in an online chatroom for an eight-minute text conversation designed to help them get to know each other. Afterward, one person in each pair was given a choice to either participate in a second five-minute conversation or skip it entirely. If they chose to skip it, their partner was left waiting alone in the chatroom without any explanation. Of the 229 pairs who completed the study, the researchers analyzed the 175 in which one partner chose to skip.
In the live experiment, the overall pattern did not hold. On average, the people left waiting did not underestimate how bad their partners felt (3.26 for those who skipped versus 3.35 predicted, on a scale where 5 meant “extremely bad”), though they did overestimate how negatively the skippers felt toward them (3.41 predicted versus 2.29 actual). Part of the explanation may be that the two sides did not always agree on what had happened. People who skipped the chat rated their behavior as less like ghosting (2.56) than their waiting partners did (3.06).
“The affective misperceptions between the ghosters and ghostees also show that the experience and subjective perceptions are sometimes asymmetric,” Zheng noted. “Therefore, the current work also argues that ghosting is a subjective experience – if at least one of the communication parties perceives their experience as ghosting, it is ghosting to this particular party. It could either be the ghoster actually wants to ghost but the ghostee doesn’t feel so, or the ghostee feels ghosted albeit the ghoster does not mean to.”
In an analysis that was not planned in advance, the researchers looked only at participants who rated the behavior as ghosting (a 4 or 5 on the 5-point scale). In that group, the original pattern reappeared: those who skipped felt worse (3.93) than those left waiting predicted (3.51). Across all pairs, the people left waiting also underestimated how much their partners wanted to develop a friendship.
These results offer a new perspective on why communication breakdowns happen and how they are perceived by both sides. The findings align with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that people who are ghosted tend to underestimate how much the person who ignored them still cares about their well-being. That earlier work focused on ghosters’ concern for the other person rather than on how bad ghosters themselves feel. Together, these studies suggest that the quiet side of a digital conversation may be more conflicted than it appears.
“If you’ve been ghosted, it may help to know that the person who hasn’t responded probably feels worse than you expected. If you’re the one who hasn’t responded, maybe consider sending a short reply before going silent,” Zheng said. “We hope to help both parties understand the other person’s perspective, reduce misunderstandings, and increase well-being for both sides.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The live experiment, the most realistic of the three, did not find the overall effect; it emerged only among participants who saw the behavior as ghosting, an analysis the researchers had not planned in advance. People left waiting were also told their partner might not return, which may have reduced the uncertainty that usually comes with being ghosted.
The interactions also involved short online chats between complete strangers, which might not capture the intense emotional weight of being ghosted by a long-term romantic partner or a close friend. Another limitation is that all the participants were based in the United States. In cultures where avoiding direct confrontation is considered polite, people might not feel as guilty about ghosting, and victims might interpret the silence differently.
There is also an ongoing debate among psychologists about how to precisely define ghosting. As the third study showed, two people can experience the exact same conversation and disagree on whether ghosting actually took place. As digital communication continues to evolve, researchers will need to keep exploring where people draw the line between a delayed response and a permanent digital exit.
Looking ahead, Zheng pointed out that complete silence is only one part of a larger puzzle. “Besides the complete silence, which is ghosting, there are many other aspects in online communication that are still underexplored,” she told PsyPost. “For example, how do people feel and predict the other person’s feelings based on the speed of a response, the length of a message, the tone of a message, whether there are emojis/punctuation or not, whether the tone is positive vs. neutral, etc. The elements in online communication dynamics are fascinating.”
The study, “The Pain of Ghosting? People Underestimate How Bad Their Conversation Partners Feel About Not Responding,” was authored by Sophia Li, Coral Zheng, and Juliana Schroeder.

The secret to a non-cloudy chicken stock | Kitchen aide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

Why is my chicken stock always cloudy?
Ryan, by email
From broths and risottos to sauces and braises, there’s no question that a good, flavourful stock will stand you in good stead. “It’s an underestimated kitchen job,” says Adam Byatt, chef/owner of Trinity, in southwest London, and author of Trinity: The Cookbook, which is published next week. “I love stock: it’s wholesome and fruitful, frugal and delicious.”
Ryan’s clarity issue, Byatt says, is “only ever caused by cooking the stock too quickly or by allowing the fat to boil back into the base liquid”. So it’s crucial to take things low and slow. You will also need a pan that’s “big and heavy enough to give the bones enough room for movement, as well as a very fine sieve for straining the stock”.
On to the actual making, and Alissa Timoshkina, author of Lozhka, goes in cold. She puts chicken legs, drumsticks or a leftover roast chicken carcass in a large pot, adds her stock veg – onions, carrots, celery, garlic, say – and aromats (bay, parsley stalks, peppercorns, for instance), then covers the lot with cold water and brings everything very slowly to a boil. She then turns down the heat and leaves it to cook on a very gentle simmer. In the event of that carefully made stock going a bit cloudy, Timoshkina would seek to mollify that by straining the lot through a fine sieve and stirring in a tablespoon of lemon juice, which has the added benefit of being “great for flavour, too”.
Lloyd Morse, chef and co-owner of The Palmerston in Edinburgh, meanwhile, likes to simmer the bones first, “shoogling them occasionally”, to bring more of the scum to the surface: “You really need to skim the life out of it.” It’s only at this point that he adds the veg: “And keep skimming that top layer,” he says, adding that it’s important to be aware that “the more agitation or the hotter the pot gets, the cloudier the stock will be”.
Essentially, “if nothing is ever actually boiled, Ryan’s stock should be nice and clear”, says Louis Lingwood, head chef at Osteria Vibrato in London, who cooks his chicken stock “on the lowest possible heat for a whole day”, before discarding the bones and leaving the stock to sit until all the fat rises to the top. Skim that off with a ladle, then reduce the stock very slowly.
Lingwood has another trick up his sleeve to guarantee a clearer stock: get it in the freezer. “Defrost it through a sieve lined with muslin (or through a lined perforated tray), and the stock will be crystal clear.” Speaking of the freezer, freezing stock in ice-cube trays, then whacking them in a sealed container, is a welcome manoeuvre for those occasions when only small quantities of stock are required.
Of course, Ryan could make his life a whole lot easier by simply cooking his stock in the oven, Morse says: “My top tip is to make it in an oven-safe dish, such as a Le Creuset [other brands are, of course, available], then pop it in the oven overnight to cook super slowly,” by which he means about 90C. “The indirect heat makes the clearest stock possible, plus, when you wake up, you’ll have a lovely smell in the kitchen.” Convenience food at its best.
- Got a culinary dilemma? Email feast@theguardian.com

Experts: Full damage of Germany's August Hanning scandal yet to be revealed

Experts: Full damage of Germany's August Hanning scandal yet to be revealed
Former German foreign intelligence chief August Hanning's detention on suspicion of espionage has raised concerns about damage to Germany's national security and the credibility of its intelligence services, Estonian experts find.
Last week, police searched the home of August Hanning, the former head of Germany's foreign intelligence service, in Nordwalde, western Germany, near the Dutch border. Hanning was detained on suspicion of espionage amounting to treason.
The allegations concern a period after Hanning had stepped down as head of the foreign intelligence service and begun providing consulting services. It emerged that he had enlisted the help of his former chief of staff, Manfred Dankesreiter, who was still working for the foreign intelligence service.
"Specifically, it is alleged that Mr. Hanning received nearly 2,000 documents from Manfred D. up until June 2022, some of which were confidential, meaning they were intended exclusively for use by the leadership of the foreign intelligence service. In one case, Mr. Hanning is suspected of using classified information to prepare an analysis for an employee of a foreign intelligence service. In another case, he is alleged to have passed information to an employee of another intelligence service following an extensive exchange of information," said German prosecutor's office spokesperson Ines Peterson.
Prosecutors have not specified which two countries' intelligence services were involved. German media have speculated about China and Azerbaijan, while Hanning's previous ties to Russia have also been highlighted. The leaked materials reportedly included primarily security assessments and documents concerning matters such as Iran's nuclear program and an analysis of the Russian armed forces.
"I think the extent of the damage is impossible to comprehend at this stage. The fragments that have appeared in the media do not allow us to properly assess its scale, partly because it is unclear which country Hanning was working for. Russia, China and Azerbaijan have all been mentioned. The timing is also important — whether he was recruited while he was still in office or after he left. When all this could have happened is extremely significant," said Arnold Sinisalu, former director general of the Estonian Internal Security Service (ISS/KAPO).
The precise extent of the damage remains to be determined. Germany's foreign intelligence service is a large organization, but its powers have so far been relatively limited. It is therefore possible that the information leaked was not particularly sensitive. However, other countries' secrets are also at stake and the overall reputational damage is enormous.
"The damage to the foreign intelligence service, the BND, is enormous. That is simply because a betrayal of this kind causes long-term damage to the BND's credibility, particularly among the intelligence partners on which it relies," said ARD journalist Michael Götschenberg.
"The other aspect is the purely symbolic damage that has been done. This affects not only Germany's intelligence service but German state institutions more broadly. How can these institutions be trusted if the head of an intelligence service has engaged in secret cooperation? At the same time, it must be emphasized that the very fact that something like this was uncovered is extremely positive," Sinisalu said.
"The Germans used to be very self-assured and believed they understood how Russia and China operated far better than we did and so on. History has made its own corrections. Perhaps this is partly a consequence of overconfidence and a sense of infallibility. I hope the substance of the case is not too serious. We will see. At present, too little is known," said Eerik-Niiles Kross, member of the Riigikogu Foreign Affairs Committee.
Hanning headed Germany's foreign intelligence service from 1998 to 2005, more than 20 years ago when Gerhard Schröder was German chancellor. Prosecutors say his alleged espionage activities took place between 2010 and 2022. How far has today's Germany moved on from that era?
"Germany is undergoing enormous change, with different forces pulling it in different directions. We are all concerned that the AfD, a far-right party that is at times openly pro-Putin, is the most popular political force. It has won some local elections. Whether that means a major shift at the next German Bundestag elections is too early to say, but the political atmosphere there is somewhat turbulent. The major established parties are doing rather poorly. At the same time, Germany is trying to move away from its highly restrained post-World War II approach. On the military front, the Germans have spent decades trying to prove to the world that they have learned from their mistakes. They have, of course, started making different kinds of mistakes, as tends to happen. Where Germany is headed is now one of the key questions for Europe's future," Kross said.
Germany is currently debating whether to grant its foreign intelligence service greater powers. Footage from last week also illustrates the contrast between the present and the past. In one clip, the current head of Germany's foreign intelligence service warns of the threats facing the country.
"Germany is at risk of being drawn into a violent conflict by Russia. The attempted attack in Leipzig is one example of this. No other country currently poses such a direct, extensive and concrete threat to Germany," said Martin Jäger, head of Germany's foreign intelligence service.
Meanwhile, former Chancellor Gerhard Schröder celebrates Russian President Vladimir Putin's birthday and visits a store belonging to a Russian retail chain on whose supervisory board he now serves.

In its statement, Hamas described the award as "an important step toward international justice," praising Pillay's involvement in investigating Israel's military operations in Gaza and calling for further international legal action against Israeli officials.
The statement followed the announcement of Pillay as the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize laureate, a decision that prompted sharp criticism from Israel's political leadership.
Hamas said the award represented international recognition of what it described as crimes committed by Israel against Palestinians, pointing specifically to the September 2025 findings of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry chaired by Pillay.
The commission's report concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, an allegation rejected by Israel, which has maintained that its military operations targeted Hamas following the terrorist organization's October 7, 2023, massacre.
"The findings of the Independent International Commission of Inquiry, which was chaired by Pillay, concerning the crimes committed in the Gaza Strip, as well as the conclusion of its report issued in September 2025 that the crime of genocide had been committed, underscore the gravity of what our people have endured," Hamas said.
The terrorist organization called on the international community to pursue Israeli officials through international courts, demanding an end to what it characterized as impunity for alleged war crimes.
UN inquiry into Gaza genocide allegations
The controversy surrounding Pillay stems in part from a September 2025 UN commission report, which determined that Israel had committed four of the five acts of genocide defined by the 1948 Genocide Convention. The commission alleged that Israeli actions demonstrated an intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza.
The commission, established in 2021, was tasked with investigating alleged violations of international law in Israel and the Palestinian territories. Pillay chaired the panel alongside commissioners Chris Sidoti and Miloon Kothari.
Israel rejected the findings, accusing the commission of relying on inaccurate information and failing to adequately account for Hamas's conduct during the war. The Foreign Ministry denounced the report as fabricated and accused its authors of acting as proxies for Hamas.
The war began when Hamas-led terrorists invaded southern Israel on October 7, 2023, killing approximately 1,200 people and abducting more than 250 others into Gaza. The massacre triggered Israel's military campaign against the terrorist organization.
Pillay, who previously served as president of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and as a judge at the International Criminal Court, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her broader career advancing international law and accountability for international crimes.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee said its decision recognized her efforts to promote peace and international legal principles, rather than specifically endorsing the conclusions of her Gaza investigation.
Hamas, however, placed the commission's allegations against Israel at the center of its response, using the Nobel announcement to renew its demands for international legal proceedings against Israeli officials.
In its statement, the terrorist organization also praised Pillay's earlier work defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa and her service on international tribunals, presenting those roles alongside her involvement in the Gaza inquiry.
Herzog condemns Nobel decision as 'moral erosion'
President Isaac Herzog sharply criticized the awarding of the Nobel Peace Prize to Pillay during a ceremony honoring Israel Bonds on Monday, describing the decision as an "affront to any life-affirming, peace-loving people."
According to remarks covered on Tuesday, Herzog condemned the Nobel Committee for recognizing Pillay, whom he accused of advancing false allegations against Israel.
"Awarding the Nobel Peace Prize to one of the leading proponents of the genocide lie is a cynical decision which celebrates a shameful display of moral erosion," Herzog said.
His remarks came amid broader criticism from Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who accused Pillay of spreading false accusations against the Jewish state.
"The Nobel Prize committee has lost its moral compass," the Prime Minister's Office said in response to the announcement.
"It has awarded its highest honor to a bigot who built her career around inventing and propagating blood libels against the only Jewish state."
The contrasting responses highlighted the dispute surrounding Pillay's work, with Hamas explicitly endorsing the UN investigation's findings while Israeli leaders rejected both the report's conclusions and the Nobel Committee's decision to recognize its former chairwoman.
Hamas concluded its statement by renewing its call for international action against Israeli officials accused of crimes in Gaza.

On US-Europe joint "peace plan"

On the possibility of an "energy ceasefire"

On intelligence sharing with Ukraine

On the Yandex situation

You know that the company is strong and powerful. Yes, it is facing difficulties now. Of course, this issue is currently being discussed in the government, but the company is taking emergency measures to deal with the aftermath of this attack."
