Indigenous women challenge Islamist oppression, call for cross-community solidarity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:57:35 UTC
20:57:35 KST

The same radical Islamist forces behind the October 7 attacks, in which more than 1,200 people were killed, are also responsible for attacks on the Druze in Syria and the mass murder and oppression of Iranians and Hindus in India and Kashmir, six women from Indigenous communities said during the “Asia & the Middle East: Conversations Across Communities” panel hosted by Indigenous Bridges on Monday night.
Hindu activist and regional analyst Kavya K, known online as “Kavya Speaks”; Israeli Druze activist Rania Dean; Kurdish speaker and educator Schilan Kurdpoor; Iranian human rights activist Honey Montzemi; and Native American and Jewish Indigenous rights activist Lani Anpo shared their experiences of oppression and silencing by Islamist forces with Ateret Shmuel, the Jewish director of Indigenous Bridges.
Despite coming from different countries, including Iran, the United States, Israel, and India, the women said they shared experiences of gender-based violence, genocide, forced assimilation, silencing, and intimidation.
Each said she had been accused of Islamophobia and subjected to death threats or doxxing for speaking about her community’s experiences. They also emphasized the need to build alliances among Indigenous communities to overcome their minority status and more effectively confront what they described as the oppressive forces of political Islam.
Both Kurdpoor and Kavya said radical Islamist forces often target women first because attacks on women also threaten families and the transmission of cultural traditions between generations.
Kavya argued that the targeting of women had led Hindu communities to adopt new gender-based restrictions, keeping women out of public life for their own protection. She contrasted these restrictions with what she described as the historically prominent role of women in Hindu communities. She cited the Hindu goddess Kali, who defeated the demon Mahishasura when the male gods could not, as an example of women's power and status in Hindu religious tradition.
Shmuel noted how it was the Kurds who were able to weaponize the misogynistic beliefs of the Islamic State against the group. The ISIS fighters believed that being killed by a female combatant would prevent them from entering paradise and receiving the rewards promised to martyrs, including the 72 virgins described in popular accounts of the group's ideology. Aware of this, Kurdish fighters in Rojava established the Women's Protection Units (YPJ), an all-female Kurdish military force operating in northern Syria.
Kurdpoor recounted how the women used battle cries to signal their presence, sometimes prompting ISIS fighters to flee. She also described the role of women in the broader Kurdish-led military effort and their acceptance within the Syrian Democratic Forces.
Kurdpoor also discussed the role of ethnic cleansing and the restrictions on indigenous languages. She argued that restricting a community's language creates a disconnect between individuals and their cultural heritage, citing restrictions in Turkey and limits on Kurdish-language education in Iran. She also highlighted the continuing struggle to learn and preserve the language in Syria, describing it as central to the Kurdish community's cultural survival.
Dean said that the Druze had historically spoken Aramaic before adopting Arabic, which she described as part of a broader effort to blend in with the surrounding occupying Arab population and protect their communities.
She argued that the community's historical efforts to assimilate had failed to ensure its safety, pointing to the July 2025 massacres in Sweida, continued attacks on Druze communities, and the ongoing siege of villages in southern Syria as evidence that conformity had not provided protection.
Dean also welcomed the growing use of Bashan, the biblical name for Sweida and the surrounding area, arguing that it signaled her community was moving away from what she described as failed attempts to secure peace with its occupiers through assimilation into their society. She also condemned the labeling of Druze calling for freedom and self-determination as “separatists,” a term several speakers said had been used to discredit or suppress calls for freedom by indigenous communities in the region.
Beyond their shared experiences of oppression and Islamist colonial occupation, the speakers also expressed concern about what they saw as a growing trend of Western women supporting regimes that would strip them of the rights and freedoms they currently enjoy.
Secular leftists paved way for Iran’s 1979 Islamic Revolution
Montazemi noted that secular leftists had helped pave the way for Iran’s 1979 Islamic Revolution, only to pay for it with their lives in the years that followed. She expressed concern at seeing women on social media wearing tank tops, clothing that would result in their arrest in Iran, while proudly displaying the Islamic Republic’s symbols.
She also pointed to Western women who had traveled to Syria to marry Islamic State members, arguing that they had surrendered their rights in the process. Montazemi said more was needed to understand the appeal these groups held for women.
Explaining the importance of the event to The Jerusalem Post, Shmuel said, “Indigenous nations across Asia, the Middle East, and Africa face the same violent colonialism, yet our stories are routinely spun for Western audiences to portray Islamists as the victims and Indigenous communities as the cause of the conflict.
We see this in Western reporting on attacks against Druze, Hindu, Kurdish, Persian, Jewish, Yezidi, Bahá’í, and other Indigenous communities. And there is a sinister reason for this narrative: to manipulate the Western public into sympathizing with Islamist jihadi groups, paving the way for their expansion into the West.”
She said she hoped the panels would help the global community better understand communities too often silenced and recognize that “the safety and sovereignty of Indigenous communities across Asia, the Middle East, and Africa are deeply intertwined.”
The panel was the first in a series of events addressing the issue of indigenous solidarity to be hosted by Indigenous Bridges. For more information, visit: https://indigenousbridges.com/

Barrett to build Northrop’s 25mm smart grenade launcher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:57:26 UTC
20:57:26 KST

- Northrop Grumman and Barrett Firearms signed a teaming agreement under which Barrett will build the 25 mm Precision Grenadier System launcher in Nashville.
- Barrett will also integrate the inductive setter that programs Northrop Grumman’s 25 mm airburst and proximity rounds.
Northrop Grumman has teamed up with Barrett Firearms to build the launcher for its Precision Grenadier System, a shoulder-fired 25 mm grenade launcher meant to let infantry squads hit enemies hiding behind cover and shoot down small drones, the companies announced on Oct. 12 at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington.
Under the agreement, Barrett will manufacture the weapon at its plant in Nashville, Tennessee, and integrate the inductive setter, the device that programs each round with the distance at which it should detonate before it leaves the barrel. Northrop Grumman will continue to lead development of the overall system and of its family of 25 mm ammunition, and says it is offering the weapon to both U.S. and international customers. The companies say pairing Northrop Grumman’s ammunition and military programs experience with Barrett’s commercial and military firearms production will let them move quickly from prototype to delivery for U.S. and allied forces.
The Precision Grenadier System is designed to give an infantry squad a precise way to reach targets in defilade, meaning enemy soldiers sheltering behind walls, trenches or terrain that direct rifle fire cannot hit, as well as to fight at close quarters and engage small drones. Northrop Grumman’s 25 mm ammunition family includes a high-explosive airburst round that detonates above or beside a target at a programmed distance, a proximity round that senses a nearby drone and explodes without needing to be programmed, a close-quarters battle round, and a training round ballistically matched to the combat rounds. The weapon feeds from detachable box magazines.
The design builds on Northrop Grumman’s experience with the XM25, a 25 mm airburst weapon the company inherited through its 2018 purchase of Orbital ATK, which U.S. Army units tested in combat in Afghanistan before the program ended in 2018. The U.S. Army launched its Precision Grenadier System effort to replace the M203 and M320 40 mm grenade launchers carried by infantry squads today with a semi-automatic, magazine-fed weapon that combines the launcher, smart ammunition and a digital fire-control sight.
Several teams are working on solutions for the U.S. Army requirement in calibers from 25 mm to 40 mm. Barrett and MARS Inc. won the Army’s xTech Soldier Lethality competition in May 2025 with a 30 mm grenade rifle, and FN America has continued testing its MTL-30 launcher under a separate Army prototype award. Northrop Grumman earlier developed its 25 mm launcher with Colt before selecting Barrett to manufacture the weapon.
The U.S. Army plans to turn the Precision Grenadier System into a formal acquisition program and award a prototype agreement, and Northrop Grumman says it is continuing prototyping and ammunition development with Barrett to meet that requirement and interest from international buyers.

High Court challenges law excluding women from Israel's Chief Rabbinate elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:57:24 UTC
20:57:24 KST

The High Court of Justice last month made a small but consequential decision that has the potential to affect how chief rabbis and members of the Chief Rabbinate Council are chosen in the State of Israel.
It issued a conditional order requiring the respondents to explain why legislation passed in December 2024 should not be interpreted to require the chief rabbis to appoint both men and women as their representatives in the electoral assembly - or, alternatively, why the provision restricting eligibility for those appointments should not be struck down.
The petition was filed on December 19, 2024, ahead of elections to the Chief Rabbinate Council. Submitted by six women with advanced religious education, Bar-Ilan University’s Rackman Center and Na’amat, it argues that the amendment passed earlier that month effectively prevented women from being appointed to the electoral assembly’s rabbinic contingent.
The case concerns the body that chooses the chief rabbis and the council’s elected members, rather than membership in the council itself.
Why doesn't the Chief Rabbinate ordain women?
Under the Chief Rabbinate Law, the electoral assembly comprises 150 members: 80 rabbinic representatives and 70 public representatives. Most seats are linked to specified offices, including rabbinic posts, local government leadership and religious councils. Ten of the rabbinic representatives are appointed by the chief rabbis, in consultation with the religious services minister and with government approval.
Those 10 appointments are at the center of the dispute.
In an earlier Rackman Center case, the court ruled on January 14, 2024, that the chief rabbis must consider appointing women with suitable Torah and Jewish-law education to those seats. Justices Dafna Barak-Erez and Isaac Amit formed the majority, against Justice David Mintz’s dissent.
The ruling did not require the appointment of particular women or their ordination as rabbis. It rather held that, for this electoral role, the statutory term “rabbis” was not confined to people formally ordained by the Chief Rabbinate.
On May 19, 2024, however, the Chief Rabbinate Council adopted a decision saying that women could not be appointed as rabbis and that even considering such appointments was forbidden under its interpretation of Jewish law. The decision, cited in the petition and reproduced in the state’s response, argued that considering a woman would itself recognize the possibility of her holding a rabbinic role.
The Knesset subsequently passed Amendment No. 8 to the Chief Rabbinate Law on December 4, 2024. It defined a “rabbi” eligible for one of the ten appointments as someone ordained by the Chief Rabbinate after passing its required written examinations, or holding a certificate of eligibility for specified rabbinic posts.
Because the Chief Rabbinate does not ordain women, the petitioners argue, the new definition closed the route the court had recognized.
A separate ruling has since changed women’s access to the rabbinate’s examinations. On July 14, 2025, a unanimous panel, in a judgment written by Supreme Court Deputy President Noam Sohlberg, ruled that the Chief Rabbinate could not bar women from taking its exams.
The court explained that the examinations serve purposes beyond qualifying candidates for rabbinic office: recognition of religious learning can also carry employment and salary benefits. Denying women access was therefore unlawful discrimination. That ruling did not, however, settle their eligibility for the electoral appointments challenged in this case.
At a High Court hearing last month (September 14), the petitioners’ lawyers emphasized that distinction: passing examinations would not by itself satisfy a law requiring ordination. They argued that women’s expertise in Jewish law was being excluded from the assembly’s rabbinic representation because of their sex.
The state’s response argued that the amendment must be considered as a whole. Alongside the disputed qualification requirement, it introduced a minimum of 31 women among the assembly’s public representatives.
The state maintained that reserving the ten appointments for rabbis recognized by the Chief Rabbinate served a legitimate purpose, and that the broader increase in women’s representation supported the amendment’s constitutionality. The Knesset joined that position. The petitioners argued that additional public-representative seats did not remedy the exclusion of women as religious scholars.
The government also argued that the petitioners’ request to halt the council elections pending a judgment would effectively suspend the statutory election arrangements. Justice Gila Canfy-Steinitz rejected that interim request on December 31, 2024, citing the caution required before suspending legislation ahead of a ruling on its merits.
The September conditional order leaves the substantive challenge open. The respondents must submit their formal answers by December 15, 2026.

Does Saudi Arabia have any good options to deal with the Houthis? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:57:17 UTC
20:57:17 KST

The deadly Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia over the last week have put pressure on Riyadh to respond.
Saudi Arabia has carried out airstrikes on the Houthis in support of the Yemeni government forces over the past month. However, Riyadh has appeared reticent to respond in a massive way to the Houthi attacks. Rumors are swirling in the region about what might come next. Analysts tend to portray the Saudis as facing an uphill struggle with the Houthis.
Does Saudi Arabia really have no good options? Various recent reports have discussed different aspects of what Riyadh may be weighing in terms of what comes next.
For instance, there is the question of the US supporting Saudi Arabia. The US and many countries have condemned the attacks. However, US President Donald Trump has left media guessing as to whether the US will do more. The US appears to be supporting Saudi Arabia in terms of intelligence and targeting, according to the BBC.
The Houthis have threatened a "swift and painful" response if the US does intervene. "If the US becomes involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond; rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the US and all its interests in the region," Houthi political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti told the AFP.
All of this must weigh on US-Saudi coordination. There are questions about how a widening war in Yemen could also lead Iran to operationalize militias in Iraq.
Who should Saudi Arabia ally with to minimize spread of war in the Middle East?
Saudi Arabia has seen this before. It intervened in Yemen in 2015 to back the Yemeni government against the Houthis. The Houthis widened the war with ballistic missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia. In 2019, Iran directly attacked Saudi Arabia. Militias in Iraq also targeted Saudi Arabia. Therefore, Riyadh knows exactly what is at stake.
Meanwhile, there are questions about whether tensions in Yemen could lead to renewed fighting with Iran. Reports indicate that Israel could be involved in strikes on Iran again, or even on the Houthis.
There is intense interest in this among Saudi Arabia’s allies in Turkey and Pakistan. Those countries joined an alliance with Saudi Arabia over the last few months.
However, Turkey would likely not want to be on the same side as Israel fighting alongside Saudi Arabia. Anadolu media in Ankara noted that Riyadh had so far rejected Israel’s “bid to join fight.” It is not entirely clear if Israel wants to get deeply involved again in Yemen.
Israel already carried out strikes on Yemen in 2024-2025 in response to numerous attacks by the Houthis on Israel. The Houthis also attacked commercial ships they claimed were linked to Israel. They seized the Galaxy Leader, only releasing the crew in 2025. They tried to make the ship into a kind of tourist attraction. The Galaxy Leader finally partially sank in April 2026, the Maritime Executive noted.
How did Saudi Arabia get into tensions with the Houthis?
Let’s review again how Riyadh got here. Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen in March 2015, leading a coalition against the Iranian-backed Houthis after the group seized Sanaa and advanced toward Aden. The intervention developed into a prolonged conflict involving airstrikes, ground fighting and Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi territory. A UN-brokered truce in April 2022 significantly reduced hostilities, and although it formally expired that October, a fragile period of relative calm followed.
That ceasefire has come under increasing pressure in 2026. Saudi strikes on Sanaa in July marked a renewed escalation, while the Houthis subsequently launched an offensive toward Bab el-Mandeb, the strategic strait connecting the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. It’s worth recalling that Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government didn’t want Sanaa airport used by Iran to fly in Iranian advisors to the Houthis.
Saudi-backed Yemeni forces launched a counteroffensive in October, supported by coalition airstrikes, to recover territory near Bab el-Mandeb and Mocha. The Houthis also escalated attacks on Saudi airports, including Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, where an October 10 strike killed 12 people and wounded 309. Riyadh vowed a firm response.
The conflict has also expanded beyond Yemen. On September 11, Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline was struck by drones that Saudi and Iraqi authorities said originated in Iraq. Riyadh temporarily shut the pipeline, a crucial alternative to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The attack highlighted growing concerns about coordination among Iran-backed terrorist groups across the region and the potential vulnerability of Saudi energy infrastructure.
On October 12, JINSA President and CEO Michael Makovsky spoke to Fox News about the latest Houthi attacks.
“It's very important that the [Saudi] Crown Prince be successful [in combating the Houthis], and it's vital for US national security. But he's alienated or distanced himself from a few key countries that could have been helpful here. I mean, he had a very well-known fight with the Emiratis, who were effective ... against the Houthis. ... He's kept a distance from the Israelis, who have ... [been] very effective at hitting the Houthis, and, at times in this war, he's been rather cool to the United States,” Makovsky said.
“I'd like to see the Saudis work with the Israelis, the Emiratis, and the U.S. to deal with the Houthi threat. It is not only a threat to the Saudis, of course, but affects the whole world because of [the Houthi threat] to international commerce. ... There has to be an international coalition," he added.
Thomas Juneau, a professor at the University of Ottawa, who focuses on Iran and Yemen and is a former Department of National Defence analyst in Canada, noted on October 11 on X that Saudi Arabia faces no good options with the Houthis.
"Military escalation was inevitable and is likely to continue - but it will hurt Saudi Arabia more than the Houthis. Negotiations are inevitable too - though not in the short term. The Houthis hold stronger cards, and they know it; their goal will be to extract maximal concessions from Saudi Arabia, which remains reluctant to pay this very high price.”
Might game theory help us understand the dilemma for Saudi Arabia in confronting the Houthis?
The challenge is modelling how complex this theater is in terms of how it is entangled with Iran, Israel, the United States, Iranian-backed militias in Iraq, Turkey and Pakistan.
The central problem is that Saudi Arabia may be militarily stronger than the Houthis, but military superiority does not necessarily translate into strategic leverage. The Houthis can impose high costs on Saudi Arabia without defeating its armed forces. Riyadh, meanwhile, must consider how its response affects not only Yemen but its economic security, regional alliances, and relations with Iran. This is what is called an “asymmetric” conflict.
This creates several overlapping strategic dilemmas. Saudi Arabia faces three calculations it has to make at the same time. It has to examine how it might deter more attacks, it has to manage its alliances, and it has to look at the regional context and potential escalation.
Game theory does not provide a clear answer, because the outcomes depend on uncertain information, different objectives, and the decisions of several independent actors. Nevertheless, it might be helpful to model this problem more because Saudi Arabia is in a difficult position, but it has many options.
Saudi Arabia can weather the storm. It has done so in the past. It has a naturally cautious leadership, similar to most Gulf countries. The West tends to prefer quick solutions, and Western media appears to think that a lack of an immediate large response, like “shock and awe,” means nothing is happening.
However, this illustrates the differences in calculations. The Iran war, for instance, has proven to be longer and more complex than many thought. This reflects the differences in thinking, perhaps, between Washington, Jerusalem, Riyadh, Ankara, and other places in the region.

IAI and SIG SAUER conduct successful live‑fire test of FIRE STORM 250 armed UAS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:57:01 UTC
20:57:01 KST

WASHINGTON - Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) and SIG SAUER have completed a live‑fire demonstration of the FIRE STORM 250, the Apus 60 VTOL tactical unmanned aircraft equipped with SIG SAUER’s MICROLIGHT Remote Controlled Weapon Station (RCWS) and the new M250 machine gun.
Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post understands that the test, conducted ahead of the AUSA 2026 exhibition in Washington, took place in Israel and showed the platform’s ability to detect, identify, and engage targets while hovering over a simulated battlefield.
During the trial, the UAS loitered over the test area and used its onboard camera to identify targets before it fired in both single‑shot and semi‑automatic modes. Engagements were carried out from different altitudes and ranges to assess accuracy, stability, and safety under varied conditions.
While it is still a functional prototype, the companies said the live-fire test validated the system’s core concept of pairing airborne surveillance with stabilized, remotely controlled firepower to give small units organic close‑support capability.
The FIRE STORM 250 is built for long‑duration overwatch and armed reconnaissance. Powered by a multi-fuel internal-combustion engine, it can remain airborne for up to three hours and be refueled in the field, avoiding battery‑charging delays and specialized logistics. Its vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) configuration allows launch and recovery from forward positions without runways or aviation support.
200 rounds at 200 meters
SIG SAUER’s M250 airborne light machine gun can be configured to carry 200 rounds of either 7.62×51 millimeters or 6.8×51 mm. ammunition, depending on customer requirements. It has a targeting range of 400-600 meters at an altitude of 200 m. The MICROLIGHT RCWS brings the system’s total combat weight to 53 pounds, including the gun and ammunition.
Sensor feeds and fire‑control data are fused into a single targeting picture, giving operators real‑time imagery, tracking information, and engagement options. Operators control the platform by using advanced control algorithms that maintain shooting accuracy even while hovering and moving.
“One of the most dangerous positions is in a turret, and the main idea is to keep the soldier out of the line of fire,” Mike Joslin, defense product manager at SIG SAUER, told D&T at AUSA. “Rather than the soldier holding the gun, he holds the interface that controls it.”
Nevertheless, the platform’s architecture keeps a human in the loop, with operators receiving real-time sensor imagery, target-tracking data and engagement options, and authorizing each use of fire.
Sali Okanin, SIG SAUER’s Israel general manager, said the test highlights how lightweight weapons can expand what small unmanned aircraft can do.
"FIRE STORM 250 brings together the most advanced technologies in the world, including IAI’s drone platform and SIG SAUER’s MICROLIGHT RCWS mounted with the M250 machine gun to deliver a new level of operational flexibility,” he said, adding that the platform has “greater range than legacy systems and weight savings that not only provide squad-level benefits but also make drone capabilities possible."
It is intended to be deployed with small tactical units and support missions including persistent overwatch, intelligence gathering, force protection, border defense and special‑operations surveillance.
Joslin explained to D&T that multiple FIRE STORM 250 aircraft can operate together to maintain continuous day‑night coverage, provide advance observation along movement routes, and support maneuvering forces during operations and extraction.
“Our concept of operations is that with the platform’s flight time, you can have loitering support with more en route to provide constant support,” he said.
Moshe Levy, executive vice president and head of IAI’s Military Aircraft Group, said the demonstration reflects a shift in how tactical unmanned systems are being designed.
“The next generation of unmanned systems will be defined not only by autonomy, but by how effectively they integrate sensing, decision-making and action within the operational environment,” he said.
“FIRE STORM 250 brings these capabilities into a single operational loop, enabling tactical forces to extend their reach and maintain continuous awareness while retaining human control over engagement decisions,” he added. “The firing test demonstrates the potential of this approach in a realistic operational scenario."
The future
The collaboration between IAI and SIG SAUER, one of the world’s largest weapons manufacturers, comes as it expands its line of unmanned aerial platforms.
“Drones are the future,” said Ryan Scott, director of Advanced Concepts at SIG SAUER.
Scott, a 22-year US Army Veteran with over a decade in unmanned systems with the Army, explained that the 250-year-old company has been investing in drone design and development for the past several years.
The company’s new direction “shows our innovative capabilities to support our troops.”
Along with FIRESTORM, SIG SAUER displayed its fixed-wing SCYTHE platform, the SABER quadcopter with the M-HORNET 22 LR payload attachment. It also displayed the prototype XRAY-9 counter-UAS platform.
According to Scott, “If Israel wanted our drones, we would sell them.”
Joslin echoed Scott’s feeling towards Israel, telling D&T that “there is no same amount of passion as Israel defense tech companies. Serving is embedded in the culture.”

Houthis and Saudis strike each other in latest escalation

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13

Houthis and Saudis show no intent to stop fighting
October 13, 2026
Iran-backed Houthi rebels on Tuesday said that Saudi Arabia had carried out overnight airstrikes targeting border regions in Yemen.
Rebel-run satellite television said two strikes had hit the Red Sea island of Kamaran and a third targeted Qanawis, north of Hodeida port.
Further strikes were reported in Jawf and rebels said their forces had downed a Saudi drone over Saada, a Houthi stronghold.
The strikes came just hours after air-raid sirens blared and loud explosions were heard in the Saudi capital Riyadh, which has come under intense fire for the past several days as fighting between the two belligerents intensifies.
The Houthis have clashed with Saudi Arabia since the kingdom stepped into Yemen's civil war to lead a military coalition against the Iran-backed fighters in 2015.
The rebels have pounded Saudi Arabia in recent days, repeatedly attacking the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. On Saturday, one of those attacks killed 13 people in what was the deadliest in the country in over a decade.
On Tuesday, Egypt's Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty called for an immediate end to Houthi attacks on the kingdom, telling Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi that there is "no justification for these attacks and they cannot be accepted."
Houthi attacks' economic impact on Saudi Arabia
Beyond reigniting fighting tied to Yemen's civil war, increased Houthi activity has come as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran, launched on February 28.
A regional proxy, the Houthis have helped Iran further destabilize the region by striking largely at the oil and transport infrastructure that brings oil and gas from US allies in the gulf to market.
Saudi Arabia is the world's top oil exporter and Houthi attacks have not only raised security issues, they have greatly hampered the kingdom's ability to get its product to market.
In its latest annual World Economic Outlook, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates Saudi GDP will contract by 3.3% on the year as a result, with Iran's chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz compounded by Houthi maneuvering in the Red Sea and attacks on Saudi oil refineries and tankers.
Saudi Arabia quickly diverted oil exports away from Hormuz as Iran's blockade dragged on, making use instead, of its overland pipelines and Red Sea access. Houthi attacks, however, have also dramatically impacted these.
Saudi Arabia stops issuing air raids
The devastation of the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have prompted the kingdom to seek help from Washington and US President Donald Trump.
Although he previously ignored Saudi requests for assistance, on Saturday Trump mused about joining the fight against the rebels.
News of this consideration drew a quick response from the Houthis, with a representative saying US interests in the region would be targeted should DC enter the fray.
Despite at least 18 people being killed and more than 300 injured in recent days, Saudi Arabia has stopped issuing air raid alerts in the kingdom.
The government has not spoken of the policy change but observers suggest it may be an effort to avoid stirring public panic as the country's security vulnerabilities come into focus.
Still, analysts warn that the change could have the opposite effect by amplifying uncertainty over the current situation.
Last week, prior to a string of airport attacks, government officials said the alerts had been halted due to citizens' complaints about being woken by them.
Further, Saudi government officials on Monday reminded residents of regulations issued in March that forbid sharing any images related to Houthi air attacks, including missile interceptions or impact craters.
Former US Ambassador to Saudi Arabia Michael Ratney told Reuters news agency that Riyadh — which initiated public warnings in May before halting them on September 29 — was trying to balance public messaging with efforts to prevent disruption in the kingdom but that in his opinion leaders had ended up adding to a sense of unease about Houthi airstrikes.

US aerospace company SpaceX launched its 35th commercial resupply mission to the International Space Station (ISS) on Tuesday morning, sending scientific research, critical hardware and operational cargo into orbit.
Loaded with more than 6,300 pounds (2,860 kilograms) of supplies, the SpaceX Dragon spacecraft launched aboard a Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.
The rocket lifted off at 6.34 am local time (1034GMT), marking the fourth orbital trip for the Dragon cargo vehicle and the eighth flight for the first-stage booster.
 
Solar arrays, medical research
The cargo manifest includes the final pair of roll-out solar arrays designed to expand power capacity for station operations, upcoming research and eventual controlled deorbit procedures. Astronauts will install the units during spacewalks planned for late autumn.
The Dragon is carrying experiments to manufacture artificial retinas in microgravity to support vision restoration on Earth, alongside three-dimensional heart tissue models and brain organoids aimed at evaluating potential therapies for neurodegenerative conditions, including Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases.
The spacecraft is expected to complete an autonomous docking with the station’s Harmony module around 11 am local time (1500GMT) on Thursday.
The resupply mission comes as the International Space Station prepares for its final phase of operations, with the orbiting facility scheduled to conclude its orbital duties at the end of 2030.

A school revolution: how systemic problems in education have led to mass protests in France
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:54:00 EEST
20:54:00 KST

A school revolution: how systemic problems in education have led to mass protests in France
On Saturday 10 October, Gabriel Attal, a former education and prime minister, as well as a potential presidential candidate, unveiled what he called a "pact for youth".
The programme was presented as a response to the anger spreading through France’s upper-secondary schools. By the weekend, France’s lycée protests had acquired a new political life. The students are planning another national day of action on Tuesday.
On Friday, 141 lycées were closed, a sharp fall from the first days of the protests. But the fact that the protests have become less widespread does not mean that the political problem has gone away.
France has spent years accumulating the conditions for this outburst.
It has neglected the ordinary machinery of public education, allowed regional inequalities to harden, and then responded to a student movement as if the principal issue were public order.
The result is a crisis that cannot be reduced either to youthful disorder or to police repression. Both are present. Neither explains the whole story.
A protest born in the classroom
The movement began around 21 September in schools in the Créteil education district, which includes much of France’s poorer eastern suburbs. The first complaints were about the daily experience of attending a school that often seemed unable to provide the basics.
A student in Aubervilliers had no French teacher while preparing for an important examination. In Sevran, pupils showed photographs of damaged chairs, holes in ceilings, mould, leaking roofs and broken toilets.
Some classrooms were difficult to heat in winter and difficult to cool in summer. Timetables stretched from early morning into the evening, with long gaps that left pupils stranded in school buildings without adequate supervision or food.
France’s public secondary schools have fewer teachers than they did in 2008, despite having roughly 250,000 more pupils. More than 70 per cent of classes in public general and technical schools have more than 30 pupils, while one in five has more than 35. Long absences without replacement have increased sharply, particularly in the Créteil and Versailles regions.
Buildings tell the same story. The average French lycée is more than six decades old. Vocational schools are older still. Only a small proportion of secondary-school buildings were built or substantially renovated in the past academic year.
The problems are not evenly distributed. In Seine-Saint-Denis, where the movement first took hold, the poverty rate is close to 30 per cent, almost twice the national metropolitan average.
France’s republican school system promises that a child’s future should not be determined by family wealth, religion or geography.
Yet pupils in the poorest areas are often asked to accept the largest classes, the oldest buildings and the most unstable supply of teachers.
The students understand the contradiction. They are not necessarily demanding a new ideology, but that the Republic honour its existing one.
The struggle over order
The protests have also produced real violence, and some schools have been damaged or ransacked. Teachers and headteachers have been threatened or injured. Incidents have been reported in Bayonne, Toulouse, Saint-Chamond, Poitiers and Saint-Étienne. In one case, a fire spread to a teacher’s car. In another, a school cafeteria was damaged.
The Education Ministry has estimated the cost of repairs at about €30 million and warned that thousands of pupils could lose teaching time.
The state’s authority cannot survive if school staff are attacked and schools become targets.
Nor is the idea that French schools are becoming unsafe entirely invented. Official surveys show substantial levels of intimidation, defiance and verbal abuse.
Many teachers report that pupils challenge their authority or mock their work. A smaller but serious minority report threats, harassment or physical assault. At the same time, the latest official data does not support the claim that French schools are simply descending into generalised violence. Most staff say they feel respected by pupils and safe inside their schools. The number of recorded serious incidents per 1,000 pupils fell slightly in the latest year.
The memory of Samuel Paty hangs over this debate. Paty was murdered in 2020 after being targeted by an Islamist extremist for showing caricatures of the Prophet Muhammad during a lesson on freedom of expression.
Dominique Bernard, another teacher, was murdered in 2023 by a former pupil in a terrorist attack. France’s schools have since become the place where arguments about secularism, religion, free speech and state authority collide with particular force.
The figures recorded during the first national commemoration of Paty showed the scale of the challenge. Hundreds of pupils were reported for provocations, refusal to participate, threats or expressions of support for terrorism. That episode should not be used to label the current movement as Islamist, most of the present protests concern staffing, buildings, timetables and inequality.
But the Paty legacy does expose a larger question: how can teachers exercise authority in an open society when the state has not reliably protected them?
The deployment of riot police has opened another dispute over how the state exercises its authority.
Images of tear gas and riot police confronting teenagers have travelled quickly through France and abroad. In Saint-Denis, the mayor, Bally Bagayoko, was filmed facing police lines while trying to shield young people. In Lens, a 15-year-old lost a hand during an incident involving a police grenade. In the Paris region, a police officer has been placed under investigation after a teenager was seriously injured. By 9 October, more than 200 pupils and over 800 police officers or gendarmes had reportedly been injured,
while more than 6,800 people had been placed in police custody, 86 per cent of them minors.
The police have a duty to prevent arson, protect school staff and stop attacks on public buildings.
They also have a duty to use force lawfully and proportionately. Student violence does not excuse unlawful policing. Alleged police misconduct does not erase the violence committed by protesters.
The state has run out of easy answers
The government has now conceded that the grievances are legitimate. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has promised rapid action on teacher replacement, school buildings, timetables and Parcoursup. The Education Ministry has said it is contacting approximately 3,000 qualified teachers who could be sent to schools facing shortages.
That is a useful emergency measure, but it os not the same as solving the recruitment crisis. The government’s plan may demonstrate political responsiveness while leaving the structural weakness untouched. Ministers have recognised the problem, but recognition is cheaper than delivery.
The same tension is visible in the education budget. The government presents a 2027 allocation of roughly €64 billion, excluding pensions, compared with €48.8 billion in 2017.
Yet wider education spending barely increased in real terms last year. Inflation, salaries, energy costs, demographic change and the maintenance of old buildings consume money before it reaches the classroom.
France can still finance its debt, but the government has far less room to finance new promises.The European Central Bank has not judged that emergency intervention is necessary. But the country is in a politically dangerous financial position.
Public debt reached about 119 per cent of GDP at the end of the second quarter.
The government is working with a deficit of roughly 5.4 per cent of GDP this year, while annual interest costs are projected to rise from about €79 billion to more than €91 billion.
The ten-year borrowing rate has approached 5 per cent, its highest level in decades. Each rise makes the government’s promised concessions harder to fund. It means that markets are becoming less willing to treat French promises as costless.
The government therefore faces a narrow corridor. It must invest more in the services that citizens believe are collapsing while convincing creditors that public spending will eventually be brought under control. It must punish destruction without allowing the police response to define the entire crisis. It must restore authority in schools without turning schools into extensions of the security state.
There is no painless solution.
The government’s online consultation gives pupils a formal channel and produces a more precise map of their concerns. But consultation can become a substitute for decision. Students have already spent years being consulted about problems that remained visible afterwards.
France’s crisis is not simply a crisis of youth. It is a crisis of state capacity.
The young people on the streets are not all representative of the country’s lycéens. The movement is uneven, sometimes confused and occasionally violent.
It has not produced a coherent national programme. But it has revealed a common experience across very different schools: the sense that institutions ask for obedience while failing to provide the conditions in which obedience can appear reasonable.
France’s ability to sustain long-term European security commitments, including support for Ukraine, depends partly on whether it can rebuild domestic authority and fiscal credibility.
Charlotte Guillou-Clerc,
Journalist, France

Investigators probe cockpit control movement in fatal cargo plane runway crash
Sound spectrum analysis and flight simulations will seek to determine whether the Boeing freighter’s thrust lever moved mechanically or was forced forward
Aviation investigators in Hong Kong are working to determine why a cockpit control on a Boeing cargo freighter moved forward during landing last year, causing the aircraft to veer off an airport runway and kill two security personnel.
The Air Accident Investigation Authority (AAIA), an independent body under the Transport and Logistics Bureau, provided an update on Tuesday on the fatal incident involving the Boeing freighter, owned by Turkish cargo airline ACT Airlines and operated on behalf of Emirates SkyCargo.
The aircraft veered off the tarmac at Hong Kong International Airport in October 2025, crashing into a ground security vehicle parked outside the runway boundary and killing two people inside.
According to an interim statement, the AAIA said one of the key focuses of the ongoing investigation was the forward movement of an engine thrust lever, which caused the aircraft to turn left during the landing roll and veer off the runway.

Germany: Nuremberg airport closed over in-flight emergency
October 13, 2026
Police gave the all-clear at Germany's Nuremberg airport after a suspected in-flight emergency involving a plane arriving from the Greek island of Corfu.
The alert prompted police to cordon off the airport and Eurofighter jets to escort the aircraft, which landed safely, an airport spokesman said.
Why was the airport closed?
The DPA news agency reported that the plane had transmitted an emergency code before landing, alerting air traffic control to a possible problem on board.
"Checks at the scene established that there is no danger," police said in a statement. The nature of the alert was not immediately clear.
Earlier in the morning, three pilots independently reported seeing an object that may have been a drone while taking off or landing at the airport.
Airport officials, border police and Germany's air traffic control service immediately launched a search involving a police helicopter, but no drone was found.
Six flights were delayed, while two arriving aircraft diverted to Cologne and Prague before continuing to Nuremberg. It was initially unclear whether the two incidents were connected.
It was initially unclear whether the incidents were connected.
Drone incidents disrupt German airports
German airports have faced drone-related security alerts previously. In August, an explosives-laden drone was found near a runway at Leipzig/Halle airport, prompting a police investigation.
In May, a possible drone sighting halted flights at Munich airport for about an hour, forcing more than 20 arriving aircraft to divert. Police found no drone.

Ust-Kamenogorsk prepares site for new CHP plant
Ust-Kamenogorsk is moving forward with a major energy project to build a new combined heat and power plant (CHP-3), designed to supply heating to 130,000 consumers. Nearly 300 hectares of land have been allocated in Ulan district for the plant and its supporting infrastructure, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Most of the heat produced by the new plant will supply the left-bank area of Ust-Kamenogorsk, where residential neighborhoods and social facilities are rapidly being developed.
Once operational, the plant is expected to meet the heating needs of new neighborhoods, address the city's heating capacity shortage for decades to come, and reduce pressure on the existing heating network.
The construction site covers 286.6 hectares opposite the village of Kassym Kaisenov. Preparatory work is already underway, with specialists identifying key utility connection points, installing perimeter fencing, and setting up temporary facilities for construction workers.
“We have begun active site preparation alongside design and engineering surveys. We need to carefully assess the plant’s generating capacity and the requirements of the entire district heating network. We expect to complete the design phase by the end of 2026,” the East Kazakhstan region Department of Energy and Housing and Utilities said.
The project is being implemented under a presidential directive, with Oskemen Energo LLP responsible for financing and construction.
According to the project schedule, commissioning and the start of commercial operations are planned for December 2029.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that five CHP plants in Kazakhstan had remained in the “red zone,” with repairs expected to be completed by the end of 2026.

Anthropic warns of self-replicating AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:46:18 UTC
20:46:18 KST

Anthropic warns of self-replicating AI
Small artificial intelligence models could be months away from copying themselves across internet-connected consumer devices without relying on data centers, Anthropic has warned, reports a Qazinform News Agency correspondent.
In its official research report, the company examined whether AI systems could move between machines, start operating on unfamiliar hardware and continue spreading without human intervention.
Researchers demonstrated that a model could run across 15 inexpensive Android TV boxes. Another small model successfully set up AI processing on eight of nine hardware types tested.
However, current small models still struggle to complete the entire replication process reliably. More capable models succeeded in simplified experiments, but required separate computing infrastructure.
Anthropic estimates that smaller models could reach the necessary capability by the end of 2026 if improvements continue at their historical pace. It stressed that this timeline is a rough projection.
“We don’t yet have a full rogue replicator,” researchers William Zhou and Daniel Freeman wrote.
The company warned that distributed AI could be difficult to shut down because it would lack a single central control point. Unlike conventional malware, it could adapt to unfamiliar hardware.
The experiments simplified the task of gaining access to devices, meaning their results do not establish reliable replication under real-world conditions.
Anthropic recommended stronger device security, monitoring unusual network traffic and isolating infected machines to limit potential spread.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Meta launched Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, describing them as its most capable AI models yet, as it expands its presence in personal AI assistants and coding tools.

Golden eagles, hawks and saker falcons featured in traditional hunting contests at the inaugural Open Asian Falconry Cup, the main competition of the fifth Shygys Salburyny International Festival.
Participants came from Kazakhstan, Türkiye, Russia, China, Mongolia, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Georgia, Spain and Hungary. Around 15,000 spectators attended the two-day event, which also featured sighthound races, the taming of unbroken horses, mounted archery, the horseback coin-picking contest, known as "tenge ilu", tug of war and other traditional strength contests.
The festival celebrates qusbegilik, Kazakhstan's centuries-old tradition of hunting with trained birds of prey. Golden eagle hunters, known as "berkutchi", demonstrated their skills alongside other falconers.
Serikbolsyn Zhalgasuly from the Zhambyl Region won the golden eagle competition, while Zaki Makhmudkhan took the hawk title and Temirali Tolegenuly won the saker falcon event.
Organisers hope the international competition will promote Kazakhstan's hunting heritage and encourage wider recognition of these traditions.

Putin’s Protector in the White House
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:46:06 UTC
20:46:06 KST

“Russia would like to make a deal... but for whatever reason, Zelensky does not want to make a deal,” Donald Trump told reporters on Oct. 10, speaking about his latest conversation with Vladimir Putin. The Russian president, he went on, was eager for peace; Zelensky could have ended the war many times; and Ukraine ought to choose a new president.
When the man at the head of the world’s most powerful democracy says such things, one has to ask what has become of American foreign policy when it casts the invader as a peacemaker and the president of the invaded country as the obstacle to ending a war that has devastated his nation for more than four and a half years.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
So Trump cannot fathom why Zelensky will not accept the agreement Putin supposedly wants. The president of the United States has at his disposal the entire American intelligence apparatus, reports from diplomats around the world, and military assessments delivered to him every day. Yet somehow one elementary fact has escaped him. Russia invaded Ukraine, seized its territory, devastated its cities, and killed tens of thousands of its citizens.
For years, Putin’s army has been trying to accomplish what its commander in chief set out to do: destroy Ukraine’s independence. Zelensky leads a nation fighting to survive, and Ukrainians have learned enough from Moscow’s promises to know how little an agreement with the Kremlin is worth.
Zelensky Says Ukraine Received No Warning From Partners Before Russian Ballistic Missile Strike on Kyiv
Perhaps, in Trump’s conception of foreign affairs, the Ukrainians’ attachment to their own country is an inexplicable quirk. Why won’t they simply hand the Russians what they demand, accept the redrawing of their borders, and allow the American president to announce another of his great diplomatic triumphs? What kind of obstinate people, after years of bombardment, thousands of funerals, and millions driven from their homes, still insist on deciding their own future? To a man who sees the world chiefly as an endless succession of deals, Ukrainian freedom must be a particularly baffling proposition.
What is especially repellent is the ease with which Trump speaks of Putin’s desire for peace. By Russia’s own stated demands, Ukraine is expected to surrender territory Russian forces have not even managed to conquer. There is no evidence whatsoever that Putin has abandoned the imperial ambitions that drove him to invade a sovereign country. Yet Putin apparently needs only to murmur into the telephone that he wants peace for Trump to take him at his word. Four and a half years of destruction count for less than a few whispered assurances from the other end of the line.
History has seen Western leaders convince themselves that an aggressor could be placated. In 1938, Neville Chamberlain signed the Munich Agreement, sacrificing Czechoslovakia to Hitler’s territorial ambitions, and returned to London convinced he had secured peace for Europe. Now imagine that after Germany invaded Poland a year later, he had told the British people that Hitler sincerely wished to reach an agreement, but that the Poles, for reasons known only to themselves, stubbornly refused to stop fighting. All that would have remained was for Chamberlain to advise Poland to elect a new president, one with a more accommodating attitude toward Berlin.
Grotesque as that imagined speech may sound, its logic is now coming from the mouth of an American president. There is, however, one historical distinction worth remembering. For all the calamity of his appeasement policy, Chamberlain declared war on Nazi Germany on Sept. 3, 1939, after Hitler invaded Poland. He eventually understood that there was a point beyond which retreat before an aggressor became a humiliation of his own country. More than four years into Russia’s invasion, Trump is still explaining to the world how much Putin wants peace and how Zelensky keeps spoiling things for him.
And if anyone doubted how affectionate this relationship has become, Putin’s adviser Yuri Ushakov was happy to oblige. After the presidents’ 90-minute conversation, Ushakov announced that neither man wanted to hang up first, so they finally ended the call at precisely the same moment. How touching. One might have thought he was describing two lovestruck teenagers on the phone after midnight, lingering through an endless succession of goodbyes, each insisting that the other hang up first, until they agree to hang up together. The only detail Ushakov omitted was which of them wished the other good night last.
The Kremlin seems so entranced by the warmth of the relationship that it believes the rest of the world deserves to hear its most tender details. While the two presidents compete over who can stay on the line longest, Russian pilots take off toward Ukrainian cities carrying bombs that will send parents scrambling to save their children that very night. Ushakov’s account becomes almost unbearable when the sentimental theater of two powerful men is set against what their politics mean for the people living beneath those bombs.
Within hours of Trump’s deal with Putin, Russian bombs struck residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia. At least 20 people were killed, including children. Reuters reported the grief of a grandfather whose six-year-old granddaughter had been pulled dead from the rubble. She was due to celebrate her birthday later in October. He stood beside her body and wept while the American president explained that Putin wanted peace.
Trump’s solicitude for Putin now has a very tangible economic expression. Following their Oct. 9 telephone conversation, the American administration issued a license temporarily relaxing sanctions restrictions on transactions involving Russian diesel. Trump announced deliveries that, by his own account, could total 4.8 million metric tons. He publicly thanked Putin for the arrangement even as European governments warned that easing the pressure on Moscow would help bankroll its war.
Consider the scale of the political humiliation involved. For years, the United States sought to restrict the Russian state’s energy revenue precisely because that money sustains its machinery of war. Now an American president personally negotiates with Putin to bring Russian fuel back to market and advertises the arrangement as a triumph. All this is happening just weeks before the congressional midterms, when diesel prices have become a serious domestic liability for the White House.
There is an almost insulting irony in Trump’s explanation. His administration is trying to relieve the extraordinary disruption in energy markets caused, in part, by the war the United States and Israel launched against Iran, yet Zelensky is a far more convenient target for blame over fuel prices. By this logic, Ukraine’s president is supposed to stop attacking Russian refineries because those attacks inconvenience American farmers and trucking companies. The American truck driver has a place in Trump’s thinking about this war; the Ukrainian child huddled in a shelter barely seems to register.
Ukraine’s strikes on Russian refineries serve a clear military and economic purpose. They disrupt Moscow’s ability to produce and supply fuel, drive up the costs of Russia’s war economy, and force the aggressor to divert resources to defend its industrial facilities. For years, Russia has systematically targeted Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in an effort to deprive millions of electricity and heat. Yet when Ukraine strikes back at facilities that matter to Russia’s war economy, Trump responds with anger and demands that Zelensky stop.
Zelensky has offered a straightforward, verifiable compromise. Ukraine will stop striking Russia’s energy infrastructure if Russia simultaneously stops attacking Ukraine’s. That is the basic reciprocity any serious mediation should require. Trump, however, had already demanded that Kyiv halt its strikes unilaterally, while Putin received relief for his fuel exports. This distribution of favors and demands allows Moscow to preserve both the military and financial advantages of its aggression, while imposing yet another constraint on Ukraine’s defense.
Damage to America
This is the gravest damage Trump is doing to American foreign policy. There was a time when it was difficult even to imagine a US president publicly echoing the arguments of a country that had invaded its European neighbor, thanking its leader as his bombs killed civilians, and demanding political and military concessions from the victim. Barely two years ago, such a statement from the White House would have stunned even those who believed Washington should negotiate with Moscow. Trump has moved the boundaries of the politically conceivable so far, and so fast, that we now have to remind ourselves almost daily how extraordinary this rupture is.
For decades, America built its international authority on alliances, security guarantees, and the defense of a principle: a powerful country does not get to seize a weaker neighbor’s territory simply because it can. America’s own foreign policy record, of course, includes grave errors and serious violations of that very principle. But the country’s claim to leadership of the free world rested on the idea that democracies share an interest in restraining aggression. Trump is replacing that idea with personal arrangements, private deals, pressure on allies, and a bewildering indulgence toward Putin. The damage will outlast his time in the White House.
For America’s democratic allies, the implications are chilling. If a US president can recast the aggressor as the peacemaker and the country under attack as the obstacle to peace, what should countries that rely on American security guarantees now expect? What would that reasoning mean for the Baltic states, for Poland, or for any country confronted one day with the demands of a much more powerful neighbor? International order does not survive on the elegance of declarations about liberty. It survives when the states with the power to uphold those declarations are willing to act on them.
Imposing elections.
Trump’s call for Ukrainians to choose a new president is especially brazen. Volodymyr Zelensky was elected by Ukrainian voters in 2019. Subsequent presidential elections have been postponed because of martial law. Holding a free, safe, and fair vote while Ukrainian cities are bombed daily, millions of people have fled, and large stretches of the country are occupied presents challenges that cannot be waved away with an offhand remark in front of television cameras. Zelensky has now offered to hold elections if Russia agrees to a full, 60-day ceasefire. Putin has yet to demonstrate that he would accept even that.
By what right, in any case, does Trump tell Ukrainians who their president should be? Does the Ukrainian people’s right to choose their government expire whenever an American politician grows impatient with their choice? If Trump believes Zelensky should go because he refuses to accept whatever Trump and Putin agree between themselves, Trump might at least show a little respect for a people who have defended their democratic choice with weapons in their hands. Ukrainians have paid far too dearly for freedom to be told from Washington which candidate would be obedient enough to deserve their future.
Trump, for his part, might exercise a little caution before recommending that other countries change presidents. Americans will vote in congressional midterm elections on November 3, and the results could significantly alter the balance of power in Washington. Congress has the constitutional authority to oversee the executive, investigate abuses, and, where there are lawful grounds, initiate impeachment proceedings. A midterm election will not itself remove Trump; conviction and removal require a two-thirds vote in the Senate. But there is a perfectly legitimate question about how long America’s democratic system can withstand a foreign policy that is wrecking the country’s international standing and damaging relations with its most important allies.
An end to Trump’s policy toward Ukraine would be welcome news for the democratic world. If American institutions were one day to establish grounds for his impeachment and removal, I doubt there would be much celebration in the Kremlin. Nor would dictators and autocrats elsewhere have much reason to rejoice. Trump’s treatment of Putin has already encouraged them to believe that American support for democracy is negotiable, subject to the president’s personal preferences and interests. Fortunately, America is larger than one man in the White House. It has institutions, a free press, Congress, courts, and citizens who have repeatedly shown that they can defend their democratic order.
Meanwhile, Trump continues to speak as though Zelensky were the one who ought to apologize for the war’s continuation.
On Oct. 11, Trump abruptly announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an energy ceasefire. Zelensky said Ukraine was prepared to honor such an arrangement but was still waiting for Moscow’s confirmation, the terms of the agreement, and credible guarantees.
At the time of Trump’s announcement, Russia had not publicly confirmed any such deal. Just hours later, a Russian drone struck a power plant in Kyiv, and Russian forces attacked the CHP-5 combined heat-and-power plant in Kharkiv.
In full view of the Russian public and the wider world, Putin once again humiliated Trump, demonstrating that the American president may proclaim as many ceasefires as he pleases, but Russian bombs will stop falling only when Putin gives the order. Putin’s promises deserve exactly the trust his record has earned them: next to none.
What pains me most about all of this is the endless expectation that Ukrainians must accommodate everyone else’s fears, interests, and political needs. They are expected to accommodate Putin’s territorial demands, Trump’s anxiety over diesel prices, Europe’s economic difficulties, and the exhaustion of Western publics after years of war.
How many of the politicians making these demands are prepared to give equal thought to the parent in Kharkiv waiting outside the wreckage of a school for word of a child, to the soldier at the front who has not seen his family in four years, or to the woman who has lost her husband and must explain to her children why their father will never come home? For too long, their suffering has entered diplomatic conversations as something to be mentioned in passing before the real business of territory, sanctions, and trade begins.
Zelensky has made mistakes during this war, as any leader facing an almost unbroken national catastrophe inevitably will. Ukrainians will decide how to judge his policies, decisions, and responsibilities. But today he possesses something that Trump, for all his power, money, and self-regard, seems less and less able to comprehend: a duty to a people who refuse to be bartered away.
Let us not forget the Ukrainians
Ukraine has endured far more than anyone could have anticipated in February 2022 because its citizens decided that some things remain worth fighting for, however terrible the price.
Trump can thank Putin, praise his alleged passion for peace, talk with him late into the night, and treat him as a partner in grand commercial ventures. He can demand Zelensky’s removal, threaten Ukrainians over strikes on Russian refineries, and try to portray resistance to aggression as the obstacle to a diplomatic breakthrough. These actions will be part of his political record. One day the American president will have to explain why he was so eager to defend Putin while Ukraine was fighting for its existence.
And Ukrainians will go on defending their country after presidents come and go, and after diplomats stop counting concessions. Their struggle has already proved that freedom is not merchandise with a price set by the powerful, nor a privilege a people may enjoy only when it elects a leader sufficiently obedient to be approved elsewhere.
Vladimir Putin will be remembered for the invasion, cities in ruins, war crimes, and Ukrainian children who never returned to their families. Donald Trump risks a place in the history of this war as the American president who thanked the aggressor and told the people under attack to replace their leader.
And when the history of Ukraine’s resistance is written, the question will not be why Zelensky refused to hand Putin territory the Russian army could not take by force. The harder question will be for those who demanded this of him while claiming to speak for the free world.
One day the war will end, and Ukraine will begin rebuilding its devastated cities. No reconstruction, however, will bring back the children killed by Russian missiles, the husbands who never returned from the front, or the years Putin has stolen from millions of lives. The history of this war will also record that the president of the United States publicly thanked the man who ordered the invasion, presented him as a sincere advocate of peace, and accused the president of the invaded country of standing in the way of an end to the fighting. Trump may seek refuge in talk of negotiations, fuel prices, and American interests. None of it can lessen the moral weight of words spoken while Ukrainians were burying their dead.
That is why I would like Donald Trump, one day, to travel to Ukraine and stand before a mother whose child was killed by a Russian missile, and repeat to her what he declared so confidently in front of the television cameras.
Let him explain that Putin sincerely wants peace, but that Zelensky, for reasons no one can quite fathom, refuses to accept it. Let Donald Trump look straight into the eyes of a mother whose child has been taken from her by Putin’s war and thank Vladimir Putin one more time.

Kazakhstan’s economy expands 4.2% in first nine months of 2026

Presenting Kazakhstan’s socioeconomic results for the first nine months of 2026, Zhumangarin highlighted several challenges facing the country’s economy this year.

At the same time, a stronger tenge has put pressure on revenues from export-oriented industries and the state budget, while slowing consumer lending has dampened domestic demand.

According to him, these trends point to a gradual transformation of Kazakhstan’s economic structure.

Privacy campaigners to ask court to ban sale of Meta AI glasses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:45:06 UTC

Privacy campaigners to ask court to ban sale of Meta AI glasses
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Two Dutch privacy organisations are seeking an injunction against Meta to ban sales of the company’s AI glasses in the Netherlands.
Offlimits and The Firewall argue that the devices, which allow users to film and record scenes that they are viewing through the lenses, breach Dutch criminal laws that protect people from being photographed and filmed without their consent.
Lawyers wrote to Meta two weeks ago demanding they withdraw the glasses from sale in the Netherlands or face legal action, but the deadline passed without a response from the company.
“Offlimits and The Firewall are demanding, by means of this letter of formal notice, that the sale of the Meta glasses in the Netherlands cease,” they wrote.
Several thousand pairs of AI glasses have been bought by Dutch customers since opticians started selling them a year ago, while worldwide more than seven million pairs have been sold.
Several music venues in the Netherlands have banned the devices after a man was caught filming women near the toilets at a festival in August. Campaigners say it is one example of how the glasses have been used to film people secretly in intimate settings such as toilets, changing rooms and sex clubs.
They also raised concerns about the potential for the devices to be used to film young children in sports halls, playgrounds or nurseries.
Drawing a line
“We are drawing a line,” Robbert Hoving, managing director of Offlimits, said. “Hiding a camera in an everyday accessory encourages online behaviour that breaches personal boundaries. Victims of these glasses are already contacting our helpline.”
Offlimits, which campaigns against online abuse and exploitation, especially of children, said it was concerned that the glasses capture images of people who are unaware they are being filmed, including minors.
Although the glasses have an LED light to show when the camera is operating, it is not always clear or visible, the lawyers wrote. “Furthermore, the LED light can easily be covered up, making it invisible to anyone,” they said.
They also pointed out that the footage is stored by Meta and used to train its AI systems, which they argue is also an offence under Dutch law. “Meta gains access to the recordings made with the Meta glasses, even when people appear in the footage who have not given their consent.”
The organisations hope the court will announce a date for a hearing by the end of the week. Dutch News has reached out to Meta for comment.
