In India, a Dark Shadow Falls on Its Vaunted Elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:45:00 UTC
20:45:00 KST

On Saturday, New Delhi, the Indian capital, was under siege. The Indian government deployed more than 20,000 police and paramilitary personnel, barricaded the city center, and suspended internet access. By evening, more than 7,000 people were detained by the police, including leaders from India’s opposition parties, lawyers, and journalists. Despite the crackdown, thousands turned out in Delhi on Monday to protest with even greater vigor.
The repressive effort sought to deter a planned protest at Jantar Mantar, a traditional protest site in New Delhi. The protest centered on two core demands: the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner and the rollback of a nationwide process known as Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
The chief election commissioner heads the national electoral body and is appointed on the recommendation of a committee headed by the prime minister. The SIR ostensibly seeks to clean up and update the electoral rolls but has removed 130 million Indians from the rolls—more than half the number of Americans eligible to vote in the midterm elections.
The troubles truly began in the summer of 2025. Several Indian states were about to hold elections for their state legislatures. Ahead of those elections, the Election Commission announced an electoral revision in those states, citing the need to “clean up” electoral rolls. Numerous voters would be required to prove that they were citizens and entitled to be on the rolls by producing one or more documents from a select list. Election Commission officials would scrutinize the documents and either accept or reject them.
Judicial avoidance
Civil society groups and political activists promptly challenged the proposed electoral revisions before the Supreme Court of India in June 2025. They questioned the power of the Election Commission to undertake electoral revisions at such a scale. India’s election law does authorize the commission to undertake a revision of electoral rolls in specific electoral constituencies, provided it records its reasons in writing. The petitioners argued that it does not grant the Election Commission overarching power to require voters already on the rolls to prove their eligibility afresh.
The petitioners also argued that Election Commission’s list of acceptable documents was exclusionary and would result in large scale disenfranchisement. In India, access to documents issued by the government depends heavily on caste, class and gender. Many people simply lack necessary documents or the ability to navigate the bureaucracy to obtain them.
For months, the Supreme Court did not rule on the legality of electoral revisions on such a vast scale, allowing the exercise to become a fait accompli. Instead, it engaged in prolonged courtroom negotiations with the Election Commission over which documents Indian voters would have to provide to remain on the electoral rolls. There was an extended debate on whether Aadhaar, India’s national digital identity document, would be accepted.
But even as the legal debates continued, exclusions from electoral rolls mounted. In the eastern Indian state of West Bengal, where Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) had never won a state election, nine million people—around 12% percent of the electorate—found themselves excluded from the rolls.
Faced with these exclusions, and still unwilling to rule on the legality of the SIR, the Supreme Court took the extraordinary step of creating an entire administrative machinery: tribunals staffed by judicial officers to hear appeals from excluded voters. When the petitioners warned that these tribunals would take years, if not decades, to resolve all the appeals, the Supreme Court judges effectively said that it was fine for excluded people to note vote in the upcoming election as long as they would eventually be put back on the rolls.
The West Bengal election went ahead using the new electoral rolls and the BJP won. One indication of how flawed the SIR may have been was that around 90% of the voters in West Bengal, whose appeals were decided, were eventually restored to the rolls. Nine out of every ten excluded voters had been wrongfully removed. Yet even as exclusions numbered in the millions in each state, the Supreme Court noted that the data did not indicate “systemic disenfranchisement.”
Unchecked bureaucrats
Eventually, when the Supreme Court finally issued its judgment in the summer of 2026, it upheld the entire exercise. It affirmed the wide powers of the Election Commission to conduct the electoral revisions as it saw fit.
A central argument against the exercise was that by requiring every elector, including those already on the electoral rolls, to prove their eligibility afresh, the Election Commission was treating each individual as presumptively ineligible to vote. This was a grossly disproportionate exercise of power, particularly because more proportionate methods were available to the election commission.
The court rejected this argument too and, I believe, effectively immunized the commission from the requirement to act in a proportionate manner. As the legal scholar Vasudev Devadasan noted, the judgement had the effect of creating a "permanent class" of disenfranchised persons who simply cannot participate in political life.
The consequences soon became apparent: the new BJP government in West Bengal threatened, on more than one occasion, to cut off welfare benefits for people excluded from the electoral rolls through the SIR. Although the Supreme Court noted that the SIR was not meant to determine citizenship, by the summer of 2026, that distinction was becoming difficult to sustain.
Beyond the threat to people’s welfare entitlements, there were widely reported cases of passport renewals being denied because applicants had been excluded from the electoral rolls through the SIR.
In 2020, the Indian government’s attempts to create a National Register of Citizens (NRC) had been widely criticized because of how it would force every individual to prove their citizenship to state authorities, and lead to widespread exclusion. After widespread protests across the country against it, the NRC was shelved. The SIR now appeared to be a way of introducing the NRC through the backdoor.
As the SIR proceeded across multiple states—with large-scale exclusions in each—patterns began to emerge: disproportionate exclusions among vulnerable and marginalized people and of religious minorities, especially Muslims; and the use of algorithms to exclude even voters who possessed the required documents, citing "logical discrepancies" such an arbitrary age gap between parent and child, judged by arbitrary criteria that varied from state to state.
Other disturbing facts also came to light. In certain neighborhoods, people had submitted pre-filled forms in bulk, seeking to have Muslims removed from off the electoral rolls by questioning their citizenship. India’s electoral law allows third parties to object to anyone’s inclusion on the electoral rolls.
In Delhi, the omission of some prominent people from the rolls provoked public outrage. The Election Commission then introduced a “VIP portal” through which their names could be restored, creating a two-tier system of class privilege.
A tenacious reporter
Against this backdrop, an investigative report by Ritika Chopra, a journalist with the Indian Express newspaper in the last week of September, landed like a bombshell. Her report showed that although the Election Commission’s decisions were supposed to be taken by consensus among its three commissioners, the chief election commissioner had been taking them unilaterally, often over the objections of, and sometimes without involving, the other commissioners. (The Election Commission responded by describing differing “views and observations” as part of “deliberation in any institution.”)
More reports followed, documenting more unilateral decisions, opaque algorithms built by private corporations, and the increasing centralization of authority within the Election Commission to add or remove voters. It was a clear departure from India’s decentralized electoral system, which is designed to guard against decisions made in bad faith.
These reports crystallized latent anger, particularly against the chief election commissioner. Under Indian electoral law, election commissioners are appointed by a committee in which the political executive holds a two-to-one majority; they are, in effect, executive appointments. The Supreme Court’s 2023 attempt to reform this system was bypassed by subsequent legislation. The court then left a challenge to that legislation on the back burner. All of this explains why the chief election commissioner became the primary focus of public anger.
The story of the SIR is both an account of large-scale voter disenfranchisement in India and one of institutional crisis. Two failures converged: the failure to entrench the Election Commission’s independence in law and in the Constitution, and the failure of the Supreme Court to intervene despite evidence of disenfranchisement placed before it. Together they culminated in the furious popular protests in Delhi and the Indian government’s crackdown.
It is difficult to see how this story ends. The right to vote is hard won and its loss keenly felt. History shows that once people lose confidence in the institutions meant to protect that right, restoring their trust is exceedingly difficult. A long shadow hangs over electoral integrity in India. Lifting it will require urgent, systemic reforms. Whether those reforms will come remains uncertain.

Iran shakes with 67 earthquakes in a week
TEHRAN – A total of 67 earthquakes have been recorded across the country in a week from September October 2 to 9, according to the seismological networks of the Institute of Geophysics of the University of Tehran.
Statistically, 64 earthquakes with magnitudes smaller than 3, three earthquakes with a magnitude between 3 and 4, and no earthquake with a magnitude above 4 have occurred in the country, irsc reported.
Of the total quakes, two had a magnitude of 3.6 on the Richter scale, the first occurred on October 4 in West Azarbajian, and the other one hit Semnan province on October 6.
Among the provinces of the country, Khorasan Razavi experienced the highest number of earthquakes with 12, followed by Yazd with 8, and South Khorasan with 7 earthquakes.
During the same period, one earthquake hit Tehran. No earthquakes were recorded in Ardabil, Alborz, Ilam, Bushehr, Chahrmahal-Bakhtiari, Zanjan, Sistan-Baluchestan, Qom, Qazvin, Kordestan, Gilan, Markazi, Hormozgan, and Hamedan provinces.
A total of 2,380 earthquakes with a magnitude of more than 2.5 on the Richter scale were recorded across the country over the past calendar year (March 2025–March 2026), according to the Seismological networks of the Institute of Geophysics of the University of Tehran, Mehr news agency reported.
Out of recorded earthquakes, 910 had a magnitude greater than 3, 130 had a magnitude greater than 4, and 15 had a magnitude greater than 5 on the Richter scale.
 
The Iranian plateau is located in a very seismically active region of the world and is known not only for its major catastrophic earthquakes but also for the disasters relating to natural hazards, especially earthquakes.
About 2 percent of the earthquakes in the world occur in Iran, but more than 6 percent of the victims of the world’s earthquakes during the 20th century are reported from Iranian earthquakes.

Baltic state bets on films and video games in militarization push
Estonia’s Defense Ministry has launched a funding competition for films and video games intended to strengthen public willingness to go to war, as Tallinn and the other Baltic states continue their military buildup citing a supposed Russian threat.
The scheme has a total budget of up to €250,000 ($280,000) and covers feature films, documentaries, animation, television series, and narrative video games, public broadcaster ERR reported on Tuesday. Applications close November 18, with the money available for use next year.
Tallinn is specifically looking for audiovisual productions that align with national defense goals and can reach different generations and make military issues accessible to a wider audience, ministry spokesman Thomas Melli explained to the outlet.
Director Ilmar Raag, who previously received ministry funding for a documentary, urged officials to favor credible portrayals over simplistic messaging, warning that overt propaganda could backfire. “Those people who give money in the ministry must see that if a filmmaker’s mind moves towards an overly simplistic propagandistic vision, it can actually have a negative backlash,” he told ERR.
The initiative comes alongside region-wide preparations for what have officials have claimed could be a confrontation with Russia by the end of the decade. The Financial Times reported earlier this month that Estonia wass acquiring missile systems capable of reaching St. Petersburg and deploying additional troops along the Russian border, particularly near the Kaliningrad exclave.
Defense Minister Martin Herem “joked” last month that if Estonia mobilized and Russia did not attack, it would be “economically more correct to attack ourselves” rather than keep troops waiting. “Then at least we will know when it will start, and we will not waste food and air in vain,” he said.
Despite already allocating a combined €9.4 billion to defense this year, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania have recently sought an additional €500 million from the EU for military drones, citing the possibility of Russia testing NATO.
The Baltic states have also pursued a sweeping crackdown on Russian language, media, and culture. Estonia and Latvia are phasing out Russian-language schooling, while all three countries have banned Russian television channels. Latvia has gone further, targeting books, video games, toys, clothing, and other goods produced in Russia and Belarus.
NATO has separately spent years researching online influence techniques. Published experiments examined fake social-media profiles, targeted advertising, and purchased engagement. The bloc described the work, examined in RT’s America Now, as defensive research.
Moscow has repeatedly denied plans to attack Estonia or other NATO members, accusing Western governments of using the supposed threat to justify militarization and restrictions on Russian culture and Russian-speaking residents.
Russian officials have warned, however, that attacks on Russian territory or attempts to blockade Kaliningrad could provoke a military response involving all weapons in the country’s arsenal.

Ukraine’s Fighter Fleet Has Quietly Tipped West—F-16s and Mirages Now Outnumber Soviet Jets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:43:38 UTC
20:43:38 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Ukraine’s Fighter Fleet Has Quietly Tipped West—F-16s and Mirages Now Outnumber Soviet Jets
Ukraine’s Air Force is no longer primarily a Soviet-designed fleet—the combined number of F-16s and Mirage 2000s has now overtaken its remaining MiG-29s and Su-27s, with Gripens and Rafales potentially next.
Ukraine’s air defense against Russia’s increasingly common jet-powered Shahed-type drones relies on far more than ground-based interceptors, with fighter aviation becoming an increasingly important part of the layered defense. According to Defense Express on October 13, the balance inside Ukraine’s combat aviation fleet has now shifted significantly toward Western aircraft.
Ukraine is using both F-16s and French Mirage 2000s to intercept fast-moving Russian drones, while work is underway to stock enough ammunition for several months of sustained operations and eliminate maintenance bottlenecks that limit how many aircraft can remain mission-ready at any given time.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Those priorities were recently outlined following discussions between Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara and journalists.
The key change, Defense Express notes, is numerical. Although MiG-29s and Su-27s still remain important to Ukrainian combat aviation, the combined fleet of Western F-16s and Mirage 2000s now exceeds the number of those two Soviet-designed fighter types still in service.
MiG-29s and Su-27s are still very much in the fight
That shift does not mean Ukraine’s Soviet-era fighters have disappeared from air-defense operations. Defense Express points to regularly published footage showing Ukrainian MiG-29s intercepting Russian jet-powered UAVs, making clear that those aircraft continue to perform combat missions alongside Western fighters.
MiG-29s and Su-27s remain useful because Ukrainian pilots and maintenance crews have decades of experience operating them, while the aircraft can still perform both interception and strike missions.
Their long-term challenge is sustainability: battlefield losses, shrinking stocks of compatible weapons, and increasingly difficult access to spare parts make it harder to maintain the fleets at their former scale.
This also explains why official discussions about fighter aviation increasingly center on F-16s and Mirage 2000s. They are not the only aircraft being used, but they are becoming the dominant part of Ukraine’s available fighter force and increasingly shape how the Air Force plans future operations.
Jet-powered Shaheds are driving fighter demand
The role of fighter aircraft has become more important as Russia introduces faster jet-powered UAVs, which give mobile ground teams less time to detect and engage incoming targets.
Fighters can patrol much larger areas, rapidly reposition as drone routes shift, and provide another interception layer between inexpensive drone-defense systems and scarce long-range surface-to-air missiles.
Ukraine is therefore working not only to increase the number of Western aircraft available but also to ensure they have sufficient ammunition and can be serviced quickly enough to sustain a high operational tempo.
According to Defense Express, one of the priorities is building missile and ammunition stocks several months ahead while addressing maintenance bottlenecks that can leave otherwise available aircraft grounded.
In September 2026 alone, Ukrainian combat aircraft reportedly conducted about 1,300 sorties for fighter cover and more than 250 missions against ground targets.
There is no public breakdown by aircraft type, but Defense Express argues that the growing numerical share of F-16s and Mirage 2000s makes it likely that Western fighters accounted for a significant portion of that activity.
Gripen and Rafale could push the transition even further
The move away from a primarily Soviet-designed fighter fleet may accelerate further. Ukraine is already looking toward Sweden’s JAS 39 Gripen and France’s Rafale as potential future additions, a transition also highlighted by the Royal United Services Institute in an August 2026 assessment.
If those aircraft eventually enter Ukrainian service, the Air Force’s center of gravity would shift even more decisively toward Western platforms, logistics, weapons, and maintenance systems.
MiG-29s and Su-27s would still remain useful for as long as they can be sustained, but they would increasingly operate alongside a fleet built around entirely different standards.
The result is an Air Force already well into a structural transition: Soviet fighters remain active and relevant, but F-16s and Mirage 2000s now hold the numerical advantage—and the next generation of Ukrainian combat aviation may be even more Western.
Previously, Ukraine’s air defense forces reported the destruction of more than 445,000 Russian missiles, attack drones, reconnaissance aircraft, and other aerial targets since the start of the full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022.

Iran eyes African markets through technology cooperation with Senegal
TEHRAN – Iranian officials have explored ways to strengthen scientific and technological cooperation with Senegal, positioning the West African country as a gateway for Iranian knowledge-based companies seeking to expand into African markets.
Hossein Roozbeh, head of the Organization for the Development of International Cooperation in Science and Technology, met with Hamid Moradkhani, Iran’s ambassador to Senegal, on Saturday to discuss avenues for expanding bilateral cooperation, IRNA reported.
The talks focused on boosting exports of knowledge-based products, transferring technical expertise for the production of agricultural drones, and finalizing a comprehensive memorandum of understanding (MoU) on technological cooperation between the two countries.
The officials also discussed ways to benefit from artificial intelligence (AI) capacities and technological infrastructures to develop bilateral economic relations.
Describing Senegal as a gateway for Iranian technology to the African continent, Roozbeh put forward several proposals to expand bilateral cooperation.
He noted that more than 11,000 knowledge-based companies operate in Iran, producing goods that meet international standards and compete with their global counterparts in both quality and price.
He also announced Iran’s readiness for joint manufacturing of products in agricultural, medical, petrochemical, and energy sectors.
His other suggestion focused on establishing and developing science and technology parks and Iranian innovation centers in Senegal.
Holding technological exhibitions, providing specialized content for media in Senegal, granting scholarships to Senegalese students, and hosting Senegalese technical delegations in the Iranian House of Innovation and Technology (iHiT) were among other points suggested by the official.
For his part, Moradkhani highlighted technology transfer and specialized training as the key pillars of the two countries’ collaborations, and called for the Vice Presidency for Science and Technology to play an active role in Iran-Africa joint commissions.
He also underscored the importance of establishing a network of experts and strengthening exchanges in the oil and energy sectors.
The official added that a draft memorandum of understanding (MoU) had been finalized and was expected to be signed during a visit to Tehran by senior Senegalese officials in January 2027.
Tehran hosts meeting of African envoys to boost science, health cooperation

“Now, we are ready to share these achievements with Africans through establishing a strategic health alliance between Iran and African countries,” Tavakoli highlighted.
Elaborating on the core areas of the strategic alliance, he said that researchers will focus on addressing real-time illnesses, such as tropical and endemic diseases, drug shortages, and health service delivery in rural areas.
Admitting African students and developing joint educational courses, with dual accreditation, as well as dispatching professors for training of trainers, will be another part of the alliance.
Other main components of the strategic alliance will include sharing technical knowledge in fields such as manufacturing vaccines, biosimilar drugs, and medical equipment by establishing a collaborative production line in African countries, Tavakoli added.
The expansion of scientific interactions between Iranian and African scientists was the last point mentioned by the official. The strategic alliance will lay the basis for boosting scientific collaborations between over 60 universities and hundreds of top research centers across the country, he further noted.
On December 8, the ministries of health and foreign affairs, in a virtual meeting with Iranian ambassadors and attachés in Africa, discussed the potential for promoting cooperation with African countries in the health sector.
During the meeting, Alireza Biglari, the deputy health minister for international affairs, highlighted the country’s capabilities in areas related to health. Referring to the existing capacity as a valuable opportunity for the expansion of health diplomacy and the favorable condition for cooperation with African countries, the official announced the readiness of the health ministry to implement decisions and operational plans, IRNA reported.
For his part, Akbar Khosravi Nejad, Assistant to Iran’s Foreign Minister and Director General for Africa, underlined the importance of Africa in Iran’s foreign policy, and said that the country’s health system is one of the main sectors for enhancing collaborations with these countries.
Tavakoli, for his part, presented an account of the current activities and programs of the university in Africa, as well as future plans to meet African ambassadors in Tehran.

Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty called Tuesday for an immediate halt to all attacks targeting Saudi territory during a phone call with his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi, according to Egypt’s Foreign Ministry.
The two ministers discussed regional developments, rapidly evolving tensions and diplomatic efforts to de-escalate the situation, the ministry said in a statement.
Abdelatty stressed the need for an immediate halt to all attacks targeting Saudi Arabia, the ministry said.
“There is no justification for these attacks and they cannot be accepted,” the minister said.
He underlined the importance of reducing tensions and containing regional escalation because of its negative repercussions for the security and stability of countries in the region and beyond, according to the statement.
The Egyptian minister also called for “prioritizing political and diplomatic solutions and returning to negotiations and dialogue between Iran and the US,” describing diplomacy as the “only path” to resolving outstanding disputes and preventing the region from sliding into further escalation and instability.
Iran’s Fars news agency also reported the call, saying Araghchi and Abdelatty exchanged views on the latest regional developments, including the situation in Yemen, as well as diplomatic efforts to reduce tensions.
Türkiye, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia issued a joint statement Sunday condemning the attacks and reaffirming support for Riyadh’s legitimate measures to counter and deter them. The statement followed a Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that killed 13 people and injured 309 others.
In September, Cairo said Egyptian and Saudi national security are “interconnected and inseparable,” while warning that continued Houthi attacks risked fueling wider regional tensions.
Saudi Arabia has faced a series of attacks in recent days on airports and civilian facilities amid an escalating military confrontation with the Houthis. The escalation began in July following a period of relative calm after a UN-brokered truce took effect in April 2022.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government.

French students staged a fresh round of nationwide protests on Tuesday, with around 200 schools closed as teachers’ unions joined calls for increased education funding and better study conditions.
Marches began in Lyon and Nantes, while students blockaded schools in Paris, Rennes and Strasbourg during the fifth round of mobilisation, French newspaper Le Parisien reported.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray told France Inter that “around 200 establishments are closed”, describing the figure as lower than the previous week.

Unions and activists join protests
Teachers’ unions FSU-SNUIPP and SNES-FSU called on members to join the mobilisation, citing shared demands over public education, working conditions and pay.
The protesters are demanding increased education spending and opposing the Parcoursup university admissions platform. President Emmanuel Macron urged demonstrators to remain calm and respect people and property.
More than 6,800 people, overwhelmingly minors, have been detained since the movement began, according to Le Parisien. France’s national police watchdog, IGPN, has opened 24 investigations into suspected police violence.

He added that 5,119 scams were recorded in August alone, a monthly record high.

Iraqi students taking Persian Language Proficiency Test more than triple
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:41:17 UTC
20:41:17 KST

Iraqi students taking Persian Language Proficiency Test more than triple
TEHRAN – A total of 268 Iraqi students have taken the Persian Language Proficiency Test at six centers across Iraq, marking a more than threefold increase from the 78 participants recorded last year.
The test was organized with the support of Iran’s scientific counselor in Iraq and administered in Baghdad, Najaf, Wasit, Karbala, Basra, and Erbil.
Proficiency in Persian helps international students communicate more effectively with professors and classmates, pursue their studies at Iranian universities, and access academic resources in the language. These capabilities can also contribute to strengthening educational and academic ties between Iran and Iraq.
 
The Persian Language Proficiency Test is held three times a year both in Iran and in the countries that have Persian Language chairs, concurrently. The test has general and academic modules.
Apart from university students, foreign nationals who want to live, work, run businesses, and establish international offices in Iran, or study in Iranian schools are required to take the test.
On January 24, Abbas Qanbari-Baghestan, an official with the Organization of Student Affairs, said: “Attaining a specified score in learning the Persian language will be a key requirement for foreign students to be admitted to Iranian universities from the next academic year, which will start in fall 2026.” The test includes listening, speaking, and writing sections, he added.
Highlighting the importance of providing quality education for international students, the official said Persian language teaching centers play a key role in attracting foreign students and preparing them to major in universities. So, they should do their best to employ experienced professors to provide the best educational courses to help foreign students learn the Persian language.
Nearly 60,000 foreign students are currently studying in Iranian universities, compared with 35,000 students in the past Iranian academic year, which started on September 22, 2024.
Despite existing challenges, Iran has managed to attract students from 101 countries, Saeed Habiba, the head of the Organization of Student Affairs, said in October 2025.
The scientific capacity of the country’s universities and their positive record in international cooperation are a valuable opportunity that must be seized to transform the presence of foreign students into a national discourse and strategic planning, the official said, adding that the students are mainly from Afghanistan, India, Iraq, and Pakistan.
Attracting 320,000 intl. students by 2028 on agenda
According to the Seventh National Development Plan (2023-2028), the country is projected to increase the number of international students to 320,000 from currently around 60,000.
To this end, the higher education system needs to adopt some institutional and developmental approaches in organizations associated with foreign students, Mehr news agency reported.
In this regard, the parliament research center has evaluated Iran’s situation in attracting international students and measures that need to be taken into account.
According to the report, the number of foreign students in the country has grown from 13,767 in Iranian year 1394 (2015 – 2016) to 68,563 in 1403 (2024 -2025). The number of educational institutions that are allowed to accept foreign students has noticeably increased from 45 to 206 over the past decade.
The report also shows that 13 acts, such as providing short-time sabbaticals, granting visas, establishing a center for foreign student graduates, and holding remedial courses, have been developed and officially accepted by the parliament as part of educational charter for foreign students; however, they have not been implemented in time.
Also major organizations and institutions of the country have no participation in planning cultural programs for foreign students.
A lack of strategic comprehensive marketing skills, and bureaucratic and time-consuming correspondence were among other recognized problems.
The parliament research center has put forward some proposals to help attract more international students. The most important one highlights adopting an approach that focuses on generating income, soft cultural power, and expanding science.
The other suggestion emphasizes the importance of boosting south-south international relations, that is developing political and economic interactions with highly populated countries like Pakistan, India, Egypt and some countries in Central Asia.
Ongoing evaluation of other countries’ policies in attracting students, developing software and hardware infrastructures, stable and secure network, as well as increasing the number of scholarships are among other suggested solutions.
Before the US-Israeli war against Iran, nearly 60,000 foreign students from 101 countries, mainly from Afghanistan, India, Iraq, and Pakistan, were studying in Iran.
The Ministry of Science has announced that educational programs for foreign university students present in the country will continue despite the unfavorable conditions caused by the imposed war.
All universities have been asked to ensure that all international students benefit from the educational facilities and capacities of the universities by adopting innovative measures, including preparing offline educational packages, developing intensive summer training courses, and anticipating the possibility of completing practical courses in the coming years, in addition to continuing online education, IRNA reported.
These measures and plans should be implemented in a way that ensures that international students do not suffer academic, training, or even financial losses due to the conditions resulting from the imposed war.
Science Minister Hossein Simaei-Sarraf has said over 30 Iranian universities had been directly attacked by the United States and Israel since the war began in late February.
Five university professors and more than 60 students had been killed in the strikes, added Simaei-Sarraf, describing attacks on Iranian infrastructure as “crimes against humanity.”
“The main reason the enemy targeted this sensitive infrastructure was that they did not want us to gain access to this technology,” he said, adding that many Iranians abroad have contacted the university, offering to help fund its restoration.

Kongsberg puts $51M into Polish counter-drone plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:40:29 UTC
20:40:29 KST

- Kongsberg will invest more than 200 million zlotys in a counter-drone factory in Poland’s Pomeranian region to support the SAN program.
- Construction is set to begin after a contract signing by year’s end, with serial production starting in the first half of 2028.
Norway’s Kongsberg will build a factory in northern Poland to manufacture and maintain counter-drone systems for the Polish SAN program, investing more than 200 million zlotys (about €45 million, or $51 million) in a plant that will create over 100 permanent jobs once it reaches full capacity, the company announced on Oct. 13 at the Warsaw Security Forum.
The plant will be built in the Pomeranian region near the Tricity area of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Sopot, with the exact site still to be announced. Kongsberg plans to sign the construction contract by the end of this year and begin building immediately afterward, with serial production starting in the first half of 2028. The factory will become part of Kongsberg’s global manufacturing network, serving Poland first and later other European customers.
“The new facility will support Polish industry and defence capabilities and strengthen KONGSBERG’s presence in Poland. The facility will be an integrated part of KONGSBERG’s global manufacturing network, to serve Poland and other future European customers,” said Eirik Lie, president and CEO of Kongsberg.
The factory follows the contract Kongsberg and Polish state defense group Polska Grupa Zbrojeniowa signed with the Polish Armaments Agency on Jan. 30 for the SAN counter-drone program, named after a river in eastern Poland. Kongsberg’s share of that deal is about 16 billion Norwegian kroner (about $1.67 billion) for 18 counter-drone batteries, while the full SAN program is valued at around 15 billion zlotys and also involves Gdynia-based company APS, which supplies the command-and-control system linking the batteries into a single network. The batteries are built around Kongsberg’s PROTECTOR family of weapon stations, including the MCT30 turret, and can carry 35 mm, 30 mm and 12.7 mm guns, interceptor drones and 70 mm guided missiles, which serve as the main weapon for SAN. Deliveries of the first elements began this year, with the whole system due to be completed within two years of the contract signing.
Poland has invested heavily in drone defense since September 2025, when more than a dozen Russian drones crossed into Polish airspace during an attack on Ukraine, prompting NATO jets to shoot several down over Polish territory. The SAN program is meant to give the Polish Armed Forces a mobile layer of guns, missiles and interceptors that can move to protect bases, cities and critical infrastructure against drones and loitering munitions.
Kongsberg has worked in Poland for more than 15 years, during which it has set up a sustainment center for the Naval Strike Missile, the anti-ship missile Poland fields in its coastal defense units, at the WZE military electronics plant, and formed partnerships with a range of Polish defense companies. The new counter-drone factory extends that presence into a second major product line and deepens defense ties between Poland and Norway, which already cooperate closely on coastal missile defense.
Kongsberg says construction on the Pomeranian site will begin in early 2027 once the building contract is signed, putting the factory on track for its first serial deliveries of SAN equipment in the first half of 2028.

Guidance: Ex-Gratia Medical Payments reviews
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:40:27 BST
20:40:27 KST

Ex-Gratia Medical Payments reviews
Guidance for former locally employed staff who were injured in the course of their service.
Documents
Details
Overview
The UK government initiated the Ex-Gratia Medical Payments (EGMP) policy to provide support to former locally-employed staff in Afghanistan who were injured as a result of their employment with the Ministry of Defence (MOD) between 2001 and 2021. The EGMP scheme was closed to new applications in 2021.
The EGMP Review was initiated in June 2020 to enable reviews of payments under the EGMP.
As of 23 July 2026, the EGMP review is closed to new applications. Those who have already applied will also no longer be able to provide further evidence on their applications.
All applications received before the scheme closed will be processed.
No new applications are being accepted.
This publication explains the eligibility criteria for the EGMP Review.
Background
Between 2001 and 2021, local staff in Afghanistan who worked with the UK government played an important part in our joint efforts towards the shared goal of a more secure, stable and prosperous Afghanistan.
Extremely brave people worked alongside our soldiers on patrol, and in some cases suffered profoundly life-changing injuries as a result of enemy action. The government committed to awarding appropriate payments for these people through the EGMP.
In 2020, the MOD initiated a process for reviewing the EGMP cases relating to individuals who wish to have their cases re-assessed. Its intent was to enable those whose condition has deteriorated beyond their original prognosis, or those who have developed a late-onset condition, to receive a fair full and final payment without prejudice.
Eligibility Criteria
To be eligible for the EGMP Review, the applicant must satisfy all of the following criteria:
- The injury must have occurred during MOD employment and have been recorded by the Department at the time;
AND
2. There must be sufficient evidence that the condition has deteriorated beyond what was assessed as the projected recovery at the time, or that a new condition has arisen as a result of the original injury;
- For EGMP Review applications received prior to 23 April 2026, these must have been reported to us within 3 years of formal diagnosis of the deterioration or new condition (as opposed to 3 years of the date of initial award payment for applications submitted on or after 23 April 2026). Consideration will also be given to cases where eligibility to the EGMP was previously considered but a payment was not awarded, where evidence supports this;
- For EGMP Review applications received after 23 April 2026 these must have been reported to us within 3 years of the initial EGMP award unless the condition could clearly not have been known to the individual within that timescale;
AND
3. The deterioration or new condition must be a significant permanent physical or mental impairment or disability, including any serious scarring or disfigurement.
These payments are not intended to provide compensation for those injuries where the individual is expected to make a complete recovery or where they may be left with some permanent or long-lasting impairment of a less serious nature, for example limited in either the degree of pain or loss of faculty.
Making a claim
New claims are no longer being accepted as of the 23 July 2026. All applications received before the scheme closed will be processed.
Prior to the closure of the scheme, claims were required to be submitted before 23 July 2026 using the Ex-Gratia Medical Review Claim Form to DARR-Medical-Casework@mod.gov.uk, together with photocopies of two forms of identification: either a passport or a driving license, and a utility bill showing the claimant’s current address dated within the previous three months.
The panel’s decision will be communicated in writing.
Receiving your payment
A decision on your application to the EGMP Review will be communicated to you electronically from DARR-Medical-Casework@mod.gov.uk.
If a Review payment is awarded to you, this will be on a full and final settlement basis without prejudice. You will be asked to sign your understanding of this before the payment can be made. You will also be asked to provide your bank details. Upon receipt of these, the payment will be made as soon as is practically possible.
Appealing the review decision
In the event you are not satisfied with the outcome of your application to the EGMP Review, you can appeal the decision within 28 days of being sent the outcome letter. You can appeal the review decision by submitting a completed EGMP Review Appeal form to DARR-Medical-Casework@mod.gov.uk. The appeal form will be published before substantive decisions are issued.
Related information
- Afghanistan Locally Employed Staff Ex-Gratia Scheme
- Supporting UK locally employed staff in Afghanistan
MOD collects, holds and uses personal data for the reasons provided in the MOD Privacy Notice and allowed under UK data protection law. To learn more, please see the MOD privacy notice - GOV.UK.

Citadel uses less ammunition than other air defense systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:40:15 UTC
20:40:15 KST

MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Russia’s state-of-the-art Citadel anti-aircraft artillery system uses less ammunition thanks to its fire control system, the state tech corporation Rostec reported.
Citadel is a 30-mm automatic artillery system designed to provide round-the-clock protection for fixed installations against multicopter and fixed-wing drones. Rostec first presented the system in May at the First International Security Forum in the Moscow Region.
"Thanks to its fire control system and shells with remote-detonation fuzes, the Citadel anti-aircraft artillery system has demonstrated significantly lower ammunition consumption per target destroyed than standard anti-aircraft artillery systems. In some cases, consumption is several times lower," a Rostec representative told the Izvestia daily.
The system independently identifies and tracks the target, automatically aims the guns, and determines when to detonate the shells. This ensures not only the destruction of the flying object but also reduces ammunition use to a minimum.
The system detects drones in the visible, infrared, and radar spectrums. Rostec previously reported that the system’s arsenal includes smart shells that can be programmed to detonate at a specific point along their trajectory. Such munitions surround enemy drones in a cloud of shrapnel at the precise moment needed, requiring significantly fewer shells than conventional munitions.
In addition, the system can be easily integrated with other UAV countermeasures as part of a layered air defense system and features a high degree of automation--from target detection to destruction.

“Nurse, Ambassador of Life” program to reach over 800 schools nationwide
TEHRAN – A national program titled “Nurse, Ambassador of Life” will be implemented in more than 800 schools across the country, with the participation of 64 universities of medical sciences, to promote life-saving skills and improve students’ preparedness for emergencies.
The initiative draws on the expertise of medical universities and nursing professionals to bring healthcare knowledge and practical experience into educational settings. By introducing students to basic emergency response skills, the program aims to strengthen social responsibility, raise public awareness and encourage informed assistance in critical situations.
Training students in basic first aid can also help them share what they learn with their families and communities, contributing to broader public preparedness and greater participation in emergency response efforts.
Abbas Ebadi, the deputy health minister for nursing affairs, highlighted the importance of expanding life-saving training during the inauguration ceremony of the program.
The event was held during Nurses Week under the theme of “Nursing Management in Accidents and Disasters.”
Referring to cooperation between the Ministry of Health and the Emergency Medical Services Organization, Ebadi said recent experiences had further underscored the need to equip the public with essential life-saving skills.
Emphasizing the importance of basic cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and first aid training, he said these skills should be accessible to everyone so that people can take essential initial steps to save the lives of injured individuals before emergency responders arrive.
Ebadi noted that greater public awareness and preparedness could help reduce the consequences of accidents and improve the chances of survival for those injured.
He added that expanding first aid education in schools would give students an opportunity to learn basic assistance techniques and understand how to respond appropriately to emergencies.
The deputy health minister also stressed the need for cooperation among relevant organizations to expand such training and establish it as a nationwide initiative, noting that a simple, timely and appropriate action could save a life.
In May 2025, the World Health Organization’s (WHO) director for the Eastern Mediterranean Regional Office (EMRO) said Iran is a leading country in expanding its healthcare system and providing access to universal health coverage.
Lauding the country’s achievements in recent years, Hanan Balkhi said expanding primary health care services, increasing access to health coverage in rural areas, maintaining high vaccination rates, and reducing maternal and newborn mortality, Iran has managed to become a successful role model in the region, the health ministry’s website reported.
In January, President Masoud Pezeshkian called the country’s health system a role model in the region and even the world, thanks to its unique, particularly primary healthcare services.

Rada passes in first reading government bill to simplify VAT administration
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:38:02 EEST
20:38:02 KST

The Verkhovna Rada has passed as a basis in the first reading bill No. 16037-d amending the Tax Code of Ukraine to simplify the administration of value-added tax (VAT), which was drafted to fulfill Ukraine’s obligations to the European Union for receiving macro-financial assistance and to the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
According to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent, during Tuesday’s vote the decision was backed by 264 MPs, with the minimum required being 226 votes, and one vote against.
According to the explanatory note, the document raises the threshold for documentary unscheduled audits of the legality of declared budget refunds and negative VAT balances from UAH 100,000 to UAH 1 million.
In addition, the bill gives individual entrepreneurs registered as VAT payers the right to choose a quarterly reporting period instead of a monthly one, and expands the functionality of the taxpayer’s electronic account, providing for pre-filling of tax reports and invoices automatically based on data from regulatory authorities.
It also simplifies the drawing up of summary tax invoices for supplies to non-VAT payers and receipt of advances from them, improves the mechanism for encouraging voluntary payment of tax liabilities following audits during martial law, and simplifies the carry-forward of negative VAT balances when enterprises are reorganized by transformation.
In addition, the bill contains provisions allowing excise tax payers to temporarily purchase excise stamps without taking anti-forestalling restrictions into account.
Earlier, on October 6, the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Finance, Tax and Customs Policy recommended adopting bill No. 16037-d as a basis.

- The company offers SQ uncrewed boats, intruder detection sonars, ROVs and aerial drones for navies, coast guards, ports and energy operators.
A former Italian Navy mine warfare officer has launched Sentiq Defence, a company based in Bordighera on Italy’s Ligurian coast that will supply navies, coast guards and port and energy operators with uncrewed boats, underwater surveillance sonars, remotely operated submersibles and aerial drones, the company announced on Oct. 13.
Sentiq starts out as an integrator, taking off-the-shelf platforms and sensors developed with international manufacturers, configuring them for each customer’s mission, and delivering them from Italy as complete systems with training and long-term support through a single point of contact. The company says it was set up to deal with a market split among many suppliers, each with its own interfaces, support arrangements and export rules, at a time when ports, energy companies, telecom operators and coast guards all need to watch large stretches of sea with limited people and money.
Its offering covers three domains. On the surface, the SQ family of modular uncrewed surface vessels can be configured for hydrographic survey, environmental monitoring, offshore inspection and persistent surveillance, as well as military tasks such as mine countermeasures and anti-submarine warfare. Under the water, Sentiq offers sonars that detect divers and other intruders, in a fixed version called SQ DDS, a portable SQ PDDS and a long-range SQ UDS, to protect ports, naval bases, coastlines and critical infrastructure, backed by inspection-class remotely operated vehicles. In the air, tactical drones extend the surveillance reach of the surface boats beyond the horizon.
The company was founded by Antonio J. Belfiore, a retired Italian Navy commander who specialized in mine warfare and served 25 years in national and international operational and staff posts. After leaving the service, he worked in business development and sales for defense and subsea technology companies in Denmark and the United Kingdom, set up his own strategy consultancy in 2025 and came up with the idea for Sentiq this year.
“I spent most of my career at sea, in mine warfare, and later training the people who do this job. I learned that technology rarely fails on its own: what fails is integration,” said Antonio J. Belfiore, founder and CEO of Sentiq Defence.
Protection of ports, undersea cables and pipelines has become a priority for European navies and infrastructure operators since the Nord Stream pipelines were blown up in 2022 and several Baltic Sea power and data cables were damaged in the years that followed, incidents that pushed governments to look for cheaper ways to keep watch on the seabed and coastal approaches.
Bordighera sits at the western end of the Ligurian coast, within reach of Italy’s naval and shipbuilding centers in Genoa and La Spezia, where the Italian Navy’s main base is located, and of the French technology hub at Sophia Antipolis and the French Navy’s base at Toulon. Sentiq’s growth plan has three steps: widening its partnerships with international technology suppliers, building an assembly, integration and test center in western Liguria, and developing training and long-term support in Italy for Italian and foreign customers.
Sentiq will make its first major public appearance at the EURONAVAL naval exhibition at Paris Nord Villepinte, which runs from Nov. 3 to 6.

Estonia's Markus Kajak wins Porsche Central Europe title
Estonian race-car driver Markus Kajak has won the Porsche Central European Circuit Series championship after finishing second in both sprint races in Hungary.
Kajak was disqualified from qualifying for a technical breach, forcing him to start from the back of the grid at the Hungaroring. He recovered to take second in both races and win the title.
Kajak, 22, is a former karting world cup winner.
The disqualification came after he had won the qualifying sessions. "Technical inspection found that one side of our car was one centimeter lower than permitted," he explained.
That penalty meant he had to start the sprint races from the back of the grid — 12th and 10th respectively. In the races themselves, the Estonian showed strong pace and finished second in both, which was enough to overtake the driver who had led the standings and take the title.
"I made strong enough first laps in both races and didn't lose much time to the leaders," Kajak said. "That allowed me to finish both sprints second. In fact, second place in the first race already secured the title, and I also won the rookie standings overall and we took first place in the team standings. So I can be very happy with the season."
Kajak also won the 100-mile endurance race at the weekend and helped the Dream 2 Drive team to the team title.
The results close out his season successfully, but preparations for next year are already underway. "There's no final clarity for next season yet, as I don't know whether I'll continue in karting," he said. "I'll certainly continue racing GT cars, but right now I don't know where, how or in which series."
The Porsche Sprint Challenge Central Europe is an officially licensed one-make series run by Lechner Racing. All drivers compete in identical 510-horsepower Porsche 911 GT3 Cup cars with no electronic aids, across six Central European countries and two 25-minute sprint races plus a 60-minute endurance race per weekend.

Drone boats used by U.S. Navy get AI-powered vision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:33:19 UTC
20:33:19 KST

- MARTAC selected SEA.AI’s AI-powered electro-optical and thermal camera system for its unmanned surface vessels, including the Devil Ray T38 used by the U.S. Navy.
- The system classifies nearby vessels and objects in real time on board, without a human reviewing the video feed.
MARTAC, the Florida maker of high-speed unmanned surface vessels used by the U.S. Navy, has selected SEA.AI’s maritime machine vision system for its drone boat fleet, adding cameras that spot and classify other vessels on their own without a human watching a video feed.
SEA.AI announced the integration on Oct. 13, saying MARTAC has made its system part of the sensor architecture for its vessels across surveillance, security and patrol missions. The MARTAC range covers the MANTAS T12 and a family of larger boats that includes the Devil Ray T18, Muskie M18, Devil Ray T24 and Devil Ray T38.
SEA.AI’s system combines electro-optical and thermal cameras with artificial intelligence that runs at the sensor itself, identifying what each contact is, which way it is heading and how close it is, and passing that on as ready-to-use information. On a crewless boat operating far beyond sight of its operators, that lets the vessel understand what is around it without someone back on shore studying hours of footage. The camera picture also fills gaps left by the other sensors such boats carry: radar shows where something is but not what it is, and the Automatic Identification System, the transponder signal ships use to broadcast their identity, can be switched off or spoofed by vessels that want to stay hidden, including fast attack craft that blend into normal traffic.
“We built SEA.AI in 2018 around a conviction that the camera alone was never going to be enough at sea. The intelligence had to be in the system, not in a person watching a screen somewhere. That requirement has only become more urgent as autonomous platforms move from trials into operational deployment,” said Marcus Warrelmann, CEO of SEA.AI.
The need for that kind of independent sensing grows with the distances MARTAC’s boats now cover. In May, a Devil Ray T38 owned by the U.S. Navy’s Naval Air Warfare Center Weapons Division completed an eight-day, fully autonomous mission off the coast of California, running for 192 hours without crew or escort at more than 400 nautical miles (about 740 km) from shore, in seas as rough as Sea State 5, while steering around real vessels it encountered along the way.
“Our platforms are built to carry whatever sensors the mission requires, and we evaluate every integration on one basis: does it make the vessel more operationally capable? SEA.AI’s machine vision, that classifies contacts autonomously and in real time, is a direct solution for closing a real gap. That is why it is on our platforms,” said Jim Harvey, chief technology officer of MARTAC.
The T38 is MARTAC’s flagship, a 38-foot (11.6-meter) carbon-fiber catamaran that can exceed 50 knots (93 km/h) and carry sensors or weapons. The U.S. Navy’s Task Force 59, the 5th Fleet unit that experiments with unmanned systems in the Middle East, brought the T38 into the Arabian Gulf in 2023 and later used it to fire Lethal Miniature Aerial Missile System munitions at targets during exercises, with a human operator ashore making the engagement decisions. MARTAC has also added capacity to build up to 100 Devil Ray vessels a year.
“Operators have sensors, platforms, and more data than their teams can process. What we add to a MARTAC vessel is not another feed to monitor, it is a system that watches, understands, and reports. This partnership with MARTAC puts that capability where it matters: on proven platforms, in real missions,” said Diogo Arreda, managing director of SEA.AI Americas.
SEA.AI, founded in 2018 and based in Austria, began by building camera systems that help commercial ships and yachts avoid collisions with small or floating objects at sea, before expanding into defense and security work, and MARTAC is now offering its vessels with the SEA.AI system to military and government customers.

Pope Leo XIV arrives at Rome's Gemelli hospital for lung operation, Vatican says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:32:36 UTC
20:32:36 KST

The pope announced the surgery on Sunday, the first time a pontiff has made a personal medical announcement of this kind.
Pope Leo XIV arrived at Rome hospital on Tuesday for an operation to remove a nodule on his lung which the Vatican said would be carried out in the afternoon.
The 71-year-old waved to well-wishers gathered outside the Vatican from the window of the car in which he was driven to the Gemelli hospital, where pontiffs are traditionally treated.
The pope announced the surgery on Sunday, the first time a pontiff has made a personal medical announcement of this kind.
The Vatican press office has said doctors expect the pope's recovery to take around a week. That would make it possible for him to leave for his visit to Latin America as planned on 6 November.
The 11-day trip will take him to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, a country close to the pope's heart as he worked there as a missionary for two decades and took on Peruvian citizenship.
What is a pulmonary nodule?
A pulmonary nodule is a small growth of tissue in the lung. Most are benign, meaning they are non-cancerous. But a small percentage can be an early stage of lung cancer.
Most small nodules cause no symptoms and are only discovered during checks for other health issues.
Larger nodules can cause shortness of breath, chest pain and persistent coughing, sometimes with blood.
The operation is normally carried out under general anaesthetic with the patient breathing through a tube.
Where is the operation taking place?
The operation will take place at Rome's Gemelli hospital, where popes are usually treated.
Pope Leo XIV's predecessor Francis spent weeks there for treatment before his death last year.
John Paul II, head of the Church from 1978 until his death in 2005, was treated nine times at Gemelli, Rome's largest hospital, and spent a total of 153 days there.
He quipped that the hospital was like "Vatican number three."
The Vatican ultimately created a top-floor apartment at the hospital site, accessed by a long corridor guarded by Italian and Vatican police.
Besides the pope's room, the suite reportedly includes a meeting room for medical staff, a kitchen, bathroom and rest areas.
There is also a small chapel.

Russell Brand has attended court for the second day of his rape and sexual assault trial and a jury has been selected in the case.
The 51-year-old comedian faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009. Brand denies all the charges.
Jury selection at Southwark crown court began on Monday morning with a warning from the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, to ignore past reporting about Brand and allegations of sexual misconduct.
On Tuesday, eight men and four women were sworn in for the trial, which is expected to last six weeks. The jurors were sent away until Wednesday morning when the prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC is expected to open the case. One reserve juror was selected to sit through the prosecution opening.
The judge told the jurors not to discuss the case or carry out any research.
“Heaven knows what’s out there,” Bennathan said on Tuesday. “If you want to, you could go and have a look – but only once you have returned your verdicts.”

Brand became a British television personality in the 2000s, presenting shows and events such as the 2007 Brit awards, Comic Relief and the MTV video music awards. He also hosted his own show on BBC Radio 2.
He made the move into Hollywood films with roles in the comedy Get Him to the Greek and the 2012 musical comedy Rock of Ages. He was married to the American pop singer Katy Perry from 2010 to 2012.

Bullfrog drone-killing gun gets radar eyes from Echodyne
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:29:00 UTC
20:29:00 KST

- Echodyne and Allen Control Systems signed a strategic collaboration agreement pairing EchoShield radar with the Bullfrog autonomous counter-drone weapon station.
- The companies have integrated the systems and will continue testing at U.S. Department of War demonstrations, with a focus on maritime missions.
Radar maker Echodyne and Allen Control Systems have signed a strategic collaboration agreement to pair Echodyne’s EchoShield counter-drone radar with ACS’s Bullfrog autonomous weapon station, combining long-range radar tracking with an AI-guided gun that fires standard ammunition at drones on land and at sea.
The companies announced the agreement on Oct. 13, saying they have already integrated EchoShield with Bullfrog and will keep testing the combined system, including at U.S. Department of War demonstration events designed to evaluate it under realistic operating conditions. The deal covers both companies’ hardware and software road maps and follows recent awards to each from Joint Interagency Task Force 401, the Pentagon office that leads counter-drone efforts, for its Domestic Shield effort and its C-UAS Marketplace.
Bullfrog uses computer vision, autonomous controls and precision robotics to turn existing weapons, such as the M240 machine gun, into counter-drone systems that detect, track, identify and engage drones on their own. Adding EchoShield’s radar data gives the gun station a continuous picture of where drones are in the surrounding airspace, letting it turn its cameras and barrel toward a target earlier, keep tracking drones as they maneuver and calculate a firing solution faster. The radar measures the precise position and speed of a wide range of drone types and flight profiles, and its open interfaces send that data both to Bullfrog and to wider command-and-control networks.
“Counter-UAS effectiveness begins with data quality,” said Eben Frankenberg, CEO of Echodyne. “Bullfrog brings together advanced robotics, AI, and widely available weapons to solve one of the most urgent challenges facing defense forces today. Combining ACS’s autonomous weapon station with the precision of EchoShield radar creates a highly capable and economically scalable solution for the United States and allied customers operating across land and maritime domains.”
EchoShield is built on Echodyne’s patented MESA architecture, which delivers the performance of an electronically scanned array radar, the kind that steers its beam without moving parts, in a small, light and low-cost unit made with commercial materials and supply chains. The companies say pairing that radar with standard-issue guns and ammunition lets forces shoot down drones without the high cost per shot and limited supply of missile interceptors.
“Bullfrog was designed to transform existing weapons into precise, autonomous defense systems and to fuse the best available data into every engagement,” said Mike Wior, co-founder and CEO of ACS. “Echodyne’s commercial radar technology provides the accurate, high-fidelity track data needed to identify threats earlier, maintain custody, and deliver effective kinetic outcomes. Our partnership also enables on-the-move defense, helping protect warfighters against drone threats while they maneuver. Together, we are creating a scalable solution that gives warfighters greater awareness, more decision time, and an affordable way to defeat drones at operational scale.”
The agreement puts particular weight on maritime missions, since Bullfrog is compact enough to mount on crewed and uncrewed vessels and EchoShield is already being fitted to uncrewed surface vessels for maritime surveillance and counter-drone work, where small size, low power draw and the ability to track targets while moving matter most. Together, the two systems give a vessel the ability to detect and track aerial and surface contacts, point the weapon station at them and let operators respond quickly, and the companies plan to offer the combination for fixed sites, vehicles on the move, expeditionary forces and ships.
Bullfrog is already in service with U.S. forces, and ACS holds contracts with the U.S. Army, U.S. Marine Corps and U.S. Special Operations Command. In July, the U.S. Marine Corps selected Bullfrog for its Light Marine Air Defense Integrated System under a prototype contract worth about $6.2 million, and the company has also signed deals to supply Bullfrog to South Korea and the United Arab Emirates. ACS is headquartered in Austin, Texas, where it builds the system, and Echodyne is based in the Seattle area.

Spanish royals begin sensitive diplomatic visit to tense Ceuta
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:27:41 UTC
20:27:41 KST

Breadcrumb
Spanish royals begin sensitive diplomatic visit to tense Ceuta
Cheering crowds waving Spanish flags lined the streets of Ceuta on Tuesday as King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia began a diplomatically sensitive visit to the North African city, following July's mass migrant influx from neighbouring Morocco.
Their trip will mark the first royal visit since 2007, when a diplomatic crisis erupted with neighbouring Morocco, which claims sovereignty over Ceuta and Spain's other North African territory of Melilla.
More than 70,000 migrants streamed into the small city of around 80,000 inhabitants in an unprecedented surge on 30-31 July. Scores died.
Most returned to Morocco in the following hours but thousands have remained for weeks in often dire conditions, sleeping rough in the streets or on the beach.
The crisis has angered locals and eroded Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's standing before a 29 November general election in which migration will feature prominently.
Felipe and Letizia greeted well-wishers lining the streets of Ceuta, stopping to shake hands and exchange a few words with members of the crowd as they made their way to city hall to meet local authorities.
People held up their phones to take pictures of the royal couple, while others waved Spanish flags and cheered as they passed, according to an AFP reporter at the scene.
Some wore T-shirts bearing the slogan "Ceuta is not for sale. Ceuta must be defended".
International law
Toni Jimenez, 56, a nursing assistant who had waited outside city hall since 9:00 am wearing a T-shirt bearing the royal couple's picture, said she hoped the visit would send a clear message to neighbouring Morocco that Ceuta and Melilla were Spanish.
"We've been waiting a long time for this visit," she said, adding that the migrant influx in July had left residents fearing for the future of the Spanish territory.
Others said the king should have visited sooner.
"The king should have come on the first or second day. And he should have come dressed as captain general of the armed forces, which is what he is," said Susana Roman, a 57-year-old jurist who is part of the "Let's Save Ceuta" platform.
The government insists it must respect international law by assessing whether the migrants are entitled to asylum, while hundreds of unaccompanied children cannot be summarily deported.
The authorities have set up thousands of places in temporary shelters and cleared the main camps on the beaches but some people continue to live on the surrounding hills and the streets.
Ana Maria Diaz, a 69-year-old pensioner, said the king should have come earlier to see the makeshift migrant encampments—and should visit the outlying areas of Ceuta where they concentrate.
"You don't see it here but if you go to the outlying neighbourhoods...it's terrible," Diaz, who was holding a Spanish flag, told AFP.
Diplomatic risks
The royals will visit a cemetery where they will pay tribute to the migrants who died—most by drowning as they tried to swim around a border barrier.
Felipe is also due to make a speech during a meeting with members of Ceuta's civil society before the monarchs travel to Melilla on Wednesday.
The visit comes at a particularly sensitive time for Spain's historically delicate relations with Morocco, as rumours swirl over the potential role Rabat may have played in the July rush.
The Spanish right has accused Morocco of orchestrating it for political motives, which Rabat and Sanchez have denied.
Moroccan King Mohammed VI broke his silence on Friday, condemning "the irresponsible statements made by certain political and media circles and their blatant instrumentalisation of the situation", in apparent reference to Spanish criticism.
Ceuta resident Mohamed Hamadi, 41, said he was unconcerned about the potential diplomatic fallout and hoped to see the royals.
"What business does the king of Morocco have here, him and his opinion, if Ceuta has always been Spanish?" Hamadi told AFP.
