James Webb reveals a massive cosmic structure that challenges our understanding of the Universe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:27:24 UTC
20:27:24 KST

James Webb reveals a massive cosmic structure that challenges our understanding of the Universe
Webb has revealed a massive, dark matter-packed galaxy cluster that formed surprisingly early, challenging scientists’ understanding of how the universe evolved.
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- Caltech IPAC
- Summary:
- NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has revealed an ancient galaxy cluster with an unexpectedly dense concentration of dark matter, challenging theories about how the universe developed. The discovery also uncovered a surprising connection between scattered starlight and invisible dark matter that could transform how astronomers study the early cosmos.
- Share:
A massive galaxy cluster dating back to an era when such enormous structures were only beginning to take shape is challenging scientists' understanding of how the universe evolved. New observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) reveal that the cluster contains an unusually dense concentration of matter, suggesting that some cosmic structures may have developed much faster than current models predict.
The galaxy cluster, known as XLSSC 122, has become the focus of three recent studies led by researchers at IPAC, Caltech's science and data center for astrophysics and planetary science. Their findings establish XLSSC 122 as the most distant galaxy cluster known to exhibit strong gravitational lensing, a phenomenon that allows astronomers to measure the mass of otherwise invisible matter. The research was presented at a press conference on June 17, 2026, during the 248th meeting of the American Astronomical Society.
Located approximately 10.4 billion light-years from Earth, XLSSC 122 stood out to astronomers because of its surprising maturity. Although it existed during a period when galaxy clusters were still assembling, it already displayed the size and organized structure typically associated with clusters in the modern universe.
Webb has now uncovered another remarkable feature. XLSSC 122 happens to lie directly in front of one or more galaxies that are even farther away. The cluster's powerful gravity bends and distorts the light traveling from those background galaxies, creating a rare effect called strong gravitational lensing. This fortunate alignment has given scientists an exceptionally precise way to measure how mass is distributed throughout the cluster.
"When we got those first images back from JWST, we said, 'wow, look at this, there's strong lensing coming from this cluster!'" said Kyle Finner, a staff scientist at IPAC and lead author of the first paper examining the cluster. "XLSSC 122 has now set the record for the most distant galaxy cluster displaying strong lensing, which is a valuable tool for astronomers."
An Ancient Galaxy Cluster Challenges Cosmic Predictions
The newly detected gravitational lensing has allowed researchers to examine the distribution of mass in an ancient galaxy cluster in greater detail than ever before. XLSSC 122 dates to a period known as "cosmic noon," roughly 10 billion years ago, when the universe was experiencing its most intense era of star formation.
During this time, galaxies were producing stars at rates up to 100 times higher than those observed in the present-day universe. Galaxy clusters were also becoming increasingly common as smaller systems gradually combined into larger structures.
Yet XLSSC 122 appears to have developed in an unexpected way. The new measurements show that a remarkably large amount of its mass is packed into its central region. According to standard cosmological models, the growth of massive structures should have been more gradual, making such a concentrated cluster particularly surprising at this early stage of cosmic history.
"XLSSC 122 is one of the first clusters we know of that formed in the universe, and it has a mass concentration that doesn't agree with our cosmological model predictions," said Finner.
To investigate the mystery further, Finner and his collaborators conducted two additional JWST studies, first authored by Zachary Scofield and Hyungjin Joo at Yonsei University. Together, the three papers provide a much more complete picture of this unusual cluster and offer new insights into galaxy cluster formation during cosmic noon.
James Webb Reveals Hidden Dark Matter
Astronomers originally identified XLSSC 122 in 2014 through an X-ray survey carried out by the European Space Agency's XMM-Newton spacecraft. Later observations with the Hubble Space Telescope helped establish its distance of approximately 10.4 billion light-years and confirmed that the cluster appeared unusually developed for its age.
However, Hubble did not reveal clear evidence of strong gravitational lensing. That changed when JWST captured distinctive curved arcs of light surrounding the cluster's center, providing the first definitive signs of this phenomenon in XLSSC 122.
"Before JWST, we couldn't do this level of science in the early, distant universe," said Finner.
The gravitational distortions are caused primarily by something astronomers cannot directly observe: dark matter.
Although XLSSC 122 contains visible stars and glowing gas, these familiar forms of matter account for only a small fraction of the gravitational lensing effect. Most of the distortion comes from dark matter, an invisible substance that has not been directly detected through light but whose gravitational influence is supported by extensive astronomical evidence.
Scientists estimate that dark matter is approximately five times more abundant than ordinary matter, which makes up stars, planets, and everything around us. Its gravity helps hold galaxies together and shapes the universe's enormous network of galaxy groups, clusters, and filaments.
Because dark matter plays such an important role in cosmic structure, determining how it was distributed billions of years ago offers a powerful way to test theories describing the universe's development since the Big Bang approximately 13.8 billion years ago.
"Strong lensing is a way to measure the dark matter without actually seeing the dark matter," said Finner. "It gives us a sensitive probe of our cosmological models."
A Wider View Reveals a Galaxy Cluster Merger
In their second paper, the researchers investigated XLSSC 122 using another form of gravitational lensing known as weak lensing.
Strong gravitational lensing produces obvious distortions, including the striking arcs captured by JWST. Weak lensing, by comparison, causes much smaller changes in the apparent shapes of distant galaxies. These subtle effects are difficult to identify individually, so astronomers rely on statistical methods to detect them.
The two techniques provide complementary information. Strong lensing is especially useful for measuring the mass concentrated near a cluster's center, while weak lensing can reveal how matter is distributed across its outer regions.
"Weak gravitational lensing can constrain mass much further out, so you can get a better picture of the surrounding cluster area," said Finner.
By combining these measurements with X-ray and radio observations from other telescopes, the scientists determined that XLSSC 122 is still undergoing a merger. Its galaxies are continuing to come together as the larger cluster takes shape.
The broader analysis also reinforced the earlier finding that an unusually large amount of mass is concentrated near the cluster's center.
Ancient Starlight Offers New Clues to Dark Matter
The team's third and most recent paper revealed another important feature of XLSSC 122: faint light produced by stars that are no longer bound to individual galaxies.
Known as intracluster light, this diffuse glow comes from stars scattered into the spaces between galaxies. Webb's observations represent the earliest known detection of intracluster light, providing another way to examine the development of galaxy clusters in the distant universe.
The widespread distribution of this light supports the conclusion that XLSSC 122 is undergoing a merger. As galaxies interact and collide, some stars are pulled away from their original galaxies and spread throughout the cluster. In XLSSC 122, many of these displaced stars appear not to have settled into its dense central region.
The researchers also uncovered an intriguing connection between these wandering stars and dark matter.
Near the cluster's center, the shape of the intracluster light closely matches the distribution of dark matter inferred from strong gravitational lensing. This suggests that the faint glow of stars between galaxies could potentially serve as a visible indicator of where invisible dark matter is concentrated.
If astronomers observe the same relationship in other clusters, particularly those from the early universe, intracluster light could become a valuable new tool for mapping dark matter across cosmic history.
"In this cluster, the intracluster light essentially traces the dark matter," said Finner. "That light tells us that the cluster is in a merging state."
Could More Ancient Galaxy Clusters Challenge Cosmology?
The next goal for Finner and his colleagues is to identify and investigate dozens of additional galaxy clusters from similarly early periods in the universe's history.
Finding these distant objects requires a different approach from studying them in detail. Although JWST is exceptionally powerful, its relatively narrow field of view makes it better suited to examining selected targets than searching enormous areas of the sky.
Instead, astronomers must first identify promising candidates through wide-area X-ray and radio surveys, similar to the observations that originally revealed XLSSC 122.
One promising technique relies on the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect, which occurs when energetic particles inside galaxy clusters scatter radiation from the cosmic microwave background, the faint afterglow of the Big Bang.
This interaction can create distinctive regions that appear as "holes" in observations of the cosmic microwave background. By searching for these signatures, astronomers can locate galaxy clusters that might otherwise be difficult to detect.
Finding more objects like XLSSC 122 could have major implications for cosmology. If other ancient clusters also contain unexpectedly concentrated dark matter and display unusually advanced development, scientists may need to revise some of their basic assumptions about how quickly large cosmic structures formed.
For now, XLSSC 122 provides an important test of existing models, but a larger sample will be necessary to determine whether its unusual properties are rare or part of a broader pattern in the early universe.
"It's still early in the JWST era," said Finner, "and if we can start to get data on tens or hundreds of these types of objects at this stage in the universe, then we can really start putting our cosmological models to the test."

Pope Leo has been admitted to hospital in Rome for an operation to remove a small growth from his lung, a discovery a top Vatican cardinal said had come “like a bolt out of the blue”.
In a rare moment of Vatican transparency, Leo, 71, said during his angelus prayer on Sunday that doctors had found a small nodule on his lung during a check-up, adding that it was “well-contained” and detected early.
“The doctors believe it would be right to intervene and so, following their advice, I have decided to have the operation to remove it,” he said to the crowds gathered in St Peter’s Square.
Leo, who in May last year became the first US-born leader of the Roman Catholic church, is being treated in Rome’s Gemelli hospital, where a large crowd greeted the pontiff.
The Vatican has not disclosed the timing of the operation, although it could take place on Tuesday afternoon, according to Italian media reports. All of his appointments have been cancelled until 20 October.
Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said he had seen Leo on Monday night. “We spoke with great serenity,” Parolin told Rai News. “He is truly a great example. The announcement came like a bolt out of the blue, nobody expected it. Thank God it was detected immediately, so the operation could take place immediately. Normally, when these things are caught in time, they can be resolved.”
The operation is deemed low risk and will determine whether the nodule is malignant.
Leo will stay in the 10-floor private-patient wing but not in the papal suite, which is being renovated.
The Chicago-born pope, who enjoys sports, especially playing tennis, is generally believed to be in good health. He often makes use of the papal retreat in Castel Gandolfo, close to Rome.
Leo travelled to France on a papal visit in September and is scheduled to go to South America in November for a 12-day trip covering 10 cities.
The weekly papal audience on Wednesday will be led by Luis Antonio Tagle, a cardinal from the Philippines who last week was elected dean of the college of cardinals – the authority that presides over papal conclaves.
The Gemelli, located in the north-west of the Italian capital, is renowned for treating reigning popes. Pope John Paul II stayed there so many times that the Vatican worked with the hospital to establish the high security papal suite.
Leo’s predecessor, Francis, spent more than five weeks in the hospital, being treated for bronchitis which developed into bilateral pneumonia. He died at home in Casa Santa Marta in Vatican City on 21 April 2025, just under a month after being discharged.

Simplifying VAT administration — the Verkhovna Rada adopted the draft law in the first reading
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:25:11 EEST
20:25:11 KST

Simplifying VAT administration — the Verkhovna Rada adopted the draft law in the first reading
Kyiv • UNN
The Verkhovna Rada supported the draft law on simplifying VAT administration. The audit threshold is proposed to be raised to UAH 1 million, while individual entrepreneurs would be allowed to choose the reporting period.
The Verkhovna Rada adopted as a basis a bill that simplifies VAT administration. The document provides for raising the threshold for unscheduled tax audits from UAH 100,000 to UAH 1 million, and also allows individual entrepreneurs who are VAT payers to independently choose their reporting period. UNN reports this, citing a parliamentary session.
Details
Draft Law No. 16037-d "On Amendments to the Tax Code of Ukraine Regarding the Simplification of Value Added Tax Administration" was adopted as a basis by 264 lawmakers.
Under the draft law, it is proposed to increase the threshold amount constituting grounds for conducting a documentary unscheduled audit concerning a VAT payer's declaration.
Currently, a documentary unscheduled audit is conducted when at least one of the following grounds exists, in particular: the taxpayer has submitted a declaration claiming a value-added tax refund from the budget and/or reporting a negative value for value-added tax exceeding UAH 100,000.
The bill proposes raising this amount to UAH 1 million.
It is also proposed to allow individual entrepreneurs registered as VAT payers to independently choose their reporting period: a month or a quarter.
For individual entrepreneurs wishing to choose a quarterly reporting (tax) period who submit the relevant application within 15 calendar days of registering as a taxpayer, the first reporting (tax) period is the period that begins on the date of such registration and ends on the last day of the first full calendar quarter.
The reporting (tax) period is changed by submitting an application to choose a reporting (tax) period.
Reminder
Since August 14, a new stage of bank monitoring of transactions involving newly established and long-inactive individual entrepreneurs and legal entities has come into effect in Ukraine. The enhanced monitoring will apply to new and "dormant" individual entrepreneurs.

New Turkish laser gun shoots down drone in live-fire test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:24:06 UTC
20:24:06 KST

- MKE’s new 20-kilowatt fiber laser for the TOLGA air defense system destroyed a drone at 760 meters during Ateş Serbest-2026 at Polatlı.
- The laser can dazzle drone sensors at up to 4,500 meters and destroy targets at ranges of 100 to 1,500 meters.
Turkish state defense company MKE has destroyed a drone at a distance of 760 meters (about 2,500 feet) with a new 20-kilowatt fiber laser weapon developed for its TOLGA close-in air defense system, scoring a direct hit during the Ateş Serbest-2026 live-fire event at Polatlı, west of Ankara.
MKE announced the result on X on Oct. 13 and released a video showing the laser turret engaging and destroying the target, with the weapon’s effects broken down by distance.
The laser can dazzle a drone’s cameras and sensors at 2,500 to 4,500 meters (1.6 to 2.8 miles), blind them completely at 1,500 to 2,500 meters (0.9 to 1.6 miles), and physically destroy a target at 100 to 1,500 meters (330 feet to 0.9 miles), placing the 760-meter shot at Polatlı well inside its destruction range. The turret carries the laser alongside a separate electro-optical sensor unit that finds and tracks targets before the beam is fired.
The laser is the newest addition to TOLGA, MKE’s short-range air defense system, and is designed to counter close-range threats in the air, on land and at sea. MKE said the Polatlı firing demonstrated its capability in high-impact defense technologies and that the company will keep building on more than a century of experience to develop future weapons for Türkiye.
A laser weapon heats a spot on a target with a focused beam until it burns through critical parts such as motors, wiring or fuel tanks, and each shot costs only the electricity needed to fire it. That makes lasers well suited to dealing with large numbers of cheap drones that would otherwise have to be shot down with far more expensive missiles or guns.
MKE’s system joins several laser weapons developed in Türkiye in recent years, including ASELSAN’s GÖKBERK, which has been shown on BMC’s AMAZON armored vehicle, and Roketsan’s ALKA directed-energy system. Türkiye is fielding these and other counter-drone systems as part of Steel Dome, a layered air defense network that combines lasers, guns, jammers and missiles to protect troops, bases and cities from drones and missiles.
Ateş Serbest is an annual live-fire demonstration held at the Polatlı training area, where Turkish defense companies show new weapons and ammunition to military and government officials, and this year’s event gave MKE’s 20-kilowatt laser its first public shoot-down of a drone target.

Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia visit Ceuta
October 13, 2026

The trip marks the first royal visit to Ceuta, and Spain's other exclave in the area Melilla, since Felipe's father Juan Carlos I toured the cities in 2007.
Excited crowds gathered to welcome the royals, with some noting that it felt like national authorities were finally paying attention to their plight.
What happened in Ceuta?
In late July, some 70,000 refugees in Morocco rushed the border fence with Spain. More than 140 people were killed in the scuffle.
The incident threw the city of some 84,000 residents into the international spotlight, with calls from right-wing governments within the European Union to suspend the Schengen free movement agreement with Spain.
However, it soon became clear that most of the refugees were quickly turned back to Morocco, and because of Ceuta's remote location, none moved on to mainland Europe except a group of at-risk children.
At the same time, locals complained that national officials did little to help with at least 10,000 migrants still in the city, and the alleged human traffickers trying to capitalize on the situation.
Meanwhile, the migrants who have been unable to return to Morocco have accused Spanish police of brutality and other abuses.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has accused organized groups stemming from Russia and Israel for spreading misinformation regarding alleged changes in Spain's immigration rules.
The incident also exposed diplomatic tensions between Spain and Morocco. Morocco does not recognize Madrid's claim to Ceuta, which has been under Spanish control for centuries. It remains to be seen how Rabat will react to Felipe's trip.

Reported by
The United Kingdom has imposed sanctions on Dutch businessman Alexander Tattersall and his Turkish company, Redwing Metal, following a joint investigation by The Kyiv Independent, OCCRP and IrpiMedia that exposed shipments of European industrial equipment to Russian factories supplying missile and fighter jet manufacturers.
Tattersall and Redwing Metal were among 38 individuals, companies and vessels targeted by the British government on October 8 as part of a broader effort to disrupt Russia’s military supply chains, oil revenues and financial networks.
The measures freeze assets under British jurisdiction and prohibit British individuals and businesses from conducting transactions with the designated parties.
The sanctions follow a June investigation by OCCRP, The Kyiv Independent and Italy’s IrpiMedia, which revealed that Redwing Metal had shipped more than $5 million worth of European-made industrial machinery to two Russian metallurgical plants in 2023 and 2024, despite EU export restrictions.
The equipment included computer-controlled lathes, metal heat-treatment furnaces, hydraulic presses and other machinery manufactured in Italy, Germany, Spain and the Czech Republic.
The recipients, Aluminum Metallurg Rus (AMR) and Stupino Metallurgical Company (SMK), produce specialized metal alloys used by Russia’s defense industry.
Financial records examined by journalists showed that the two plants had supplied more than 40 Russian defense manufacturers since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, including companies producing cruise missiles, fighter jets, tanks and artillery.
Both plants are controlled by Russian businessman Nikolay Timokhin, the son-in-law of Igor Zavyalov, a senior executive at Russia’s state-owned defense conglomerate Rostec.
The investigation also found that Redwing Metal had shipped another $1.3 million worth of European-made shipbuilding equipment to a company in Timokhin’s business group. The equipment was intended for two vessels associated with Russian naval programs.
According to corporate records, Tattersall, a Dutch national residing in Switzerland, owns 40 percent of Redwing Metal, which was established in Turkey shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
When contacted before the investigation was published, Tattersall acknowledged his ownership stake but described himself as a part-time consultant with limited knowledge of the company’s operations. He denied knowing of any involvement in schemes to ship sanctioned goods to Russia.
The European Union sanctioned AMR in July, but Tattersall, Redwing Metal and the other Russian companies identified in the investigation remain outside the bloc’s sanctions list.
Roman Steblivskyi, director of policy and advocacy at Ukraine’s Economic Security Council, told The Kyiv Independent that the British designation would likely disrupt Redwing Metal’s supply chain and discourage European banks and companies from doing business with it.
He said the sanctions could also affect the company’s relationships with Turkish partners.

Pope Leo XIV arrived at Rome's Gemelli hospital Tuesday to undergo surgery to remove a small nodule from his lung, a procedure expected to help doctors determine whether the growth is cancerous and whether further treatment is needed. The 71-year-old pontiff walked into the hospital and waved to dozens of well-wishers gathered outside its main entrance.
Earlier, Leo waved to reporters from the back seat of his SUV as he left Vatican City. The Vatican said he is expected to remain hospitalized for at least a week and has canceled his audiences through October 20. It has not specified the surgical technique doctors will use.
The pope disclosed the nodule during his Sunday noon prayer, saying doctors had discovered a small, localized growth during routine medical checks and recommended its removal. The operation marks the first publicly announced major health concern of his 17-month papacy, and Leo has been unusually transparent about his condition.
Dr. Lorenzo Spaggiari, director of thoracic surgery at the European Institute of Oncology in Milan, said the outlook could be favorable if the lesion is indeed small and confined to one area. Spaggiari, who is not involved in the pope's care, said doctors may perform a biopsy and remove part of the affected lung during the same procedure.
Both procedures can be performed using minimally invasive robotic technology available at Gemelli, he explained. The technique involves small incisions through which surgeons operate robotic instruments. Spaggiari said the approach could allow doctors to conduct the biopsy and surgery under the same anesthetic, although the Vatican has not disclosed its medical team's plans.
If tests reveal cancer, doctors would also examine nearby lymph nodes to determine whether the disease has spread. When a tumor is detected early and completely removed, additional treatment may not be necessary, Spaggiari said. Lung nodules are not necessarily cancerous and can be either benign or malignant.
Cardinal Tsutomu Kikuchi, the archbishop of Tokyo, who met Leo on Monday, said the pope felt well and had decided to undergo surgery promptly to avoid disrupting his planned November trip to Latin America. Kikuchi said Leo had given no indication that the procedure was an emergency.
The pope is scheduled to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17. The ambitious itinerary covers more than 31,000 kilometers and includes approximately a dozen flights, two helicopter journeys and significant changes in altitude.
Spaggiari said his institute generally advises patients against flying for three weeks after lung surgery, potentially leaving Leo only a narrow recovery window before departure.
The pontiff will not stay in Gemelli's traditional papal apartment because the rooms, which include a private chapel, are undergoing renovations. Instead, he will occupy a nearby hospital room.
The Vatican has not announced any changes to Leo's travel schedule. The operation and subsequent laboratory findings will determine whether additional treatment is necessary and how quickly he can return to his duties.

Zelensky prolonging fighting to avoid answering for corruption – Polish MEP

Zajaczkowska-Hernik’s remarks came after Zelensky demanded a 60-day “total truce” to prepare for a presidential election, which he has repeatedly postponed since his term expired in spring 2024, citing martial law. Moscow dismissed the request as a pretext to buy time to rearm Ukrainian forces and prolong the conflict.
“Vladimir Zelensky’s term in office expired long ago, yet by dragging out the war, he manages to evade accountability, specifically for corruption,” Zajaczkowska-Hernik told Poland’s Zet Radio on Monday.
According to Zajaczkowska-Hernik, the Ukrainian leader had many opportunities to make peace but “rejected [them] every time precisely to avoid facing the consequences, since he knew that [peace] would necessitate holding elections, which Vladimir Zelensky might lose.”
Zelensky’s popularity at home is “not so great,” the MEP argued, attributing it not only to the prolonged fighting but also to “massive corruption” within his inner circle. “The Ukrainians see it,” Zajaczkowska-Hernik said.
Ukraine has been rocked by a series of high-profile corruption scandals since last year, with the largest centering on a $100 million kickback scheme at state nuclear operator Energoatom reportedly led by Timur Mindich, a former business partner of Zelensky. Zelensky hit back by telling ABC that, if Trump “really wants some changes,” he should “tell [Russian President Vladimir] Putin, give us two months, 60 days off.”
Moscow, however, said it was ready to suspend strikes on Ukraine only on the election day itself, despite Kiev having launched an “unprecedented” drone attack on Moscow during Russia’s parliamentary elections last month. Russian officials also said Ukrainian strikes had damaged or destroyed 74 buildings housing election commissions.
Zelensky’s goal is “very simple: to bargain for time in order to secure a respite,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said on Monday. During that period, Europe would be able to supply him “with new weapons to continue the terrorist war against the Russian people.”

Ardebil governor urges facilitation of land transit, expanded border cooperation with Azerbaijan
TEHRAN- During a trip to the Republic of Azerbaijan and in meetings with high-ranking officials of the country, the Governor of Ardebil emphasized facilitating the land travel of traders and tourists and expanding bilateral border interactions in the economic, logistical, and crisis-management fields.
Masoud Emami Yeganeh said on Tuesday in meetings held during the Interior Minister’s trip to the Republic of Azerbaijan, referring to the 370-kilometer shared border between Ardebil Province and Azerbaijan: “Azerbaijan is Iran’s gateway to the Caucasus region, and creating the necessary facilities for the land travel of businessmen and tourists will play a strategic role in strengthening communications and developing exchanges between the two sides.”
Recalling the follow-ups carried out to streamline transit, the Governor of Ardebil said: “Finalizing and operationalizing the land travel of tourists and traders will have a direct impact on the development of economic relations in Ardebil Province and even for both countries.”
He referred to the importance of goods transit and stated: “Currently, about 500 trucks cross daily from Ardebil Province’s border into Azerbaijan, and facilitating the movement of trucks at Bileh Savar Customs while observing all security requirements is one of our work priorities for increasing regional trade.”
Emami Yeganeh announced previous agreements to launch a rail logistics yard and described its implementation as one of the infrastructure necessities for developing economic exchanges.
In addition to trade capacities, he pointed to the agricultural capabilities of Ardebil Province and declared the province’s readiness to transfer technical knowledge in the field of modern irrigation to the Republic of Azerbaijan.
In another part of his trip, in a meeting with the Minister of Emergency Situations of the Republic of Azerbaijan, the Governor of Ardebil emphasized the importance of the role of border provinces in controlling natural crises and said: “Given the geographical conditions of the region, Ardebil is fully ready to enhance its cooperation with the relief forces of the neighboring country by holding joint operational and field exercises.”

Also, Azerbaijan’s Minister of Emergency Situations, welcoming Iran’s relief plans, described the exchange of experiences between the two countries as a useful step for better responding to emergencies.
On October 12, the Governor of Ardebil, along with the Interior Minister and several national officials, traveled to Azerbaijan to follow up on the approvals of previous trips and economic issues between the two countries.
Ardebil, with rich water resources, fertile lands, a diverse climate, and capable human resources, is an attractive destination for foreign investment, especially from the Republic of Azerbaijan. Establishing specialized agricultural towns, utilizing the capacity of the free trade-industrial zone, and developing food industries and renewable energies with the participation of Azerbaijani investors can ensure sustainable development and job creation in the province.
Linguistic, religious, and historical commonalities, along with Ardebil’s secure border with the Republic of Azerbaijan, have provided a suitable foundation for strengthening economic and cultural ties, and these advantages make Ardebil a key player in Iran’s transit, economic, and cultural interactions with the Caucasus.
Ardebil Province has a 370-kilometer shared border with the Republic of Azerbaijan, and the active international border customs of Bileh Savar in the north of the province plays an important role in the trade and border relations between the two sides.
In late September, Shahin Mustafayev, Deputy Prime Minister of the Republic of Azerbaijan, speaking on the sidelines of the meeting of the heads of the Joint Committee for Economic Cooperation between Iran and the Republic of Azerbaijan, stressed the friendly and brotherly relations between Tehran and Baku and said: Despite existing tensions in the region, relations and cooperation between the Republic of Azerbaijan and the Islamic Republic of Iran are developing in various fields, and this trend will continue.

Oshkosh starts building Dutch marines’ Kaaiman vehicle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:18:20 UTC
20:18:20 KST

- Oshkosh Defense began building the first prototype of the JLTV-based Kaaiman patrol vehicle for the Royal Netherlands Marine Corps.
- The Netherlands ordered 150 Kaaiman vehicles in June 2025, with deliveries scheduled for 2028; the contract value was not disclosed.
Oshkosh Defense has started building the first prototype of the Dutch Expeditionary Patrol Vehicle, a version of its Joint Light Tactical Vehicle known in the Netherlands as the Kaaiman, for the Royal Netherlands Marine Corps, the company said on Oct. 13.
The Netherlands Ministry of Defence ordered 150 of the vehicles in June 2025 at a signing ceremony in Doorn, with deliveries to the Dutch marines, known as the Korps Mariniers, scheduled for 2028. Neither Oshkosh nor the Dutch ministry has disclosed the value of the contract, how many prototypes will be built or when testing of the first one will begin.
The Kaaiman is an unarmored variant of the JLTV, the four-wheel-drive tactical vehicle Oshkosh designed to replace the Humvee in U.S. service, tailored to a Dutch requirement for a patrol vehicle that can operate along coastlines and in shallow water. When the Dutch Defence Materiel and IT Command opened the competition in 2024, it asked for a vehicle able to work in extreme coastal conditions, wade through salt water and supply enough electrical power to take on weapons or sensors later. Oshkosh says the Dutch version adds better off-road mobility and reworked suspension, corrosion protection for maritime use, optional add-on armor, upgrades for hot and cold climates, and integrated mission systems.
“The start of DXPV prototype production is an important step in delivering next-generation capability to the Netherlands,” said Jeff Heggemeier, vice president and general manager at Oshkosh Defense. “Just as importantly, it demonstrates the strength of an active production base and our ability to continuously evolve proven vehicle technologies to address the changing needs of our customers and their missions.”
The Kaaiman is being built on the same JLTV production line in Oshkosh, Wisconsin, that is also turning out JLTV-based counter-drone vehicles for a customer the company described only as having an urgent need. Oshkosh argues that working from a vehicle already in production lets it move from design to prototype much faster than a clean-sheet program.
“Because we’re building on a mature platform from an active production line, we can move from concept to prototype much faster than traditional vehicle development. That allows us to deliver capability quickly while maintaining the quality and reliability our customers expect,” said Heggemeier.
More than 20,000 JLTVs have been delivered to the U.S. Army and U.S. Marine Corps since full-rate production began in 2019, and the vehicle has been bought by several European allies, including the United Kingdom, Belgium, Lithuania, Montenegro, North Macedonia and Slovenia. Oshkosh lost the U.S. follow-on JLTV production contract to AM General in 2023, but it remains the only company authorized to sell the vehicle to foreign customers through direct commercial sales, the route the Netherlands used for the Kaaiman.

‘My son was killed’ France faces backlash over proposed police firearms law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:17:54 UTC
20:17:54 KST

‘My son was killed’: France faces backlash over police firearms bill
As protests rage across France, activists warn proposed law could deepen impunity.
Paris, France – Issam El Khalfaoui’s teenage son Souhail was shot and killed by a police officer in 2021 in Marseille.
“When my son was killed during a police traffic stop, we realised how difficult it was to bring the truth to light. The police and the justice system took different actions to cover up the evidence. We realised that this was a deeply systemic issue,” El Khalfaoui told Al Jazeera. “The IGPN [National Police] lost the video that captured my son’s murder. The witnesses were not interviewed, and the case file completely disappeared from the court. That is the reality.”
France has one of the highest numbers of fatal police shootings in Western Europe. At least 69 people were killed by police or gendarmerie officers in 2024, compared with 49 in 2023 and 50 in 2022.
Now, French police are again facing scrutiny, this time over their tactics during clashes in education protests. A 15-year-old lost a hand from a police stun grenade, and another officer threw a tear gas canister at close range, shattering a 14-year-old’s jaw and several teeth. The use of stun grenades has since been halted. Authorities say 700 police have also been injured.
The unrest comes as a controversial bill that would presume police officers acted in self-defence when using firearms faces a vote in the Senate.
Khalfaoui launched a petition against the draft law that received more than 700,000 signatures. The measure, which critics describe as a “licence to kill”, was approved by the National Assembly in July.
Several advocacy groups, including Stop State Violence (SAVE), the Human Rights League (LDH) and Amnesty International, as well as left-wing lawmakers, organised protests in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Toulouse, which drew nearly 50,000 people on September 20.
Under the proposed law, police officers and gendarmes would be presumed to have acted in self-defence if they used weapons in the line of duty, placing the burden of proof on the complainant.
For El Khalfaoui, who co-founded SAVE after his 19-year-old son’s death, passing the law would only increase the police’s strength.
“In France, there has been a seizure of power by police unions,” El Khalfaoui said. “There’s a militarisation of the police that has no equivalent in Europe, and resources have been allocated to the police to ensure the police’s loyalty to the government.”
The draft law could entrench a sense of impunity, El Khalfaoui noted.
“It will be impossible to refute this presumption of self-defence,” he said.
Bruno Bartocetti, a regional representative for the police union, told French news channel BFMTV the El Khalfaoui case was an act of “self-defence beyond any doubt” and said Souhail wanted to “start a fight”.
The judicial case was closed in December 2021, but reopened when the family’s attorney filed a complaint for “obstruction of the discovery of truth” after surveillance camera videos disappeared. A new judge was appointed in 2025, and the court’s investigation is ongoing.
‘Draft law enables police impunity’
Nathalie Tehio, president of France’s Human Rights League (LDH), also fears the bill “enables police impunity”.
“If there’s no investigation anymore, that means the police officer can no longer be held responsible for anything,” she told Al Jazeera. “France is a European leader in the number of people killed by the police.”
A 2017 law permitting police officers to wield firearms if a vehicle does not comply with a traffic stop has led to five times as many fatal shootings, according to researchers. At the time, the law had broad political support, although several left-wing politicians have opposed the recent draft bill and participated in protests.
“All parliamentary groups voted in favour of this law in 2017 by a very large majority. There was support across the political spectrum, from the left to the right and the far-right,” Sebastien Roche, a researcher at France’s National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS), specialising in police and democracy, told Al Jazeera.
After legislative elections in 2024, French President Emmanuel Macron’s party was unable to form an absolute majority to pass legislation without entering a coalition with other parties.
“Successive governments under Emmanuel Macron, especially during his second term, have adopted ideas from the far right,” Roche said.
With France’s presidential elections in six months, political parties are vying for electors, Roche noted.
“The competition is already under way, and in this competition, the right is trying to win over far-right voters because the right in France has lost a great deal of its political strength to the far-right in national and European elections,” he said.
When a police officer shot and killed 17-year-old Nahel Merzouk, a boy of Algerian descent, in 2023, riots spread across the country.
Discrimination leads to more traffic stops, said Roche, and ultimately people of colour are at more risk of violence.
“The way the police monitor people’s behaviour is unfavourable to non-white people,” he said, citing studies he conducted in Bouches-du-Rhone in the Marseille region. “The probability of being stopped (by the police) is more than 50 percent higher for people who are not white.”
In 2001, Omer Mas Capitolin was in a work meeting when a disturbance from a police intervention on the street outside shook the building. Mas Capitolin went downstairs to ask the officers to move, but the police entered the association and handcuffed Mas Capitolin.
“They used a chokehold and pinned me to the ground. I couldn’t breathe or speak,” Mas Capitolin told Al Jazeera.
He later founded the Community House for Supportive Development (MCDS), a grassroots non-profit against police violence and discrimination. In 2021, six NGOs, including MCDS filed a class action suit against the French government, alleging systemic racial discrimination in police identity checks.
“We can call these identity checks discriminatory, along with everything that goes with them, including the refusal to comply, contempt of authority, resistance, and, increasingly today, the issue of illegal and excessive fines imposed on young people,” Mas Capitolin said.
In October, 2023, France’s high court recognised racial profiling during police identity checks, a ruling described by Human Rights Watch (HRW) as “historic”. But the court did not order French authorities to take the “necessary measures to end this long-standing, abusive practice” as it handed down the verdict in the case filed by the six groups, HRW said.
Also in 2021, the French state was condemned for “gross negligence” in an identity check of three high school students in Saint-Denis, north of Paris. Last year, the European Court of Human Rights condemned France for racial profiling of Karim Touil.
Despite these rulings, “everything is moving in the opposite direction”, Mas Capitolin said. “France is dealing with kids using military-grade weapons. Police officers are over-equipped and over-armed. I’m devastated.”

Europe paid Russia $209bn for energy since 2022, far below Moscow’s $320bn claim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:17:24 UTC
20:17:24 KST

The European Commission pushed back against what appear to be inflated claims by Russia — and the United States — regarding the bloc’s spending on Russian energy since 2022.
The European Commission disputed Russia's claim on Tuesday that the EU spent $320.7 billion (€286 billion) on energy from Moscow since 2022, citing a significantly lower figure, according to a Commission spokesperson.
Contrary to Moscow's claims, Russia supplied the EU with €197 billion ($209 billion) worth of energy between March 2022 and July 2026, the Commission spokesperson said, citing COMEXT data, the official reference database managed by Eurostat.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said late Monday that the EU had purchased €302 billion ($320.7 billion) worth of Russian energy resources since 2022, highlighting the bloc’s continued reliance on Moscow despite Brussels’ efforts to sever energy ties, even as the EU faces gas shortages this winter.
But Brussels rejects those claims, stressing that the bloc's efforts to ditch Russian energy have already borne fruit.
"The EU would have spent €475bn — an additional €278bn on Russian fossil fuels if REPowerEU hadn’t been launched," the Commission spokesperson added, justifying the efficacy of the bloc's plan to ditch reliance on Russian fuels.
REPowerEU was designed to reduce dependence on Russian energy through diversification, lower consumption and a faster transition to alternative energy sources shortly after Moscow invaded Ukraine.
By 2023, only 6% of the EU’s total fossil fuel expenditure went to Russia, according to the Commission spokesperson.
The Commission’s figures cover payments for energy imports through July 2026, while Novak refers to supplies since 2022 without specifying the commodities included, the valuation methods used or the exact period covered.
"I'm not in the position to confirm other people's numbers. What I can confirm is that we have a clear declining trend of our dependency on Russia from 42%-45% in 2022 to 12% now," Commission spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen told reporters on Tuesday.
Russia, US, float different figures
The figures also complicate US President Donald Trump’s claim on 12 October that the EU paid Russia $250 billion (€223 billion) for energy, which he has used to defend his “America First” approach, Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Moscow’s estimate is about $112 billion (€100 billion) higher than the Commission’s figure, while Trump’s claim is around $41 billion (€36 billion) higher.
The discrepancy reflects competing accounts of the EU’s energy trade with Russia at a time when Brussels is seeking to demonstrate that sanctions and its strategy to ditch reliance on fuel imports from Moscow have sharply reduced the bloc’s exposure to Russia.
Moscow’s message: Europe still needs Russian energy
Speaking to Russian state broadcaster Vesti, Novak said Russia had supplied €302 billion ($320.7 billion) in energy resources to EU countries from 2022 to the present.
"The figure for the period from 2022 to the present stands at $320.7 billion — that is the total volume of energy resource supplies to European Union countries," the Russian minister said.
He added that deliveries worth $21.3 billion had already reached Europe in the first nine months of 2026, despite sanctions.
His remarks portrayed Western sanctions as insufficient to sever the energy relationship and presented Russia as a continuing supplier capable of responding to global market disruptions.
Novak said Russia was meeting its contractual obligations and supplying energy through routes where exemptions remained in place — such as the Arctic route, which has given Moscow €9.7 billion in the first nine months of the year for its liquefied natural gas (LNG).
He also argued that additional Russian diesel exports, including to the United States, could help ease market pressures caused by disruption in the Strait of Hormuz and reduced global refining capacity.
Trump turns Europe’s energy bill into a political argument
Meanwhile, Trump’s $250 billion (€223 billion) figure is being used to reinforce his argument that European countries have continued financing Russia while relying on the United States for security.
His social media post framed the figure as evidence that his America First policy was the right choice for US interests.
However, the Commission’s data suggests that the EU’s energy relationship with Russia is more complex than either Washington’s political narrative or Moscow’s headline figure suggests.
The EU has continued to import some Russian energy despite sanctions, particularly through remaining supply routes and specific exemptions.
The ongoing exemptions were a concession to landlocked countries like Hungary and Slovakia, as well as to long-term contract holders, to avoid legal penalties.
"For the time being, it is still allowed to import some energy from Russia, given that the last deadline for these imports will take place next year," Itkonen added.
Under the bloc's REpowerEU, Brussels plans to "completely phase out gas and LNG from Russia" by 1 January 2027.

EBRD increases guarantee fund for insuring Ukraine's war risks to EUR 150 million
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:17:23 EEST
20:17:23 KST

The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and Aon, a leading global professional services firm, are expanding the size and capabilities of the Ukraine Recovery and Reconstruction Guarantee Fund (URGF) for war risk insurance from EUR 110 million to EUR 150 million.
"As the existing capacity of EUR 110 million is now fully used by Ukrainian insurers and their clients, the bank is increasing the scheme to EUR 150 million so that more companies in Ukraine can obtain war risk insurance and address the current problems caused by the war," the EBRD said on its website.
It is noted that the scope of such insurance has also been broadened. The coverage will now also include transportation and storage of gas-related assets, as well as goods temporarily stored in warehouses, in addition to domestic cargo, damage to vehicles and railway rolling stock, which are already covered by the existing scheme.
The additional capacity is backed by donor coverage from the European Union under its Ukraine Investment Framework. This will allow insurance companies INGO, Colonnade and UNIQA, as well as two new Ukrainian insurers, USG (owned by Vienna Insurance Group) and Universalna (owned by Fairfax Financial Group, Canada), to offer more war risk coverage.
Through the URGF, which is managed by Aon, the EBRD guarantees to global reinsurer MS Amlin coverage of losses from war-related risks that are reinsured from participating Ukrainian insurers.
"The initial guarantee of EUR 110 million, backed by donor coverage from France, Norway, Switzerland, the United Kingdom and the TaiwanBusiness-EBRD Technical Cooperation Fund, remains fully in force and supports reinsurance coverage of more than EUR 500 million for goods and vehicles under almost 10,000 policies. Premiums received under these policies currently exceed the amount of insured events, and MS Amlin has not had to call on the EBRD guarantee, which shows that the war risk insurance and reinsurance markets in Ukraine can operate commercially," the EBRD said.
It is also reported that the URGF expansion comes amid intensified Russian attacks on energy, transport, logistics and civilian infrastructure, as well as the renewed blockade of Black Sea ports.
The EBRD is Ukraine's largest institutional investor. The bank has significantly increased its investment in the country since Russia's full-scale invasion, placing EUR 11 billion there since 2022, including a record EUR 2.9 billion in 2025.

Across China: Back in saddle, Tibetan ex-wrestler gives horse traditions a modern twist
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
19:16:35 CST
20:16:35 KST

CHENGDU, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- As more herders on the grasslands of southwest China's Sichuan Province turn to motorcycles and cars instead of horses, Rinch Wangyel is heading in the opposite direction, opting to get back into the saddle.
The 34-year-old former wrestling champion returned to his native Hongyuan County seven years ago to build a business around horses. What began with two horses has since grown into a ranch with 44.
In peak season, up to 20 visitors a day ride with him across hills and rivers and into remote grasslands and forests, sometimes spotting hares or wolves.
"My goal is to let people see the grasslands and experience nomadic culture," he said. "Many people know little about horses and yaks, and they are curious about how herders live and what they eat."
For Rinch Wangyel, horses were part of life long before they became his livelihood.
Born into a herding family in the Aba Tibetan and Qiang Autonomous Prefecture, he rode almost daily as a child. But it was wrestling that first took him beyond the grasslands.
At 13, he traveled by bus to a competition in Maerkang, the prefectural capital. Back then, transport links in the region were limited, and the trip took nearly a full day. Having rarely ridden in a car, he threw up on his coach halfway.
Wrestling later took him much farther. He won several provincial championships in Sichuan and a national title.
After retiring as an athlete, he moved to Beijing to study something he had known all his life: horseback riding.
"I wanted to do something connected to my own culture," he said.
He spent four years studying modern horsemanship, earning riding and coaching qualifications from Chinese and French equestrian associations. He learned to train horses, use equipment safely and communicate through body movements.
In 2019, he returned to Hongyuan.
At an average elevation of more than 3,600 meters, Hongyuan takes its name from the grasslands crossed by the Communist Party of China-led Red Army during the Long March, a roughly 12,500-kilometer military odyssey from 1934 to 1936.
From 1935 to 1936, the three main forces of the Red Army passed through this region. Bitter cold, thin air, treacherous marshes and unpredictable weather made the grasslands of northwest Sichuan one of the most grueling stretches of the Long March.
The take-off of modern traffic infrastructure is among the most visible changes in these formidable grasslands.
Before 1949, the Aba plateau had no modern roads. Highway construction began in the early 1950s, with airports, expressways and railways following.
Today, Rinch Wangyel said, the journey from Hongyuan to Maerkang or the provincial capital Chengdu takes just three or four hours. Tourists can now even visit the once-remote grasslands over a weekend.
Tractors, trucks and motorcycles spread through pastoral areas in the 1980s and 1990s, followed by cars. Some herders now drive new energy vehicles.
Horses, once essential for getting around, have gradually taken on a different role.
Hongyuan, known for its Tibetan equestrian traditions, has around 20,000 horses. Increasingly, they are used for racing, tourism and cultural experiences rather than daily transportation.
Rinch Wangyel first offered tourists short horseback rides at Moon Bay, a popular local attraction. But riding beside a road for an hour, he felt, did little to show visitors what the grasslands were really like.
He then opened his own ranch, offering rides lasting hours or even a full day, deeper into the countryside.
"Our guests tend to be well-off," he said. "But they're also looking for something more than just sightseeing."
Some guests stay for days, switching horses and routes. A Frenchman living in Shanghai in east China has returned several times, and the ranch has attracted thousands of repeat visitors from both China and abroad.
For city dwellers seeking a break from hectic urban life, the grasslands offer a different pace. But taking inexperienced riders into remote terrain required Rinch Wangyel to rethink traditional practices.
He modified traditional saddles and stirrups, made helmets and protective gear mandatory, and helped develop safety standards for local horseback-riding businesses.
His approach to training horses also changed. "We have moved away from the traditional practice of training horses with whips and use the methods I learned in Beijing, communicating with them through body language," he said.
He even washes the horses with shampoo and carefully grooms them, hoping first-time visitors will see the local Hequ breed at its best.
"I've always believed horses have personalities just like people," he said.
Hequ horses, a traditional Chinese plateau breed, are known for their courage, steady temperament and endurance in cold, high-altitude conditions.
These animals have also become part of a wider effort to build a tourism industry around the region's equestrian traditions.
In recent years, Hongyuan has upgraded more than 100 horseback-riding sites and expanded horse breeding and training. Equestrian competitions and music festivals, notably, have brought more visitors.
During a series of events in 2025, the county received 220,000 tourist visits and generated 218.5 million yuan (approximately 32.47 million U.S. dollars) in tourism revenue.
The country's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), released in March, calls for promoting county economies via local strengths, expanding distinctive rural industries, and developing new rural industries and business models such as leisure tourism, cultural experiences and rural e-commerce.
Rinch Wangyel films and edits videos of grassland rides to attract customers and trains local herders to serve as part-time riding instructors during peak season. His ranch made a profit of approximately 600,000 yuan in 2025.
Now he has another ambition.
Rinch Wangyel has begun breeding imported British horses with local Hequ horses, hoping to produce taller animals while retaining the endurance and hardiness of the plateau breed.
Eight horses have been bred this year. If all goes well, a new generation of foals will arrive next spring, increasing his herd to more than 50.
"One day, I hope horses bred and trained in Hongyuan can leave the grasslands and compete in show jumping in Beijing and Shanghai," he said. "And I hope that will help more people understand our nomadic culture." ■

BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- China's central bank has approved an application from a subsidiary of Visa to set up a bank card clearing institution in China, a step forward in the country's financial opening up.
Visa Information Technology (Beijing) Co. Ltd. is required to complete its preparations and apply to commence operations within a year, the People's Bank of China (PBOC) said on Tuesday.
The bank card clearing business license will be issued after the PBOC and the National Financial Regulatory Administration jointly approve the application.
"The approval of our Application to Prepare marks a significant step forward in Visa's long-standing commitment to China," said Ryan McInerney, CEO of Visa. "For more than 40 years, Visa has been an active contributor to China's dynamic payments landscape."

Under current regulations, once it is approved to commence operations, Visa will be able to provide clearing services and issue bank cards denominated in renminbi (RMB). The company is currently permitted to provide such services in China only in foreign currencies.
PBOC Governor Pan Gongsheng met with Visa CEO McInerney on May 15 this year. They exchanged views on issues including China-U.S. economic and trade relations, and Visa's development in China.
American Express secured approval in 2018 to establish a bank card clearing institution through its Chinese joint venture, Express (Hangzhou) Technology Service Co., which launched operations in 2020, becoming China's first foreign-funded bank card clearing institution. Mastercard likewise secured approval in 2020 and started operations in 2024. ■

COLOMBO, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- The International Monetary Fund (IMF) expected Sri Lanka's economic growth to slow to 4 percent this year and further to 3.7 percent in 2027.
The projections, released on Tuesday in the IMF's October 2026 World Economic Outlook, mark a clear step down from the 5-percent growth Sri Lanka recorded in 2025.
IMF estimated the country's inflation to climb to 5.3 percent, as the war in the Middle East drives up energy prices across import-dependent economies.
The turnaround in prices is sharp. Sri Lanka's consumer prices fell by 0.5 percent in 2025, but the IMF now projects inflation of 5.3 percent in 2026 and 5.4 percent in 2027, marginally above the Central Bank of Sri Lanka's 5 percent target.
The country's external position is also expected to weaken, with the current account moving from a surplus of 1.6 percent of GDP in 2025 to deficits of 0.5 percent in 2026 and 0.3 percent in 2027.
In addition, the IMF projects unemployment to hold at 3.9 percent over the three years. ■

Letter from Mideast: A vest marked "PRESS" was no shield
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
19:16:08 CST
20:16:08 KST

by Taher Abu Hamdan
BEIRUT, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- The tripod lay on its side, the camera and other equipment scattered across the hilltop. A media car burned nearby. Moments earlier, a group of journalists had been filming. The word "PRESS" was still visible on the vests amid the wreckage.
It was Oct. 13, 2023, days after fighting began along the Lebanon-Israel border. Cameraman Issam Abdallah was killed and six other journalists wounded, all wearing press vests. Independent investigations traced the shells to the Israeli side, while the intent remained disputed.
Until then, we had carried an assumption none of us said aloud: as journalists, we stood outside the fighting. After that afternoon, the vest no longer felt like armor. It felt like a word we had trusted too much.
Since Oct. 8, 2023, one day after the latest Gaza conflict erupted, we had gathered almost daily in a square in the border city of Marjeyoun overlooking Israeli positions.
We filmed Israeli airstrikes on towns around Marjeyoun and Bint Jbeil, then watched the strikes spread to the western Bekaa and Baalbek. In the opposite direction, we recorded Hezbollah rockets arcing toward Israel, sometimes intercepted above us.
At first, the confrontation looked contained. Then the distance between us and the war narrowed, day by day.
We began studying where we stood, which vehicles we used, how long we lingered, and how far we were from military positions. But the war advanced faster than our habits.
On Nov. 21, 2023, journalist Farah Omar and cameraman Rabih Maamari, both with Lebanese broadcaster Al Mayadeen, were killed while covering the fighting.
Nearly a year later, an Israeli strike hit a building in Hasbaya where about 18 journalists were staying, killing three.
Before each reporting trip, we no longer asked only what was happening there. We also asked: Is the place where we are standing safe? Is the word "PRESS" on our vests and vehicles enough to protect us?
As Israeli forces entered border villages, we no longer watched only the shelling. Tanks moved in, bulldozers reshaped the landscape. Houses were reduced to rubble. Villages once minutes away became dangerous to reach.
A ceasefire in November 2024 offered a fragile pause, but fighting surged again in March 2026. By May, Israeli forces had crossed the Litani River. Evacuation orders spread, and strikes continued even after further ceasefire announcements.
Each time we thought the war had reached its limit, it pushed that limit farther.
The endless fighting has reshaped the south. According to Lebanese authorities, at the peak of the 2026 flare-up, some 1.2 million residents were displaced across the country, most of them from the south.
For residents, a shifting front line is more than a change on a map: it decides whether they can return home, tend their farms, or reach the services they need.
As journalists, we leave after filming, but the place does not leave us. Some sounds remain: explosions, the buzz of drones, cries for an ambulance, and the long silence after an airstrike -- sometimes more painful than the blast itself.
Three years on, our footage records how far the war has spread. It cannot tell us where it will stop, or when those still displaced will be able to go home. ■

Australian study tests acupuncture for acute pain in emergency departments
China
Unknown Publisher

19:16:04 CST
20:16:04 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- An Australian research project is testing whether acupuncture can be integrated into hospital emergency departments as a non-drug option for patients experiencing acute pain.
The Personalized add-on Acupuncture service at Northern Hospital Emergency Department for Acute Pain (PANDA) explores how registered acupuncturists can work alongside emergency department clinicians to support patient comfort, improve care experiences and potentially reduce time spent in hospital, according to a statement released Tuesday by Australia's RMIT University.
Unlike clinical trials that assess treatment effectiveness under controlled conditions, the project -- led by RMIT and Northern Health, a public health service provider in Australia's Melbourne -- focuses on how acupuncture can be delivered effectively in a busy emergency department, the statement said.
Early findings of the PANDA team show strong interest in non-drug pain management options, with more than 90 percent of surveyed emergency department patients saying they would consider acupuncture if it helped them avoid or reduce medication use.
Meanwhile, 90 percent of surveyed healthcare workers wanted non-drug options for their patients, the team found. The project has adopted the panda as its symbolic mascot, reflecting its goal of bringing relief and reassurance to patients in distress. ■

EU has paid Russia US$209bn for energy since March 2022
From March 2022 to July 2026, European Union countries paid Russia around €197 billion or approximately US$209 billion for fossil fuels.
Source: an EU source with a reference to official European Union statistical data, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Following the start of the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine, the EU spent approximately US$209 billion on Russian fossil energy, which refutes the claim made by US President Donald Trump about US$250 billion spent during this period.
Meanwhile, according to European institutional estimates, without the launch of the REPowerEU plan (the EU's planned phase-out of Russian energy resources), this figure could have reached around €475 billion.
The source calculated that reducing dependency on Russian fossil fuels had allowed the EU to avoid additional expenditure of approximately €278 billion.
The official recalled that as early as 2023, supplies from Russia accounted for only about 6% of the European Union's total expenditure on fossil fuels.
Background:
- Trump wrote on his social media network that the European Union had paid Russia US$250 billion for energy.
- On 9 October, Trump said he had spoken to Putin and reached an agreement with him on supplying Russian diesel fuel to the US and global markets.
- The agreement between Trump and Putin sparked outrage in Ukraine and European capitals.
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy strongly criticised Trump's actions, describing the easing of sanctions as an "absolutely terrible" move.

Estonia's new plain language standard aims to make public writing clearer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:15:00 UTC
20:15:00 KST

Estonia's new plain language standard aims to make public writing clearer
Estonia's first plain language standard took effect in early October, offering guidance on writing clear, reader-focused public communications.
Adopted ahead of International Plain Language Day on Tuesday, the standard aims to make public-sector writing clearer and communication more effective.
Kristel Ress, who chairs the technical committee that developed the standard, said writers should first consider who will read a text and in what circumstances.
Instructions for a fisherman reading on a phone in a cold boat, for example, need to account for very different conditions than something read at home or standing at a bus stop.
Ress nonetheless emphasized that the standard is just one tool, offering broad principles rather than detailed rules on word choice or grammar.
"The advantage of the standard is that, for the first time, all this advice has been brought together in one concise guide," she explained.
This guide, she continued, can help anyone who writes for work, including editors, teachers and researchers — but also office workers and even students.
"This isn't just for language professionals anymore," Ress said.
Putting the reader first
ERR language editor and adviser Ester Põldma said the guidance will be particularly useful for people writing online, where brevity and clarity are essential.
"Readers should be able to understand on the first read what a sentence is trying to convey," Põldma said.
Under the international definition, a text is written in plain language when its intended readers can find the information they need, understand it and act on it.
"Putting the reader first is the most important thing," Põldma said. "We need to think about who we're writing for or who we're making a program for. That determines the words we use, the sentences we write and what the text should look like."

Olympic champion Zakharova and NGO Sports Context challenge presence of Russian organizations in FIG
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:13:13 EEST
20:13:13 KST

Taras Samborsky, co-founder and expert at the Sports Context NGO and a specialist in legal and institutional sports matters, announced the submission of complaints to the Gymnastics Ethics Foundation (GEF) of the International Gymnastics Federation (FIG). These complaints document violations related to the presence of Russian sports organizations within the FIG and the inclusion of athletes from the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine in their ranks.
"We prepared the documents and engaged not only legal specialists but also OSINT experts. We enlisted specialists to document unlawful actions committed by Russian organizations, specifically the Russian Gymnastics Federation, regarding the recruitment of athletes and organizations from the temporarily occupied territories. As of today, this package of documents, detailing the violations and our legal assessment, and prepared in compliance with all procedures set out in the FIG Code of Ethics, has been submitted to the relevant FIG body. The goal is to secure a legal assessment and a decision regarding the continued presence of Russian organizations within the International Gymnastics Federation," Samborsky said during a press conference at the Interfax-Ukraine agency on Tuesday.
According to him, the formal appeal was submitted by Olympic champion Stela Zakharova, Vice President of the Ukrainian Gymnastics Federation (responsible for artistic gymnastics), who initiated the separate filing. "We helped her compile the relevant package of documents," stated the co-founder of the NGO Sports Context.
Samborsky added that the document package has already been "accepted and is undergoing assessment by the International Gymnastics Federation," and that the organization is prepared to "bolster its position with additional documentation if necessary."
Zakharova, for her part, emphasized that the events unfolding in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine "cannot be viewed as unrelated to sports."
"When sports organizations, coaches, judges, athletes, or competitions from internationally recognized Ukrainian territory are incorporated into another state's sports system, a very specific question arises: whose sports system do they represent, and who should defend the Ukrainian gymnast's right to her own territory and jurisdiction? To me, the answer is obvious: first and foremost, we ourselves—people to whom Ukrainian sport has given the opportunity to compete, win, become Olympic champions, and work within national federations—must not only avail ourselves of these opportunities but also stand up for ourselves. That is precisely why my appeal to the GEF—the International Federation's Gymnastics Ethics Foundation—reflects not only a civic stance but also a professional responsibility," she said during a press conference.
According to the Olympic champion, "we are submitting facts and documents and requesting an assessment of them in accordance with international gymnastics regulations."
"I do not know what the final decision will be, and I believe it is wrong to predict it before the procedure concludes. But I know one thing for certain: if a protection mechanism exists, we must trigger it; if rules exist, we have the right to demand that they apply equally to everyone. Therefore, what matters to me is not just the act of filing the complaint, but the fact that we are changing our approach—moving beyond merely talking about the problem to professionally defending Ukrainian gymnastics by utilizing the international sports system itself," said Zakharova.
She also emphasized the importance of ensuring that Russian athletes are not admitted to FIG international competitions. "I took this step deliberately, fully aware that certain organizations might respond with actions that could be considered inappropriate. I understood that risk, but for me, the priority is ensuring that our sport has every opportunity to prevent their admission into international sports organizations. I hope that will happen," Zakharova said.
Samborsky described the goal of the appeal as enabling Ukrainian sports institutions to defend their rights and "create conditions under which the return of Russian and Belarusian athletes to the international sports arena would be, if not impossible, then extremely difficult."
"We are not currently asking international sports organizations to agree with Ukraine politically, nor are we asking for an exception for Ukraine or for an assessment of the political actions of the organizations and aggressor nations currently causing us harm. We are asking for an assessment, a legal assessment of the actions, taken by Russian sports organizations that violate the statutes of international organizations. That is precisely the foundation upon which we propose basing Ukraine's position..."

Russia and Ukraine on Tuesday traded accusations concerning overnight air strikes that killed at least four people and injured over 60 others.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (DSNS) said in a statement on Telegram that three people were killed and 15 others injured when a Russian missile strike destroyed a section of a four-story residential building in the Kholodnohirskyi district of Kharkiv, the country’s second-largest city.
The DSNS reported that the strike occurred on Monday evening and also targeted the city’s Shevchenkivskyi district, noting that four people were rescued, though some may still be trapped under the debris.
“Despite the threat of repeated strikes, rescue workers, police, medics, volunteers, K-9 units, and municipal crews are working at the scene,” the DSNS added.
The DSNS later updated the death toll to four and the number of injured to 41.
Meanwhile, the Kiev City Military Administration said one person was injured in a strike that affected a residential building in the Darnytskyi district.
Khmelnytskyi Governor Serhii Tiurin said four people were injured in the western region after drones targeted it over the past day, adding that the windows and entrance area of a regional medical facility were damaged during one of the attacks.
In the northwestern Rivne region, Governor Oleksandr Koval said 20 people were injured, one critically, in a strike on the regional capital that damaged an educational building.
Separately, Heorhii Reshetnikov, acting governor of the southern Mykolaiv region, said a cargo terminal and an unspecified number of warehouses were damaged in Russian strikes.
Ukraine’s Air Force claimed air defences shot down 88 out of 108 drones launched by Russia overnight. It added that Russia launched five Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles from the border region of Bryansk.
The Russian Defence Ministry, meanwhile, said it launched coordinated strikes against a workshop and locomotive depot in Kiev, as well as a logistics centre, a warehouse and dry cargo ship in the southern Mykolaiv region, which it said are “involved in delivering military cargo to Ukraine.”
‘Ukraine did not receive early warning from partners on overnight strikes in Kiev’
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country received no early warning from its partners about the strikes in Kiev, and that it has not carried out strikes on Russia's energy sector in general for the two days since US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire.
"But Russia did not heed the American President. During this time, the Russians have attacked both our energy facilities and our critical infrastructure, sending absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes on Ukraine," Zelenskyy said in a statement on X.
"Our position remains unchanged: Ukraine is ready for reciprocal steps toward de-escalation, and effective pressure on Russia is needed to make de-escalation happen. Wars end when the aggressor realises that it cannot prolong the war," he added.
Separately, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told a panel of the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland that Kiev continues to receive intelligence data from the US.
“Yes, we continue this cooperation (with the American side). And, also, it is true that yesterday’s attack, or night attack, (the) air raid alert was launched with a delay. But it is because of (the) special type of the weaponry which was used by (the) Russian side,” Sybiha said.
The Financial Times, citing people familiar with the matter, reported over the weekend that US envoys, in talks with their Ukrainian counterparts on Friday, raised the possibility of cutting off intelligence sharing to Kiev if it did not heed Washington’s warning to halt energy strikes in Russia.
Strikes in Russia
Russia’s defence ministry claimed that air defences shot down 604 Ukrainian drones over 15 regions and over the Sea of Azov.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin alleged that 417 drones were heading towards the region surrounding the Russian capital between 8.30 pm on Monday (1730GMT) and 7 am on Tuesday (0400GMT), with 65 of them destroyed.
Kaluga Governor Vladislav Shapsha said 73 drones were downed in his region overnight, damaging a school building, two private houses, and one car in the Mosalsky district.
The governors of the Tula and Voronezh regions reported Ukrainian drones being downed over their respective regions without any consequences, while Stavropol Governor Vladimir Vladimirov said damage was recorded in the industrial zone of the city of Nevinnomyssk.
“According to preliminary reports, there are no casualties, and there is no damage on the ground in Solnechnodolsk. … Inspections of the impact sites and damage assessments are ongoing, and repair work has begun,” Vladimirov said.
Yegor Kovalchuk, acting governor of the border region of Bryansk, said three firefighters were injured and hospitalised while extinguishing a blaze caused by a drone attack in the town of Zhukovka.
Independent verification of the claims is difficult due to the war, which continues for more than four years.
Moscow and Kiev have intensified strikes in recent months, targeting each other's logistics centers, ports, and energy infrastructure.
Both countries deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities only.
