Iran may be digging in for next war, raising stakes for US, Israel and Gulf allies - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:00:06 UTC
20:00:06 KST

Iran is fortifying its defenses and preparing for a possible new round of fighting with the US and Israel, satellite images indicate, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday.
“Iran is fortifying its defenses, rallying loyalists and threatening a wider, harsher response against the US and its Gulf allies as it prepares for potential American attacks after the midterms and seeks to deter them,” the report noted.
The findings come amid a series of reports suggesting that the US or Israel could resume military operations against Iran. Maariv reported over the weekend that the US had pressured Israel to carry out strikes against Iran. Both Israel and the US have upcoming elections, and renewed military action could have implications for those votes.
PBS reported on October 11 that “Iran has continued to reject a deal with the US. The head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council says Tehran finds the latest response from the United States ‘insufficient’ as efforts at negotiations to end the war and fully open the Strait of Hormuz limp along.”
The emerging picture is of an Iran continuing its efforts to rebuild its missile and drone programs despite the damage inflicted by previous US and Israeli strikes.
In March, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Iran could no longer produce ballistic missiles because of the extensive damage caused by US and Israeli attacks. There were also optimistic assessments of the number of Iranian missile launchers destroyed and missiles effectively “corked” inside storage facilities after strikes collapsed access routes.
However, The New York Times reported in April that Iran was repairing its missile bunkers. Tehran has shown it can rebuild military capabilities despite sustained attacks.
The WSJ reported that “Iran has also reinforced protection around its nuclear sites and other security-related bunkers. Last month, it built passive defense measures such as makeshift dirt mounds around its Pickaxe Mountain and Natanz nuclear sites to impede any attempted raid by ground forces, according to Vantor satellite images analyzed by the Institute for Science and International Security, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit.”
The report also quoted Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.
“In both word and deed, the Islamic Republic is actively preparing for the next war,” Behnam Ben Taleblu said.
Iran's vast territory complicates efforts to identify and eliminate its military threats. The country is approximately 75 times the size of Israel and 150 times the size of Lebanon.
Israel's difficulties in defeating Hezbollah in Lebanon and eliminating all the threats posed by the terrorist organization illustrate the challenges involved in locating and destroying Iran's military capabilities across a much larger territory.
Iran strengthens defenses and prepares population for renewed conflict
The new Wall Street Journal report raises further concerns about the scale of Iran's preparations for another confrontation.
“Satellite images show Iran is strengthening sensitive locations, including nuclear sites and border areas, to make them more resilient to attacks. The government is also preparing Iranians for renewed war, sending paramilitary forces to read war stories to kindergartners, advertising training in firing shoulder-mounted anti-aircraft missiles and holding rallies,” the report added.
According to the report, Iran is preparing to defend against several types of airstrikes. Tehran has likely drawn lessons from the 12-day war in June 2025, as well as the subsequent round of strikes that began in February 2026 and continued until May.
Iran is also continuing to threaten shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a strategically important waterway for global energy supplies.
The US has sought to ensure that commercial vessels can continue passing through the strait while limiting the impact of the crisis on energy prices. Nevertheless, Washington's efforts have not resolved the broader conflict with Iran, which remains an open-ended challenge.
The WSJ reported that “Iranian officials have hinted that their forces could conduct land incursions into neighboring countries, according to people familiar with the warnings.”
The withdrawal of US troops from Iraq on September 30 could provide Tehran with additional opportunities to act.
For example, Iran could attempt to infiltrate neighboring countries through Iraq or use Iranian-backed militias there to launch further attacks. Those militias have already attacked a key pipeline in Saudi Arabia.
Although US Central Command and Saudi Arabia carried out retaliatory strikes in July, Riyadh has been reluctant to confront the militias in Iraq while simultaneously dealing with the Houthi threat.
The possibility of a broader regional confrontation makes the Wall Street Journal report particularly significant.
“Tehran has separately warned Arab officials that it could strike regional targets including Saudi oil facilities in the event of a renewed conflict, some of the people said.”
Saudi Arabia is already weighing how to respond to the threat posed by the Houthis, who have targeted Saudi airports in recent days, killing and wounding people.
Could renewed strikes produce different results?
The central question is whether renewed US or Israeli military operations against Iran would achieve more lasting results than previous campaigns.
Iran is seeking to rebuild its capabilities while adapting to lessons learned from earlier confrontations. Those efforts include expanding its drone arsenal alongside its missile programs.
Tehran has also demonstrated its ability to strike US military bases across the region.
Iranian officials can assess publicly available reports describing damage to US facilities and aircraft, as well as the repositioning of American military assets following previous attacks.
Such information could help Tehran evaluate the effectiveness of its operations and shape its preparations for another confrontation.
The challenge for Washington and Jerusalem is therefore not simply whether they can strike Iranian military infrastructure again, but whether renewed operations would prevent Iran from rebuilding its capabilities and threatening US forces, Israel, and neighboring countries.

So that’s already a complicated step. And then it’s able to move almost a hundred muscles in your tongue, in your jaw, and in your larynx to vibrate air in this exquisitely precise way.
Sanders: But then, even more magic happens when those vibrations move into someone else’s ear.
Stavisky: Those vibrations are going to fly through the air and they’re going to hit someone else’s eardrum and it’s going to vibrate that, and it’s going to vibrate the hair cells. And it’s going to send a bunch of nerve signals to their brain and they’re going to first make sense of the sounds you’re making amidst all of the other sounds, whether there’s background conversation or a train rumbling by or a dog barking. But then beyond that, they’re going to not just hear the words you just said, but remember all the previous words, put them together and like get the same idea in their brain. I mean, it’s telepathy through mechanical means.
Sanders: Telepathy through mechanical means. When you step back and think about it, it’s an absolute marvel. So here I am floating these ripples out toward my microphone. And then through more technology, they are reaching you, where your own amazing machinery senses those ripples and turns them into meaning. So with these ripples, I’m putting something into your mind.
Stavisky: We have this like shared scaffolding of understanding where I can pretty much visualize anything I want and with enough words, make someone else put that into their mind. And I think that’s a really remarkable ability. And that’s like the basis of civilization and learning and science and connection.
Sanders: But there’s something happening before all of this muscle moving and air rippling, and it’s something that Stavisky just mentioned. My words first started taking shape somewhere else. They started in my brain. Certain clusters of my synapses fired as I thought about what to say. This intricate path from brain to muscles to sculpted air is behind every word we say.
Sanders: Hi Casey.
Casey Harrell: Hello there and thanks for being patient with me as I was running a bit late.
Sanders: When I met Casey Harrell on Zoom, I asked him to tell me a little bit about himself.
Casey: That is both the easiest and the hardest question to answer, right? So my name is Casey Harrell, and I am 47 years old. I grew up in the Atlanta area and have lived in the Bay Area for the past 23 years, most of them with my wife, Levana, and our seven-year-old daughter, who is going on 17. I spent most of my professional career as a climate campaigner and have went all over the globe, fighting companies who are destroying the earth and trying to bring some justice to our planet and the people who inhabit it.
Sanders: Like Jules, Casey has ALS. The disease has taken a lot from him. He can no longer move most of his body. That includes speech muscles.
Casey: I began to lose my ability to talk shortly after my diagnosis in 2020. 
Sanders: With time, he could no longer talk clearly enough to be understood. 
Casey: Then it became a slow-motion car crash of multiple years before almost no one would be able to understand me. A few other friends who were around often would be able to understand some of what I was saying. I relied upon my assistant and my wife to basically serve as my translators to other people. I did not go anywhere, even a video call without them, either one or both.
Sanders: Casey’s life in the Bay Area was changing in difficult, almost impossible ways. Like Jules, Casey had received an ALS diagnosis in 2020. Like Jules, he had a kid, a partner, a career, a big, full life. And then wham, life threw them one of the biggest curveballs you can imagine. These two men, separated by 3,000 miles, Jules in Miami, Casey in Oakland, were both facing big losses. And one of the biggest of all was their ability to talk. 
Speech-language pathologist Kate Nilson walks me through some of the standard approaches that she uses when she’s working with people who face similar futures. There’s a process called voice banking.
Nilson: So voice banking is the idea of recording specific sentences that you might not actually say in real life, but predetermined sentences that you record that give the software the combinations of sounds that it needs to make a computer voice that sounds like you.
Sanders: That process has actually improved quite a bit in recent years.
Nilson: When I started doing this, it was 1600 sentences. Now it can be an app on your phone that you do at home. It can be a website that you go to. The software that I use most of the time is 50 sentences. It can be done in like 15 minutes. It’s really come a long way and the voices are pretty darn amazing in how how true to the person they are. But they are still a computerized voice, right? They’re they’re they’re taking combinations of sounds and splicing them together. So it sounds computerized.
Sanders: Voice banking has the benefit of being flexible. This voice can say anything a person wants, but it sounds off. There’s another approach. This one’s called message banking.
Nilson: So the idea of message banking is we just record an entire message. So instead of using that computer voice to say, “Good night, honey, I love you,” we can just record someone saying, “Good night, honey, I love you,” with their voice, like, with their true inflection and meaning.
Sanders: The beauty of these messages is that they capture the quirks of a person’s voice.
Nilson: You know, I live in Minnesota, and so there’s a lot of ooftas and doncha knows, and those kinds of things that do not come out right when you type them into a computer.
Sanders: Nilson encounters these sorts of sounds when she’s helping people save recordings of their voice for the future.
Nilson: You gotta get all those right sayings with the right, you know, “o’s” in them.
Sanders: These recorded messages are often things like an inside joke with the exact right timing or a favorite little nickname for someone special.
Nilson: It can be really emotional. And that’s, when you’re recording the sentences that are predetermined and they’re not sentences that you would normally say, that can be easy. But when your family has written down a list of meaningful words that they want to hear in your voice and you know that you’re recording it because you might lose your voice, that can be really emotional. And it can be hard. And I fully understand that, but we can also have fun with it.
Sanders: Pre-recorded jokes come up pretty often when people are choosing what messages to preserve for later use. And swear words come up surprisingly often too, Nilson tells me.
Nilson: I had someone come in just the other day, and they had an entire category of recorded cuss words. So that’s important. Well, right? I mean, you don’t want them to be monotone when you’re frustrated. You want the right emphasis to come out on that.
Sanders: It takes the sails out of it for sure if it’s monotone. 
Nilson: Yeah, exactly. I mean, that’s communication, right? That’s important communication. So I guess it doesn’t really surprise me anymore, but it’s fun nonetheless.
Sanders: She says some people come to her with entire folders of swears, folders that she refused to share with me for the story, by the way.
Nilson: The best part is it was a swear folder with all these different swear words and like different sayings and whatever. And then just one of them had a call-out to a specific person. And I was like, what did that person do to you that he’s the only one that has a specific? And then he laughed and he typed out, “If you knew him, you’d understand.”
Sanders: All of these quirks, the swears, the smiles in the voice, the familiar jokes, all of these things make a particular voice special. Jules created a banked voice. He didn’t love the result.
Jules: What I learned from banking my voice was that it really wasn’t my voice. It was more like a robot trying to emulate my voice. It had no emotion or tone behind it.
Sanders: This was a problem because it got in the way of something Jules wanted to do. The turmoil of ALS forced some clarity for him about what he wanted out of life, what he wanted to spend his time doing. And one of those answers, it turns out, was comedy. After his diagnosis, while he still had his voice, he performed stand-up a few times.
MA: And that was amazing, right?
Sanders: But as his voice got harder to use, things changed. Jules could still talk, but it took a lot of work, especially since he was often using a mask for extra oxygen.
MA: He was wearing the mask pretty much the entire time. So his voice was very labored, because you have to take the breath in to utter anything. So it was very choppy. But he did have a voice.
Sanders: With time, a live performance with his original voice became impossible. The next option was to use a banked voice, but that wasn’t good enough for a comedy performance.
MA: So then he started to lose his voice and he was like, I don’t, you know, I can’t pull this off with a banked voice because it’s so robotic. It’s monotone. You can’t really do it.
Sanders: Jules couldn’t pull off a comedy show. But could there be a different way, a different voice?
I’m going to step back here and give you more context about Jules and about ALS. ALS is progressive and relentless, which means over time, more and more of the motor neurons in the brain and spinal cord are affected, and symptoms get worse.
And though this progression varies quite a bit from person to person, the median survival time after an ALS diagnosis is about 30 months. Time is short here. This diagnosis forces big choices about how to live and what a person wants their remaining time to include, for them and for their family. In the middle of everything else going on, Jules was facing a choice that many people in his situation must confront, whether or not he would get a tracheostomy.
That’s a procedure in which doctors place a tube in the throat. This tube is then connected to a ventilator that breathes for a person.
The procedure can leave a person unable to speak again, with whatever residual voice they might have left. Now, we have spent this episode on what it feels like to lose your voice. Jules was losing his. So it might seem like this part of the decision wouldn’t matter all that much. But to a person who’s losing their voice, and to their family, this moment marks an end point. It’s a hard stop.
On the next episode.
MA: He was someone who didn’t want to do a tracheostomy. He was opting for, once I’m done, that’s it. And that was our plan.
Sanders: As Jules and MA confront this decision, could a different sort of voice change the story?
Jules: So when I first heard my cloned voice, it felt like I reappeared. When my wife first heard it, she cried because of how close it sounded like me before I lost my voice.
Sanders: This is The Deep End. Talk to me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast, tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot.

Wikipedians Believed AI Would Come and Go. They Were Wrong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Long before the storm of AI struck Wikipedia, the Wikimedia Foundation was making preparations. Wikipedians battened down the hatches and made confident-sounding predictions that it would break and wash over them. Large language models might even improve Wikipedia, it was said, automating more of the housekeeping—formatting, sources, citations, missing links—and so freeing up humans to do creative work. It was not so simple. In 2019, then-Wikimedia Foundation head Katherine Maher wrote an op-ed in The New York Times under the headline “Without Humans, A.I. Can Wreak Havoc.” “Too often,” she wrote, “artificial intelligence is presented as an all-powerful solution to our problems, a scalable replacement for people.” The issue confronting Wikipedia, retaining human control over machines, was the same one soon being faced everywhere.
Already in 2018 Google was training AI to write “Wikipedia-like articles,” and by October 2024, a Princeton University study found that about 5 percent of nearly 3,000 newly created articles on English Wikipedia in a single month (August 2024) contained a substantial amount of AI-generated content. There were signs. ChatGPT was fond of em dashes—parenthetical statements that look like this one—and curly quotation marks. Sometimes, residues from the prompts used to compose articles were left behind (“Here is your Wikipedia article,” they might say.)
At first, Wikipedians tried to shape and control AI, to make its output “acceptable and constructive,” or to fix or remove if it proved otherwise. Generic fluff like “praising a village for its fertile farmlands, livestock, and scenic countryside” and fake sources were weeded out. By March 2026, AI content was found to violate its core principles so often that writing with large language models was banned outright, and their role restricted to translation and minor proofreading.
A much-read essay titled “Death of Wikipedia” explained this defensive posture. It predicted a ripple effect: As contributors reduced their contributions in response to AI pervading the platform, there might be a temptation to replace their work with still more AI, creating a downward spiral. One viral X post lamented that artificial intelligence seemed to be changing things in the wrong direction: “I want AI to do my laundry and dishes so that I can do art and writing, not for AI to do my art and writing so that I can do my laundry and dishes.” The “Death of Wikipedia” warned against something similar: Rather than AI performing Wikipedia’s “housekeeping” roles, it might compose its articles instead, leaving humans relegated to formatting and cleanup. The result would trap editors in an endless curatorial project derived not from human priorities but from the frostbitten harvests of machines.
“The potential ‘whittling down’ each year of our pool of talented writers is the greatest threat to Wikipedia,” another Wikipedian wrote, “as we must increase the number of editors, especially expert editors, to be able to fix the sprawling hellscape of weak, inaccurate and incomplete articles that drag down the project.” A Wikipedia written and read by machines threatened to create a new, deracinated Wikipedia, stripped not only of its context, but of its animating passion. It would be artless, and soulless. When the Wikimedia Foundation says that the care and commitment of Wikipedians to “reliable encyclopedic knowledge is something AI cannot replace,” that is not the same as saying that it will not be replaced.
Once Google introduced AI Overviews in search, they quickly became as central to the experience as Wikipedia was until recently. (This also means Wikipedia still does play a crucial role as a source, only at one step removed.) Anyone who uses AI agents knows that they give plausible, almost intuitive answers, which can pass a superficial review of their sourcing. They are also often wrong. If Wikipedia itself becomes corrupted by artificial intelligence, by what means will we prove when they are wrong?
Implicit in the idea of a single, machine-edited encyclopedia to rule them all is that such a phenomenon should act as a final authority. Its appeal, to the kind of people who find it appealing, is that it will be coolly rational, a kind of digital King Solomon that can act as a disinterested arbiter. There is no reason to think such cold logic would not be cruel instead. Its aesthetic failings are a clue: “Slop” is a useful word for the product of artificial intelligence, which implies something unvariegated and monotonous, absent not only of nutritional value but also of the flavor that makes nutrition a pleasure.
There is also no reason to believe an AI encyclopedia, or any other encyclopedia, should be unifying. Whatever its shortcomings and eccentricities, Wikipedia is the closest thing to an “encyclopedia of everything” we have ever had. Once smartphones became widespread after the iPhone’s launch in 2007, the old speculations, however far-reaching, were realized: Wikipedia was costless, portable, immediate, and electric. Enormous and omnipresent, it really became an approximation of the “sum of all human knowledge.” But so what? What did access to this oracle mean for human flourishing? What good has Wikipedia done?
A documentary maker, wanting to bring Wikipedia’s story to the screen, asked me a sharpened version of this question. Yes, Wikipedia was the little encyclopedia that could. It had overcome humble origins to become massive. But the dictates of streaming television needed something more. Were there, she asked, any real-life episodes where Wikipedia had “saved the village”? Has Wikipedia saved lives? The answer is “probably,” though not in dramatic or famous ways. Quick-fire encyclopedic knowledge has helped with accidental poisoning, and there are signs that Wikipedia is accessed with special frequency during natural disasters. But these anecdotes are difficult to corroborate, and often, when Wikipedia’s role is scrutinized, it turns out to be incidental. If someone calls for help in an emergency, it is not the phone which is the hero.
Does Wikipedia perform a public good? This seems self-evident but is much harder to measure and, in a way, is out of the project’s hands. In 2013, when an online poster posed the question “If someone from the 1950s suddenly appeared today, what would be the most difficult thing to explain to them about life today?” the top answer went viral as a mordant sign of the times: “I possess a device, in my pocket, that is capable of accessing the entirety of information known to man. I use it to look at pictures of cats and get in arguments with strangers.” Elsewhere, the “arguments with strangers” line was expressed in less lighthearted ways. “The greatest threat to democracy may no longer derive from human agency but from new forms of technology, which have the capacity to undermine democracy without anyone having intended it,” the academic David Runciman wrote two years later. “The forces from which democracy needs rescuing are no longer pressing on it from the outside. They come from within.”
No one is credited with foreseeing Wikipedia more clearly than H. G. Wells, a reputation built on a series of essays collected in his book World Brain, and its advocacy for a “Permanent World Encyclopaedia.” But Wells expounded on this idea many times, and his other writings were much more equivocal, and he even satirized his own obsessions in The Camford Visitation: “He wants a universally educated world, educated on the same lines, with every artificial difference eliminated. He is a cantankerous, disagreeable little nobody and yet at times one feels he has got hold of something most exasperatingly vast and right.” Soon after World Brain was published, Wells had lost faith in his encyclopedic vision altogether and succumbed to late-life pessimism. Humanity had orchestrated to create a world war, not a world brain, and in the civilizational race between “education and catastrophe,” as he put it, catastrophe looked to have a winning lead.
Less obvious to us now is that World Brain was also an antidote. The most significant new European encyclopedias that preceded it, the Great Soviet Encyclopedia and the Enciclopedia Italiana, were direct expressions of nationalist and totalitarian intent, so much so that the entry on “Fascism” in the Enciclopedia Italiana was credited to Benito Mussolini himself. Wells understood that “internationalism” needed its own encyclopedia as a counterweight, but that did not make it a simple force for freedom. He assumed that the World Brain would assist a world government in projecting its power, and though democratically available, his Permanent World Encyclopaedia would make such a world government omnipotent. A world government that was all-seeing as well as all-knowing would inevitably be repressive; a sinister side to Wells’ ideas seemed to have partly inspired George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four.
Orwell also critiqued Wells more explicitly in his 1941 essay “Wells, Hitler, and the World State.” One of its more perceptive observations is that Wells was not, in fact, a futurist. He was a nostalgic, Orwell thought, a “nineteenth-century liberal” who had spent 40 years repeating the same idea: that history was a battle between “the man of science who is working towards a planned World State” and “the reactionary who is trying to restore a disorderly past.” With Orwell’s help, we can see that Wells’ World Brain was an old idea, not a new one. Versions of it had preexisted Wells by centuries, and this particular encyclopedic worldview sprang from his Edwardian conception of Progress with a capital P.
The encyclopedia handed down to us from the Enlightenment is much more than a collation of facts in a book or on a website. It is a whole mode of seeing and doing, a lens through which a clear, scientific vision of all things can come into view, unobstructed by superstition. Witness the world in this way, and the world changes. So far-reaching is this idea that the philosopher Alasdair MacIntyre classed “encyclopaedia” as one of the three major approaches of Western ethics, what he called “rival versions of moral enquiry.” The others were “tradition,” starting with Thomas Aquinas and Aristotle, and “genealogy,” which began with Nietzsche. Tradition was a marriage of faith and reason. Genealogy emphasized hidden power relations. Encyclopaedia relied on reason alone, trying to build an objective picture of the world that could determine how to act, thanks to a consensus version of the truth. The purest expression of this was to be found in the 19th century, in the ninth edition of Encyclopaedia Britannica, which promised “the available facts of human history, collected over the widest areas … carefully coordinated and grouped together, in the hope of ultimately evolving the laws of progress, moral and material, which underlie them.”
When Three Rival Versions of Moral Enquiry was published in 1990, MacIntyre’s notion was already criticized for being out of date. One reviewer complained that it saddled “the encyclopaedists with their 19th-century dogmatic statements in Britannica and plays down the fact that few if any of their heirs hold such views today.” Yet there were some places that rational-liberal outlook did survive in an unapologetic form. It remained at the very forefront of Encyclopaedia Britannica—the 1987 edition opened with the motto of its associate, the University of Chicago: “Let knowledge grow from more to more and thus be human life enriched.” Most pertinently, it undergirded the beliefs of Wikipedia’s cofounders. Not only did Wikipedia’s text-heavy format reflect a centuries-old Enlightenment tradition, it was also created by two men who still believed, earnestly, that discovering the facts and learning lessons from them was not only the purpose of an encyclopedia, but the central task of a life well lived.
The divergent paths of Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger offer a kind of parable for the fate of this worldview and the cultural crosscurrents that swamped it. Twenty-five years after Wikipedia’s founding, Wales is still a Davos Man, an international person for an international project, who lives in the capital of the United Kingdom and makes frequent criticism of the MAGA movement. Sanger never left Ohio, where he homeschooled his children, became a vocal vaccine skeptic during the Covid-19 pandemic, and voted for Donald Trump. In 2025, he announced that he had given up his long-standing agnosticism to become a professing Christian, and wrote a book-length philosophical proof for the existence of God. If Wales remained wedded to the MacIntyre-style notion of “encyclopedia”—Enlightenment rationalism, with an added Objectivist trim—Sanger had returned to “tradition.”
As Wikipedia affirmed its status as a knowledge institution, it also lost its immunity from the crises afflicting knowledge institutions everywhere. The only surprise was that it had been exempt for so long. At the end of her tenure as head of the Wikimedia Foundation, Sue Gardner had likened the experience to living on a peaceful tropical island as “cruise missiles flew overhead.” Culture war had broken out all around, and now Wikipedia was an island no more. In the 2010s, “disinformation,” “misinformation,” and “fake news” were all selected as words of the year in short order, and the saturation of information was just as blameworthy as its corruption. Instead of adjudicating between facts like judges, audiences acted like lawyers assembling a brief and took only what they wanted. The results of “doing your own research,” an off-kilter version of the Enlightenment demand “dare to know,” were algorithmically personalized pseudo-informational systems. Mired in this uncertain environment, Wikipedia approached its 25th anniversary facing unprecedented political, cultural, and technological threats.
All of this added an elegiac note to its birthday celebrations in January 2026. The Pew Research company marked the occasion by quantifying the encyclopedia’s staggering reach—in the decade between 2015 and 2025, Wikipedia had been viewed 1.9 trillion times, an average of 508 million views per day. These immense numbers nevertheless contained an unmistakable arc of decline. In the days prior to the anniversary, a long-time Wikipedian, Christophe Henner, published a long and detailed “wake-up call” for the Wikipedia movement. Since 2022, the encyclopedia had lost almost a quarter of its readership, more than 1.1 billion visits per month, a missing audience who, presumably, were seeking out AI summaries instead. Even when answers offered by AI agents contain links, readers tend not to follow them: One figure showed that the click-through rate from AI chatbots was only 0.33 percent; for the Google search engine, it had been closer to 9 percent. For a model whose lifeblood was readers becoming editors, it was a disaster.
Artificial intelligence was an existential risk to Wikipedia, Henner warned, and the encyclopedia risked being remembered as a “historical artifact that AI once trained on … a footnote in the training data of models that have moved on without us.” An editing crisis meant that fewer and fewer editors were performing more and more labor, “a smaller club working harder to maintain something fewer people see,” as he put it. Past moments of opportunity—for example, when Wikipedia might have harnessed the growth of the internet outside Western countries—had mostly been squandered. The energy generated by places like India and Nigeria going digital had passed Wikipedia by, and in the wake of all this, the encyclopedia risked becoming a “temple,” maintained by the last in a priest class of superannuated Wikipedians. Once sacrilegious ideas, like paying editors for their work, had to be considered anew. Otherwise, the whole of Wikipedia might be reduced to an abandoned cathedral.
Media coverage marking the occasion was just as bittersweet. In Nature, Dariusz Jemielniak wrote that “academic indifference” and artificial intelligence threatened Wikipedia’s survival, accusing agentic AI of exploiting a “parasitic relationship” that “endangers the last bastion of freely accessible, human-curated knowledge and undermines the premise of collaboration on which many of Wikipedia’s knowledge-sharing practices rely.” “Wikipedia’s Existential Threats Feel Greater Than Ever” was the headline for a Stephen Harrison piece in WIRED, a catalog of threats beleaguering the project. More dangerous than hostile think tanks and lawmakers was an increasingly indifferent public, slowly drifting away from its founding ideals. “Economic precarity [has] trained many Gen Zers to see any unpaid labor as a scam,” Harrison wrote. In the cold light of the dawning era, becoming a Wikipedia super editor during a period of unemployment seemed a distant luxury, or outright perplexing, “thankless work that AI companies strip-mine for a profit.”
The tide turning on Wikipedia was more than the advent of artificial intelligence or a fragmentation of reading habits. Christophe Henner thought the “AI summaries” were only a “convenient explanation.” “I’m skeptical,” he wrote:
Even this undersold the quantum of change. Something far older was fast losing relevance as well: It was the beginning of the end of the encyclopedic age. Near the front of the French Encyclopédie there is a diagram called the “figurative system of human knowledge,” which is now sometimes called “The Tree of Diderot and d’Alembert.” The Tree is a system for not only ordering “the parts of knowledge,” but connecting them in a logical chain so long it can wreath the universe. It represents a bold idea: that an encyclopedia’s unifying force will show how everything in existence is linked. It suggests that knowing everything will lead to knowing One Big Thing about everything. This old-fashioned idea was resuscitated in the computer age, and gathered momentum with the concept of AGI, artificial general intelligence, the moment machines surpass every form of human understanding. If realized, it will represent not only the end of encyclopedias, but their culmination. Human-written encyclopedias will still exist after AGI, but only as secular scriptures in the mind of a digital god.
The longest-standing critique of “encyclopaedia” is religious: It is the belief that human activity on a godlike scale is a doomed act of conceit. It was only during the Enlightenment that absolute knowledge came to be considered beneficial (and today, “know-it-all” is still an insult, not a compliment). Beforehand, desire for absolute knowledge was viewed as a sin or a crime, a proscription that continues in many cultures. Greek mythology is full of cautionary figures like Pandora and Prometheus, who knew too much and suffered for it; when the Norse god Odin seeks the sacred well waters granting wit and wisdom, a single drink costs him one of his eyes. In the very first book of the Bible, two different stories, the Tower of Babel and the Garden of Eden, carry variations on the same moral: Total understanding must be God’s alone. Curiosity is not only a sin, but the first sin.
One of the many artworks inspired by Wikipedia speaks to this phenomenon. In the 2010s, the bio-artist Joe Davis declared that he would engineer a real, living Tree of Knowledge, the tree described in the Bible that holds forbidden fruit and results in the fall of humankind. To do so, Davis planned to take a 4,000-year-old strain of apple trees and copy the English-language edition of Wikipedia into the letters of its DNA. He called the project Malus ecclesia, which in Latin is a pun that means both “evil church” and “apple tree church.” In interviews, Davis refused to say whether he would eat the Tree’s fruit; because of laws around genetic modification, ingesting an apple or even planning to may have been a criminal act. Mired in red tape, this tantalizing idea never came to fruition, but its forbidding message remains: The sum of all knowledge is cursed.
The real existing Wikipedia feels less melodramatic than that, and the most lasting dividend of Wikipedia may not be its contents but its process, which holds a promise quite unlike the Tree of Knowledge or even the Tree of Diderot. For years, the annual Wikimania conference has sustained a fledgling tradition: At the opening ceremony, Wikipedians wear their national dress. When almost three-quarters of the nations on earth are in attendance, this produces a real spectacle, even against a backdrop of convention center carpet. All around the room are people wearing hanboks and kaftans and kimonos (the practice was initiated by a Japanese Wikipedian), and when they intermingle, the effect is like those old, quaintly hopeful pictures canvassing the “Peoples of the World.” Appreciating the depth and variety on display takes longer. Those golden headdresses, called serimpak, are worn by the seafaring tribes of Borneo, and that is why they are shaped like ships. The chapan robes that seem to swirl under their resplendent colors are from central Asia; those heavy ponchos, overkill against the air-conditioning, have come all the way from the Andes. Someone offers Jimmy Wales a conical nomad’s hat from Burkina Faso, but he cannot accept all the paraphernalia presented to him. There is too much.
Those might be lederhosen in the distance, although someone jokes that the real German national dress is sandals with socks. At least one tech type seems to be wearing Hawaiian shorts for a similar reason, as the official livery of Silicon Valley. Everywhere there is embroidery, silk and brocaded colors, headscarves and skullcaps, a pageant of signs and patterns from parts unknown. Once congregated, the people wearing this garb do not generate an atmosphere of hubris. In this room their shared mission seems humble. Their talk is the slow, uncertain work of mutual understanding, graced with the tentative socializing of the shy. They are bounded by human fallibility, the same thing that ennobles them. Together, they call to mind a Latin phrase very different from Malus ecclesia. E Pluribus Unum—out of many, one.

Israeli extremist settlers use sheep farms, intimidation to expand West Bank control, CBS reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:59:59 UTC
19:59:59 KST

Extremist settler sheep farmers in the West Bank have been using their flocks in an attempt to drive out Palestinians living in the area, according to a CBS News 60 Minutes investigation, broadcast on Sunday.
According to the investigation, the settlers' flocks have "taken over" around 20% of the West Bank.
"Over 100 Palestinian communities have been displaced or erased by the settler violence and the ever-encroaching sheep," CBS's Lesley Stahl said in a voiceover at the end of the broadcast.
A local Palestinian mayor told CBS that the settlers "actually seized the land with their sheep."
"They enter, they open the gate of the house and take the sheep inside to eat the trees around the house," a man identified as a Palestinian schoolteacher added.
Sheep grazing 'delineates' border, Jewish West Bank farmer argues
Stahl spoke with Mordehai Minster, one of the co-founders of a sheep farm in the area.
"Sheep are amazing. They're dumb, but they're amazing creatures," Minster said.
"So the idea is you send your sheep down to graze, and then you can say, 'That's my land because my sheep are grazing on it?'" Stahl asked.
"When you have sheep, everyone understands. Arabs tend to fight over grazing land among themselves. It's a language that we understand, and they understand. And it's a way to delineate the border. This is where I graze my sheep. You don't take your sheep here. You don't plant here. You don't build here," Minster said in response.
"A lot [of the farms], including this one, have used violence against the [Palestinian] villages down around you," Stahl said.
"Whenever you have ethnic religious communities, especially in the Middle East, fighting over land and resources, that conflict sometimes gets ugly. The fact that violence exists doesn't change the merit of the right that we have to this land," Minster responded.
Stahl asked Minster about a group of extremist settlers, often called the "Hilltop Youth," who formed part of the movement.
"Those are kids that are ranging [in] age between, I don't know, 15 and 25. They don't do great in school. They don't get into the army that easily because maybe behavioral problems. So some of them end up in places like this, taking care of sheep, doing construction. Some of the kids may have drug problems. They smoke [and] grow pot (Cannabis)," Minster said.
Stahl raised that US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee had called violence against Palestinian farmers "terrorism," as well as "thuggish and disgusting."
"I wouldn't classify it as terrorism, but are there some children who overreact and act in thuggish ways and need to be controlled and held in? Yeah, definitely," Minster said.
Stahl flagged that Palestinians have died as part of the violence.
"Yes. None of this is great, and none of this changes the fact that our right to be here is legal and it's ancient," Minster said.
Hilltop Youth 'succeeding' in pushing out Palestinians, Arab family says
Stahl also spoke to Palestinians living in the area.
Mahmoud Faraj, his cousin Hassan, and Hassan's daughter Salma, spoke about their village, Jannatah [Arabic for Paradise], and how residents of the area feel amid rising extremist settler violence.
"They come over here, and they shepherd here," Mahmoud said.
"Actually, it was a paradise until March 26 when a group of settler invaders entered our land, our property, private property, and they established a tent. They were something like 20 people, 25 people, and they started to behave like they owned everything," Hassan said.
"This is my cousin's house over there. He's not allowed to go there at all," Mahmoud said.
Hassan said that Hilltop Youth are "succeeding" in getting Palestinians to leave. "If you go around them, you will see many houses they [Palestinians] just left really empty. Abandon; they abandoned their property. They [Hilltop Youth] steal electricity from the locals, and they also steal water. This is their strategy: to make the area unlivable."
The Faraj family also claimed that every time they try to approach their house, teens from the hilltop outpost "rush down to beat them up."
"Within few seconds, they started to attack us in small groups with wood sticks and with stones. And they have tear gas. And three of them, they were armed. So one of the armed guys, he started to shoot. He shot my cousin in his head. And it didn't stop here. They came, and they started to beat my uncle and his son, who was dead, with wood sticks," Hassan said.
The Faraj family took Stahl to the family's house they were discussing, but were intercepted by Hilltop Youth teens wearing black hoodies.
CBS highlighted that the Hilltop Youth were not the only Jewish activists at the scene.
Sons of Abraham act to protect Palestinians from extremist settler violence
Members of Bnei Avraham (Sons of Abraham), a group of Jewish activists who attempt to protect Palestinians from extremist settlers by stepping in between the extremists and Palestinians, were also present.
"They are trying to push us back. They don't want us to enter with cameras. So they are pushing and waiting for someone to react with their hands, so they have an excuse for more extreme violence," Roie, one of the Sons of Abraham, said.
According to the Sons of Abraham, "Judaism calls on them to protect, not expel, their neighbors," Stahl said.
"When the settlers see you, they get even angrier because they see you as traitors," Stahl said to one of the activists.
"I think they are angrier because we threaten them ideologically. And also, I'm not coming from outside [the movement]. I also grew up as a settler. I tell them I changed my ways. I know what you're doing, and I know it's not the right way," she answered, adding that sometimes they know and recognize each other when she interacts with the extremists.
One of the Hilltop Youth asked Stahl who she was, with the reporter replying that she is "an American journalist - television."
"Are you in with Hamas?" the extremist asked, to which Stahl replied, "No."
This extremist settler was then shown in the broadcast headbutting Hassan Faraj in the face.
"This is my land, and you won't stay. These are my roots," Hassan replied, before the same extremist settler headbutted him again.
The Palestinians and Sons of Abraham then attempted to leave. An IDF captain and squad of soldiers appeared, "seemingly out of nowhere," according to Stahl. The soldiers went to rescue the two Sons of Abraham activists trapped by extremist settlers, before the captain instructed everybody to leave the scene.
Stahl noted that the IDF allowed the Hilltop Youth to return to the disputed house but did not let the Faraj family pass through.
"The army's priority is the settlers. Some soldiers are settlers themselves and occasionally join the violence. Though there've also been cases where the soldiers have been attacked by the young settlers," Stahl said in a voiceover.
Stahl voiceover continued by saying that the Israeli government has "poured tens of millions of dollars into expanding the sheep farms, arming them and giving them American-made off-roaders."
"People call it 'settler violence.' I don't agree with that. It is state violence. There is a violence of a government," Roie, one of the Sons of Abraham activists, said.
Sons of Abraham released a statement following the 60 Minutes broadcast.
"Last week, we went to the village of Jannata, near the 'Kochav Yehuda' outpost, an offshoot of the violent 'Eitam Farm' outpost, to accompany a Palestinian man to the home from which he had recently been evicted," the statement said.
"The structure has since been 'converted' into the outpost's latrine. Settlers blocked our path and injured the homeowner, while soldiers forced both us and the homeowner away from the area," the Sons of Abraham said, noting that the 60 Minutes crew were at the scene, documenting it.
"At Sons of Abraham, we are a group of over 200 activists who head out into the field four times a week. We believe the Torah commands us to rescue the oppressed from the hand of the oppressor, driven by the conviction that this Holy Land can bring blessing to all who dwell in it," the group said.
Stahl asked Minster if he cares about US public opinion towards extremist settler violence, and possible ramifications of Israel losing American military aid.
"I do...I am bothered by the fact that America's turning on us, and we're turning on America. It's like, I see it as losing a friendship. And I'm also concerned that, as a military ally, as a political ally, we may lose America as well. It looks like it's going in that direction. But Israel will find other allies," Minster said.
"You're not worried enough about it to dial back?" Stahl asked.
"No. I am worried about that. But I don't look at it as an existential threat," he replied.

From Brexit to Breturn: What prompted UK's U-turn on EU and what it means to the grouping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:59:54 UTC
19:59:54 KST

More than a decade after Britain voted to leave the European Union in a contentious referendum, the country appears to be reconsidering its relationship with the bloc amid mounting economic pressures and a shifting political landscape.
The 2016 referendum exposed deep divisions within the British political establishment over the country's future, as populist movements gained ground across Europe and the United States.
Three years after the vote, as Britain continued negotiating its withdrawal from the EU, Brexit helped propel one of its chief architects, Boris Johnson, to power. His landslide victory in the 2019 general election appeared to signal the country's determination to chart its own course outside Brussels.
But the years that followed fell short of the "beginning of the new golden age" Johnson had promised. His vision of national renewal rested on restoring British sovereignty and reclaiming control of the country’s borders, but it did not deliver the “stunning success” he had predicted.
Instead, Britain entered a period of political instability and mounting economic difficulties. Johnson's premiership ended in 2022, paving the way for Liz Truss, who resigned after just 45 days in office, becoming the shortest-serving prime minister in British history.
Her successor, Rishi Sunak, could not reverse the Conservatives' declining political fortunes. The 2024 general election delivered a crushing defeat to the party and handed Labour a substantial parliamentary majority.
Yet Labour Prime Minister Keir Starmer, who had been reluctant to advocate a political rapprochement with the EU that might include rejoining the 27-state bloc, also struggled to navigate Britain's changing political landscape. He resigned in July 2026, two years after taking office.
A decade after the referendum, the economic consequences of Brexit have become increasingly difficult to ignore. Leading economists estimate that Britain's economy has suffered a 6 to 8 percent loss in GDP, alongside a 12 percent decline in foreign investment.
Against this backdrop, Britain's new prime minister, Andy Burnham, has signalled a significant shift in the country's approach to Brussels, making closer ties with the EU, including the possibility of rejoining the bloc, a political priority.
“There are three main reasons for that: growth, geoeconomics and electoral positioning,” says Mehmet Babacan, a professor of economics at Marmara University who previously served on an auditing committee at Türkiye's central bank.
According to Babacan, Brexit's economic consequences, US tariffs affecting Britain and growing public support for closer ties with the EU are helping drive the country's changing position.
Economic argument
While some studies have highlighted Brexit's potential economic benefits through unilateral free trade and deregulation, successive UK governments have yet to fully implement these policies. As a result, the substantial economic gains Brexit supporters anticipated have so far failed to materialise.
“Burnham argues Brexit triggered ‘a decade of low growth’ and other trade deals offer little: the Australia and New Zealand deals together are estimated to add only 0.1% to the GDP over a decade,” Babacan tells TRT World.
A recent study led by Paul Mizen, a professor of economics at King's College London, alongside researchers from Stanford University, the Bank of England and the University of Nottingham, has also highlighted the economic costs of Brexit.
The study found that Brexit has left the UK economy “significantly smaller than it would otherwise have been”.
According to Babacan, economists broadly agree that Brexit has had negative economic consequences for both the UK and the EU, although the impact has been considerably greater on Britain.
As a result, “the case for some form of Britain’s return to the EU seems to be strong in economic terms as evidence points one way,” he says.
“Based on different models, a new deep alignment of the UK with the EU could recover around half of the estimated cost associated with Brexit.”
Beyond Brexit's economic consequences, US tariffs have pressured both London and Brussels, strengthening the case for closer economic cooperation.
According to Babacan, these trade pressures are prompting both sides to reconsider their post-Brexit relationship and explore ways to reintegrate their economies.
Local politics
Beyond the economic argument, Babacan points to another factor driving Burnham's rapprochement with the EU: a shift in British public opinion, with recent polls suggesting growing support for closer ties with Brussels.
A September survey by the Messina Group (TMG) found that Labour could gain up to seven percentage points in electoral support if Burnham pursued closer ties with the EU and offered voters a new referendum on rejoining the bloc.
In the 2016 referendum, 51.89 percent of voters backed Leave, compared with 48.11 percent who voted Remain. A decade later, the TMG survey found that 52.4 percent of respondents believed leaving the EU had been the wrong decision, while only 29.7 percent considered it the right one.
“The Labour party’s base is strongly pro-European," Babacan says.
He draws a parallel with Canada's Mark Carney, who used Trump's threats against Ottawa to strengthen his electoral appeal while seeking closer ties with Brussels.
According to Babacan, Burnham appears to be pursuing a similar strategy, positioning closer cooperation with the EU as a response to Trump's policies while seeking to counter Nigel Farage's Reform Party, which has aligned itself with the MAGA movement.
But Farage sees an opportunity in Burnham's approach.
With Reform polling closely with Labour, Farage believes the prime minister's renewed push towards Brussels could give him “the biggest boost” of his political career.
This competing political pressure, Babacan argues, means Burnham must carefully consider how far and how quickly to pursue closer relations with the EU.
He warns that the prime minister must approach each step on “the ladder of rapprochement” cautiously, moving from sector-specific agreements to a possible customs union, participation in the single market, and, ultimately, full EU membership.
He says this gradual approach could help Burnham avoid reigniting the Brexit-related political divisions that contributed to the downfall of several Conservative leaders, including Johnson and Sunak.
While deeper integration with the EU could deliver greater economic benefits, Babacan also cautions that it could involve significant political trade-offs over sovereignty, currency arrangements and migration, issues that have fuelled populist movements across Europe and the United States.
“The most plausible sensible path for the time being seems to go for deep sectoral alignment” until full EU membership becomes a durable cross-party consensus in British politics, the economist says.
He warns that another British departure from the EU, even after a future return to the bloc, could cause lasting damage to relations between London and Brussels.
How the EU will react
The rise of far-right movements across Europe has posed growing political challenges for Brussels.
These movements have opposed not only EU enlargement but also policies ranging from the Green Deal to migration, arguing that the bloc's approach undermines national sovereignty.
At the same time, American tariffs and US criticism of NATO spending and EU policies have added to the pressure on Brussels.
Washington's warning of Europe's potential "civilizational erasure" has further strained transatlantic relations, prompting the 27-member bloc to reconsider its partnerships, including with the UK, a major European economy with nuclear capabilities and extensive global financial ties.
If the UK rejoins the EU, “the strategic gain would be significant”, Babacan tells TRT World.
“Britain would bring back in a military and nuclear power capability, a global financial centre, deep capital markets and some additional diplomatic reach, which also fits Europe’s new defence push in the Trump era as well as reindustrialisation efforts on both sides.”
Some studies suggest potential trade gains of roughly $32.9bn for the UK and $29.7bn for the EU, benefiting both sides.
EU accession negotiations are complex and can take years, depending on a candidate country's economic and political circumstances, its alignment with EU requirements, and existing members' willingness to approve its entry.
The process has also drawn criticism over perceived inconsistencies in how Brussels treats different applicants.
Some European politicians, however, believe Britain's previous membership could speed up the process considerably.
“As a former member, and with much of the regulatory framework already in place, I personally do not see any serious reason why an application from the UK would not be achievable within one parliament,” said Sandro Gozi, chair of the European Parliament's Delegation to the EU-UK Parliamentary Partnership Assembly.
Yet Brexit's political divisions could complicate any attempt at reunification.
“The main fear is a UK that rejoins and later leaves again, which is why the EU has inserted a ‘Farage clause’ (an informal term used by the EU diplomats to describe a proposed financial penalty or termination provision in draft EU-UK Brexit reset negotiations) into the reset deal,” says Babacan.
Beyond concerns about the durability of any future agreement, Britain would also face potentially less favourable membership conditions than those it enjoyed before Brexit.
Under any circumstances, the UK's terms for rejoining the EU “would be worse than before: no rebate, no opt-outs, and a commitment in principle to adopt the euro eventually” because the EU will not allow “cherry-picking” this time, says Babacan.

Orbán denied ordering the confiscation of Ukrainian money and gold in the "golden convoy" case
Kyiv • UNN
Orbán denied ordering the confiscation of $82 million worth of Ukrainian valuables. Hungary is investigating the detention of seven Ukrainians and the actions of law enforcement officers.
Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán denied ordering the authorities to seize two Ukrainian vehicles carrying $82 million worth of cash and gold, dismissing the claims as politically motivated. UNN reports this, citing Reuters.
Details
Seven Ukrainians who were transporting the assets were briefly detained by Hungarian authorities in March on suspicion of money laundering. The case heightened tensions between Hungary and Ukraine ahead of the April elections, which ended Orbán, an ally of Russia, 16 years in office as prime minister, the publication writes.
Ukraine's Oshchadbank said that its employees, who were transporting cash and gold from Austria to Ukraine, were involved in a routine operation similar to the one it had carried out every week since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Hungarian prosecutors launched an investigation into the handling of the case, including allegations of the unlawful detention and mistreatment of Ukrainian citizens.
In June, prosecutors named János Hajdu, the former head of Hungary's counterterrorism forces and now head of the security service of Orbán's Fidesz party, as a suspect.
Orbán was not questioned, but politicians from the ruling Tisza party called on him to say whether he had been involved.
"Viktor Orbán! Address the Hungarian people and say it clearly, directly, and in a manner worthy of a true leader: Did you order the 'gold convoy' to be stopped or not?" Defense Minister Romulus Rusin-Szendi wrote last week.
On Monday, Orbán called the transit of Ukrainian cash and gold "the biggest corruption case in Europe."
"I did not have to make specific decisions or take measures because, fortunately, the Hungarian authorities did their job of their own accord. But I would have done it anyway if they had not done so themselves," Orbán told Hir television.
"Now they want to take me to court for this? ... This has nothing to do with corruption, nothing to do with abuse of power. It is about wanting to eliminate the right wing," Orbán said.
Context
Oshchadbank reported the groundless detention of two cash-in-transit vehicles and the disappearance of seven employees in Hungary on March 5. This occurred during Viktor Orbán's tenure as Hungary's prime minister.
Later, Hungary stated that the seven Ukrainian citizens detained with cash-in-transit vehicles carrying a consignment of money and gold in Hungary had already been expelled from the country on March 6.
The National Police of Ukraine launched criminal proceedings over the abduction of Ukrainian citizens and a service vehicle belonging to JSC Oshchadbank in Hungary. The information was entered into the Unified Register of Pretrial Investigations under articles concerning unlawful deprivation of liberty and hostage-taking.
Hungary returned to Ukraine Oshchadbank's funds and valuables seized by Hungarian special services in March of this year, in early May, after the election victory of Péter Magyar, who later became Hungary's prime minister.
Oshchadbank noted that the total value of the assets held in the two cash-in-transit vehicles amounted to $40 million, €35 million, and 9 kilograms of bank gold.

Washington’s diesel deal: A door in the sanctions wall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:58:03 UTC
19:58:03 KST

On Friday, President Trump described his phone call with Vladimir Putin as “highly successful.” By Monday, oil traders had reason to agree. Kyiv had reason to feel betrayed.
In a single weekend, Washington dismantled part of the sanctions architecture it had spent four years building against Russia, all to shave a few cents from the price of diesel three weeks before an American election.
The mechanics are straightforward. Russia banned its own diesel exports on 8th July after Ukrainian drone strikes crippled its refineries and constricted domestic supply. That ban, combined with the disruption the Iran war inflicted on Gulf shipping, helped drive diesel prices toward record highs worldwide.
On 9th October, Trump announced that Putin had agreed to release diesel back onto the market: 300,000 tons “immediately,” another 500,000 in November, a million more “immediately thereafter,” and as much as 4.8 million tons in total, depending on how quickly Russia’s bombed refineries could recover.
The US Treasury moved just as swiftly. It issued a waiver suspending American sanctions on Russian diesel until 7th April 2027. Moscow, however, authorized only 500,000 tons for the time being, a smaller and slower first step than Trump’s announcement had implied.
Trump portrayed the agreement as a triumph of personal diplomacy, linking it to the other front of his energy strategy.
“Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” he wrote on Truth Social.
Markets moved on the headline. Diesel futures fell more than 4 percent on the day of the announcement. Within hours, the US diesel refining margin had dropped by more than six dollars a barrel.
Yet the scale of what was promised tells a different story.
READ: Trump’s national security team holds unannounced Camp David talks on Iran war, Yemen: Axios
At roughly 7.45 barrels per ton, the first 300,000-tonne tranche amounts to about 2.2 million barrels. That is roughly 14 hours of American distillate consumption and about 2 percent of existing US commercial stocks.
Even the full 4.8 million tons, delivered over three months, would average around 400,000 barrels a day. The global diesel market consumes close to 29 million barrels daily.
Clayton Seigle, an energy expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, put it bluntly. The agreement “probably won’t have much impact on prices” but represents “a tremendous benefit to Russia and Putin,” allowing Moscow to offload aging summer-grade diesel before winter demand shifts to a different blend.
One analyst’s note to clients went further: “We expect this deal to fail economically… We remain short US assets.”
If the economic case is thin, the political cost is not.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the move “a weak decision of strong partners” and warned that “Russia will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy.”
Rather than absorb the criticism, Trump told reporters that it might be time for Ukraine to find a new president who could strike a deal with Moscow. The remark landed in Kyiv exactly as intended: as pressure, not solidarity.
Behind the scenes, the bargain’s asymmetry was starker still. Putin aide Yuri Ushakov said that during the same call that produced the diesel agreement, Putin ruled out peace talks altogether. Russia, he insisted, would continue fighting until it had achieved “all its objectives.”
Washington surrendered sanctions leverage. Moscow surrendered nothing except diesel it could not use at home anyway.
Nor has the domestic reaction divided neatly along party lines. Critics in both parties have warned that the agreement would “only lead to more slaughter” by subsidising the Kremlin’s war chest while allowing Russia to dispose of surplus fuel.
Two days later, Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, urging both sides to stop attacking each other’s energy infrastructure. Within hours, Russia struck a Ukrainian power plant.
The sequence captured the episode in miniature: a declaration made for effect, followed by a reality that refused to obey it.
This is not Washington’s first retreat from Russian energy sanctions this year. That is the deeper problem.
The administration had already eased restrictions on Russian oil in the spring, when the war with Iran strained global supply. Treasury’s new six-month waiver comes barely three weeks after Trump signed legislation on 18th September designed specifically to tighten sanctions on Russian energy exports.
READ: Putin says US-Iran ceasefire proved ‘too fragile,’ assures Tehran of support
A law intended to constrain Moscow’s revenue now coexists with a waiver that reopens a market for it. The contradiction diminishes the credibility of both.
The sanctions regime assembled after 2022 was never a single wall. Price caps, shipping restrictions, insurance bans, and financial penalties formed a system of interlocking constraints. Each reinforced the others. Each depended on traders, insurers, and allied governments believing that the rules would hold.
The EU and the UK have kept their sanctions on Russian diesel in place, pointedly declining to follow Washington’s lead. An American carve-out now sits awkwardly within an otherwise intact European wall, creating an opening allied governments neither requested nor welcomed.
Every exemption, however “temporary” its label, teaches the market something: the wall has a door, and the right phone call can open it.
Traders price that lesson in. Insurers reassess the risk. Moscow learns which levers move Washington and files the knowledge away for the next shortage, the next election, the next moment of American impatience.
That is the true shortsightedness of the agreement. The diesel relief may be economically small. The precedent is not.
A sanctions regime survives on the expectation that it will not bend under short-term political pressure. Trump’s own Treasury has now demonstrated, twice in a single year, that it will.
The next time Moscow seeks leverage, it will not need to persuade Washington that sanctions relief is deserved. It need only wait for the next price spike that happens to coincide with an American election.
None of this resolves the diesel shortage. Its structural cause—refineries in two war zones operating below capacity—cannot be remedied by a phone call; however, it is “highly successful.”
It can only be papered over. The price will be measured not in barrels, but in the erosion of the one instrument the West built to make the invasion of Ukraine costly.
Three weeks from now, American voters may or may not notice a few cents missing from the price at the pump. Kyiv, and every government that joined the sanctions architecture in good faith, will remember exactly what those few cents cost.

Amcha Yisrael, with 1.8 percent, and Blue and White, with 0.9 percent, would both fall short of the 3.25 percent electoral threshold.
The poll was conducted by the Midgam Institute, headed by Mano Geva, in cooperation with iPanel, among 509 respondents surveyed online and by telephone. The margin of error was 4.4 percentage points.

EBRD Expands Ukraine War-Risk Insurance to $168M
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:56:00 UTC
19:56:00 KST

The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) is raising the capacity of its war-risk insurance scheme for Ukrainian businesses from €110 million ($123.2 million) to €150 million ($168 million), after Ukrainian insurers and their clients used up the existing limit, the bank wrote on Tuesday, Oct. 13.
The scheme, known as the Ukraine Recovery and Reconstruction Guarantee Facility (URGF), will expand its coverage to include the transport and storage of gas-related assets and goods temporarily stored in warehouses, the EBRD said. The facility currently covers inland cargo, motor vehicle damage, and railway rolling stock.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The additional capacity is backed by donor coverage from the EU under its Ukraine Investment Framework. It will allow existing insurers INGO, Colonnade, and UNIQA to offer more war-risk cover, along with two insurers joining the scheme: USG, owned by the Vienna Insurance Group, and Universalna, owned by Canada’s Fairfax Financial Group.
The EBRD developed the URGF with Aon, a global professional services firm that manages the facility. Under the scheme, the EBRD guarantees global reinsurer MS Amlin against losses on war-related risks underwritten by participating Ukrainian insurers. The insurers, in turn, can obtain reinsurance coverage and widen their war-insurance offering.
The bank linked the expansion to the pressure on Ukraine’s economy. It cited intensifying Russian attacks on energy, transport, logistics, and civilian infrastructure, as well as the renewed blockade of Black Sea ports. Notably, reliable war-risk insurance is essential for companies to manage risk and keep operating.
Japan Signs Contract for Ukraine's SkyFall Interceptor Drones
As per EBRD reports, the initial €110 million ($123.2 million) guarantee is fully deployed. It was backed by donor coverage from France, Norway, Switzerland, the UK, and the TaiwanBusiness-EBRD Technical Cooperation Fund. It supported more than €500 million ($560 million) of reinsurance coverage for goods and vehicles across nearly 10,000 policies.
The EBRD and Aon introduced the bank guarantee in December 2024 to help private-sector insurers in Ukraine cover domestic cargo, motor vehicle damage, and railway rolling stock. Francis Malige, the EBRD’s Managing Director and Head of the Financial Institutions Group, had exclusively announced the facility three months earlier, in September 2024.

Russia exports grain via Arctic port of Murmansk for the first time
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:55:00 EEST
19:55:00 KST

Russia exports grain via Arctic port of Murmansk for the first time
Russia has begun using the Arctic port of Murmansk for the first time to export grain from Stavropol Krai amid problems with grain exports through the Black Sea.
Source: Latifundist.com, citing Russian media outlets, as reported by Ukrainska Pravda
Details: In October, Russia dispatched 40,000 tonnes of wheat from Stavropol Krai via the Arctic port of Murmansk.
"Russia is developing the new route amid problems with traditional grain export routes through the Black Sea. At the same time, transporting wheat to Murmansk costs 3 to 5 times more than through southern ports," the publication notes.
Potential grain transshipment volumes in Murmansk are estimated at 60,000 to 90,000 tonnes per month, or approximately 0.7 to 1.1 million tonnes per year.
For comparison, 46.3 million tonnes of grain were previously exported through the ports of the Azov-Black Sea basin.
"Thus, even at full capacity, Murmansk will be able to provide only a small fraction of these volumes," the report says.
One of the main problems with the new route is the need to deliver grain by rail from the southern regions of Russia to the Arctic port.
In addition, the infrastructure for grain cargo transshipment in Murmansk is currently underdeveloped.
Background:
- Russian grain exporters are trying to find new supply routes: the ports of the Azov-Black Sea basin are blocked, and exporting through the Baltic ports is too expensive.
- In Russia, grain shipments in the second ten days of September fell to 381,000 tonnes, compared to 1.6 million tonnes last year, as a result of Ukrainian Armed Forces strikes on grain terminals in Novorossiysk and vessels in the Sea of Azov.
- Since July 2026, the Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) have managed to disable 300 vessels of Russia's so-called "shadow fleet".
- It was previously reported that Russian grain exports, which bring about US$15 billion into the aggressor country's economy annually, have been almost completely paralysed by Ukrainian strikes on ports in the Azov and Black seas.
- In the first two weeks of August alone, the export of Ukrainian grain fell by 75% compared to the same period last year. Russian strikes almost halted transportation through Black Sea ports at the height of the harvest.

Libya seizes nearly $1 million worth of hashish (PHOTOS)
The Libyan authorities have seized around 400 kg of hashish worth nearly $1 million near the eastern coastal city of Tobruk, officials reported on Sunday. Several suspects were arrested in the operation, with investigators saying the drugs were smuggled across the border from Egypt.
The shipment, valued at approximately 6 million Libyan dinars ($934,000), was discovered on Saturday at a house in an agricultural area southeast of Tobruk, according to Ahmed al-Mismari, an information and documentation officer at Libya’s anti-drugs agency. The suspects included Libyan and Egyptian nationals, although officials did not confirm the number detained.
“The preliminary investigations revealed the shipment had been smuggled across the border with Egypt and was intended for local marketing and distribution within the Libyan market,” Mismari told Reuters.
Photographs released by the agency showed large quantities of hashish packed in gold-and-black wrappers. The packages carried several markings, including a horse symbol and the year 2026.
The seizures follow another major drug interception in September, when Libyan security officers discovered approximately 100,000 ecstasy tablets smuggled from Europe. The pills, shaped like the face of former Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, were concealed inside a cargo van, the Deterrence Agency for Combating Terrorism and Organized Crime said.
In another operation in Tobruk on June 10, Libya’s anti-drugs agency reported seizing 86,900 tablets of Tamol and tramadol worth approximately 2.17 million Libyan dinars ($338,000) during a raid on a farm. An Egyptian national was arrested after officers also found a bottle of imported alcohol and a piece of hashish at the property.
Libya has emerged as a major North African transit hub for synthetic drugs and other narcotics targeting domestic and regional markets, according to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC). The UN agency notes that trafficking networks are actively exploiting the security vacuums and political fragmentation left in the wake of the 2011 NATO-backed overthrow of Muammar Gaddafi. Today, the nation remains divided between the Government of National Unity based in Tripoli and the eastern administration backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar.
In 2025, Libya’s eastern-based anti-drugs agency seized over 6.4 tonnes of hashish, 68.4 kg of cocaine, and nearly 1.9 million narcotic tablets worth a total of $34.3 million, according to the Libyan News Agency.
