China sentences 3 people to death for running scam centers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:53:26 UTC
19:53:26 KST

China sentences 3 people to death for running brutal scam centers in Myanmar
A Chinese court sentenced three members of a criminal gang to death on Tuesday for operating a network of brutal scam centers in Myanmar's Kokang region on the border with China, while jailing dozens more.
China has stepped up cooperation with Southeast Asian nations to crack down on a vast industry that has flourished in the region in recent years to fleece people out of billions of dollars.
Those conducting the online scams are sometimes willing con artists, and other times trafficked foreign nationals -- many Chinese -- tricked themselves into work and held in prison-like compounds.
Quanzhou Intermediate People's Court said in a statement on Tuesday that it had sentenced Wei Huairen, Chen Dawei, and Liao Jingfang to death for their involvement in the "Wei family criminal gang."
The gang was involved in crimes including drug trafficking, organizing prostitution, operating illegal casinos, telecommunications fraud, and the murder of at least two Chinese citizens, the court said.
Wei Huairen was identified as one of the group's leaders and found guilty of several crimes including murder, the court said.
The gang's operations netted more than 12.2 billion yuan ($1.8 billion).
Another three gang members were handed life sentences, while 55 more were given prison terms ranging from 24 years to three years and three months, the court said.
Analysts describe the Wei clan as one of the "four families" running crime syndicates in Kokang.
China's state broadcaster CCTV on Tuesday called them the "most violent criminal force in northern Myanmar", having created an "iron triangle of political, military, and business criminal activities."
It described the gang as operating 14 "large-scale" scam compounds and luring "large numbers" of Chinese to Myanmar through fake promises of high wages.
Police had also discovered remains of victims bound with iron chains and with bullet holes in their skulls, CCTV said.
Members of the Wei family were first indicted in October 2025.
In January, China executed 11 people, including members of the "Ming family criminal gang."
The following month, four members of the notorious Bai clan were executed for crimes including "fraud, intentional homicide, intentional injury, kidnapping, extortion."
A growing, illegal international business
The United Nations warned that Chinese and Southeast Asian gangs are raking in tens of billions of dollars a year through cyber scam centers.
Sprawling compounds where internet tricksters target people with romance and business cons have thrived along Myanmar's loosely governed border during its civil war, which was sparked by a 2021 coup.
While Myanmar's border region has been a hotbed of the illegal activity, the industry has spread to South America, Africa, the Middle East, Europe and some Pacific Islands, according to the U.N. Office on Drugs and Crime.
A CBS News investigation in 2024 revealed the massive fraud operations targeting unsuspecting Americans from scam centers in Ghana, where young Ghanaians are lured into potentially lucrative lives of cyber fraud, but quickly become tools of transnational criminal syndicates that work in what's become a billion-dollar industry.
The U.N. estimates that hundreds of thousands of people are working in scam centers globally, and the flourishing centers in Myanmar have drawn many workers from Southeast Asia as well as China.
Experts say Myanmar's military, which has ruled over the country since seizing power in the 2021 coup, has long turned a blind eye to the scam centers, profits from which are believed to go to its militia allies, who are crucial collaborators in their fight against rebels.
But the junta has also faced pressure to shut down scam operations from its military backer China, irked at its citizens both participating in and being targeted by the scams

Iran sitting volleyball target historic fifth consecutive Asian Para Games gold
TEHRAN - Iran’s men’s sitting volleyball team will head into the upcoming Asian Para Games in Nagoya with a clear objective: extend their remarkable dominance and capture a fifth consecutive gold medal at the continental multi-sport event.
With an impressive championship record, a squad featuring some of the world’s most recognizable sitting volleyball stars, and a proud tradition of success, Iran will once again be among the leading contenders for the title.
The Iranian team are scheduled to face Thailand on Oct. 20 and Kazakhstan on Oct. 21, with both matches set to play an important role in determining the team’s progress through the competition. The opening fixtures will provide an early test of Iran’s preparation, consistency and ability to handle the pressure that comes with defending a long-standing winning record.
Iran’s record at the previous four editions of the Asian Para Games speaks volumes about the team’s quality and consistency. Having won gold at each of the last four editions, the Iranian side have established themselves as the powerhouses in men’s sitting volleyball and set a benchmark that their rivals will be eager to challenge.
Winning a single major championship requires talent, teamwork and determination. Maintaining that level of excellence across four consecutive editions, however, demands much more. Iran’s sustained success reflects years of experience, a strong competitive culture and the ability to perform when the stakes are highest.
The challenge in Nagoya will be to translate that history into another title. Past achievements provide confidence, but they also bring additional pressure, as every opponent will be motivated to end Iran’s winning streak. The Iranian players will therefore need to approach each match with focus and discipline, treating every contest as a new challenge rather than relying on their reputation.
A fifth consecutive gold would represent another major milestone for Iranian sitting volleyball, further strengthening the country’s position among Asia’s leading nations in para sport.
Iran’s hopes will be boosted by the presence of established stars such as Morteza Mehrzad, Sadegh Bigdeli and Meysam Alipour. Their experience and individual qualities could prove valuable as the team seeks to navigate the tournament and maintain its position at the top of the podium.

Nobel peace laureate Navi Pillay urges US to defend human rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:50:32 UTC
19:50:32 KST

US should become rights defender once more, Nobel peace laureate Pillay says
THE HAGUE, Oct 13 - Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay urged the United States on Tuesday to resume its traditional role of defender of human rights and freedom for the rest of the world as Washington campaigns to undermine the International Criminal Court.
"My message is: 'You have to get back to playing your serious role as a leader, playing a liberatory role for the rest of the world'," Pillay, 85, told Reuters in The Hague, where she is currently a judge at the United Nations' highest legal body, the International Court of Justice.
Hours after Pillay was announced as the winner of the Peace Prize on Friday, the United States announced sweeping sanctions aimed at her former employer, the International Criminal Court.
She said the timing of the sanctions, an unprecedented attack on an institution founded by international treaty, could not be coincidental.
"I think it's very unfortunate. However, the plans of targeting international criminal justice through the ICC were brewing all the time," Pillay said.
UN INQUIRY FOUND ISRAEL COMMITTED GENOCIDE IN GAZA
"That's why the first thing I did when I returned from Nuremberg to The Hague is to go to the staff of the ICC to show solidarity for their work in promoting international criminal justice and to protect those who've already been sanctioned."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday called the ICC a "rogue court" that would never be allowed to prosecute Americans. The sanctions included a six-month grace period, and some exemptions for transactions for telecoms, software, payment of pensions and those related to detainees.
The US has long been hostile to the court, especially the statute that says the ICC has jurisdiction not only over nationals of member states but also over others alleged to have committed atrocity crimes on the territory of member states.
President Donald Trump was furious in particular with the arrest warrants issued in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant, and the administration has in recent months escalated its campaign against the ICC.
Pillay last year chaired a UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory that concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Israel dismissed the report at the time as "scandalous".
PILLAY IS ONLY TWENTY-FIRST WOMAN TO WIN NOBEL PEACE PRIZE
On Tuesday, Pillay called the backlash against the report "false propaganda by lobbies that promote Israel".
Her first thought when she learned she had won the Nobel Peace Prize was that she was only the 21st woman to win it since 1901. "That in itself speaks to how entrenched inequality against women is."
During her time as a judge on the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda in the 1990s, Pillay was part of a bench that issued a landmark judgment that rape and sexual violence could constitute acts of genocide.
Even now, she said sexual violence was still not being pursued enough in war crimes cases, in part because mainly male prosecutors believed that doing so would detract from their cases.
Rather than withdrawing into private life once she finishes her term at the ICJ, Pillay plans to work on addressing that issue:
"There is a solid base, laid not only by the Rwanda tribunal but by subsequent international tribunals, that you can no longer ignore sexual violence as collateral damage or as a 'reward for soldiers'." REUTERS

david altrath on architectural photography as an experience of space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:50:16 UTC
19:50:16 KST

david altrath on architectural photography as an experience of space
in a personal reflection on his practice, the architectural photographer considers what happens between experiencing a building in person and translating that experience into a photograph.
[ADVERTISEMENT]
before the first photograph
Sometimes I arrive at a building and don’t take a photograph for the first hour. I walk around. I look at the light, the floor, the ceiling, the way one room leads into another. I pay attention to the materials and how they change depending on where I stand. Sometimes I know the building well from photographs. Sometimes I have travelled a long way to see a place I have been curious about for years. Other times, I arrive with very little idea of what to expect. Usually, I have an idea of what I am looking for. It is quite often wrong.
Once I am actually there, the building starts to feel different. A photograph can give you an idea of a place, but it can never really tell you what it feels like to stand inside it. You don’t know how the shadows fall, how the light moves through the room, how loud the space is, how cold the concrete feels, or how your perception changes as you walk through it. I think this is one of the reasons I became interested in photographing architecture in the first place. I like the moment when a building stops being an object and becomes an experience.
LOOKING BEYOND THE FAMILIAR IMAGE
I don’t enter a building thinking about how to make it look impressive. Especially with places that are already well known, I am more interested in finding something beyond the images I have seen before. There might be a famous view, a perfect symmetry or a photograph that seems to represent the building. When I finally stand there, that image is inevitably somewhere in the back of my head. But I don’t want to simply reproduce it. I want to find out what I see when I am actually there.
Sometimes that means looking for a different viewpoint. Sometimes it is a detail that would be easy to overlook: a shadow moving across a wall, a reflection, the way two surfaces meet, or a person crossing a space at just the right moment. Often, it is simply about waiting. The light might not be right, or I might not have understood the space yet. So I walk around some more, trying to work out what catches my attention and why.
LEARNING TO SEE THROUGH THE CAMERA
I often wonder whether I would look at buildings in the same way if I wasn’t photographing them. Probably not. The camera has made me much more aware of things I might otherwise walk past. I notice distances, edges, repetitions and small changes in light. I look at how a dark opening frames another room, or how a single person changes the scale of an enormous space.
The camera also forces me to make decisions. Where do I stand? What do I leave outside the frame? How much of the room do I actually need? Sometimes moving half a metre changes the entire image. Photographing architecture is not simply about documenting what is there. It is about choosing a particular way of seeing it. Two people can stand in exactly the same room and come away with completely different photographs. The building hasn’t changed, but the position of the person looking at it has.
WHEN A BUILDING BECOMES MORE THAN AN IMAGE
I am drawn to architecture with a strong visual language: monumental concrete structures, large churches, repetitive facades and vast interior spaces. But I don’t photograph these places simply because they are spectacular. In fact, the spectacle can sometimes get in the way. I am more interested in what happens when the first impression wears off and I begin to notice things that are less obvious. The Barbican in London is a good example. It is an incredibly recognisable place, and there are countless photographs of its architecture. But spending time there changes the way you see it. The concrete is only one part of the experience. There is the vegetation, the water, the people, the light and the small domestic details. The building becomes less like an image and more like a place.
Something similar happens in churches, although each space offers a very different experience. At Grundtvigs Kirke in Copenhagen, the scale and almost overwhelming repetition of the brick architecture make an immediate impression. After spending some time there, however, my attention shifts towards quieter details: the way the light falls into the space, the rhythm of the columns, the subtle changes in colour and shadow. At the CBR Building in Brussels, I find myself looking at the relationships between forms rather than the building as a whole. Repetition, geometry and the way different elements come together begin to shape the image. The longer I look, the less I am interested in capturing the building in a single, defining photograph. Instead, I start noticing smaller relationships that might otherwise go unnoticed. For me, this is often where photographing architecture becomes interesting: when the building stops being a single object and becomes a series of observations.
In places like these, photography becomes less about showing what a building looks like and more about understanding how you experience it. The same applies to spaces that are not monumental at all. In a greenhouse, for example, the relationship between architecture and nature becomes just as important as the structure itself. Glass, steel and concrete meet plants, changing light and humidity. The architecture shapes the environment, but the living things inside it also change how the space feels. What interests me is often this relationship between different elements, rather than any one of them on its own.
WHAT PHOTOGRAPHY CAN AND CANNOT CAPTURE
Of course, something is lost when a physical space becomes a photograph. An image removes sound, temperature, smell and movement. It flattens distance and turns something you can walk through into something you can hold in your hands. A photograph of a church doesn’t tell you how your footsteps sound inside it. A photograph of a greenhouse doesn’t convey its humidity. A photograph of a concrete wall can’t tell you how cold it feels.
And yet, something else can appear. The camera can isolate a relationship that is difficult to notice while you are simply moving through a space. It can bring together elements that were physically far apart, or make a small detail suddenly feel monumental. Sometimes I only understand what attracted me to a space after I have photographed it. You don’t always know exactly what you are looking at until you see the picture.
This is also what makes the photographer’s role interesting to me. When I enter a building, I am not only looking for a picture. I am trying to understand how the space can be experienced. Where does it make you slow down? Where does it direct your movement? What does it hide, and what does it reveal? As a photographer, I am a spectator, too. I react to the architecture like anyone else, but I can choose to freeze one particular moment of that experience.
INVITING OTHERS TO LOOK AGAIN
Once the photograph is made, however, I am no longer the only person looking. The image becomes someone else’s starting point. The person looking at it has never stood where I stood. They don’t know what happened just outside the frame, how long I waited or what the room sounded like. They bring their own memories and expectations to the image. They might see something completely different from what I saw when I made it, and I like that.
The longer I photograph architecture, the less interested I become in simply showing what a building looks like. I am more interested in what makes us stop and look. Why do we pause in one particular place? Why does one room stay in our memory while another disappears? Why can a certain quality of light suddenly change the way we understand a space? Photography doesn’t really answer these questions. It just makes me pay attention to them. Perhaps that is what I am looking for when I photograph a building: not the perfect view, and not necessarily the most spectacular one, but the moment when looking becomes an experience in itself.
The camera is an excuse to stop, to wait and to look again. And then, hopefully, to make someone else want to look, too.
David Altrath is a Hamburg-based photographer specializing in architecture and reportage. Since graduating from Merz Akademie in Stuttgart in 2018, he has worked on a range of commissions and independent projects, with work featured in magazines, websites, and corporate and public-sector projects.

photographer: David Altrath | @davidaltrath

Source: Philippe Sands in an interview with the German publication Börsenblatt
Details: Sands said this will be his fourth book exploring the themes of international crimes, justice and the search for accountability, following his previous works, East West Street: On the Origins of Genocide and Crimes against Humanity, The Ratline: Love, Lies and Justice on the Trail of a Nazi Fugitive and 38 Londres Street: On Pinochet in London and a Nazi in Patagonia.
Sands noted that he had not initially planned to extend the trilogy, but the fourth book is set to be released in 2030.
He said the book will focus on the creation of the special tribunal through the story of the killing of Victoria Amelina, whom he knew personally. Amelina died in 2023 following a Russian missile attack on a restaurant where she was eating pizza. At the heart of all Sands' works is the search for ways to prosecute international crimes. He said he has realised it is helpful to recount a great historical, political and legal drama through the prism of a personal story, as this makes it easier for people to understand the connections.
Details: In 2022, Philippe Sands and Victoria Amelina appeared together at the Lviv International BookForum, where they spoke about accountability and justice during wartime.
Sands is one of the initiators behind the creation of a special tribunal to investigate the crime of aggression against Ukraine. He said the new body is intended to plug a legal gap, as the International Criminal Court lacks the relevant jurisdiction. The search for effective ways to punish international crimes remains the central theme of all of Sands' works.
For reference: Victoria Amelina was a Ukrainian writer and public figure, a winner of the Joseph Conrad-Korzeniowski Literary Prize and nominee for the Angelus Central European Literature Award.
When the full-scale invasion began, Victoria paused her fiction writing and joined Truth Hounds, an organisation documenting human rights violations.
She also took part in charity trips with PEN Ukraine writers to recently liberated territories.
Victoria was injured in a Russian missile strike on a restaurant in Kramatorsk on 27 June 2023. At the time she was accompanying a delegation of Colombian writers and reporters on a trip to eastern Ukraine.
Despite doctors' efforts, Victoria died on 1 July 2023.
Philippe Sands is a lawyer and professor of international law at University College London. He also works at the UN International Court of Justice in The Hague as a human rights lawyer. Sands has been involved in international law cases concerning Augusto Pinochet and the Chagos Archipelago.
In addition to his legal and academic work, he writes narrative non-fiction.
Sands's father originated from what is now Lithuania and his mother was from Lviv. Sands himself was born in London.

Sweden's centre-left opposition bloc won 176 seats in parliament, versus 173 for outgoing Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's right-wing bloc, which includes the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats, in the 13 September election.
Sweden's Social Democratic party leader Magdalena Andersson said Tuesday she had failed to form a government with the three other parties in the left-wing bloc following last month's election.
"My overall assessment is that progress has been made, but at the same time, the conditions are currently not in place to form a government that can be tolerated by the parliament," Andersson told a press conference.
She spoke after reporting back to parliament speaker Andreas Norlen, who had tasked her with gauging conditions to form a government after the September 13 elections.
Shortly after Andersson's announcement, Norlen told a separate press conference that parliament would still be asked to vote on whether to make her prime minister.
Norlen said there had been agreement from the beginning that Andersson's talks on forming a government "would conclude with a prime ministerial vote regardless of how the exploratory talks had gone".
The speaker said a vote would be scheduled for Thursday, while conceding that Andersson would likely fail to be voted in as premier.
After that vote, Norlen said he would speak to the party leader once again to reassess who the next candidate should be.
Sweden's centre-left opposition bloc won 176 seats in parliament, versus 173 for outgoing Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's right-wing bloc, which includes the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats, in the September 13 election.
In Andersson's bloc, the Centre Party has said it will oppose a government that includes cabinet posts for the Left Party, which has in turn insisted it will only support a left-wing government of which it is a member.
Under the Swedish system, a prime minister can secure office so long as a majority in parliament does not vote against them.
Norlen first tasked Andersson with starting government talks on September 18, but she gave up on September 28, after failing to unite the three other parties in her group due to deep ideological differences.
With no apparent changes in the parties' positions, Andersson was tasked with trying again.
After Andersson's attempt, Norlen is expected to assign the task to Kristersson, who currently leads a caretaker government.
Speaking to reporters, Norlen said he considered Kristersson a natural candidate but the speaker did not wish to commit to that too soon and would "respect the process."
Kristersson would need to convince an opposition party to support him or at least not vote against him.
The speaker of parliament has four attempts at proposing a prime minister for parliament to vote on. If the fourth attempt fails, a snap election must be called.

Food worth millions of euros spoiled in cyberattack on French stores
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:49:30 UTC
19:49:30 KST

Hundreds of French supermarkets have been hit by a cyberattack that caused refrigerators and freezers to warm up, spoiling fresh and frozen food worth millions of euros, reports the BBC.
Cybercriminals gained control of the software monitoring temperatures in the refrigerators and freezers and forced the units to heat up to 50 degrees Celsius. The CEO of Coopérative U stated that several of the company's supermarkets faced an attack of unprecedented scale and severity. More than 100 of the company's stores were affected, and 180 Intermarché stores were also targeted. A company representative said that another 100 stores were disconnected from the internet to prevent the attack.
Other food retailers—Carrefour, Monoprix, and E.Leclerc—were also affected by the cyberattack. All the companies hit by the attack used software developed by the Danish firm Danfoss, which allows for the remote regulation of temperatures in refrigerators and freezers. Under normal conditions, supermarket freezers undergo a brief defrosting cycle at night, during which the temperature rises only slightly. Meanwhile, cybercriminals caused the equipment to overheat and maintain high temperatures. Danfoss has not confirmed reports regarding the specific temperatures reached by the units. The company merely stated that the cyberattack affected older models of freezers and refrigerators whose software could not be updated to mitigate the risks, adding that it had long recommended replacing equipment utilizing the remote control software.
The full extent of the attack remains unknown; however, information provided by certain supermarket chains indicates that 400 out of approximately 15,000 supermarkets in France were affected.
Carrefour reported that the refrigeration control systems in 80 of its stores (out of a total of 6,000) were compromised. Monoprix stated that about 5% of its more than 400 stores were affected and that food products whose safety could not be guaranteed were withdrawn from sale. The Mousquetaires Group, which owns the Intermarché and Netto supermarket chains, told the BBC that some fresh and frozen food display units were still not functioning on the afternoon of the 12th of October. The stores reportedly took all necessary measures and removed products from the affected display cases, and staff are working to restock the shelves as quickly as possible.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

The redesigned structures appear intended to address these limitations while improving aerodynamic performance and potentially accommodating different weapon configurations.
The Mi-8AMTSh-VN, also known as the Sapsan, is a specialized version of Russia’s Mi-8 transport helicopter developed to support special operations missions, including troop deployments in difficult environments.

In response to the Iranian authorities arbitrarily executing five people convicted in relation to the January 2026 protests in the space of a week, between 30 September and 5 October – Ali Hemmati Sistanian, Alireza Raisi, Alireza Sepahi, Majid Nikandish and Siavash Jamshidi Kheirabadi – following grossly unfair torture-tainted trials, Diana Eltahawy, Deputy Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa at Amnesty International said:
“The arbitrary executions of these five young men serves as another chilling reminder of how the Iranian authorities weaponize the death penalty to render the cost of dissent so high that it terrorizes the population into silence and deters further mass uprisings challenging their repressive decades-long rule.
“These executions followed reports illustrating a frightening and familiar pattern: denial of access to lawyers during interrogations, refusal to investigate defendants’ claims of torture and other ill-treatment, accusations of involvement in the killing of members of security forces and other violent and non-violent acts during protests, the use of televised forced ‘confessions’ as evidence, and trials before Revolutionary Courts that are inherently unfair. For instance, Alireza Sepahi reported being subjected to torture and other ill-treatment and was denied access to a lawyer during interrogations at the investigation stage. Such proceedings make a mockery of justice, laying bare the Iranian authorities’ utter disregard for the right to life.
“Scores of people including dissidents and protesters remain at risk of politically motivated executions as authorities intensify repression citing ‘wartime conditions’ and national security threats, increasing the urgent need for coordinated diplomatic pressure on Iran to halt all planned executions.
“Systemic impunity has emboldened Iran’s authorities to continue their assault on the right to life and other human rights, underscoring the urgent need for the referral of the situation in Iran to the International Criminal Court by the UN Security Council and the establishment of an international criminal justice mechanism for Iran through the UN General Assembly.”
Background
Alireza Raisi and Alireza Sepahi were executed in Esfahan on 5 October 2026. According to Mizan News Agency, the judiciary’s media outlet, they were part of the “Alikhani Square” mass trial in which authorities accused defendants of various violent and non-violent acts during protests that took place in Esfahan on 8 January 2026, including blocking streets, destruction of property, arson, and involvement in the deaths of four security agents. The men were sentenced to death after a grossly unfair trial in which their forced “confessions” were broadcast on state media on 23 January 2026, prior to their trial. Amnesty International learned that agents subjected Alireza Sepahi to torture and other ill-treatment in detention, including prolonged solitary confinement, beatings and electric shocks. According to Mizan News Agency, the men were sentenced to death for “‘membership in an armed rebellion group (baghi); ‘waging war against God’ (moharebeh) through drawing weapons and creating fear, terror and insecurity in the surrounding area; and “corruption on earth” (efsad-e fel arz) through acts against individuals’ physical integrity and national security that severely disrupted public order and created widespread insecurity, incitement to war and killing, and other criminal acts, including acts against national security”. Five other men convicted in the same case were previously executed and at least eight others are at risk.
Majid Nikandish and Ali Hemmati Sistanian were executed on 30 September 2026 in Mashhad, Razavi Khorasan province. According to Mizan News Agency, they were accused of various violent and non-violent acts during protests in Mashhad on 8 January 2026 that authorities labelled a “coup”, including blocking streets, destruction of property, arson, and involvement in the deaths of four members of the security forces. Their televised forced “confessions”, including those taken at the scene of their arrest and subsequent interrogations when they had no access to a lawyer, were used as evidence to convict and sentence them to death. According to Iran Human Rights, an independent human rights organization based outside Iran, Majid Nikandish was subjected to torture and other ill-treatment, including through prolonged solitary confinement and suspension from his arms, resulting in a dislocated shoulder and broken jaw.
Siavash Jamshidi Kheirabadi was executed on 3 October 2026 in Shahr-e Kord, Chaharmahal and Bakhtiari province. According to Mizan News Agency, he was convicted and sentenced to death in relation to protests that took place on 8 January 2026 in Shahr-e Kord on the charges of “’waging war against God’ (moharebeh) through drawing a firearm and firing it” and “gathering and colluding to commit crimes against national security”. Amnesty International has consistently documented the use of the latter charge against protesters, dissidents and human rights defenders for taking part in protests and other gatherings. Siavash Jamshidi Kheirabadi forced “confessions” were televised and used as evidence to convict him and sentence him to death.
Iranian authorities have executed at least 34 individuals in relation to the January 2026 uprising, during which security forces used unlawful lethal force on a massive scale, killing thousands of protesters and bystanders on 8 and 9 January. Politically motivated executions intensified further following the unlawful US-Israeli attacks on Iran on 28 February 2026, while executions for drug-related and other offences have continued.
Amnesty International opposes the death penalty unconditionally, for all crimes and under any circumstances.

NATO Unveils “Theory of Victory” to Stop Russian Attack With Drones and Missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:48:50 UTC
19:48:50 KST

- Category
- World
NATO Unveils “Theory of Victory” to Stop Russian Attack With Drones and Missiles
NATO has outlined a new defense strategy, dubbed the “Theory of Victory,,” designed to repel a potential Russian attack by halting its initial offensive, preventing further advances, and systematically weakening enemy forces.
According to The Wall Street Journal on October 12, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, General Alexus Grynkewich, presented the strategy during the Warsaw Security Forum, revealing that its classified version had been finalized three months earlier.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Drawing on lessons from Ukraine’s battlefield experience, the strategy prioritizes investment in what Grynkewich called “affordable mass,” focusing on relatively low-cost drones to supplement NATO’s advanced weapons systems, according to the publication.
Under the plan, NATO’s immediate priority in the event of a Russian attack would be to stop the initial assault.
“Enemy formations will be starved of replenishment. Enemy commanders will be unable to control their forces. Enemy forces and support capabilities will be reduced and destroyed,” Grynkewich said.
The NATO commander emphasized that the Alliance’s objective would not be to defeat Russia as a state or undermine its government, but rather to repel any attack against NATO territory.
According to The Wall Street Journal, the strategy builds on earlier work by General Chris Donahue, a former commander of US Army forces in Europe and NATO’s Allied Land Command.
The approach is intended to address concerns that Russia’s geographical advantages and extensive defense industry could enable it to launch an offensive against the Baltic states, Poland, or other NATO members before the Alliance could organize a substantial military response.
A central element of the strategy involves establishing a large autonomous zone in which unmanned aerial vehicles and ground-based robotic systems would be deployed to disrupt and suppress Russian attacks while minimizing casualties among allied forces.
At the same time, NATO would use long-range missiles to strike Russian command centers and air defense systems in the Kaliningrad exclave, near St. Petersburg, and in Belarus. According to The Wall Street Journal, these operations would aim to weaken Russia’s ability to control the airspace, creating conditions for the US Army’s V Corps and other NATO ground forces to launch counterattacks.
NATO air forces would also move rapidly to target Russian reinforcements approaching the battlefield and strike additional military assets behind enemy lines.
The operations would be supported by a secure information-sharing network known as a “data backbone,” allowing NATO forces to exchange classified targeting data almost instantaneously through a cloud-based system. According to reports, components of the network have already been tested in the Middle East during the US war with Iran.
The broader concept, known as the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative, is intended to strengthen NATO’s ability to respond rapidly to potential Russian aggression.
According to US military officials cited by The Wall Street Journal, the initiative ultimately aims to deter Russian leader Vladimir Putin from launching an attack against the Alliance.
The strategy also reflects NATO’s broader shift toward integrating emerging technologies into military operations, particularly those that have demonstrated their effectiveness on Ukraine’s battlefield.
On August 12, Bild reported that NATO was increasingly prioritizing drones, satellite technology, advanced sensors, and artificial intelligence as part of its efforts to modernize its military capabilities.
The move toward greater automation draws on Ukraine’s experience deploying AI-powered drone swarms capable of identifying targets, coordinating their movements, and conducting strikes autonomously, even when Russian electronic warfare disrupts communication with human operators.

MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Design engineers from the Moscow Aviation Institute (MAI) National Research University and Tupolev JSC have begun working on modifications to flight controls of the Tupolev Tu-214 medium-range passenger aircraft in order to reduce the cockpit crew from three to two, the university’s press office told TASS.
The Tu-214 is a Russian twin-engine medium-haul airliner with a flight range of up to 4,500 kilometers.
"The designers face a challenge that is crucial for commercial viability: to make changes to the aircraft’s control system that will reduce the workload on the crew and cut the number of people in the cockpit from three to two by eliminating the flight engineer position. Specialists have already begun analyzing the onboard equipment system and have identified the components that require optimization or replacement. At the same time, they're trying to keep costs to a minimum for the work and subsequent certification procedures. The solution must fit within the project’s strict deadlines," the statement reads.
Participants in the MAI continuing education program will prepare a preliminary cost estimate, a work schedule, and a roadmap for collaboration with industry partners. The design of an integration test bench for the avionics suite - necessary to prepare the upgraded system for ground and flight testing - will also be considered. The S.P. Gorbunov Kazan Aviation Plant, a subsidiary of Tupolev JSC, where the Tu-214 is currently in serial production, will serve as the production base for the program.
"We see that our partners are interested and ready to actively participate in this project. In the near future, work will be carried out to develop a roadmap, a cooperation framework, and the structure of the team that will be responsible for the design and integration of the complex," said the program director, MAI Rector Mikhail Pogosyan, whose remarks are quoted in the press release. In addition to technical specialists, Tupolev JSC is represented by Managing Director Yury Abrosimov and his deputy, Chief Designer Yevgeny Deyanov.
The program is expected to run through the end of October and conclude with a final evaluation. The leadership of MAI and Tupolev JSC will summarize the results of the work and assess the impact of the proposed organizational and technical solutions on the project’s economics.

Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-runs and drunk driving by U.S. military personnel have long triggered protests on the southern Japanese island, which has for years urged other regions of the country to share the burden of hosting U.S. troops.
"We plan to hold discussions including whether the existing rules are effectively functioning," Motegi said, adding that "matters such as patrols and curfew management" would be under review in talks with the United States.
The high-level bilateral consultations will examine off-duty conduct and the "liberty" policy governing off-base private activities of U.S. military personnel, he said.
The existing policy, updated in 2024 following a string of sexual assaults by U.S. military personnel in Okinawa, includes a ban on them drinking in public off-base between 1 a.m. and 5 a.m. or going to bars during those hours.
Japanese police arrested a U.S. Marine stationed on Okinawa early this month on suspicion of killing a 39-year-old woman at a hotel in Naha, the capital of Okinawa Orefecture. Word of the arrest drew outrage.
The U.S. military enacted a two-day operational pause after the Marine's arrest to reinforce discipline and standards, followed by a monthlong midnight-to-5 a.m. curfew.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Tuesday that "we began high-level, working-level consultations between Japan and the United States last week on what effective measures should be taken."
"The Japanese government will continue to do everything in its power both to address this case and to ensure that it does not happen again," she told a legislative committee session.
Motegi spoke by phone over the weekend with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who offered his "sincere condolences" over the alleged crime and pledged U.S. cooperation in the investigation.
Crimes committed by U.S. personnel have long been a thorn in relations between the close security allies.
A Japanese court sentenced a U.S. Marine accused of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison last year.
In 2017, a former U.S. Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
The United States has approximately 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa.

This tiny jurassic predator helped pave the way for the human brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:44:22 UTC
19:44:22 KST

This tiny jurassic predator helped pave the way for the human brain
A tiny, 165-million-year-old Jurassic predator reveals an evolutionary breakthrough that helped pave the way for modern mammals and the human brain.
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Bonn
- Summary:
- A 165-million-year-old fossil has revealed an extraordinary Jurassic predator that may help explain how mammals developed one of their most important evolutionary advantages. Although only 20 inches long, Megacauda sungei was a heavyweight among early mammal relatives, swimming through ancient waterways and hunting prey with specialized teeth. Its advanced swallowing anatomy reveals an early step toward the ability to safely nurse on milk, a key development in mammalian evolution.
- Share:
A furry predator that lived 165 million years ago is offering scientists an unexpected glimpse into the evolution of mammals. Known as Megacauda sungei, this ancient hunter measured only about half a meter (20 inches) from nose to tail, yet it was remarkably large compared with most of its Jurassic relatives. It hunted in the water, using teeth with backward-curving cusps to grip slippery prey.
Its most significant feature, however, was not its size or hunting ability. Researchers discovered evidence of a sophisticated soft palate that separated the mouth from the pharynx, the passage connecting the mouth to the throat. This anatomical development helped make it possible to swallow while maintaining the ability to breathe, an essential adaptation for mammals that nurse their young. The findings, from researchers in Shenyang, Chicago, and Bonn, have been published in the journal Nature.
How an Ancient Predator Reveals the Evolution of Swallowing
Many animals lack a soft palate and instead rely on a relatively simple arrangement of hyoid bones in the throat. Without the complex swallowing mechanism found in mammals, feeding can require very different movements.
Crocodiles, for example, lift their heads and make sudden jerking motions to move unchewed food down their throats. "This is achieved with the aid of gravity," explains paleontologist Prof. Dr. Thomas Martin from the University of Bonn.
Mammals have a more elaborate hyoid structure that allows them to swallow even when gravity is working against them. Humans, for instance, can drink through a straw while upside down and still breathe.
This ability has played an important role in mammalian evolution. It allows young mammals to consume nutrient-rich milk safely, preventing liquid from entering the nasal passages. By supporting effective nursing, this adaptation provided an important survival advantage.
"It was this adaptation that made brain development, eventually leading to humans, possible," stresses Martin. "The soft palate and the shaping of the oral cavity and pharynx are directly linked to the evolution of mammals."
Remarkably, Megacauda sungei already possessed evidence of this anatomical development millions of years before modern mammals appeared.
A 165-Million-Year-Old Predator Built for Swimming
With its short fur and broad, flattened tail, Megacauda sungei would have looked somewhat like a modern otter, beaver, or platypus. Its body was also well suited to moving through water.
Scientists used computed tomography scans of the fossil to create detailed three-dimensional reconstructions of its anatomy. These models suggest that the animal propelled itself through the water by paddling with its front legs and moving its tail in an undulating motion. Its hind legs likely helped it change direction.
"It is the earliest evidence of an aquatic lifestyle in mammals," says the paleontologist from the University of Bonn.
Its teeth revealed another unusual adaptation. Along with the backward-curving cusps that helped it catch aquatic prey, the animal possessed specialized canine teeth with three roots, a distinctive feature that surprised the researchers.
By comparing the fossil with other prehistoric specimens and living animals, the team determined that Megacauda sungei belonged to the docodonts, an extinct group of early mammal relatives known as mammaliaforms. These animals were especially widespread during the Jurassic Period. The fossil itself was discovered in Xiayingzi, Inner Mongolia.
A Tiny Giant in the Age of Dinosaurs
"The new species Megacauda sungei is the largest of the mammaliaforms from the Jurassic," says Thomas Martin.
At roughly half a meter long and weighing about two kilograms (4.4 pounds), this prehistoric "top predator" would seem insignificant beside modern giants such as elephants, rhinoceroses, and whales.
But size was relative in the Jurassic world.
The Mesozoic Era, which lasted from approximately 230 million to 66 million years ago, was dominated by dinosaurs. Early mammal relatives generally remained small, with many weighing only a few grams.
Against that backdrop, Megacauda sungei was unusually large. Although tiny by today's standards, this aquatic hunter was a heavyweight among the early mammal relatives that shared the planet with dinosaurs.
An Extraordinary Fossil Discovery in Inner Mongolia
The scientific importance of Megacauda sungei might never have been recognized without a fortunate series of events.
Years ago, the Paleontological Museum of Liaoning in Shenyang (China) acquired the fossil, which had been unearthed in Inner Mongolia, as part of a collection of specimens. Its exceptional features became apparent when three scientists examined it together: Prof. Dr. Chang-Fu Zhou from Shandong University (China), Prof. Dr. Zhe-Xi Luo from the University of Chicago (USA), and Prof. Dr. Thomas Martin from the University of Bonn.
Recognizing that the specimen represented a previously unknown species, the researchers chose to honor Prof. Sun Ge, the Honorary Director of the Paleontological Museum of Liaoning.
They combined the name "large tail" (Megacauda) with the species designation "sungei," creating the scientific name Megacauda sungei.
Establishing the animal's identity required years of detailed analysis, comparisons, classification, and documentation.
"It is the result of a long period of teamwork," says Thomas Martin.
The research has provided important new insights into the early history of mammals, particularly how rapidly their ancestors developed specialized bodies and lifestyles.
Other Jurassic docodont fossils show that members of this group were already adapting to very different environments. Some lived in trees, others burrowed underground like moles, and species such as Megacauda sungei were adapted to life in water.
"This shows how widespread docodonts were in the Northern Hemisphere and that this diverse group of animals developed very different lifestyles at an incredibly early stage," summarizes Martin.
Together, these discoveries reveal that long before modern mammals became dominant, their ancient relatives were already experimenting with an impressive range of ways to survive.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Bonn. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Y. Li, P. Li, A. I. Neander, H. Zhang, C.-F. Zhou, T. Martin, Z.-X. Luo. A Jurassic mammaliaform swimmer and transformation of the mammalian pharynx. Nature, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11107-0

The crew ignored orders from the authorities, and a collision occurred during the chase. One suspect was seriously injured and later died.
The two others, both foreign nationals, were arrested and will be brought before a judge at the Justice Campus in Lisbon, where any potential charges and pre-trial detention will be decided.
Code-named "Mare Nostrum", the operation was carried out under the Maritime Analysis and Operations Centre – Narcotics (MAOC-N), in coordination with the Portuguese Navy, the Maritime Police, Spain’s Guardia Civil and Italy’s Guardia di Finanza.

Estonia's plans to tighten health data access face conflicting bills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:41:00 UTC
19:41:00 KST

Estonia's plans to tighten health data access face conflicting bills
Estonia plans to require court approval for access to people's health data without their consent, but two bills proposing changes to the rules appear to contradict each other.
Current law allows health data to be disclosed without consent to establish the facts in criminal or other offense proceedings, however the chancellor of justice has said the provision is too broad and needs to be clarified.
Now the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs and the Ministry of Social Affairs have drafted separate bills, dubbed the Pakosta and Joller bills after the ministers involved.
Social Affairs Minister Karmen Joller (Reform) said her bill would merge three major health databases: the prescription and treatment-billing databases under the Estonian Health Insurance Fund (EHIF) and the centralized national health information system managed by the Health and Welfare Information Systems Center (TEHIK).
"It does not directly address how data is disclosed or when consent is needed or not," she noted.
The Pakosta bill, by contrast, sets conditions for officials to access health data, Joller added.
Attorney Carri Ginter warned that the Joller bill would essentially expand health data access while the Pakosta would sharply restrict it.
"I can't imagine the Riigikogu simply approving and rubber-stamping both government bills, because that would leave us with both very broad access to health data and an extremely narrow version of access at the same time," he said.
Joller explained regardless that under the planned changes, investigative authorities would need court approval to obtain health data without a person's consent.
"Until now, authorities have requested data not only from health databases but also directly from healthcare providers, such as hospitals and family doctors' offices," the minister said. "Going forward, healthcare providers will only be able to release such data under court order or with court approval."
Other agencies welcome greater clarity
Roger Kumm, head of the Prevention and Criminal Proceedings Bureau at the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA), said police support clearer rules.
What law enforcement needs, he said, is clarity on what police can request and in what cases — including "whether in criminal proceedings specifically or in offense proceedings more broadly, since some drug offenses are misdemeanors."
Health data can also serve as evidence in traffic collision investigations, Kumm continued.
"If someone is injured in a traffic collision, that is evidence in the proceedings and police process that kind of data too," he explained.
TEHIK director Margus Arm also welcomes clearer rules, saying the center would follow any new legal safeguards.
"Once additional safeguards are in place, we will act in accordance [with the law]," Arm said.
He said TEHIK has recently received numerous inquiries about the use of health data, but noted that people can most easily review their own data through the national Health Portal (Terviseportaal).

Putin-Trump deal about ‘much more’ than diesel – Serbia’s Vucic to RT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:38:47 UTC
19:38:47 KST

Putin-Trump deal about ‘much more’ than diesel – Serbia’s Vucic to RT
US President Donald Trump’s diesel deal with Russia is part of a broader geopolitical strategy to draw Moscow away from Beijing, Aleksandar Vucic has told RT Balkan in an exclusive interview.
According to Vucic, who recently stepped down as Serbian president to run for prime minister, Washington, which sees China as its main rival, hopes to weaken Beijing’s partnership with Russia by improving ties with Moscow.
Trump announced the deal following talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin on October 9. Moscow agreed to release more than 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets immediately, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and one million tons thereafter. Washington subsequently waived sanctions on Russian diesel until April 7, 2027.
Ahead of the deal, Trump blamed soaring fuel prices on Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries, although markets have also been disrupted by the US war with Iran, which has affected shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
“As far as Donald Trump is concerned, he is doing a smart thing for America, he is trying to do something to bring down the price per gallon… But I don’t think this is just about diesel,” Vucic said, noting that the initial 300,000 tons would cover less than a day’s US consumption.
With the US midterms approaching and Trump’s standoff with Tehran increasingly unpopular, Vucic suggested the deal could partly be aimed at winning over voters by lowering fuel prices. However, he suggested there was a larger geopolitical calculation behind the agreement.
“I think it is about something much more than this. Donald Trump knows that his main competitor is China. And is trying, in a sophisticated way, to move Russia somewhat away from China and bring it closer to the US.”
Asked whether Trump was seeking closer ties with Moscow, Vucic replied: “Of course.”
“If he is in conflict with Russia, he will only push Russia closer to China,” he explained. “Trump is trying, I assume, to draw Russia, China’s powerful and strong ally, at least a little away from that alliance.”
The Trump administration has long treated China as a major strategic rival. Its 2025 National Security Strategy calling for a rebalancing of economic ties with Beijing. Trump nevertheless hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington last month for talks on trade, Taiwan and Iran. The two sides agreed to extend their trade truce until January, but tensions over tariffs, technology and security persist.
Russia and China, meanwhile, have only deepened their strategic and energy cooperation in light of Ukraine-related Western sanctions on Moscow. Beijing has become Moscow’s biggest oil customer and a major buyer of Russian gas, with supplies expanding through the Power of Siberia pipeline as Russia redirected energy exports away from Europe.
Talking about Russia-US ties, Vucic also pointed to Washington’s diplomatic push to resolve the Ukraine conflict, saying its parallel negotiating channels with Moscow and Kiev show it is serious about reaching a settlement. However, he sees little prospect of an imminent breakthrough.
Vucic expressed hope that a peace deal could be reached within five to six months. Asked whether he fears that the conflict could evolve into a direct confrontation between Russia and the EU, Vucic replied: “I fear that, but I hope it won’t happen.”
Serbia has maintained close ties with Russia and, under Vucic, has resisted EU pressure to impose sanctions on Moscow over Ukraine, despite Belgrade’s ambitions to join the bloc. In the interview, Vucic again stressed the need to preserve Serbia’s traditional ties with Moscow despite external pressure, saying leaders must “keep a cool head and make rational and wise decisions.”
Vucic resigned during his second presidential term last month ahead of snap parliamentary elections scheduled for October 25. Barred by the Serbian constitution from seeking a third term, he is now seeking the prime minister’s post as a candidate for the ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).

Employment by algorithm: Lithuania moves to tighten rules for platform work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:37:00 UTC
19:37:00 KST

Lithuania’s parliament has taken the first step toward tightening rules for digital labour platforms – such as food delivery or ride hailing apps Wolt and Bolt – with proposed legislation aimed at improving working conditions and increasing transparency in algorithmic management.
The amendments, presented to lawmakers Tuesday by Deputy Social Security and Labour Minister Aušra Putk, would make it harder for platforms to classify workers as independent contractors if they cannot freely negotiate service prices or access essential job details, such as rates and addresses, before accepting assignments.
Lawmakers asked whether the changes would increase service prices.
“I cannot assess the impact on prices, as that depends on business practices, but naturally, protecting workers can increase costs,” Putk said.
The main amendment to the Labour Code received 85 votes in favour, with none opposed and eight abstentions. The proposals will now be reviewed by parliamentary committees before further votes in the full Seimas. The legislation has already been approved by the government and would require the president’s signature to take effect.
The measures implement an EU directive intended to improve the employment status of people working through digital platforms, strengthen oversight of algorithmic management and increase transparency.
Under the proposed rules, employment status would be determined primarily by the actual working relationship rather than the wording of a contract. Indicators of an employment relationship could include subordination and a lack of freedom to choose working hours, provide similar services to other clients, or accept or reject assignments without negative consequences.
Platforms would also face restrictions on collecting sensitive or private information unrelated to work, such as data about workers’ emotional states or conversations outside working hours. Workers would have the right to request explanations of automated decisions affecting them.
The Social Security and Labour Ministry estimates that about 28 million people work through digital platforms across the EU, with 5.5 million potentially misclassified.
In Lithuania, about 141,000 people worked through platforms, including around 33,000 ride-hailing drivers and couriers, according to Vilnius University data for 2024. The number of platform workers is projected to rise to 157,000 by 2028.
There are some 140 service platforms operating in the country, the most popular among them being Wolt, Bolt Food, Bolt, Uber, Ziticity, LastMile, Barbora, Trobos.
The ministry says platform workers in Lithuania are generally classified as self-employed and therefore lack access to certain benefits, including unemployment and workplace accident compensation.
The changes are scheduled to take effect December 2, with fines related to reclassification of employment relationships due to begin a year later, on December 2, 2027.
Implementation would require about €1.1 million in additional funding for the State Labour Inspectorate to cover staffing needs.

Study: Nearly 20% of Ukrainians view current Ukrainian-Polish relations as friendly or hostile
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:36:40 EEST
19:36:40 KST

According to a study by the Operative Sociology organization, 18.6% of Ukrainians consider the current state of Ukrainian-Polish relations to be friendly, while 19.5% view it as hostile.
Specifically, the survey, presented in Kyiv on Tuesday, asked respondents to assess the current state of relations between Ukraine and Poland.
The results showed that 2.4% described relations as entirely friendly, 16.2% as predominantly friendly, 57.6% as somewhat friendly and somewhat hostile, 15.5% as predominantly hostile, and 4% as entirely hostile; 4.1% found it difficult to answer.
Additionally, in a section dedicated to historical figures, Ukrainians were asked about their attitude toward Polish head of state Józef Piłsudski (1867–1935). Responses indicated that 8.7% held a completely negative view, 9% a mostly negative view, 12% a mixed (somewhat negative/somewhat positive) view, 7.5% a mostly positive view, and 3.7% a completely positive view; 52.3% stated they did not know who he was, 6.7% found it difficult to answer, and 0.1% declined to answer.
The study was conducted by the Operative Sociology organization, commissioned by the Ukrainian Institute of National Memory, between July 10 and July 18, 2026. The sample consists of 2,007 respondents from across Ukraine, excluding occupied territories. For this sample, the maximum margin of error is 2.2% at a 0.95 confidence level.

He also reported that another vessel was struck 17 nautical miles east of Krapets and subsequently sank, with one crew member rescued.

Land, water, clay shape Çanakkale Biennial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:33:34 UTC
19:33:34 KST

Spanning 15 venues, the biennial turns Çanakkale’s urban and rural landscape into an exhibition space.
Like tides that reshape coastlines, the 10th Çanakkale Biennial examines how nature, memory and human experience are transformed through the constant interaction between water and land, bringing together more than 60 artists from nine countries in northwestern Türkiye.
Titled “Metcezir // Ebb & Flow,” the biennial opened on Oct. 10 at the Troy Museum, drawing on Çanakkale’s coastal geography, ceramic traditions and archaeological heritage to explore the traces left by these encounters. Spread across 15 venues in the city center and surrounding rural settlements, the exhibition makes the region itself part of the experience.
The movement of the tides offers a framework for thinking about change: Shorelines erode and accumulate sediment, while landscapes preserve evidence of what has passed through them. The biennial extends this natural cycle to questions of cultural memory, material production and humanity’s relationship with the environment.
The setting lends the theme particular resonance. Situated along the Dardanelles, which connect the Aegean and Marmara seas, Çanakkale has long been shaped by the movement of water, its coastal livelihoods and its cultural history. The artworks explore how the natural world shapes human experience and how people, in turn, leave their mark on the environments they inhabit.
Ceramics take center stage
The Troy Museum anchors the biennial’s first “Special Focus: Ceramics,” bringing contemporary works by artists including Füreya Koral, Elif Uras and SEDNA into dialogue with the region’s archaeological heritage.
Among the participating artists is Lara Ögel, exhibiting ‘Gravity,’ who sees clay as more than a material, describing it as a body that reflects and carries lived experience. “The cracking, shedding, expanding and contracting of the clay are all deeply significant,” Ögel said. She views these physical changes as a visual map of inner experiences, with the material’s layers mirroring the emotional and existential changes people undergo. Working with ceramics, she added, requires patience, understanding and time, becoming a form of confrontation with one’s own soul.
SEDNA presents two new works inspired by memory and transformation. “İz” (Trace) draws on marks left by the sea on sand and the impressions experiences leave on the body and spirit. Its twisted form evokes sisterhood, interconnectedness and resilience. “TAÇ” (Crown), meanwhile, combines handmade glass scenes, plants collected from the museum garden and references to the sun and life cycles, presenting accumulated experience as a record of memory.
In the city center, Mavi Ev (Blue House) brings together ceramic and glass works, painting and digital art. Gülden Ataman’s ‘For Eyes That Listen, For Hands That Watch’ challenges conventional ideas about the material’s fragility and function. Rather than considering them musical instruments, she describes each piece as a “sound-seeking device” for acoustic exploration. “Their output depends entirely on the performer’s manual dexterity and acute listening skills,” Ataman said. The sounds that emerge depend on touch and the combinations chosen by each performer, potentially producing entirely new acoustic experiences. Local musicians explore these possibilities in a video installation at the venue.
German artist Gerrit Frohne-Brinkmann, meanwhile, juxtaposes a handcrafted ceramic snake with a mass-produced singing fish toy in ‘Pack.’ Drawing on Çanakkale’s historic ceramics, known for their animal motifs, he brings traditional craftsmanship into conversation with a familiar object of popular culture. “I really enjoy the confrontation between these two different styles of sculpture,” he said, highlighting the contrast between handmade and mass-produced objects that depict animals but carry different values and meanings.
The biennial extends into buildings whose previous uses reflect the city’s history. The Korfmann Library, housed in a former school and tobacco warehouse, presents works engaging with archaeological heritage and traditional building techniques, including Funda Susamoğlu’s response to a terracotta figure at the Troya Museum and Eymen Aktel’s work with adobe.
Along the Sarıçay riverbank, former acorn warehouses now house several exhibition spaces. MAHAL features Johannes Vogl’s Summer Rain – The Smell of Memories, which explores the scent of rain on Aegean soil and vegetation. The neighboring DemirHAN presents works by artists including Ozan Atalan and Mesut Öztürk, whose pieces draw on video, ceramic fragments and firebricks.
The Balıkhane, a working fish market, hosts works addressing marine ecosystems and coastal landscapes. These include Carmen Bouyer’s project connecting the Gediz and Rhône deltas and Annika Boll’s digitally constructed underwater environment. At the ASTİM industrial estate, visitors can see works by A. Serkan Aka and Gözde Mimiko Türkkan at Helin Boztepe Studio and by Manfred Heinze at Süleyman Yılmaz Studio. British artist Kay Aplin’s site-specific public artwork at Çanakkale Biennial Park draws on Troy’s nine archaeological settlement layers. Nine ceramic tile designs combine local botanical motifs with forms drawn from archaeological finds. Produced with the support of Kale Group, the installation is intended to remain in the city after the biennial closes.
Further afield, ORMOS in Yukarı Tartışık village hosts works by Can Altay, Renée Levi and Stijn Ank. The Adatepe Olive Oil Museum presents works by Andreas Treske and Fulya Çetin, while restored stone houses at İda Blue in Adatepe display works by Dilara Akay, Hakan Yılmaz and Meliha Coşkun.
The biennial also marks the 20th anniversary of the Çanakkale Biennial Initiative (CABININ), which has worked to sustain contemporary art in a city outside Türkiye’s main cultural centers. Together, the exhibitions, running until Nov. 20, invite visitors to consider change not as a clean break with the past, but as an ongoing process in which landscapes, materials and human experiences continually shape one another.

'Haunting' Israeli sexual abuse of Palestinian children exposed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:33:15 UTC
19:33:15 KST

Breadcrumb
'Haunting' accounts of Israeli sexual abuse of Palestinian children prompt calls for justice
Accounts of Palestinian schoolgirls afraid to cross Israeli military checkpoints after soldiers exposed themselves to women and girls stayed with Dr Rubin Minhas long after he reviewed the evidence.
For Minhas, a co-author of a new opinion piece in The BMJ, a leading medical journal, the descriptions were "haunting" – not only because of the sexual abuse, but because Palestinian children were forced to navigate military checkpoints simply to reach their classrooms.
"I think it just brought home to me how absolutely bizarre it is that having to go to school and pass through military checkpoints is the norm before we even get to the sexual violence," he told The New Arab.
The accounts include Palestinian schoolgirls in Hebron who feared passing through a checkpoint where Israeli soldiers had exposed their genitals to women and girls, according to a UN investigation cited by the authors.
Published on Tuesday, the article brings together evidence of conflict-related sexual violence against Palestinian women, men and children, exposing patterns of abuse across Israeli detention facilities, military checkpoints, raids and displacement sites, and demanding independent investigations and accountability.
Drawing on survivor testimonies, UN investigations and medical, humanitarian and human rights reports, the five authors examine how sexual violence has been used against Palestinians under Israeli occupation, and the devastating physical and psychological consequences for victims.
The purpose, Minhas said, was to draw together evidence "dispersed across accounts of detention, gendered abuse, humiliation, and displacement, and harm to children, to actually paint a picture of what was going on".
Conflict-related sexual violence, or CRSV, refers to sexual violence directly or indirectly linked to conflict. It encompasses rape, sexual torture, sexualised humiliation and reproductive harm, among other abuses.
'Occupation is violence'
For Palestinian children, the consequences of Israeli sexual violence extend far beyond the immediate abuse, affecting their education, relationships, psychological wellbeing and sense of safety.
The article cites a 2025 Save the Children report in which more than half of 165 Palestinian children, aged 12 to 17 at the time of detention, reported witnessing or experiencing sexual violence in Israeli detention, including rape threats, forced stripping and genital assault.
A separate 2026 UN investigation documented sexual and gender-based violence against Palestinian children during arrest and detention, including forced public nudity, sexual humiliation, rape threats, genital violence and allegations of rape.
In one particularly degrading incident documented in humanitarian and UN reports, a Palestinian boy was stripped and urinated on.
The Save the Children report also revealed the lasting psychological toll of Israeli detention, with former child detainees experiencing anxiety, panic attacks, nightmares, depression and social withdrawal.
Twenty percent reported intentional self-harm, while 45% did not return to school after their release. The figures reflect the wider consequences of detention, rather than harm attributed exclusively to sexual violence.
"We’re now moving away from the immediate act and are thinking about the long-term effects, the effects on their education, psychology, their development – it becomes intergenerational," Minhas said.
The evidence also documents sexual violence and humiliation against Palestinian women and girls at checkpoints, during military raids, in detention and in communities facing displacement.
Women described being forcibly undressed, sometimes in public or in front of their children, sexually touched during searches and threatened with rape.
Some were beaten after refusing to undress, while others faced rape threats in front of their children, threats to publish degrading footage online and the denial of sanitary pads while menstruating in detention.
The authors also cite Israeli soldiers posting photographs and videos of Palestinian women's underwear taken from homes in Gaza. Many of the images were subsequently removed, while the soldiers' social media accounts were closed or made private.
In the occupied West Bank, Israeli settlers have used sexual violence and humiliation to intimidate Palestinian communities, including exposing their genitals, threatening rape, attempting to touch women's bodies and stalking women on their way to latrines.
Fear of such violence has prevented women from going to work and girls from attending school, while some families have resorted to early marriage for their daughters.
Among 39 displaced households interviewed in Area C of the occupied West Bank, more than 70% identified threats to women and children, particularly sexualised violence, as a decisive reason for leaving, the authors write.
The article also details severe sexual torture inside Israeli detention facilities, including forced nudity, rape threats, genital violence, rape and assault with objects.
Palestinian detainees have suffered serious genital and rectal injuries following sexual torture involving batons and electric shocks.
One documented case involved a detainee whose rectum was ruptured, requiring surgery and the creation of a stoma. Other accounts describe detainees losing one or both testicles after being beaten on their genitals.
The authors also cite a February investigation by the Committee to Protect Journalists, which interviewed 59 Palestinian journalists released from Israeli detention. Seventeen, or 29%, described experiencing sexual violence, including two who recounted rape.
Minhas told The New Arab that these accounts exposed a reality of Palestinian life that remains poorly understood.
"People have very little understanding and awareness of what actually is going on and what the daily life of Palestinians entails, the kind of indignities that people have to suffer," he said.
"There is a fundamental aspect of living under military occupation that involves violence. And you know, at its very core, occupation is violence. You know, that’s the fundamental transaction that takes place, and it will manifest itself in various ways."
Sexual violence as a systematic yet underreported issue
The authors argue that the extensive evidence demonstrates recurring patterns of sexual violence against Palestinians rather than isolated incidents.
They cite a 2025 UN Commission of Inquiry finding that specific forms of sexual and gender-based violence "de facto form part of" Israeli security forces' "standard operating procedures" towards Palestinians.
The commission also concluded that sexualised torture, including rape and genital violence, was carried out with either explicit orders or implicit encouragement from senior Israeli civilian and military leaders.
It found that Israeli military and civilian justice systems were failing to ensure accountability for sexual crimes against Palestinians.
Despite the extensive evidence documented by human rights organisations and UN investigators, Minhas said medical research into sexual violence against Palestinians remained strikingly limited.
"The interesting thing here, from a medical perspective, was the remarkable lack of documentation and publication of conflict-related sexual violence in this setting," he said, contrasting it with the much larger body of research into sexual violence in other conflicts, including Ukraine.
He suggested that political pressures could discourage academics and researchers from investigating abuses against Palestinians.
"I think there’s a degree of personal and professional exposure for academics and for researchers seeking to try and study and understand this subject," he said.
The BMJ article brings together existing investigations and testimonies rather than presenting new primary research. Its authors warn that sexual violence remains significantly underreported, particularly among men and children, while restrictions on independent investigations have helped sustain impunity.
They also cite figures from Israeli rights group Yesh Din showing that, of 1,260 cases involving alleged offences by Israeli soldiers against Palestinians known to the military law enforcement system between 2017 and 2021, just 11, or 0.87%, resulted in indictments. The figures concern alleged offences more broadly, not sexual violence alone.
The authors identify the denial of independent access as a major obstacle to documenting abuse and holding perpetrators accountable.
The UN Commission of Inquiry has lacked access to Israel and the occupied Palestinian territories since October 2023, while the International Committee of the Red Cross has been unable to visit Palestinians held in Israeli custody.
Although Israel's Supreme Court ruled in June 2026 that the prohibition on Red Cross visits must be lifted, access had not resumed by the time the article was published.
The authors demand full, unrestricted access for independent investigators and medical and humanitarian organisations, arguing that accountability is impossible without scrutiny of the places where abuse occurs.
"The first instance is we need to get independent investigators into those settings," Minhas said. "And it’s only once you’ve got independent investigators in those settings that there’s actually a prospect that people may find that the impunity that they’ve enjoyed disappears."

Europe must switch to ‘war-mode’ defence production, Polish defence minister says

2026-10-13
