====================================================================================================

Israel must redraw Syria red lines to prevent confrontation with Turkey, think tank argues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:23:44 UTC
19:23:44 KST

Israel needs to draw more limited red lines on Turkish activities in Syria instead of the more aggressive approach it has taken since the old Syrian Assad regime fell in December 2024, the Institute for National Security Studies think tank argued.
On August 17, Israel struck an emerging Turkish position at the Abu al-Duhur base in Syria, leading to a high-profile diplomatic conflict between Israel on one side and the US, Turkey, and Syria on the other side.
In addition, on Friday of last week, the IDF targeted a vehicle near the Lebanese-Syrian border carrying Yusuf Ali al-Hassoun, who may be associated with Iran terror managers.
In repeated position papers since early 2025, INSS has warned that staying in Syria indefinitely without engaging in dialogue with Damascus about long-term security arrangements could lead to forfeiting many of the security gains that the IDF achieved upon the fall of Assad.
At the time, the IDF destroyed most of the Assad regime's military's higher-profile threats at sea, on land, and in the air, while also taking over a significant buffer zone in southern Syria to make it harder for any potential hostile jihadist force associated with the new Syrian government to initiate an invasion.
Authored by former senior IDF intelligence advisor and current INSS Head of Syria research, Carmit Valensi, and Amal Hayek, another INSS researcher, the most recent think tank report recommends that Israel walk a complex and nuanced tightrope in Syria, which splits "restoration of Syrian infrastructure and the establishment of a Turkish presence" into multiple components.
"A distinction should be made between technical assistance, training, and the rehabilitation of facilities for the Syrian state, on the one hand, and the establishment of independent Turkish command-and-control infrastructure, on the other," stated the think tank.
Israel has confirmed with Valensi that the report still holds following the most recent events in Syria, which includes the statement regarding deployment of systems in northern Syria: "From an operational standpoint, there is little practical difference between the deployment of Turkish radar, electronic warfare, or air defense systems in northern Syria and their deployment in southern Turkey or northern Cyprus."
"Their coverage ranges are similar, and the presence of such systems in northern Syria therefore does not in itself constitute a red line warranting the use of Israeli force," the position paper contended.
'Turkish navy has inherent advantage in eastern Mediterranean,' INSS argues
According to INSS, these same principles of nuance apply to the maritime domain: "The Turkish navy enjoys an inherent advantage in the eastern Mediterranean, and a limited presence along the Syrian coast would not fundamentally alter the balance of power."
This INSS position clashes with the current position of the navy, which wishes to be more aggressive in confronting Turkish naval expansion in the Mediterranean, including growing Israel's naval fleet from six to eight over future years.
Part of the INSS recommendations stems from an analysis that even if Turkey helped build Syrian leader Ahmad al-Sharaa's regime, "the relationship between Ankara and Damascus is therefore more complex than is sometimes perceived in Israel and is not free of tension."
"Evidence of this can be found in a series of structural changes recently implemented by Damascus in the ranks of the Syrian army, indicating an intention to reduce the autonomy of these forces and the extent of Turkish influence over them," wrote INSS.
For example, "As of August 2026, the Turkish military presence in Syria is undergoing a process of reorganization. Ankara is gradually downsizing some of the smaller outposts and facilities it established during the years of war – particularly in areas where the security situation has changed – and transferring authority and responsibility to Syrian state institutions."
Israeli security officials generally say these are cosmetic changes designed to fool the West, but some Mossad officials have expressed openness to testing out whether Syria's new regime may choose stability over conflict with Israel, and INSS warned that being perceived as not giving the Syrians a chance could paradoxically endanger Israeli national security.
After all of the above advice for Israel to come to terms with a more restrained approach against Syria and Turkey, INSS does still believe in red lines.
Its view is that central and southern Syria are critical areas and that "While Turkey justifies its presence in northern Syria as necessary to prevent threats to its territory, the establishment of Turkish bases farther inside the country, in central Syria, and even more so in the south, is not dictated by such security needs."
Further, INSS said that such a Turkish presence "would also bring potential friction closer to the Israeli front and constitute a problematic shift in the regional balance."
Israel should focus on thwarting terror elements in Syria, INSS says
In addition, INSS stated that Israel must avoid the "Entrenchment of terror proxies in southern Syria. Israel should focus on thwarting terrorist elements, particularly Hamas, and preventing them from enjoying freedom of action or safe haven under Turkish or Syrian auspices in the southern region adjacent to Israel’s border."
In other words, INSS would be less tolerant of jihadist elements, especially Hamas, getting anywhere near Israel's border in southern Syria, versus Turkey growing its presence in northern Syria.
Bringing all of these views together, INSS stated that, "Turkey’s presence and influence in Syria are an established reality that is unlikely to disappear through the use of military force alone."
In that sense, "Israel’s challenge is not to eliminate Turkish involvement altogether, but rather to contain and balance it."
Moreover, "Relying exclusively on military force and striking targets of marginal operational value, without a parallel diplomatic track with Damascus, jeopardizes Israel’s security interests and could drag the parties into a direct confrontation that neither side desires."
This last statement by INSS engages the debate about whether the target radar which the IDF struck in Syria was truly a game-changer in terms of tracking Israeli aircraft, or whether other nearby existing radars are already carrying out the same detection activities.
"Israeli decision-makers must therefore combine focused military deterrence with direct and indirect dialogue, utilize deconfliction mechanisms, and clearly define the areas in which Israel is prepared to allow Syria to rebuild its capabilities, before the situation deteriorates into dangerous regional escalation," said INSS.
Next, it stated, "blanket Israeli opposition to any process of Syrian military rehabilitation could prove counterproductive, pushing Damascus toward greater dependence on Ankara."
Moreover, INSS wrote, "the broader regional and diplomatic context should be taken into account: Damascus is currently drawing closer to Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates and gaining growing legitimacy from the United States and European countries."
In early 2025, Valensi and several other national security officials suggested that Israel must draw up a list of conditions, such as demilitarized zones in Syria, that could lead it to withdraw from some or all of the buffer zone.
When the IDF first took over the buffer zone in Syria, multiple IDF officials told the Post during a visit to the new security zone that the military's presence was very temporary and would end once it was clear that the new Syrian leadership was not trying to invade Israel.
While Sharaa's background is as a jihadist and some of his associated forces have perpetrated multiple massacres against Syrian Druze and Alawites since taking power, there has been no hint of action against Israel for nearly two years.
"Israel’s actions are increasingly perceived as seeking to destabilize Syria, and in this context Israel is at times even compared to Iran. In this framework, greater attention may be directed toward the issue of the Golan Heights, as recently raised by [US Ambassador Tom] Barrack, while regional, and particularly international, pressure could intensify for Israel to withdraw to the lines established under the 1974 Separation of Forces Agreement, possibly even without significant political concessions in return," concluded INSS.
This raises the threat that while Israel has held the Syrian buffer zone to both be safer and as leverage to gain security concessions from Syria, a failure to make any concession offers for the last two years could eventually lead Trump, who now heavily supports Sharaa, to force a withdrawal with few pluses for Israel.

Pegasus spyware scandal deepens as Poland questions Israeli tech, strengthens ties with Turkey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:23:17 UTC
19:23:17 KST

WARSAW - Polish prosecutors said Monday that NSO Group, the Israeli manufacturer of Pegasus spyware, retained technical access to sensitive surveillance data collected by Poland’s anti-corruption bureau, raising new questions about Warsaw’s reliance on Israeli security technology as Turkish defense companies expand their presence in Poland and across Europe.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the findings “a crime against the state,” accusing his predecessors of allowing an Israeli company and potentially Israeli intelligence to gain access to sensitive information about Polish citizens, opposition politicians, and independent prosecutors.
The findings emerged on the opening day of the Warsaw Security Forum, where Polish defense strategist Jacek Bartosiak identified Turkey, rather than Israel, as one of Poland’s principal security partners.
“Let’s not cry about it,” Bartosiak told The Media Line when asked about Israel’s reluctance to supply Ukraine with weapons. “Our key allies are Ukrainians, Swedes, Finns and Turks.”
The Pegasus revelations add another complication to Polish-Israeli relations, already strained by disagreements over Israel’s conduct in Gaza and its policies toward the Palestinians. Yet Poland continues to purchase Israeli defense systems, illustrating the competing political and military considerations that shape European arms procurement.
According to Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office, experts from the Internal Security Agency, known as ABW, determined that the Central Anti-Corruption Bureau, or CBA, “did not have full control over the Pegasus system.”
The bureau lacked passwords to some administrative accounts, while the server module responsible for infecting mobile phones remained under NSO’s “exclusive control.” Data collected through the system traveled through servers outside Poland that the bureau could not control.
Investigators found that NSO had the technical ability to access intercepted material, but they could not establish whether the company actually examined information collected during specific surveillance operations.
Tusk went further, saying it was “beyond any doubt” that NSO cooperated with Israeli intelligence. In a video posted on X, he accused the previous Polish government of surrendering control over sensitive surveillance information to an Israeli company and potentially the Israeli state.
His assertion that information reached the Israeli side goes beyond what investigators established about access to specific intercepted records.
A parliamentary commission investigating Pegasus presented its findings the same day and announced that it had prepared 11 criminal referrals. Its chairwoman, Magdalena Sroka, said the CBA had purchased and operated the spyware without the required security accreditation.
According to the commission, judges who authorized surveillance operations were not informed that Pegasus could extract virtually the entire contents of a mobile phone.
Poland acquired Pegasus in 2017 under the Law and Justice government, known by its Polish abbreviation PiS, using money from a Justice Ministry fund intended to assist crime victims and combat crime. The system was subsequently used to monitor hundreds of people, including political opponents. Tusk disclosed last year that his wife and daughter were among those affected.
In February, prosecutors charged former heads of Poland’s internal security and military counterintelligence agencies over their roles in approving the system. Both deny wrongdoing.
PiS maintains that Pegasus was necessary to fight crime and that its use was authorized by courts. Former CBA chief Ernest Bejda disputed Monday’s findings, denying that Israeli authorities had obtained Polish surveillance data.
NSO Group has previously maintained that its government customers operate Pegasus and control their surveillance activities. The company has not publicly responded to the latest Polish findings.
The controversy comes at a difficult time in relations between Warsaw and Israel.
In August, Poland summoned Israel’s ambassador after Israeli military authorities discontinued their investigation into the 2024 killing of Polish aid worker Damian Soból in Gaza. Warsaw also condemned Israel’s seizure of a United Nations facility in East Jerusalem.
Poland, alongside Britain, France declared restrictions on trade with Israeli settlements in West Bank.
In September, Poland joined 11 other countries, including Britain and France, in declaring their intention to introduce, support, or consider restrictions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
The political disagreements have not ended defense cooperation. In July 2025, Poland signed a contract worth approximately $110 million for 18 coastal-surveillance radars from Elta, a subsidiary of Israel Aerospace Industries, to detect ships and low-flying threats over the Baltic Sea. Deliveries are scheduled for 2027 and 2028.
Polish forces also use Israeli-designed Spike anti-tank missiles manufactured under license by the Polish company Mesko.
Bartosiak, founder of the Warsaw-based Strategy & Future think tank, said the Pegasus affair was unlikely to significantly change Poland's purchasing decisions.
“Right now, Poland is not buying too much of Israeli security, and I’m not sure if it’s going to change,” he said.
Future contracts, he added, “will depend on the capabilities on the battlefield” and on the “European stance towards Israeli policy. So there is a political problem here.”
The Warsaw Security Forum, held October 12 and 13, brought together political leaders, military officials, diplomats, and defense specialists to examine the war in Ukraine, Russia’s threat to European security, and questions about continued American involvement in the continent’s defense.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy addressed the gathering by video, accusing Russia of attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure despite President Donald Trump’s announcement of a ceasefire covering such targets.
Israel’s position on Ukraine remains a source of frustration for some European security experts.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has resisted supplying Kyiv with weapons while maintaining relations with Moscow, which historically helped Israel conduct military operations in Syria. In July, The Washington Post reported that Netanyahu had blocked the transfer of American-owned Iron Dome missile-defense batteries to Ukraine because of concerns that the technology might eventually reach Iran.
The forum nevertheless included an Israeli-founded defense technology company. Heven AeroTech, established in Israel in 2019 by former Israeli army reconnaissance commander Bentzion Levinson, is now headquartered in the United States and manufactures hydrogen-powered drones, with operations in Israel as well.
Levinson joined former Ukrainian Prime Minister Oleksiy Honcharuk for a discussion of drone warfare and the lessons emerging from the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
“We’re looking at an era of drones,” Levinson told the panel. “Ukraine is amazing. Russia also became very close,” he said.
He argued that other countries had fallen behind and needed to accelerate development and production. Manufacturers willing to establish local operations in Europe could gain access to military customers, he added.
The importance of drones to European security is creating opportunities for Turkish manufacturers, whose products have gained international attention through their use in Ukraine and other conflicts.
Turkey has also developed a substantial defense relationship with Poland.
At the MSPO defense exhibition in September, Turkish electronics manufacturer ASELSAN signed an agreement with Polish armored-vehicle producer AMZ-Kutno to supply additional reconnaissance and surveillance systems. The deal followed a $410 million electronic-warfare contract ASELSAN won in December 2025.
During the same exhibition, Turkey’s state-owned arms manufacturer MKE and Poland’s PGZ defense group signed a memorandum concerning TOLGA, a Turkish counter-drone air-defense system.
Poland also purchased 24 Turkish Bayraktar TB2 armed drones in 2021, becoming the first European Union member and the first NATO member outside Turkey to acquire the system.
Bartosiak viewed these relationships through the longer history of Polish and Turkish efforts to counter Russian power.
“Turkey is deterring Russia from expanding into the Middle East, Mediterranean, Black Sea,” he said. “We have been having wars against Russia for many centuries. So it’s always about Poland and Turkey together.”
He also argued that Poland’s strategic interests were closely tied to the security of Ukraine and its northern European partners.
“Everything that strengthens them strengthens us. Everything that weakens them weakens us,” he said.
The growing Turkish presence in European defense markets, however, does not mean that Ankara faces no obstacles.
Security Action for Europe, or SAFE, the European Union’s €150 billion defense loan program, is designed to strengthen European manufacturing and joint military procurement. Poland is its largest recipient, with an allocation of approximately €43.7 billion.
The program imposes restrictions on components originating outside the EU, the European Economic Area’s European Free Trade Association countries, and Ukraine. Such components generally cannot exceed 35% of the estimated component cost of eligible defense products.
These rules create difficulties for Turkish and Israeli manufacturers seeking access to EU-financed contracts, although partnerships and manufacturing operations within Europe may provide ways to participate.
Greece and Cyprus have also opposed expanding Turkey’s access to European defense initiatives.
Suat Kınıklıoğlu, a former Turkish parliamentarian and senior foreign policy analyst in Ankara, said Turkey regarded Poland as a partner rather than a rival.
“Turkey doesn’t see Poland as a competitor. On the contrary, we value our relationship with Poland,” he told The Media Line.
“Historically, we always valued Polish independence and continue to see it as a key country in countering Russian influence in the region.”
Turkish manufacturers, he said, were finding ways to work with European partners despite regulatory restrictions, including “by setting up companies in Europe or bilateral cooperation agreements such as with the Italians.”
“We Turks are very much disappointed by this exclusionary approach at a time when Europe needs a stronger [Turkey] by its side,” he said.
Turkish defense manufacturers are already establishing a stronger industrial presence inside the EU.
Drone maker Baykar’s joint venture with Italy’s Leonardo became operational in July, while armored-vehicle manufacturer Otokar is working with Rheinmetall’s Romanian unit on local production of Cobra II vehicles ordered by Romania.
Spain offers another example of Turkey’s growing position in the European defense market.
Madrid has canceled plans to purchase new Israeli-designed Spike anti-tank missiles and moved away from Israeli technology in a rocket-artillery program. At the same time, Spain has committed approximately €2.6 billion to a pilot-training program involving 30 Turkish-designed Hürjet aircraft, which will be adapted and integrated by Airbus in Spain.
The Spanish decisions reflect political objections to Israel’s military campaign in Gaza as well as efforts to increase domestic and European control over defense technology.
Turkish participation in European defense manufacturing is not without contradictions. Olena Tregub, secretary general of the Independent Anti-Corruption Commission in Kyiv, told The Media Line that Western electronic components continued to reach Russian drone factories “through intermediaries in countries such as China, Turkey, and the UAE,” often through shell companies.
In one case, she said, “a company presenting itself as an adult-toy manufacturer was supplying Russia with Western microelectronics.”
Tregub also warned that Russian-Iranian cooperation in drone technology “is increasingly becoming a two-way relationship.”
For Ankara, broader access to European markets is only one of several strategic challenges. Relations with Washington, including Turkey’s ambitions to acquire F-35 fighter jets, remain important.
Kınıklıoğlu said President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan “has a very special relationship with Trump,” but added that “Ankara recognizes that there is a time limit attached to it.”
He warned that a “more domestically preoccupied US president” after the American midterm elections could complicate Turkey’s efforts to obtain the aircraft.
Israel’s defense manufacturers face similar European procurement restrictions, as well as growing political opposition in several countries.
The Cypriot newspaper Philenews has reported that Elbit Systems, Israel Aerospace Industries, and Rafael have considered establishing production facilities in Cyprus that could improve access to EU-funded defense projects. The companies have not confirmed those plans.
Spain and Slovenia have imposed arms embargoes on Israel, while France barred Israeli offensive weapons from the Eurosatory defense exhibition in Paris in June. Germany and Italy, by contrast, have opposed broader EU measures against Israel.
Norway, this year’s partner nation at the Warsaw Security Forum, restricts exports of Norwegian defense equipment to Israel. Oslo recognized Palestinian statehood in 2024, and its sovereign wealth fund has reduced its Israeli investments.
At the same time, Norway lifted restrictions on arms exports to Turkey in 2024, reversing measures introduced in 2019.
Despite these political pressures, Israel’s defense industry continues to record substantial international sales.
Figures released by Israel’s Defense Ministry in June showed that arms exports reached a record $19.2 billion in 2025, the fifth consecutive annual high. Europe accounted for 36% of those sales, or approximately $6.9 billion, compared with 54% in 2024, when Germany’s major Arrow 3 missile-defense purchase helped increase the European share.
Danny Citrinowicz, a senior researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies in Tel Aviv and former head of the Iran branch in Israeli military intelligence, said Israel was counting on Europe’s concerns about Russia to sustain demand for its military technology.
“Israel is building on the fact that Europe needs Israeli equipment because of the Russian threat,” he told The Media Line.
But Israel’s conduct in Gaza and its policies in the West Bank create political limits on that relationship, he said.
“At the end of the day, it’s a glass ceiling thing,” Citrinowicz said. “There is a glass ceiling for the Israeli capacity to use some arms for its own greater good,” even if European countries “definitely need that.”
He also warned that excluding Israel from European security discussions could work against Europe’s own interests.
Israel “is a formidable force within the Middle East,” Citrinowicz said, with influence “for good or for bad.” Excluding it from European security discussions means “you’re missing a lot.”
The competing demands of military capability, political alignment, and industrial independence are particularly acute for Poland, which faces Russia’s military threat while reassessing its relationships with suppliers and allies.
Bartosiak recalled a conversation with Turkish diplomats a decade ago that he said captured the strategic questions facing his country.
“You used to have a great empire. Where are you guys?” he remembered them asking.
“American power is ebbing away from Eurasia. Wake up!”

Zionist Iranian dissident Ramin Parsa granted residency in Israel after years-long battle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:22:53 UTC
19:22:53 KST

Ramin Parsa, an Iranian dissident and pro-Israel activist living in Jerusalem, was granted a one-year temporary residency permit last month after a three-and-a-half-year legal and bureaucratic battle with the Interior Ministry.
Parsa, who was born in Shiraz before converting from Shia Islam to Christianity and fleeing the Islamic Republic, is a public speaker and activist who has spent years volunteering and advocating for Israel. Nevertheless, despite his Israeli wife and child, he was twice denied legal status in Israel by the Interior Ministry. Last month, however, following what Parsa credited to an intervention by God, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, that finally changed.
“It was a miracle, actually, a miracle of God,” Parsa told The Jerusalem Post on Sunday. “But Ambassador Huckabee really helped. He took our case and presented it to the government, to Prime Minister Netanyahu and his office, and they took it seriously.”
According to Parsa, the intervention prompted officials to revisit his case after years of legal proceedings and repeated applications.
“They basically had an inquiry into the case – what’s happening – and then they realized that it had been stuck there for a while,” he said. “So they granted me my temporary residency after three and a half years.”
Parsa said he credited Huckabee, Netanyahu, and members of the prime minister’s national security team with helping bring the matter to a resolution.
The permit gives Parsa temporary status for one year. After that, he said, he will have to apply again, with the possibility of eventually seeking permanent residency.
“We have one year, and then after a year I will reapply again, and so this is one good step in the right direction, and I’m grateful for that,” Parsa said.
“I believe that next year we will also apply and will get it. I’m confident of that, but you never know,” he continued. “I believe that it’s going to work out, and we’re going to have another miracle. And eventually, I can apply for permanent residency.”
Parsa said his temporary residency was granted through a discretionary provision that he referred to as “Section Nine,” rather than through the ordinary process based on his marriage to an Israeli citizen.
“The way my residency was granted was not based on marriage, but based on Section Nine,” he said, adding that the decision was based on his being considered a benefit to the state.
“I’ve been a Zionist, a Christian Zionist, for almost 20 years,” he said. “I’ve been supporting Israel even before I met my wife, before I got married, before I even imagined I would be living in Israel.”
Parsa stressed that, as he understood the decision, it did not automatically establish a pathway for other applicants in similar circumstances.
“It’s not a law that basically they have to give it to everyone based on the same rule,” he said. “It’s discretion, so they can decide to do it or they can decide not to do it.”
The change in status has already opened doors that had previously been closed to him. When the Post interviewed Parsa earlier in the process, he said his uncertain legal situation had prevented him from traveling abroad, including to events where he had been invited to speak in support of Israel.
Parsa has booked trips to South Africa, Germany, United States to speak on Israel’s behalf
Now, he said, he has already booked trips to South Africa, Germany, and the United States to speak on Israel’s behalf.
“A few days ago, I got a message from the Foreign Ministry that they want me to speak to a group of pastors who came from South Africa,” Parsa said.
“I want to use my time in the best way possible, in the wisest way possible, to support Israel, to combat antisemitism, and to basically tell the world [about] the real Israel that I live in.”
Parsa said he did not view his experience with the Interior Ministry as representative of Israeli society as a whole.
“I don’t want to blame Israel for the mistake of a few people in the Ministry of Interior because that doesn’t represent the country,” he said. “What represents the country is the good people of Israel.”
For Parsa, the case is also personal beyond his legal status. His wife is an Israeli Jew, the couple has a young son, and they are expecting another child.
He described their family as symbolic of what he hopes could one day become a broader reconciliation between Israelis and Iranians.
“My marriage with my wife is a prophetic picture of two nations coming together,” he said. “We have a beautiful son, and we have one on the way, so the fruit is so beautiful when these two nations come together.”
Asked what he hoped that relationship might look like in the future, Parsa pointed to his hometown.
“I’m hoping and praying for a day that we have a direct flight from Tel Aviv to Tehran, from Tel Aviv to Shiraz,” he said.
“I see the day that the regime will fall and Israelis and Iranians will become friends.”

Yemen: Taiz faces humanitarian disaster as Houthis tighten siege
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:21:29 UTC
19:21:29 KST

Breadcrumb
Yemen's Taiz faces humanitarian disaster as Houthis tighten siege
Yemeni government forces are managing to stall the Houthi offensive on the besieged city of Taiz, analysts told The New Arab, as residents increasingly fear a repeat of previous sieges earlier in the war.
Ameneh Mehvar, Senior Analyst for the Middle East at ACLED, told The New Arab that, despite the recent encirclement by the Houthis and continued gains, "government forces, backed by Saudi airstrikes, appear to have stalled further significant Houthi advances in recent days."
Fighting around the city's suburbs and hills has continued in recent days, with Houthi attempts to advance along the western and southern approaches, including around al-Misrakh, where government-aligned fighters reportedly fended off a Houthi infiltration attempt, according to Yemeni analyst Muhammad al-Bashar.
However, the Houthis tightened their siege on Monday after closing all four exits from the government-held city, according to military sources cited by AFP.
A Yemeni government field officer said Houthi forces had established fire control over the exits and were shooting at vehicles attempting to pass through them.
The Houthis also attacked government positions defending the city's southern and western approaches, seizing new positions despite Saudi airstrikes.
Government-aligned forces lost 22 fighters in 24 hours of fighting, while the Houthis lost at least 40, according to AFP, citing military sources from both sides.
Mehvar noted, however, that the battle for the city highlights the limits of the government's recent offensive on the coast, which has been offset by the Houthis' stranglehold on Taiz.
"The Houthis do not need to capture Taiz outright to weaken government control, as prolonged isolation could erode the defenders' ability to sustain their positions while further deepening a humanitarian crisis."
The Houthi encirclement of Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, was effectively completed after the group took the town of al-Turbah, severing the supply road to Aden, on 4 October.
It is not the first time the Houthis have occupied and encircled the city. The group previously captured Taiz in 2015 and laid siege to it until 2016, when government forces pushed them out, although the Houthis retained positions around the city.
Baraa Shiban, an Associate Fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told The New Arab that the Houthis' strategy in Taiz is informed by their previous attempts to capture the city, with fighting now focused on its surrounding suburbs and hills.
"The Houthis had before tried to take control of the city itself, and then it proved to be very costly," he said, noting that urban fighting eventually forced the group out.
"What they did instead is that they then placed snipers and artillery on the hills overlooking the city, and that was what the situation [was like] when I was there. So, the bombing of the city was constant."
With urban fighting proving costly, Houthi advances have concentrated on the hills and peaks surrounding the city and the wider province, eventually leading to its encirclement.
“There's fighting literally from one hill to the other, from one road to the other,” he said, adding, “the fight is really concentrated on trying to take control of the main road, because if you control the main road, then you effectively are in control of the district."
Humanitarian crisis deepens as Taiz is cut off
The encirclement has triggered a worsening humanitarian crisis, with the Studies and Economic Media Center (SEMC), a Taiz-based civil society group, warning in a recent report that the city is "facing near-total isolation from food, medicine, and energy supplies."
SEMC said petrol stations had run out of fuel, while wheat and flour stocks were sufficient for just 19 days of consumption.
Saeed Saif, the UN Population Fund's (UNFPA) West Coast and Taiz Coordinator, told The New Arab that roads into the city had been completely cut off, with prices for basic commodities doubling and fuel prices tripling.
He warned of critical shortages of medical supplies, with only two of the eight UNFPA-supported health facilities inside the city still operational.
"High transportation costs prevent women, girls, and vulnerable populations, particularly pregnant women from accessing essential services," Saif said.
The deteriorating security situation has forced UNFPA to suspend some of its activities, leaving vulnerable residents with even fewer options for healthcare.
Saif, who returned to his hometown of Taiz in April after 25 years away, was himself forced to flee as fighting intensified.
He left the city on 13 September, travelling at night to al-Turbah along deserted roads and through military checkpoints.
During his six days there, he visited displacement sites just five kilometres from the front lines, where artillery shelling could be clearly heard.
On 18 September, following an emergency relief distribution, security warnings prompted him to evacuate again, this time with his family to Aden.
The journey took more than five hours through difficult terrain amid heavy rain and flash flood warnings, with the sound of bombardment along the way.
Saif said the experience was particularly distressing for his 13-year-old daughter and brought back memories of the family's evacuation from Sanaa during intense airstrikes in 2018.
"There is widespread fear and anxiety," he said, warning that a further wave of displacement could affect up to 100,000 households.
According to the UN's migration office, 57% of the more than 200,000 people displaced by the recent fighting across Yemen have come from Taiz province.
Yemen's Human Rights Ministry also warned on Monday that the tightening siege threatened to disrupt life-saving medical services, including emergency surgery, intensive care, dialysis and neonatal care.
In a statement carried by the official Saba news agency, the ministry held the Houthis responsible for blocking supply routes and called on the United Nations and international humanitarian organisations to intervene urgently to secure access to food, medicine and fuel.
Shiban said conditions in the city were reminiscent of earlier sieges during the war.
"There is a genuine fear, and that reflects itself on the prices of goods, food, and other main materials."
Can government forces break the siege?
Although Houthi advances have slowed, government forces lack the firepower needed to reverse the group's gains around Taiz.
Government troops and newly formed local resistance forces are largely equipped with unarmoured pick-up trucks and Kalashnikov rifles, while the Houthis possess drones, artillery and tanks.
Shiban said "the situation doesn't play in their favour."
He argued that the government's best chance of breaking the siege could depend on the success of its parallel offensive along Yemen's western coast.
"If their [government] operation on the West Coast succeeds, pushing from the Bab al-Mandab up and then to the Mokha port, then they can enter [the city] using the same road that the Houthis entered into Taiz districts," Shiban said.
Such an advance could allow government forces to bring heavier weaponry into the city and challenge the Houthi encirclement.
"Other than that, it's going to be difficult because now the city is encircled."

Trump team eyes Turkish diplomat who accused Israel of war crimes for UN chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:21:10 UTC
19:21:10 KST

A former Turkish foreign minister who accused Israel of war crimes, the FIFA president who presented Donald Trump with a special peace prize, the diplomat overseeing negotiations on Gaza's future and a senior Emirati official who condemned the October 7 massacre are among the names now being discussed as possible candidates for the next United Nations secretary-general. Their emergence follows reports that the Trump administration is dissatisfied with all seven candidates currently seeking to succeed António Guterres.
According to Politico, citing officials familiar with internal administration discussions, Washington is searching for a candidate capable of fundamentally transforming the UN, which is struggling with a deep financial and political crisis.
"There are no reformers of the kind the United States wants on the entire list of candidates. Some even appear likely to continue business as usual," an administration official told Politico. A State Department official explained that Washington is looking for someone willing to shake up the organization, rather than necessarily choosing a career diplomat who rose through its ranks.
Turkish diplomat who accused Israel of war crimes
One of the most intriguing names, and potentially one of the most concerning for Jerusalem, is Feridun Sinirlioglu, Turkey's former foreign minister and the current secretary-general of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
Sinirlioglu served as Turkey's ambassador to the United Nations from 2016 to 2023, frequently using the international organization's platform to criticize Israel. During Operation Guardian of the Walls in May 2021, he condemned Israeli airstrikes in Gaza, accused Israel of deliberately targeting schools operated by the UN Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) and described such attacks as war crimes.
"If a classroom full of children had been blown up somewhere else, how many days would it have taken the Security Council to convene a public meeting?" he asked at the time. He accused the council of maintaining a silence that encouraged Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to continue Israeli military operations.
His relationship with Israel was not always confrontational. In 2016, Sinirlioglu led Turkey's negotiating team during talks to restore diplomatic relations between Ankara and Jerusalem after six years of tensions following the Mavi Marmara incident. He signed the reconciliation agreement on Turkey's behalf, opposite Dore Gold, then director-general of Israel's Foreign Ministry.
Sinirlioglu is reportedly considering entering the race for UN secretary-general with encouragement from the White House. However, he has not formally announced his candidacy.
Trump's Gaza envoy and the FIFA president
Another figure being considered in Washington is Nickolay Mladenov, the Bulgarian diplomat serving as the senior representative of Trump's Board of Peace, the international body established to address Gaza's future.
Mladenov, a former UN special coordinator for the Middle East peace process, maintains close relationships with Israeli and Palestinian officials. He is currently leading negotiations over Hamas' disarmament and the establishment of an alternative governing mechanism in Gaza.
Despite those relationships, Mladenov has also criticized Israeli policy. In August, he accused the Israeli government of jeopardizing the ceasefire and undermining efforts to disarm Hamas. Addressing the Security Council, he questioned whether another attack on an ammunition depot would prevent Hamas from rearming or strengthening its control over Gaza, and answered that it would not.
At the same time, Mladenov has insisted that Hamas must surrender its weapons and dismantle its tunnel network. He has indicated, however, that the organization could continue operating as a political movement if it abandoned its military activities. Israeli President Isaac Herzog praised Mladenov's proposal, saying he was impressed by the central importance it placed on Israel's security.
Perhaps the most unconventional name mentioned in Trump's circle is Gianni Infantino, president of FIFA, world soccer's governing body, and a close associate of the US president.
In December 2025, Infantino presented Trump with FIFA's inaugural Peace Prize during a ceremony in Washington. The decision drew attention, particularly because the precise criteria and justification for the award remained unclear.
Infantino's record regarding Israel has been more favorable to Jerusalem than that of some other potential candidates. He resisted demands from Palestinian officials and pressure from other quarters to suspend Israel from international soccer following the war in Gaza.
In March, FIFA decided against taking action over Israeli clubs competing in West Bank settlements. Separately, the organization fined the Israel Football Association 150,000 Swiss francs after finding violations of its rules on discrimination and racism.
Infantino has not announced any intention to seek the UN position and is also pursuing another term as FIFA president.
The UAE diplomat who condemned October 7
Another potential candidate is Lana Nusseibeh, a senior diplomat from the United Arab Emirates who previously served as her country's ambassador to the United Nations.
Following the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack, Nusseibeh condemned the murder of Israeli civilians and the abduction of hostages, emphasizing that Hamas did not represent the Palestinian people.
She subsequently criticized Israeli bombing operations in Gaza, describing them as indiscriminate, and called for a ceasefire and greater humanitarian access to the territory.
In December 2023, Nusseibeh played a significant role in advancing a UN Security Council resolution aimed at expanding humanitarian assistance to Gaza.
The frontrunner with family ties to Israel
Washington's search for alternatives poses a particularly serious challenge for Rebeca Grynspan, the former vice president of Costa Rica who remains the leading candidate in the race.
Grynspan, whose family includes Holocaust survivors, could become both the first woman and the first Jewish person to serve as UN secretary-general.
She also maintains close personal ties to Israel. Her sister lives in Mevaseret Zion, near Jerusalem, her nephews have served in the IDF, and she has additional relatives living in the West Bank.
Nevertheless, a Republican congressional official told Politico that Grynspan was too critical of Israel and too accommodating toward China. The official warned that her appointment could make it difficult to secure Republican support for continued US funding of the United Nations.
Under Grynspan's leadership of UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD), the organization has published reports attributing a significant part of the Palestinian economy's collapse to Israeli policies and military operations in Gaza.
A report published in September estimated that Gaza's recovery and reconstruction would require $71.5 billion.
Grynspan herself condemned the October 7 massacre and called for the release of the hostages, while also criticizing harm to Palestinian civilians during the war.
Despite the concerns in Washington, she continues to lead the Security Council's confidential informal straw polls. In the latest round, she received nine votes of encouragement and six votes of discouragement.
Another candidate still in contention is Rafael Grossi, the Argentine director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency. Grossi maintains working relationships with Israeli officials and is respected by some in Washington for his handling of the Iranian nuclear issue. Russia, however, is among the countries expressing reservations about his candidacy.
October 16 vote could reshape the race
The next critical moment in the succession contest is expected on October 16, when the Security Council is scheduled to conduct another informal vote that could provide further indications of opposition among its permanent members.
The United States, Russia, China, Britain and France each possess veto power, meaning that opposition from any one of them can prevent a candidate from securing the council's recommendation.
Guterres is due to complete his term on December 31. If Trump continues to oppose the existing candidates and no alternative emerges with sufficient international support, the UN could approach the new year without an agreed successor.
For Israel, the stakes extend well beyond the identity of the next secretary-general. The appointment could help determine whether its strained relationship with the United Nations continues after Guterres leaves office, or whether a new leadership opens the possibility of a different chapter.

Saudi Arabia prepared for various scenarios amid Houthi attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:21:05 UTC
19:21:05 KST

Saudi Information Minister Salman Al-Dosari said Monday that the kingdom was prepared for various scenarios, regardless of their likelihood, stressing that life was continuing normally despite repeated Houthi attacks, Anadolu Agency reported.
Speaking at a government press conference in Riyadh, according to the Saudi Press Agency, Al-Dosari said: “Life in the kingdom, praise be to God, continues normally.”
“Increasing readiness does not mean anxiety; rather, it reflects the state’s preparedness for various scenarios, whatever the likelihood of their occurrence,” he added.
Riyadh has faced repeated Houthi attacks in recent days, with strikes on King Khalid International Airport over two days forcing the temporary suspension of operations.
Despite the attacks, the World Petroleum Congress opened Sunday in Riyadh with broad international participation. Saudi Arabia is hosting the event for the first time, with proceedings scheduled to conclude Thursday.
READ: Bloomberg: Saudi Arabia disappointed by limited support from Western allies
Al-Dosari also highlighted the changes underway in the capital.
“Riyadh today is one of the cities whose transformation you can most clearly see as you travel along its roads: in transport activity, urban expansion and the growth of projects, through to its global presence as a capital for business, investment and decision-making,” he said.
Since 5th October, five Saudi airports have been targeted in 10 attacks carried out by the Houthi group, killing 20 people and injuring hundreds, according to an Anadolu tally. The attacks have also caused material damage and disrupted air traffic.
The strikes come amid continued military escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis since July, including attacks on civilian aviation facilities and energy installations in the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen’s government against the Houthis since March 2015. The group has controlled the capital Sanaa and several provinces since September 2014.

India detains top ‘cockroach’ leaders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:20:35 UTC
19:20:35 KST

Indian authorities have closed metro stations, cancelled trains and restricted mobile internet access ahead of the protest. (AFP Photo)
India’s youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) said on Oct. 13 that key leaders had been detained after entering an iconic protest site in New Delhi blocked by police.
Opposition parties and supporters of the movement have taken to the streets in recent days, defying a security clampdown to demand the resignation of the head of India’s election commission, accusing it of manipulating voter rolls to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party.
The Election Commission of India, which oversees the voting process in the world’s most populous nation, has denied any wrongdoing.
Delhi Police said on Oct. 12 that Jantar Mantar in the heart of the capital had been taken off the list of designated official protest sites.
The site has been sealed off for several days by yellow metal barricades and guarded by a heavy police presence.
But a video posted online by CJP leader Abhijeet Dipke on Oct. 13 showed protesters clambering over the barricades, running into the empty space and waving the national flag, before police chased and detained them.
“CJP sneaks inside to reclaim Jantar Mantar,” the group said in a post on social media, adding that those detained included leaders Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka and Ajinkya Shinde.
“All of them have been detained by Delhi Police,” it added.
Modi, in comments at a business conference in New Delhi on Oct. 13, called India the “mother of democracy,” but did not refer directly to the protests.
“In our country, people openly debate a wide range of issues and discuss different perspectives,” he said.

Ukraine shoots down up to 85% of Russian jet-powered drones - Air Force
Kyiv • UNN
Yuriy Ihnat reported that Ukraine shot down and suppressed 58 of 74 jet-powered UAVs in one night. Recently, the figure reached 85%.
Ukrainian forces are shooting down and suppressing a significant portion of Russian jet-powered drones. According to Yurii Ihnat, spokesman for the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, this figure recently reached 85%. He said this during a telethon broadcast, reports UNN.
Details
"Our reports also show that we have already divided the regular UAVs — "Shaheds," "Herberas," and "Parodies" — into one line, while jet-powered UAVs are identified separately in the second line. So, this night, out of 74 jet-powered UAVs, 58 were shot down or suppressed. If you calculate the percentage, that is a considerable proportion shot down. If you look further down through our reports, you can see that there really is an increase in the percentage. It is obvious here. Sometimes it was even 85%, it seems, recently, for jet-powered drones shot down," Yurii Ihnat stated.
Let us remind you
On the night of October 13, Russia launched five ballistic missiles and 117 drones at Ukraine, including nine "Banderols." Eighty-eight drones were shot down or suppressed. There were strikes at 17 locations, as well as loitering munitions in Kharkiv.

"American PR": Ukraine denies European involvement in "peace plan" leaked to Washington Post
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:20:00 EEST
19:20:00 KST

"American PR": Ukraine denies European involvement in "peace plan" leaked to Washington Post
Dmytro Lytvyn, communications adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has responded to a report in The Washington Post which claims Europe and the US are drawing up a peace plan for Ukraine and Russia that envisages territorial concessions. Lytvyn said the information presented in the article is merely the American team's perspective.
Source: European Pravda, citing Lytvyn's comments to journalists
Quote from Lytvyn: "It is not 'the US and European countries'. This is an outline of the view of some members of the US team at the meeting in Florida, which was attended by the Americans, Ukrainians and Europeans. Good PR by the Americans."
Details: Lytvyn said the WP report reflects specifically American views that were expressed during a meeting of representatives from Ukraine, the US, the UK, France and Germany in Miami on 9 October arranged by US presidential special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
The report claims that during the meeting, the Americans asked the Ukrainians to cease attacks on Russian oil refineries and warned that Trump would make a deal with Russia regarding diesel fuel.
Background:
- On 12 October, The Washington Post reported that the US and Europe are discussing a joint four-point peace plan that envisages both territorial concessions by Ukraine and Russia and security guarantees and agreements aimed at improving both countries' post-war economies.
- On 9 October, Trump announced that he had spoken to Russian ruler Vladimir Putin and reached an agreement with him on the supply of Russian diesel to US and global markets.
- According to media reports, Witkoff and Kushner informed the Ukrainian delegation at the negotiations in Miami that the agreement permitting the export of Russian diesel fuel is part of an effort to bring Russia back to the negotiating table.

Sea Breeze 2026 Conference - a commitment to Allied cohesion in Black Sea region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:19:51 UTC
19:19:51 KST

News
Sea Breeze 2026 Conference - a commitment to Allied cohesion in Black Sea region
Tuesday 13 October 2026 12:03
Tuesday, 13 October 2026, 12:03
Vice Admiral Jeffrey Anderson
PHOTO Romanian Naval Forces (Forțele Navale Române)
Font size
Security in the Black Sea has long ceased to be merely a regional issue and has become an absolute European priority. Today, the Black Sea is an extremely volatile geopolitical space and a critical point for regional security. Constanța, on Romania’s Black Sea coast, recently hosted the third edition of the Sea Breeze 2026 Conference of Black Sea naval commanders, an event that brought together strategic leaders and NATO allies, as well as representatives of NATO’s Allied Maritime Command – MARCOM – from around 20 countries. Against the backdrop of the war in Ukraine, US Sixth Fleet Commander Vice Admiral Jeffrey Anderson explained the main pillars of the strategy in the region and how autonomous technologies are becoming vital in addressing hybrid threats and drifting mines.
He said that he was pleased to be back in Constanța and that a wide range of issues had been discussed during the conference. He stressed that efforts to restore peace, security and stability in the Black Sea were important not only for the Black Sea nations, but also for European naval forces. He said the discussions had focused on ways to cooperate on emerging capabilities, including unmanned surface vessels, robotics and autonomous systems. The participants had also discussed a number of such initiatives, as well as ways of helping protect navigation and the maritime environment against the threat posed by sea mines. Finally, he said, they had discussed initiatives aimed at monitoring and protecting critical maritime and underwater infrastructure in the Black Sea.
One of the most important objectives of the Allied presence on the Eastern Flank is the ability of forces to operate together. This tactical cohesion is the result of complex exercises conducted jointly by military personnel, an aspect highlighted by the senior US official. He noted that the conference was taking place shortly after the Sea Breeze exercise, which is held annually in the Black Sea. This year, he said, there had been two editions of the exercise. He stressed that whenever tactical units from the Black Sea nations and other nations from across the European theatre were able to come together, integrate and collaborate, share best practices, rehearse and demonstrate existing capabilities as well as their tactics, techniques and procedures, this made the participating forces more effective. Such cooperation, he added, would improve their readiness, capability and capacity.
Beyond military strategies and equipment, the strongest message coming from this conference is one of unity and resilience, while the real stakes in Constanța remain deeply geopolitical. The Black Sea is a vital artery for the region’s economy and stability, and maintaining constant dialogue among allies is opening up new strategic avenues for cooperation. NATO allies and European partners are here to protect, support and guarantee a secure future on the Eastern Flank, Vice Admiral Anderson said. He stressed that the effort was about promoting security and stability in the critically important Black Sea region, not only for the nations in the area, but for the entire European theatre and for Europe’s prosperity. He said the allies were working to develop ways to continue protecting the Black Sea against the threats it faces, while promoting and supporting these efforts.
It is a clear and firm message of unity, stability and resilience from the Eastern Flank, where the partnership between Romania and the United States guarantees that the security of the Alliance is not something to be negotiated, but strengthened through concrete action and trusted partnerships.
Source: Agenția Media a Armatei (Media Agency of the Romanian Army)

The night Trump announced a diesel deal with Putin, drones knocked out more than half the tanks at a Russian fuel-export terminal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:19:46 UTC
19:19:46 KST

A drone strike on 10 October put more than half of the large fuel tanks out of action at an oil-loading terminal in Russia’s Rostov-on-Don, Russian news Telegram channel Astra found. The terminal loads fuel onto river and sea tankers for export, and it burned for two days while a local channel wrote that reeds might be on fire. Neither Kyiv nor Moscow has officially acknowledged the hit. It came hours after US President Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
Russia has spent the autumn hammering Ukraine’s power grid ahead of winter. Ukraine’s long-range drones keep hitting the refineries, depots, and terminals that fuel Russia’s army and earn it export revenue. Every burned tank turns that revenue into repair bills, while Moscow is already subsidizing its own fuel pumps. A refinery-only truce of the kind the White House described a day after the strike would shield the Russian plants that feed terminals like this one.
Seven of 12 tanks out of action
Astra’s analysts concluded from eyewitness footage that at least seven of the terminal’s 12 large tanks had been knocked out. Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ counted seven burned-out tanks and one more scorched by the fire.
The fire was still burning in the early hours of 12 October. Local channel Rostov Glavny posted video of the burning tank farm, passing on rumors that reeds were on fire and noting the city’s second day under smoke, The Moscow Times reported. Footage filmed in the daytime on 12 October showed no more open flames, only gray smoke, according to Astra.
A terminal that loads fuel for export
The site is the oil-loading terminal of the Novoshakhtinsk Oil Products Plant, formerly known as Yug Rusi, in Rostov-on-Don’s Zheleznodorozhny District. It receives, stores, and transships fuel onto river and sea tankers, including for export, Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ said.
The terminal also supplies fuel to the Russian army and earns Moscow hard currency, ZN reported. The Moscow Times put its loading capacity at 3.5 million tons a year and its tank farm at about 60,000 cubic meters, roughly 16 million gallons.
Trump’s Russian diesel deal, which drew fury in Ukraine, is unlikely to lower prices, experts say
The refinery itself stands in the town of Novoshakhtinsk near the border with Russian-occupied Luhansk Oblast. The terminal sits on the Don River with access to the Sea of Azov, Ukrainian military outlet Militarnyi noted. Ukraine hit the refinery in June, and Ukraine’s General Staff reported striking the Yug Rusi terminal on 9 July, placing it in Bataysk.
A night of drones over the region
Exilenova+ posted images of the burning terminal in the early hours of 10 October. It presented them as the site after Trump’s phone call with Putin. The channel later shared NASA satellite fire data showing the blaze.
Rostov Oblast Governor Yuri Slyusar claimed the attack injured six people. Slyusar further stated air defenses downed more than 100 drones over the region. Radio Liberty’s Russian Service noted that neither side had officially confirmed the hit on the terminal.
Hours after the US-Russia diesel deal
The strike came hours after Trump announced on 9 October that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to US and global markets. The US Treasury then cleared the trade with a sanctions license.
On 11 October, Trump declared an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine. Under it, he expects Ukraine to stop striking Russian refineries, a White House official told Axios.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that evening that Ukraine’s armed forces had received all relevant orders. Neither Ukrainian monitoring channels nor Russian officials have reported a new strike on a Russian oil facility since. On 13 October, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was ready to guarantee an energy ceasefire if Russia took matching steps.

Palestinian killed, others injured in Israeli attacks in Gaza despite ceasefire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:19:13 UTC
19:19:13 KST

Ramzi Mahmud and Mohammad Sio
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
A Palestinian was killed and several others, including a woman, were injured Tuesday in an Israeli airstrike and gunfire across the Gaza Strip, while the army demolished residential buildings, medical and local sources said.
The attacks came amid continued Israeli violations of the ceasefire agreement in force since Oct. 10, 2025, and more than three years after the start of Israel’s genocide on Gaza.
One Palestinian was killed and others were injured when an Israeli drone struck a vehicle in the Al-Mashahara area of the Tuffah neighborhood in eastern Gaza City, a medical source told Anadolu.
In southern Gaza, another medical source said a woman was injured by Israeli gunfire in Hamad City, north of Khan Younis, while another Palestinian was wounded near Al-Amal Hospital west of the city.
Israeli military vehicles opened heavy fire toward Palestinian homes and tents sheltering displaced people in several areas of Khan Younis, injuring the woman and the man, local sources told Anadolu.
In northern Gaza, a medical source said a Palestinian sustained moderate injuries from Israeli gunfire near Kamal Adwan Hospital in Beit Lahia.
In the same area, the Israeli army demolished homes and evacuated buildings north of the hospital, near areas under its control.
Witnesses told Anadolu they heard a powerful explosion from the demolition operation, with no casualties immediately reported.
Separately, Israeli naval vessels opened machine-gun fire and launched shells toward the Gaza City coast, with no injuries reported.
Israeli violations of the ceasefire had killed 1,493 Palestinians and injured 5,299 others as of Monday, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Since October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured in Gaza by Israeli genocide, while around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed.

Taiwan’s Chunghwa Telecom carbon project passes review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:18:18 UTC
19:18:18 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Chunghwa Telecom’s bamboo forest carbon project has become the first corporate project in Taiwan based on a bamboo forest management methodology to pass a registration review by the Ministry of Environment, the company said Tuesday.
The project is part of a natural carbon sink and biodiversity conservation initiative led by the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency under the Ministry of Agriculture. It focuses on managing bamboo forests to absorb carbon while protecting local ecosystems, per CNA.
Chunghwa Telecom Chair Chien Chih-cheng (簡志誠) said the company had reduced emissions by 152,000 metric tons through the third quarter, reaching 96% of its full-year target. He said the company would pursue net-zero emissions through technology-driven reductions and natural carbon removal.
Chien said the company would follow strict monitoring, reporting, and verification procedures while managing bamboo forests through cultivation, bamboo production, and subsequent use. The project also aims to preserve traditional bamboo-harvesting skills and forest knowledge.
The project will create opportunities for Indigenous communities to participate in forest management and support local green livelihoods, Chien said. He added that it could serve as a model for developing natural carbon sinks in Taiwan.

Istat said in a report on Tuesday
that its consumer-price index rose by 63% overall between 2000
and 2025.
The national statistics agency added that several categories
registered rises of over 100%, including spending for housing
and utilities, which were driven up by the rising cost of
electricity and fuel, for alcoholic beverages and tobacco, and
for financial and insurance services.
It said there were increases of less than 30% for education and
health services, and a decrease of nearly 60% in the cost of
information and communication goods and services.

French students say they are determined to press the government to address the problems of too many absent teachers, dilapidated buildings, overcrowded class schedules and other grievances.
Swedish activist Greta Thunberg joined high school pupils campaigning for better learning conditions in France on Tuesday ahead of fresh nationwide demonstrations, with authorities and participants wary of further violence.
The 23-year-old, who became famous as a teen for school strikes to demand action on climate change, stood among pupils demonstrating outside a school at the heart of the movement in the capital's largest suburb of Saint-Denis.
Thunberg arrived at the Paul Éluard high school, as lawyers in their robes formed a human chain to protect teens after numerous allegations of police brutality.
"Young people are not being included in the conversation. Our future is being robbed away from us," Thunberg told the AFP news agency.
The mobilisation, which is backed by unions and the far-left opposition France Unbowed party, was to include a midday march through Paris, along with marches in other cities.
"They're not listening to us, so we're going to them," university student union l'Union etudiante wrote in a post on X.
More than 70,000 people took to the streets last Thursday in the last major event of a movement that started in late September.
French authorities had been hoping that the protests would start to ease ahead of half-term holidays.
"We should be at around...200 schools closed, which is fewer than last week," Education Minister Édouard Geffray said on radio station France Inter on Tuesday morning, adding some near protest routes were closing to avoid damage.
In the Paris region, teenagers had blockaded the entrances to several schools before dawn.
In the southern city of Marseille, students slowly pushed dumpsters on wheels in front of their high school.
'Aren't being heard'
French students say they are determined to press the government to address the problems of too many absent teachers, dilapidated buildings, overcrowded class schedules and other grievances.
The protests since last month have seen teenagers pile up dumpsters and light security barriers outside hundreds of France's 3,700 lycées for students mostly aged 15 to 18.
They have mostly been peaceful, but seen clashes occasionally break out with police.
The education ministry said eight members of teaching staff were injured on Monday, mostly in the Paris region and cities of Bordeaux and Lyon, in relation to the protests.
"Students aren't being heard enough...not their proposals to authorities and elected officials," a 19-year-old graphic design student in Paris, Leo, said on Monday.
He added that the protesters, many of whom were minors, were "disturbed by the level of repression never before seen for a student movement."
Thousands of arrests
Authorities said fireworks fired through a tube injured two school workers in Reims, one school worker in a Paris suburb and a police officer outside a school in Marseille.
Tuesday's demonstrations supporting the students were to be followed on Saturday by wider public rallies against the rising cost of living.
Naila, a 17-year-old student in the city of Rennes who said she would participate in Tuesday's demonstration, hoped it would "converge" with the wider one on Saturday.
President Emmanuel Macron, speaking to reporters at a car show on Monday, urged restraint from protesters.
"These are issues that deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect," Macron said just months before elections to replace him.
More than 6,800 people, largely minors, have been taken into police custody over the course of the protests, according to the justice ministry.
Police have opened internal investigations into 24 allegations of brutality against demonstrators.
After last week's nationwide demonstrations, the government promised some 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days to replace absent staff at the 114 worst-affected high schools.
The education minister said on Tuesday that 35% had already been assigned.
High school students are demanding a €10 billion boost in investment for the country’s lycées.
