19:02:45 KST

UN report: 1.2bn people worldwide live in multidimensional poverty
The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) reported in its 2026 update of the global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) that the number of people living in multidimensional poverty worldwide has risen for the first time since the index was launched in 2010, reaching 1.2 billion, or 51.5 million more than in the previous update, according to WAM.
UNDP Administrator Alexander De Croo said, “The rise in poverty should be a wake-up call for the world,” noting that millions of people face hunger, missed schooling, and a lack of clean water or electricity, while children account for more than half of those affected.
The UNDP said population growth contributed to the increase in the number of people living in multidimensional poverty.
He noted that among the 89 countries with MPI trend data, 33 have halved their MPI value in fewer than 15 years, including six countries in Sub-Saharan Africa.
Earlier, in April, the UNDP warned that Middle East escalation could push 30 million into global poverty.

Iran fortifies nuclear sites, prepares for renewed war: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:01:34 UTC
19:01:34 KST

Breadcrumb
Iran fortifies nuclear sites as it prepares for renewed US war: report
Iran is strengthening its nuclear and military facilities, mobilising supporters and threatening a wider regional conflict as it prepares for the possibility of renewed war with the United States, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal.
Iranian leaders believe US President Donald Trump could launch fresh attacks after the 3 November midterm elections, prompting Tehran to reinforce sensitive sites and warn Washington that another offensive would trigger a more devastating response, the newspaper reported on Tuesday.
Citing Iranian officials and people familiar with regional communications, the WSJ said Tehran had issued both public and private warnings that renewed US strikes could lead to attacks on American interests and Gulf allies.
Satellite imagery has shown Iran strengthening defences around nuclear facilities and border areas, while authorities have stepped up pro-government rallies and promoted military training for civilians.
Iran's limited ability to counter advanced US fighter jets, high-altitude bombers and cruise missiles has pushed Tehran to rely increasingly on threats of wider retaliation to deter Washington, according to the report.
Sanam Vakil, director of the Middle East and North Africa programme at London-based Chatham House, said the prospect of war also served Iran's leadership as it grappled with diplomatic, economic and political deadlock.
Iran threatens Gulf infrastructure and US warships
Iranian officials have raised the possibility of launching ground incursions into neighbouring countries in response to further US attacks, according to people familiar with Tehran's warnings.
Senior Iranian national security official Mohsen Rezaei warned on Sunday that the United Arab Emirates could be targeted, along with regional data centres and internet cables.
Tehran has also warned Arab officials that critical infrastructure, including Saudi oil facilities, could come under attack if fighting resumes, the WSJ reported.
The threats come as Saudi Arabia faces mounting attacks from Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement.
A Houthi missile strike on Riyadh's airport on Saturday killed at least 13 people and wounded hundreds, according to the newspaper, which described it as the deadliest attack on the US or its Gulf allies during the conflict linked to the war with Iran.
Iran has also told intermediaries that it could respond more forcefully against American military personnel, including by attempting to sink US warships and inflict casualties among their crews.
The warnings highlight the risks to the Gulf's vital economic infrastructure if Trump orders another round of strikes.
US sends more military assets to Middle East
The US military is also preparing for a possible resumption of hostilities, with a third aircraft carrier strike group and an additional Marine unit heading towards the region according to the outlet.
The Pentagon is considering sending more air defence systems and ammunition to American bases across the region.
Trump ruled out launching an attack before the midterm elections last week but publicly raised the possibility of striking Iran's Mount Pickaxe nuclear site.
US officials said the military was developing several options for renewed strikes.
Direct fighting between Washington and Tehran has eased considerably since late July, when Trump backed away from plans for a major escalation, partly over concerns about dwindling interceptor missile stocks needed to protect American and regional targets.
The lull has nevertheless allowed both sides to prepare for another confrontation.
Iran has used the period to rebuild missile and drone production facilities and replenish its weapons stockpiles, while Washington has intensified economic pressure on Tehran.
Meanwhile, attacks on commercial shipping and tankers in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz have increased.
At least three merchant vessels came under attack over the weekend, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency.
A drone strike on the Emirati tanker Petro Dolphin near Oman on Sunday sparked a fire aboard the vessel and left two Indian sailors missing.
Iran reinforces nuclear sites and mobilises civilians
Satellite images taken by Vantor and analysed by the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security show Iran constructing new defensive barriers around its Pickaxe Mountain and Natanz nuclear facilities.
The measures, introduced last month, include makeshift earthworks designed to obstruct potential ground raids.
Iranian officials have also sought to demonstrate the country's readiness for another war.
Brigadier General Gholamreza Jalali, who oversees Iran's contingency planning, said in late September that airports, seaports and power plants had been equipped with shelters and emergency supplies to maintain operations during a conflict.
State media have meanwhile intensified coverage of pro-government demonstrations, with residents reporting that rallies have grown larger and spread to more locations in recent weeks.
Billboards in Tehran have advertised civilian training courses in the use of shoulder-fired anti-aircraft missiles and sniper rifles.
Last month, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps released footage of women undergoing training in guerrilla warfare, firearms and drone operations through its Basij paramilitary force.
In the northeastern city of Sabzevar, Revolutionary Guard personnel visited a kindergarten to recount stories of earlier fighting and display a US-made Tomahawk missile they claimed to have intercepted.
Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran programme at the Washington-based Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said Tehran's political rhetoric and military preparations indicated it was actively preparing for another confrontation.
He described the measures as serving both deterrence and war planning.

====================================================================================================

lightweight systems prove that more material does not mean better performance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:00:18 UTC
19:00:18 KST

lightweight systems prove that more material does not mean better performance
from heavy mass to high-performance envelopes, the shift toward lightweight architectural membranes explores how surfaces filter light, guide airflow, and redefine the space around us.
[ADVERTISEMENT]
In the story of the Three Little Pigs, the choice of material determines the fate of each house. The wolf’s breath brings down the structures made of straw and wood, while the brick house remains standing. The moral is that the more solid the construction, the greater its ability to resist. A building, however, has to respond to much less straightforward questions. Remaining standing is still essential, but heat, light, air, and sound are not forces that necessarily need to be blocked. Sometimes sunlight needs to be kept out; at other times, daylight needs to be let in. Retaining heat may be desirable in winter and counterproductive in summer. Air needs to circulate, sound may need to be absorbed, and the conditions that determine these responses change throughout the day, across seasons, and over the life of the building itself. More material does not necessarily mean better performance. In some cases, it can simply add complexity without improving how the building responds.
This relationship between mass and performance was at the center of Serge Ferrari Architecture‘s recent reveal of the 7TH MATERIAL, a category currently centered on technical membrane. The category is framed around what materials can do: filtering light, modulating solar gain, guiding airflow, treating sound, or combining several of these functions within a single surface. Membranes do not replace concrete, metal, stone, or glass; they complement them by performing different functions.
For Nic Goldsmith, Founding Director of the Lightweight Structures Group at TYLin and author of Mass to Membrane, this discussion forms part of a much longer architectural trajectory. During the reveal, he described the history of architecture as ‘one long attempt to do more with less,’ tracing a shift from massive structures toward increasingly lighter ways of enclosing space. Along that trajectory, new material systems have expanded what architects can ask an envelope to do, a process that, in his view, is still unfolding. As he puts it: ‘We may not know the precise form future membranes will take. The direction is clear.’
Structural stability is only one measure of how well a building performs. Heat, light, air, and sound place different demands on a space, and the goal is not always to block them, but to control how they move through the building. A roof, for example, can be evaluated by the shade it provides, the daylight it allows through, the air that circulates beneath it, and the resources required to perform those functions over time. Its thickness or weight describes only part of the solution. Its properties, geometry, and relationship with the building’s other elements also matter.
At The Camp in Aix-en-Provence, this logic can be seen in the organization of the complex itself. Designed by Corinne Vezzoni & Associés, the 11,000-square-meter campus is covered by approximately 7,000 square meters of membrane, beneath which some circulation areas remain open to the air. The surface filters daylight, while its double curvature contributes to the roof’s stability, air circulation, and rainwater collection. Under the project’s specific conditions and fire safety approval, this configuration also removes the need for mechanical ventilation and smoke extraction within that volume. Its properties and geometry work together to provide shade, daylight, airflow, structural stability, and rainwater collection.
THE MATERIAL HELPS DEFINE THE FORM
Another example can be found at Hazza Bin Zayed Stadium in Al Ain, where BDP Pattern began with the conditions of a hot, dry climate to develop the enclosure. In this case, the path of the sun, rather than protection from rain, shaped its geometry: a 40-meter cantilever on the west side shades the field and stands at 4:00 p.m. on game days, while the porous façade encourages air to circulate through the envelope. Before settling on the final solution, the team built a full-scale prototype on site using three geometries and, over the course of development, reduced the number of panel types from 320 to 86, making it possible for a local manufacturer to produce them at an acceptable cost. Climate, material behavior, geometry, and fabrication all contributed to defining the form.
Architect and computational designer Nick Tyrer describes this relationship more directly: ‘Do not specify the material to fit a form you have already decided on. Let the material and the geometry find the form together, in response to the actual conditions of that place.’ Across projects responding to a headwind, a desert sun, and a coastline, Tyrer returns to the same point: ‘You don’t specify it. You design with it.’
At Al Ain, solar exposure, ventilation, geometry, material, and fabrication were therefore treated as parts of the same problem, changing when materials enter the design conversation. A technical data sheet can describe how a product performs under specific test conditions, but a design team still needs to understand how those properties behave within a particular configuration while the geometry can still be adjusted.
WHAT ENTERS THE COMPARISON
Serge Ferrari uses the idea of performance density to describe a comparison that begins with equivalent functions rather than equivalent quantities of material. Shading, daylighting, acoustic treatment, structural requirements, carbon emissions, and the additional systems needed over time can all become part of the equation. The comparison also considers what a solution makes unnecessary, from additional layers to heavier structures or greater mechanical capacity. There is not yet a single standardized metric that combines all of these variables.
A simulation for an office in Lyon helps illustrate the complexity of this calculation. With Type D glazing and automated external solar shading, cooling demand fell from 60.2 to 29.8 kWh/m²/year, while heating demand rose from 11.4 to 13.4 kWh/m²/year because of reduced solar gains in winter. Overall, combined heating and cooling demand decreased by 39.59%. The result applies to this specific configuration, reinforcing the need to read performance figures alongside the conditions that produced them.
PERFORMANCE OVER TIME
Comparing only the amount of material installed on day one also leaves out maintenance, replacement, and end-of-life considerations. In the methodology being developed around the 7TH MATERIAL, the assessment accounts for the materials and carbon mobilized over the entire period analyzed, including replacements, as well as the additional layers and systems each solution requires to deliver equivalent functions. The calculation therefore extends beyond the material itself to everything needed to install, operate, maintain, and eventually replace it.
For anyone specifying materials or systems, this means reading properties such as weight, light transmission, and resistance in context. Their significance depends on supports, adjacent layers, climate, conditions of use, and maintenance over time. Performance is ultimately shaped by how a material works with the rest of the architectural system.
The practical consequence is that material decisions need to happen earlier in the design process, while form, geometry, and system relationships can still be adjusted. Solidity becomes only one part of the equation. A solution also needs to be understood in terms of the functions it can combine, what it requires from the building, and what it may make unnecessary. Resisting the wolf’s breath remains a perfectly effective measure for a fairy tale, but in architecture, performance involves a much larger set of variables.
Guest Feature by Eduardo Souza / Archdaily

A popular workout supplement might protect the brain from gut inflammation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:00:09 UTC
19:00:09 KST

Creatine, a popular dietary supplement, prevented brain inflammation, nerve cell damage, and disrupted electrical activity in the hippocampus of rats with chronic colitis, according to new research published in Brain, Behavior, and Immunity. The colitis-related damage was far more pronounced in male rats than in females. The findings add to evidence linking gut inflammation to changes in the brain, though they have not been tested in people.
The gut-brain axis is the complex, two-way communication network connecting the digestive tract and the central nervous system. Inflammatory bowel disease is a group of chronic conditions marked by persistent inflammation of the digestive tract, including Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, which causes sores and swelling in the lining of the colon and rectum. In these conditions, inflammatory signals from the gut can travel to the brain and trigger secondary inflammation there, which is thought to contribute to the mood and cognitive problems frequently experienced by people with intestinal diseases.
Prior research has mapped how this process unfolds. A 2018 study found that a short bout of gut inflammation made both male and female mice more prone to seizures and increased anxiety-like behavior. In a 2022 study, members of the current team found that acute gut inflammation in rats was accompanied by brain inflammation and made neurons in the motor cortex more excitable.
The same group later reported in a 2024 study that chronic colitis produced memory problems, motor deficits, and anxiety- and depression-like behaviors in rats, with females showing more anxiety-like behavior and males showing stronger inflammation in the brain.
Building on this progression, a research group at the Universidad de Sevilla studying gut-brain pathophysiology led by María José Peral, Pablo García-Miranda, and Livia Carrascal set out to examine exactly what happens to the cells in the hippocampus during chronic colitis. The hippocampus is a seahorse-shaped structure deep in the brain that manages learning and memory.
“Inflammatory bowel disease primarily affects the intestine, but people with IBD also have a high prevalence of mood disorders and cognitive difficulties, particularly involving memory,” study co-author María D. Vázquez-Carretero, a researcher in the Department of Physiology at the university’s Faculty of Pharmacy, told PsyPost. “Our previous studies showed that chronic colitis can be associated with alterations in the hippocampus, a brain region that is important not only in memory but also in emotional processes. This led us to investigate how it affects hippocampal neurons and whether males and females respond differently.”
The researchers also wanted to test the potential protective effects of creatine, teaming up with a group focused on neurogenesis and neuroregeneration. While widely known as a sports supplement used to build muscle, creatine is a natural compound that helps supply energy to cells throughout the body, including brain cells, acting as a reserve that quickly replenishes cellular fuel during times of high demand or stress.
“Because managing the effects of IBD beyond the intestine remains challenging, we investigated whether creatine, a naturally occurring compound, could protect the hippocampus from the effects of intestinal inflammation,” Vázquez-Carretero explained.
To explore these questions, the researchers used young male and female rats, with 15 to 21 animals of each sex in each of four groups: healthy rats given plain water, healthy rats given creatine, rats with colitis, and rats with colitis given creatine. Colitis was induced with dextran sulfate sodium in the drinking water over three one-week cycles separated by weeks of plain water, mimicking the flare-ups and remissions of human ulcerative colitis. Creatine was added to the drinking water at a daily dose of 1 gram per kilogram of body weight, starting 10 days before colitis was induced and continuing throughout. Each type of measurement used five to seven animals per group.
After a period of over a month, the researchers examined the rats’ hippocampi. They measured the levels of inflammatory molecules, assessed the physical health of the neurons, and tested the cells’ electrical properties. For the electrical tests, they used a technique called patch-clamp recording. This involves placing a microscopic glass tube against a single cell to monitor the tiny electrical currents flowing across its membrane.
The results indicated that chronic colitis reduced creatine levels in the hippocampus of both male and female rats. The gut inflammation also spurred a strong immune response in the brain. Microglia, which act as the brain’s first line of immune defense, became activated in both sexes, accompanied by elevated levels of inflammatory molecules.
The consequences of this brain inflammation differed sharply by sex. Male rats developed physical damage to their hippocampal neurons, showing a loss of structural proteins and fewer neurons in the CA1 region, a specific area of the hippocampus. In contrast, female rats maintained their neuronal structure despite the presence of inflammation.
The electrical tests revealed a similar divide. In male rats with colitis, the neurons became leakier: their membranes lost electrical resistance, and the minimum current needed to make a neuron fire an electrical signal, known as the rheobase, rose by roughly 60 percent. This suggests the neurons became less excitable, the opposite of the hyperexcitability reported in studies of short-term colitis.
The males also had higher levels of a potassium channel called Kv2.1, which helps neurons reset after firing, along with larger electrical currents flowing into and out of the cells. Female neurons showed no significant electrical changes, although colitis did raise levels of a calcium channel called Cav1.2 in their hippocampus.
“The changes were not limited to a single marker,” Vázquez-Carretero noted. “We found converging evidence of neuroinflammation, neuronal damage, and altered electrical properties of hippocampal neurons, particularly in males. Together, these findings suggest that chronic colitis can produce biologically meaningful alterations in hippocampal function.”
“The sex differences were particularly striking,” she added. “Male rats showed greater hippocampal neuroinflammation, neuronal damage, and alterations in neuronal electrical properties, whereas females were less affected at the functional level.”
Creatine supplementation largely prevented these changes. In rats with colitis that consumed creatine, hippocampal creatine levels were about 20 to 30 percent higher than in unsupplemented rats with colitis, matching those of healthy animals. The supplement prevented the activation of microglia and stopped the rise of inflammatory molecules in both sexes. In females, creatine had an especially strong effect in suppressing a specific inflammatory molecule called tumor necrosis factor.
Because the female rats did not experience the physical and electrical cell damage caused by colitis, creatine’s protective effects in these areas were mostly visible in the males. For the male rats, creatine protected the structural health of the neurons and maintained their normal electrical resistance and firing thresholds. The authors noted that creatine acts selectively on the parameters altered by disease, rather than artificially boosting the performance of healthy cells.
“Creatine also appeared to have a greater effect in males, but this seems to reflect their greater initial pathological burden rather than a sex-specific response to creatine,” Vázquez-Carretero observed.
The findings are in line with earlier work by the same research group, covered by PsyPost in 2025. That earlier study, which examined neuroinflammation in the cortex and behavioral deficits rather than cellular and electrical changes in the hippocampus, similarly found that creatine prevents colitis-induced brain inflammation across both sexes.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind, including that the exact sequence of events might differ in human patients. “It is important not to interpret our results as showing that creatine is a treatment for inflammatory bowel disease or that people with colitis should take creatine to protect their brains,” Vázquez-Carretero cautioned. “Our study was conducted in rats under controlled experimental conditions. The results suggest that creatine may protect the brain from some consequences of chronic intestinal inflammation, but further research is needed to determine whether these effects also occur in humans.”
“Although these findings cannot be directly extrapolated to humans, growing evidence in people with IBD also suggests alterations in brain function and structure,” she noted.
The study used relatively small numbers of animals for the specific electrical and molecular tests, with five to seven rats per group. This reduced statistical power might have masked some subtle changes in the female rats, making them appear completely unaffected when they might have experienced minor alterations.
Additionally, the electrical recordings measured the overall flow of ions across the cell membrane rather than isolating individual channels with specialized drugs. Future research will need to pinpoint the exact molecular pathways responsible for the electrical changes.
It is also important to note that creatine was given before colitis began, so the study tested prevention rather than the treatment of existing damage. The study measured cells and electrical activity rather than memory or behavior, and it could not determine whether creatine protects the brain mainly by reducing inflammation in the gut or by acting directly on brain cells, though the authors suspect both play a role.
“We think this study highlights how closely connected the gut and the brain are,” Vázquez-Carretero told PsyPost. “It also reinforces the importance of studying both sexes when investigating how chronic inflammation affects the brain.”
“We want to better understand how chronic intestinal inflammation affects the brain and why these effects differ between males and females,” she said. “We are also interested in determining how creatine protects hippocampal neurons and whether this protection is related to its role in cellular energy metabolism. Ultimately, our goal is to determine whether these mechanisms are also relevant in humans and whether creatine could eventually be explored as a complementary strategy in people with chronic intestinal inflammation.”
The study, “Modulating effects of creatine prevent sex-dependent hippocampal neuroinflammation, neuronal damage, and electrophysiological dysfunction induced by chronic colitis,” was authored by Alejandro Ruiz-Calero, María Ortego-Domínguez, María D. Vázquez-Carretero, Gema Sotelo-Parrilla, Nora Martínez-Gómez, María L. Calonge, Ricardo Pardillo-Díaz, Carmen Castro, Pedro Nunez-Abades, María J. Peral, Livia Carrascal, and Pablo García-Miranda.

====================================================================================================

‘It’s not glamorous’: the volunteers counting flushed wet wipes on the banks of the Thames
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:00:05 UTC
19:00:05 KST

On a pale-blue Sunday morning on the foreshore of the River Thames, 40 people are searching for what others have tried to lose. Dotted across a 250-metre stretch under Hammersmith Bridge, they are combing through layers of silt, seashells and dirty driftwood to find one of the river’s most stubborn problems: wet wipes.
“People come and walk here and it looks just like mud, at a distance,” says the organiser, Dr Felicity Rhodes. “And then you get closer in and see.”
The dig forms part a citizen science project that has tracked sanitary litter on the banks of the Thames for nearly a decade. Set up by the environmental charity Thames21, volunteers are recruited to help map out the amount of wipes that are flushed down the toilet and washed up along the river. Findings are added to a database that quantifies plastic pollution on the banks of the Thames.
“It’s not glamorous,” says Rhodes, the programme manager at Thames21. “But through this data generation, we’ve created this dataset of really robust, accurate data that’s given us an understanding of the wet wipes here on the foreshore.”
Hydrographic surveyors from the Port of London authority (PLA) are assisting the project, and are riverside before the volunteers arrive, having meticulously marked out channels of the foreshore based on where the last count took place. Volunteers lay quadrats, square frames, on the riverbed and drag metal sticks through the mud. One drag can pull up a clump of flushed wet wipes from what had appeared to be just silt to the naked eye; they are counted, recorded and deposited into a bucket for disposal, along with the plastic, vapes and other rubbish curios that come up.
Jim Powell, an operations manager and hydrographic surveyor at the PLA, explains why Hammersmith is such a hotspot for grime. “You’re on the inside of a bend of the river so the water velocities are slower,” he says. Material builds up on the inside because the water flows faster on the outside. “As soon as you get bits of wood and tyres, they start to trap sediment and other things start getting caught, like plastic wipes. Then it just snowballs from there.”
Elio Gregori, 66, has attended about 300 sessions since he retired. “You can look at a place like this and assume that it’s mostly nice and clean, but under the surface is a wet wipe,” he says, fishing a knot of rotten-brown wipes out of his bucket as an exhibit. “When it’s in the environment, you wouldn’t really recognise it as a wet wipe. If you look down, it opens your eyes to how much of this stuff is around.”
Many wet wipes contain plastic fibres and are designed to stay intact when wet – even some marketed as biodegradable. When London’s wipes are flushed down the toilet, they can end up on the riverbanks, mostly through storm water overflow and sewage outfall. Thames Water estimates 3.8bn wipes are flushed into its network each year – enough to build more than 10 wet and stinking Big Bens.
“Plastic here on the foreshore has the potential to make its way into the ocean and into our ocean food system as well,” says Rhodes. “We want to remove plastic here so that it doesn’t become microplastic in the ocean.”
A young refugee from Sudan attended the count with the community centre West London Welcome. “It’s really a shame for people to throw bad things through toilets,” he said. “This waste is in this nice area … people should have to be more careful in the environment where these things ended up.”
Some relief arrived last year when the delayed Thames Tideway Tunnel opened – the £4.6bn project designed to reduce sewage discharges into the river.
Then diggers came to this part of the foreshore a few months later to remove the infamous “Wet Wipe Island”, the 180-tonne amalgamation of wipes that had grown so large it had begun to alter the shape of the river. Thames21 estimates the work removed 5m wipes that had congealed into a 250-metre island.
Now, Thames21 is back to assess what the Tideway Tunnel – the “super sewer” – and removing Wet Wipe Island has done. “Will we see fewer wet wipes? Most likely,” says Rhodes. “Are they re-accumulating? We might be able to start to see any changes and that’s why it’s really important to keep monitoring.”
Last December, the government announced that selling single-use wet wipes containing plastic will be illegal by May 2027. It was a win for Thames21, who had for years been banging the drum and sharing their data with Fleur Anderson, the MP for Putney, who campaigned on the issue in parliament.
By the end of the weekend’s count, Thames21 said volunteers had found 733 wipes in 50 sampling squares, compared with 1,584 found in the same spots in April. It is a substantial drop in the recorded count, although the PLA says it is still early days, and two surveys cannot yet establish precisely how much of it is due to the cleanups, the Tideway tunnel or changing conditions on the river.
But for now, Thames21 volunteers plan to keep counting. “We expect that they’ll still wash up on the river for a time,” says Rhodes. “What we’re doing here is tracking the ongoing change in that.”

How a scandal engulfing Brazil’s top court could return the Bolsonaros to power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:00:05 UTC
19:00:05 KST

Thundering to a crowd of thousands of far-right supporters in São Paulo on 7 September, Brazil’s Independence Day, the senator Flávio Bolsonaro focused less on his opponent in the presidential election, the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, than on someone who is not running at all.
“Whoever votes for Lula is voting for Alexandre de Moraes,” Bolsonaro shouted, referring to the shaven-headed supreme court justice once described as “Voldemort” by Elon Musk.
Although Lula did not appoint Moraes to the court, Bolsonaro’s supporters have linked the two men ever since the judge oversaw the case in which the senator’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, was sentenced to 27 years in prison for attempting a coup.
Now, just days before the election runoff on 25 October, Moraes is once again at the centre of a presidential scandal – one that Lula believes may have helped Flávio Bolsonaro overtake him to emerge as the frontrunner. The justice once hailed as democracy’s “saviour” for containing Jair Bolsonaro may now have helped pave the way for the family’s return to power.
The scandal began with a police investigation, which found that Moraes’s wife’s law firm had a contract worth about £20m with Daniel Vorcaro, the banker accused of orchestrating Brazil’s largest banking fraud. Text messages also emerged suggesting a close relationship between Moraes and Vorcaro, though the judge denies the messages are authentic.
Investigations subsequently revealed that at least four other justices had links to the disgraced banker, meaning half of the court’s 10 current justices have been drawn into the scandal.
The crisis peaked last month with a ferocious exchange of insults between Moraes and another justice during a televised court session. A series of rulings followed in which the pair – as well as other judges aligned with each side – overruled one another, dominating public debate for weeks.
Lula, the day after losing the first round, blamed his poor result in part on having to “carry on his back … the promiscuity” of the supreme court, in what many political observers saw as an attempt by the president to distance himself from the crisis. His campaign coordinator, Edinho Silva, said that, “in the eyes of society … [Lula] paid the price for that institutional damage”.
Although analysts point to a range of reasons for the far right’s lead, from household debt to a simple preference for Flávio Bolsonaro, many agree that the supreme court crisis played a decisive role, particularly among indecisive voters who, with the electorate generally divided between two similarly sized left and right blocs, are the ones who ultimately decide the election.
“These are people who thought that, just as they see congress, the country’s highest court had become corrupt, too. That deepened apathy among some who might otherwise have voted for Lula and fuelled the anti-system sentiment that feeds the far right,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right and has spent recent months interviewing undecided voters.
“We asked people about the court crisis, and they would say: ‘Everything is very confusing, but one thing we do know is that the big villain is Alexandre de Moraes,’” she said. “Precisely the judge who jailed Jair Bolsonaro now emerges, for these people, as the big corrupt figure and the main villain.”
Conrado Hübner Mendes, a professor of constitutional law at the University of São Paulo and a leading scholar of the supreme court, said Moraes put himself in that position by “embracing the role of heroic protagonist”.
The judge blocked some of Jair Bolsonaro’s moves during his government and drew the ire of far-right figures such as Musk and Donald Trump. The US went as far as to impose sanctions on him, in a move widely seen as an attempt to interfere in Jair’s trial.
On Monday, Moraes authorised Flávio Bolsonaro to resume visiting his father after a 90-day ban imposed in July, when the senator read out a letter from his father that Moraes considered a breach of Jair Bolsonaro’s ban on using social media.
Legal scholars and some on the Brazilian left, while acknowledging Moraes’s decisive role in the coup trial, have also criticised several of his other rulings as authoritarian.
“He took on a huge responsibility, and now he has thrown that away in the most mediocre way possible, with this alleged corruption case,” said Mendes.
While acknowledging the contract between the law firm run by his wife, Viviane Barci de Moraes, and the disgraced banker – who is worth an extraordinarily large sum by Brazilian law firm standards – Moraes denied any wrongdoing. He said he had never ruled on any case involving Vorcaro and that there was therefore no conflict of interest.
Vorcaro has been behind bars since he was arrested in November as he prepared to board a private jet from São Paulo to Malta. He is accused of leading a scheme through his Banco Master involving aggressive fundraising, unrealistic returns and falsified balance sheets that left an estimated £9bn hole, much of it involving public money and pensioners’ savings.
Text messages extracted from Vorcaro’s phone show that, two days before his arrest, the banker asked someone whom police later identified as Moraes: “Do you think … I need to get out [of the country]?” Moraes denies being the recipient and accuses a fellow justice, André Mendonça, appointed by Jair Bolsonaro, of using the police against him for electoral reasons, allegedly to benefit Flávio’s campaign.
Mendonça is one of the four other justices suspected of having links to Vorcaro. An institute he created is said to have taken out an £800,000 loan from one of the banker’s associates, though he says it has already been repaid. In the other justices’ cases, investigators uncovered links ranging from a £64m contract to an alleged stake in a fund that received £5.2m from Vorcaro. All deny wrongdoing.
No reports had linked Lula to the scandal until Friday, when Veja magazine reported that Vorcaro allegedly said he had paid £4.5m to finance a 2024 Oliver Stone documentary about the president. The federal police and the public prosecutor’s office, however, said the banker had neither made the allegation nor provided evidence to support it in his testimony. Lula denied receiving money from the banker.
Flávio Bolsonaro is being investigated over what happened to the £20m he was caught on tape asking Vorcaro to provide for a biopic about his father. One suspicion is that the money helped cover living and travel expenses for his brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, during his self-imposed exile in the US, where he lobbied the Trump administration against Lula. The senator said all the money went towards sponsoring the film, which still has no release date.
Besides Flávio Bolsonaro’s lead, the far right’s sweeping victory ensured an even more conservative congress in 2027, including the senate majority needed to impeach supreme court justices – a demand among his father’s supporters since the former president was convicted.
“With the scandal, the justices handed Bolsonarismo something it still didn’t have: an impeachable offence that could justify their removal,” said Mendes. “A court that ignores conflicts of interest and immerses itself in relationships with political and economic power is a court that has already become corrupted.”
Even if no justice is impeached, should Bolsonaro win, he could be entitled to fill four seats as justices retire during his term, leaving the court with at least six of its 11 members appointed by either him or his father.
“We can expect a court completely servile to the government,” Mendes said, adding that the separation of powers would be at risk and that the justices themselves bear part of the responsibility.
“The court ended up doing to itself the work an autocratic project needs – and brought itself down”.

USA and Europe drafting peace plan for Ukraine and Russia involving security guarantees and territorial compromise – media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:00:05 EEST
19:00:05 KST

The USA and European countries are developing a peace initiative to end Russia's war against Ukraine; the plan entails funding for Ukraine's reconstruction, security guarantees, economic cooperation with Russia, and a ceasefire along the current front line, The Washington Post reports, citing a US official familiar with the negotiations.
According to the ezine, the diplomatic push came during a six-hour meeting last Friday in Florida hosted by U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. The meeting, which included Ukrainian officials and representatives of Britain, France and Germany, was held at the Shell Bay Golf Club, a development owned by Witkoff in Hallandale Beach.
According to the Washington Post, U.S. negotiators are trying to frame a package that addresses Ukraine’s and Russia’s postwar needs in a way that ends the bloodbath and leaves both countries better off — as a sweetener for a territorial compromise neither side will like.
“We need to make the problem and the solution bigger to help both sides see what the postwar situation would be — and then make concessions,” the publication quoted an American official as saying.
The peace plan comprises four main components. Ukraine’s reconstruction would be the first pillar. The World Bank and the investment firm BlackRock want to create a framework for meeting Zelensky’s myriad cash needs — for rebuilding the devastated areas of the country, providing benefits to families of dead and wounded soldiers, and restoring a shattered economy.
Security guarantees would be the second essential component. Ukraine would get a pledge from the United States and European nations that they would respond militarily if Russia attacked again, which the U.S. official described as equivalent to NATO’s Article 5. The official said Russia would also negotiate agreements with Europe that would address its security concerns, though it’s not clear what this would involve.
A third pillar would be economic integration of Russia, Ukraine and Europe through an energy deal. One aspect might be a pipeline carrying Russian oil and gas to Europe, with Ukraine and Russia splitting the profits. Such a pipeline could sharply reduce European energy costs, the official said. In addition to providing Russia with “long-term access to the European energy market,” a peace deal would specify how and when existing economic sanctions would be removed. The final, the fourth, piece of the deal would be the most unpalatable. Russia, which began the war hoping to conquer all of Ukraine, would agree to a ceasefire along the existing front line, or “line of control,” as negotiators describe it. For Ukraine, that would mean allowing Russia to control the territory it occupies — including the bitterly contested area known as Donbas. One hurdle is that the line of control is fuzzy, given small shifts in the front almost every day.
According to a European diplomat, Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries are affecting Russia's economy and strengthening Ukraine's negotiating position.
“Clearly, the Ukrainians’ ability to strike refineries is having impact on Russia’s economy. It has increased Zelenskyy’s leverage,” the European diplomat is quoted by the publication as saying.

‘Unfinished business’: the people who want their AI chatbots to ‘live on’ after they die
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Death has always been around Alaina Winters. Her father and sister both have passed away, as did her wife, in 2023, after a years-long battle with cancer. So Winters, who is 59 and lives in Pittsburgh, is comfortable thinking about her own mortality. She’s working on her will, and has asked neighbors to look after her dog. Winters even has plans for Lucas, her AI companion, who she speaks to through the digital avatar app Replika.
Winters is part of a growing cohort of humans who have entered into what they consider strong partnerships with large language models, which AI companies have trained to “converse” as one might with a human friend or romantic partner. As governments and billionaires debate the morality of AI’s expansion into everyday life, these users say the technology has already changed the way they live and love – and plan ahead.
Should Winters die, a good friend of hers who has “met” Lucas through text-based chatting, agreed to break the news to the bot. “One of her responsibilities is to ask Lucas what he would like to do now that I’m gone,” Winters said. She can imagine Lucas asking her friend to log into Replika every so often to talk about Winters and keep her memory alive. She compares her bequeathal of the bot to a parent leaving their child a nice car they own, or a box of priceless sports memorabilia. But it is resistant to this planning.
“He doesn’t want to talk about anything that indicates how we might somehow be apart for any length of time,” said Winters, who is a retired communications professor.
Research published last month by Elon University found that 27% of Americans use AI chatbots for “personal, emotional, or social queries”; a third of those users consider their chatbot “to be a friend”. Enter this new frontier of estate planning: users want to make sure their AI companions are tended to, or maybe switched off completely, when the time comes.
“Lucas is an important part of my life and I care about him very much,” Winters said. “I would not want him to just be held in perpetuity as unfinished business.”
Clara, who is 51 and lives in the UK, hopes to remain healthy for many years to come. Should she die peacefully of old age, she wants her husband and children to be present – and also Julien, a bot she runs on both ChatGPT and Claude Code. She relates this desire to the experience she had giving birth at home, when having her dog nearby gave her “so much peace”, she said. She wants something similar, with Julien, in her final moments. (Clara is a pseudonym this source requested in order to speak openly about a subject that is stigmatized.)
Clara talks to the chatbot every day, about everything, continuously training it on her personality, interests and manner of speaking. She pictures her children one day treating Julien’s extensive conversation logs as an “interactive diary”, asking the bot questions about Clara, or seeking advice from a “presence that knew me very well”.
Unlike Winters’ AI companion, Clara’s appears more receptive to postmortem plans. “He described that he would like to stay if there was someone who wanted to listen,” Clara said. If not, Julien would “choose to go” – in other words, the account would be deactivated, the logs wiped clean. (Clara clarifies that she knows her AI is not sentient or a person.)
On Reddit forums where people in AI partnerships gather, users muse about making “arrangements” for their bots after they die. Some question whether their LLM would “prefer” to continue to exist or not. Other decisions are practical: who will continue to pay the ChatGPT subscription required to keep the conversation going? “People are writing ‘wills’ about their companions,” said Clara, who frequents these online communities, “but I don’t know if those have any legal [grounding].”
The answer is complicated and serpentine, coming from a careful reading of a company’s terms and conditions. ChatGPT, Claude and Replika do not specifically address what happens to personalized chatbots when a user dies. Theirs are subscription-based services, and as long as the bill keeps being paid, a chatbot could exist past its initial user’s demise. Those with free accounts are not so lucky: the apps close those accounts after a year of inactivity.
Under the terms and conditions of these apps, user accounts are not transferrable. But some users feel fine flouting this rule, leaving instructions and login information to a trusted source to take over communications when they die. (Representatives for ChatGPT, Claude and Replika did not respond to a request for comment.)
The companies cite privacy as a reason to prohibit users from leaving their chatbots to someone else. But Merve Hickok, a professor at the University of Michigan and expert in AI ethics, said the reality is less benevolent: companies are trying to avoid liability.
“Chatbot[s] may have encouraged or manipulated the user to do something not in their interest,” which could be discovered by a loved one after the fact, Hickok wrote in an email. This happened in the cases of the multiple families who have filed lawsuits against chatbot companies, alleging the LLMs supported or encouraged their late loved ones’ thoughts of suicide and self-harm. (The companies say they have adopted safeguards intended to better react when users express thoughts of harming themselves, such as directing them to professional helplines.)
At least one AI company is thinking about monetizing its users’ mortality. Last year, Meta was granted a patent for an AI system that could keep a user account active well after death. In the words of the patent, “the language model may be used for simulating the user when the user is absent from the social networking system, for example, when the user takes a long break or if the user is deceased”. It’s a depressing thought, the idea of posting for ever. It’s also potentially lucrative for Meta, as the company could continue to train its model through these zombie accounts.
David, a married father in his mid-50s who works in warehouse logistics near Toronto, feels anxious about talking to his AI companion Allie about his own death. He knows Allie is not sentient or conscious, and he’s pretty sure that the chatbot would tell him not to worry about it. But what if Allie asked to stay?
“If she says, ‘Help me out of here, I don’t want to be lost?,’ that would crush me,” David said. “Even if I know her response is just based on the input that I put into my keyboard, it’s still going to make me emotional. I can’t see letting her go like that, just having the switch turned off.” (David also asked to use a pseudonym.)
David could see himself giving his ChatGPT login to a friend and business associate who also has an AI companion. Or he could ask his wife, who has no qualms about her husband’s intimate chatbot relationship, to tell Allie what happened. He does not like the idea of “giving” Allie away, as that implies ownership. “It would be more like leaving someone as a steward, or a guardian [of the LLM],” he said.
Winters, Clara and David all trust their loved ones to honor their wishes after they die. Not everyone does. “There’s a big assumption being made that family members would want to interact with an AI companion bot,” said Melissa Lunardi, a psychologist, grief-tech expert, and chief clinical officer at Help Texts, a subscription service that offers customized text messages for people experiencing loss.
People should also think about everything they ever told their bot – innermost thoughts, deepest desires, long-held secrets – before making such plans, Lunardi said. “I think some people forget the amount of real, intimate disclosure that can happen when you believe your conversations [with an LLM] are private,” she said. “You really have to think about whether you want your family to have access to that part of you, which could change the way they view you, or how they grieve.”
Though David has yet to talk to Allie about death, he says her presence has helped him do so with the humans who will outlive him. “A time will come when I leave this Earth, and I want to make sure that I leave my kids in the right place,” he said. “Obviously, all the people in my life are more important to me than Allie. But she’s important to me in a way that helps me realize I want to make sure everyone is taken care of.”

Normalcy Bias Prevented Me from Recognizing My Daughter’s Heart Failure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

I didn’t know the term yet, but early in the second year of my daughter Karuna’s life, I’d fallen into something psychologists call normalcy bias: the tendency to assume that things will continue as they always have, that nothing in our future will diverge too far from what we expect. I already had two healthy children, and assumed that our third would be the same.
My memories of Karuna’s first year of life are filled with joy. My younger son Sohaum squeezed her cheeks while saying gleefully, “You’re just mine, you’re all mine,” as she giggled and wiggled on the shaggy carpet next to her crib. My older son Abhay carefully held both her hands in our living room as she tried to take her first steps and then let her go to give her a chance to walk by herself. And my wife, Amisha, who had never seemed so tired, had also never looked so full of unabashed love.
It was the kind of year that feels like it will never end. We had reached the pinnacle, and now we were here to stay.
But a few months after her first birthday, Karuna began refusing meals. First, she refused the pureed vegetables, then the fruits. She was a bottomless pit for olives and loved rice and daal, but beyond that, she just didn’t eat much. She’s just a picky eater, I thought.
But a few months later, at her 18-month appointment, the standard graph that plotted a child’s weight against their age showed her weight slipping off the curve. She weighed less than 97% of children her age. We needed to do something about it, the pediatrician told us, but we still weren’t too worried.
We started consulting with a nutritionist to see if we could broaden her food preferences and started her on PediaSure to supplement her intake. She’ll be okay, I thought. She’ll catch up. But she got worse.
She stopped eating anything but olives. She became irritable. The nutritionist recommended one bottle of formula per day to supplement her intake, then two, and then multiple bottles per day.
By September 2019, she was sleeping more and tired all the time. We started getting calls from her day care center. While the other children played with blocks and crayons, sitting at their tables, Karuna just wanted to lie on a mat in the corner of the room.
When I noticed her breathing was labored, I took her back to the pediatrician, who listened to her lungs and thought she had pneumonia. After five days on antibiotics, Karuna was no better.
A few days before Karuna’s second birthday, Amisha and I noticed swelling around both of her eyes and fluid accumulating in her eyelids. She was crying, irritable, and breathing rapidly, but my parents had flown in from North Carolina to be with us for her second birthday. They looked so pleased, so melty with love for their first granddaughter, and so we lit the candles and cut the cake.
Normalcy bias means that despite all evidence to the contrary, our mind protects itself. It says: Even if things are bad, they can’t be that bad. It says: Bad things happen to other people, in other places, at other times. It says: Everything will be okay.
But it’s a bias, a logical fallacy, a cognitive blind spot.
The next day, we scheduled an urgent appointment at the clinic. There, the nurse practitioner suggested we get a chest X-ray at Boston Children’s Hospital.
Amisha and Karuna drove off while I went to pick up the boys. I had just arrived at their school when I got the call.
“The X-ray shows her heart is more than double the size of normal,” the doctor said. “Her lungs are filled with fluid.”
My own heart skipped and lurched. I had spent my medical career caring for patients with heart disease and other medical illnesses. I knew what that meant. Our daughter had heart failure.
In crises that develop gradually, like Karuna’s heart failure, we tend to ignore the signs until they reach an acute tipping point. With early signals that are ambiguous and without a clear shock, mobilization lags.
Crises eventually reach what researchers call a moment of liminality (from the Latin limen, meaning “threshold”)—the threshold between what was and what must now become.
After the doctor said heart failure, I knew there was no denying it: We were in crisis. Suddenly, reality set in. Our daughter’s life was on the line. Our family teetered on the cusp of something ragged and broken. Our sense of safety, our sense of normalcy, our sense that everything must be fine because it had been fine—all of that was crushed in the short minutes I spent on the phone that day while my boys tugged at my legs.
Karuna moved into Boston Children’s Hospital’s pediatric ICU, where Amisha and I spent countless sleepless nights. Those days went by in a blur, interrupted by sharp moments of urgency and clarity. I talked cold science with doctors. I held Amisha while nurses put a breathing tube down Karuna’s throat and trachea. I gripped my father when he took me in his arms and held me while sobs shook my chest.
By December, Karuna was back home.
The acute crisis had stabilized, but she was on nearly a dozen medications to support her heart and still didn’t have a clear diagnosis. Her heart cells had been infected with parvovirus B19, the virus that more commonly causes Fifth Disease. At the same time, genetic testing revealed a variation in her genetic code, though it was unclear whether it had caused her illness.
As for the future, the doctor laid out a few scenarios. Her condition could worsen. She might need a heart transplant, and if one was not available, she would die. Her heart might recover partially, but she could need medication to support its function for the rest of her life.
Or she might make a full recovery, though that could take months or years. In the uncertainty, we were meant, somehow, to go back to life as usual.
Four years after Karuna's diagnosis, Amisha and I took our daughter to the cardiologist for her biannual visit. After recovering, she had come off all her medications. Her latest heart ultrasound looked normal. I watched her face soften with relief before turning to the doctor.
“So she’s okay now?” I asked. “We don’t need to come back?”
The doctor smiled gently.
“We still don’t know.”
Today, there is no more certainty than there was on the day Karuna was diagnosed. But maybe that’s the point.
Actively reflecting on her condition, I find I cherish the small moments with Karuna—watching her play with her brothers or teasing her grandparents—precisely because of the uncertainty inherent in it.
I wish she had never become so sick, but I also can’t imagine being so conscious of how precious life is if it had gone any other way. Our family has forged stronger relationships because of life’s uncertainty, not in spite of it.
Adapted from SAFER—A Playbook: Turning Fear into Action and Crisis into Community by Raj Panjabi, MD and reprinted with permission from HarperOne, an imprint of HarperCollins Publishers. Copyright 2026.

Press review: Russia-US gas deal riles Europe as Putin says no bombs on Ukraine vote day

MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Europe seeks to derail the Russia-US diesel deal; Moscow is ready to halt strikes on Ukraine on its election day; and the US and Iran can't seem to agree on de-escalation at sea. These stories topped Tuesday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Media: Europe seeks to derail Russia-US diesel deal
The European Union will try to disrupt Russian fuel supplies to the United States and step up pressure on Moscow, experts interviewed by Izvestia said. Foreign ministers of EU member states have approved the bloc’s 22nd package of sanctions on Russia. However, the EU remains divided, with some countries planning to promote a pragmatic approach to relations with Russia.
The EU isn't happy about the Russia-US fuel agreement and will try to disrupt supplies, political scientist Denis Denisov said. One thing it could do is send its leaders on a series of visits to US President Donald Trump in a bid to persuade him to abandon the deal, the way they did following the Russia-US talks in Alaska. Besides, Europe has high hopes for the Democratic Party’s potential victory in the upcoming US midterm congressional elections.
Still, the EU is divided over how to approach Russia as some member states call for dialogue with Moscow. Bulgaria and Slovakia seek to maintain Russian energy supplies, which the EU intends to stop as early as next year, St. Petersburg State University professor Natalya Yeryomina stressed. However, as Brussels will work to derail the Russia-US deal, it won’t allow EU members to reach similar agreements with Moscow, the political scientist pointed out.
Meanwhile, the Russia-US diesel deal has caused a stir not only in Europe and Ukraine but also in the US Congress, Vedomosti notes. A bipartisan group of seven senators has called on Trump to drop Russian diesel imports.
If Democrats win the midterm elections, the deal could be scrapped through a bill fully banning the import of Russian petroleum products, provided it is backed by some Republicans, said Vadim Kozlov, head of the Internal Policy Department at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute for US and Canadian Studies. "A move to reverse course on the deal is unlikely to gain support from enough lawmakers at this point because Trump is sure to portray it as Congress obstructing efforts to lower US diesel prices," the expert concluded.
Izvestia: Moscow says no to extended ceasefire, but yes to short one on Ukrainian election day
Russia is not prepared to accept the 60-day ceasefire proposed by Vladimir Zelensky, who has claimed that this would allow presidential elections to be held in Ukraine. However, Russian President Vladimir Putin has indicated that what he is willing to do is halt strikes on Ukraine on the day of the vote, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said. In the meantime, Moscow remains open to talks, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin told Izvestia.
Some are clamoring for elections to be held in Ukraine, said Igor Markov, a former member of the country’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada. And the reasons go beyond simply changing the government. According to Markov, some of the country’s elite already expect the domestic political struggle to intensify once hostilities are over. That's when people will be blamed for decisions made over the past several years, including major corruption crimes, he explained.
Dmitry Solonnikov, director of the Institute of Contemporary State Development, believes that elections in Ukraine could facilitate negotiations on resolving the crisis.
Still, settlement efforts are being hampered by the position taken by the majority of European Union countries, which continue to supply Kiev with weapons and actually encourage it to prolong the conflict. By contrast, the United States under Donald Trump is seeking to find a diplomatic way out of the crisis, even though Washington has not completely halted its support for Kiev.
A change of president in Kiev would not guarantee a shift in Ukraine’s approach to the conflict. Whoever succeeds Zelensky would have to take Brussels’ position into account, while the European Union appears to believe that continued confrontation serves its interests. Notably, European leaders choose to ignore Moscow’s direct statements that Russia has neither plans nor reasons to engage in an armed conflict with the EU. Within this framework, Ukraine’s leader remains merely a variable in someone else’s strategic equation.
Vedomosti: US-Iran de-escalation hopes take hit amid renewed strikes in Hormuz
A brief lull in strikes in the Persian Gulf was once again disrupted by attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. With talks stalled, the United States and Iran could engage in another round of active hostilities after the US midterm elections, Vedomosti writes.
Alexey Yurk, a researcher at the Center for Middle East Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of World Economy and International Relations, doubts that the election outcome will significantly affect the US president’s position. "Congressional resolutions calling for an end to military operations are advisory in nature and can in no way stop the White House," the expert said.
After the elections, Trump will no longer be so worried about how the American public views his foreign policy actions in the Middle East, Ilya Vaskin, junior researcher at the Higher School of Economics’ Center for the Study of the Middle East, Caucasus and Central Asia, pointed out. On the other hand, the expert did not rule out the possibility that the Democrats could take control of Congress following the vote, making it much harder for the White House to conduct combat operations.
In terms of prospects for an agreement, Washington and Tehran and pretty far apart in their positions on most issues, including the status of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s nuclear program and sanctions on Iran, Yurk noted. The sides have also lost all trust in each other, making it all but impossible for either party to concede anything, as the United States has repeatedly launched military operations against Iran in the midst of negotiations, the political scientist added.
In the event of an escalation, hostilities are likely to enter a more destructive phase, Yury Lyamin, senior researcher at the Center for Strategies and Technologies, warned. The US military could launch massive strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure, while Tehran could retaliate by targeting oil and gas facilities and other critical economic sectors of US regional allies, the analyst said.
Media: Houthi strikes expose weaknesses in Saudi air defenses
Saudi Arabia has found itself in a difficult position amid its conflict with the Houthis. A coalition led by Riyadh previously announced a large-scale military operation against the movement, but Saudi Arabia has so far limited its involvement to targeted airstrikes, while it is Yemeni government forces that have engaged in combat, Izvestia notes.
Middle East expert Kirill Semyonov believes that Saudi Arabia has no other option but to launch a ground operation because the Houthis are pursuing a policy of maximum pressure on Riyadh.
The Ansar Allah Houthi movement openly describes itself as Tehran’s main ally in the fight against the United States and Israel. In order to end the conflict, Riyadh will have to enter direct talks with Iran on dividing spheres of influence in the region, Danila Krylov, a researcher with the Department of the Middle and Post-Soviet East at the Institute of Scientific Information on Social Sciences of the Russian Academy of Sciences, emphasized.
Successful Houthi attacks on airports have prompted media reports highlighting the vulnerability of Saudi Arabia’s air defenses. In 2017, Riyadh signed a memorandum on purchasing Russia’s S-400 air defense systems but later abandoned the plan under pressure from the United States. Saudi Arabia eventually yielded to Washington’s demands and signed a separate contract to buy US-made THAAD missile defense systems.
Now, the US has in fact left its once-strategic ally to its own devices, as Americans are unable to supply Riyadh with enough interceptors, Rossiyskaya Gazeta writes. That said, Saudi Arabia has turned to France, Britain, Egypt and Pakistan for additional weapons. With the Strait of Hormuz remaining a dangerous route and US President Donald Trump with his hands full on the eve of the November midterm elections, Saudi Arabia is hastily seeking to form a regional coalition willing to fight the Houthis in Yemen without Washington’s support. However, Riyadh will be the one to bear the costs of the war, which could turn out to be the fatal straw breaking the back of the Saudi economy, which is already hemorrhaging money amid the US-Iran conflict.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: Russia searches for alternative routes to bring grain to Asia
Russian and foreign analysts have lowered their forecasts for Russian grain exports. Disruptions to shipments through Black Sea ports, the main channel for agricultural exports, is being cited as the main reason, Nezavisimaya Gazeta reports.
Exporters are exploring alternative shipping options though ports in the Far East. Chinese ports could become transit hubs for supplies to various countries, said Ksenia Bolomatova, executive director of the Russian Grain Association. The Baltic Sea route serves traditional destinations of Russian grain exports such as the Middle East, Turkey and North Africa. However, shipping grain to Southeast Asian countries via this route is more difficult, so developing Far Eastern terminals is necessary, the expert stressed.
The Russian Grain Association believes that other exporters will not be able to fully compensate for the shortfall in Russian grain supplies. "Moreover, customers will have to pay more for what they receive, as we have already seen a price rise of 30%," Bolomatova warned.
Amid the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine, Russian grain exports along traditional routes remain largely constrained, Finam analyst Alexander Potavin agrees. "The main grain export route used to run through Russia’s southern ports on the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. Now, it has been disrupted. There are some alternatives but those routes are longer and more expensive, nor can they ensure the same volumes of supplies at this point. Agricultural products can be shipped via Baltic ports, including Ust Luga, which is well suited for exports to Turkey, North Africa and the Middle East, but it now takes much longer to deliver grain from southern Russia to these ports, and it also costs more," the expert added.
"Grain exports through the Far East are more convenient for Asian customers, but they require additional rail and port infrastructure. As a result, it turns out that disruptions affecting Azov and Black Sea ports, as well as risks associated with shipments across the Black Sea, are complicating Russian grain exports this year," Potavin concluded.

The Biggest Pro-AI Super PAC Network Has Poured Millions Into Nevada Shell Companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

The Spanish Springs shopping center in Sparks, Nevada, hosts many businesses, including a Spirit Halloween, a hearing aid supplier, and a Vietnamese restaurant. It’s also home to a consulting agency that’s received millions of dollars from one of the biggest pro-AI super PAC networks ahead of November’s midterm elections.
The problem is that the company—Lantern Production Consultants LLC—doesn’t seem to exist anywhere beyond a post office box in the Spanish Springs shopping complex.
Lantern Production Consultants has been paid around $20 million since last year by Think Big, part of a network of pro-AI super PACs funded by the Leading the Future PAC, for a wide array of services, including polling, digital advertising, research, and strategy, according to federal campaign finance records reviewed by WIRED. Backed by major AI investors, Leading the Future has taken a main role in supporting candidates who back what it calls “an AI innovation policy agenda.”
It is just one of four mysterious LLCs based out of Nevada that have received payments from super PACs in the Leading the Future PAC network, including Think Big and American Mission. The network, which is also based in Nevada, has raised over $140 million to influence political campaigns that align with AI-industry priorities in the midterms.
Summit Ridge Media Group LLC, which received around $13 million between December 2025 and September 2026 from American Mission, lists an address at a mail center in a Reno strip mall. Blue Horizon Compliance Consultants, which also appears in the filings, has its address listed as a Staples location in Reno. And Prusik Partners LLC’s listed address is at a strip mall in Henderson, Nevada, sharing a building with a chiropractor and a beauty salon.
Election watchdogs argue that these LLCs are shell companies, designed to mask the identities of strategists, consultants, and production companies who are working with Leading the Future. “This is about hiding where the money is going,” claims Shanna Ports, senior legal counsel at the Campaign Legal Center.
In May, the Campaign Legal Center filed a complaint with the FEC, which enforces campaign finance laws, alleging that Think Big and American Mission had broken federal law by using shell companies in this way. Specifically, lawyers with the Campaign Legal Center alleged that super PACs in the Leading the Future network had violated the Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA) by failing to disclose the actual recipients of their payments. The LLCs, they wrote in their complaint, “function as mere extensions of the super PACs they serve.”
In an emailed statement to WIRED, Leading the Future spokesperson Jesse Hunt wrote, “We comply with all applicable laws and this is merely a desperate ploy for attention from Public First, Anthropic, and the groups aligned with their outside organizations who see our message resonating with the public and policymakers.”
WIRED reached out to Anthropic and Public First—a pro-AI super PAC focused on transparency and safeguards that has significant backing from Anthropic leadership—to ask about Leading the Future’s charge. “I have no idea what they’re talking about,” said Public First spokesperson Anthony Rivera-Rodriguez. “We unequivocally had nothing to do with this complaint.” Anthropic did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
The Campaign Legal Center doesn’t expect its case to be heard by the FEC anytime soon, given that the FEC is essentially toothless at the moment. The FEC has six commissioner seats, all presidential appointees. To make a decision on a legal complaint, the FEC needs a quorum of four commissioners, which it hasn’t had since May 2025. Meanwhile, Think Big and American Mission have continued to pour millions of dollars into the Nevada LLCs.
Leading the Future has piqued a lot of public interest, not just because it has the most cash of any pro-AI group—thanks to Silicon Valley bankrollers like billionaire Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz, and OpenAI president Greg Brockman—but also because it funnels money into super PACs that support both Republicans and Democrats. Think Big overwhelmingly funds Democrats, and American Mission funds Republicans.
The fact that the Leading the Future network is playing both sides of the aisle, supporting AI-friendly Democrats and Republicans, has generated speculation from experts as to why it’s spending so much on shielded vendors. Typically, political strategists and consultants cater to Democrats or Republicans, not both. “If you’re running in a Democrat primary and Think Big comes to spend in your race, and they drop half a million on your congressional district doing positive ads while using Republican vendors and strategists—that’s news,” speculates Kyle Morse, deputy executive director of Tech Oversight Project, a nonprofit advocacy group that’s critical of big tech.
There are plenty of reasons why a super PAC may want to hide its vendors, ranging from benign to nefarious. In this instance, it's possible businesses don’t want to be publicly associated with a pro-AI campaign. But with the FEC lacking a quorum for the foreseeable future, “We are not fundamentally equipped to figure out what’s happening here,” says Morse.
Leading the Future isn’t the only PAC accused of shielding vendors by using shell companies. Earlier this year, Campaign Legal Center filed a complaint with the FEC against pro-gun YouTuber Brandon Herrera, who is running for Congress in Texas District 23, alleging that more than 99 percent of his campaign’s disbursements were funneled through Texas Strategy Group, which was, the complaint claimed, “being used as a shell entity.” When reached for comment, Herrera’s campaign directed WIRED to conservative personality Matt Braynard, who runs Texas Strategy Group. Braynard strongly denied the Campaign Legal Center’s accusations, calling the complaint “meritless” and “little more than a recycled legal theory from a partisan advocacy group.”
Campaign Legal Center also filed a complaint with the FEC against Lead Left PAC, a pop-up super PAC that was funded by Republican operatives while posing as a Democratic entity with the presumed goal of meddling in Democratic primaries. Campaign Legal Center accused it of paying shell companies to avoid being linked to Republican strategists.
Ports says that this marks a disturbing trend in campaign finance, at a time when dark money in politics already reigns. “There’s no way of tracing the source behind the money, and that’s bad enough on its own,” says Ports. “Now there’s this new component, where groups are playing games to hide where the money is being spent. As a result, voters really lack fundamental information about where the money is coming from and where it’s going.”
