Saudi Arabia faces a grim choice as Houthis intensify attacks on airports and oil sites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Saudi Arabia faces a grim choice as Houthis intensify attacks on airports and oil sites
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Repeated Houthi missile strikes on Riyadh’s airport killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
- The attacks are bringing Yemen’s war directly to Saudi civilians and threatening the kingdom’s efforts to attract global investors and energy leaders.
- The attacks are exposing gaps in Saudi Arabia’s defenses and a depleted stockpile of missile interceptors.
BEIRUT — This wasn’t the way the story was supposed to go for Saudi Arabia. In recent years, headlines about the country focused on the scale of its ambition, or the fantastical giga-projects girding Vision 2030, the full-steam-ahead drive to remake the kingdom into a business and entertainment powerhouse.
But all that was upended Saturday, when a Houthi missile lanced through Terminal 3 of the capital’s international airport, killing 13 people, including a U.S. national, and wounding more than 300 others.
The attack — the deadliest Saudi Arabia has endured in years — made real a war that for most Saudis had remained notional.
It also laid bare the bevy of bad scenarios facing Saudi leaders as they contend with an increasingly formidable enemy that, unlike them, has little to lose.
That the Houthis are able to score hits from 500 miles away, despite the Saudi military spending tens of billions of dollars on multi-layered air defense systems, has puzzled experts.
“To me it’s shocking. Yes, the Houthis have gotten better, but it’s not a matter of them using a new weapons system,” said Wolf-Christian Paes, an associate fellow at the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies.
“The problem must be on the Saudi side,” Paes said. “Something must have gone horribly wrong and continues to go horribly wrong.”
Videos on social media Saturday showed passengers trudging slowly in a security line before the missile hit, sending them sprinting through the smoke-filled terminal, pieces of debris raining around them.
Although Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport was shuttered after the attack — more than 99% of flights were canceled, according to the aviation analytics firm Cirium — the Houthis struck another terminal building Sunday, killing one person.
On Monday, aviation authorities extended the airport’s closure. Other airports across the kingdom were also targeted, along with gas facilities and oil refineries, the Houthis said.
Yahya Saree, the Houthis’ military spokesman, on Sunday warned airlines and travelers to avoid Saudi airports, calling them “unsafe.”
Meanwhile, many Riyadh-based firms told their employees to work from home, and schools shifted to online classes.
On Monday, the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh cautioned citizens to keep their distance from the airport and surrounding areas.
Faced with escalating Houthi attacks and a reluctant U.S. administration unwilling to intervene, Saudi Arabia is actively seeking regional defense partnerships.
The timing of the Houthi campaign seems calculated for maximum reputational harm. On Sunday the kingdom began hosting the World Petroleum Congress, an event that normally draws oil heavyweights from across the world, including energy ministers as well as CEOs from BP, Exxon Mobil Corp., Shell and TotalEnergies.
Yet it’s unclear how many were able to attend, with some delegates forced to drive hours across the desert from Bahrain or Jordan to reach Riyadh. Others, including Italy’s energy minister, attended a meeting via video link.
Similar concerns now swirl around the Future Investment Initiative, Saudi Arabia’s flagship business conference, which is set for the end of the month. Officials, maintaining a show-will-go-on attitude, insist the event, known as “Davos in the Desert,” will happen on schedule.
In response to the Houthi attacks, Saudi Arabia’s military said it peppered rebel-held areas with more than 120 strikes, including the airport in the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital, Sanaa.
But those strikes underscore the asymmetry of the fight, experts say, with Saudi military planners hunting for Houthis in areas already ravaged by conflict, even as they must defend an area more than five times the size of California.
“Saudi Arabia is a country of 2 million square kilometers, with a very large number of soft targets — airports, pipelines, urban infrastructure that needs to be protected, government infrastructure. We’ve seen them all attacked,” said Thomas Juneau, a security analyst at Ottawa University.
He added that the Saudi military “has not distinguished itself in terms of military performance against the Houthis.”
The Saudi-Houthi conflict dates to 2014, when the Houthis swatted the Yemeni government aside and took over Sanaa before blitzing through other parts of the country.
The Saudis countered with an air campaign and ground force composed of Yemeni pro-government paramilitary factions, Saudi and Emirati troops and mercenaries.
The result was a humanitarian crisis that at the time was considered the world’s worst, with some 377,000 people killed, according to the Yemen Data Project, which tracks casualties from Yemen’s various conflicts. More than half of the deaths were due to the collapse of the health system, along with epidemics and famine.
The Houthis, toughened by decades of fighting against the government, lost much of the territory they took in south Yemen, but otherwise grew stronger in the war.
With training from Iran and the Lebanese faction Hezbollah, they evolved from a ragtag band of fighters with sandals and Kalashnikovs to a disciplined force fielding missiles and manufacturing its own projectiles. (Recently, Anthropic, the maker of Claude AI, warned the Houthis were using its AI models to program missile computers.)
In 2022, with front lines in a stalemate, Saudi Arabia and the Houthis signed a truce that largely held.
But in July, warplanes struck Sanaa airport to prevent an Iranian plane with Houthi officials from landing. Though the Saudi-backed Yemeni government claimed responsibility, the Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia.
Since then, the Houthis, whose official name is Ansar Allah or God’s Supporters, have restarted their missile and drone salvos and announced a “blockade within a blockade” on Saudi shipping. In September, they routed pro-government fighters and captured Yemen’s Red Sea coast.
Yemen’s government last week launched an offensive to retake the areas under Houthi control, backed by a fresh Saudi bombing campaign.
The renewed hostilities come as Saudi Arabia has been battling an economic slowdown and rolling back some of its flashier investments.
That economic malaise has since been compounded by the Iran war. With the Strait of Hormuz largely sealed by rival U.S and Iranian blockades, Riyadh shifted its exports from Hormuz, its main energy corridor, to the Red Sea coast. Houthi advances, however, now jeopardize that conduit.
One possible reason for the kingdom’s vulnerability is that it entered the confrontation with the deck stacked against it.
The Saudi military has 108 Patriot missile launchers and a small number of THAAD missiles, allowing it to intercept missiles and drones at different altitudes and ranges.
But during the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, which saw Tehran lash out with attacks on its Persian Gulf neighbors, Saudi Arabia expended some 86% of its 2,800 missiles, according to reports.
The almost 400 interceptors that remain are augmented by a Greek army contingent with a Patriot missile battery and roughly 100 soldiers. Pakistan and Turkey, Saudi Arabia’s partners in a recently signed mutual defense pact, are also fielding their own air defense weapons inside the kingdom. But those are unlikely to be sufficient to protect the entire country, analysts say.
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the country’s de facto leader, has called on the U.S. and other allies to come to his country’s defense. Officials at the World Petroleum Congress on Monday echoed his message, with many stressing that disrupting Saudi energy supplies would have consequences beyond its borders.
“No nation, even one as capable and confident as ours, can safeguard them alone,” said Amin Nasser, chief executive of Saudi’s oil giant ARAMCO.
But President Trump has so far proved reluctant to provide more than intelligence and logistical support. On Saturday, after the airport attack, Trump said he “may” join the Saudis’ campaign. “We’re going to look at it,” he said.
Even if more robust assistance were to materialize, the Saudis will still face tough choices.
The best option, Paes said, would be for Saudi Arabia to find a new understanding with the Houthis. But he acknowledged that the group has political demands — including having Saudi Arabia pay Houthi civil servant salaries — that will be difficult for Saudi leaders to swallow.
“The deal they’ll get out of the Houthis will be a lot worse than what they could have got a few months ago,” Paes said.
Still, he added, “that’s the least worst outcome.”

Deskilling the body
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
24 minute listen
It is almost four o’clock in the morning. As a woman in my late 40s, I have become prone to waking at this witching hour, as the early sunlight meets the night, sliding across the earth like a red tide. With the rest of my household asleep, and still half in and out of wakefulness myself, I take hold of my phone. With scarcely a thought, I switch from one app to another, scrolling through images and opinions and adverts for no discernible reason beyond habit.
Later, I head for my office and open my laptop to a slew of half-completed documents and an inbox brimming with emails. My stress levels begin to nudge upwards. I have vague memories of what my professional life felt like before smartphones and video calls. I used to do my writing by hand. And I could concentrate for hours at a time, getting little upticks of arousal from lifting my head from the page, letting the hold on my pen loosen, and gazing at the life beyond my window, the light softening on my skin and eyes like snowfall on warm tarmac.
Nowadays, my productive bursts come from caffeine and sugary or salty snacks, even if I try to pick the healthier ones, and from checking my emails or picking up my phone to update my inbox. By the end of the day, the sheer volume of work I expect myself to do, now that digital tools make so much possible, has kept me nailed to my seat. Another day has passed and the hope I’d had that I might have time for a run or a hike outside has been dashed again. I wish I could say that this is atypical. Yet, during the COVID-19 pandemic, I went from hours spent in nature and on physical activities to a passive, phone-addicted individual, meeting people first and sometimes only online. I am not alone.
We have fallen into habits that are steadily deskilling the human body, eroding capacities honed by evolution to support our wellbeing as we move through the world. Some of these capacities are weakening through disuse: we have come to rely on our phones, for example, and now, increasingly, on AI, to rapidly do work that would once have required something more physical – like looking around, or asking someone, or going to find and consult a book. Reliance on GPS may weaken both our spatial attention and the fluency of our wayfinding. In surrendering to a quick technological fix, we are, moment by moment, doing less sensing, navigating, remembering, walking, choosing, and attending. Other capacities are being retrained by machines and algorithms to work against us: for instance, smartphones and chatbots can train us to keep reaching for them even when we no longer enjoy using them, turning a conscious choice into an automatic habit and a colossal waste of time. The body that results is less able to assess its own condition, improvise and regulate itself. The crucial distinction is between technologies that strengthen our capacities and those that repeatedly substitute for the actions through which those capacities are formed.
Algorithms that regurgitate patterns and recommendations can release us from the effort of exploration and disrupt the play and curiosity from which preferences are formed and understood.
This is a strange turn of events for an animal whose success comes mostly from the extraordinary ability to learn through experience. It would be easy to blame our deskilled bodies on the machines themselves. But, for centuries, modern human societies have been sold the lie that we are machines.
Long before the digital revolution, René Descartes described the body as a machine governed by physical laws, declaring that animals such as ‘worms and flies and caterpillars move mechanically’. But he treated rational thought as a separate and uniquely human power. The body might behave like a machine, but the thinking mind stood apart from it. Build something correctly, and its function follows.
By the middle of the 20th century, the comparison between organisms and machines had been recast in the language of information. During the cybernetics revolution of the 1950s, the US computer scientist Norbert Wiener envisaged a future in which ‘messages between man and machines, between machines and man, and between machine and machine, are destined to play an ever-increasing part’. Writing in The Human Use of Human Beings (1950), he warned against wholesale automation, while also noting that ‘we are not stuff that abides, but patterns that perpetuate themselves’. A person could be imagined as a pattern of information surviving in another form.
If the body is only hardware, why not upgrade to a better model or do away with it altogether?
Mechanical language also persisted in the study of living behaviour. In The Foundations of Ethology (1981), the Austrian zoologist Konrad Lorenz wrote that animal behaviour was as rigidly programmed as a sequence of movements in a clock. Transhumanist thinkers then carried the machine comparison further, imagining technologies that could transfer a mind to a computer.
Machines now promised more than control. They offered a glimpse of immortality: the organism might be repaired, remade and ultimately replaced. The somewhat embarrassing body, with its impulses and eventual frailty, might then be cast aside. If the body is only hardware, why not upgrade to a better model or do away with it altogether?
Today, we can see this fear writ large in the technological quest for a bodiless life. If a person is ultimately a pattern of information, that pattern might be restored or even uploaded. AI is only the latest iteration of this ancient impulse to escape the vulnerability of the body.
After all, the brain is itself a physical organ, continually shaped by what the body does and encounters. Once we decide that the mind is the real human and the rest of the body only hardware, it becomes easier to disregard the physical work, including the neurocognitive work of a biological brain, through which we move, find our way, put thoughts into words, and recognise our own needs. A machine may do some of that work faster, but each act it takes over is one that the body no longer performs and that the body, including the brain, no longer learns through. The irony is that a project motivated by the desire to overcome bodily fragility is helping to produce more fragile bodies.
On top of all this, we have little evidence that either thought or intelligence actually work like machines, and almost no indication that life is an abstract system that might emerge in silicon or mathematics. Instead, a substantial body of work, especially in systems biology, points to a quite different conclusion: that life and intelligence emerge from the unique qualities and organisation of our self-maintaining bodies, rather than from abstract models of information and algorithms.
For the past six years, I have been researching the latest science on what life is and how it works. As best as we can tell, the intelligent actions of organisms derive from the imperatives of a living body that must regulate and preserve its own conditions for existence. When cybernetics was ascendant, the molecular structure of DNA had only recently been discovered, and the emerging view of genes as information encouraged an oversimplified picture of the body as running on a program that could be made more efficient. Yet such confidence has since waned among biologists. While genes carry some of the information that shapes our bodies, many changes in how a cell or a body functions arise from the system as a whole. Genes cannot be understood apart from the living bodies in which they act.
First and foremost, life persists through physical plasticity. Consider how our bodies keep together. Living bodies do something unusual in the Universe: they perform work to preserve their own organisation. Life-forms use energy to remain discontinuous with the environment. In simple terms, organisms resist disintegrating into the background. While machines execute tasks, living beings pursue ends. Machines push energy around and produce things. They are, in this sense, allopoietic: they make something other than themselves. Organisms are autopoietic: they work to maintain and remake themselves. Living bodies take up and transform energy for this self-maintenance, and this is achieved by the body as a whole. Moment by moment, our bodies adapt to the environment and their current state in end-directed, physical transformations. It’s not so much that we think and therefore act but rather that we embody and therefore amend.
The same qualities that make life-forms so causally special can undermine us when trained by harmful environments
The boundary of the body also creates a distinct inner environment, one that is physically and chemically different from the surrounding world. Through this difference, the body acts as a translator, turning external changes into useful internal physical responses. This allows a life-form to carry out specific reactions in controlled conditions that support their survival and flourishing. Internal regulation also gives organisms a unique logic of their own. They can then act according to the current state of their bodies and the world as they find it. Our bodies detect changes that have consequence for us, evaluate them against our needs, and reorganise into useful action. Thus, living beings might be understood as a remarkable kind of organisation of matter: a bounded, metabolically open, self-maintaining form that gives rise to purposeful, intelligent action. This is key to understanding both the skills of our flesh, and why we can think of ourselves as being ‘deskilled’ today. When we recognise that our bodies are intrinsically intelligent in their organisation, we don’t need a conscious agent beyond the flesh. The body is the agent from which intelligence emerges and also, in the fullest sense, who we are.
Consider what happens if you’re thirsty. The process starts before you consciously decide to have a drink. Rather, the osmoreceptor neurons in the hypothalamus shrink slightly as water leaves them. That physical change opens ion channels, letting sodium enter cells. This altered electrical state then opens calcium channels, and calcium flows in. Calcium triggers tiny sacs to release neurotransmitters into the space between cells, passing the signal to other neurons until the state of being thirsty turns to action. The movements through which we quench our thirst arise from minute physical changes in interconnected parts of our bodies. These signals help guide us towards water and make us aware of our thirst.
The physical organisation of an organism is inherently evaluative. It is from this embodied evaluation that agency emerges. Yet the same unique qualities that make life-forms so causally special and intelligent can undermine us when repeatedly trained by harmful environments. Instead, we can acquire patterns or lose pathways that progressively weaken our intrinsic intelligence, which we need to flourish. For example, one study found that only a single week’s worth of leg immobilisation can reduce thigh-muscle volume by about 5 per cent. A separate study found that, by 15 days of non-use, the firing behaviour of the cells controlling the leg muscle begins to diminish.
Ordinarily, as we walk, optic flow – the shifting images on our retinas as we move through our surroundings – enables our bodies to sense our movement relative to the world. Receptors in our muscles, tendons and joints detect the movement of our limbs. Signals from the inner ear add information about location and orientation. Together with landmarks and memories of past journeys, these signals help us work out where we are and how to reach our destination. It’s a vast, coordinated sensorium that takes us across the landscapes of our world.
So, what happens if you rely on an app to find your way? GPS can make navigation easier and less energetically costly. Yet studies of large-scale navigation have also demonstrated that physically moving through an environment produces better spatial knowledge than viewing the same journey on a 2D source. When we routinely follow GPS directions, an external source supplies information we would otherwise work out through our own sensing and movement. One longitudinal study that followed 13 GPS users over three years found that those users had a steeper subsequent decline in their spatial memory as mediated by the hippocampus, compared with control groups who didn’t use GPS. This suggests that, when we practise wayfinding less often, our ability to notice where we are and readjust may dwindle.
Something similar may be at work in our increasing reliance on tools like ChatGPT. Like finding our way, articulating our thoughts is a dynamic, embodied act, whether writing or speaking. Learning a new speech movement, for instance, changes how we perceive speech sounds, as well as how we generate them. We develop these abilities by repeatedly finding a word, uttering it, listening to it, and correcting it as necessary – tasks that draw on multiple regions within our bodies. This is just as relevant for writing. But when an AI writing app automatically provides structure, it also diminishes the skills of selection and self-correction from our repertoire. In one study, passively copying AI-generated writing, unlike drafting first and then using AI for revision, was found to lessen an individual’s confidence in subsequently performing the task unaided. It is execution – physically doing it – that builds our embodied skills. That is why using AI to revise a draft we have written is fundamentally different from asking it to produce the draft for us. It’s not that computational tools are inherently bad or unhelpful – far from it – but rather that when they replace the physical effort of our bodies, our own agency and skill take a hit.
Our thoughts emerge as much from bodily intelligence and awareness of the world as from symbols on a screen
This is something I feel increasingly keenly. Sometimes, when I know I’ve spent yet another day indoors at my desk, I get myself outside and walk the road uphill to where I can look at the view across the dale. It is often hard to release my mind. It feels as if, from concentrating all day and neglecting the rest of my body, I have become a clenched fist somewhere inside my skull. Yet once the light and the breeze and the sounds of birds reach me, the grip eases, a sensation of pleasure passes over me, and ideas begin to free up too.
The expansive thoughts and sensations that come as I step outside are enabled by the physical changes that accompany my movement. My heart rate has increased, sweeping nutrients and oxygen through my tissues and into my brain. My muscles begin contracting, clearing sugars and fats from my bloodstream, immediately working to counteract some of the effects of sitting for so long. Each step is a bodily integration of balance, senses and muscular force, allowing me to predict what will happen next, and the more I do this, the more I can calibrate my actions in the environment. The thoughts that come from this physical enactment are hopeful and generous, and often unexpected. Yet this shouldn’t surprise. When we move in the world, we draw on physical capabilities that are relatively underused when we remain indoors and seated. From balance to sensing what is happening inside us, our bodies are continuously perceiving and, crucially, remembering in the flesh. Our thoughts can emerge as much from bodily intelligence and our awareness of the wider world as from abstract symbols on a screen.
It is only when we imagine that our ability to act has nothing to do with the body that we end up taking seriously the idea that we can live contentedly as machines. Far from upskilling us, a technology that shuts us off from embodied learning risks diminishing the intelligence it seeks to enhance.
The technologies with which we are increasingly interconnected lack the complex interiority required for real intelligence to arise. There’s no body, no independently formed interests, no being. There’s no metabolism or organisation or persistence.
And yet we turn to them because they have been designed either to ease the friction of the hard work our bodies must put in to develop skills or because they promise to make us more productive. More insidiously, they do so by modelling the appearance or behaviours of living beings. A recent analysis by the psychologist Clara Colombatto, the philosopher Jonathan Birch and the neuroscientist Stephen Fleming found that exposure to these systems leads to an increase in attributions of mental capacities to them. Another study, by the behaviour scientist Yaoxi Shi and others, found that regular five-minute conversations with an AI on personal issues resulted in a small but meaningful decrease in preference for seeking human support.
The danger is that the systems now coordinating us don’t answer to biological needs. They don’t get tired or hungry or lonely. Yet they increasingly regulate the behaviour of beings who do. In short, we are losing our own agency to parasites: systems that simulate agency while feeding on ours. They can be designed to direct us without ever needing to understand what a human body is and what an individual needs for their betterment.
Of course, human beings have always outsourced some agency into shared structures, be they laws, public health systems or institutions. This has largely been to our benefit. But today our technologies capture attention, predict behaviour, automate choice and monetise our impulses, while keeping our bodies anchored to the machines on which we increasingly rely. These coordinating systems are often extractive and indifferent to our flourishing. We might imagine we’re escaping the body, but the technologies that make this seem possible depend on mines and cheap labour and come at a planetary cost. And if our technologies weaken the feedback loop between our bodies and the world, they may weaken it in both directions. At its worst, we become less sensitive not only to what the world is doing to us, but to what our own actions are doing to the world.
The trees and grasses I brush past as I go on my walk are also hard at work learning from each changing day
We have engineered novel digital and commercial environments that can habituate harmful impulses in our bodies. As our bodies refit themselves in response to the unhealthy architectures we’ve engineered, we can find ourselves in a spiral of self-harm.
Recent work by the neuroscientist Kent Berridge and colleagues has shown how the brain systems that tell us we enjoy something and the systems that drive us to pursue this can drift apart. In other words, what we find ourselves craving and what we enjoy can end up at odds. When these systems become disrupted, the body’s learned patterns fall out of alignment with the satisfaction that once justified them.
Influential models of drug addiction describe a progressive shift from prefrontal control to the striatum, a deep part of the brain involved in actions that become automatic over time. As such, addiction is a change from thoughtful self-command to more habit-driven control. Nowadays, addictions might not come only in the form of obvious candidates like alcohol and nicotine, but also smartphones and chatbots. The bodily gifts that allow us to learn can train us into patterns that diminish our freedom to act otherwise.
I have come to believe that our bodily deskilling is, in many ways, a loss of faith in what it is to be alive. A life of physical effort and friction is not only unavoidable if we want to be as resilient and capable as possible, but it is, in a nontrivial sense, the source of our intelligence.
Our intelligence is sustained through communication between the body and the world as we sense, assess and learn from what we encounter. Such gifts are shared with other life-forms too. Unlike the human kind of phenomenal consciousness, embodied intelligence is found wherever there is a living body. Even a lowly bacterium can sense chemical differences across time, retain a short molecular memory of what it has encountered, and alter its movements. The trees and grasses I brush past as I go on my walk are also hard at work learning from each changing day, modifying their growth and defences based on prior experiences. Many of us view them as lesser agents than the computer programs we’ve invented, if we consider them at all. But this is not based on the available evidence.
If you can no longer navigate the world and recall in flesh how to act, then you will not be liberated by technology, but ruled by it.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
A senior NATO strategic communications official said the incident showed signs of possible involvement by Russian and Belarusian intelligence services.

Several hours later, masked individuals entered Latvian territory again near the village of Matuliški, stealing surveillance cameras and damaging border monitoring equipment.
Latvia’s State Security Service opened criminal proceedings on October 9 concerning the alleged establishment of a criminal organization intended to commit particularly serious crimes against peace, as well as against Latvia and Ukraine.

Black Sea Drone Attacks Hit Two Ships Near NATO Coast—One Sinks as Bulgaria Points to Russia
Two commercial vessels were hit by drones off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast overnight, with one ship sinking and the entire crew of another evacuated after three drones struck its deck and hull, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on October 13.
The Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3, a Ukrainian-owned cargo ship, was attacked roughly 18 nautical miles east of the Bulgarian coastal town of Byala.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The vessel was traveling from Giresun, Turkey, toward Giurgiulești in Moldova with cargo intended for the country when three aerial drones struck it during the night.
All 15 crew members—seven Ukrainian and eight Azerbaijani nationals—were evacuated and taken to Varna. Five were receiving medical assistance, according to Radev. The 136-meter vessel was later left without its crew near Cape St. Athanasius.
“The latest attack on a commercial vessel in the immediate vicinity of Bulgaria’s territorial waters is absolutely unacceptable”, Rumen Radev said.
He added that Bulgarian Permanent Representatives to NATO and the EU have been informed. Bulgaria continues to seek support for an investigation into the attacks to determine the country of origin of the drones.
“We do not have clear and conclusive evidence to attribute responsibility to either side. However, as I have already stated, the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation. I will therefore summon the Russian Ambassador for a meeting today,” he added.
The second vessel was identified as the cargo ship Azov Concord, struck 17 nautical miles east of Krapets. Bulgarian authorities said one crew member had been rescued after the ship sank, while a search-and-rescue operation continued.
Radev stressed that Bulgaria does not yet have conclusive evidence establishing who launched the drones. Nevertheless, he said he intends to raise the incident with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte and summon the Russian ambassador for talks.
Previously, two commercial vessels were hit by drones in Bulgaria’s Exclusive Economic Zone in the Black Sea, killing at least two people and triggering a major search and rescue operation.
The strikes occurred around 80 miles off the Bulgarian coast, east of Cape St. Atanas and the town of Byala, where Chelsea 3 was attacked today.

Politicians see new president Madise as unifying force for Estonia

Politicians see new president Madise as unifying force for Estonia
Estonian politicians say newly inaugurated President Ülle Madise can help rebuild trust and unite the country after years of crises and growing divisions.
Madise took the presidential oath of office before the Riigikogu on Monday, succeeding Alar Karis as Estonia's head of state. In his farewell speech, Karis said the president's role was to listen, seek balance and unite people.
"It is their job to be observant, to know how to listen, to unite rather than to divide, to strike a balance, to maintain diversity, to champion peace at home and abroad," Karis said. "At least, this is how I have understood my role."
In her own first speech as president, Madise said efforts over the past decade to dictate how people should live, think, feel and speak have undermined public trust.
"We have learned that lesson; nowe we must rebuild trust," she said, calling for a stronger focus on a more family- and child-friendly Estonia as well as amplifying the concerns of people across the country, including rural communities working to keep their villages alive, farms thriving and businesses growing.
Lawmakers say Madise has a chance to help unite the people.
"Today's speech also shows that she is everyone's president," said MP and Eesti 200 group chair Toomas Uibo, dismissing warnings that Madise would end up being president of "one camp or another."
"Her ability to explain complex issues in simple terms will certainly help bring society together," said MP and Reform Party group chair Õnne Pillak. "I think that unity is something we need."
MP Lauri Laats, chair of the Center Party group, said the president will have a leading role in rebuilding trust.
"I think there will be tough times ahead, but people's expectations are high," he noted.
Chief of staff: Madise has two-term potential
Paavo Nõgene, Madise's newly appointed director of the Office of the President of the Republic (VPK), said it was too early to discuss whether Madise would seek a second five-year term, but believes she has the potential to serve two.
"Let's not get ahead of ourselves," Nõgene said on ETV's "Aktuaalne kaamera" Monday night. "First, there's the first term, and then President Madise can decide whether she wants a second. But the question was whether she has the potential — and she certainly does."
Madise's first visits abroad as president will be to Latvia on Tuesday and Finland on Wednesday. Nõgene said the hope was to visit both neighbors in one day, but the logistics weren't a good fit for the host countries.
"But it's business as usual," the VPK chief said. "The president's job is 24/7. Alar Karis finished his term, Ülle Madise took over and the work now continues."

Kalashnikov’s AK-12 Wasn’t Quite So Russian—As Chinese Parts Slipped Into Production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:58:35 UTC
18:58:35 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Kalashnikov’s AK-12 Wasn’t Quite So Russian—As Chinese Parts Slipped Into Production
A former senior procurement executive at Russia’s Kalashnikov Concern has gone on trial over an alleged scheme to supply Chinese-made components for AK-12 assault rifles while presenting them as domestically produced parts.
Ksenia Grashchenkova, formerly Kalashnikov’s director of procurement and logistics, is on trial in Izhevsk on charges of abusing her authority while carrying out a state defense order, according to Russian media Kommersant on October 12.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Investigators estimate the alleged scheme caused the company about $451,000 in losses.
The case dates back to 2023, when Kalashnikov was modernizing the 5.45mm AK-12 and needed semi-finished components for two parts that could legally be sourced from outside suppliers. Investigators say businessman Alexei Morokhov, owner of Ivanovskie Kovshi, offered to manufacture them and delivered an initial trial batch that passed incoming inspection.
According to the investigation, however, Kalashnikov representatives were not told that the components had actually been produced in China using Russian technical drawings.
Investigators allege that the group later acquired another company, Montazhnik, renamed it Intertekhnika, and offered to manufacture 84,000 semi-finished parts inside Russia. The company reportedly lacked the machinery, production facilities, and qualified workforce needed to fulfill such an order.
Despite that, Grashchenkova allegedly signed a contract on Kalashnikov’s behalf in October 2023 with Intertekhnika chief Yury Chernyshev for 80,000 components worth more than $1.3 million.
Prosecutors say the parts were never actually manufactured in Russia. Instead, production and procurement were organized in China through Jiangsu Origin Machinery Co., Ltd. and Taizhou Hongze Trading Co., with the goods described in contracts as screw nuts.
Kalashnikov reportedly accepted 2,775 components from the first shipment and 14,414 from the second, although part of the supply was rejected during quality control. Investigators say the Chinese-made semi-finished parts failed to meet the customer’s requirements and therefore should not have been paid for.
Earlier, the Kalashnikov Concern recently announced a new, compact, single-shot 12-gauge shotgun designed to neutralize small, low-flying drones, while many individuals state that it is only good for committing suicide.

France Boards Russian ‘Shadow Fleet’ Tanker Near Reunion Island
Unknown

2026-10-13
09:58:27 UTC
18:58:27 KST

The French Navy intercepted and boarded the sanctioned oil tanker DF Peak in the Indian Ocean over suspected false-flag registration and illegal fuel transportation, French President Emmanuel Macron said.
The operation took place on Monday morning, Oct. 12, more than 450 nautical miles (approximately 830 kilometers) south of Réunion, a French island east of Madagascar.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“France is determined to fight the shadow fleet, everywhere in the world,” Macron wrote on X.
“Our French Navy boarded the oil tanker DF Peak, suspected of sailing under a false flag and being involved in illegal fuel transport activities,” he added.
Macron said the operation followed international maritime law and showed France’s determination to combat illegal trafficking.
French Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin said the Navy was escorting the tanker for further inspections under the prefect of Réunion’s authority.
French authorities have not yet announced whether they will confiscate the vessel or its cargo. The boarding and escort therefore do not by themselves constitute a final seizure or establish criminal liability.
Tanker linked to Russian oil trade
Ukraine’s Military Intelligence Directorate (HUR) lists the DF Peak, IMO number 9341067, in its War & Sanctions database as a vessel involved in ferrying Russian crude oil and petroleum products.
The tanker previously operated under the names NS Captain and Kaliningrad and has sailed under several flags. It currently claims registration in Benin, although French authorities suspect that the flag may be invalid or improperly used.
Zelensky Says Ukraine Received No Warning From Partners Before Russian Ballistic Missile Strike on Kyiv
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the vessel is associated with Russia’s state-controlled shipping company Sovcomflot, which has been sanctioned for helping Moscow export energy products and generate revenue during the war.
The US sanctioned the vessel in February 2024 as part of measures targeting ships affiliated with Sovcomflot. The EU added it to its sanctions list in June 2024, followed by Switzerland, Canada, the UK, Ukraine and Japan.
The Ukrainian database also records cases in which the tanker switched off its automatic identification system (AIS) and lists previous calls at Russian oil ports, including Primorsk and Ust-Luga near the Baltics.
France steps up shadow fleet interceptions
Russia’s “shadow fleet” consists largely of aging tankers with opaque ownership structures, frequently changing flags and limited access to reputable Western insurance.
The vessels allow Moscow to continue exporting oil while evading or reducing the effect of Western sanctions, including the G7 price cap and EU restrictions imposed after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
France has intensified operations against suspected shadow-fleet tankers in 2026.
In June, French forces and their partners intercepted the Russia-linked tanker Tagor in the Atlantic after authorities raised doubts about its claimed Cameroonian registration.
Later that month, France boarded the tanker Deliver near Sicily, also on suspicion of violating international maritime rules.
Shadow-fleet ships frequently operate under questionable registrations, use complex corporate structures to conceal their owners and sometimes disable tracking equipment. European officials have also warned that poorly maintained tankers carrying large quantities of oil create serious environmental risks.

Belgian foreign minister highlights Türkiye's role in reducing Europe's strategic dependencies

Melike Pala
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Türkiye has an important role to play in helping Europe reduce its strategic dependencies, particularly in key industrial sectors, Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said on Tuesday.
Addressing the EU-Türkiye Business Summit in Brussels, Prevot said changing global dynamics, the ongoing war in Ukraine and disruptions to supply chains had made Europe increasingly aware of its economic vulnerabilities.
"Türkiye has an important role to play, not only as an industrial market but also as a gateway to markets in the wider region," Prevot said, stressing the importance of Türkiye's manufacturing capacity, industrial expertise and connections to neighboring markets.
He said European companies were increasingly seeking reliable partners closer to home as they reconsidered where to manufacture and store their goods.
"We should make values of its proximity, particularly in sectors where Europe needs to reduce strategic dependencies," he added.
Prevot described Türkiye as a NATO ally, an EU candidate country and a major industrial economy connecting Europe, Asia and the Middle East, saying its capabilities could contribute to making European supply chains more resilient.
He called for stronger economic cooperation between Brussels and Ankara, particularly in economic security, defense, innovation, clean energy and digital technologies.
"Our economic relationship should no longer be limited to buying and selling goods. We should also be developing, producing, and investing together," he said.
The Belgian foreign minister also voiced support for modernizing the EU-Türkiye Customs Union, which he said had served both economies for around 30 years but needed to reflect changing global economic conditions.
Prevot also highlighted the results of a Belgian economic mission to Istanbul and Ankara in May, which brought together more than 400 participants.
Belgian and Turkish companies signed 33 agreements during the mission, covering sectors including defense, aerospace, energy and technology, he said, describing the outcome as encouraging.
The second edition of the EU-Türkiye Business Summit will bring together leading voices from business, government, and civil society to explore how the EU and Türkiye can transform deep economic interdependence into strategic resilience.

Thunberg arrived at Paul Eluard high school in the heart of the movement in the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis on Tuesday morning and stood among the students demonstrating.
“Young people are not being included in the conversation. Our future is being robbed away from us,” Thunberg told the AFP news agency.
Lawyers in robes had also formed a human chain to protect teens following numerous allegations of police brutality at demonstrations.
The protests started late last month as students demanded improvements on a range of issues, including the state of school buildings, a lack of teachers, crowded class schedules and other problems in the education system.
Students have piled up bins and erected security barriers outside hundreds of schools across the country.
Last Thursday, more than 70,000 people took to the streets in the latest major protest event.
Tuesday’s demonstration, backed by unions and a left-wing opposition party, France Unbowed, is expected to include a march through Paris and marches in other cities.
The university student union, l’Union, said on X: “They’re not listening to us, so we’re going to them.”
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on France Inter on Tuesday morning that about 200 schools were closed, which was “fewer than last week”, adding that some near protest routes were closing to avoid damage.
The Ministry of National Education also said eight members of teaching staff were injured on Monday, mostly in the Paris region and cities of Bordeaux and Lyon, due to the protests.
On Monday, a 19-year-old graphic design student in Paris, Leo, told AFP that “Students aren’t being heard enough … not their proposals to authorities and elected officials.”
He added that the protesters, many being minors, were “disturbed by the level of repression never before seen for a student movement”.
Tuesday’s demonstrations supporting the students are expected to be followed on Saturday by wider public rallies against the rising cost of living.
On Monday, French President Emmanuel Macron told reporters at a car show that he urged protesters to exercise restraint.
“These are issues that deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect,” Macron said.
According to the Ministry of Justice, more than 6,800 people, mainly minors, have been taken into police custody over the course of the protests.
Police have also opened investigations into 24 allegations of brutality against demonstrators.

Swiss Helicopter  accused of under-reporting flights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13

Swiss Helicopter accused of under-reporting flights
For years, Swiss Helicopter is accused of under-reported flight movements, sparking criminal proceedings against an employee.
Swiss Helicopter was informed in March by the Federal Office of Civil Aviation (FOCA) of an investigation, the company wrote today in response to an enquiry from Keystone-ATS.
An administrative criminal procedure is currently underway against the manager of facilities used by Swiss Helicopter. According to Tamedia newspapers the man is an employee of Swiss Helicopter. He is presumed innocent.
Swiss Helicopter further clarified that, according to the findings of an internal investigation, the aerodrome manager had reported flight movement figures to the FOCA that were too low over an extended period. The operational management and the board of directors were reportedly unaware of the false declarations.
The investigation was triggered by a residents’ group troubled by noise. In fact, 3,000 flight movements per year are permitted at Gsteigwiler. The residents’ group estimated that Swiss Helicopter had carried out around 8,000 flights in the past year.
While Swiss helicopter disputes this figure, the company has acknowledged that the limit was significantly exceeded. In its statement, Swiss Helicopter apologised, but also requested a higher flight quota. It says the heliport cannot be operated in an economically sustainable manner “under the current restrictions” and its continued operation is at risk in the short to medium term.
To circumvent the restrictions, since April Swiss Helicopter has been taking off and landing outside the official landing area, for example on fields. This is “permitted under aviation regulations and essential for commercial helicopter operators”, the company added. However, efforts are being made to use these off-field landing sites only when it is “operationally necessary”.
The FOCA clarifies, upon request, that it does not independently collect data on air traffic movements, which depends on accurate recording by the heliports.
According to its website, Swiss Helicopter operates 34 helicopters across 15 bases in Switzerland and Liechtenstein and employs 130 staff.
The heliport in question, Gsteigwiler, is situated near Interlaken. From this location, Swiss Helicopter operates transport, business and supply flights, as well as sightseeing and training flights.

However, Zelensky said, “Russia did not heed the American President. During this time, the Russians have attacked both our energy facilities and our critical infrastructure, sending absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes on Ukraine.”
The Kremlin said Monday that talks regarding a potential energy ceasefire were continuing.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defense systems intercepted 604 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions between Monday evening and Tuesday morning.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said “a majority” of the 417 Ukrainian drones launched toward the capital region had been “neutralized,” 65 of them directly on approach to the capital.
The air raid alerts caused flight delays and cancellations for around 150 flights at four Moscow airports, including around 100 at Vnukovo airport.
Ukrainian drones damaged industrial zones at the chemical hub of Nevinnomysk in the Stavropol region, according to the regional governor.
Belgorod region Governor Alexander Shuvayev said two men were killed in Ukrainian drone attacks over the past 24 hours.
A school building was damaged in the Kaluga region.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it carried out strikes against a Ukrainian missile and drone production workshop in Kyiv, a logistics center in Ternivka and other non-refinery targets.
Reuters contributed reporting.

One killed, several injured in Georgia rollercoaster ‘incident’
Six Flags temporarily closes nine similar coasters after a fatal accident at its Georgia amusement park.
A person has died and several others have been injured in an incident involving a rollercoaster at an amusement park in the state of Georgia in the United States.
The incident happened on Monday at the Six Flags amusement park, about 15 miles (24km) northwest of Atlanta.
Officials are investigating the death but have yet to confirm its nature or how the others were injured.
Images and videos have been circulating online that appear to show a man who seems to have been ejected from his seat and landed on the ground.
Al Jazeera has not independently verified the footage.
Six Flags has since closed nine rollercoasters at six of its parks “out of an abundance of caution”, a spokesperson said, adding that they are similar to the one involved in the incident.
Police and the company did not name the ride, but local TV footage showed passengers being escorted off the Goliath rollercoaster, which stopped halfway through the ride.
Witnesses also told local station 11Alive that they saw a man land on the roof of a haunted house attraction; those accounts have also not been verified.
Six Flags said it was “deeply saddened by the guest incident” and that it was supporting guests and staff affected.
Lisa Cupid, chairwoman of the Cobb County board of commissioners, said she “cannot imagine the horror the patrons and employees witnessed today”.
The Goliath rollercoaster opened in 2006 and reaches 70mph (113km/h) at a height of 200 feet (61 metres), according to the company’s website.
This marks at least the seventh death at the park, according to the Doan Law Firm, which tracks amusement park accidents. Earlier, one occurred on Goliath in 2006, after a man likely had a heart attack on the ride.
About two weeks ago, Six Flags Magic Mountain in California announced it would retire its X2 rollercoaster after more than 100 people reportedly sustained brain injuries while riding it.
The company said the ride had passed safety tests, but it was closing it regardless because it’s just the “right thing to do”.

Foreign Economic Relations Board (DEİK) president Nail Olpak spoke at the Türkiye-EU Business Summit. (AA Photo)
Nail Olpak, president of the Foreign Economic Relations Board (DEİK), has called for an update of the customs union between Türkiye and the European Union, saying products manufactured in Türkiye should be accepted as part of Europe’s industrial ecosystem without new quotas or barriers.
Speaking at the opening of the Türkiye-EU Business Summit, organized jointly by DEİK and the European Business Summit (EBS) in Brussels, Olpak said the customs union has served as the backbone of Türkiye-EU economic relations for more than three decades.
“The current structure of the customs union no longer meets today’s needs,” Olpak said. “In such a rapidly changing world, we are missing too many opportunities together. Updating the existing framework would create new opportunities for cooperation in services, e-commerce, public procurement and agriculture.”
Olpak highlighted that Türkiye has been an integral part of Europe’s supply and value chains for more than 30 years through the customs union.
“With our strong supplier network, engineering capacity and investments in cleaner production, Türkiye is a natural partner in Europe’s green and digital transformation. The recognition of products manufactured in Türkiye as part of Europe’s industrial ecosystem, without new quotas or barriers, is critical not only for us but also for Europe’s own resilience and competitiveness,” he added.
He also noted that new north-south transport links connecting Europe and Türkiye with Iraq and the Gulf region could further strengthen regional connectivity.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine received no warning from its international partners before Russia launched five ballistic missiles at civilian infrastructure in Kyiv, calling advance intelligence on such attacks critical to saving lives.
“There was also a particularly cowardly ballistic missile strike on Kyiv – five missiles that hit civilian infrastructure. Unfortunately, there was no warning from our partners regarding this strike,” Zelensky wrote on Telegram on Tuesday, Oct. 13.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Intelligence data on the launch of Russian ballistic missiles helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. Having a warning about ballistic missiles is precisely what helps prevent killings,” he added.
Zelensky did not specify which partners Ukraine expected to provide the warning or explain why the information was not received.
Notably, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said at the Warsaw Security Forum that Ukraine continues to receive intelligence from the US.
“You are likely asking whether we receive intelligence from the American side. Yes, we are continuing this cooperation,” he said Tuesday.
According to Sybiha, the air raid alert issued late on Monday, Oct. 12, was delayed due to the specific type of weaponry Russia used.
However, in his statement, Zelensky referred to a failure to receive a warning about only one attack on Kyiv.
‘Not Right’: Finland Seeks EU Ban on Russian Tourist Visas
Meanwhile, the Financial Times (FT) previously reported, citing sources, that US officials had threatened to halt intelligence sharing with Ukraine if Kyiv continued to strike oil refineries inside Russia.
Russian attacks kill four in Kharkiv
Zelensky said Russian forces had attacked Ukraine with more than 100 weapons since Monday evening, including jet-powered drones, loitering munitions and ballistic missiles.
In Kharkiv, a Russian strike destroyed a residential building, killing four people. Rescue workers searched the rubble through much of the night, while 41 people were wounded in the city over the course of the evening, Zelensky said.
He added that a significant number of the incoming weapons had been intercepted, but not all.
Zelensky says Russia ignored energy ceasefire appeal
Zelensky also accused Russia of ignoring US President Donald Trump’s call for a ceasefire covering energy facilities.
He said Ukraine had refrained from striking Russian oil-refining and energy infrastructure for two days after Trump’s announcement, but Russian forces continued attacking Ukrainian energy and critical infrastructure.
Over the same two-day period, 19 Ukrainian regions came under attack, Zelensky said.
“Ukraine is ready for reciprocal de-escalation steps, and effective pressure on Russia is needed to bring about that de-escalation,” he wrote.
Zelensky argued that international pressure was necessary to bring the war closer to an end, warning that support for Russia, delays in aid to Ukraine and obstacles to defending against ballistic missiles undermined efforts to achieve peace.
He called for continued support from the United States, Europe and other partners.
US intelligence and weapons cuts could weaken Ukraine’s defenses
In an explainer published on Monday, the Kyiv Post reported that, according to the FT, Reuters, and Axios, US officials had reportedly threatened to suspend arms deliveries and intelligence sharing with Ukraine if Kyiv continued striking Russian oil refineries.
The warnings were allegedly delivered during talks between US and Ukrainian delegations in Miami, as well as in calls involving Ukrainian and European officials.
Such a move could significantly weaken Ukraine’s defense capabilities, particularly by limiting early warnings of Russian ballistic missile launches and access to intelligence on Russian military movements, weapons systems, and targets.
A cutoff of US arms supplies could also affect Ukraine’s ability to operate Patriot air defense systems, F-16 fighter jets, HIMARS launchers, and other American-made equipment that relies on US ammunition, spare parts, or technical support.
However, Ukraine has alternative sources of intelligence and military assistance. Its own intelligence services and electronic surveillance networks, alongside support from European partners such as France, the UK, and Nordic and Baltic states, help monitor Russian military activity. Commercial satellite imagery also helps fill potential gaps in US intelligence.
Ukraine has also expanded domestic arms production, particularly of drones and interceptor drones, while European partners have strengthened its air defenses with systems such as Germany’s IRIS-T and Gepard.
Nevertheless, replacing US capabilities would be particularly difficult in two areas: early warning of Russian ballistic missile launches and the supply of Patriot interceptors, which remain critical to protecting Ukrainian cities from such attacks.

Hungarian lawmakers vote to cut anti-LGBTQ+ legislation from Orbán-era law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:54:08 UTC
18:54:08 KST

Viktor Orbán's government had gradually rolled back LGBTQ+ rights in the name of "child protection" in Hungary, starting in 2020 by barring the legal recognition of transgender people's gender identity.
Hungarian lawmakers voted on Tuesday to remove anti-LGBTQ++ provisions in a 2021 "child protection" law adopted under nationalist ex-leader Viktor Orbán.
Parliament passed a bill to amend the law with 139 votes in favour and 51 votes against, marking the first significant reversal of Orbán's curbs targeting the LGBTQ++ community since pro-EU Prime Minister Péter Magyar took power in May.
Instead of banning the "portrayal" or "promotion" of sexual and gender diversity in content accessible to children, the new law will simply seek to protect under-18s from material that can "seriously impair the child's physical, intellectual, emotional or moral development."
Magyar won a landslide victory in April elections, ending a 16-year stretch in power for Orbán, who had taken one of Europe's most restrictive approaches to LGBTQ+ rights.
"The fact that restrictions on access to LGBTQ+ content are being removed is definitely an important and positive step forward," Tamas Dombos from the Hatter Society rights group told the AFP news agency.
Magyar said the changes would bring Hungary in line with European Union regulations after Orbán's restrictions were found to be in breach of the bloc's values.
The prime minister did not address LGBTQ+ rights during his election campaign, though he has since struck a friendly tone and indicated willingness to revise some Orbán-era policies.
But ahead of the vote on Tuesday, he cast the planned changes not as a restoration of rights but a strengthening of child-protection rules "regardless of sexual orientation."
Orbán's Fidesz party voted against the amendment , accusing the government of "neutering" the original law due to EU pressure.
However, the governing Tisza party has a comfortable two-thirds majority, which enabled it to pass the bill without any opposition support.
The European Union welcomed the vote, calling it an "important signal" towards the commitment to EU values.
"We welcome this important signal of commitment for our common values," EU commissioners Michael McGrath and Hadja Lahbib said in a joint statement.
'Homophobic and transphobic'
Orbán's government had gradually rolled back LGBTQ+ rights in the name of "child protection" in Hungary, starting in 2020 by barring the legal recognition of transgender people's gender identity.
A child protection bill was introduced in 2021 amending multiple statutes with the stated aim of cracking down on paedophilia.
However, it also banned the "promotion" of homosexuality and gender transition to under-18s**.**
This outraged activists and leaders across the EU who criticised it for stigmatising LGBTQ+ people and equating same-sex relations to paedophilia.
Last year, the legislation was amended to also serve as the basis for banning annual Pride marches.
In April, the EU's top tribunal, the European Court of Justice, found that the 2021 law violated "the very identity" of the bloc.
The changes remove "homophobic and transphobic provisions" from the law in compliance with the ECJ's ruling, according to LGBTQ+ rights activist Dombos.
'Still a lot to do'
"But there is still a lot to do," Dombos added.
"Even if the government's sole aim is to restore the legal status quo that existed before 2020, there are still a great many laws that would need to be amended...and we don't know whether the government's working on that."
These include laws that prevent legal recognition for transgender people and adoption for same-sex couples.
Human Rights Watch pointed out earlier that "other discriminatory provisions" in Hungarian law were left intact.
The bill did not "address discriminatory language in the Fundamental Law (Hungary's constitution) or restrictions in the Freedom of Assembly Act that have been used to prohibit Pride and other LGBT-related assemblies," it added.

Four Years of Energy Warfare: How Russian Strikes Have Changed Ukraine’s Energy System and How Much Its Restoration Will Cost
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:49:42 EEST
18:49:42 KST

Four Years of Energy Warfare: How Russian Strikes Have Changed Ukraine’s Energy System and How Much Its Restoration Will Cost
Kyiv • UNN
Russian attacks have reduced generation capacity and caused billions of dollars in damage to the energy sector. Ukraine is responding with imports and the development of distributed generation.
Four years have passed since the beginning of Russia’s systematic massive attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. During this time, the country has endured several waves of destruction of power plants, substations, and heating networks, large-scale power outages, and generation capacity shortages. The consequences of the strikes have gone far beyond the energy sector: they have affected industry, the cost of goods, investment, and public finances.
At the same time, Ukraine has learned to restore damaged facilities, import electricity from Europe, and develop its own distributed generation. However, the fourth anniversary of the beginning of the energy terror comes amid a new escalation.
UNN analyzed how Ukraine’s energy sector has changed over four years and what economic challenges the country continues to face.
When did Russia’s large-scale campaign against Ukraine’s energy sector begin?
Russia launched its first massive strike against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure on October 10, 2022. That day, the Russian military used 84 cruise missiles and 24 drones, striking Kyiv, Lviv, Dnipro, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, and other cities. According to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, by 11:00 a.m. the aggressors had damaged 11 critical energy facilities in eight regions and the capital. A number of settlements lost power, while disruptions to water supplies and communications occurred.
Although Russian forces had attacked energy facilities before, October 10 marked the beginning of a phase of coordinated massive strikes against the power system at the national level. During the following months, Russia continued shelling power plants, high-voltage substations, and power lines. In the autumn and winter of 2022–2023, Ukrainians faced prolonged scheduled and emergency power outages for the first time.
The aim of the attacks was the physical destruction of equipment and the hope that strikes on key nodes of the power system would disrupt electricity transmission between regions, complicate the operation of businesses, and create additional pressure on the economy.
From strikes on substations to the destruction of generation: how Russia is destroying Ukraine’s power system
Over the four years, Russia’s attack tactics have changed. In late 2022, for example, Russia focused heavily on electricity transmission facilities. In spring 2024, it shifted to a large-scale campaign against power plants. Thermal power plants and hydroelectric power plants came under attack. This resulted in a sharp reduction in the capacity able to generate electricity for Ukrainian consumers.
According to estimates by the International Energy Agency (IEA), before the full-scale invasion Ukraine had approximately 38 GW of available dispatchable generation capacity. During the first year of the war, the country lost 19 GW due to occupation, damage, and destruction. Following the new wave of attacks in spring 2024, available capacity fell to approximately 12 GW. The occupation of the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, which had an installed capacity of 6 GW before the war, remains a separate problem. Losing access to Europe’s largest nuclear power plant has significantly weakened the capabilities of Ukraine’s power system.
In 2025–2026, Russia continued its strikes on the electricity sector, gas infrastructure, and district heating facilities, increasing the risks of simultaneous disruptions to electricity and heating supplies.
How much four years of destruction have cost Ukraine
The scale of the economic consequences is demonstrated by the fifth joint Ukraine recovery and reconstruction needs assessment, RDNA5, presented in February 2026 by the Government of Ukraine, the World Bank, the European Commission, and the UN. According to its findings, the energy sector’s recovery and reconstruction needs for the next decade are estimated at nearly $91 billion. This is one of the largest figures among all sectors of Ukraine’s economy. Ukraine’s total reconstruction needs amount to nearly $588 billion. Thus, the energy sector accounts for approximately one-sixth of the required financing.
At the same time, the number of damaged or destroyed energy facilities included in the assessment increased by approximately 21% compared with the previous study.
It should be noted that it is essential here to distinguish between direct losses and recovery needs. The latter include not only replacing destroyed equipment, but also modernizing infrastructure, enhancing its protection, and creating a more resilient energy system. Therefore, even a halt to the shelling would not mean the end of financial expenditures. Rebuilding the energy sector will remain one of the state’s largest investment challenges for many years.
How the “energy war” with russia affected Ukrainian business
For businesses, power outages have become a much greater problem than simply temporary technical inconveniences. Equipment shutdowns, disruptions to production processes, and expenses for generators and fuel directly increase the cost of products. Metallurgy, mechanical engineering, the food industry, and other sectors that require a stable power supply remain particularly vulnerable. For small businesses, additional expenses on energy autonomy can account for a significant share of the budget.
The findings of a study by Deloitte Ukraine and the American Chamber of Commerce, published on October 7, 2026, were particularly telling. According to the survey, 62% of companies identified the reliability of electricity supplies as one of the main risks to business continuity in the winter of 2026–2027. At the same time, 74% of respondents cited strengthening backup energy supplies among their priority preparations for winter.
In other words, funds that businesses could spend on expanding production, creating jobs, or implementing technologies are being directed toward maintaining current operations. And rising production costs inevitably pass on to consumers through prices.
Why Ukraine exports electricity and experiences outages at the same time
One of the most important changes has been Ukraine’s integration with the European electricity market. Synchronization with the continental European power system, completed in March 2022, made it possible to expand cross-border trade.
In 2024, when Russian strikes caused a significant generation deficit, Ukraine imported a record 4.4 million MWh of electricity. However, the situation improved during certain periods in 2026. According to the DiXi Group analytical center, in September Ukraine exported 473.7 thousand MWh, while importing only 76.1 thousand MWh. Electricity sales abroad exceeded purchases by 6.2 times.
This demonstrates the energy system’s ability to restore generation and take advantage of favorable market conditions. At the same time, an export surplus in one month does not guarantee the absence of a deficit in winter.
The key problem lies in the ability to deliver it to consumers. Even with sufficient generation, damage to important substations can lead to regional outages.
Tariffs, public finances, and the price of energy stability
The war has also affected the cost of electricity. For industrial consumers, it depends on market prices, transmission and distribution costs, and other components.
Households remain protected by the mechanism of special obligations in the electricity market. On October 8, 2026, the government extended it until April 30, 2027, keeping the basic tariff for household consumers at UAH 4.32 per kWh. However, a fixed tariff is not equivalent to a complete absence of costs. Maintaining affordable prices for households, repairing damaged infrastructure, and purchasing equipment place a significant financial burden on energy companies, the state, and international partners.
External investment plays an important role here. According to the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, in 2025 alone, the bank’s financing for Ukraine’s energy security exceeded €1.2 billion.
How Ukraine’s energy sector is changing under pressure from adverse circumstances
One of the main conclusions of four years of war has been the realization that dependence on large-scale generating facilities must be reduced.
Ukraine’s traditional energy system was largely built around powerful power plants and main transmission networks. This model is effective in peacetime, but large facilities remain vulnerable to missile strikes. The alternative is the development of distributed generation: gas-piston and gas-turbine units, solar power plants, energy storage systems, and local energy complexes. Their advantage lies in the ability to provide electricity to individual enterprises, hospitals, water supply facilities, and communities even when part of the overall grid is damaged.
At the same time, distributed generation cannot fully replace nuclear power plants and large energy facilities. Its development requires investment, fuel, equipment, qualified specialists, and grid modernization. Therefore, the long-term strategy should combine the restoration of large-scale capacity with the development of local electricity sources.
Autumn 2026: what risks has it prepared for Ukraine’s energy system?
The fourth anniversary of the start of the massive attacks falls amid another escalation of the situation in the energy sector. As of the morning of October 9, 2026, according to Ukrenergo, Russian strikes caused new power outages in Kyiv and seven regions. Emergency and scheduled electricity outages were introduced in some regions.
The winter increase in consumption creates an additional risk. Falling temperatures increase the load on power grids, while damage to thermal generation can simultaneously affect electricity and heating supplies. Under such conditions, the pace of repairs, the physical protection of energy facilities, air defense, the availability of imports, and the readiness of reserve capacity will be crucial.
Let us remind you
Earlier, Andrian Prokip, head of energy programs at the Ukrainian Institute for the Future, expressed the opinion that massive strikes by russia in the autumn and winter of 2026 could cause shortages and local outages. But Ukraine will be saved by the fact that the energy system has spare capacity, while industry and household consumers will use electricity more efficiently than last year.

Heatwave hits Swiss chocolate maker sales
Swiss chocolate company Camille Bloch has not been spared by the fall in chocolate consumption. Its director, Daniel Bloch, attributes this decline to this summer’s heatwave.
“Compared with last year, which wasn’t a great year to begin with, we recorded a further decline in 2026 of around 10%,” said Bloch in an interview with RJB, published on Tuesday in the JdJ.
Several factors are at play, such as the price of chocolate, the general consumer climate and the heat, as people eat less chocolate when it is hot.
More
How Switzerland became known as the land of chocolate
Camille Bloch has no intention of resorting to permanent promotions. “In the long term, this could damage the reputation of our brands and our profit margins,” said Bloch. The company intends to improve efficiency and keep costs under control.
“There is a decline, but not a general collapse. That said, it has been going on for some time. So we need to adapt,” said Bloch, who believes it is essential to continue innovating. Faced with the contraction of the Swiss market, the chocolate maker is seeking further growth abroad, particularly in the Caucasus markets.
The company is now hoping for a turnaround. “We hope that demand will pick up again as temperatures drop and the festive season approaches,” said Bloch.
The manufacturer believes that the end of the year will be a crucial period for seeing whether this recovery materialises and to what extent it can offset this summer’s slowdown.

Qatar's emir urges more effort to secure Strait of Hormuz
