Qatar's emir has called for greater efforts to secure the passage of oil and gas through the Strait of Hormuz, urging Gulf states to maintain cooperation and coordination as the regional crisis disrupts maritime traffic.
Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani said on Tuesday that the security, sovereignty and stability of Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries could not be compromised.
Speaking to the Shura Council, he also called for stronger efforts to secure navigation in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz and to protect energy, water and civilian infrastructure.
“We will continue working with our brothers and our international and regional partners to keep our region stable and secure,” he said.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which much of the Gulf's oil and LNG exports pass, remains a major focus of international diplomacy amid continuing disruption to maritime traffic and energy flows during the conflict between Iran and the US.
Tehran has threatened to target vessels using routes other than those designated by Iranian authorities, or attempting to cross the waterway without permission.
Qatar's role in global energy
Qatar accounts for a major chunk of liquefied natural gas (LNG) trade, the emir said, warning that any disruption affecting the country quickly reverberates across international markets and consumers.
“Qatar supplies around one-fifth of global LNG trade, and anything that affects it is quickly reflected in markets and consumers everywhere,” he told the council.
He said the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and direct damage to some energy facilities in Ras Laffan Industrial City had disrupted a significant portion of Qatar's exports, though the economic impact had been concentrated mainly in the energy sector.
QatarEnergy halted LNG production in early March after drone attacks struck energy facilities in Mesaieed and Ras Laffan, the world's largest LNG export hub. Qatar's Defence Ministry said two drones originating from Iran targeted the facilities.
Sheikh Tamim said work on expanding Qatar's North Field gas development was continuing as planned to increase the country's LNG production capacity. He added that the Golden Pass LNG project in the US had made significant progress, while QatarEnergy continued to expand its investments and international partnerships.
Defence without escalation
The emir said Qatar had shouldered three responsibilities during the crisis: protecting its sovereignty, fulfilling its role in global energy and economic security, and keeping diplomatic channels open.
He said Qatar's strategy rested on four elements: defending the country firmly without being drawn into war; maintaining public services, supply chains and economic activity; contributing to efforts to secure a ceasefire and reopen waterways; and encouraging negotiations to seek peaceful solutions.
Qatar had been attacked by Iran in a violation of its sovereignty and international law, he said, adding that Qatari armed forces and security agencies had carried out their duty to defend the country.
Stressing that dialogue did not mean compromising on national defence, he said Qatar's right to defend its sovereignty "does not conflict with our keenness to prevent the war from expanding."
Favouring dialogue
Sheikh Tamim said Qatar had consistently favoured resolving disputes through dialogue, negotiation and diplomacy, arguing that recent developments had again demonstrated the interconnected nature of regional and global security.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. Tehran responded with missile and drone attacks across the region and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, while Washington later imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports.
The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June on freedom of navigation in the strait, but implementation stalled over disagreements related to security in the waterway.
As cross-border aerial attacks have targeted civilian infrastructure and airports, the GCC has reinforced a collective security framework, saying the defence and stability of each member state are tied to the sovereignty of the wider bloc.

Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:47:22 UTC
18:47:22 KST

Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- Oxford physicists have recreated a bizarre quantum effect in which a particle responds to a magnetic field without ever traveling through it. Using a hybrid quantum computer, they demonstrated how introducing a simulated magnetic flux could completely halt a particle's movement through quantum interference. The experiment brings a decades-old prediction into a new setting where matter and quantum fields influence one another.
- Share:
A particle does not have to pass through a magnetic field to be influenced by it. That surprising feature of quantum physics has now been recreated by researchers at the University of Oxford, who used a hybrid quantum computer to demonstrate how an invisible magnetic influence can bring a simulated particle's movement to a complete stop.
The experiment reproduced a phenomenon known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, in which a charged particle traveling around a region containing magnetic flux experiences a measurable change in its quantum state, even though its path never takes it through the magnetic field itself.
The Oxford team achieved this using a quantum system that combines qubits, the basic units of quantum information, with quantum oscillators, which represent vibrating motion. Their findings, published in Nature Physics, demonstrate how this combination could help scientists investigate fundamental interactions between matter and fields that are increasingly difficult to simulate using conventional computers.
A Strange Quantum Effect Predicted in 1959
In everyday physics, a charged particle responds to the electric and magnetic fields it encounters. Quantum mechanics, however, reveals that particles can behave in ways that have no straightforward counterpart in our ordinary experience.
In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle could be affected by magnetic flux even if it traveled entirely outside the region containing the magnetic field. Rather than experiencing a conventional magnetic force along its path, the particle would undergo a change in its quantum phase.
Quantum phase describes an aspect of a particle's wave behavior that influences how different possible paths interfere with one another. Although the phase itself is not directly visible, differences in phase can produce measurable effects.
The prediction became known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect and was eventually verified in experiments involving real electrons. It remains one of the clearest demonstrations that the quantum world operates according to rules that go beyond the familiar laws of classical physics.
Researchers are now exploring how this phenomenon behaves in more complex theoretical systems known as lattice gauge theories.
These theories describe how matter interacts with fields associated with fundamental forces. They represent space as a grid, with matter located at individual points and fields associated with the connections between them. Such models are particularly important in particle physics and high-energy physics, where scientists study the basic particles and interactions that make up the universe.
The challenge is that the mathematics becomes extraordinarily demanding as these systems grow more complicated. Even powerful conventional computers can struggle to calculate how all the interacting components evolve.
Quantum computers offer a different approach. Instead of attempting to calculate every aspect of a quantum system using classical computing methods, scientists can construct another quantum system that follows the same underlying rules. They can then observe its behavior directly, an approach known as quantum simulation.
How Scientists Built the Quantum Experiment
The Oxford project began in 2022, when lead author Dr. Sebastian Saner, Dr. Oana Bazavan, and their colleagues started developing a way to simulate lattice gauge theories using a hybrid quantum system. They collaborated with Dr. Alejandro Bermudez of the Instituto de Física Teórica in Madrid.
Their experimental design relied on two different quantum components that performed separate functions.
The first consisted of qubits encoded in the internal states of trapped ions, which are electrically charged atoms held in place using electromagnetic fields. These qubits represented the gauge fields in the theoretical model.
The second component used quantum oscillators, created by the vibrations of those same trapped ions. These oscillators represented matter.
By combining the two, the researchers constructed a simple loop that served as a basic building block of a lattice gauge theory. Two oscillators represented matter at two different locations, while two qubits represented the fields connecting those locations.
Although the arrangement was small, it was sufficient to reproduce an important interaction between matter and magnetic flux.
Quantum Entanglement Creates a Surprising Solution
The researchers next placed the two qubits into an entangled quantum state. Entanglement is a phenomenon in which quantum systems become linked in ways that cannot be fully explained by classical physics.
Within the team's simulated lattice gauge theory, this entangled state represented magnetic flux passing through the center of the loop.
Initially, the researchers had planned to introduce the magnetic flux as a fixed background condition. However, creating the necessary interaction would have required capabilities that their quantum hardware did not possess.
Encoding the flux directly into the qubits provided a practical alternative. More importantly, it allowed the magnetic flux to become part of the evolving quantum system rather than remaining an unchanging external influence.
"For us, the exciting step was to encode the magnetic flux in a gauge field that was itself dynamical," says Dr. Saner. "Rather than having matter evolve in a fixed background, the matter and gauge field become part of the same quantum dynamics."
What began as a technical workaround ultimately enabled the researchers to explore a more interesting version of the phenomenon, one in which matter and the field could participate together in the quantum dynamics.
A Quantum Effect That Stops Particle Motion
With their simulated loop in place, the scientists examined how a matter particle moved between locations through a process known as quantum tunneling.
Quantum tunneling allows particles to move between states in ways that would not be possible under ordinary classical rules.
When the researchers ran their simulation without magnetic flux, the particle could tunnel freely around the loop.
Introducing the simulated flux produced a strikingly different result.
The particle had two possible paths around the loop, but the magnetic flux changed their relative quantum phases. As a result, the two paths interfered destructively, meaning their quantum contributions canceled each other out.
This interference completely suppressed the tunneling, leaving the simulated particle frozen in its original state.
The outcome demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect within a lattice gauge theory containing a dynamical field. Rather than simply reproducing the familiar behavior of a particle moving around a fixed magnetic influence, the experiment showed how the phenomenon can emerge when matter and the field are both represented by interacting quantum components.
A New Tool for Exploring Fundamental Physics
The Oxford findings were published alongside a related study by researchers at the University of Maryland, led by Professor Norbert Linke.
The Maryland team also used a hybrid quantum system, but their experiment focused on simulating the Yukawa potential, a mathematical description of an interaction relevant to nuclear and particle physics.
Although the two research groups developed their methods independently, they later coordinated the submission of their studies to Nature Physics.
Together, the experiments demonstrate how hybrid quantum computers could become valuable tools for investigating fundamental interactions that are difficult to reproduce using classical simulations.
By combining different types of quantum components, researchers can build systems in which matter and fields are represented in ways that more closely reflect the physics they want to study.
The Oxford experiment provides an example of that potential. A phenomenon first predicted in 1959 and later observed with electrons has now been recreated in a quantum simulator where the field itself participates in the dynamics, offering scientists another way to explore the unusual rules governing the quantum world.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Oxford. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal References:
- S. Saner, O. Băzăvan, D. J. Webb, G. Araneda, C. J. Ballance, R. Srinivas, D. M. Lucas, A. Bermúdez. Aharonov–Bohm interference in a $${\\pmb{\\mathbb{Z}}}_{\\bf{2}}$$ lattice gauge theory on a hybrid qubit–oscillator quantum computer. Nature Physics, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03400-6
- Anton T. Than, Saurabh V. Kadam, Vinay Vikramaditya, Nhung H. Nguyen, Xingxin Liu, Zohreh Davoudi, Alaina M. Green, Norbert M. Linke. Quantum field theory dynamics on a spin–phonon quantum computer. Nature Physics, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03402-4

Israeli forces raid Palestinian NGOs in occupied West Bank
Snipers have been deployed outside entrances to the Palestine Medical Complex, Wafa reported.
Israeli forces have raided the offices of two Palestinian nongovernmental organisations (NGOs) and the courtyard of the Palestine Medical Complex in the occupied West Bank.
Israeli forces searched the Union of Palestinian Women’s Committees and the Addameer Prisoner Support and Human Rights Association in the city of Ramallah on Tuesday.
Israeli snipers were also deployed around the entrances to the Palestine Medical Complex in Ramallah, the official Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
The hospital is the largest government medical facility in the West Bank.
Reporting from Ramallah, Al Jazeera’s Nida Ibrahim said Israeli forces were confiscating equipment belonging to Addameer, an NGO that focuses on prisoner rights.
“Israeli forces have been raiding one of the compounds that belongs to Addameer. The NGO has been closed before by the Israeli forces. It has been deemed by the Israeli army and establishment as a terrorist organisation,” Ibrahim said.
“This is a daylight raid that is happening in the centre of Ramallah, causing a lot of panic. Palestinians [currently] have children at school. Others have [relatives] at work. People are worried because they know Israeli forces can open fire on them. Earlier, that happened: Israeli forces fired stun grenades at journalists covering this raid.”
Al Jazeera Arabic also reported that a journalist was injured after Israeli forces fired tear gas during the attacks.
The Palestinian Health Ministry reported that a child was injured by Israeli live ammunition and several others had suffered from suffocation due to the ongoing raids in Ramallah and Al-Bireh.
The raid on the NGOs is the latest act in an Israeli campaign of aggression against Palestinian civil socirty organisations.
In 2021, Israel designated six Palestinian organisations, including Addameer and the Union of Palestinian Women’s Committees, as “terrorist” organisations.
At the time, the defence ministry claimed that the organisations used activism as a cover but “in practice belong and constitute an arm of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, the main activity of which is the ‘liberation of Palestine’ and destruction of Israel.”
Founded in 1991, Addameer works to support Palestinian prisoners held in Israeli and Palestinian prisons, offering free legal aid and advocating their rights at the national and international level, according to its mission statement.
The Union of Palestinian Women’s Committees was founded in 1980 to empower Palestinian women on all levels and to “contribute to the Palestinian national struggle against the Israeli military’s illegal occupation of the Palestinian territories”, according to its Facebook page.

Veilig Thuis asks for €70m as domestic abuse reports mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:46:53 UTC

Veilig Thuis asks for €70m as domestic abuse reports mount
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
People who report suspected child abuse or domestic violence are waiting an average of 2 months for national domestic violence network Veilig Thuis to act, and the agency itself now says it can no longer guarantee it will pick up every sign of danger in time.
The network of organisations told broadcaster NOS on Tuesday that it needs €70 million from the cabinet over the coming years to take on extra staff and push through reforms.
By law, Veilig Thuis must carry out a safety assessment within 5 working days of receiving a report. Roughly half of reports have missed that deadline in recent years, and some families wait more than 6 months.
“Normally the waiting list gets a little shorter over the summer, but that hasn’t happened this time,” Ida Ouweneel, a board member of the national network, told NOS. Reports usually rise in the autumn, she said. “We can’t get through them. It can’t go on like this.”
All incoming reports are screened, she said, and cases of acute danger skip the waiting list and are dealt with immediately.
Growing backlog
Reports to Veilig Thuis rose 5% to 136,000 last year, according to national statistics office CBS. The agency says it welcomes the greater awareness, but that cases are also becoming more complex.
“Every day when I start up my computer, I see the number of reports getting bigger,” said Colinda Guiljam, who works for Veilig Thuis in Zeeland. “At the start of this year there were just over 30 reports on the waiting list in Zeeland. Now there are almost 400.”
Ouweneel said the backlog is driven by shortages and waiting lists across youth care, which leave vulnerable children without help and lead to more reports. “Our waiting list is a consequence of youth care grinding to a halt,” she said.
Budget debate
The health and youth care inspectorate IGJ has warned about waiting times for years. Criticism grew in May when it emerged that a 6-year-old girl in Stadskanaal had been severely abused despite several reports to the agency, which has said it acted on them immediately.
Mirjam Sterk, the centrist Christian Democrat (CDA) minister responsible for youth care, told NOS she will meet local council executives, local authorities association VNG and Veilig Thuis soon to discuss what is needed. She did not say whether extra money would be made available.
MPs will debate the health budget, which covers Veilig Thuis, on Wednesday and Thursday.
If you have experienced or are experiencing domestic or sexual violence, Veilig Thuis (Safe at Home) offers confidential advice 24 hours a day on 0800 2000 or at veiligthuis.nl. In an emergency, call 112.

The United Nations Human Rights Office in the Occupied Palestinian Territory has verified the deaths of 1,076 Palestinians in the Gaza Strip between October 2025 and the end of July 2026, warning that continued Israeli attacks during the ceasefire period raise serious concerns about possible war crimes.
In a report released on Monday, the office said Palestinian medical sources had recorded more than 1,400 deaths since the ceasefire was announced on 10th October 2025.
Of the 1,076 deaths verified by the UN office, 268 were children and 126 were women, together accounting for approximately 37 percent of the total.
The report also noted that more than 20,000 children have been killed in Gaza since 7th October 2023. It indicated that the proportion of civilian deaths may be higher than the available figures suggest, as the breakdown does not account for civilian men among those killed.
Ajith Sunghay, head of the UN Human Rights Office in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, described the continuation of violations during a period intended to be a ceasefire as appalling.
He warned that Palestinians were facing attacks within increasingly restricted areas, amid the continued deployment of Israeli forces and difficulties accessing essential supplies and services.
According to the report, Israeli forces controlled approximately 53 percent of Gaza’s territory when the ceasefire was announced, with plans to expand their deployment to approximately 70 percent.
UN monitoring also found that the boundaries of the so-called Yellow Line, marking areas of Israeli military deployment, were neither fixed nor clearly defined. The report documented continued Israeli military incursions and advances into residential areas.
Between October 2025 and July 2026, the office verified the deaths of 331 Palestinians near the Yellow Line, including 66 children and 27 women.
The UN office stressed that deliberately targeting civilians who are not directly participating in hostilities may constitute a war crime, regardless of their location.

EU ends anti-corruption funding curbs on Hungary, freeing €4.2bn

Unknown Publisher

The Council of the EU has ended the 2022 conditionality mechanism imposed on Hungary over corruption risks, releasing €4.2 billion and restoring access to Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe after Péter Magyar’s new government adopted anti-corruption reforms.
The Council of the EU has brought an end to the conditionality mechanism imposed on Hungary to address corruption risks in the country.
The decision unfreezes €4.2 billion in funding and allows Hungary to rejoin the Erasmus+ student exchange programme and the Horizon Europe research initiative.
The EU introduced the conditionality mechanism in 2022 under the government of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, making access to EU funds dependent on respect for the rule of law. The move also led to the suspension of a substantial amount of EU funding to Hungary.
Following the landslide election victory of the centre-right Tisza Party, led by Péter Magyar, the new government adopted a series of anti-corruption and transparency measures to unblock the funds.
Magyar agreed with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on the release of a total of €16.4 billion in exchange for reforms and investment plans. The money had been frozen over rule-of-law and corruption concerns under Orbán.
“A new chapter starts today. For Hungary and for Europe,” von der Leyen posted on social media.
In addition to the €4.2 billion released now, Hungary is applying for €10 billion from the EU’s post-pandemic recovery funds, and €2.2 billion is linked to improvements in academic freedom.
At the end of August, Hungary said it had fulfilled all the conditions required to access the funds. The European Commission is currently assessing whether the requirements have been met.
If the evaluation is positive, Budapest could gain access to the money by the end of the year, following approval in the autumn.

The Tel Aviv District Planning and Building Committee approved plans for a permanent United Arab Emirates embassy in Herzliya Pituah on Tuesday, six years after the signing of the Abraham Accords and the establishment of diplomatic relations between Israel and the UAE.
The approved plan allows for the construction of a building of up to 15 stories, housing the embassy's offices as well as residences for the ambassador and diplomatic staff.
The approval clears the way for progress on the UAE diplomatic mission's permanent headquarters in Israel, at a time when regional tensions are affecting relations between the two countries.
Herzliya planned as location for permanent embassy for months, mayor previously confirmed to 'Post'
In October, The Jerusalem Post reported that the permanent embassy would be built in Herzliya, after receiving exclusive confirmation from the city's mayor.
"We welcome the fact that the building of the Embassy of the United Arab Emirates in Israel will be constructed in Herzliya," Mayor Yariv Fisher told the Post at the time.
Herzliya has long-term plans to strengthen its ties with the countries of the Abraham Accords, "as well as with other nations that we all hope will join these agreements in the near future, in areas such as education, transportation, technology, tourism, and environmental quality: particularly initiatives that will strengthen understanding and the importance of coexistence and peace in the Middle East,” Fisher added in October.
"The process of locating the land was complex and included negotiations with various parties," the Israel Land Authority told the Post in October.
The land authority noted at the time that the request to search for a permanent location came from the Prime Minister's Office.

====================================================================================================

Stellantis, Filosa: "Too much capacity in Europe", strikes deals to avoid closures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:44:17 UTC
18:44:17 KST

Chief executive Antonio Filosa says sharing factory capacity could help keep plants open, as Stellantis invests in new platforms and European batteries.
Stellantis wants to use partnerships with Chinese carmakers to keep its European plants open as it tackles excess production capacity, chief executive Antonio Filosa said in Paris.
Speaking at the Paris Automotive Summit, held alongside the Paris Motor Show, Filosa outlined plans to share factory capacity with partners including Leapmotor and Dongfeng.
"We have excess production capacity, especially in Europe, but we do not want to shut plants," he said.
The aim is to make better use of existing factories while matching production to demand, without introducing vehicles that compete directly with the group’s own brands.
Stellantis bets on partnerships with Chinese manufacturers
The collaboration with Leapmotor, Filosa explained, makes it possible to combine the Chinese company’s technology with Stellantis’s factories and access to markets. Production in Europe could help serve local customers and expand the range of affordable electric vehicles.
Stellantis is pursuing similar partnerships with other Chinese companies and partners in markets such as India. It aims to combine their technology with its manufacturing experience, sales network and knowledge of customers to develop new models faster and make better use of its plants.
More battery gigafactories in Europe
The shift to electric vehicles will also require further investment in battery production. Stellantis already has European gigafactories developed with two partners, but Filosa said more would be needed to support demand and meet “Made in Europe” requirements.
He stressed that carmakers need enough time to make these investments, with European battery production a key part of efforts to make the industry more competitive.
STLA One platform to launch with Peugeot
Stellantis is preparing to launch its new global STLA One platform, which will initially be used by Peugeot in France before being rolled out to the group’s other brands in Europe and North America.
The project is part of the FaSTLAne 2030 plan, which sets out €60 billion in investment. Of that, 40% will go towards platforms, powertrains and technologies shared across brands and markets.
Stellantis also plans to develop shared powertrains for use in several regions. The aim is to avoid duplicate spending and reduce costs by producing at scale. The remaining 60% of investment will go towards individual brands and products.
Filosa urges swift agreement on emissions rules
Filosa also called for a swift agreement on changes to European CO2 emissions rules and measures to support production in Europe. He said the industry agreed on most objectives but needed to resolve the remaining differences.
"We all agree on 90 per cent of the issues," he said, stressing the need to finalise the rules quickly.
The talks also involve the diplomatic initiatives of France and Germany and meetings with manufacturers and suppliers promoted by French President Emmanuel Macron.
Ahead of the Paris Motor Show, Stellantis unveiled six of the nine concept cars planned for the event at a preview called The Night Before.
The models from Alfa Romeo, Citroën, DS Automobiles, Fiat, Opel and Peugeot offer a glimpse of the group’s FaSTLAne 2030 strategic plan, presented in May by Filosa, to accelerate model development and strengthen the group’s competitiveness.

US, Europe drafting four-point plan to settle Ukraine conflict — newspaper
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:44:12 UTC
18:44:12 KST

WASHINGTON, October 13. /TASS/. The United States and Europe are working on a four-point proposal to settle the Ukraine conflict, The Washington Post columnist David Ignatius reported, citing sources.
According to the sources, Washington and Brussels are moving toward a joint peace proposal that would deliver financial and security benefits to both Ukraine and Russia as a baseline for a territorial settlement. A US official said the package would have four basic components, including a proposal for Russia to reach an economic and security deal with Europe that would restore stability to the region.
"Ukraine’s reconstruction would be the first pillar," Ignatius said, adding that the negotiators had asked Kiev for detailed cost estimates.
Security guarantees for both Ukraine and Russia would constitute the second essential component. However, it remains unclear what security arrangements are expected to be offered to Moscow.
"A third pillar would be economic integration of Russia, Ukraine and Europe through an energy deal. One aspect might be a pipeline carrying Russian oil and gas to Europe, with Ukraine and Russia splitting the profits," the columnist noted. The proposal would also provide Russia with long-term access to the European energy market and specify when economic sanctions would be removed.
The fourth and final piece of the deal would be a ceasefire along the existing front line.
According to The Washington Post, "the diplomatic push" for the plan came at a recent meeting in Florida involving US, European and Ukrainian negotiators.

Red Cross fears for civilians in Riyadh and Yemen attacks
The President of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), Mirjana Spoljaric, has condemned the impact on civilians of the recent attacks in Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
On Tuesday in Geneva, she called on the parties to the conflict to protect the civilian population.
Attacks by Yemeni Houthi rebels on Riyadh airport on Saturday left 13 people dead. According to Spoljaric, they highlight the “devastating” toll on civilians in the region.
In Yemen too, the number of people killed, those injured and the damage to infrastructure are rising at “an alarming rate”, added the ICRC president. She reiterates that the parties to the conflict must not target civilians or civilian sites, in accordance with international humanitarian law.
An escalation of the fighting would be “disastrous” for tens of millions of people, Spoljaric added. In Yemen, more than 210,000 people have been displaced by the violence in the space of a month.

WP learned about a &quot;peace plan&quot; for Ukraine with four pillars - what it entails
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:38:26 EEST
18:38:26 KST

WP learned about a "peace plan" for Ukraine with four pillars - what it entails
Kyiv • UNN
The plan provides for the reconstruction of Ukraine, security guarantees, energy integration, and addresses the territorial issue.
As part of efforts to end Russia's war against Ukraine, a U.S.-European settlement is taking shape. The plan has four main pillars. David Ignatius, a Washington Post columnist covering foreign affairs, writes about this, reports UNN.
Details
According to the publication, U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff asked the Ukrainians at Friday's meeting to stop attacks on oil refineries and warned that Trump would make a deal on diesel fuel, according to a U.S. official.
According to the publication, a U.S. official said, "if Zelenskyy agrees to stop attacks on oil refineries," then "we get back to business and go to Moscow." "But what will Ukraine receive — and what will it give up — as part of the U.S.-European settlement that is taking shape?" the author of the publication writes, listing the points below.
"The package will have four main components, according to a U.S. official. The message to Putin will be this: do not simply stop the war with Ukraine. Conclude an economic and security agreement with Europe that will restore stability in the region after the upward spiral of escalation," the article says.
First — reconstruction
As noted, "the reconstruction of Ukraine will be the first pillar." "The World Bank and investment firm BlackRock want to create a framework" to meet financial needs — "to rebuild the country's devastated regions, provide assistance to the families of killed and wounded soldiers, and restore the destroyed economy."
"The negotiators asked Kyiv to provide detailed cost estimates — and guarantees that the money will not be looted by postwar profiteers. So far, the Ukrainians have not provided the figures, but they are expected to do so over the next few days if the peace efforts do not fail," the publication says.
Second — security guarantees
According to the report, "security guarantees will be the second major component." "Ukraine will receive commitments from the United States and European countries that they will provide a military response if Russia attacks again, which, according to the U.S. official, is equivalent to Article 5 of NATO. The official said that Russia would also negotiate with Europe on agreements that would take its ‘security concerns’ into account, although it is unclear what this entails," the publication says.
Third — economic integration
"The third pillar will be the economic integration of Russia, Ukraine, and Europe through an energy agreement. One aspect could be a pipeline transporting Russian oil and gas to Europe, with Ukraine and Russia sharing the profits from it. Such a pipeline could sharply reduce European energy costs, the official said. In addition to providing Russia with ‘long-term access to the European energy market,’ the peace agreement would determine how and when existing economic sanctions would be lifted," the article states.
Fourth — the territorial issue
"The final part of the agreement will be the most unpleasant. Russia, which launched the war hoping to seize all of Ukraine, will agree to a ceasefire along the existing front line, or the ‘line of control,’ as the negotiators call it. For Ukraine, this would mean allowing Russia to control the territory it occupies, including the fiercely disputed territory known as Donbas. One obstacle is that the line of control is unclear, given the small shifts on the front almost every day," the publication says.
What Europe thinks
According to the report, "although European leaders were angered by Trump's diesel deal, they appear determined to continue the diplomatic process led by Kushner and Witkoff." "This is the moment to de-escalate the situation and get back to work," a European diplomat explained.
"The rationale for a settlement now is that this war has turned into a horrific battlefield. (...) It is a war of attrition with enormous losses. In winter, it will turn into an economic battle, as each side tries to undermine the other's economy and intensify the suffering of civilians," the author of the article notes.
And he points out: "Trump has rightly been trying to end the war since taking office. But he still seems unable to understand that putin, the aggressor, wants victory, not a ceasefire." "putin does not appear to be serious about peace," said the European diplomat, citing intelligence reports.
"With his sanctions-busting deal on diesel fuel, Trump is tragically making it easier for putin to continue this horrific war," the publication concludes.

NEW DELHI: Union home minister Amit Shah on Tuesday called for stronger regional cooperation among BIMSTEC countries to combat terrorism, disrupt terrorist financing and organised crime, and prevent terrorist networks from finding safe havens in the region.Addressing the first Home Ministers’ Meeting of BIMSTEC countries in Delhi, Shah said India follows a policy of “zero tolerance” towards terrorism and stressed the need for collective action to strengthen regional security.
“Hosting the first BIMSTEC Home Ministers’ Meeting is a matter of great pride and fortune for India. BIMSTEC, in a way, has become an essential platform for regional integration, economic cooperation and collective security. With the spirit of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, India is going ahead today," Shah said.We have always been committed to peace, coexistence and human welfare. We continue to be committed to these even today. India has never believed in attacking any country or establishing dominance over them. India has always believed in upholding the sovereignty and territorial integrity of every country and peaceful resolution of differences,” he added.
Shah said the trust among BIMSTEC members was strengthened by the belief that the security arrangements of each country should contribute to the security of the others.He called for a collective resolve to ensure that terrorist networks could not find shelter, establish bases or training facilities, mobilise resources or carry out activities against other member countries.“India has always adopted a 'zero tolerance' policy against terrorism. The trust in our cooperation is strengthened by the sense that the security mechanism of every member country becomes helpful in the security of other member countries. Our mutual resolution should be to ensure that there is no scope or space for harbouring, recruiting, training, procuring resources, or carrying out activities against neighbouring nations in any part of the region,” he said.The home minister also urged member countries to cooperate on mutual legal assistance and extradition in accordance with their national laws and applicable agreements. The illegal proceeds from drugs provide financial strength to organised crime and are also used for terrorist financing. The diversion of precursor chemicals and transactions through the dark web make this challenge even more complex,” he said.

US and Europe prepare peace plan to improve post-war state of Ukraine and Russia – The Washington Post
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:35:00 EEST
18:35:00 KST

US and Europe prepare peace plan to improve post-war state of Ukraine and Russia – The Washington Post
The United States and Europe are discussing a joint four-point peace plan that foresees both territorial concessions from Ukraine and Russia, as well as security guarantees and agreements aimed at improving the economic condition of both countries.
Source: The Washington Post, citing comments from a US official familiar with the negotiations
Quote from The Washington Post: "The package would have four basic components, according to the US official. The message to Putin would be: Don't just end the war with Ukraine. Make an economic and security deal with Europe that would restore stability to the region after an upward spiral of escalation."
Details: The Washington Post explains that the peace plan currently being developed by the US and European nations relies on the principle of "whenever you run into a problem you can't solve, make it bigger".
Specifically, driving diplomatic efforts, US Presidential Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner organised a meeting in Miami on 9 October with representatives from Ukraine, the United States, the United Kingdom, France and Germany. During the session, they asked the Ukrainians to cease strikes against Russian oil refineries and briefed them on Trump's deal with Russia regarding diesel fuel.
Quote from the official: "We need to make the problem and the solution bigger to help both sides see what the postwar situation would be – and then make concessions."
Details: As part of the US-European peace settlement, the US is seeking to formulate a package of measures that accounts for the post-war needs of both Ukraine and Russia to improve their standing following a territorial compromise that will be unpalatable to both sides.
According to the official, the package will consist of four core components. First will be the reconstruction of Ukraine. The World Bank and investment firm BlackRock aim to establish a financial mechanism to rebuild the country's damaged regions, provide assistance to families of fallen and wounded soldiers and restore the shattered economy. Negotiators have already requested detailed cost estimates from Kyiv alongside guarantees that funds will not be embezzled post-war. The Ukrainian side has not yet provided exact figures but is expected to do so in the coming days.
The second component of the peace settlement will be security guarantees. Ukraine would receive commitments from the US and European nations regarding military intervention in the event of a new Russian attack – which the US official stated is equivalent to Article 5 of the NATO Treaty. They noted that Russia would also enter into agreements with Europe addressing Moscow's security concerns, though specific terms remain unclear.
The third direction will be the economic integration of Russia, Ukraine and Europe through an energy agreement. One proposed aspect could be a pipeline transporting Russian oil and gas to Europe, with revenues split between Russia and Ukraine. Such a pipeline could sharply reduce European energy costs, as the official noted.
Aside from granting Russia long-term access to the European energy market, the peace agreement would also define how and when current economic sanctions against Russia will be lifted.
The fourth point of the plan will prove most unacceptable to both sides, as the official claims. It envisions that Russia, which launched the war hoping to conquer all of Ukraine, would agree to a ceasefire along the current front line. For Ukraine, it would mean allowing Russia to control occupied territory.
However, a major hurdle for such an agreement is that the "line of control", as negotiators call it, remains fluid due to small daily shifts along the front line.
Background: According to media reports, Witkoff and Kushner informed the Ukrainian delegation at negotiations in Miami that the agreement permitting the export of Russian diesel fuel is part of an effort to bring Russia back to the negotiating table.

Transport Board: Don't wait to switch to winter tires
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:32:00 UTC
18:32:00 KST

Transport Board: Don't wait to switch to winter tires
The Transport Board (Transpordiamet) is advising drivers to switch to winter tires as soon as possible. Temperatures are forecast to drop below zero at times this week.
Winter tires become mandatory on December 1, but can be used at any time. The studded variety — banned in the warmer months — can be used from this Thursday, October 15.
The arrival of colder conditions this week, combined with the wet, may make roads more slippery. Drivers starting early or traveling late should be especially careful. Surface temperatures can be low even when the air is above zero, the board noted.
"When choosing and changing tires, it's worth thinking about how much, when and on which roads you usually drive. If you cover long distances or often drive early and late, don't wait until the mandatory deadline," said Jürgo Vahtra, head of the Transport Board's technical department.
"Driving on summer tires on a slippery road endangers both your own life and those of other road users. At low temperatures, the rubber compound in summer tires changes and grip can decrease. It's wise to switch before road conditions force it," he added.
Winter tires without studs must carry the three-peak mountain snowflake symbol, or 3PMSF marking. That shows the tire meets standardized snow grip requirements. M+S alone does not mean the tire has passed the same standardized test.
For friction tires, the Transport Board recommends those with an ice grip marking in addition to 3PMSF. Those are designed for Nordic conditions and have been assessed for ice grip as well as snow grip. That is useful in Estonian winters, where temperatures fluctuate around zero and melting and freezing create icy stretches. Check the markings on the sidewall before buying or fitting.
Used tires should be assessed for tread depth and overall condition. Winter tire tread must be deeper than three millimeters. There should be no cracks, bulges or visible damage, and wear should be even. If tires have been in use for several seasons, check their age as well. Performance can degrade over time even when there is tread left.
Autumn is also the time to check the rest of the car's readiness for dark and wet conditions. The windshield, wipers and lights must ensure good visibility. Lights must be correctly adjusted. A clean windscreen matters in low sun, which can significantly reduce visibility through a dirty or fogged window.
"In winter conditions, choose your speed according to visibility and road state, and keep a sufficient following distance. In the dark and wet, avoid sudden maneuvers and bear in mind that braking distance can increase considerably on slippery roads," Vahtra said.
Studded tires can be used from October 15 to March 31 of the following year. If wintry conditions linger into April, an extension can be granted to the end of that month too. Since studded tires damage road surfaces once the snow and ice has melted, their use is forbidden for the rest of the year. Non-studded winter tires can be left on the vehicle, but it is wise to change them for summer tires in any case, to preserve them for the following winter.
The Transport Board urges drivers to check their tires in good time and book a tire change where needed. The changing season at the beginning and end of winter is a peak time for tire changing (often advertised as "Rehvitöö," "Rehvivahetus" or "Rehviremont") businesses, so longer wait times should be factored in too.
Current road conditions across Estonia can be checked via the TarkTee portal.

Bulgaria’s capital Sofia leads a new ranking of the 10 best city breaks in Europe, which also includes Lisbon in Portugal, Bristol in the UK, Leuven in Belgium and Verona and Italy.
Sofia has been named as Europe’s best city break destination for 2027 in a new ranking.
According to the report by European Best Destinations, which “brings together 10 cities with very different personalities”, Bulgaria’s capital took the top spot thanks to “ancient history, contemporary culture and the mountains”, which create an “especially rewarding combination”.
Recently voted the world's happiest travel destination, Lisbon was ranked second on the 2027 city break list with Copenhagen, Cannes and Basel making up the top five. Completing the top 10 were Bristol, Leuven, Milan, Calpe and Verona.
The ranking is based on a 33-day vote involving 11,614 subscribers to the European Best Destinations newsletter. Each respondent could cast up to three votes from a shortlist of 64 European destinations selected by independent travel journalists. The top 10 are listed in order of votes received.
“A great city break gives you plenty to do and enough time to enjoy it,” said European Best Destinations. “There is room here for a romantic escape, a weekend with friends, a few days by the sea or a special occasion worth celebrating in style.”
Best city breaks in Europe 2027
- 1. Sofia, Bulgaria
- 2. Lisbon, Portugal
- 3. Copenhagen, Denmark
- 4. Cannes, France
- 5. Basel, Switzerland
- 6. Bristol, UK
- 7. Leuven, Belgium
- 8. Milan, Italy
- 9. Calpe, Spain
- 10. Verona, Italy
The top three cities in focus
Sofia was praised for offering city breakers a “variety of experiences within a relatively compact area”, said European Best Destinations. Aside from “cultural discoveries, good food and evenings out”, visitors are also able to enjoy forest trails and mountain views during the same trip.
Once known as Serdica, Bulgaria’s capital was among the most important cities in the Byzantine Empire, Dianne Apen-Sadler said in her Sofia city guide for Euronews Travel. This is a city where old meets new “quite literally”. A city to enjoy from “morning coffee to the last view of the river”, Lisbon suits travellers who “like a little structure and plenty of freedom”, the report said. If you are visiting Portugal’s capital, choose a neighbourhood to explore, make a dinner reservation and “let the hills decide the route”. One top tip for visitors? Save time for art, time for the historic centre, and time to linger over a meal, European Best Destinations advises.
Copenhagen, ranked third on the 2027 city break hotlist, “makes a strong case for spending a weekend enjoying the everyday details of a city”. The Danish capital is an “appealing choice” for friends and couples who enjoy design, neighbourhood restaurants and exploring by bike. “A few carefully chosen stops can shape the day, with plenty of space between them for another coffee or a waterside pause,” the report said.

Inside India’s protests over voter roll revisions and alleged electoral bias
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:31:36 UTC
18:31:36 KST

Tens of thousands of protesters have taken to the streets of New Delhi to demand the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner over a controversial revision of voter lists.
The demonstrations have drawn opposition parties, student groups and youth activists into a confrontation with authorities.
The protests centre on allegations that the Election Commission’s revision of electoral rolls has unfairly removed voters, potentially benefiting Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in some of the recent state elections and raising concerns that it could do so in future polls.
The commission denies wrongdoing, saying the exercise aims to remove duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries.
More than 130 million names have been removed from voter lists since the revision began last year, according to media reports. Critics say the deletions disproportionately affect women, Muslims and other minorities, while election authorities maintain that people whose names were wrongly removed can re-enrol.
Why are protesters demanding the election chief’s resignation?
Demonstrators want Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to step down, arguing that the scale of the deletions threatens voters’ access to the ballot and could influence future elections.
The controversy intensified after The Indian Express reported last month that Kumar’s two deputies had raised concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems.
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi of the Congress party led a protest march on Monday and later challenged the revision exercise in a petition filed with the Supreme Court. The BJP has accused the opposition of undermining legitimate electoral processes by questioning the work of constitutional institutions.
The protests have been driven in part by the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which has mobilised supporters through social media. The movement has pledged to continue demonstrations until Kumar resigns.
Intense police crackdown deepened the rift
Authorities have deployed thousands of security personnel across central Delhi, erected metal barricades and closed major metro stations.
Police also removed Jantar Mantar, a long-established protest site, from the list of designated demonstration venues, announcing three alternatives.
On Tuesday, CJP said several of its leaders, including Ashutosh Ranka, Saurav Das and Ajinkya Shinde, were detained after activists climbed barricades to enter the site and demanded the right to protest there.
The latest confrontation follows a weekend crackdown in which thousands of protesters were detained, according to local media reports. Most were subsequently released, including several CJP leaders.
The movement has previously organised demonstrations over issues including government school infrastructure, jobs and examination paper leaks. A weeks-long sit-in earlier this year contributed to the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over an examination scandal.
Journalists report rough treatment and detentions
The police response has also drawn criticism from journalists and press freedom organisations, who say officers detained reporters covering the demonstrations, seized their phones and used excessive force.
Nearly three dozen journalists from outlets including The Indian Express, Scroll and Newslaundry were detained for hours during the weekend protests, according to Reuters interviews with journalists.
Some said they were detained despite being clearly identifiable as members of the press.
Newslaundry reporter Anmol Pritam told Reuters that an officer grabbed his microphone, dragged him, seized his phone and detained him alongside his producer while they were interviewing people held on a bus. He said he was detained for nearly three hours on October 10.
Delhi Police did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the reported treatment of journalists. Police have previously said some protesters posed as journalists and interfered with officers’ work.
The detentions continued despite India’s Supreme Court ruling in favour of a request seeking to ensure journalists and lawyers could perform their duties during the protests, according to journalists who said some arrests took place after the order.
The Press Club of India called the police action an attack on press freedom, while Reporters Without Borders said detentions, surveillance and restrictions on reporting risked suppressing coverage of the demonstrations.
A wider test of public dissent
Modi described India as the “mother of democracy” at a business conference on Tuesday, saying people in the country openly debate a wide range of issues. He did not directly address the demonstrations.
The government has rejected broader allegations that it is restricting democratic freedoms, while critics point to pressure on journalists, civil society groups and political opponents.
For protesters, the immediate demands remain the resignation of the election chief and a halt to the disputed revision.
The dispute also widens into a confrontation over the right to demonstrate, the treatment of journalists and public confidence in India’s electoral process.

Australia's winter crop forecast to fall in 2026/27
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:30:38 CST
18:30:38 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Australia's winter crop production is forecast to fall 7.9 percent from last season's harvest to 62.9 million tonnes in 2026/27, but remain above the five-year average, agricultural lender Rabobank said on Tuesday.
The forecast volume would be 2.6 percent above the five-year average, following last season's second-largest harvest on record, according to the agribusiness bank's latest Australian Winter Crop Forecast.
Rabobank said firmer grain prices, supported partly by geopolitical disruptions to global exports, were providing some support to growers, although high fertilizer, diesel, agrichemical and freight costs continued to squeeze grower margins.
Report lead author, RaboResearch senior grains and oilseeds analyst Vitor Pistoia, attributed the outlook to "sharply contrasting seasonal conditions" across Australia, with below-average rainfall expected to reduce output in the states of Queensland and New South Wales, while favorable moisture levels and strong yields support production increases in the states of South Australia and Victoria.
Wheat production is forecast to fall 13.3 percent year on year to 31 million tonnes, while barley output is expected to decline 1.2 percent to 16.5 million tonnes. In contrast, canola production is forecast to rise 5.3 percent to a record 8.1 million tonnes, the report said.
The state of South Australia's winter crop is estimated to reach a record 12.44 million tonnes, up 43.7 percent from last season, while Queensland's output is forecast to drop 47.6 percent to 2.03 million tonnes, primarily driven by well-below-average rainfall across much of the state's wheatbelt, according to the Rabobank forecast. ■

UK holiday demand may have peaked amid cost of living squeeze, says travel industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:30:20 UTC
18:30:20 KST

The UK’s cost of living squeeze means fewer people plan to ringfence money for holidays abroad next year, the travel industry has warned.
Despite war, wildfires and EES border checks, the numbers of Britons taking holidays climbed back to pre-pandemic levels this year – but rising costs may mean the numbers have peaked, according to an annual travel industry report on Tuesday.
Numbers taking holidays at home and abroad continued to rise, although late bookings and shorter city breaks have been an increasing feature of holidays through 2026.
Confidence in travel dropped slightly year on year but rebounded as fears over jet fuel shortages and flight disruption faded since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran in February, according to research from the industry body Abta.
Overall, 88% of Brits took a holiday this year, matching the 2019 pre-pandemic peak, with a new high of 74% in the UK and 62% abroad.
However, Abta’s report found that almost one in three people were planning to spend less on travelling abroad next year, suggesting that the annual holiday is no longer sacrosanct. Fewer people now say they are willing to reduce spending on phones or other gadgets than the holiday abroad.
Abta said the holiday business remained resilient, despite a dip in its travel confidence index to +50 – this measures the net proportion of people who felt secure in going abroad, compared with those who were worried. But it said that score had rebounded since disruption from the Middle East conflict and fears about fuel availability and the EU’s entry/exit system (EES).
The Abta chief executive, Mark Tanzer, said it had been a tough year for the travel industry. But he added: “Demand has held up well despite a range of challenges this year, and that looks set to continue, as does the willingness to prioritise spending on travel over other discretionary items.”
Speaking at the annual Abta travel convention in Madeira, Tanzer added: “It’s been a stop-start year but the market did come back in the summer.
“We saw people switching their holiday plans and booking later, waiting and seeing – maybe hoping for better deals but also managing the uncertainty.”
He said the industry would continue to lobby ministers hard to reduce aviation taxes and increase help in the switch to sustainable aviation fuels, to help cut costs and support an industry that contributed £57bn to the UK economy.
Tanzer said the investment in tourism continued but he admitted: “The pressures of the last few months are not going to go away in the next 18 months.”
Spain increased its dominance of the British outbound market. The number who said they visited Spain was up four percentage points to 36%, while Portugal moved up to sixth in popularity for holidays.
Polling next year’s travel intentions, only 26% said they were planning to visit Spain, with places such as Japan and Norway cited in the top 10. However, previous surveys have underlined that, despite dreams of somewhere more exotic, Britons head resolutely back to Spain.
Travel to the convention was provided by Abta

SOFIA, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Drones have attacked two merchant ships in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria, and at least one of them has sunk, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said in a statement on Tuesday.
At an extraordinary meeting with the country's security council, Radev said one ship was attacked around 1:30 a.m. local time (2230 GMT Monday), about 18 nautical miles east of the town of Byala.
Bulgarian authorities rescued all 15 crew members aboard the vessel, including seven Ukrainian nationals and eight Azerbaijani nationals, Radev said.
The ship, named "Chelsea 3," was flying the Maltese flag, registered in Odesa, Ukraine, and Ukrainian-owned, according to Radev. The crew said three aerial drones struck the vessel.
The crew members were safely transported to the port of Varna, where five of them received medical care, he added.
Radev said authorities had also received information that another merchant ship had been hit about 17 nautical miles east of Krapets. The vessel sank, and one crew member was rescued. "We are still clarifying the situation," he said.
The incident marked the second drone attack on merchant ships near Bulgaria within a week. On Oct. 6, unidentified drones sank one merchant ship and set another on fire about 70 nautical miles east of Byala, within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
"Another attack on merchant ships in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters is absolutely unacceptable," Radev said.
Bulgaria's permanent representatives to NATO and the European Union have been notified, Radev said, adding that he was due to speak with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.
The prime minister also said Bulgaria was seeking support for an investigation into the attacks on the ships to establish precisely which country the drones that struck vessels near Bulgarian territorial waters had come from.
Radev added that Bulgaria would continue to seek support to strengthen its air and maritime surveillance and enhance its response capabilities. ■

AI cuts wildlife monitoring workload for Indigenous rangers in Australia: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:30:12 CST
18:30:12 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Artificial intelligence (AI) has reduced image-processing workloads for Indigenous rangers in northern Australia by 81.4 percent, according to recent research.
Researchers explored the use of AI in Indigenous-led community-based wildlife monitoring in the Warddeken Indigenous Protected Area in West Arnhem, Northern Territory, according to a statement released Tuesday by Australia's Charles Darwin University (CDU).
The program uses camera traps to monitor animals of cultural and conservation concern and involves Traditional Owners and Indigenous rangers in land management.
Researchers from Warddeken Land Management, CDU and the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organization, Australia's national science agency, applied the AI animal-detection model MegaDetector to 1,572 hours of data collected by rangers.
The technology reduced the number of images requiring analysis from 925,088 to 172,290, cutting processing time from six months to two months.
The time saved allowed rangers to focus more on land management and species identification, while documenting languages and developing educational resources, the researchers said. ■

2024.

from Italy.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) responded Tuesday to Legislative Yuan Speaker Han Kuo-yu’s (韓國瑜) criticism during his National Day speech, defending the need to exercise what he called “countersignature power.”
In his speech Saturday, Han said the Cabinet’s refusal to countersign bills passed by the legislature represented a crisis in Taiwan’s democracy, per TVBS. He called on President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) to resolve tensions between the legislative and executive branches, warning that Taiwan’s democracy could be viewed by the rest of the world as a “dictatorship disguised as a democracy.”
Han’s remarks drew pushback from the government and DPP politicians. DPP Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) accused Han of deepening the conflict between the two branches of government and called on him to lead by example, per Liberty Times.
Responding to Han’s speech, Cho argued that his decision not to countersign bills passed by the legislature was a reactive but necessary step to uphold the nation’s constitutional order, per CNA. He said the Cabinet was willing to consider the legislature’s recommendations as long as the bills were constitutional and fiscally responsible.
Cho said the legislative and executive branches held different views on the separation of powers and constitutional order. He added that measures already taken, including reconsideration requests and interpretations by the Constitutional Court, had failed to “procure just results,” per UDN.
Cho’s remarks drew criticism from the opposition. KMT Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) argued that the separation of powers would become unworkable if the executive branch were given unilateral authority to veto legislative decisions, per Mirror Daily.
Hsu accused Cho of blocking legislation at Lai’s behest. TPP Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Hung Yu-hsiang (洪毓祥) said whether bills took effect depended on the DPP’s position, arguing that the party would refuse to countersign legislation passed by the legislature if it deemed the bills undesirable, per UDN.
Cho’s interpretation of “countersignature power” has continued to draw criticism. He previously argued that because the president has no constitutional authority to veto legislation, the premier should exercise “countersignature power” in support of the president.
Legal experts remain divided on the issue. Soochow University professor Hsu Yu-wei (許有為), a nominee for the Control Yuan put forward by Lai, argued that “countersignature power” has long been a tool available to the executive branch.
Meanwhile, Kuo Ming-sung (郭銘松), a reader at the University of Warwick School of Law, argued that the countersignature requirement had become an “ultra-executive veto” that could be used against the opposition-controlled legislature. Stanford University’s Hoover Institution Research Fellow Kharis Templeman said Cho’s move was politically understandable but remained “blatantly unconstitutional.”

Taiwan housing costs hit 20-month high

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s residential living costs rose to a 20-month high in September as higher utility bills, building management fees, and home repair costs outpaced slower rent increases.
The Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics on Tuesday reported that the consumer price index for housing rose 2.38% from a year earlier, the highest annual increase since January 2025. Water, electricity, and gas costs led the increase, rising 4.63%, followed by household management fees at 4.2% and residential maintenance costs at 3.77%.
Household goods prices also climbed 2.93% year over year in September, reversing declines recorded during much of 2025. Meanwhile, the rent index remained below 2% annual growth for the ninth consecutive month, suggesting that rental inflation has moderated even as other housing-related expenses continue to rise.
Tseng Ching-te, a project manager at Sinyi Realty, told UDN that the figures show rising residential costs extend beyond rent to include utilities, household goods, building management, and maintenance. Higher labor costs have contributed to rising management and repair expenses, while surging oil prices following the outbreak of conflict in the Middle East have also driven up prices for petroleum-based goods, Tseng said.
The overall housing index followed a U-shaped trajectory, with annual growth falling to a low in July 2025 before recovering in 2026. The index rose from 1.87% in January to 2.38% in September, indicating renewed pressure on household budgets.
Building management fees have risen as residential communities face higher costs for security guards, cleaning staff, and other services, UDN reported. Older buildings also require more spending on elevator upgrades and equipment maintenance, adding to residents’ burden.
Tseng said some residential communities have changed property management companies in response to rising costs but retained existing security guards under new uniforms to maintain service continuity. He added that adjusting to new contractors can temporarily disrupt service quality even as communities seek to control expenses.

Franco–German deal on cars and ‘Made in Europe’ is ‘hours or days’ away, says EU industry boss
Speaking at POLITICO’s Competitiveness Summit in Paris, Stéphane Séjourné said he hoped the agreement would help “break the deadlock, particularly in the European Parliament” on the IAA.
PARIS — A deal between France and Germany to strengthen protections in the Industrial Accelerator Act in exchange for a loosening of combustion engine rules should be finalized “in the next few hours or in the next few days,” the bloc’s industry chief Stéphane Séjourné said Tuesday.
Speaking at POLITICO’s Competitiveness Summit in Paris, Séjourné said he hoped the agreement would help “break the deadlock, particularly in the European Parliament” on the IAA.
Séjourné’s comments come a day after French President Emmanuel Macron said a grand bargain with Germany was “imminent.”
Advertisement
The French commissioner said he was open to more “flexibility” on the combustion engine ban and emission rules — so long as decarbonization targets are not fully abandoned — if that helps to unlock talks on the IAA.
“This agreement, in fact, is a European agreement, and that is why it is so important. It should make it possible to green-light the IAA,” Séjourné added.
POLITICO revealed the Franco–German bargain in July. Séjourné is hoping the agreement will ease tensions in the European Parliament, where a minority of lawmakers from the center-right European People’s Party — mostly from the German delegation — have sought to reject or substantially weaken the proposal.
The IAA dispute lies between supporters of an opt-in system — where trading partners would need to qualify before receiving preferential treatment on the European market — and backers of an opt-out system in which the EU would move to exclude partners that fail reciprocity or other conditions. Many of those who back the opt-out option are German EPP lawmakers.
Séjourné called the debate irrelevant, stressing that what matters most is reciprocity with countries the EU works with.
“European public funds should be used primarily for public procurement,” he said. “Our goal is to keep production running smoothly, so we can’t expand the scope of Made in Europe indefinitely if our goal is to manufacture in Europe.”

Javelin output nearly doubles as global demand rises
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:25:58 BST
18:25:58 KST

The Javelin Joint Venture has nearly doubled its annual All-Up-Round production capacity over the past two years, and has delivered the first of a new lightweight launcher to the United States Army, according to Lockheed Martin.
Lockheed Martin is increasing output on its existing manufacturing line and through the missile’s supply chain partners, and is putting money into accelerating the long-lead parts and equipment that higher production rates require.
Rich Liccion, vice president of the joint venture and programme director for Javelin at Lockheed Martin, said: “By scaling our Javelin production line to meet increasing global demand, we’re extending Javelin’s legacy of performance excellence for years to come. Our increased output ensures that warfighters worldwide continue to rely on an anti-tank missile system that has delivered unmatched precision for over 30 years.”
The venture was awarded the largest single-year Javelin production contract to date in May 2025, a follow-on under an indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity production contract first awarded in May 2023.
All test stations critical to the ramp are due to be built by the end of this year, verifying that the missile and its subcomponents meet environmental, performance and functional requirements. Sixteen further test stations that duplicate essential capabilities will then be upgraded, modernising legacy equipment and sustaining production capability over the longer term.
The Lightweight Command Launch Unit is the next-generation launcher for the system, built to work with all current, past and future Javelin variants. Raytheon has invested $22 million in modernising the factory that builds it, at Tucson in Arizona, to increase speed and expand capacity, and annual production there is being increased in collaboration with the US Army.
Jenna Hunt Frazier, president of the joint venture and Javelin programme director at Raytheon, said: “Delivering the LWCLU into soldiers’ hands underscores our commitment to accelerating meaningful capability upgrades. Our investment in modernisation and production capacity ensures the Army can field this advanced launcher more quickly, giving soldiers better awareness and greater lethality on today’s battlefield.”
The new unit offers twice the target detection and recognition range of the launcher it replaces while cutting size by thirty per cent and weight by twenty-five per cent, with improved optics and a day and night surveillance capability.
Javelin is built by the joint venture between Raytheon at Tucson and Lockheed Martin at Orlando in Florida, which has produced more than 55,000 missiles and more than 12,000 reusable command launch units to date.
