====================================================================================================

Air France says it will follow Israeli rule barring crew from some nations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:21:29 UTC
18:21:29 KST

Air France says it will follow Israeli rule barring crew from some nations
The reported restrictions could put airlines that comply with Israel at odds with the national laws under which they operate.
Air France has confirmed that it is complying with new Israeli restrictions limiting who can fly to and over Israel based on their nationality, a controversial policy that some experts say could expose the airline to discrimination lawsuits.
The new Israeli restrictions, reported by Israeli media and French investigative publication Mediapart, list 31 Muslim-majority countries, including Algeria, Tunisia, Iran, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Niger, whose nationals are no longer allowed to fly into Israel’s airspace.
“Like all airlines, Air France is required to comply with the entry regulations established by the authorities of the countries it serves, both for its customers and employees,” Air France told Al Jazeera in a statement.
According to Israel’s N12 broadcaster, the Ministry of Transport and Road Safety told foreign airlines on October 1 that pilots and cabin crew operating flights into Israeli airspace must not hold the nationality or dual nationality of countries that lack diplomatic relations with Israel. The directive came a day after an Omani copilot allegedly attempted to hijack a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv and crash it into Israel’s Ben Gurion airport on September 30, according to Emirati and Israeli authorities. The copilot is accused of attacking the plane’s Indian pilot, who has been recovering in hospital.
“The staff concerned have been informed of the new regulations implemented by the Israeli authorities for flights to Tel Aviv,” Air France told Al Jazeera.
Dozens of airlines affected
The Israeli directive could affect dozens of airlines that fly to, from or over that country. Al Jazeera contacted the Israeli Transport Ministry for comment but had not received a response by the time of publication.
Al Jazeera also contacted 15 major international airlines operating flights to Israel, asking whether they had received the directive and changed crew assignments in response.
Smartwings, the largest Czech airline, confirmed that it had received the new Israeli directive, and while it said its operations were not impacted at the moment, it added that it would comply with the restrictions.
“We received the directive from the Israeli authorities in September 2026. We have carefully reviewed the directive and continue to monitor and comply with all applicable requirements issued by the relevant authorities. At present, the directive does not have any impact on our operations, crew management procedures, or the deployment of crew members on flights to and from Israel,” Vladimira Dufkova, a spokeswoman for Smartwings, told Al Jazeera.
United Airlines responded, saying only that they “don’t have anything to share”. The US airline did not confirm whether it had received the Israeli directive or acted on it.
An internal memo to Air France pilots and cabin crew, seen by Mediapart, warned that “failure to comply with this directive would expose Air France and the employee to potential sanctions”.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify the memo.
‘Discriminatory bias’
The reported restrictions could put Air France at odds with French employment law, said Paris-based anti-discrimination lawyer Clara Gandin, raising questions about whether an airline can comply with a foreign government’s security requirements while ignoring its obligations to its workers.
“The measure rests on a collective presumption which amounts to a discriminatory bias: Every national of these 31 countries, most of them Arab or Muslim-majority, is treated as a potential security threat,” Gandin told Al Jazeera.
She said Air France’s adoption of the directive amounts to outright “discriminatory harassment”.
“Article L1132-1 of the French Labour Code prohibits any discriminatory measure based on a person’s actual or perceived nationality, in particular regarding assignment, pay and discipline,” Gandin said.
“Removing employees from certain flights because they hold Algerian, Tunisian, Iranian or another of Israel’s listed nationalities is therefore direct discrimination – even without loss of pay.”
With the countries listed on Israel’s list of barred nationalities largely Arab or Muslim-majority, the measure could also constitute “indirect discrimination based on origin, and possibly on perceived religion”, she added.
Gandin explained that French law does make a caveat for a difference in treatment in cases where it is an “occupational requirement”, where a move pursues a “legitimate aim” that is proportionate, and where it is linked to the nature of the job.
“Evidently, nationality is not a requirement for flying an aircraft. Air France also lets the same pilots and crew operate every other route, which demonstrates it does not regard them as a safety risk,” she said.
The lawyer said Air France holds no valid legal justification for adopting Israel’s policy.
“Air France’s aim is commercial: keeping access to the Israeli market. But economic considerations cannot justify discrimination in the eyes of the law,” Gandin said, explaining that the safety objective is Israel’s, not the company’s, and that French law looks at the aim pursued by the employer itself, not its clients.
“More specifically, a third party’s wishes cannot turn a protected characteristic into an occupational requirement,” she added, referencing a 2017 ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union adopted by France’s highest court that same year.
“A proportionate response to a security concern relies on individual assessment, which French aviation security vetting already provides. It cannot rest on nationality alone,” Gandin said.
Airspace sovereignty vs national laws
However, the question of whether the restrictions amount to discrimination under French law is distinct from a state’s authority to regulate access to its airspace and territory.
Analysts pointed to international civil aviation law, which recognises state sovereignty over territorial airspace under Article 1 of the 1944 Chicago Convention and, subject to specified conditions, the recognition of flight crew licences issued by other contracting states under Article 33.
Vincent Correia, a professor of air law at McGill University in Canada, also pointed to Article 13 of the Convention, which allows states to enforce their laws and regulations governing the admission of passengers and crew into their territory.
“Hence, a state can impose immigration restrictions on crews from other countries, on the basis of nationality, given that crew members must go through immigration and customs when flying on international routes,” Correia told Al Jazeera.
Pilots and other crew from countries that Israel does not have diplomatic relations with were already barred from flying there, making the new measure applicable only to dual citizens, which explains why airlines like Air France might have complied, he explained.
Still, Gandin said, a state’s authority to impose entry restrictions does not necessarily exempt airlines from their obligations under other applicable laws, including national anti-discrimination and employment legislation.
While Air France could make an argument about state sovereignty over airspace, it “does not change the fact that the measure is discriminatory”, she said.
Besides, the lawyer pointed out, Air France has options: It could choose not to operate the route under these conditions, or challenge the directive through the French state, the French Civil Aviation Authority (DGAC), or the EU.
The DGAC had not responded to Al Jazeera’s queries by the time of publication.
The flagship French airline could, therefore, be setting itself up for legal consequences.
Affected employees could claim damages for harm suffered, and trade unions could file proceedings, said Gandin. Such a measure could also fall under criminal law – punishable by up to three years’ imprisonment and a fine of 45,000 euros ($50,300), said Gandin.
Meanwhile, data protection laws stipulate that information requested from employees must have a direct and necessary link with their job – a register of employees holding one of the 31 listed nationalities may reveal ethnic origin and could be in violation of this, the lawyer said.
According to Mediapart, Air France had considered asking flight crew members to come forward themselves if they were affected by the circular. However, Alter, the union representing the flight deck crew, had managed to persuade management to forgo that action, stating in a leaflet to its members that it would amount to “discrimination based on nationality”, reported the French outlet.
Alter did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
While the wider implications of Israel’s policy for other airlines remain unclear, Correia warned that it could set a precedent for other states to introduce nationality-based screening of international flight crews, complicating airline operations.
“At a time of pilot shortages, this will create additional constraints for airlines when scheduling flights to and from Israel. If other countries adopt similar measures, it could quickly become extremely difficult to manage,” the air law expert said.

Foiled attack

- Law enforcement operations made it possible to expose and disrupt the illegal activities of a Russian woman who had been recruited by a Ukrainian intelligence officer during a trip to Ukraine in 2022.

- FSB officers responded immediately after receiving intel, promptly detaining the accomplice of Ukrainian intelligence agencies and preventing the act of sabotage before it was carried out, thus containing the potential consequences of the Kiev regime’s actions against the military facility, the FSB said.
Confessions
- The woman confessed to cooperating with the Ukrainian intelligence service, according to a video released by the FSB.
- She said she had been living in Ukraine when Russia launched its special military operation.
- According to the suspect, a Ukrainian intelligence officer recruited her and suggested that she travel to Russia to carry out his orders in exchange for a cash reward.
- On his instructions, she traveled to Voronezh and rented a garage near the military airfield, the woman said.
- She added that she had retrieved drones and explosives from caches, brought them to the garage and assembled them as instructed by her handler.
- The woman also said that she had planned to return to Ukraine after completing her mission.
Investigation
- The suspect has been taken into custody.
- Efforts are ongoing to establish all circumstances of the crime and identify all those involved," the FSB said.

Türkiye records $4 billion current account surplus in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:18:33 UTC
18:18:33 KST

Türkiye posted a current account surplus of $4 billion in August, while the 12-month rolling deficit stood at $42.1 billion, according to central bank data on Oct. 13.
The Central Bank announced that the current account excluding gold and energy indicated a net surplus of $8.2 billion during the month.
The country’s goods deficit realized at $3.75 billion in August, the bank stated.
Net inflows from services recorded $9.7 billion in the same period. Under the services item, travel revenues reached $7.28 billion and transportation revenues hit $3.26 billion.
Direct investment saw a net inflow of $141 million, as non-residents recorded a net inflow of $719 million. Non-residents recorded a net inflow of $719 million and residents’ external assets increased by $578 million. 
Portfolio investments registered a net outflow of $1 billion in August. Non-residents’ investments in equity securities and investment funds and government domestic debt securities market recorded net purchases of $1.05 billion and $77 million, respectively.
“As regards the real estate investments, residents purchased $142 million of real estate abroad, while non-residents realized net purchases of $244 million in Türkiye,” the Central Bank said.
The official reserves of the country increased by $7.14 billion during the same period.
According to the annualized data, Türkiye’s current account deficit amounted to $42.1 billion in August, up from $41.5 billion in July, while the goods deficit was $78.4 billion against the deficit of $77.5 billion in the previous month.
“As regards the annualized figures, the current account deficit was mainly financed through portfolio investment with a net inflow of $5.5 billion, loans with a net inflow of $47.1 billion and trade credits with a net inflow of $0.5 billion,” said the bank.
The current account deficit stood at $31.5 billion in the January-August period, up from $19.7 billion in the same period of 2025, the bank’s data showed.
The country’s goods deficit grew from $44.2 billion in the first nine months of last year to $53.3 billion in January-August 2026.
The government’s Medium-Term Program (OVP) projects the current account deficit at $47.5 billion in 2026, equivalent to 2.6 percent of GDP.
According to the program, the current account deficit is forecast to decline to $38.5 billion in 2027, or 1.9 percent of GDP.

Türkiye’s first 1,000-megawatt offshore wind Renewable Energy Resource Zone (YEKA) project could be gradually commissioned between 2030 and 2032 if development proceeds as planned, Turkish Wind Energy Association President Ibrahim Erden has said.
Erden said the project is expected to be tendered in the first quarter of 2027 and could take four to six years to develop and implement.
The project would not only contribute to electricity generation but also help develop Türkiye’s wind energy industrial infrastructure and create new investment opportunities, he stated.
He said offshore wind energy could create new opportunities for shipyards, equipment manufacturers and other industrial sectors, paving the way for a new wind energy ecosystem.
“The development and implementation of the first 1,000 MW offshore wind YEKA project could take around four to six years. A gradual rollout between 2030 and 2032 would be a realistic expectation,” Erden said.
The sector expects at least 1.5 gigawatts of wind energy YEKA tenders to be announced annually through 2035, Erden said.
Offshore wind farms can cost 2.5 to three times as much to build as onshore projects, he added.
“An offshore wind investment with a capacity of 1,000 MW requires around $3 billion, while an onshore project of the same capacity costs approximately $1 billion,” Erden said.
Projects of this scale could also offer opportunities for international financial institutions and investment partnerships, enabling Türkiye to benefit from foreign financing and technology partnerships, he added.

18:15:37 KST

Finland has called for a complete EU ban on issuing tourist visas to Russian citizens while Moscow continues its war against Ukraine.
Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen said on Monday, Oct. 12, that the European Commission should tighten its guidance on Russian visa applications and propose the legislative changes needed for an EU-wide ban.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“As long as Russia continues its invasion, Russian citizens should not be issued tourist visas,” Valtonen said.
“It is not right that Russians can travel to Europe to enjoy the way of life and freedoms here while their country bombs the homes of Ukrainians,” she added.
Finland stopped issuing visas to Russians for tourism and other non-essential travel under a government decision adopted in 2022. Valtonen said the same restriction should finally be introduced across the EU.
Nearly 500,000 visas issued in 2025
According to Finland’s Foreign Ministry, Schengen countries granted Russian citizens close to 500,000 tourist visas in 2025.
Finland argues that restrictions imposed by individual member states are insufficient because a Schengen visa issued by one country generally allows its holder to travel throughout most of the passport-free zone.
Valtonen has invited other EU governments to join a letter asking the European Commission to develop a common approach.
Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo has also said he intends to raise the proposal at the next European Council meeting.
Russia Reportedly Strikes Dnipro With Guided Bombs, Wounding 64-Year-Old Man
“One concrete measure that I will present at next week’s European Council meeting is for Europe to stop issuing tourist visas to Russians,” Orpo told Finnish broadcaster Yle.
He linked the proposal to security concerns over alleged Russian sabotage operations inside Europe.
“Why on earth are we letting them into European territory as tourists, where they can move freely?” Orpo said.
The proposal concerns tourist and other non-essential travel. It would not automatically prohibit entry on humanitarian grounds, for family reasons, or for Russians seeking protection from political persecution.
Putin’s circle, athletes, and combatants also targeted
Finland’s proposal goes beyond ordinary tourist visas.
Helsinki is also seeking a ban on Schengen visas for members of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s inner circle and people or organizations under EU sanctions.
The letter proposes restrictions on Russian athletes and members of sports teams with close ties to the Kremlin. Finland also wants the EU to effectively enforce an agreed entry ban covering current and former Russian combatants who participated in the war against Ukraine.
The European Commission previously proposed barring people who have served in the Russian Armed Forces since the invasion, arguing that Europe should remain inaccessible to those who joined Moscow’s war.
EU officials and several member states have described Russian veterans as a potential security threat, particularly amid allegations that Moscow is recruiting individuals to conduct sabotage, arson, and surveillance operations across Europe.
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna earlier warned that the EU needed a coordinated system for identifying and blacklisting former combatants, declaring that there could be “no path from Bucha to Brussels.”
An EU-wide tourist visa ban has not yet been adopted and would require agreement among member states as well as changes to the bloc’s common visa rules.

Last weekend the public jury voted the shrimp croquette from Restaurant North as the best croquette at Ostend's Shrimp Croquette Festival. The expert jury chose the croquette from Restaurant Leffe Beach. In total, the 8,400 visitors devoured some 60,000 croquettes – an all-time record.
The 8,400 tickets for the 6th edition of the Shrimp Croquette Festival in the West Flemish seaside resort of Ostend sold out quickly. Visitors were clearly very hungry, as the 60,000 croquettes they ate set an all-time record.
But the visitors didn’t just come to fill their bellies. They were also able to rank their top three favourite croquettes from a selection of 15 restaurants serving them.
For the fifth year running, the public voted Restaurant North’s croquette as the very best in Ostend. Toope came second and Hotel Cocoon third. There was heated debate amongst the diners: at many tables, lively discussions took place about flavour and texture. 7,000 visitors cast their votes.
Technical perfection
The jury of experts, which included chef Piet Huysentruyt and actor Manu Van Acker, came up with a completely different top three. They deemed Leffe Beach’s croquette to be the best. Seafront restaurant Océan took second place and eatery ‘t Zeezotje came third.
For the jury, Leffe Beach stood head and shoulders above the rest. “The flavour, the crust and the texture are all the very best,” it said. “The fact that the croquette is served ‘naked’, without any garnish, testifies to the creators’ refined vision. Leffe Beach’s shrimp croquette comes close to technical perfection.”
The children’s jury awarded first place to ‘t Zeezotje.
The croquettes entered must weigh 40 grams and be made with North Sea shrimps. Otherwise, the chefs are free to follow their own recipes.
Next year, the festival will return from 9 to 11 October 2027.

- Russia’s spending plans for 2027 almost certainly represent a real-terms reduction compared to 2026. But military spending is set to increase. Compared with updated expected spending for 2026, the plan forecasts a nominal spending increase of 0.5 per cent, well short of inflation, which the Bank of Russia estimates at 6.3 per cent. - The draft 2027 budget allocates 17.1 trillion rubles (USD $202.6 bn) towards national defence, which is around 35 per cent of total federal government spending. This is a 40 per cent increase compared to what was initially planned in 2026. However, Russia will almost certainly overspend on defence by at least 4-5 trillion rubles (USD $47-59 b in 2026 included in updated 2026 total spending plans). As a result, the actual increase in defence spending will almost certainly not be as high as 40 per cent.
- The 2027 budget forecasts that the budget will be less reliant on oil revenues than in previous years. Oil revenues are forecast to amount to 16 per cent of total federal revenues in 2027 compared with a 22 per cent in 2026. This change is down to a reduction in the oil-price threshold at which Russia saves additional revenues into its National Wealth fund: USD $50 per barrel in 2027 down from USD $59 per barrel in 2026.

“Live long, die fast”: How Russia’s  propagandist poets try to make sense of a senseless war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:12:26 UTC
18:12:26 KST

Over the past five years, poetry by so-called “patriots of Russia” has demonstrated just how rapidly the image of the war is changing. Whereas before 2022 poetry promised a swift triumph of the Russian will, it now accustoms the reader to war as a process that can last forever. Pro-war poets claim allies wherever they can even plausibly find them — from Mozart and early 20th-century author Osip Mandelstam to the metaphorical forces of light and darkness. This hodgepodge reflects the Kremlin’s lack of coherent arguments for continuing a “special military operation” that, after nearly five years, remains nowhere close to achieving its stated objectives.
The war is short, the war is long
Over the nearly five years of full-scale war in Ukraine, neither Russian film, nor theater, nor even literature has produced any memorable works about the “special military operation.” In this respect, pro-war poetry provides the only exception — likely owing to the peculiarities of the genre. A poet is forced to be concise, and therefore more meticulous in the choice of images and words. As for the underlying messages, the pro-war poets, if they waver at all, do so in perfect alignment with the official narrative.
According to literary scholar Mikhail Edelstein, all “patriotic” poetry after Feb. 24, 2022, offers a brief recap of the events that had unfolded since 2014. Many authors who have made a name for themselves in this genre extolled, glorified, and even called for war before 2022, promising Russia a swift victory and world domination.
For example, the poem “Pre-Winter” by Igor Karaulov (from the poetry anthology “I Am the Wounded Earth: Russian Poetry on the Crimean Spring and the War in Donbas,” 2017) reflects classic dreams dating back to tsarist times:
What we will eat tomorrow,
Or how our clothes will be cut — are trifles.
Many winters passed, and we’re alive again
As long as there is vodka, Crimea, and the straits.
The word “straits” in 19th-century propaganda meant roughly what Crimea does in modern-day Russia: the epitome of the empire’s existence. The straits in question were the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles, which would finally give Russia access to the southern seas. (These hopes, needless to say, have still not been realized.)
The word “straits” in 19th-century propaganda meant roughly what Crimea does in modern-day Russia: the epitome of the empire’s existence
War was expected to fulfill a range of personal hopes. Ultranationalist poet Alexander Pelevin (not to be confused with bestselling novelist Viktor Pelevin) offers his reflection on the popular expression “war will write everything off”:
War will write it all off: your debts, payments, bills,
Your deadlines, projects, books you never wrote,
A clean slate, your new chapter in life,
Last year’s draft you never meant to complete.
(2018)
“Patriots” also pinned their hopes on a war to cleanse Russian society from the “liberal delusion” of perestroika and the 1990s — along with purging culture of the much-hated “postmodernism,” which they tend to use as an umbrella term for all things alien to a patriotic heart.
“Having cleansed itself of the delusion of the liberal agenda — LGBT+, postcolonialism, radical feminism, permissiveness bordering on Satanism, and other postmodernist discourse — [poetry] has become visible again,” poet and critic Oleg Demidov writes when explaining the origin of pro-war poetry.
In a 2022 interview, the poet Olesya Nikolaeva (wife of Russian Orthodox Church priest Vladimir Vigilyansky) characterized the war in Ukraine as “a clash of civilizations: Christian, on the one hand, and one that has renounced Christ and sunk into paganism, if not Satanism, on the other.” The Satanists, one must understand, are Western civilization.
Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 turned out to be neither swift nor victorious, with Russian troops taking months to capture every tiny village — only to lose it after a few more weeks of intense fighting. For now, Mala Tokmachka remains as inaccessible for Russian patriots as the straits for the 19th-century empire. Yet throughout 2022, inertia inspired poets to keep holding onto their pre-war mood of swaggering overconfidence.
That year, Igor Karaulov wrote a humorous poem that begins with the line: “Let us split Poland right in half, like the sweet iceberg of a Kyiv cake...” — as if the division of the “Kyiv” cake were still a foregone conclusion, a prelude to Russia’s conquest of its old lands further west.
The poet Maria Vatutina, whose poems are now available both on the YouTube channel of Russia’s National Guard and on the TV channel Russky Mir, borrows images of “liberator warriors” from Soviet propaganda:
The old men wept upon his chest,
The roadside villages shone bright,
They’re planting flowers in Mariupol,
And bringing textbooks to the schools.
Hopes for a swift redrawing of the borders across the post-Soviet space are reflected in Alexander Pelevin’s “In the City of Limonov” (2022), in which the author renames the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv, the hometown of Russian writer Eduard Limonov (1943-2020):
In the city of Limonov 
Padded jackets fill the streets
Public holidays and street names 
Will be changing before long.  
As we’re rising in our millions, 
Like we did when we were young, 
In the city of Limonov, 
Kharkiv Region — that’s the one.  
We are not bad people — our history is the problem
By 2026 the full-scale invasion of Ukraine had long since evolved into positional, trench warfare — striking in the irrational number of casualties taken for every captured kilometer. Poetry has to somehow justify such a high price, but after 2023, the names of captured settlements appear less often in propagandist art while the poet’s gaze turns to the metaphysical depths of the war. This change of optics helps to soothe the anxious reader — and the poet’s own conscience.
As could be expected, pro-war poetry usually chooses the “warrior of light” as its lyrical hero. But in moments of doubt, a characteristic ethical reversal kicks in, familiar to us from the Kremlin propaganda after 2014. Generally, “we” are the best, kindest, and most honest. But in the absence of extolling arguments — as in the case of Russian athletes caught doping — the “ethical reversal” kicks in, with propaganda whispering that “everybody does it; we are not the bad guys — everyone else is no better.”
The poet Alexander Pelevin employs this device when reflecting on the future:
There will be no “good Russian” passports for you,
Who’s good and who’s bad — who can tell from a trench?
We live in grim times, and since we are the bad guys,
Well, glory to Russia — what more can I say?
This marks an important turn: the “patriotic” poet realizes that a “good war” is no longer possible, and advises his readers to get used to being bad. He grasps at big ideas to justify this new position: the image of an ominous “History” appears in Pelevin’s poetry, an entity that simply exists regardless of people’s will. And this “History” of his is by definition a malevolent, cruel actor, meaning outsiders are not entitled to hold our actions against us:
History smells of death, history smells of sh*t,
History is burned-out vehicles, rust-covered metal scrap,
History is when they say: wherever you see him, kill him.
History is what happens when some people kill other people.
Propaganda in 2023-2024 also turned to a “historical” argument as justification, portraying the war against Ukraine as inevitable — the legacy of the Soviet Union’s collapse postponed by 30 years, something that “had to happen” and “could not have been avoided” (a thought Dmitry Medvedev expressed in one of his articles in the spring of 2023).
Seeking resonance with these ever-changing “root causes” of the war, propagandist poets mimic the state’s arguments: “we did not start it,” “we were set against each other,” and besides, Ukraine is “torn by civil war.”
Propagandist poets mimic the state’s arguments in their poems: “we did not start it,” “we were set against each other,” and besides, Ukraine is “torn by civil war”
The poet Sveta Litvak works in the genre of playful performance — a deliberate device reminiscent of “children’s poems” in the spirit of Agniya Barto. A brisk stepped-line verse seems intended to help readers memorize the theses of propaganda by heart:
You know, Sergeant, we’ll have company tonight.
The hostile silence shrouds the town before the fight.
As long as brother murders brother,
After one battle comes another,
Placing an end to war beyond our sight.
The wind from the Atlantic brings us hostile hordes,
One nation set against the other by their lords.
(2024)
In trying to explain the length of the war, nationalist poetry first relies, in the spirit of state patriotism, on the thesis that this war is not new but rather a “continuation of the Great Patriotic War,” which supposedly never ended:
Our great-grandfather drove out the plague,
was captured and escaped,
and held his head high in Berlin, and to us
bequeathed his fate — to beat the enemy
Imagine that, one with its center in Kyiv.
(A poem by a mobilized man named Nikita that came out in 2023 in the collection “Resurrected in the Third World War,” distributed free of charge through the public services portal Gosuslugi)
There is also another argument, borrowed from the Soviet playbook of the Cold War era, that has come to the pro-war poet’s aid. This is “not just any war” but the Third World War, the worst fear of all Soviet children. The anthology of pro-war poetry that came out in early 2023, edited by pro-Kremlin author Zakhar Prilepin, is called exactly that — “Resurrected in the Third World War.” (It sold roughly 10,000 copies).
Following Putin, who has repeated many times that the “special military operation” will last as long as it takes to achieve the mysterious “goals” known only to him, the poet Anna Dolgareva — nicknamed the “Valkyrie of the special military operation” — gives this message a simple and clear form:
Death is inevitable (here, a shot booms like a chord).
“How much longer?” As long as your sense of duty can last.
For in Russia one must live long
And die fast.
Russian pro-war poetry stands out from among other genres of propaganda by sometimes letting slip the truth — even if inadvertently. In the classic definition of a totalitarian state, a citizen has only one duty: to die for their fatherland quickly, without thinking and without asking questions.
Igor Karaulov, a representative of an older generation, is in no hurry to give straightforward explanations. In a 2023 interview he frankly admits that he had not expected the war to drag on. And to the question “Who are we fighting?” he gives what seems to him a paradoxical and wise answer: “Ourselves.”
Russian pro-war poetry stands out from among other propaganda genres by sometimes letting slip the truth — if inadvertently
The main prewar mythologem held that, as a result of a hypothetical war, Russian society was supposed to “be cleansed.” But since society has yet to cleanse itself fully or sufficiently, the war cannot end in victory. This presents an example of outstanding semantic acrobatics on the part of poet Karaulov, who demonstrates just how elastic a patriot’s logic can be: cause and effect, the horse and the cart, easily switch places if need be — whenever and however is convenient for the author.
To justify the number of casualties and the length of the invasion, pro-war poets have to keep expanding its purpose. Karaulov himself writes:
A stock of warmth, a stock of hardtack,
My dear old lumbering bear,
Our motherland’s rockets streak overhead,
A Mandelstam lying facedown by the bed.
In a bout of remarkable cynicism, the author rhymes Osip Mandelstam — who was tortured and killed by the Stalinist regime and was far removed from any motives of military conquest — with Putin’s missiles.
Remarkably, this device closely follows the state’s own approach. In 2017, educational posters printed to mark the occasion of Moscow’s 870th anniversary appeared on the capital’s streets and in the subway, illustrating the city’s history with the fates of its outstanding residents. The city administration did not hesitate to claim for itself the achievements of Great Terror victims like the geneticist Nikolai Vavilov or the poet Osip Mandelstam.
Not all metaphorical allies have to be native-born. The poet Olesya Nikolaeva, claims for herself a composer from a country that modern-day Russia treats as unfriendly:
Who stands with us? Our kin, our blood,
The running river, rustling forests, love,
The golden skies, the secret breath of spring,
And all of Mozart, and prophetic dreams.
And yet, in the fifth year of war, poets and composers alone will not do: higher powers have to be called in. As a result, in Anna Dolgareva’s poems, God, angels, and camouflage-clad saints often descend into dugouts, don body armor, smoke with soldiers, and share the hardships of war. This running plot can be seen in other pro-war poets as well.
God is with us; so is the sun; and so is the rain
that loaded its sniper rifle.
(Anna Revyakina, the poem “The Miner’s Daughter”).
In Sofia Yudina’s poem “To the Hospital,” God comes in a greatcoat (in this image one recognizes, however, rather an earthly god — Joseph Stalin):
It is as though God comes home every night,
Takes off his shabby army greatcoat, hangs it
On a hook, then stomps to shake the snow off his boots,
Turns on the light, and looks — and through the blizzard
Starlight begins to glimmer over weary earth.
Alongside furious appeals to the forces of light, propagandist poetry also takes pride in a secret ability to “make hell” on earth. Speaking on behalf of the light, poets do not miss the chance to wink at the lower tier. Dolgareva again:
The commander said it as a simple fact:
“We raised hell
On sectors facing not battalions —
But whole brigades.”
They were foretold
To burn up, not hold out for long.
They offered a preview —
Showed what hell is like.
Chumminess with hell is a distinct feature of Russian pro-war poetry — a device that could be interpreted as a perverse way of “making peace with the war.” Hell, blood, coffins, and the cross that must be borne are frequent images in the work Dolgareva and others, where blood, guts, and mud are invoked not to appall the reader but as a kind of paean to this hell on earth:
And yet,
Even if my tongue should die,
I will pronounce this all the same
Into this
Horror mixed with the remains of bodies,
Into this sunset pink
And air blue,
To my last breath:
“Russia,
Glory be with you.”
As literary scholar Oleg Lekmanov noted in 2024: “The candy-sweet prettiness with the epithet and the noun swapped places (‘sunset pink,’ ‘air blue’) is no accident next to ‘the remains of bodies’ — these images are meant to be perceived in one row. It looks as if today’s [pro-war] poets have gotten hooked on the cruelty and blood of war like heavy narcotics.”
Finally, one more way to justify war is a paradoxical and deliberate admiration for it, a kind of infernal bravado. The collection by the poet Dmitry Artis is titled “He Walks Through the War,” cynically paraphrasing Gennady Shpalikov’s anthem of the Sixties generation. Philologist Mikhail Edelstein calls Artis “one of the bloodthirstiest poets in this crowd.” His deliberate cruelty contains a disinterested rapture before death:
War is a piece of happiness,
a blood-soaked chunk,
A gem of freedom
without a slavish cut…
War is the very best mother
That we could have,
The taste of porridge
She gave us when we were young.
Over the past five years, the meaning of the war in Russian “patriotic” poetry has performed an astonishing somersault from the promise of a swift national victory in 2022 to a wish in 2026 for everyone involved to have “a good death.”
At his infamous meeting with the mothers of killed mobilized soldiers in 2022, Vladimir Putin quoted lines by the celebrated Soviet poet and songwriter Vladimir Vysotsky: “To go this way is better than from vodka and from colds.” The Kremlin’s attempt to enlist even Vysotsky as an ally in its deadly escapade is no more cynical than everything else. After all, the very idea of a “sacrificial, meaningful death” is a trademark device of Soviet propaganda. Unsurprisingly, this motif also appears in the poems of Igor Karaulov:
Others flee to the front to escape their death.
Where steel goddesses rage, where the guns never tire.
Where the grain that must perish will never expire.
The image of fallen soldiers “sprouting” after death in the form of grass is another popular trope — in the work of Maria Vatutina, in particular:
Like stalks, we shoot up, bud by bud,
We sprout, dead, through tight-packed soil,
We lift our heads, beginning to be heard.
Soon we will reign as kings, as wordsmiths of the world.
Literary scholar Mikhail Edelstein unambiguously interprets this passage as presenting an image of the resurrected dead who will come to “reign as kings,” and more than that, this infernal side of pro-war poetry also marks the evident exhaustion of rational arguments for the war among poets and officials alike. This is called magical thinking: when reality does not match the basic myth, one has to pile up ever more new myths.
Instilling the idea that one must get used to an endless, pointless war is the only purpose poetic propaganda can serve today. The same goes, indeed, for Kremlin propaganda as a whole.

designboom listens: jacques monneraud finds inspiration between music and silence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:12:23 UTC
18:12:23 KST

designboom listens: jacques monneraud finds inspiration between music and silence
from childhood road trips and french rap to film scores and absolute silence, the french ceramic artist reveals how music shapes his creative process, memories, and moments of concentration.
[ADVERTISEMENT]
jacques monneraud’s creative world, in sound
For French ceramic artist Jacques Monneraud, creativity moves between moments of intensity and stillness. Best known for his Carton series, which transforms the fragile appearance of cardboard packaging into enduring ceramic vessels, he approaches making as a process of experimentation, doubt, and discovery. Music accompanies these shifts, from the restless momentum of Philip Glass’s compositions to the silence he seeks when he needs to think clearly.
In this edition of designboom listens, Monneraud shares the soundtrack of his creative universe, revealing a musical taste as varied as his approach to ceramics. Film scores, French rap, progressive rock, and contemporary pop all find a place in his playlists, alongside songs tied to childhood road trips and the decision to leave advertising behind and devote himself to pottery. Together, his selections offer a glimpse into the memories, emotions, and moments of concentration that inform his practice. Explore the sounds that shape Monneraud’s practice through his answers below, and tune in to the full playlist.
inside the playlist: from road trips to late-night listening
What song best captures your creative practice?
Jacques Monneraud (JM): That’s not an easy question! I’d say the third movement of Philip Glass’s Violin Concerto No. 1. The creative process isn’t calm and serene for me, and this piece captures quite well the alternation between the breathless rush of ideas and the tumultuous crash of doubts that come along and shake things up.
 What is the very first track you play to clear the air and get inspired when starting a new project?
JM: Justin Hurwitz – Another Day of Sun. I really love Justin Hurwitz’s work on the La La Land soundtrack. I’m a big fan of film scores, and their composers share my playlists with artists like Neil Young and Billie Eilish.
 Is there a song that instantly takes you back to a specific memory or place from your past?
JM: Supertramp – School. It takes me back to the hours we spent in the car as kids, driving off on holiday with my father, surfboards strapped to the roof of our Passat estate. I really like Supertramp because they knew how to work with silence.
 What song is stuck in your head right now?
JM: Beyoncé – 16 Carriages. I love this album. I listen to a lot of different kinds of music. I think that, just like with pottery, it’s variety that makes things beautiful.
 What is your ultimate 2 AM studio track — the one you secretly know every word to?
JM: I was going to say Demain c’est loin by IAM, but since we’re talking about guilty pleasures, I have to admit that I’m a huge fan of JUL’s freestyles — those performances outside of his albums where he really gets to rap. They’re actually fairly unknown tracks, but JUL is an excellent rapper. Rap generally has a pretty special place in my playlists. Lately I’ve been listening to a lot of Ben PLG, BB Jacques, Youssoupha and Alpha Wann.
 What song do you put on when you’re stuck and need a breakthrough?
JM: Absolute silence. That’s not the name of an album. I really need to be able to hear myself think at those moments.
 What track is dominating your speakers this week, and is it influencing what you’re making right now?
JM: Daft Punk – Contact, and actually the whole Random Access Memories album, which I’ve been playing on repeat. It’s Daft Punk’s last album. The more I listen to it, the more I feel that you can sense they knew, while making it, that it would be their last. With that in mind, I think they really wanted to leave behind a positive message, a message of love. That touches me a lot, and I think yes, it does influence what I’m making.
 What song helps you slow down and focus on the tiny, quiet details?
JM: Fyrs – Lost Seas,  Hermanos Gutiérrez – Nuevo Mundo, Pink Floyd – Shine On You Crazy Diamond, Philip Glass – Akhnaten. These pieces help me reach a particular level of concentration. I think concentration works a little bit like sleep, and that you can sink into a very deep state of focus. When you reach that state — what athletes call ‘the zone’ — your senses change. In my case, my hearing becomes muffled, as if I were underwater, truly inside a bubble where time doesn’t exist. Smell and taste disappear and make way for touch and sight, whose acuity becomes almost maximal. It’s a very pleasant feeling.
If people were wearing headphones while experiencing your latest work, what one song should be playing?
JM: Sirens, from the The Odyssey soundtrack. Ludwig Göransson is to me what Beyoncé is to a 25-year-old American. His albums are Christopher Nolan’s films — and ever since Nolan discovered him, he seems unwilling to let him go — and I look forward to each new one with great anticipation.
What is your favorite album cover art?
JM: System of a Down – Steal This Album!. I remember when I first discovered this album. I was 14. It was a time when the musical experience began with a physical encounter with the CD and its cover. In the record store I used to go to, the simplicity and sheer force of this invitation to anarchy really hit me like a slap in the face. That’s when I understood the political power of music.
 What track best describes your favorite project you’ve worked on so far?
JM: Stromae – Défiler. It was playing on repeat in my headphones when I decided to leave my job and devote myself to ceramics. Stromae is one of my favorite artists.
project info:
artist: Jacques Monneraud | @jacquesmonneraud

Ukraine's future in Putin's hands, Russian victory all but assured — British politician
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:11:16 UTC
18:11:16 KST

BEIJING, October 13. /TASS/. The future of Ukraine will be decided by Russian President Vladimir Putin and the Russian government as Moscow's victory in its special military operation is a foregone conclusion, George Galloway, leader of the Workers Party of Britain, told TASS.
"It will be decided by president Putin and the Russian government, in particular. Because the war (Russia’s special military operation - TASS) is won [by Russia]," he said following a lecture hosted by the Russian Cultural Center in Beijing. "And the question is, now, what terms they will impose on the Ukrainian regime, both in terms of its own dissolution, for the solution there must be cannot possibly have [Vladimir] Zelensky continue in office," he added.
The key to bringing the situation in Ukraine to normal is not holding a presidential election there, the British politician argued. "It's not a new president with cleaner hands <…>. The change that's required is in the nature of any remaining rump Ukrainian state," Galloway explained. "Is that rump state going to be used in the future, in the new generation, perhaps as a knife in the back of Russia, or is it going to be a friendly government towards Russia and absolutely neutral," he wondered.
Ukraine’s new status
According to the politician, this neutrality means that the former Soviet republic cannot be part of NATO, nor should the North Atlantic Alliance be in Ukraine, Galloway continued. "I wouldn't trust the current political class in Ukraine at all. Nor Zelensky, nor any of the pretenders to his throne," he emphasized. "I would like to see Ukraine have the same relationship to Russia as Belarus does. Why can't they all be members of a union state?" he asked rhetorically.
Such a status for Ukraine would guarantee to the Russian side "no recurrence of the circumstances which led to the special military operation," according to Galloway. "Whether that's what happens or not, we cannot have, after all, this blood, all this treasure, all this wreckage of international relationships. People being confiscated, sanctioned, killed even," he added.
The Ukraine problem "has to be resolved once and for all," the leader of the Workers Party of Britain insisted. "The Russian speaking territories, all of them will have to be returned to Russia. Down to the Odessa, includes Transnistria, and whatever is left," he maintained.
As regards a recent statement from US President Donald Trump who announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, it will hopefully lead to a "permanent resolution of this conflict," Galloway said. "Too much dislocation and disruption to the international system has already occurred, <…> [and this problem] has to be resolved now, once and for all," he concluded.

Ex-gang leader faces maximum penalty of life in prison for Tupac Shakur murder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:10:32 UTC
18:10:32 KST

Ex-gang leader faces maximum penalty of life in prison for Tupac Shakur murder
LAS VEGAS, Oct 13 - A former gang leader was set to be sentenced on Tuesday for orchestrating the 1996 drive-by shooting death of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur in Las Vegas, capping the lone prosecution of a long-unsolved murder that shaped the golden age of rap music.
Duane "Keffe D" Davis, 63, found guilty of first-degree murder in August, was scheduled to return to a Las Vegas courtroom facing a maximum penalty of life in prison without the possibility of parole.
Davis has said he would appeal his conviction.
Until Davis' 2023 arrest, the killing of Shakur, shot dead in the passenger seat of an SUV driven by his record executive, Marion "Suge" Knight, had stood for nearly three decades as one of America's most notorious cold cases.
The murder, which silenced one of rap's most commercially successful and influential artists, heightened the image of violence permeating 1990s hip-hop culture while stoking the infamous East Coast-West Coast "gangsta" rap feud of the era.
Despite Davis' conviction, the question of who pulled the trigger in the fatal shooting of the 25-year-old rap legend has never been conclusively decided.
Davis was tried and convicted for hurriedly masterminding the murder to avenge the beating of his nephew by Shakur and members of the rapper's entourage inside the MGM Grand casino on the Las Vegas Strip on September 7, 1996.
FATAL SHOOTING SPARKED BY CASINO BRAWL
The clash at the casino stemmed from hostility between two Los Angeles-area street gangs — the South Side Compton Crips, of which Davis was the self-described leader, and Mob Piru, which was associated with Shakur, Knight, and their music label, Death Row Records.
Members of both groups were in Las Vegas to see a world heavyweight title boxing match that night between Mike Tyson and Bruce Seldon.
Within hours of the casino brawl, Davis ushered his nephew and two other associates into a white Cadillac and went looking for Shakur and Knight, determined to settle scores, according to an account Davis later gave police in an unrelated investigation and that prosecutors cited during his murder trial.
Davis said he passed a gun to the two men seated behind him in the Cadillac, one of whom opened fire through the window when they caught up with, and pulled alongside of, Knight and Shakur’s vehicle in traffic.
Shakur was struck four times and died in a hospital six days later. Knight, who suffered a minor injury from a bullet fragment that grazed his head, is now serving a 28-year prison term on an unrelated voluntary manslaughter conviction.
Authorities said they long believed Davis was involved in Shakur's killing but lacked sufficient evidence to charge him.
That changed when he went public with his story in media appearances and a memoir that, along with tapes of his secret meetings with investigators, formed the bulk of the prosecution’s murder case.
In his book, "Compton Street Legend," Davis himself wrote that he was considered a suspect in the murders of both Shakur and Christopher Wallace, a rival rapper.
Wallace, who performed as the Notorious B.I.G. under the New York-based Bad Boy Entertainment label, was shot dead in Los Angeles in March 1997.
Although the Wallace killing remains unsolved, there has long been speculation that he was gunned down in retaliation for Shakur's killing months earlier.
While Davis was never accused of actually firing the shots that killed Shakur - Nevada law allows someone to be charged with murder as a participant in the crime - prosecutors have never named a suspected gunman.
All three other men in the Cadillac with Davis that night have since died. REUTERS

Deloitte Erased $672M in Assets for Oligarch Abramovich, Investigation Reveals

- Category

Deloitte Erased $672M in Assets for Oligarch Abramovich, Investigation Reveals
One of the world’s largest accounting firms, Deloitte, helped forge documents to conceal the wealth of Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich and assist him in tax evasion, according to an investigation by the BBC on October 12.
Deloitte Cyprus signed off on financial statements from which $672 million of Abramovich’s assets—including superyachts, luxury estates, and private jets—disappeared.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The firm also reportedly helped develop a tax evasion scheme involving forged documentation. Legal expert Andrew Mitchell stated that evidence gathered by reporters points to tax evasion.
Abramovich’s lawyers stated that he denies dodging taxes or hiding wealth, adding that journalists provided no proof he was aware of or ordered document falsification. Representatives for Deloitte Cyprus stated that the firm acts in accordance with applicable laws.
The BBC revealed that the earliest backdating case identified by journalists dates back to 2006, when Cyprus passed a law requiring companies to publish financial disclosures. Deloitte Cyprus drafted a 2003 financial statement for Amiscan Investments, a Cyprus firm linked to Abramovich, listing $672 million in assets.
The list contained a West Sussex estate, luxury apartments in London, a mansion in the south of France, as well as helicopters, private jets, and several yachts, including the $147.5 million Pelorus. According to the investigation, Deloitte Cyprus advised Abramovich’s company on a tax avoidance scheme.
To hide the assets from public disclosure, individuals in the oligarch’s inner circle and the firm MeritServus transferred them to Amiscan Investments’ parent company in the British Virgin Islands. The transfer date was backdated by three years to make the transaction appear as though it took place in 2003.
Deloitte Cyprus reviewed the backdated documents and deemed them an adequate basis for removing the assets from Amiscan’s statements. In 2006, Deloitte signed off on the 2003 statements, erasing the homes, jets, and yachts, leaving listed assets of just $75 thousand.
Beyond the documents processed by Deloitte, Abramovich’s advisors at MeritServus forged another set of records involving over $10 billion in business assets held by his Cyprus company, Electus Investments, as reported by the BBC.
MeritServus backdated documents to create the impression that Electus did not hold these assets, transferring them on paper to a firm of the same name registered in the British Virgin Islands, where public financial reporting is not required.
Speaking ahead of a meeting of the EU Foreign Affairs Council in Luxembourg on October 12, 2026, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha argued that sanctions pressure on Russia had to continue to increase throughout Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
He stated that the EU’s decision on September 22 to remove two Russian oligarchs, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, from its sanctions list was a wrong step. Consequently, Ukraine planned to propose imposing sanctions on ten more Russian oligarchs, while Sybiha expressed hope that the EU would adopt its 22nd sanctions package against Russia as soon as possible, further isolate Moscow, and make full use of frozen Russian assets.

EU electric, hybrid car trade grows in 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:09:27 UTC
18:09:27 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
The European Union's electric and hybrid car trade saw notable growth in 2025, while these vehicles accounted for nearly 40% of the bloc's overall auto production.
The EU imported €45.1 billion ($50.44 billion) worth of hybrid and electric cars in 2025, marking a 4% increase from €43.4 billion in 2024.
Exports grew to €64.7 billion, up 10% compared with €58.7 billion in the previous year.
Overall, this trade saw a significant increase since 2017, when the share of electric and hybrid cars accounted for only 10% of total car imports and 3% of total car exports.
The share of full electric cars in 2025 stood at 20% for EU car imports and 18% for exports, up from 0.8% and 1.1% in 2017, respectively.
Plug-in hybrid cars represented 17% of car imports and 9% of car exports, while the share of non-plug-in hybrid cars was 23% for imports and 14% for exports.
Out of the 12.6 million cars produced in the EU in 2025, nearly 40%, or 4.8 million, were hybrid or electric cars, representing an increase of almost one million units compared with 3.9 million in 2024.
Last year, 17% of the cars produced in the EU were electric, 7% were plug-in hybrids, and 14% were non-plug-in hybrids.
The production value of electric and hybrid cars reached €139 billion in 2025, up from €123 billion in the previous year.
Among these vehicles, electric cars held the highest value at €68 billion, followed by non-plug-in hybrid cars at €38 billion and plug-in hybrid cars at €33 billion.
This equaled a value share of the total EU production of 21% for electric cars, 12% for non-plug-in hybrid cars, and 10% for plug-in hybrid cars.
China was the top EU import partner, accounting for 42% of all electric car imports, followed by South Korea with 27% and Japan with 9%.
The top three export partners for electric cars were the UK with 35%, and the US and Norway with 14% each.

Scientists looked at a net zero future. One climate risk remained
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:09:18 UTC
18:09:18 KST

The world is on the cusp of an historic El Niño, a climate pattern centred in the Pacific that could reshape weather across the planet.
El Niño is hardly a new phenomenon, but the coming one could be the biggest ever recorded. Research suggests extreme El Niño years will become more common as the world rapidly warms, driven by humanity’s greenhouse gas emissions.
Our new research examines the reasons why El Niño is changing, and how this climate pattern may evolve if we reach our net zero goals. Our findings suggest extreme El Niños will become more common if we remain reliant on fossil fuels, but reaching net zero earlier should limit how often they occur.
Shaping global weather
El Niño has long influenced weather across the globe by driving variations in temperature and rainfall beyond the Pacific Ocean. Here are several exceptional examples.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
In 1982, a strong El Niño dumped vast volumes of rain on South America, with some rivers in Peru filled with 1,000 times more water than usual. On Kiritimati Island (part of Kiribati in the central Pacific), heavy rainfall flooded seabird nests and caused entire colonies to vanish. Meanwhile, southeast Australia was crippled by drought, culminating in the fires that claimed 75 lives.
The El Niño of 1998 carried enough rain to fill a new lake three metres deep in Peru’s Sechura Desert, one of the driest places on Earth. With it came record numbers of mosquitoes and widespread malaria. In Indonesia, months of severe drought allowed devastating forest fires to burn for weeks.
In 2016, a strong El Niño coupled with already warming oceans triggered the bleaching of more than two-thirds of the Great Barrier Reef.
The current El Niño forming in the tropical Pacific is expected to be among the strongest on record, with its effects lasting well into 2027. For Australia, this could heighten the risk of hot, dry conditions and a fierce bushfire season. Its presence is already being felt across the globe, slowing the shipping of goods through the Panama Canal and forcing fish to migrate to cooler waters.
El Niño in a warmer world
Scientists have always understood El Niño to be a phenomenon that temporarily alters global weather, with conditions returning to “normal” when it dissipates. However, climate change is expected to change what “normal” looks like.
As the planet warms, extreme El Niño years are likely to become more common. Our research suggests the tropical Pacific could remain in an El Niño-like state for centuries — even if the world reaches net zero carbon emissions — and extreme El Niño years would occur more often.
We used climate models to test two possible climate futures: one in which carbon emissions continue to rise, and the other in which the world meets its net zero goals. To see if timing matters, we also examined what would happen if we curb emissions at different points during this century.
A warning from the Pacific
The Pacific Ocean covers about a third of the planet, stretching along the equator from Indonesia to South America.
Its western side is normally several degrees warmer</a> than its eastern side. This temperature difference is linked with the trade winds that blow from east to west and pull cold water up from the deep eastern ocean. During an El Niño, this temperature gap shrinks, causing the easterly trade winds to slacken and rainfall to shift east, away from Australia.
Under continued warming, climate models show the eastern Pacific warming faster than the west, reducing this temperature difference. Scientists are yet to observe this happening, with the eastern Pacific even cooling in recent decades.
However, this warming trend is expected to emerge if the world keeps burning fossil fuels. Once it does, our findings suggest this west-to-east temperature difference will be reduced for centuries after emissions reach net zero, rather than recovering.
This is because oceans are slower to respond to warming. Research suggests global temperatures would stop rising soon after the world meets its net zero target. By contrast, ocean temperatures would keep rising for centuries.
This means the world’s oceans, particularly the Southern Ocean surrounding Antarctica, will keep warming long after emissions stop. This would draw tropical rain belts closer to the equator, as their position depends on the temperature contrast between the northern and southern hemispheres. This would keep the trade winds weak and the eastern Pacific warm.
More extreme El Niños to come
A smaller west-to-east temperature difference would mean the eastern Pacific sits closer to El Niño conditions. Heavy tropical rain needs warm water and, with the eastern Pacific projected to warm faster than the west, it would take less of a push for rainfall to shift east. This means a larger share of El Niño events would become extreme.
Our research suggests the longer we take to reach net zero, the more extreme El Niños we will likely face. Further delay could create a less hospitable climate with more risks and higher costs for generations to come.

Haredi parties may refuse to endorse both Netanyahu, Eisenkot after Israeli election, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:07:27 UTC
18:07:27 KST

Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ) may refrain from recommending either Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu or Gadi Eisenkot to President Isaac Herzog to form the next government after the election, according to assessments by haredi sources familiar with developments in the parties.
The sources believe neither party is inclined to recommend a candidate to the president after the election. At the same time, they do not expect either party to actively seek Netanyahu's replacement or help the opposition bloc oust Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana.
According to the sources, Shas and UTJ would prefer to remain in the opposition, at least initially, until a solution is found to the dispute over the haredi conscription law. Even if the legislation passes the Knesset, concerns that the High Court of Justice could strike it down may continue to delay their entry into a coalition and government, should one be formed.
At this stage, these are assessments from sources familiar with the haredi political establishment, not decisions by the parties' rabbinical leadership.
The assessments come as parties in the opposition bloc prepare for the possibility that the election will produce no clear winner. Parties in the bloc are considering replacing Ohana after the new Knesset is sworn in.
Netanyahu faces uncertain coalition prospects
The proposed move is intended to give the bloc greater influence over the parliamentary agenda and allow it to advance legislation, including the establishment of a state commission of inquiry into the October 7 attacks and a two-term limit for prime ministers, among other initiatives.
Under the plan being considered, the parties would seek to establish the Knesset House Committee and the Constitution, Law and Justice Committee after electing a new Knesset speaker. They would then try to secure majorities on those committees that would let legislation advance even before a government is sworn in.
In such a scenario, the opposition bloc could pursue certain parliamentary initiatives while Netanyahu continues to serve as caretaker prime minister. However, electing a new Knesset speaker would not guarantee a majority to pass legislation, nor would it end the outgoing government's term.
The haredi sources, for their part, believe that if the opposition bloc secures a majority to replace the Knesset speaker, it may also gather the support needed to form a government.
Such an arrangement could include a minority government relying on external support from Ra'am, or potentially even a government in which Ra'am participates as a coalition partner.
Haredi sources: Agreements could emerge after October 27 election
According to the sources, party leaders' current objections could change after the election if they are presented with a realistic opportunity to replace Netanyahu.
Although MKs may agree to replace the Knesset speaker while refusing to support the swearing-in of a particular government, the haredi sources believe that agreements on forming a government could also emerge after the election.
The sources nevertheless assess that Shas and UTJ are unlikely to actively support the opposition bloc's effort to replace Ohana.
It remains unclear whether the two parties would vote against such a move, abstain, or absent themselves from the vote.
The sources believe both parties would prefer to await the election results and a clearer picture of the possibilities for forming a government without committing themselves to either side in advance.
Their assessment that the haredi parties may refrain from recommending Netanyahu should not be interpreted as a willingness to help the opposition bloc replace him.
Conscription law remains central obstacle to coalition talks
One of the main considerations is the ongoing crisis over the conscription law.
One possibility under consideration is for the opposition bloc to advance conscription legislation before a government is formed, in an attempt to remove an obstacle to the haredi parties joining a coalition at a later stage.
However, haredi sources doubt that passing the legislation would be sufficient as long as concerns remain that the High Court of Justice could strike it down.
According to the sources, even a commitment by a future government to advance a conscription arrangement would not guarantee that the haredi parties would agree to join it.
They believe that even if the Knesset approves a conscription law, the haredi parties will want to know whether the arrangement can withstand judicial review and remain in force over time.
Another possibility raised in closed discussions is to initially establish a government without the haredi parties and then attempt to bring them into the coalition after the conscription law passes the Knesset.
Haredi sources do not rule out a change in the parties' positions if they receive a concrete proposal.
However, they currently believe that neither Shas nor UTJ is likely to commit to joining a government headed by Netanyahu or Eisenkot.
In either case, the sources expect the conscription issue to continue complicating negotiations.

Participants heard testimony from former hostages, relatives of those killed and wounded Israelis about the attacks and their aftermath.
The week’s program included meetings with President Isaac Herzog, government officials, diplomats and business leaders, alongside visits to communities near Gaza.
Delegates also toured Yad Vashem, Israel’s Holocaust memorial in Jerusalem; the Old City and Church of the Holy Sepulchre; the City of David; and the Friends of Zion Museum. Other stops included Masada, the Dead Sea, ancient Shiloh and sites in the Galilee.
FOZ said the summit aimed to strengthen ties between Israel and Christian communities worldwide and encourage participants to share survivors’ testimony through their congregations, community networks and social media audiences.

“We don’t need to hit the entire plant”—Ukraine’s drones go for refinery parts sanctions make hard to repair
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:06:44 UTC
18:06:44 KST

Ukrainian drones have helped push Russia into its worst fuel crisis since the Soviet Union fell, The Washington Post (WaPo) reported on 11 October.
Diesel is where this war reaches American drivers. US President Donald Trump blames rising diesel prices mostly on Russia’s war in Ukraine, while experts blame mainly the US war with Iran. Some of his allies now accuse Kyiv of trying to sway the US midterms.
Drones go for the first stage of refining
The Washington Post looked at dozens of strikes between 1 April and 31 August. Three refinery experts then examined satellite images of 54 strikes with visible damage. In over half, the damage seems to be to the desalting and distillation units, known by the Russian acronym ELOU-AVT. These units clean the crude of water and salt, then split it into separate compounds, the first steps toward gasoline and diesel. More than a third appear to have hit secondary units, which turn those compounds into jet fuel, gasoline, and liquefied petroleum gas.
From April through August, drones struck two-thirds or more of the 36 big Russian refineries that S&P Global Energy tracks, a strike every third day. Some took as many as five hits. On 16 June, drones set the Moscow refinery’s distillation towers on fire. That strike and a second one days later kept the plant offline into September, WaPo reported, citing data firm Kpler. Ukraine targeted the refinery again on 20 September.
Trump’s Russian diesel deal, which drew fury in Ukraine, is unlikely to lower prices, experts say
“We don’t need to hit the entire plant,” a Ukrainian drone battalion commander with the call sign Tango told The Washington Post. Ukraine knows where to strike so that a refinery stops and stays down, he said. His unit, Ukraine’s 1st Separate Center of Unmanned Systems, runs long-range strikes deep inside Russia.
Sanctions slow the repairs
The EU banned exports of oil-refining equipment to Russia the day after the 2022 invasion, and the US followed days later. WaPo reported that the bans cover the distillation and secondary processing units Ukraine keeps hitting. The bans make spare parts hard to get, Alexander Kolyandr of Eurasia Group told the paper, and the strikes come faster than repairs.
Since last year, Ukraine has doubled the size of each wave, decoys included, a person involved in the strike campaign told WaPo. The decoys are unarmed and draw Russian fire, wasting air-defense ammunition, WaPo explained. Without them, the person said, Ukraine would simply lose expensive systems. András Rácz of the German Council on Foreign Relations told WaPo that even if only 2–3% of drones get through, the damage is significant.

He appeared in court last Friday, October 9, where a judge ordered him to be detained for a further 14 days. Police are carrying out further inquiries.

World Cup revenge, Olympics firing Mooney beyond 100
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:05:08 UTC
18:05:08 KST

World Cup revenge is driving Beth Mooney as the Australian women's cricket star eyes long-term goals even as she gets set for a career milestone.
Mooney will face Bangladesh in her 100th career ODI in Brisbane on Wednesday, but she is considering pushing on to the 2029 Women's Cricket World Cup and beyond.
Mooney says she is still disappointed after Australia's World Cup semi-final loss to India last year.
Veteran batter and wicketkeeper Beth Mooney is a star performer of the Australian women's cricket team, and there is plenty of incentive for her to continue well beyond her 100th ODI.
The 32-year-old will reach the milestone in the third and final one-day international against Bangladesh at Allan Border Field on Wednesday.
She is seventh on the all-time Australia aggregate list in ODIs with a stellar 3,288 runs at an average of 49.81, including six centuries.
Last year's loss to India in the World Cup semi-finals still sticks in the craw.
Australia previously lost the crown in 2017 when England beat India in the final, and that was a big driver for Mooney and the Australians to win back the trophy in 2022, which they did.
Now it is a case of deja vu after what transpired last year.
"I think there was a lot of bitter disappointment from that World Cup loss in India 12 months ago now, and looking ahead, we've obviously come off a T20 World Cup win, we've got a Champions Trophy, there are a lot of ICC events and Ashes series and big series coming up," Mooney said.
"But the 50-over one is what you want to win as well, so I guess the motivation for me now is to play well enough in the next few years to put my hand up for selection in that (2029) World Cup, but also contribute in a positive way to a format of the game that is constantly changing and evolving."
Cricket will be played at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics and likely again in 2032 in Brisbane, Mooney's hometown these days.
She will be 38 in 2032, but do not discount her still being around.
"Certainly the Olympics is definitely an enticing one for players to hang around a bit longer," Mooney said.
"We're obviously seeing the game a bit more modern and are remunerated well, so it's probably more likely people will start retiring a bit later. But I think the exciting part is there's always something on the calendar, so it'd be pretty hard to retire at this point."
Mooney said that if she was still performing and contributing to the success of the team, a swan song in 2032 was on the table.
"Hopefully I'm still around, but that's a long way away," she said.
"There's a lot of cricket to be played between now and then, a lot of tournaments to play with this Australian team and in franchise cricket, so my main focus is to contribute as much as I can to those, and also help the younger players along the way as well."
Current openers Georgia Voll and Phoebe Litchfield, who added 162 inside 20 overs in the nine-wicket win over Bangladesh in game two of the series, are two young guns changing the way the game is played.
"I guess that's what excited me the most is the fact that the 50-over game is becoming a lot more modern, and we're seeing Phoebe and Georgia really take the game on," Mooney said.
"Who knows how many runs we might be able to score in a 50-over game one day? That's sort of driving me at the moment."

Germany detains Turks suspected of sabotaging Starlink station in Poland on behalf of Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:04:55 UTC
18:04:55 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Two Turkish men suspected of carrying out last month’s arson attack on a satellite internet ground station in Poland used by Starlink have been detained in Germany. The Polish authorities say that the sabotage was carried out on behalf of Russia.
On Monday evening, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk first announced that the pair had been taken into custody “at the request of the Polish security services”.
He said that the Turkish men’s actions had been “a further act of hybrid warfare” – the term used for sabotage and other hostile activity carried out in Europe by Russia – and that “the perpetrators will answer before the Polish justice system”.
Na zlecenie polskich służb niemiecka policja zatrzymała dwóch obywateli tureckich podejrzanych o podpalenie stacji Starlink na Mazowszu. To kolejny akt wojny hybrydowej. Sprawcy sabotażu odpowiedzą przed polskim wymiarem sprawiedliwości.
— Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 12, 2026
Shortly afterwards, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński revealed that the arrests had taken place in cooperation between Poland’s police and Internal Security Agency (ABW) and Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA).
He said that the charge the suspects are likely to face in Poland would be “sabotage on behalf of a foreign intelligence service”, a crime that carries a minimum prison sentence of 10 years, ranging up to life.
Later on Monday, Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of the security services, confirmed that Poland believes the attack was carried out “on behalf of the Russian security services”.
The incident in question took place on 23 September at a ground station in Poland used by Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite internet company. The facility is used to provide internet services across the region, including in Ukraine, which has relied heavily on Starlink connections since Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Firefighters were called out that evening to a fire at the facility, which is owned by Polish state telecommunications operator Exatel. The next day, digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gakowski revealed that the blaze had been started deliberately and “the modus operandi is clearly Russian”.
Poland has been one of the primary targets for Russian sabotage operations in Europe. Those have included a series of arson attacks, including one that burned down Warsaw’s largest shopping centre and another at a drone factory that is used to supply the Ukrainian military.
A fire last night at a Starlink ground station in Poland that is used to provide internet services to Ukraine was caused deliberately and "the modus operandi is clearly Russian", says digital affairs minister @KGawkowski https://t.co/p2DEn7XexF

On Monday evening, at a press conference alongside Kierwiński and Siemoniak, the commander of Poland’s police, Marek Boroń, revealed that one of the two Turkish suspects had resident status in Germany while the other did not.
He said that the Polish authorities had been able to document their movements in Poland, and had recordings, fingerprints and DNA of the suspects.
Simoniak added that there was a “high probability” that other individuals were involved in the attack, but that he could not divulge further information about them currently. He also thanked the German authorities for their cooperation.
“We have no doubt that Russian intelligence services are behind this act of sabotage,” said the minister, quoted by the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. “And it’s worth adding that Russian intelligence services are increasingly using people connected to the criminal world. They never use their own citizens.”
Russia uses individuals already present in Europe – and often already involved in criminal activity – to carry out most of its hybrid operations. On Monday, in a separate case, three Ukrainians and one Belarusian went on trial in Warsaw accused of being behind a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania.
