Euro depreciates amid regional financial, political turmoil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:56:28 UTC
17:56:28 KST

Bahattin Gonultas and Emir Yildirim
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
The common currency of the 21 EU member states continues to depreciate against the US dollar amid mounting financial and political uncertainty in the bloc.
Concerns have reignited in the eurozone over fears of a repeat of the 2012 debt crisis, driven by France’s deepening fiscal indiscipline, political crisis and ongoing street protests, alongside Spain’s snap elections and Italy’s debt vulnerability.
The Middle East crisis continues to drive up energy costs, adding to volatility in the global bond market, while persistent inflation has cemented the downward pressure on the euro’s value as a medium-term trend.
The euro/US dollar exchange rate has been on a gradual downward trend since testing its January high of 1.21. The exchange rate dropped to 1.11 amid ongoing developments, hitting its lowest level since May 2025.
The euro has depreciated by around 5% this year, and the currency has now come under the spotlight as a sign of persistent fragility in the financial world despite having been largely unaffected by bond market volatility in recent months.
Developments in France, the second-largest economy in the eurozone, have been driving the euro’s depreciation.
France’s 10-year bond yield hit its highest level since 2002, nearing 5% amid geopolitical risks and leading to global bond sell-offs.
France’s overall public budget deficit widened to 5.8% of gross domestic product (GDP), exceeding the EU’s 3% threshold, according to the French National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (INSEE) and Paris.
The country has failed to post a budget surplus since 1974, while nominal growth rates have dropped below borrowing rates, dragging the country further into structural debt.
France’s total nominal debt stock hit a historic €3.6 trillion ($4 trillion), accounting for 119% of GDP and exceeding the 60% Maastricht criterion.
The spread between French and German borrowing costs reached its widest level since the major debt crisis of 2012.
Meanwhile, uncertainty in the eurozone has not been limited to France, as the crisis in Spain has also contributed.
Spain’s housing market policies brought political risks to the EU’s fourth-largest economy after Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez decided to call snap elections in November.
The US, on the other hand, is not facing global repercussions despite its historic debt burden exceeding $40 trillion and its inability to maintain spending discipline due to upcoming midterm elections.
Global capital continues to flock to the US dollar as a safe haven amid tensions in the Middle East.
Analysts say movements in the exchange rate stem directly from the euro’s weakness caused by developments in France, while the fragmented structure of national financial markets in the eurozone leaves the region vulnerable to such shocks despite sharing a common currency.
The European Central Bank’s (ECB) room for monetary policy maneuver is being limited by the financial and political turmoil.
The bank had been expected to hike rates three times next year, but these expectations have shifted to two 25-basis-point rate hikes due to the economic slowdown in the region and debt risks, alongside the loss of confidence and the widening interest rate gap between the US and Europe.
Selling pressure on the euro is expected to persist as long as structural problems remain unresolved and political tensions continue, analysts say.
While analysts think a new debt crisis is not inevitable and that France will not be driven into bankruptcy, they believe the euro is highly unlikely to strengthen against the US dollar under current conditions.
Carsten Brzeski, chief economist at ING Germany, recently said the deepening political turmoil in France reflects structural problems threatening the economic stability of the bloc. He noted that the country had already changed prime ministers six times since 2020 and urged the European Commission and the ECB to take action against Paris, as the government had managed to bring the budget deficit below the 3% goal only twice in the past two decades.
He added that political instability and uncertainty would take a toll on the economy and push France toward stagnation.
Chris Turner, head of global markets research at ING, said the euro/US dollar exchange rate would continue to be capped within the 1.10-1.15 range over the next two quarters due to the Fed’s hawkish stance and rising bond yields.
He added that further losses in the euro could be prevented by a fiscal consolidation program adopted by the French parliament, while the White House’s strategies after the midterm elections would determine the exchange rate’s direction.

FSB detains Russian woman over Ukraine-backed plot to attack military airfield

"The Federal Security Service in the Voronezh Region has foiled a large-scale act of sabotage and terrorism orchestrated by the Security Service of Ukraine, which planned to attack the Russian Defense Ministry’s Baltimor military airfield with short-range drones," the statement reads.
Law enforcement operations made it possible to expose and disrupt the illegal activities of a Russian woman who had been recruited by a Ukrainian intelligence officer during a trip to Ukraine in 2022. "Acting on instructions from her handler, she traveled to Voronezh and rented a garage, where she planned to assemble and launch drones meant to be used to destroy infrastructure and aircraft, as well as kill military airfield staff," the FSB said. The drones were supposed to be operated remotely by personnel based in Ukraine.
According to the FSB, the woman retrieved nine drones equipped with explosive devices, along with drone control equipment, from previously established caches and took them to the garage. Each drone carried 500 grams of foreign-made explosives.
"FSB officers responded immediately after receiving intel, promptly detaining the accomplice of Ukrainian intelligence agencies and preventing the act of sabotage before it was carried out, thus containing the potential consequences of the Kiev regime’s actions against the military facility," the agency stressed.
The suspect has been taken into custody. "Efforts are ongoing to establish all circumstances of the crime and identify all those involved," the FSB added.

Unions want Estonia's minimum wage to exceed €1,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:55:00 UTC
17:55:00 KST

Unions want Estonia's minimum wage to exceed €1,000
The Estonian Trade Union Confederation and the Estonian Employers' Confederation have begun negotiations on next year's minimum wage.
Estonia's minimum wage currently stands at 43 percent of the average wage or €946 per month. The Estonian Trade Union Confederation wants it to rise by more than 4 percent next year, bringing it above €1,000.
"We entered negotiations today (Monday — ed.) with the wage level agreed upon in the 2023 goodwill agreement, which would put the minimum wage at 47.5 percent of the average wage next year," said Kaia Vask, chair of the Estonian Trade Union Confederation.
Employers will present their counteroffer in subsequent rounds of negotiations. However, they consider the increase proposed by the trade unions too steep.
"The minimum wage needs to rise and the average wage has also increased, but the rate of increase must be something businesses can afford, particularly those located outside Tallinn and Tartu. Otherwise, jobs could simply disappear in some places. That is why this agreement has quite significant implications," said Hando Sutter, CEO of the Estonian Employers' Confederation.
Vask said that under the agreement signed three years ago, the minimum wage should eventually reach 50 percent of the average wage.
"The minimum wage needs to be raised so that everyone in Estonia can make a living from their wages. When prices keep rising and everything becomes more expensive, it gets increasingly difficult to make ends meet on a low wage," Vask said.
According to Sutter, any increase in the minimum wage must reflect what the economy can afford.
"Although we have seen some modest economic growth, there is still a great deal of uncertainty. Energy prices this coming winter will drive inflation and put pressure on economic growth, while input costs are also rising," Sutter said.
At the beginning of the century, the minimum wage stood at 30 percent of the average wage, rising to 41 percent a couple of years ago. Around 20,000 people in Estonia earn the minimum wage. It also affects the minimum rate of parental benefits, unemployment insurance benefits and, in some areas, kindergarten fees.

Ship sinks in new drone attack off Bulgaria, PM summons Russian ambassador
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:52:48 BST
17:52:48 KST

Bulgaria summons Russian ambassador after ship sinks in Black Sea drone attack
- Published
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has summoned the Russian ambassador after two merchant ships were struck by drones off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast.
Eleven crew members are missing and one sailor was saved, according to local officials, after one of the vessels sank 17 nautical miles (31km) east of the village of Krapets.
The other vessel, Ukrainian owned, was hit by drones 18 nautical miles from the town of Byala and all 15 crew were rescued.
The attacks come a week after two other commercial ships were hit by sea and aerial drones in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone. One of the ships, the Alfa Watan, sank and all 10 crew, including nine Syrians, are presumed dead.
Radev convened an emergency meeting on Tuesday and said he had summoned Russian envoy Eleonora Mitrofanova. Although there was no conclusive evidence of blame on "either side... the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation", he said.
Mitrofanova was later quoted by Bulgarian media as telling Radev she had no information from Russia's defence ministry relating to the latest attacks. She also said these strikes could have been a provocation by a third party.
Bulgaria is a Nato member, and Radev also spoke to secretary general Mark Rutte about the latest attacks.
"Nato will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea," Rutte said after the talks.
"We have already strengthened our posture along the eastern flank and will continue to monitor the security environment, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed," he added.
The two ships were struck just outside Bulgarian territorial waters.
If this had happened just a few nautical miles to the west, Article 5 of the Nato treaty could have been triggered. The article defines an armed attack on one member of the military alliance as an attack on all.
Radev had earlier asked Nato and the EU for technical assistance in investigating the previous attacks that took place on 6 October, indicating it was unclear who was behind them.
Radev came to office during the summer and has since rejected suggestions that he is "pro-Russian".
Ukraine has directly blamed Russia for the latest attacks and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen spoke on Tuesday of the Black Sea becoming "another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable".
Russia's military has not publicly commented on the issue. It has recently intensified its strikes on vessels in the Black Sea, particularly the western side, as part of its war against Ukraine.
The same day that two ships were targeted off Bulgaria last week, Ukraine hit an oil tanker in the Russian Black Sea port of Sochi.
Moscow says it is targeting ships delivering weapons and dual-use cargo to Ukrainian ports - and cited attacks in the ports of Mykolaiv and Chornomorsk last week, along with one in the Black Sea.
However, Kyiv and its European allies say merchant vessels carrying grain and other civilian cargo are being attacked.
Meeting with his security chiefs on Tuesday, Bulgaria's prime minister said: "Another attack on merchant ships in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters is absolutely unacceptable".
Radev identified one of the hit vessels as the Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3, which is registered in Ukraine's Odesa, saying that five of its crew members were being treated for minor injuries. He gave no further details about the vessel that had sunk.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said "Russia's latest attack on commercial vessels near Bulgaria's territorial waters... once again demonstrates Moscow's deliberate disregard for civilian lives and maritime security in the Black Sea".
"The Black Sea is a lifeline for global food security. Russia is attacking it to weaponise hunger and hold the world hostage. This must be met with strength," he added.
Both Russia and Ukraine are major grain-exporting countries and Turkey has called on both countries to halt attacks in the Black Sea.
Moscow has repeatedly rejected calls by the US and Europe for a naval ceasefire in the Black Sea, blaming Ukraine for attacking Russian merchant ships in the area.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

A talking glove, a 90-second health check and a drone interceptor: Meet Uzbekistan’s young inventors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:51:33 UTC
17:51:33 KST

At an engineering competition in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, 90 finalists were selected from 1,925 applications. The award-winning projects range from early prototypes to devices already in use at clinics and industrial sites, according to their creators.
A sensor-equipped glove designed to convert sign language gestures into speech, a device that takes six basic health measurements in around 90 seconds, and a mining innovation aimed at reducing energy consumption are among the inventions developed by young engineers in Uzbekistan.
The projects featured in Kelajak muhandislari (Engineers of the Future), a national competition organised by Uzbekistan's Ministry of Higher Education, Science and Innovation.
The competition attracted 1,925 applications, with 90 finalists selected and the winners honoured in Tashkent on 29 September.
The award-winning inventions are at different stages of development. Some remain prototypes, while others, according to their creators, are already in use beyond university laboratories.
A smart glove to bridge a communication gap
Among the winners was engineering student Abduqodir Latifjonov, whose project, ImoVox, took second place in the student category for Best Idea.
He developed a sensor-equipped glove after witnessing the difficulties some sign language users face when communicating with people who do not understand them.
“I started thinking: in this age of technology, why can’t we create a solution that understands their signs and turns them into speech that everyone can understand?” he told Euronews.
Adapted to Uzbek sign language, the prototype uses sensors to track finger and hand movements in three dimensions.
Individual gestures are recorded and assigned meanings, allowing the device to recognise them and convert them into speech. AI then helps combine individual signs into more natural sentences.
Six health measurements in 90 seconds
Another award-winning invention has moved beyond the laboratory. Asadbek Urunov, a master's student at Turin Polytechnic University in Tashkent, won third place in the student Best Project category for Body Tester, a device his team calls a “robot doctor”.
The machine measures height, weight, pulse, blood oxygen levels, body temperature and blood pressure in around 90 seconds, storing the results digitally and offering preliminary recommendations.
Urunov says the same measurements can take 20 to 25 minutes when performed separately using conventional equipment.
“This is only a preliminary assessment. We should not use it to make a final medical conclusion,” he told Euronews.
According to Urunov, the device is already in use in around 30 organisations, including public institutions and clinics.
Reducing energy use in ore processing
Bekzod Gafforov won first place in the student Best Invention category for a redesigned lining used in industrial ball mills, which grind ore before further processing.
Inside these rotating machines, heavy metal balls crush and grind the ore. The lining protects the machinery from wear and influences how the balls move, affecting grinding efficiency.
A master's student at the Graduate School of Business and Entrepreneurship, Gafforov developed the new lining with specialists from Navoi State University of Mining and Technologies, combining wear-resistant steel and cast iron.
He says it is already in use at facilities operated by Navoi Mining and Metallurgical Company.
“According to the results, its service life increased by between one and a half and two times, grinding efficiency improved by 30 to 35%, and energy consumption fell by 5 to 10%,” he told Euronews.
A robotic platform moves towards production
Dilmurod Rustamov of Turin Polytechnic University in Tashkent won second place in the student Best Project category for BARLOS, a hybrid unmanned ground vehicle that can operate on electricity or petrol. Its modular design allows different equipment to be fitted for different tasks.
Rustamov says the platform was demonstrated to the head of Uzbekistan's State Security Service and has publicly described it as military technology.
According to the developer, his team has produced nine vehicles after receiving an order for eight units in four configurations. The team says it has also been tasked with producing 100 units in 2027.
A drone designed to intercept drones
The competition's first prize in the student Best Project category went to Biloliddin Ismoilov, a second-year student at Tashkent University of Information Technologies, for Shunqor-8, a locally developed drone interceptor.
“We are creating something new, something that has not been done here before,” Ismoilov said.
Designed to counter unmanned aircraft, the system can reportedly reach speeds of up to 450 km/h and intercept targets 8–10 kilometres away, according to information released by Uzbekistan's Ministry of Higher Education, Science and Innovation.
Ismoilov says the technology has undergone eight rounds of field testing, with further trials planned.
Controlling computers with hand movements
Davron Polojanov, who took third place in the student Best Invention category, developed the Hand Control Mouse K10G.
The device uses hand movements in three dimensions to control computers and other electronics without a conventional mouse.
“While an ordinary mouse works on a flat surface, our Hand Control Mouse works in the air, along the X, Y and Z axes,” Polojanov explained. “It allows us to control computers, equipment and other devices through movements in the air.”
One potential application is in education. Teachers could move through presentations while walking around the classroom, rather than repeatedly returning to their computers.

Former DR Congo president Kabila joins M23 rebels in a new coalition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13

17:50:49 KST

Former DR Congo President Kabila joins M23 rebels in a new coalition
Kinshasa braces for potential conflict as Kabila allies with M23 rebels, challenging President Tshisekedi’s regime.
Former Congolese President Joseph Kabila has launched a new political and military coalition, including the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group, which has captured vast areas of the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
Kabila introduced the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) at a news conference on Monday at his residence in the eastern city of Goma, which the M23 has controlled since January 2025.
Kabila said he will head the FRN with rebel leaders, including Corneille Nangaa, the former leader of the Congo River Alliance (AFC) and the political wing of M23, serving as his deputies.
Claude Ibalanky, a coalition adviser, said the group aims to unite all resistance forces “to put an end to tyranny by any means necessary, including the use of force”.
There was no immediate response to the announcement from the DRC government.
Reporting from Goma, Al Jazeera’s Alain Uaykani said there were growing fears that fighting in eastern DRC could escalate.
“Kabila addressed the nation, explaining his plan. People are making comments across the country that this is another level of the conflict,” Uaykani explained.
Uaykani said rebels already hold Goma, Bukabu, the airports and key border crossings with Rwanda and Uganda, and that the government has been unable to push them back. Talks to resolve the conflict have also failed, with each side blaming the other.
“The government has shown no sign of defeating these people,” he said.
Uaykani noted that Kabila is a former army chief and said there were fears that government troops could defect.
“He’s still a soldier; he has led an army. People are worried that more soldiers from the government may join him as well”.
Yvon Muya, a researcher at the University of Ottawa in Canada, said the announcement increases the chances of a confrontation between Kabila and DRC President Felix Tshisekedi, and could lead to more fighting in eastern DRC.
“You don’t make an announcement like this without having prepared the actions that follow,” Muya said. “We will likely witness an escalation on the military front.”
Representatives from the DRC government and the M23 movement were expected to meet in Qatar in November for talks, but analysts warn that the new coalition could undermine the process.
Kabila led the DRC from 2001 to 2019, taking office at 29 after his father, President Laurent Kabila, was assassinated.
A DRC military court sentenced Joseph Kabila to death in absentia last year on charges of treason, war crimes and crimes against humanity, finding that he collaborated with Rwanda and M23.
Kabila has called the case politically motivated and denies the charges.
The US imposed sanctions on him earlier this year over his alleged role in funding rebel groups.
The DRC, the United States and United Nations experts accuse Rwanda of backing M23, an allegation Rwanda denies.
Tshisekedi’s second term ends in 2028, and his allies have been preparing public opinion for changes to the constitution’s two-term limit, as rebel activities intensify in the east.

Biotech industry calls for €450m investment in food innovation

Biotech industry calls for €450m investment in food innovation
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The agriculture sector has called on the government to invest €450 million in food technology to maintain the Netherlands’ status as a world leader.
Biotech companies and research institutions such as Wageningen university say €1 billion is needed by 2040 for plant breeding and innovation, partly to deal with the challenges of climate change.
Some 50 companies and research institutions petitioned economic affairs minister Heleen Herbert and junior agriculture minister Silvio Erkens to allocate more funding to the sector in a meeting at Wageningen this week.
Sjoujke Heimovaara, president of the executive board at Wageningen University and Research, said the industry needed its own equivalent of Project Beethoven, the government-back scheme to invest €2.5 billion in the Eindhoven region to support major technology companies such as ASML.
“Crops need to be constantly bred to withstand new diseases, higher temperatures because of climate change and the higher salt content in ground water,” she told the Telegraaf.
“We are still a world leader in this area, but if we don’t take action we will soon be selling our seeds and machines for harvesting these crops in China.”
Heimovaara said investing public money in facilities for the agriculture industry was justified by the wider economic benefits. “It is basic infrastructure,” she said. “You wouldn’t ask Albert Heijn to pay separately for using the motorways.”
Erkens tempered expectations that the cabinet could find €450 million for the sector, but he said there could be opportunities to use existing subsidies for food innovation.
“For example, money has been set reserved to limit the use of crop protection measures,” he said. “We could use some of that for these purposes.”

Finnish foreign minister calls on EU to ban Russian tourist visas, slams Trump lifting sanctions on diesel from Russia
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:48:03 EEST
17:48:03 KST

Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen (NCP) has called for a complete EU ban on issuing tourist visas for Russians until Russia ends its war in Ukraine.
"As long as Russia continues its invasion, Russian citizens should not be issued tourist visas. Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine is now in its fifth year. It is not right that Russians can travel to Europe to enjoy the way of life and freedoms here while their country bombs the homes of Ukrainians," Valtonen said in the release.
In recent years, Schengen countries have been issuing more tourist visas to Russian citizens. Last year, nearly 500,000 tourist visas were granted to Russians across the Schengen area.
"Issuing visas to Russians for non-essential travel was banned by government resolution in Finland already in 2022," Valtonen pointed out. "The same must finally happen at the EU level."
Valtonen has invited other EU states to sign a joint letter to the European Commission.
"In addition to the complete ban on tourist visas, the letter proposes a ban on Schengen visas to [Russian] President Vladimir Putin's inner circle, visa restrictions for Russian athletes, and the effective implementation of the visa ban on Russian (ex)combatants agreed by the EU Member States this summer," the ministry explained in the release.
Valtonen slams US-Russian fuel deal
Valtonen has also sharply criticised a deal between US President Donald Trump and Putin.
Aiming to lower diesel pump prices in the US, Trump has decided to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports.
In an interview with news agency Reuters, the Finnish foreign minister said that as the leader of the free world, the US should stand with Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression.
"The rest of the world should be on the side of the victim and certainly those countries who want to still be strong for the concept of freedom," she told Reuters.
Valtonen also commented on her proposal to other EU member states to restrict tourist visas for Russians.
"I hear from all of my colleagues in the European Union an agreement to the principle and I am so sure that all of the European Union countries will start restricting tourist visas to Russians even more strongly now, especially because Russia is also waging a hybrid war against Europe," she said, according to Reuters.

Hurricane Simon hitting western Mexico after tropical systems kill 5
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13

17:47:50 KST

Hurricane Simon still hitting western Mexico after tropical systems kill 5
Hurricane Simon continued to move slowly up the coast of west-central Mexico early Tuesday bringing wind and flooding rain after tropical weather systems caused five deaths and damage in Pacific coastal towns and resorts.
The eye of the hurricane remained offshore as its outer bands of winds and rain slammed communities between the Sierra Madre and the Pacific Ocean near Puerto Vallarta.
Simon's 90 mph strongest sustained winds made it a Category 1 storm, but the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami said it had technically become a small tropical cyclone. Simon was some 100 miles west of Cabo Corrientes and heading northwest at 3 mph.
Forecasters said it may weaken a bit but will likely maintain hurricaine strength through Wednesday. Hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 10 miles from Simon's core and tropical-storm-force winds extended outward up to 45 miles.
Hurricane Simon rain and flood forecast
About 5 to 10 inches of rain are expected from Simon across coastal west-central Mexico with as much as 15 inches in the state of Sinaloa by Thursday.
Moisture associated with Simon is forecast to bring the potential for flash flooding from this evening through Friday morning to parts of Texas, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Kansas and Missouri, according to CBS News meteorologist Nikki Nolan. Rinfall could total 6 inches and perhaps 8 in some spots.
Tropical weather turns deadly
In Mexico's Baja California state, rescuers on Monday combed parts of the coastal city of Ensenada, where floodwaters swept away vehicles and damaged homes. At least four people died in the state due to the impact of post-tropical cyclone Rachel.
Resident Johana Nuriulu said the flooding began during the night, shortly after heavy rain knocked out electricity. "We heard a loud noise that sounded like ocean waves, but really loud," she said.
Nuriulu said she went outside and discovered that a nearby stream had overflowed, sending water rushing through the neighborhood. The waters inundated streets and homes, sweeping away vehicles and other belongings. "Everything was being dragged away," Nuriulu said.
Several communities were cut off by landslides and overflowing rivers elsewhere in Baja California.
In the afternoon, the Mexican military used helicopters to rescue 32 people - 22 of them foreigners - from a ranch in Ensenada. Baja California Gov. Marina del Pilar Ávila said 13 were youths.
The state Secretary of Security, Gen. Laureano Carrillo, said some of the group were missionaries meeting at the ranch and that among them were Germans and Americans.
Baja California Civil Protection Coordinator Ignacio Lozoya said Monday evening that four bodies had been recovered in Ensenada: a 13-year-old girl on Sunday and two women and a 4-year-old boy Monday. Lozoya said six people remained missing: four in Ensenada and two from the town of San Felipe, a father and son who went fishing Saturday and didn't return.
According to Ávila, some 14,000 federal and state personnel had been deployed across Baja California to assist affected residents and respond to the emergency.
To the south, Simon downed trees and electricity poles, blocked roads and flooded homes in coastal towns of Guerrero state, including the major seaport of Acapulco, Gov. Evelyn Salgado said at a news conference.
A 71-year-old man died after a wall collapsed in Chilpancingo, Guerrero's capital, Salgado said.
In Puerto Vallarta, workers removed wooden panels from boarded-up storefronts and businesses reopened Monday as rains eased. The popular tourist destination's international airport suspended operations until Tuesday morning.
"Personally, I think we should remain on alert because we don't really know whether it will arrive, move elsewhere or dissipate," said Noelia Carrillo, a tourism agency worker.
U.S. impact from storms 
Rachel weakened into a post-tropical cyclone as it moved north into Southern California. The storm battered the coast with unusually large waves, which tore apart a boardwalk and smashed into homes in Long Beach. Some residents were forced to evacuate.
Las Vegas tied an all-time daily rainfall record for October when it received 1.08 inches of rain into Sunday morning, according to the U.S. National Weather Service. The record was set in 1947.
Videos posted on social media showed a torrent of water rushing through a street near the Las Vegas Strip, with a Ferris wheel and casinos in the background.
Flood advisories were mostly lifted by late Monday in Utah, Arizona and elsewhere in the Southwest.
In Utah, dozens of runners and volunteers who were part of the Moab 240 ultramarathon were evacuated Sunday after being stranded by flooding. The race goes through Canyonlands and Arches national parks.
The additional rainfall isn't associated with Rachel, but a different weather system moving across the West, forecasters said. The precipitation is expected to end by Wednesday.
Power was gradually being restored after Hurricane Isaias hit the U.S. Southeast.
At least four deaths have been linked to Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, which came ashore as a Category 2 hurricane Friday near Destin, Florida, a Gulf Coast vacation spot filled with high-rises and tourist shops. The storm then roared into Alabama with tropical-force winds before dissipating farther north.

Lower income for young Swiss women despite educational advantage

17:47:21 KST

Lower income for young Swiss women despite educational advantage
Despite having an educational advantage, young women in Switzerland continue to earn less than men. Whilst the pay gap has narrowed significantly, it still stands at 14% for those born in 1995.
This is shown by a study by the University of Lausanne and the Fors Centre of Excellence in Social Sciences, in the journal Social Change in Switzerland. For this study, researchers Daniel Oesch and Oliver Lipps analysed data on over 215,000 people aged between 25 and 34 from the Swiss Labour Force Surveys covering the period from 1991 to 2024.
In a press release accompanying the study, the researchers describe this trend as a “catch-up”. Among 25 to 34-year-olds born in 1965, women’s total earned income was still 55% lower than that of men. For those born in 1995, the gap has narrowed to 14%.
More
Switzerland leads the way in the fight against ‘unexplained’ wage gaps
The genders have also been converging in terms of labour force participation and working hours. The difference in weekly working hours fell from 17 hours to less than four hours. The gap in standardised hourly wages narrowed from almost 20% to less than 5%.
Children widen income gap
According to the study, a key driver of this trend is the reversal in educational attainment. In 2025, 54% of young women in Switzerland held a tertiary qualification (university, university of applied sciences, higher vocational education), compared with only 48% of young men.
Women are also increasingly moving into occupations with higher earning potential.
This catch-up is also reflected in international comparisons. Whilst the 1965 cohort had the second-largest income gap compared with France, Sweden, Britain and the United States, the 1995 cohort now has the smallest gap among these countries.
According to the study, parenthood remains a key dividing line. Once a family is established, the income gap widens significantly. Among childless women, the income gap narrowed from 27% to 7% between the 1965 and 1995 cohorts. Among parents, it also narrowed, but remained significantly larger at 51%.

Germany's China calculation shifts as import pressures eclipse export benefits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:47:00 UTC
17:47:00 KST

Why Germany is backing tougher EU trade defenses against China
October 13, 2026
Germany's cautious approach toward Beijing is cracking. For years, Berlin blocked a harder line on what the European Union describes as China's unfair trade practices.
In the last few months, that caution — a fear of Chinese retaliation that could hurt German exporters — has given way to a willingness to escalate.
Last week, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron wrote jointly to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen seeking a new tool to cut a trading partner off from the EU's single market if unfair practices continue.
Clearly aimed at Beijing, the letter warned the measure was necessary against countries that "deliberately seek to undermine ... fair market conditions by political or economic means."
China's Commerce Ministry warned Europe would "suffer the consequences" if it adopted such a "kill-switch" plan, which was timed to coincide with crucial EU-China trade talks in Beijing last week.
The cost of standing still
Noah Barkin, a senior adviser with research consultancy Rhodium Group's China practice, told DW that the threats to Germany's export powerhouse "have convinced Merz and his closest advisers that the benefits of action outweigh the costs of inaction."
Before the COVID pandemic, the two economies rose in tandem and German industry benefited from China's ascent.
Since 2021, however, China has fallen from Germany's second-largest export market to its ninth, according to data from Germany Trade & Invest for the first half of 2026.
Chinese competitors have quickly closed the technology gap and benefit from much lower costs and state subsidies. That pressure is being felt especially in Germany's automaking, precision engineering and chemicals industries.
Why Berlin's China policy is changing
German vehicle makers have suffered a large sales drop in China, which was once their second-largest market. According to data from Rhodium Group, German car exports to China plummeted by 66% between 2022 and 2025.
Big German brands now face heavy rivalry from a new wave of Chinese electric vehicle (EV) manufactures in other major markets, including Europe, which is forcing a wave of layoffs and possible factory closures.
In Germany alone, imports of new Chinese-made cars rose 121% in the first seven months of the year, according to Destatis, the federal statistics agency. Overall, Chinese-made vehicles accounted for nearly 14% of total vehicle imports.
"After continuously losing market share in China ... it [the rivalry] seems to be hitting their business within the European automotive market," Andreas Mischer, an associate fellow at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW.
Mischer said pressure from Germany's powerful automotive lobby was key to Berlin's "shifting attitude toward trade defense instruments."
Industry pressure grows for trade defenses
Among the many German business leaders who have demanded a more hard-line approach in recent months, Oliver Richtberg, head of foreign trade at VDMA, Germany's mechanical engineering association, was perhaps the most blunt:
"We are currently being deindustrialized through unfair measures — and most companies are no longer willing to accept this," Richtberg told Welt am Sonntag newspaper in August.
According to Eurostat, the wider EU's goods deficit with China was around €360 billion ($402 billion) last year — effectively €1 billion per day — and widened again in the first half of 2026.
While Brussels has been pushing back against the dumping of cheap Chinese goods, a separate industrial protection law and other anti-coercion measures are running into trouble from Beijing and at home.
Business groups question industrial policy proposals
The EU's Industrial Accelerator Act, proposed in March, aims to pull manufacturing investment back to Europe by favoring EU-based firms in public contracts and subsidies.
Foreign investments in key sectors would only be approved if European partners keep majority control, which Beijing has framed as discriminatory.
The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) warned last month that the draft act does little to counter the threat from cheaper Chinese rivals. In a position paper, it said the incentive to produce within the bloc has to be large enough to "cancel out the extra cost of producing locally."
Berlin's chief concern was that China could place new export curbs on rare earth minerals and the magnets made from them. China has a stranglehold on these elements, which are essential for German automotive, renewables and defense manufacturing.
Bloomberg last week cited unnamed German officials as saying that a new EU kill-switch could be a "second-strike weapon" if Beijing blocked those exports. Brussels is also considering unilateral limits on how many hybrid cars China can export to the EU, according to the same Bloomberg report.
EU weighs additional trade measures
Perhaps to avoid such an open confrontation, the EU and China reached a "shared understanding" last week at the EU-China trade talks in Beijing that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the European Union by more than half, according to EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic, who headed the European delegation.
Reports say the agreement would cap such Chinese imports at 350,000 vehicles annually, with the limit increasing by 6% each year over four years.
Overall, new hybrid-electric cars in the EU reached nearly 37% of all new cars registered from January to August, according to ACEA data.
MERICS, meanwhile, calculated that the EU is a more critical export market for China than the US. In the first half of the year, Chinese exports to the EU were $254 billion (€354 billion), versus $172 billion to the US.
This could give EU negotiators a firmer hand as they seek to avoid a trade war while protecting Europe from China's latest export glut.
"The EU has more leverage than it sometimes thinks," MERICS' Mischer told DW.
Edited by: Tim Rooks

Montenegro provisionally closes 3 more chapters in EU accession talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:46:20 UTC
17:46:20 KST

Talha Ozturk
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Montenegro provisionally closed three more negotiating chapters in its accession talks with the European Union, bringing the total number of provisionally closed chapters to 21, officials announced Monday evening.
The chapters, covering economic and monetary policy, statistics, and social policy and employment, were closed during an intergovernmental conference in Luxembourg.
Prime Minister Milojko Spajic said on US social media company X that the three chapters represent key pillars of European integration: responsible economic governance, reliable policymaking and social progress.
Thanking the European Commission and all 27 EU member states, Spajic congratulated the heads and members of the working groups involved in the negotiations.
“At this point, the government of Montenegro has fulfilled literally all obligations within its competence required for the final phase of negotiations,” he said.
Spajic expressed confidence that the necessary political consensus and compromise would be reached at other levels to bring the accession process to a successful conclusion.
“We continue to move forward decisively with our European partners toward Montenegro’s full EU membership in 2028,” he added.
EU urges further reforms
EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos welcomed the progress, saying reforms under the three chapters would contribute to price stability, provide governments with reliable data for better decision-making and strengthen workers’ rights and workplace safety.
Kos noted that nearly two-thirds of all negotiating chapters have now been closed, describing the finish line as within reach.
She urged political parties in both the government and opposition to put the interests of Montenegrin citizens first, work together and implement the remaining reforms without delay.
Montenegro’s Foreign Minister Ervin Ibrahimovic also welcomed the development, describing it as an important step toward strengthening the country’s economic system, improving statistical capacities and developing labor market and social policies.
“Every closed chapter represents a concrete result of our work, but also an additional responsibility to continue decisively and with dedication to fulfill all remaining obligations on the European agenda,” Ibrahimovic said.
He noted that the latest progress followed a successful Berlin Process ministerial meeting in Przno, where participants expressed strong support for the European future of the Western Balkans, particularly Montenegro’s accession efforts.
Ibrahimovic thanked EU member states, fellow foreign ministers and Commissioner Kos for their continued support.
He reaffirmed Montenegro’s commitment to completing accession negotiations and becoming a full member of the EU, saying the closure of three additional chapters demonstrated that the country’s European future was being built through concrete results.
Montenegro is widely regarded as the frontrunner for EU membership among Western Balkan candidate countries, having made the most progress in accession negotiations and aiming to join the bloc by 2028.
Montenegro declared independence from its state union with Serbia on June 3, 2006, following a referendum held on May 21 in which 55.5% of voters supported independence.
The Balkan country applied for EU membership in December 2008 and was granted candidate status in December 2010.
Montenegro formally launched accession negotiations with the EU in June 2012, becoming one of the frontrunners in the Western Balkans’ EU integration process.
The country joined NATO in June 2017 and has since maintained EU membership as a key foreign policy priority.
Montenegro has opened all 33 negotiating chapters and, with the latest three closures, has provisionally closed 21.
The government aims to complete accession negotiations and secure full EU membership by 2028, although accession will ultimately require approval from all EU member states.

Red Cross warns escalating Mideast hostilities could have 'disastrous' consequences for millions

08:45:44 UTC

Beyza Binnur Donmez
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) warned Tuesday that escalating hostilities in the Middle East could have "disastrous" consequences for tens of millions of people, urging immediate efforts to protect civilians.
"Civilians are paying an unacceptable price as a result of military operations in the Middle East," ICRC President Mirjana Spoljaric said in a statement.
She highlighted recent deaths, injuries, and destruction in Saudi Arabia, warning of the devastating impact of hostilities on civilians.
Deaths, displacement, and damage to civilian infrastructure in Yemen, including in Aden and Sanaa, have been mounting at an "alarming rate," Spoljaric noted.
"Civilians and civilian objects must be spared from attack," she stressed, reminding parties to conflicts of their obligation to distinguish between civilian and military targets.
Spoljaric warned that strikes on ports, airports, and essential infrastructure could have severe consequences for communities dependent on them.
"A further intensification of hostilities would be disastrous for tens of millions of people," she said, calling for urgent de-escalation to prevent further civilian suffering.
Saudi Arabia has faced a series of attacks in recent days on airports and civilian facilities amid an escalating military confrontation with the Yemeni Houthi group.
Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, before a Saudi-led coalition intervened in March 2015 in support of the country’s internationally recognized government.
The escalation began in July this year following a period of relative calm after a UN-brokered truce took effect in April 2022.

Yemeni army strikes Houthi forces in Taiz amid escalation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:45:08 UTC
17:45:08 KST

Aziz Ahmadi, Mohammed Sameai and Mohammad Sio
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
- UN says 216,000 people displaced in Yemen since August
Yemeni government forces carried out nine airstrikes Tuesday targeting Houthi fighters and military equipment in the southwestern Taiz province as escalation continues to rage across the country, according to the army.
The Taiz Military Axis Media Center said warplanes belonging to the Yemeni armed forces carried out five strikes in the Al-Dhabab area and four others in Al-Misrakh district.
The strikes targeted Houthi personnel and military equipment, the center said.
It added that clashes were also ongoing between government forces and Houthi fighters on the Al-Shaqab front south of Taiz.
The military did not provide details on casualties or damage.
Meanwhile, the Taiz office of Yemen’s Human Rights Ministry said in a statement late Monday that six civilians, including a girl, were killed and others were injured in Houthi shelling that struck densely populated villages in rural Taiz on Sunday.
In Taiz city, the office said 17 civilians, including five women and six children, were injured and seven homes were damaged in Houthi shelling over the previous 24 hours.
The office did not specify the nature or severity of the injuries or the extent of the damage
Early Tuesday, the non-governmental Taiz Human Rights Center accused the Houthis of shelling the area around Al-Safwa Hospital, a private facility in central Taiz city.
It said a shell landed near the hospital, causing material damage to patient rooms and frightening patients and medical staff.
Thousands displaced
Amid the continuing escalation, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said Monday evening that 216,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since August, including more than 172,000 from Taiz province.
The UN and humanitarian partners have so far reached around 143,000 people with emergency assistance, including food, hygiene supplies and cash support, the agency said.
On Saturday, local authorities in Taiz warned that the Houthis have tightened their siege on the province, threatening the lives, security and livelihoods of more than 6 million residents.
The Yemeni army launched Operation “Dawn of Yemen” last week, aimed at restoring state institutions and ending Houthi control of the capital Sanaa.
The developments are part of a military escalation that began in July, the most extensive since the relative calm that followed a UN-brokered truce that began in April 2022.
Yemen has been engulfed in war since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several of the country’s 22 provinces in September 2014, prompting an Arab coalition led by neighboring Saudi Arabia to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.
The Houthis fully control most northern and western provinces, including Sanaa, Saada, Amran, Dhamar, Al Hudaydah, Ibb, Al Mahwit and Raymah, while maintaining partial control over parts of Hajjah, Al-Bayda, Marib, Al-Jawf, Al-Dhalea and Taiz.
Government forces and their allies control the interim capital Aden, the eastern provinces of Al-Mahra and Hadramout, the southern provinces of Shabwa and Abyan, most of Lahj and Al-Dhalea, and parts of Taiz, Marib, Al-Jawf, Hajjah and Saada.

fifty oak trees and stone-paved clearing shape contemporary italian piazza by ghisellini architetti
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:45:07 UTC
17:45:07 KST

fifty oak trees and stone-paved clearing shape contemporary italian piazza by ghisellini architetti
ghisellini architetti reorganizes public square madre francesca cabrini around shaded gathering areas, layered planting, and integrated rainwater systems that reconnect the town center with the surrounding lowland landscape.
[ADVERTISEMENT]
a grid of oak trees frames porphyry-paved piazza in northern Italy
Ghisellini Architetti has redesigned Public Square Madre Francesca Cabrini as a contemporary Italian piazza framed by architecture and trees. Located in a small town in the lower Lodi area of Italy, the project reinterprets the open clearings of the region’s former lowland forests, creating a defined public space enclosed by three planted edges and the existing town hall.
Ghisellini Architetti reimagines the square as a tree-lined clearing
A continuous paving surface of Italian porphyry extends from north to south, aligning with the town hall’s facade and volume. Fifty oak trees representing three species are arranged in a 7-by-7 grid, providing shade and forming sheltered green spaces around the square. Paths weave through flowers, lawns, shrubs, and shade-tolerant undergrowth, while wooden benches, drinking fountains, trash bins, and bike racks support public use. The design team at Ghisellini Architetti uses concrete monoliths to separate pedestrian areas from vehicles.
A dual-level lighting system illuminates the square after dark
A two-level lighting system combines multi-projector poles with ground-level fixtures to illuminate the square after dark. The landscape and paving also integrate rainwater management and climate-responsive measures. Permeable surfaces and lawns help replenish groundwater and reduce summer heat, while the porphyry paving directs rainfall to an underground storage system. Collected water is reused to irrigate trees, lawns, and undergrowth, with excess water gradually released into the drainage network during heavy rainfall.
project info:
name: FOREST JUMP | Public Square ‘Madre Francesca Cabrini’
architect: Ghisellini Architetti | @ghisellini_architetti
location: Public Square Madre Francesca Cabrini, Lodi, Italy

Cyberattack on Supermarket Fridges in France Highlights Food Systems’ Vulnerability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:45:00 UTC
17:45:00 KST

Cyberattacks aren’t just stealing your passwords; they’re spoiling your food.
The Paris prosecutor’s office opened an investigation on Monday into an overnight cyberattack on refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets. Hackers raised the temperature of refrigerators and freezers, sparking fires and causing food to spoil.
In a statement to TIME, French retailer Les Mousquetaires, which runs supermarket chains Intermarche and Netto, said damage from the attack could amount to several million euros in losses.
“Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented,” Dominique Schelcher, CEO of French supermarket chain Cooperative U, posted on X.
France’s National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) confirmed to TIME that it is investigating the attack “both at the national level, to accompany potential victims, and at the European level to coordinate with its counterparts.”
The incident has raised concerns about the threat of cyberattacks on food security as food supply chains increasingly rely on network-connected systems.
Christophe Hansen, the European Union’s food and agriculture commissioner, condemned the attack, noting in a post on X: “Food security requires more attention at all levels, because the exploitation of food has become a reality.”
Hackers target connected refrigerators, spoiling food across hundreds of stores
BFM-TV, which first reported the attack, said hackers “managed to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores.” The French broadcaster said the cyberattack involved forcing a continuous defrost cycle, setting temperatures to 50°C (122°F). French newspaper Le Monde reported that hackers also extended the defrost cycle in some freezers and cold-storage rooms from one hour to eight hours to delay alarms.
Supermarkets typically use central control panels to manage multiple refrigeration units. Many of these control panels are connected to the internet to allow maintenance companies to remotely access them. But the French government said Monday that exposing a management interface to the internet is “contrary to best practices,” and that remote administration should be restricted to trusted IP addresses if it is necessary.
Monday’s attack affected two refrigeration management product series by Danish company Danfoss, AK-SC and AK-SM, according to an ANSSI alert.
Danfoss told news outlets that it was “aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems.” The company said the affected units “were running outdated firmware” and that it “long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions.”
Investigators have yet to publicly identify how attackers gained access to the Danfoss systems.
Around 180 Intermarche or its Netto brand supermarkets were targeted, parent company Les Mousquetaires told TIME, although BFM-TV reported a higher count of 300. At least 100 Cooperative U stores, 80 Carrefour outlets, 30 Monoprix stores and several E.Leclerc outlets were also affected, the retailers said. Independent grocery stores and butchers that use the same refrigeration system may also have been affected.
Intermarche CEO Thierry Cotillard told BFM-TV that the “unprecedented” attack resulted in losses amounting to “tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day.”
Two supermarkets in Alsace, Intermarche and Super U, reported losses of 270,000 euros, according to BFM-TV. An Intermarche in La Haye, Normandy, posted on Facebook that temperatures reached 80°C (176°F), causing some equipment to melt. Supermarket owners described throwing out nearly a dumpster’s worth of frozen food.
TIME has reached out to Danfoss and major French retailers for comment.
Growing cyber threat to food and agriculture
France’s ANSSI told TIME that it is coordinating with European counterparts given that stores in other countries may also use the same software and be at risk. Reuters reported, citing a cyber threat intelligence analyst, that Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany, and Belgium were affected. Internet scans found Danfoss refrigeration controllers exposed in South Africa, the U.S., the U.K., and other countries. France had the largest observed concentration, holding nearly 60% of the world’s exposed Danfoss controllers detected by scans, according to cyber intelligence firm U.K. Cyber Defence.
No other countries have confirmed related breaches so far.
The attack is also not the first time cyber incidents have disrupted food systems.
In late August, at least six U.S. military commissaries reported refrigeration outages, resulting in spoiled chilled and frozen products. Military investigators are investigating the outages, but have not commented on the nature of the investigation.
In June 2025, U.S. food distributor United Natural Foods also temporarily took certain systems offline during a suspected breach, which impacted order fulfillment and distribution.
Also on Monday, Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize took several systems offline as a precautionary measure amid “a security issue within its network.” The retailer operates the Netherlands’ biggest supermarket chain Albert Heijn, as well as several U.S. grocery brands, including Stop & Shop, Hannaford, and Food Lion. In a Monday statement, Dutch retail brands Albert Heijn, Etos, and Gall & Gall said they were dealing with a cybersecurity incident. There is no established link between these incidents and the French cyberattack.
Food systems are becoming increasingly exposed to cyberattacks as farms, processors, distributors, and supermarkets rely on network-connected equipment throughout their supply chains, analysts have warned. The Food and Ag-ISAC, a nonprofit industry group based in Washington, D.C., tracked 227 ransomware incidents in the food and agriculture sector from January through July, up 62% from the same period last year.
The European Union’s cybersecurity agency ENISA also noted that food production, processing and distribution were among the sectors most affected by ransomware claims in its latest E.U. threat assessment.
Prior to Monday’s attack in France, cybersecurity firm Claroty published an August report that showed how flaws in Danfoss’s AK-SM 800A controller could allow an intruder to bypass a login and gain control of software used to control supermarket refrigeration. Danfoss’s firmware updates included fixes for those flaws.

Warsaw Security Forum on the "theory of victory”, security, the future of NATO and the war in Ukraine
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:44:35 CEST
17:44:35 KST

Warsaw Security Forum on the "theory of victory”, security, the future of NATO and the war in Ukraine
12.10.2026
- The choice of place was not arbitrary - we picked Warsaw to show the theory of victory, as Poland has been demonstrating for the last few years how to place large investments for freedom to have strength with which to defend itself - said the Deputy Prime Minister W. Kosiniak-Kamysz during the Warsaw Security Forum.
On Monday, 12 October in Warsaw, the Deputy Prime Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz and Deputy Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka took part in the Warsaw Security Forum.
During the event, the Deputy Prime Minister met with the Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR), gen. Alexus Grynkewich. The Minister of National Defence has also attended a number of bilateral meetings and gave opening remarks for the panel “How Can Europe Build the Military Power It Needs?”.
- What to do for Europe to be stronger – that’s the topic of today’s debate. How to forge the difficult achievements and experiences of these last few months into being able to build strength and the resilience and defence potential for the whole of Europe? I will begin by saying that Europe has to take greater responsibility on itself. This is not just a buzzword anymore, but something European countries are fully aware of since the decision from the Hague in 2025 on spending 5% of GDP for defence by 2035. (…) We are the leader of using European funds from the SAFE programme – 44 billion euros, or almost a third of the entire amount went to Poland, and of that sum, two thirds has already been given to the Polish defence industry. Europe has to make its defence industry supply chain independent, that is the task that needs to be fulfilled first. (…) Military mobility is another matter with which the European Union has been struggling with for years now, and there is still no decision allowing for the free movement of troops without prior approval of all the regions or lands. This needs to end as soon as possible. (…) Poland wants to take greater responsibility for its partners, especially on the eastern flank of NATO. The more American soldiers are stationed in Poland, if we were to have a permanent base and presence of US troops, the more responsibility for the eastern flank of NATO we can take. (…) Europe has to do more not to replace America. We want an alliance with the United States. A lasting, predictable alliance, not just in the areas of intelligence exchange or military capabilities, but also for our defence industries. I believe that the defence industry strategy should be highlighted as part of plans for NATO 3.0, show it prominently. Things like moving production lines and service centres to Europe, for example those for the Patriot missiles
- said the Minister of National Defence during the Warsaw Security Forum.
Earlier, the Deputy Prime Minister was present for the discussion of gen. Grynkewich with prof. Katarzyna Pisarska, the head of Warsaw Security Forum, entitled: “The Theory of Victory: How To Achieve Military Success in Deterrence and Defence Against Russia?”.
- NATO is a defensive alliance. However, no one should mistake our defensive nature for weakness or lack of determination. If anyone was so reckless as to attack us, we will fight. (…) If we are attacked, we are ready to fight tonight, but we will not fall into complacency. We will still prepare and train every day, so tomorrow we will be even more ready, and even more the day after that. (…) If an adversary will threaten escalation, rattling their sabre, or actually decides on escalation during a conflict, this will not fracture our Alliance. On the contrary – it will make us even more united
- noted the Supreme Allied Commander Europe gen. Alexus Grynkewich, presenting his „theory of victory” during the Warsaw Security Forum.
Warsaw Secuirty Forum is an annual conference, organised by the Casimir Pulaski Foundation. WSF is a place for exchanging experiences and views on the security policy of the member states of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation and the European Union, as well as partner countries. The guests are high-level country representatives, ambassadors, politicians and experts in international affairs and security.
- We do not want to waste time. Poland remembers, especially from the time of the Second World War, when not everything was yet ready, that the only boundless thing was the bravery of the Polish soldier and everything else had limits – the alliances had limits, deliveries had limits, supplies had limits. We do not want to have this history lesson, which our ancestors have learned once before, in their experience and the experience of all the Polish families, we do not want to repeat it
- noted the Deputy Prime Minister.
On the sidelines of the Forum, the Deputy Prime Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz met with the US Permanent Representative to NATO Matthew Whitaker, the Chair of the NATO Military Committee, adm. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone and the Ministers of Defence of the Netherlands, Hungary, Norway, Kosovo and Belgium.
- I believe that this is the moment when the US government and companies will agree to co-production with Europe. The cooperation between the European Union and America is necessary. We have the SAFE instrument. We have decided to invest almost all the funds into our defence industry to make ourselves independent from other supply chains. (…) The lesson from Ukraine is that on the first day it is important how much equipment we have in place, but on the second and further days it is important to maintain what we have. This is something we are preparing for. Is Poland open to companies from other countries? Yes, this is one of the ideas present in the Ministry of National Defence. If a company wants to sell something to the Polish government, then we don’t look only at the price and quality. We are looking at four additional conditions. The first is a maintenance centre, co-production, local suppliers or at least investing in local training. So there is no chance for anyone to sell us something without investing in the region. This is also a matter of maintenance
- stressed the Secretary of State in the Ministry of National Defence Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who took part in the panel entitled: “How Can Europe Build the Military Potential It Needs?”.

Ukraine’s swimming robot can tow 10 tons, its maker says. Hook up a gun, and the shells ride aboard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:43:52 UTC
17:43:52 KST

Ukraine’s amphibious ground robot UNEX UGV can tow artillery guns, its project lead said in a video interview, Militarnyi reported on 13 October. The electric platform from ABRIS Design Group (ABRIS DG) also swims, climbs, and hauls cargo on its own deck.
The Defense Ministry’s robot tally, kept in its DELTA system, counts supply and evacuation runs. It logged 25,143 of them in August, a monthly figure that has climbed all year. In April, then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said the goal was for robots to handle all frontline logistics. A robot that brings a gun and its shells to a position adds artillery moves to that workload.
A gun behind, shells aboard
The robot can pull a gun or another wheeled vehicle of up to 10 metric tons (about 22,000 lb), the project lead said. Ammunition can ride aboard, so the gun and its rounds reach the position together. No crew has to go with them, he said, and the team has already demonstrated the setup. On its own deck, ABRIS DG says, the robot carries up to 1.7 tons (3,750 lb) on land and 1.25 tons (2,760 lb) on water.
ABRIS DG said US Army testers ran UNEX through scenarios that included towing Joint Light Tactical Vehicles (JLTVs), which are armored US military trucks. The trials took place at the Army’s XTech competition in Vilseck, Germany, in March 2026. UNEX was picked as one of five winners, the company said.
Swims, climbs, backtracks
The robot can float for more than an hour. The team has already crossed the Desna River and narrow stretches of the Dnipro with it, the project lead said. Ultra-low-pressure tires spread its weight over soft ground and swamps. ABRIS DG says it climbs obstacles up to one meter (3.3 ft) high and drives out of water onto ice.
Ukraine turned ground robots into a frontline workhorse. Its first competitive tender may reward cheap copies over proven machines, an officer warns
Operators steer it via Starlink or radio. An escort drone can add an overhead view to the robot’s own cameras. If the link drops, the robot retraces its route to where the signal last held.
It runs on a Ukrainian-made 78 kWh battery. The project lead puts its work time at up to six hours and its range at up to 120 km (75 miles), with a top speed of 20 km/h (12 mph). Load and terrain cut into those figures, he added. With a generator now in development, a mission should stretch to about 12–14 hours, he said.
The robot is not built for the zero line, the project lead said. It works 20–30 km behind the front, at night, where armor would add little. Developers also plan demining and air defense versions. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry codified the robot and cleared it for use in its forces in April 2025.

- Ukraine’s Frodo robot carries wounded soldier in first reported evacuation

The escalation in Yemen is a turning point
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:42:55 UTC
17:42:55 KST

The escalation in Yemen is a turning point
The risk of a region-wide war is increasing, but if cooler heads prevail, a peaceful arrangement can still be reached.
Yemen is witnessing a major military escalation that has once again brought the western coast and the area around the Bab al-Mandeb strait to the forefront of regional developments. Operation Yemen’s Dawn, launched by the forces loyal to the internationally recognised Yemeni government, has produced some results.
Government forces have advanced towards the strait of Bab al-Mandeb and are now fighting against reinforced Houthi positions. Clashes continue in parts of Dhubab District and around Dhubab Airport.
The central question now is whether these military moves can bring about a lasting change in the balance of power and whether they will widen the confrontation or open the way for a new negotiating process.
Control of Bab al-Mandeb
Fighting has concentrated around Bab al-Mandeb because of its strategic position in global trade and energy flows. It is especially significant to the parties to the Yemeni conflict because control of the coastline, islands and surrounding highlands offers varying capabilities for surveillance, military deployment and threats to maritime traffic.
An advance along the coast may enable government forces to retake key positions and restrict the Houthis’ space for manoeuvre. However, it does not, by itself, guarantee the security of the strait or eliminate threats to navigation.
Even if the Houthis lose coastal positions, they could still retain their ability to launch attacks in the Red Sea. Threats to maritime traffic do not necessarily depend on direct control of the strait; they also depend on the availability of missiles, drones, launch platforms, supply networks and the ability to operate from other locations.
As operations move from the coastal strip into the highlands, particularly the Kahbub Mountains in Lahj governorate and the highlands to the west and south-west of Taiz governorate, the challenges posed by the terrain, defence, movement and supply become more severe.
In this context, three distinct levels must be differentiated: retaking coastal positions, consolidating military control over them and establishing a sustainable capacity to secure the strait and its surrounding area. Confusing these levels may lead either to an exaggerated assessment of the operation’s results or to an underestimation of the adversary’s ability to continue fighting.
Unity and cohesion
Recent statements by Dr Rashad Al-Alimi, president of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, signal a shift in objectives: from containing the Houthi threat to restoring state institutions and liberating Sanaa.
This shift gives the ongoing fighting a national dimension that goes beyond limited gains on the ground. Its success, however, remains contingent on the government forces’ ability to unify command, secure supplies and coordinate the various military formations.
Containing divisions within the components of the government—particularly over the southern issue—is essential to preserving gains and preventing the confrontation from turning into an internal conflict.
Success requires coordination among participating formations, avoidance of competition over spheres of influence and the linking of military gains to security and political governance capable of preventing fighting between factions.
This is especially important because the formations playing the most effective role in the coastal battles, the Southern Giants Brigades, originate from the southern governorates.
The regional dimension
The Houthi escalation is difficult to understand in isolation from the Iran war. Iran’s support for the group is well-known, but recent media reports have also revealed the extent of it. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps reportedly has directed Houthi movements along the coast and encouraged escalation against Saudi Arabia, with commitments to provide further support.
Control of Bab al-Mandeb is strategically important to Iran and its allies, as increased pressure there can provide more leverage in the Iran conflict.
For Saudi Arabia, involvement in the Yemen conflict is driven by direct security concerns and a desire to reduce threats to its territory and nearby maritime routes.
Against this backdrop, a Saudi response to the deadly airport attacks appears highly likely. Riyadh may be less inclined to limit itself to familiar exchanges along existing front lines and could instead target sites or capabilities of greater importance within the Houthis’ military structure. What form the response takes may reflect efforts to impose significant costs without immediately widening the confrontation into a broader regional war.
At the Gulf level, collective military participation appears less certain. The attacks could prompt an emergency GCC meeting, stronger political statements, or greater defensive coordination, but reviving a joint military campaign against the Houthis would be more difficult. Gulf states no longer share the same degree of strategic alignment over Yemen, while differences, particularly between Saudi and Emirati priorities, continue to constrain collective action.
Pakistan and Turkiye, for their part, have announced support for Saudi Arabia under the Mecca Pact, although the exact parameters of their participation are yet to be defined. The current escalation may therefore test whether these partnerships remain political and defensive frameworks or translate into practical military support, including stronger air defence deployments.
US involvement also remains possible, but any direct role would likely be limited. Previous US intervention in Yemen has focused more on deterrence, maritime security and containing threats rather than on decisively shifting the battlefield balance in favour of the government forces.
An expanding confrontation does not automatically mean that all parties seek an open war. Some may use escalation to improve their deterrence or negotiating position, although the risk of miscalculation remains.
What happens next
Developments in the Yemen war in the near future depend on the government forces’ ability to hold the positions they have retaken, secure the area around the strait and the connecting roads and remove the Houthi threat from the highlands. If these conditions are met, the balance of military and political pressure could shift, though this would not necessarily end the Houthis’ maritime threat.
However, if the advance stalls at positions that are difficult to overcome and the Houthis are able to continue using missiles and drones to conduct counterattacks, this could create a protracted confrontation. A war of attrition could have a devastating humanitarian and economic impact not just on Yemen, but across the region.
The risk of escalation and region-wide war may still push the parties to seek an understanding or an arrangement to halt the fighting. Turning military advances into a settlement, however, would require addressing broader political and security issues, including power-sharing arrangements, mutual guarantees and the security of maritime routes.
In other words, the ongoing coastal battle could become a gateway to a broader change in the course of Yemen’s crisis rather than another round in a protracted war.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

MI5 chief Ken McCallum confirms Russia did interfere in Brexit referendum - but says it had little impact
Dan Sabbagh
Dan Sabbagh is the Guardian’s defence and security editor.
MI5 chief Ken McCallum said today that Moscow did attempt to interfere in the 2016 Brexit referendum with anti-EU coverage on RT and Sputnik media and via troll social media accounts. But there was a big difference between “what may have been attempted and what actually resulted”, he added.
The head of the Security Service said that he agreed strongly with what the prime minister had said on Sunday and Monday, when he raised the issue of attempted Russian interference a decade ago – though Burnham then backed off when he was challenged by the Conservatives as to whether this meant he regarded the Brexit vote as illegitimate.
McCallum did not put any new evidence into the public domain but cited already known concerns about Russian broadcasters who “came in pretty strongly around the time of the referendum” in favour of Brexit. He also said that “there was a second line of interference attempted through [internet] trolls”.
However, he argued there was no evidence to suggest the result of the Brexit vote had been swayed as a result of the effort, which is generally believed to have been marginal, and said that it would be to Russia’s benefit if the issue was talked about further.
He explained:
It is up to us how far we allow our adversaries to divide us.
I’m a little bit worried that if we all stay in this debate for another few days, the Russian trolls who didn’t appear to do all that much at various points over the years, they’ll be delighted they are front page news once again despite the comparative unimpressedness of what they do at all points along the journey.
How MI5 chief's comments undermine Tory claim Burnham was spreading 'conspiracy theories' about Brexit referendum
The statement from Ken McCallum confirming Russian interference in the Brexit referendum is a bit awkward for Katie Lam, the shadow communities secretary. On Sunday she wrote an open letter to Angela Rayner, the communities secretary, about Andy Burnham saying Russia did interfere in the 2016 vote. Lam said in her letter these claims were “unproven” and in a post on social media she said: “The prime minister is spreading conspiracy theories about the Brexit referendum.”
(You can argue that the claim Russia decided the outcome of the referendum is a conspiracy theory, but this is not something Burnham did say in his Rest is Politics interview, or ever has said.)
