Standards watchdog warns Burnham of growing concern that wealthy donors exercising 'undue influence' on politics
Andy Burnham has been warned that progress on beefing up ethical standards in public life is “stalling”.
The comment came in the first annual report to the PM from the Ethics and Integrity Commission, the body set up last year to replace the Committee on Standards in Public Life.
Doug Chalmers, the former deputy chief of defence staff and master of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, has to report every year to the PM on “the health of standards in public life” and he has delivered his first update in the form of an open letter.
In it, he says:
A number of positive steps have been taken since the July 2024 general election towards strengthening England’s standards system, but progress is at risk of stalling. Your personal leadership is needed to accelerate standards reform and to ensure that the core values and standards expressed in the principles of public life remain at the heart of government and our public services.
In particular, Chalmers says there is a growing concern that wealthy donors are exercising an “undue influence” on UK politics because parties are ever more reliant on them for money.
He says:
The longstanding debate around the merits of a universal annual cap on permissible donations is receiving increased attention from parliamentarians and the media in light of the trend for large donations to originate from a small number of donors.
Political parties play a vital role in our democracy and need significant sums of money to function, yet the reliance on large donations from a limited number of sources creates the risk that donors may exert undue influence, or may be perceived to do so, which is damaging for trust in politics.
Chalmers does not mention Reform UK in his letter, but his comment seems in part influenced by the alarm generated by the news last month that two cryptocurrency billionaires are between them giving £72m to Nigel Farage’s party.
Whether the donations will comply with a new election law going through parliament remains to be determined, but ministers are under pressure to tighten the law further, with some MPs saying the amount an individual can give to a party should be capped.
In his letter, Chalmers says a cap is “likely to affect the major parties in different ways” and he says any reform should not be seen as partisan. “This will also ensure reforms have democratic legitimacy and are more likely to endure,” he says.
The letter also urges Burnham to press on with action to strengthen standards in other areas, including local government and lobbying.

Andy Burnham will take Britain back into European Union, Neil Kinnock claims
Good morning. In his long statement to MPs yesterday, Andy Burnham was evasive when asked whether he wanted his planned renegotiation of Britain’s relationship with the EU to result in a Labour-led government, after the next election, rejoining. Yes, sure, sure, sure. His commitment is authentic. He really does understand from the grassroots up why restoring what I think of as normality in our continent is vital for every party economically, politically, culturally, all in security terms, and is able to articulate it in language that people can understand. So yeah, he is definitely.
Asked about Burnham playing down his desire to revisit the referendum result during the Makerfield byelection campaign, Kinnock claimed this was just a matter of deciding when to have this debate.
Andy’s not changed direction. He’s always been a committed pro-European. In the byelection, he rightly didn’t make a noise about it. That’s tomorrow’s debate. Simply because the byelection wasn’t about Europe. It was about winning Makerfield in order to enable him to become leader of the party. That’s all it was about.
Kinnock was interviewed by Antonello Guerrera who asked how, as someone who inherited a leftwing party and dragged it to the right, Kinnock felt about a sucessor taking Labour to the left. Kinnock said he thought Burnham’s approach was right.
It’s common sense. It’s not left and right. Andy’s view of the engagement of the state is about what Winston Churchill did in the 1950s, and I don’t remember Churchill being thought of as on the left. Andy’s a socialist, but he’s a very common-sense socialist. He’s very rational. He’s cool, not just with his dark blue T-shirt, but in his thinking, and he’s advanced a hell of a lot in the last 10–12 years in terms of his understanding of the absolute importance of utility, of usefulness in politics.
That’s what puts us, basically, he and I, on the same spot. Of course he’s on the left. I’m on the left. We’re socialists, but we are prompted by the usefulness of the application of ideas.
We have got a lobby briefing later and no doubt No 10 will clarify that its understanding of Burnham’s position on rejoining the EU is not quite the same as Kinnock’s. Kinnock is a former vice president of the European Commission, and an ardent pro-European, and perhaps there is some wishful thinking in what he says. But he is also a good friend of Burnham, and an astute observer of Labour politics. You will have to decide for yourself if he is right.

LVMH sales miss growth forecasts as China luxury demand slows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:41:04 UTC
17:41:04 KST

LVMH, the world's leading luxury group, said its sales edged higher in the third quarter despite a slowdown in demand in China hitting its fashion and leather goods segment.
The fashion giant, once Europe’s most valuable listed company, reported revenue of €18.5 billion in the three months to the end of September.
The firm, whose brands include Louis Vuitton, Dior, Celine and drinks maker Hennessy, saw a revenue increase of 1.2% year on year in the third quarter, after a 0.1% rise in the second quarter and a 5.9% fall in the first.
However, organic sales growth, which excludes currency movements and changes to the group's business portfolio, fell short of expectations. Growth slowed to 1% in the third quarter from 3% in the second.
Overall, in the first nine months, sales were €57.1 billion, with organic sales up 2%.
The company praised its diverse business portfolio in a statement, saying it provided resilience in an uncertain geopolitical and economic environment.
LVMH said sales growth was good in the United States, Europe and Japan, but it faced a less favourable environment in China.
As a result, the fashion and leather goods segment saw sales drop 5% on an organic basis as weaker demand in the world's second-largest economy weighed on the business. The decline was steeper than the roughly 2% fall expected by analysts, according to Deutsche Bank.
Louis Vuitton also saw its public image take a hit in China after suing local tea company Molly Tea for copying its logo. While it won the case, the dispute provoked a wave of indignation on social media and calls to boycott the brand.
Overall, the quarter proved to be a setback for the fashion and leather goods segment, as the drop in sales followed the division posting its first organic sales gain in two years in the previous quarter.
But LVMH's selective retailing division, which includes the Sephora perfume and cosmetics retail chain, posted an 8% organic sales increase, while the watches and jewellery and wines and spirits segments both managed 6% organic gains.
Deutsche Bank analysts said the results could prompt further cuts to earnings forecasts for the second half of 2026 and 2027.
“It is hard to see what could change investor sentiment in the short term,” they wrote, although they viewed the weakness as cyclical rather than structural.
"Overall, recovery is taking longer due to the weaker Chinese demand, but the company do not see it as a structural issue. Brand initiatives are producing results and they expect these bottom-up measures to be more gradual," they wrote.
LVMH's share price has dropped nearly 40% since the start of the year. In September, L'Oréal overtook the group as France's most valuable listed company. LVMH’s share price was down more than 1.6% at around 10am CEST in Paris.

Lithuanian fintech is growing abroad and strengthening the export of financial services

In Lithuania, licensed electronic money and payment institutions had 2.5 million active customers in 2025 – 14 percent more than a year ago. As many as 87 percent of them were foreign customers, according to data from the Bank of Lithuania. According to the Lithuanian Fintech Association, these results reveal the improving opportunities for the country’s fintech companies to grow in international markets and strengthen the export potential of Lithuania’s financial services.
The international orientation of the sector is also visible in the business client segment. Of the 146 thousand legal entities served by electronic money and payment institutions, only slightly more than a fifth were established in Lithuania. This shows that foreign companies also widely use the payment services of institutions licensed here.
As Greta Ranonytė, CEO of the Lithuanian Fintech Association, notes, the large share of foreign clients shows that the services of payment companies licensed in Lithuania are in demand on the international market. According to her, this provides opportunities for companies to grow and strengthen Lithuania’s role as a financial services center.
“Lithuania’s small domestic market does not limit the opportunities of payment companies operating here. The expertise of specialists, technological solutions, payment infrastructure and opportunities provided by the regulatory environment accumulated in our country help them to serve foreign residents and businesses. For Lithuania, this is an opportunity to expand the fintech sector, export of financial services and create high-value-added jobs here, even though the users of the services are in other EU countries,” she says.
Both income and payment volumes grew
The expansion of the customer base was accompanied by growing revenues of electronic money and payment institutions, which constitute an important part of the Lithuanian fintech sector. According to the Bank of Lithuania, the revenues of these institutions from licensed activities in 2025 increased by 13 percent and reached EUR 643.1 million. The total amount of payment transactions increased by 5 percent over the year to EUR 161.6 billion.
At the end of 2025, there were 117 electronic money and payment institutions operating in Lithuania.
As G. Ranonytė notes, when assessing Lithuania’s positions in the international financial technology market, it is important to take into account the ability of companies operating here to expand their activities and earn income.
“It would be too narrow to judge the development of the sector solely by the number of licenses issued. What is also important is the scale of activities carried out by companies, how many clients they serve and whether they are able to retain them. Growing income and payment volumes show that licensed institutions in Lithuania are expanding their activities. For the further growth of the fintech sector, it is important to invest in the quality of services, technologies and people who help compete in different markets,” she says.
Currently, there are a total of almost 250 financial technology companies operating in Lithuania, employing about 7.8 thousand specialists.

AI models improve long-term flood forecasting: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:38:25 CST
17:38:25 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- An international research team has developed artificial intelligence (AI) models that could improve long-term flood forecasting, helping communities get warnings weeks ahead of floods.
Researchers used two decades of historical precipitation and streamflow data from the DuPage River basin in Illinois, the United States, to develop deep learning models incorporating attention mechanisms to identify patterns in rainfall and river flow, according to a statement released Tuesday by Australia's University of Technology Sydney (UTS).
By combining the models' predictions, the team improved forecasting accuracy, with the ensemble deep learning models reducing prediction errors by about 38 percent and the proposed fusion framework improving predictive performance by about 47 percent, according to the study published in the Journal of Hydrologic Engineering.
The approach remained highly accurate for forecasts up to 12 weeks ahead, said UTS Professor Amir H. Gandomi, the study's co-author, stressing that additional warning time could help communities prepare for floods.
The findings could have implications for flood risk management, including disaster preparedness, infrastructure resilience and water resource management, according to the team.
"Ultimately, the goal is not simply to predict floods more accurately, but to turn better predictions into better decisions," Gandomi said. ■

SOFIA, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Drones have attacked two merchant ships in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria, and at least one of them has sunk, the country's Government Information Service said on Tuesday.
At an extraordinary meeting with the country's security council, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said one ship was attacked around 1:30 a.m. local time (2230 GMT Monday), about 18 nautical miles east of the town of Byala.
Bulgarian authorities rescued all 15 crew members aboard the vessel, including seven Ukrainian nationals and eight Azerbaijani nationals, Radev said.
The ship, named "Chelsea 3," was flying the Maltese flag, registered in Odesa, Ukraine, and Ukrainian-owned, according to Radev. The crew said three aerial drones struck the vessel.
The crew members were safely transported to the port of Varna, where five of them received medical treatment, he added.
The information service said authorities also received information about another merchant ship that was hit about 17 nautical miles east of Krapets. The vessel sank, and one crew member was rescued.
The incident marked the second drone attack on merchant ships near Bulgaria within a week. On Oct. 6, unidentified drones sank one merchant ship and set another on fire about 70 nautical miles east of Byala, within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
"Another attack on merchant ships in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters is absolutely unacceptable," Radev said.
Bulgaria's permanent representatives to NATO and the European Union have been notified, Radev said, adding that he was due to speak with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. ■

2026-10-13
08:38:00 UTC
17:38:00 KST

Türkiye’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations Ahmet Yıldız called on Israel to end its "reckless acts” in Syria and fully comply with the 1974 Disengagement Agreement.
"Lasting stability is essential for Syria to rebuild its economy, attract investment, and participate in regional energy and connectivity projects,” Yıldız told a session of the U.N. Security Council on Monday.
"Israel’s continued violations of Syrian sovereignty and territorial integrity undermine these prospects and show disregard for international law,” he said.
"The situation is particularly alarming in southern Syria, where continued military incursions and expansionist actions and words are getting out of control,” he added.
Yıldız said Israel’s recent resumption of activities along the so-called "Sufa 53 line” in Quneitra was a further attempt to undermine the 1974 agreement and impose a fait accompli on the ground. "These reckless acts must stop,” he said.
He urged Israel to comply with the 1974 agreement and relevant Security Council resolutions, particularly Resolution 497, and to withdraw from the occupied Syrian Golan Heights. "A stable, sovereign and unified Syria capable of securing its borders, defeating terrorist organizations and contributing to regional peace and economic cooperation serves the interests of all, including Israel,” he added.
"The dissolution of the so-called SDF has opened a new chapter in the integration process,” Yıldız said. "Remaining arrangements should be finalized and fully implemented without delay, in a manner that reinforces Syria’s sovereignty, unity and social cohesion,” he added.
Yıldız described the fight against terrorism as "a critical priority” and welcomed Damascus’ cooperation with the global coalition for the enduring defeat of Daesh. "Security and economic recovery must advance hand in hand,” he said.
On refugees, Yıldız said the number of Syrians under temporary protection in Türkiye once exceeded 4 million and now stands at around 2.2 million.
He said returns have been gradual because of economic conditions, security concerns and Israeli incursions. Since Bashar Assad’s fall on Dec. 8, 2024, Israel has expanded its military operations in Syria, moving troops into the Golan buffer zone and nearby positions. Syria demands the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the areas they occupied and maintains its commitment to the 1974 Disengagement Agreement. Israel claims its movements are driven by security considerations.
Addressing the same session, Syria’s U.N. representative Ibrahim Olabi said those claiming to seek security "should not be killing Syrian citizens within Syrian territory.”
"They should know very well that there is only one path towards security, which is international legitimacy and the resolutions of the (U.N. Security) Council,” the envoy said.
"Every time they open fire on Syria, they are, as the world has witnessed, at the same time opening fire on itself locally and internationally,” he added. Olabi also urged support for economic recovery, investment, job creation and reconstruction. He called for help rehabilitating schools, hospitals and water and electricity networks and for resources and expertise to clear mines and other remnants of war.

Xi calls for decisive progress in Healthy China advancement
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:37:48 CST
17:37:48 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, delivers an important speech during a national meeting on health in Beijing, capital of China. The meeting was held in Beijing on Monday and Tuesday. (Xinhua/Xie Huanchi)
BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping has called for efforts to firmly follow a path with Chinese characteristics in developing the country's health programs, to secure decisive progress in the Healthy China Initiative over the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030).
Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks at a national meeting on health held in Beijing on Monday and Tuesday.
Xi stressed that people's health is a key benchmark of a nation's prosperity and strength.
Since the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012, the Party has made a major decision to launch the Healthy China Initiative, promoting the establishment of the world's largest systems of medical services, traditional medicine, disease prevention and control, and healthcare security, said Xi, noting that the country has achieved historic accomplishments and made all-round progress in healthcare.
He said the goal is to build a Healthy China, where health services are ensured in a balanced, inclusive, high-quality and efficient manner.
Xi stressed that people's health should be factored into all policies and reflected in every aspect of work.
Prevention, he said, is the most cost-effective and efficient approach to protecting public health. He called for greater emphasis on foundational health work, addressing risks at their source, and encouraging the public to adopt a sound understanding of health and take an active role in managing their own well-being.
He also called for a stronger disease prevention and control system to guard against large-scale outbreaks.
Xi underscored the need to optimize the functions and structural layout of medical institutions so that people can access medical care close to home and receive effective treatment.
He also urged efforts to improve mechanisms for the preservation and innovative development of traditional Chinese medicine, strengthen basic research and original innovation in the health sector, and enhance the patient experience.
Xi stressed that coordinating the development and regulation of medical services, medical insurance, and pharmaceuticals should be a key priority in reforming China's medical and healthcare systems.
He also called for efforts to train and develop a sufficient number of highly qualified medical professionals.
Efforts will also be made to actively promote the building of a global community of health for all, work with other countries to address major challenges in the health sector, and continuously improve the health and well-being of people around the world, he said. ■

Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:37:22 CEST
17:37:22 KST

Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti
said the government will continue to take a prudent approach to
managing the public finances as there are storm clouds ahead as
he presented its Public Finance Planning Document (DPFP) in the
Lower House on Tuesday.
                                    
The DPFP features the government's plan to use the escape clause
granted by the EU for 0.3% budget deviations for both energy and
defence investments in the 2027 budget law.
                                    
"Planning three years ahead (in the DPFP) is highly complex
especially amid great turbulence, and updates come weekly, as
IMF data show," Giorgetti said.
                                    
"The fundamental premise underlying our reasoning is that when
the weather forecast predicts a storm, it is wise to check the
vessel's condition before heading out to the open sea, and that
is precisely what we have sought to do in recent years.
                                    
"We believe it is essential to stay on this course at a time
when storm clouds are gathering on the horizon.
                                    
"This document is a reflection of that approach, aiming to
adhere to the path of fiscal consolidation and meet the targets
set by the new European governance framework, with a view to
exiting the (excessive-deficit) procedure in the spring,
conditions permitting".
                                    
Italy's budget deficit needs to come within the 3% of GDP
threshold for it to be able to emerge from the procedure.
                                    
Giorgetti has said he is expects this to be the case for 2026,
after the deficit came in at 3.1% for 2025, before going up to
3.4% in 2027 with the use of the escape clause.
                                    
"The request to adjust the budget in order to activate the
national escape clause for defence and energy is a deliberate
departure from the prudent stance I have previously advocated,"
Giorgetti said.
                                    
"These are measures that the Commission acknowledges, and that
the markets have deemed sustainable within the framework of
ensuring the long-term sustainability of Italian public debt".

Chiang rejected claims that his campaign had proposed Oct. 31, saying the date came from the two broadcasters. He said organizers needed at least two weeks to prepare, making Oct. 31 the earliest possible date, per Newtalk.
Chiang said his team had agreed to the date despite existing commitments. He criticized Shen's representatives for leaving the talks without approving it, questioning whether they had the authority to make decisions.

Police detain leaders of India’s ‘cockroach’ movement at New Delhi protest

Police in the Indian capital have detained leaders of the country’s youth-led “cockroach” movement after they jumped barricades to enter a popular protest site in New Delhi while calling for the resignation of the country’s chief election commissioner (CEC) over voter list revisions.
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Ashutosh Ranka, Saurav Das and Ajinkya Shinde were among about 20 volunteers who “sneaked” into Jantar Mantar to “reclaim” the popular protest site and were detained on Tuesday.
CJP supporters and opposition parties have held protests nearly every day this month to demand CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over the revisions, which critics say favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Thousands joined a protest march on Monday, after a clampdown foiled CJP plans for a weekend demonstration. Earlier, police detained thousands of protesters, including CJP leaders, over the weekend.
Following the mass detentions, Human Rights Watch urged the government to stop “the ill-treatment” and “arbitrary” arrests of protesters and to allow people to protest peacefully.
“The Modi government should stop throwing young protesters in jail and instead engage with them to address concerns over the right to vote and fairness of elections,” Elaine Pearson, HRW’s Asia director, said in a statement on Tuesday.
“Peaceful protest and freedom of expression are fundamental rights protected under the international human rights law that India’s leaders claim to uphold,” she added.
The Delhi Police announced on Monday that the Jantar Mantar open-air astronomical observatory was no longer designated an official protest site and that three new venues had been identified for demonstrations.
However, CJP leaders and supporters went ahead with their protest plan at Jantar Mantar and were taken into custody.
“You cannot denotify the resistance,” CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke said on X after their detention.
A video posted to his account shows about a dozen volunteers jumping a gate and barricades to reach the site, where they waved the Indian flag and chanted slogans as police arrived and detained them.
The Delhi Police did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Reuters news agency.
In an earlier post, Dipke said the government’s efforts to block the site would do nothing to deter their campaign.
“If Modi thinks taking away Jantar Mantar will put an end to protests, he is mistaken. Jantar Mantar is not just a location but a spirit of resistance that nobody can ever take away,” he said.
The youth-led movement, which has mobilised protests in recent months over a range of issues, is among the biggest political challenges to the BJP and Modi in his 12 years in power.
The Election Commission has denied favouring any party with its revisions to the voter list and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Shareholders of Taiwan Cement Corp. (TCC) approved a plan Monday to take subsidiary Cimpor International Holdings public in Europe.
Chair Nelson Chang (張安平) said the listing would provide funding for TCC’s European operations and broaden the company’s access to local capital markets, per Anue.
Following the listing, TCC would retain control of Cimpor International, the subsidiary that will house its cement and concrete businesses in Turkey, Portugal, and Africa. The company would continue to include the subsidiary in its consolidated financial statements.
Potential listing venues include the London Stock Exchange and Euronext, TCC said. Cimpor International’s public float will be at least 10% of its total issued shares.
Europe accounts for a growing share of TCC’s revenue, Business Next reported. According to data released during the shareholder meeting in May, Europe contributed 42%, surpassing Taiwan at 38% and China at 19.47%.
In recent years, TCC has sought to transform itself from a cement maker into a diversified energy group with operations across Asia, Europe, and Africa, per Business Next.
In 2024, TCC fully acquired the Portuguese cement group Cimphor’s businesses in Europe and Africa through OYAK Group, a Turkish holding company.
In September 2026, TCC authorized its Dutch subsidiary to acquire Ivano-Frankivsk Cement, Ukraine’s second-largest cement maker, for up to 750 million euros (NT$27 billion). The deal remains subject to government approval.
Chair Chang said AI is creating new demands for the cement industry. TCC will continue developing low-carbon, durable materials, upgrading its plants, improving energy efficiency, and investing in renewable energy, energy storage, and recycling, he said.
The European listing plan requires approval from regulators in both Europe and Taiwan, Chang said. The offering price, number of shares to be issued, and final listing venue have yet to be determined.

Fertility Treatment in Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:35:42 UTC
17:35:42 KST

This article explores why Iran has become an option for international patients seeking fertility treatment. It covers the global prevalence of infertility, Iran’s position in reproductive medicine, and factors such as specialized treatments, accessibility, and comparatively lower costs. The article also introduces VitaLife Fertility Center and its support for international patients seeking IVF, egg donation, surrogacy, and other fertility services in Iran.
Infertility is no longer a health challenge limited to a small group of couples. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), approximately one in six people of reproductive age experience infertility during their lifetime, making access to effective and affordable fertility care a growing global health priority.
As demand for assisted reproductive technologies continues to grow, patients are increasingly looking beyond their home countries for fertility treatment. Cost, access to advanced reproductive technologies, legal restrictions, waiting times, and the availability of specialized services can all influence where international patients seek care.
Among the destinations receiving increasing attention is Iran, where assisted reproductive medicine has developed substantially over the past several decades.
Infertility can result from male factors, female factors, a combination of both, or unexplained causes. Treatment may involve medication, surgery, intrauterine insemination (IUI), in vitro fertilization (IVF), egg donation, embryo-related genetic testing, or other assisted reproductive technologies.
The challenge, however, is not simply whether treatment exists. Access matters.
WHO notes that fertility treatments remain inaccessible or unaffordable for many people, with the high cost of assisted reproduction creating a significant barrier in numerous countries.
This has contributed to the growth of cross-border reproductive care, in which patients travel to another country to obtain fertility services that may be more accessible, affordable, or legally available there.
Research examining international reproductive care has found that cost and the legal availability of assisted reproductive technologies are among the most frequently reported reasons patients seek treatment abroad, alongside cultural and practical considerations.
Where Does Iran Stand in Fertility Treatment?
Iran has developed a substantial medical infrastructure for assisted reproduction. Assisted reproductive technologies have been used in the country since the 1980s, and a national report published on Iranian ART centers documented tens of thousands of IVF/ICSI cycles across dozens of centers. Researchers concluded that Iran has considerable potential to provide IVF services not only to Iranian patients but also to patients from other countries in the region.
Iran's position has also been highlighted by Iranian medical authorities. In a report published by Mehr News, Hamid Choubineh, head of the Iranian Scientific Association of Infertility and Reproductive Health, described Iran as being among the top 10 countries in the world for infertility treatment, while emphasizing the country's access to modern assisted reproductive techniques.
The country's reproductive medicine sector includes IVF, ICSI, genetic testing, donor programs, and gestational surrogacy. Iranian research has also documented the use of preimplantation genetic diagnosis for conditions such as beta-thalassemia, aneuploidy screening, and sex selection.
For international patients, this combination of medical expertise and comparatively lower treatment costs can make Iran an option worth investigating.
Why Do International Patients Consider Iran?
The reasons vary from patient to patient, but several factors frequently influence the decision.
Access to Specialized Fertility Services
Some reproductive treatments are heavily restricted in certain countries. Regulations concerning donor eggs, donor embryos, gestational surrogacy, and embryo testing vary significantly around the world.
Iran occupies a distinctive position within the Muslim world in this regard. Islamic bioethics literature notes that the late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei issued a fatwa permitting certain third-party reproductive arrangements, including egg donation and surrogacy, and that these practices subsequently became incorporated into Iran's reproductive medicine framework.
This religious and legal context differs from the position adopted by many Sunni authorities regarding third-party gamete donation. For international patients, therefore, Iran can provide an alternative where certain fertility treatments are available within a Shia Islamic legal and medical framework.
At the same time, eligibility is not unlimited. Iranian fertility programs operate within local medical and legal requirements, and international patients should confirm their eligibility before traveling. For example, VitaLife's current program information specifies eligibility requirements for international intended parents and states that its surrogacy pathway is designed for legally married heterosexual couples.
Surrogacy, Egg Donation and Gender Selection
For patients who cannot safely carry a pregnancy, surrogacy in Iran can provide another reproductive pathway. In gestational surrogacy, an embryo created through IVF is transferred to a gestational carrier.
Egg donation is another important option for patients whose own eggs may not be suitable for treatment. Iran has developed clinical experience with donor-assisted reproduction, making it an area of interest for some international patients.
Another service sought by some international couples is gender selection through IVF and preimplantation genetic testing. Iranian medical research has documented PGD-based sex selection in clinical settings, although the medical, ethical, and legal circumstances surrounding its use should always be discussed with a qualified fertility specialist.
The important point is that international fertility care should not be viewed simply as a search for the cheapest treatment. Patients need to consider medical suitability, legal requirements, laboratory standards, documentation, and the process for returning home with a child born through assisted reproduction.
How VitaLife Supports International Patients
For someone traveling abroad for fertility treatment, the medical procedure is only one part of the journey.
International patients may also need help with medical records, treatment planning, translation, travel arrangements, legal documentation, surrogate coordination, and communication with clinics.
This is where an international surrogacy agency and fertility coordinator can play an important role.
VitaLife Fertility Center in Iran works with international intended parents seeking coordinated fertility and reproductive services. Its programs include IVF, egg donation, gestational surrogacy, embryo-related genetic services, and support with the practical aspects of treatment in Iran.
The center's international support model is designed to coordinate different stages of treatment rather than leaving patients to manage each component independently. According to VitaLife's published program information, this includes medical coordination, surrogate matching, legal documentation support, international patient coordination, and assistance throughout the treatment process.
For intended parents considering treatment abroad, this type of coordinated approach can make an otherwise complicated process easier to navigate.
Choosing Fertility Treatment Abroad
Choosing fertility treatment abroad involves more than cost. International patients should consider the medical team, clinic facilities, legal requirements, treatment eligibility, timeline, total costs, and support throughout the journey.
Fertility treatment cannot guarantee pregnancy or live birth, as outcomes depend on individual medical factors such as age, reproductive history, and embryo quality.
Your Treatment Journey with VitaLife
At VitaLife Fertility Center, international patients are supported throughout their treatment journey in Iran, from the initial consultation to delivery. Mobina Hosseini, a midwifery specialist with a master’s degree in midwifery, serves as the dedicated patient coordinator, helping international intended parents navigate their treatment from A to Z.
Medical care is provided under the supervision of Dr. Farah Ghasemi, the treating physician, with IVF procedures carried out at Baharan Negar Infertility Treatment Center. For patients undergoing surrogacy, delivery takes place at Nikan Aghdasieh Hospital, providing a coordinated pathway from fertility treatment through pregnancy and birth.
This integrated approach allows international patients to have one coordinated team supporting their medical, communication, and practical needs throughout the process.
A Growing Role for Iran in International Fertility Care
Iran’s experience in assisted reproduction, specialized fertility services, and comparatively accessible treatment costs has made it an option for international patients. For intended parents, choosing the right pathway means finding medically appropriate, legally compliant, and well-coordinated care. VitaLife Fertility Center supports international patients throughout their fertility journey in Iran.

NATO's top commander outlined tough military response in the event of "foolish" Russian attack
Kyiv • UNN
General Alexus Grynkewich said that NATO would make an attack on any ally completely futile. He also vowed to dismantle the entire system of warfare.
NATO's Supreme Allied Commander warned Russia on Monday, October 12, that his forces would destroy "everything and everyone" that could be involved in any attack if Moscow were "foolish enough" to launch an assault on alliance territory. UNN reports this with reference to Reuters.
Details
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, U.S. Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich emphasized that NATO is a defensive alliance. But he outlined a three-pronged approach of blocking, blunting and breaking enemy forces to make any attack "utterly futile."
His remarks came amid rising tensions between Europe and Russia and continued concern among European allies about U.S. President Donald Trump's commitments to NATO's mutual defense pact.
In recent days, Trump announced an agreement with Kremlin chief Vladimir Putin allowing Russia to supply diesel fuel to world markets, and renewed his criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the publication writes.
European governments accuse Moscow of intensifying a campaign of sabotage, drone incursions, and cyberattacks against them, while Russia warned last month that it could use nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off its exclave, the Kaliningrad region.
EU commented on Russia's nuclear threat against NATO over Kaliningrad01.10.26, 16:32 • 4710 views
Grynkewich did not mention Russia by name, but much of his message was clearly directed at Moscow, the publication writes. NATO's 2022 Strategic Concept describes Russia as the most significant threat to the alliance's security.
If anyone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight. In short, we will ensure that any attack on any ally proves absolutely futile
Grynkewich said NATO's response would not be limited to the forces involved in the initial attack.
"If the adversary decides to continue the attack or commit its reserves, we will break the warfighting system that is being waged against us," he said.
"This includes not only the attacking forces themselves, but everything that supports, sustains, and controls those forces," Grynkewich noted.
Putin said this month that Russia does not plan to attack any European country and wants to coexist peacefully. Such statements have not reassured European leaders, given that Russia made similar statements before invading Ukraine in 2022, the publication points out.
Russia has also repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage and other hybrid operations.
Grynkewich said he decided to speak publicly about NATO's plans because recent acts of sabotage and arson had made people across the alliance nervous.
"I want to assure the one billion citizens of our alliance that we will deal with this. We know what we need to do. We know how we will do it," he said.
He said he also wanted to send a message to anyone considering the possibility of harming NATO members.
Grynkewich sought to downplay concerns about Washington's commitment to the alliance, recalling that Trump spoke of "love" at the NATO summit in Ankara in July.
"I was in the room and I felt the love," he said.

Global: New report exposes human rights failures at 2026 Men’s World Cup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:34:34 UTC
17:34:34 KST

Coalition calls for upcoming FIFA presidential election to centre human rights
The 2026 Men’s World Cup exposed a failure of FIFA’s leadership to implement its own human rights policies, with the pursuit of record revenues prioritised over fairness and equality, the Sport & Rights Alliance and Football Supporters Europe said in a joint report released today. The 50-page report, “Profit Over People: The 2026 FIFA Men’s World Cup,” documents a tournament marked by a climate of fear given the backdrop of mass immigration detentions and deportations; discriminatory visa bans; cost and accessibility barriers for fans, players and journalists; unclear safeguarding and eligibility standards; and lack of effective access to remedy.
“The 2026 World Cup exposed how the priorities and direction set by FIFA’s leadership put profit over people,” said Andrea Florence, Executive Director of the Sport & Rights Alliance. “For everyone touched by the tournament, access and participation were limited by economic status, nationality, immigration status, disability, gender identity and sexual orientation or political circumstance. Not only did FIFA fail to use its leverage to uphold human rights obligations, it chose to lift up a government that is actively violating human rights by awarding an unvetted ‘FIFA Peace Prize’ to U.S. President Donald Trump.”
As a 48-nation, 104-match tournament hosted for the first time in three countries – Canada, Mexico, and the United States – the 2026 Men’s World Cup was the biggest mega sporting event in history, and one that, as FIFA promised would be a tournament where everyone “feels safe, included and free to exercise their rights.” The tournament was the first World Cup to be hosted under FIFA’s recognition and adoption of international business and human rights obligations, through its 2017 Human Rights Policy, integration of human rights criteria in the bidding process, and a dedicated “FWC26 Human Rights Framework” for 16 local host committees. Yet due to rising concerns about potential human rights abuses at the tournament, over 65,000 people joined Amnesty International’s call for FIFA and host nations to address risks and guarantee a World Cup for everyone.
ICE raids surged, protests were blocked and discriminatory visa policies kept many fans from enjoying what was billed as ‘the most inclusive World Cup ever’.
Frank Conde Tangberg, Policy Advisor at Amnesty International
“The unity and joy we saw on the pitch and in the stands were a world away from the fear and division beyond the stadiums. ICE raids surged, protests were blocked and discriminatory visa policies kept many fans from enjoying what was billed as ‘the most inclusive World Cup ever’,” said Frank Conde Tangberg, Policy Advisor at Amnesty International. “Many of these violations stemmed from repressive and abusive government policies, but FIFA failed to use its leverage to protect fans and local communities. It spent its political capital on maximising revenue rather than standing up for human rights.”
The report details how excessive ticket pricing, coupled with expensive visa requirements and a lack of affordable inter-city transport, as well as U.S. travel restrictions on over 39 nations, disproportionately excluded fans with disabilities, with limited incomes and/or from the Global South. Participating teams and officials faced severe disruptions: members of the Iranian national team had U.S. visas delayed or denied, and for two U.S. matches the team had to enter and depart the country on the same day – while Somali referee Omar Artan, despite having a valid visa, was denied entry at Miami International Airport following an 11-hour interrogation. These and other barriers unfolded alongside aggressive U.S. immigration enforcement, with, as Human Rights Watch documented, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) conducting over 167,000 arrests in and around 11 World Cup host cities leading up to the tournament. Although reporting of ICE detentions inside World Cup venues was limited, enforcement surged during the tournament, including over five days in late June when approximately 10,000 people were arrested.
“Supporters were treated as objects to be exploited rather than the heart of the game,” said Ronan Evain, Executive Director of Football Supporters Europe. “When ticket prices are at the highest in World Cup history, legal accessibility requirements for fans with disabilities are ignored, and dedicated supporters face discriminatory visa rejections or militarized border enforcement, you no longer have a global celebration – just an exclusive, sanitized spectacle meant only for the elite.”
The report also documents other human rights abuses in Mexico, where police confronted planned protests with tear gas and detained two journalists. In Canada, preparations were marked by street sweeps displacing unhoused residents in host cities – and immigration authorities rejected more World Cup visa applications, which came mostly from Global South applicants, than they approved. Within FIFA’s direct control, questions remain about whether FIFA failed to enforce its own in-competition policy explicitly requiring athletes to declare they have never been investigated for a sexual or other violent offence, given that at least eight players facing pending sexual assault cases or allegations competed in the 2026 World Cup. Independent journalism was also severely constrained by FIFA’s opaque media accreditation processes, U.S. visa barriers, and a lack of regular press conferences with top leadership.
“In recent years, the U.S. – the country hosting the majority of World Cup matches – fell from 45th to 64th in our Press Freedom Index, and journalists have faced violence, detention, and deportation,” said Clayton Weimers, Executive Director of Reporters Without Borders (RSF) USA. “Yet FIFA’s lack of clarity on media accreditation, coordination with visa processes, and blasé attitude toward media briefings underscored FIFA’s failures to uphold human rights. On top of this, FIFA’s continued lack of advertising for its grievance mechanism for journalists, players, fans, workers and community members means we don’t know the true extent of the harm.”
FIFA is in clear need of systemic governance reform that embeds human rights and good governance into leadership and decision-making structures, provides an independent system of checks and balances, and ensures meaningful accountability when its commitments are not met.
“The lesson of the 2026 World Cup is not that international sporting bodies can guarantee the conduct of sovereign governments, but that human rights risks must shape how tournaments are awarded, planned, contracted, monitored, and delivered – and that top leadership at FIFA and other sport governing bodies must be prepared to act, especially when circumstances change,” said Florence.
As detailed in the report, the Sport & Rights Alliance and Football Supporters Europe call on FIFA, and all candidates in the 2027 presidential election, to:
- Make human rights requirements binding, and set enforceable conditions in host agreements for all future Men’s and Women’s World Cups, backed by independent monitoring and clear consequences for non-compliance;
- Establish a transparent, survivor-centered eligibility framework for athletes and officials facing serious misconduct or sexual violence allegations, replacing case-by-case discretion;
- Ensure meaningful access without discrimination to future tournaments for fans, athletes, journalists, and other accredited participants, and ensure the rights to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and press freedom are guaranteed in the context of FIFA tournaments;
- Guarantee equal ticket access and free companion seating for supporters with disabilities, while preventing predatory ticket pricing; and
- Make FIFA’s grievance and remedy mechanisms visible and accessible, re-establish a permanent and independent Human Rights Advisory Board, comprehensively reform the FIFA Ethics Committee, and create a permanent Remedy Fund for individuals and communities harmed by past and future tournament operations.

Netanyahu seeks prosecution of soldiers who testified in Gaza documentary: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:34:10 UTC
17:34:10 KST

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the security establishment and the country’s attorney-general to identify and prosecute soldiers and officers interviewed in the investigative documentary NAZA about Israel’s mass killings of civilians in Gaza, Israeli media reported on Monday.
In a letter to army Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir, Shin Bet chief David Zini and Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, Netanyahu accused those who participated in the documentary of committing “serious information security offenses, and criminal defamation” and causing harm to “Israel’s diplomatic and security interests,” according to Haaretz newspaper.
The award-winning documentary examines Israel’s use of artificial intelligence and automated surveillance systems in targeted killings and military offensives during its genocidal war on Gaza.
The film’s title, "NAZA," refers to an acronym used by Israeli military intelligence to denote the number of civilians expected to be killed in an air strike.
During the war, the Israeli army has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others since October 2023 in a brutal offensive that has left the entire enclave in ruins.
Netanyahu claimed that the film has presented a “false, misleading and biased narrative” that defames Israel and its military and damages the country’s international standing.
“There is concern that those involved in the defamatory film committed serious criminal offenses by exposing highly classified information and creating a breach in the information security of a highly sensitive intelligence unit,” he said in the letter.
The film, based on testimony from 24 Israeli soldiers and intelligence personnel, won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival last month.
Following the award, Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar asked the Interior Ministry to consider revoking the citizenship of the film’s creators, describing the documentary as “vile” and accusing them of “treason.”
Zamir separately ordered Military Intelligence, the Military Advocate General’s Corps and the Israeli Air Force to identify the soldiers featured in the film and determine whether they were active-duty troops, career officers or reservists, according to Haaretz.
During discussions on the issue, Military Advocate General Itai Ofir said that there would be no legal basis for criminal prosecution unless participants were found to have committed information-security violations or disclosed classified material.
He said disciplinary or command measures could, however, be taken if military orders were violated.
The Israeli army claimed that the documentary’s portrayal of its targeting procedures in Gaza contained “substantial factual errors.”
The Guardian, which produced the documentary, defended the film, saying the process used to assess the credibility of the testimonies was “rigorous” and included classified documents, verification of specific strikes and corroboration from additional confidential sources.
The newspaper said it had interviewed more than 100 people familiar with Israeli military systems used during the war on Gaza, including senior commanders involved in authorising strikes.
In November 2024, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
The International Court of Justice, the UN’s principal judicial organ, is also hearing a case brought by South Africa and joined by several countries accusing Israel of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

Bulgaria’s population decreased by 14,153 people in 2025. At the beginning of 2026, the country’s population stood at 6,423,207, a decline of 0.22% compared with the previous year. Over the past 10 years, the population has shrunk by 9.56%, according to the National Statistical Institute.

abroad. The largest numbers arrived from Türkiye, Ukraine and Germany. The main reason for the population decline remains negative
natural growth.

Ethiopia opens first gold refinery (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:33:16 UTC
17:33:16 KST

Ethiopia opens first gold refinery (VIDEO)
Ethiopia has opened its first gold refinery to increase earnings from its mineral resources and offer African producers an alternative to processing their gold overseas, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has announced.
Abiy inaugurated the National Precious Metals Refinery on Saturday at the Bole Lemi Special Economic Zone in the capital, Addis Ababa. The $50 million venture is majority owned by the Ethiopian Investment Holdings (EIH) and Dubai-based Sam Precious Metals.
The facility can process more than 600 metric tons of precious metals annually and has “the capacity to serve not only Ethiopia but also the broader East African and pan-African markets,” Abiy wrote on X on Saturday. It is intended to boost export earnings, create skilled jobs, support the jewelry industry, and serve East African and wider African markets, he said.
“It enables neighboring countries and regional mining companies to bring their gold to Ethiopia for advanced refining, certification, value addition, and sale, eliminating the need to export it outside the continent,” he added.
The launch came five days after Abiy was reelected for another five-year term, pledging to continue economic reforms, advance major infrastructure projects, and defend Ethiopia’s national interests.
Gold is a major source of foreign exchange for Ethiopia, generating $5.6 billion last year, according to government figures. Abiy said African countries have long exported raw materials cheaply while importing finished products at substantially higher prices.
African leaders have increasingly demanded local mineral processing and rejected a repeat of colonial-style resource extraction as Western powers seek greater access to critical minerals. Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama took that message to the UN General Assembly last month, warning that Africa would not remain a “passive arena for a new scramble for resources.”
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa similarly told the BRICS Business Forum in New Delhi last month that Africa must reject a future of supplying minerals while “value addition and manufacturing take place elsewhere.”
Ghana has required licensed self-financing gold aggregators to refine their gold locally before export since September 1. Burkina Faso opened its first gold refinery, Raffinor-BF, on September 28 as the transitional authorities seek greater economic sovereignty after cutting ties with traditional Western partners. DR Congo, where the US brokered a peace deal tied to access to critical minerals, has banned copper and cobalt concentrate exports to encourage domestic processing. Zimbabwe has introduced lithium concentrate export quotas and required producers to commit to building local processing plants ahead of a planned January 2027 ban on concentrate exports.
The National Precious Metals Refinery, constructed within the Bole Lemi Special Economic Zone, has the capacity to serve not only Ethiopia but also the broader East African and pan-African markets. By providing internationally credible refining and testing services, it enables neighboring countries and regional mining companies to bring their gold to Ethiopia for advanced refining, certification, value addition, and sale, eliminating the need to export it outside the continent.

Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti
said the government will continue to take a prudent approach to

he presented its Public Finance Planning Document (DPFP) in the
Lower House on Tuesday.
                                    
The DPFP features the government's plan to use the escape clause
granted by the EU for 0.3% budget deviations for both energy and
defence investments in the 2027 budget law.
                                    
"Planning three years ahead (in the DPFP) is highly complex
especially amid great turbulence, and updates come weekly, as
IMF data show," Giorgetti said.
                                    
"The fundamental premise underlying our reasoning is that when
the weather forecast predicts a storm, it is wise to check the
vessel's condition before heading out to the open sea, and that
is precisely what we have sought to do in recent years.
                                    
"We believe it is essential to stay on this course at a time
when storm clouds are gathering on the horizon.
                                    
"This document is a reflection of that approach, aiming to
adhere to the path of fiscal consolidation and meet the targets
set by the new European governance framework, with a view to
exiting the (excessive-deficit) procedure in the spring,
conditions permitting".
                                    
Italy's budget deficit needs to come within the 3% of GDP
threshold for it to be able to emerge from the procedure.
                                    
Giorgetti has said he is expects this to be the case for 2026,
after the deficit came in at 3.1% for 2025, before going up to
3.4% in 2027 with the use of the escape clause.
                                    
"The request to adjust the budget in order to activate the
national escape clause for defence and energy is a deliberate
departure from the prudent stance I have previously advocated,"
Giorgetti said.
                                    
"These are measures that the Commission acknowledges, and that
the markets have deemed sustainable within the framework of
ensuring the long-term sustainability of Italian public debt".

Swiss family business Wagner shuts down with 69 job losses

Unknown Publisher

Swiss family business Wagner shuts down with 69 job losses
Swiss industrial company Wagner is closing down permanently with the loss of 69 jobs. Following an unsuccessful consultation process, business activities will be gradually transferred to other partners.
Production is set to continue on a larger scale than originally planned until the end of March 2027, the family business announced. The reason for this is said to be additional customer orders.
Wagner specialises in metal die-casting and plastic injection moulding. The company supplies the automotive industry and the mechanical and plant engineering sectors.
The redundancies and resignations of the 69 employees will take place in stages. A voluntary redundancy scheme has been agreed for those affected, in consultation with the administrator.
Despite intensive restructuring efforts and discussions with investors, it was not possible to find an economically viable solution for the company as a whole.
Wagner cites a difficult demand situation, significant overcapacity, international competitive pressure and the framework conditions for industrial production in Switzerland as the reasons. Even additional funding from the owners was unable to prevent the closure.
The consultation process, which began on September 23, was concluded on October 9. No proposals were received that would have enabled the orderly closure to be adjusted.
“The definitive closure of our family business is an extraordinarily painful step for us,” said CEO and co-owner Silvan Halter. According to the statement, he is the third generation to run the family business, which has been in operation for over 80 years.
The aim now is to carefully manage the handover of the projects, support staff in finding new employment and ensure a fair and orderly process.
The continuation of the insolvency proceedings still requires court approval as well as the subsequent consent of the creditors.

India to buck global slowdown and grow 7% for two years – IMF
India will be the world’s fastest-growing major economy despite the drag from higher oil prices and slowing global growth, the International Monetary Fund has said. 
The IMF raised India’s GDP forecast for 2026-27 to 7%, from its July figure of 6.4%, in its latest World Economic Outlook released on Tuesday. It also upgraded its growth projection for the country in 2027-28 to 7%, from the previous 6.7%. 
The upgrade reflects stronger-than-expected economic momentum, supported by domestic demand and services activity. India’s expanding domestic market, favorable demographics, and continued structural reforms have also strengthened its growth potential, the IMF said. 
The Indian economy expanded 7.8% in the financial year ended March 2026, and maintained the same pace in the April-June quarter. The latest revision follows similar upgrades by other major institutions. The World Bank raised India’s growth forecast for 2026-27 to 7.1% last week, citing strong domestic demand and exports. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) also increased its projection for the current financial year to 7.1%. 
India’s expansion is also supporting growth across South Asia, where the World Bank expects the country to remain a major driver of regional economic activity. 
The upgraded Indian outlook contrasts with slower global growth. The IMF expects the world economy to expand 3.1% in 2026, down from 3.5% last year.
China’s economy is projected to grow 4.5% this year, while the US is expected to grow 2.3%.
The Middle East conflict continues to weigh on energy-importing economies, while investment in AI infrastructure has helped support global growth, the IMF said.
Inflation remains a concern in India, with consumer prices rising 5.54% in September, close to the RBI’s upper tolerance limit of 6%. The central bank raised its benchmark interest rate to 5.5% last week amid broader price pressures.
The IMF also expects India’s current account deficit to widen to 1.5% of GDP this financial year from 0.7% a year earlier amid higher energy import bills.

The potential targets of such ground operations were not specified. Tehran has also privately warned Arab officials that renewed fighting could trigger attacks on Saudi oil facilities and other strategic infrastructure across the Gulf.
Iranian national security official Mohsen Rezaei warned Sunday that Tehran could strike the United Arab Emirates, which has largely avoided attacks since late spring, as well as data centers and internet cables across the region. Separately, Iranian officials have told mediators that their forces could intensify attacks on American personnel, including attempts to sink US warships in the Middle East and kill their crews, according to people familiar with the warnings cited by the Journal.
The threats follow a series of attacks that have heightened regional tensions. At least three commercial vessels were struck over the weekend in and around the Strait of Hormuz, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency. A drone attack also set an Emirati tanker ablaze near Oman, leaving two Indian sailors missing. President Donald Trump has ruled out strikes before the midterm elections but has publicly discussed targeting Iran's Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility.

Iranian missiles had previously come close to American warships during attacks in September, highlighting the risks facing US forces in the region.
Meanwhile, Tehran has used the relative pause in direct fighting to rebuild missile and drone production facilities and replenish its arsenal, while strengthening defenses around sensitive sites. Satellite imagery analyzed by the Institute for Science and International Security shows that Iran recently constructed earthen barriers around the Pickaxe Mountain and Natanz nuclear facilities, apparently intended to obstruct possible ground raids.
Iran's preparations extend beyond military installations. State media has intensified coverage of pro-government rallies, while billboards in Tehran advertise civilian training in shoulder-fired antiaircraft missiles and sniper rifles. The Revolutionary Guard has publicized training for female commando units and even sent personnel to a kindergarten in Sabzevar, where they recounted wartime experiences and displayed what they described as a neutralized American Tomahawk missile.
The Journal noted that Iran's ability to defend against advanced American aircraft and cruise missiles remains limited, making threats of regional escalation a central element of its deterrence strategy. The preparations suggest that Tehran is attempting both to discourage another US attack and to ready itself for a conflict that could extend far beyond Iranian territory.

Mapping Africa’s energy wealth and 560 million who remain without power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:25:54 UTC
17:25:54 KST

Mapping Africa’s energy wealth and 560 million who remain without power
Africa is rich in energy, yet hundreds of millions Africans still live without electricity, most of the world’s total.
Africa holds billions of barrels of oil, trillions of cubic metres of gas and produces most of the world’s cobalt and manganese for electric car batteries.
This week, energy ministers, investors and oil executives are meeting in Cape Town for African Energy Week, which runs until October 16. The conference focuses on investment in oil and gas, energy finance and ending energy poverty.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera maps where Africa’s oil, gas and critical minerals are found, how its electricity is generated and who still goes without it.
How much oil does Africa have?
Africa holds about 125 billion barrels of proven crude oil reserves, representing 7.2 percent of the global total. Proven reserves are oil that has been discovered and can be extracted commercially with existing technology, but is still in the ground.
Libya and Nigeria account for nearly 70 percent of Africa’s reserves, with 48.4 billion and 36.9 billion barrels, respectively. Algeria ranks third, with 12.2 billion barrels. Angola follows with 7.78 billion barrels, while South Sudan and Egypt hold 3.75 billion and 3.3 billion barrels, respectively.
Nigeria was Africa’s largest oil producer in 2024, accounting for about 23 percent of the continent’s output. Algeria and Angola followed with about 17 percent each, and together the three produced 56 percent of Africa’s oil. The top five producers accounted for more than 80 percent. Africa as a whole produced 7.6 percent of the world’s crude oil, roughly in line with its share of global reserves.
Libya, which holds Africa’s largest proven reserves, ranked only fourth in production. Italy’s Eni, France’s TotalEnergies and Spain’s Repsol are among the foreign companies operating in the country, where political disputes and blockades have repeatedly disrupted output.
Where are Africa’s natural gas reserves?
Africa held almost 18 trillion cubic metres of proven natural gas reserves at the end of 2023.
Nigeria and Algeria hold about 58 percent of the total, followed by Mozambique with 2.84 trillion cubic metres, Egypt with 2.21 trillion and Libya with 1.51 trillion.
Algeria and Nigeria are also among Africa’s leading gas exporters, while much of Mozambique’s reserves, discovered offshore in the 2010s, remain largely undeveloped.
Where do the critical minerals come from?
The African continent supplies a large share of the minerals used in electric vehicles, batteries and renewable energy technologies.
In 2025, African countries accounted for 71.2 percent of global cobalt production and 72.4 percent of manganese production.
Cobalt is used in rechargeable batteries. Manganese is mainly used to strengthen steel, but it is also used in some electric vehicle batteries and in batteries that store renewable energy.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo produces nearly 70 percent of the world’s cobalt. Some of it is dug by hand by artisanal miners, and Amnesty International has documented dangerous and often deadly conditions in some of the country’s mines.
South Africa produces nearly 38 percent of global manganese, followed by Gabon with nearly 25 percent. Together with Ghana, the three countries account for 72.4 percent of global production.
Zimbabwe, Africa’s largest lithium producer, accounted for 9.6 percent of global production in 2025. Lithium is used in rechargeable batteries that power electric vehicles and store electricity from solar and wind.
Madagascar, Mozambique and Tanzania produced a combined 222,000 tonnes of natural graphite in 2025, or 11.9 percent of the global total. Graphite is used in the anodes of most lithium-ion batteries, the negative electrodes that store and release energy, as well as in steel manufacturing, lubricants and pencils.
How many African countries produce electricity from renewables?
Renewable energy accounted for all electricity generated in Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2024. Uganda, Namibia and Eswatini each generated more than 96 percent from renewables, mostly hydropower.
At the other end, renewables made up less than 5 percent in Algeria, Libya, Niger and Tunisia, which rely mainly on gas or oil.
Ethiopia’s electricity comes mostly from hydropower, led by the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile, Africa’s largest hydroelectric project. The dam began generating power in 2022 and was officially inaugurated in September 2025.
Where do people have access to electricity?
In 2024, six African countries reported universal electricity access: Algeria, Egypt, Mauritius, Morocco, Seychelles and Tunisia. Together, they are home to about 215 million people, or roughly 14 percent of Africa’s population.
Elsewhere, access varies widely. In South Sudan, only 5.4 percent of people had electricity. The figure was 15.6 percent in Malawi and 22.5 percent in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, even though the DRC generates all its power from renewables.
Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country, had an access rate of 62.5 percent, leaving roughly 85 million people without electricity, the largest number of any country in the world.
In rural areas, where access is far lower than in cities, many families still rely on kerosene lamps, candles or torches to light their homes after dark.
Africa has vast energy resources, from oil and natural gas to the minerals powering the global energy transition. Yet more than 560 million people in sub-Saharan Africa lack access to electricity, accounting for about 86 percent of the global total, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

UK shoppers seek deals as grocery price inflation rises again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:21:13 UTC
17:21:13 KST

Grocery price inflation in the UK has picked up further, prompting shoppers to turn to special offers to keep their bills down – while the price of chocolates has fallen in the run-up to Halloween.
Supermarket prices were 2.5% higher than last year in the four weeks to 4 October, up from 2.3% last month, according to data from the retail analysts Worldpanel by Numerator.
Spending on promotions over the last month was more than £250m higher than a year ago, with many shoppers using special offers to keep their grocery bills in check or to make pricier items and larger packs more affordable, Worldpanel said.
Fraser McKevitt, the head of retail and consumer insight at Worldpanel, said: “With the autumn budget fast approaching [on 28 October], the cost of living continues to weigh heavily on the minds of shoppers. And the cost of filling up a car is only adding to the pressure on household budgets.
“More than half tell us they’re very or extremely worried about petrol prices, and almost one in three say it’s already taking a real toll on their finances. Until the chancellor sets out his plans, we expect that caution to carry on showing up at the till, with shoppers leaning more heavily on promotions to keep their grocery spend under control.”
However, in some good news for households stocking up on trick or treat supplies for Halloween, chocolate confectionery prices are 3% lower than a year ago.
About 1.2 million households bought a pumpkin over the latest four weeks, up 10% year on year, while more than 250,000 households treated themselves to a pumpkin spice coffee.
McKevitt added: “Halloween and Christmas are two of the most important moments of the year for chocolate confectionery, so falling prices will be welcome news for shoppers and retailers alike.
“After the double-digit increases of 2025, a 3% drop won’t fully reverse what consumers have paid in recent months, but it should help ease some of the pressure on household budgets as the festive season approaches.”
While sales of hot chocolate and soup surged in September compared with August, by 41% and 35% respectively, they fell sharply when compared with last year, by 20% and 4% respectively.
A separate report from NielsenIQ showed total till sales at major UK supermarkets grew 1.4% in the four weeks to 3 October, down from 1.8% growth in the previous month, as shoppers remain cautious about spending.
Summer favourites remained popular as September was unusually warm this year, with strong sales of mineral water (+17.4%) and ice-cream (+11.7%), while sales of hot chocolate (-11%) and ready-to-eat soup (-5.4%) declined year on year.
Asda was the only big grocer to report a drop in sales, of 0.5%, in the 12 weeks to 4 October, Worldpanel said.
The German discounter Lidl led in market share gains and now controls 8.6%, on the back of a 7.1% increase in sales driven by fruit, vegetables and wine.
Sales at the online grocer Ocado increased by 12.4%, outpacing online sales across the sector at 5.5%.
Spending through the tills was 1% higher at Tesco and 1.3% higher at Sainsbury’s, with the two retailers holding 27.8% and 15.2% of the market respectively.
Asda’s share now stands at 11.5%, while Aldi holds 10.5% of the market, with sales at the discounter up 0.4% year on year.
Beyond the supermarkets, grocery sales at Marks & Spencer rose by 14.9%.

Three drones struck the Ukrainian-owned vessel Chelsea 3, sailing under a Maltese flag, about 18 nautical miles (roughly 33 kilometers) east of the city of Byala. All 15 crew members — seven Ukrainian citizens and eight Azerbaijani citizens — were evacuated. According to preliminary reports, five sailors sustained minor injuries.
Another ship sank about 17 nautical miles east of the village of Krapets. One crew member from that ship was rescued.
“This is absolutely unacceptable: yet another attack in close proximity to Bulgaria’s territorial waters,” Radev said in a televised address. He added that he has a call scheduled with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.
According to Radev, there is not yet “solid and unambiguous evidence to bring accusations,” but “logic suggests the outcome benefits the Russian Federation.” Bulgaria intends to summon Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova over the incident.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said that “Russia’s latest attack on commercial vessels near Bulgaria’s territorial waters, which injured Ukrainian and Azerbaijani citizens, once again demonstrates Moscow’s deliberate disregard for civilian lives and maritime security in the Black Sea.” He called on partners to increase pressure on Russia.
A week earlier, drones attacked two other cargo ships off Bulgaria’s coast, about 110 kilometers (68 miles) from shore. The crew of one ship was evacuated, while the other sank. Reuters reported that this was the first known drone attack on civilian ships in Bulgarian waters since the start of the war in Ukraine.

Meta launches new AI models to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:17:31 UTC
17:17:31 KST

Dilara Hamit
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Meta has launched two new artificial intelligence models as the technology company seeks to compete more directly with leading systems developed by OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.
Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full are Meta’s most capable models to date and are designed for personal and professional AI agents, the company said in an announcement on Monday.
The models can perform long-running tasks, use computers, and work in specialized areas including law, finance, and health. Meta said they can also handle complex coding projects, delegate work to smaller AI agents and recover from errors without abandoning the original goal.
One of their main features, Active Memory, allows the AI to retain important information about a user across multiple conversations and retrieve it when relevant.
Another feature, Active Focus, is intended to keep an AI agent working when it encounters difficulties by trying alternative approaches, adapting to new information, and seeking clarification when necessary.
Meta said the models could help users perform tasks ranging from understanding a lease or navigating an insurance claim to analyzing finances and building an application.
Muse Wonder is now available to developers through the Meta Model API and the company’s Muse Code programming tool. The more capable Muse Wonder Full is available through paid Muse Code subscriptions, with plans starting at $50 per month for access to Meta’s most advanced models.
Muse Wonder will later be incorporated into Meta’s Muse personal assistant, initially for subscribers.
Meta published benchmark results that it said showed the models matching or outperforming some systems from OpenAI and Anthropic on selected coding, memory, and professional tasks. The broader performance of the models will still need to be assessed through independent testing.
The company said it trained the Wonder family to protect private information, refuse assistance with harmful activity, and strengthen defenses against cyberattacks. A more detailed safety report is expected to be released later.
The launch forms part of Meta’s broader push toward what CEO Mark Zuckerberg has described as “personal superintelligence,” AI systems capable of understanding users’ goals, preferences and long-term needs.
Unlike some earlier Meta models released with downloadable weights, the company did not announce plans to make the Wonder models open source.
