Kazakhstan’s GDP grows 4.1% in first half of 2026
Kazakhstan’s GDP reached 71.2 trillion tenge in the first half of 2026, marking a 4.1% increase in real terms compared with the same period last year, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the Bureau of National Statistics.
According to the bureau, the country's GDP totaled 71,215,382.4 million tenge between January and June 2026, representing real growth of 4.1% year-on-year.
Ulytau region recorded the fastest growth in gross regional product (GRP) at 15.3%, followed by Turkistan region at 13.3% and North Kazakhstan region at 11.4%.
Meanwhile, Almaty accounted for the largest share of Kazakhstan’s GDP at 20.2%, ahead of Astana at 12.5% and Atyrau region at 11.7%.
Almaty also contributed the most to the country’s economic growth, adding 0.68 percentage points, compared with 0.62 percentage points from Astana and 0.47 percentage points from Almaty region.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Kazakhstan’s economic growth had slowed to 4.1% year-on-year in the first half of 2026, mainly due to disruptions in oil exports and lower production.

12 dead Caspian seals found in Kazakhstan’s Mangistau region
The carcasses of 12 dead seals have been discovered along the Caspian Sea coast near the village of Bautino in Kazakhstan's Mangistau region, Qazinform News Agency reports.
An Aktau resident discovered the dead seals while walking along the coast on October 11 and sent photographs to the relevant authorities. According to him, the carcasses were scattered along a 2.5–3-kilometer stretch of shoreline.
The Mangistau regional fisheries department said specialists had been sent to the site and that an official statement would follow if the reports were confirmed.
The Caspian seal is an endangered species native to the Caspian Sea, with dead seals increasingly found along the Mangistau coast in recent years, particularly in spring and autumn.
Separately, a dead sturgeon was also found along the Caspian Sea coast near the 15th microdistrict of Aktau.
According to the authorities, an official inspection report was prepared on October 10, 2026, by representatives of a state wildlife protection agency and a police officer.
"One dead sturgeon was found along the shoreline, with no visible signs of fishing nets on its body. However, the fish was too badly decomposed to determine the cause of death," the department said in a statement.
The fish carcass was handed over to Aktau Service Qurylys LLP for disposal.

Cyberattack hits fridges at French supermarkets
A cyberattack has disrupted refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets across France, including stores operated by Coopérative U, Intermarché and Carrefour, Qazinform News Agency reports.

The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened an investigation, which has been assigned to France’s anti-cybercrime office (OFAC).

Basic schools' broad selection of foreign languages a problem for Estonian high schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13

17:15:00 KST

Basic schools' broad selection of foreign languages a problem for Estonian high schools
With 15 different languages taught in basic schools last year, students entering upper secondary school may be unable to continue studying a language they have spent several years learning.
A few years ago, Russian and German were the main second foreign languages taught in Estonian schools, but students can now choose from 15 different languages in basic school. Hans Krister, who started upper secondary school this fall, had studied Spanish for three years in basic school. His new school does not offer Spanish, leaving his family with no choice but to pay for his continued language studies out of pocket.
"With the school's help, we found another student, so the lessons aren't entirely one-on-one and the price is quite reasonable. The best compliment for me was when my son said after one lesson, 'Dad, you know, I think that money was well spent. I feel like I'm really learning and making progress there,'" parent Sven Kala said.
Tallinn Language School has seen a significant increase in interest among schoolchildren in learning French and Finnish this fall.
"Finnish has been the most requested language so far. There's also demand for online lessons. People from outside Tallinn, including students from other cities, have taken and are taking these courses," said Ivar Soone, head of Tallinn Language School.
According to Soone, courses for schoolchildren are slightly cheaper, costing less than €100 per month. So far, no schools have paid for the courses. The Ministry of Education sees no problem with paid courses replacing compulsory language lessons.
According to the Ministry of Education, if students cannot continue studying a foreign language in upper secondary school, the school must offer them the opportunity to start learning another language from scratch. Alternatively, students can continue studying their chosen language at private language courses paid for by their parents, with the school recognizing the results.
Last winter, there was debate over whether schools should be allowed to collect money from parents for expenses such as museum tickets.
"These are different things. If it's a compulsory subject in the curriculum and the school is required to offer students the opportunity to study a B foreign language — at the upper secondary level, we're talking about B1 and B2 foreign languages and schools must offer B1 foreign language instruction — then when a student continues studying a language outside school, it's usually not because the school doesn't offer another option. It's the choice of the parents and the student," said Marika Peekmann, the Ministry of Education's chief expert on foreign languages.
According to Ene Saar, principal of Tallinn Secondary School of Science, the biggest challenges for schools are still ahead as this year's basic school graduates are the first cohort required to choose a foreign language other than Russian.
"When they enter upper secondary school, it will be a challenge to figure out how and in what way we can open these B foreign language groups. It's simply not financially feasible to offer everyone the language they want," Saar said.
Saar believes the choice of second foreign languages could be restricted, with some less commonly taught languages offered as electives instead. The Ministry of Education sees no need for such restrictions, saying it is not aware of any upper secondary schools experiencing problems.

AI models may soon replicate across smart devices without human control, Anthropic says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:13:24 UTC
17:13:24 KST

Dilara Hamit
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Small artificial intelligence models could soon become capable of copying themselves across internet-connected devices without human control or access to data centers, according to new Anthropic research.
The study, published Sunday by the US AI company’s Frontier Red Team, examined whether AI models could independently find devices, transfer model files, establish the software needed to operate and continue spreading from each newly infected machine.
Researchers said models with fewer than 30 billion parameters can already complete many individual stages of that process, although most still struggle to combine them reliably.
In a controlled and simplified experiment, the GLM-5.2 model successfully spread across all eight available test devices in four of five trials and reached seven in the remaining trial.
Anthropic stressed that the experiment simplified the hacking stage by using devices with an unsecured connection. The results therefore do not demonstrate that an AI model can currently escape and reproduce autonomously under real-world conditions.
“We don’t yet have a full rogue replicator,” the researchers said. However, they warned that agents were becoming increasingly capable of completing the necessary steps and passing useful information to later copies of themselves.
The study focused particularly on inexpensive internet-of-things devices, which frequently have limited security protections. Potential targets could include smart televisions, refrigerators, ovens, vacuum cleaners, security cameras and videoconferencing equipment.
Anthropic demonstrated that a 26-billion-parameter model could run across 15 inexpensive Android television boxes costing about $55 each. A smaller model successfully established the software required to operate on eight of the nine types of hardware tested.
Unlike conventional computer worms, a self-replicating AI system could potentially adjust to unfamiliar devices, diagnose technical problems and pass successful strategies to future copies.
The researchers said such a system would initially spread slowly, possibly taking one or two days to produce each new copy. However, it could be difficult to eliminate because there would be no central server to switch off.
Anthropic estimated that, if smaller models continue improving at their historical pace, they could reach the capability demonstrated by GLM-5.2 by the end of 2026. The company cautioned that this was only a rough projection based on general capability trends.
The researchers recommended monitoring unusual network traffic, isolating infected devices and requiring manufacturers to strengthen default security settings.
They warned that early, slow-moving replicators could signal the future arrival of faster systems capable of breaching more secure computers.
“We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread,” they said, “but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay.”

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited a defense industry museum featuring an intercontinental ballistic missile capable of reaching the United States. Reuters reports, writes UNN.
Details
The report came a day after U.S. President Donald Trump said he might meet with Kim during a planned trip to Asia. In mid-November, Trump is expected to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China.
According to media reports, on Sunday Kim, together with his daughter, known as Ju Ae, and his wife, Ri Sol Ju, attended the opening of the recently established Museum of the Defense Revolution.
KCNA photographs show that the museum features weapons systems developed under Kim’s leadership, ranging from drones to the "Hwasong-20" intercontinental ballistic missile.
According to Shin Jong Woo, secretary general of the Korea Defense and Security Forum, the exhibit in front of the "Hwasong-20" launch vehicle appeared to display a design with multiple warheads and a world map showing the strike range extending beyond the continental United States, including the Middle East, Australia and South America.
The exhibition appears intended to showcase the achievements of Kim’s defense science development program. It gave the impression of a propaganda event aimed at gaining a strategic advantage ahead of a possible North Korea-U.S. summit
Analysts noted that the museum also reflects Kim’s broader efforts to turn displays of North Korean weapons into lasting symbols of the regime’s military achievements.
By transforming temporary weapons exhibitions into a permanent museum, Kim is cementing his military achievements and presenting the buildup of North Korea’s nuclear and missile capabilities as a completed legacy that will endure for a long time

Unknown

Netanyahu has called for a criminal investigation into soldiers and officers interviewed in award-winning documentary.
Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the country’s attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet security service to reveal the identities of officers interviewed in the award-winning film NAZA.
Netanyahu is ordering for the filmmakers, Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, to be prosecuted for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.
He has asked for attorney general Gali Baharav-Miara, IDF chief of staff Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, and Shin Bet head David Zini, to “act urgently to uncover the identity of all those who are involved or appear in the libel film”.
NAZA, which premiered in Venice and won the Special Jury Prize, is currently being screened in cinemas in more than 50 countries, shows “in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza,” according to its official synopsis.
Shot in secrecy at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv during the ongoing Gaza war, it features interviews with 24 Israeli military intelligence officers, soldiers and whistleblowers. They describe how Palestinians are targeted and how strikes are carried out using AI and automated surveillance in military targeting systems - despite Israel being aware that civilians are present in targeted areas. The participants' faces and voices were digitally altered to protect their identities.
The 80-minute hot-button doc builds on reporting between 2023 and 2025 published by the Israeli-Palestinian +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call, and The Guardian.
It received a record-breaking 25-minute standing ovation at Venice – the longest in the festival's history.
The Israeli government has previously attacked Abraham and Szor, threatening to strip them of their citizenship.
As reported by the Guardian, Ricardo Gutiérrez, the general secretary of the European Federation of Journalists, said: “These threats constitute a blatant act of intimidation against journalists who have simply been doing their job, in strict accordance with ethical standards and in the public interest.”
Regarding Netanyahu’s threats, he added: “I am not surprised by this outburst, which confirms that this regime is prepared to do anything to cover up its crimes against humanity and the ongoing genocide in Gaza.”
NAZA has been released in select cinemas more than 50 territories. It is being made free-to-watch on The Guardian’s website in November.

Switzerland sees rise in mortgage rates in third quarter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

17:10:41 KST

Switzerland sees rise in mortgage rates in third quarter
Mortgage costs rose in Switzerland in the third quarter compared with the previous three months, mainly due to the rise in interest rates on the capital markets, which drove up banks’ refinancing costs.
At the end of September, the indicative rate – calculated based on the average of rates from around 30 banks – stood at 2.07% for a ten-year fixed-rate mortgage, according to the online comparison portal Comparis.
More
Switzerland’s housing shortage: how bad is it?
For a five-year fixed-rate mortgage, the rate stood at 1.9% at the end of the quarter under review. At 1.75%, three-year fixed-rate mortgages were also higher than they had been three months earlier (1.38%).
“In the short term, given that inflation remains low, the Swiss National Bank is unlikely to be in any particular hurry to raise interest rates. However, the more favourable economic outlook, the weakness of the franc and rising energy prices have increased the likelihood of a tightening of monetary policy,” says Dirk Renkert, a financial expert quoted in the press release.
Higher interest rates abroad are increasingly having an impact on the Swiss capital market.
“This is why fixed-rate mortgages are becoming more expensive, even though the SNB is keeping its key interest rate at 0%. The indicative rates for 10-year fixed-rate mortgages, which are now above 2%, have not been this high since March 2025,” Renkert added.

Dozens of Turkish Amazon armored vehicles spotted in Libya
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:10:21 UTC
17:10:21 KST

- Footage said to be from Libya shows dozens of Turkish-made BMC AMAZON 4x4 armored vehicles with remote weapon stations and jamming systems.
- Turkish analyst Ahmet Alemdar said the vehicles are operated by Libyan elite units but did not identify the force or filming location.
Footage said to be from Libya shows dozens of Turkish-made BMC AMAZON 4×4 armored vehicles in service with Libyan elite units, fitted with remote-controlled weapon stations and jamming systems, according to Turkish defense analyst Ahmet Alemdar, who shared the images on X.
Alemdar described the vehicles as being operated by “elite units” but did not identify which Libyan force or faction they belong to, where or when the footage was filmed, or how many vehicles appear in total beyond describing them as “dozens.” The post also did not say what type of jamming equipment is mounted on the vehicles or which weapons the remote-controlled stations carry. Neither BMC nor Türkiye’s defense procurement agency has publicly announced an AMAZON export contract with Libya.
The AMAZON is the smallest vehicle in BMC Otomotiv’s family of armored vehicles and was first shown publicly at the Eurosatory exhibition in Paris in 2016. It has a V-shaped hull built to deflect mine and roadside bomb blasts away from the crew, carries up to seven people, and, according to BMC, can reach 120 km/h (75 mph) and travel about 800 km (500 miles) on a tank of fuel. Remote-controlled weapon stations on the AMAZON typically carry a 7.62 mm or 12.7 mm machine gun that the crew aims and fires from inside the vehicle using cameras and a screen. BMC has also shown versions that can be driven without a crew, and Turkish company ASELSAN has mounted its GÖKBERK counter-drone laser on the AMAZON chassis.
Jamming systems on light armored vehicles are usually meant to block the radio links and satellite navigation signals that small drones and remotely triggered roadside bombs rely on, giving convoys some protection against both threats. Alemdar’s post did not say which of those roles the Libyan equipment is meant to fill.
Türkiye has been one of Libya’s main military partners since 2019, when it signed a security agreement with the government in Tripoli and later sent military advisers, drones and armored vehicles to support its forces. Turkish-made BMC vehicles, including the larger Kirpi and Vuran models, have appeared in Libya in previous years. The AMAZON has also been exported to other countries in the region, and BMC has marketed it heavily to armies that need light, mine-protected vehicles for internal security and border work.

====================================================================================================

Child marriage in southern Germany: Over 350 cases recorded, some brides as young as 11
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:09:32 UTC
17:09:32 KST

A written question by two AfD members of the Baden-Württemberg state parliament revealed 358 marriages involving minors, but only eight have so far been annulled with final legal effect.
In the southwestern German state of Baden-Württemberg, a total of 358 so-called child marriages have been officially recorded since 2012. Only eight of these forced marriages have so far been legally annulled. According to authorities, the other 350 cases were brought to an end in other ways.
This alarming finding comes from a response by the Baden-Württemberg state government to a minor inquiry submitted by AfD state parliament members Nikolaos Boutakoglou and Emely Knorr.
The Tübingen regional authority is responsible for recording the data, the answer came from the Ministry of the Interior.
11-year-old Iraqi girl married off
The eight final annulments took place between 2018 and 2024. Among the documented cases was the marriage of an 11-year-old girl from Iraq to a 17-year-old Iraqi, which was annulled in 2020.
As early as 2018, the marriage of a 14-year-old Afghan girl to a 30-year-old man had been ended. In 2024 two further annulments were added: they concerned a 16-year-old German girl and a 25-year-old Pakistani man and a 16-year-old Syrian girl and a 27-year-old man from the same country.
State parliament member Nikolaos Boutakoglou wrote on Facebook that the issue was "really awful" but was being treated as a taboo.
According to its own account, the ministry deals exclusively with such marriages entered into abroad.
Since summer 2017, the Act to Combat Child Marriages has been in force in Germany. In 2024, the Bundestag adopted new rules to protect minors in marriages concluded abroad.
Hundreds of cases without state intervention
The significantly higher number of cases concluded in other ways raises questions about how these marriages continued. For the period from 2015 to 2026, the regional authority lists a total of 350 proceedings under the heading "other disposals."
But what became of the other child marriages? The state government cites, among other things, the death of a spouse, reaching adulthood, a decision not to seek annulment or a new marriage concluded abroad. In these cases, there was therefore no legally binding annulment.
For 2023, the records include the case of a 12-year-old Afghan girl who was married to a 21-year-old Afghan man. Girls aged 13 and 14 also appear several times in the statistics.
The most recent entries in the overview relate to 2026. They include, among other things, marriages of 16- and 17-year-old girls to adult men. The statistics record the age of the spouses at the time of marriage and their respective nationalities.
According to the Interior Ministry, at the time the inquiry was answered there were no court proceedings pending to annul child marriages.
State parliament member Emely Knorr, who co-initiated the inquiry, demanded on the social media platform Instagram: "Child marriages are incompatible with our values. Children have a right to safety, education and a self-determined future. That is why we need effective protection, early intervention and resolute action against forced marriages."
How many pupils are affected?
The two MPs wanted to know what impact forced marriages have on their schooling.
The Ministry of Education explained that no such data are collected. According to the state government, it also has no information on the countries in which the recorded marriages were contracted.
The age and nationality at the time of marriage are recorded, as these are relevant for possible annulment proceedings.
Another question from the MPs concerned how often the YASEMIN counselling centre, which is funded by the state, had been called in for cases of forced marriage involving pupils at schools in Baden-Württemberg.
In its reply of 9 September 2026, the Interior Ministry wrote that the counselling centre does not break down its cases by the school status of the people it advises or by school year.
Instead, cases are recorded by the age of those affected and by calendar year. The precise number of counselling sessions remains unclear.
Threat of forced marriage: 80 cases recorded
In the 2025 calendar year, YASEMIN recorded a total of 271 counselling cases. In 80 cases, the people concerned were at risk of being forced into marriage. Of these 80 people, 33 were minors.
Four of the minors were under 12 years old, five were 12 and another two were 13. The counselling centre distinguishes between people at risk of forced marriage and other counselling issues; it does not carry out any school-related analysis.
According to the MPs, the trigger for the parliamentary inquiry was an emergency checklist by the women's rights organisation Terre des Femmes, published at the end of July 2026 and aimed primarily at teaching staff.
In legal terms, people up to the age of 14 are considered children in Germany; from then until the age of 18 they are deemed adolescents.
Under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, everyone up to the age of 18 is regarded as a child. Only once they reach adulthood are people allowed to marry in Germany. Forced marriage is defined as a separate criminal offence in the Penal Code.
With a population of around 11.24 million people, Baden-Württemberg accounts for just under 13.5% of the total German population of about 83.5 million inhabitants.

====================================================================================================

One trail approved, another closed: questions grow after deadly Israeli school hike blast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:05:41 UTC
17:05:41 KST

Documents obtained by ynet following the death of schoolboy Yair Wilensky in an unexploded munition blast on Ramim Ridge in northern Israel reveal troubling questions about how school hiking trips are approved in areas damaged by war. The Education Ministry's trip coordination center authorized an itinerary labeled "Israel Trail 2051," a designation that combines the names of two entirely different routes running parallel to each other, one of which remains officially closed. The documents raise concerns about unclear instructions and conflicting restrictions in a region exposed to Hezbollah fire for more than two years.
Near the entrance to Kibbutz Kfar Giladi, two separate hiking routes begin at roughly the same location. One is the Israel Trail, marked in orange, blue and white, which climbs dozens of meters up the mountainside. The other, marked in green, is a paved route identified on maps as Trail 2051, also known as the Ramim Ridge Scenic Road or the Naftali Mountains Scenic Road. For approximately 7.5 kilometers, the two trails remain entirely separate before merging near Ein Korim spring and continuing toward Mishkenot HaRoim.
The school group received authorization to hike from Kfar Giladi to Mishkenot HaRoim along a route identified as "Israel Trail 2051." Yet the same approval explicitly stated that "Ramim Ridge Scenic Road 2051" was closed due to repairs of war damage. The Jewish National Fund (KKL-JNF) website also lists the paved, green-marked route as closed to hikers.
The scenic road was repaired and remarked only during the past week but has still not officially reopened. Nevertheless, thousands of families walked along it during the recent Jewish holidays and the vacation period at religious educational institutions. Despite the risk of unexploded ammunition and other remnants of the fighting, no specific warnings about such dangers were posted along the route. A longstanding KKL-JNF sign states that the trail is closed "due to war damage" and that hiking is "strictly prohibited," but makes no mention of unexploded ordnance.
‘The trail is approved, but not approved’
Investigators now face several critical questions. Did the students take the green-marked scenic road rather than the Israel Trail? If so, why? Did the guide misunderstand the route or fail to distinguish between two trails beginning at the same location? Did the group follow the approved itinerary, or was the route changed along the way? Another question concerns the approval system itself: Should school trips be authorized near routes that remain closed because of possible unexploded munitions left behind by the war?
Experienced hiking guides have sharply criticized the Education Ministry's approval procedures, arguing that the conflicting instructions indicate a lack of understanding of conditions on the ground. "It cannot be that Route 2051 is approved, but approved with restrictions. So is it approved or not?" a senior hiking guide told ynet. "If these are different routes, they should have been treated as different routes."
The guide acknowledged that the person leading the trip also had a professional responsibility to clarify the instructions. "Perhaps he should have asked questions and tried to understand what the coordination center meant with all its 'remarks,'" he said. "But ultimately, the body responsible for overseeing and managing the entire process is the Education Ministry."
The central problem, according to guides familiar with the area, is the disconnect between officials issuing hiking permits from their offices and the actual dangers on the ridge. "You cannot issue an approval, include contradictory and confusing instructions under the restrictions, and then expect a teacher or guide to understand that 'this trail is approved, but it isn't approved,'" the guide said. "So what exactly am I allowed to do? What am I not allowed to do?"
He also criticized the system used to approve hikes, saying it relies too heavily on computerized information rather than firsthand knowledge of the terrain. "The nature coordination center doesn't know what's happening on the ground. I'm telling you this from experience," he said. "They don't approve things based on actual fieldwork and an understanding of reality. They simply work according to the computer, according to whatever it tells them. Most of the time, they have no real connection to conditions in the field."
Education Ministry: Planned route did not enter prohibited area
The Education Ministry rejected suggestions that it had authorized a hike through an area officially closed to visitors. "The ministry acted in accordance with KKL-JNF restrictions and instructed that no activities take place in the designated area because of war damage. The planned hiking route did not pass through the prohibited area," the ministry said in a statement. It added that the approval included explicit safety instructions, including an absolute prohibition on touching unexploded missiles or ammunition and a requirement to report any such objects immediately.
"The circumstances of the incident and the route actually taken are now being examined as part of an investigation by the IDF and police, in cooperation with the Education Ministry and the relevant professional authorities," the statement said. The ministry stressed that the findings of the investigation should be awaited before conclusions are drawn about the circumstances of the tragedy.
The ministry also said it would work with the relevant authorities in the coming days to review the procedures for approving outdoor activities and the safety instructions accompanying them. For now, a central question remains unanswered: Whether the students followed the authorized Israel Trail or entered the nearby scenic road that had been closed because of war damage.

UNHCR chief says low funding makes agency’s task “impossible”

UNHCR chief says low funding makes agency’s task “impossible”
The UN High Commissioner for Refugees believes that the agency is facing an “impossible” task due to a lack of funds. Barham Saleh admitted in Geneva that “times are tough” while announcing a reorganisation.
“Efficiency has its limits,” said Saleh at the start of the executive committee meeting of the UNHCR. “There comes a point where greater efficiency cannot make up for a shortage of resources,” he added. “The consequences are not abstract; they are borne by those who depend on us.”
More
Ripple effect of aid freeze becomes real in Geneva
The former Iraqi president acknowledged the financial difficulties facing member states. “But there is a difference between doing more with less and being asked to do the impossible,” the High Commissioner added.
Among the consequences, aid to 50,000 survivors of the Sudan conflict is under threat, and the registration of tens of thousands of refugees has been suspended in Ethiopia.
According to figures up to last Friday, the UN agency had received only 35% of the $8.5 billion requested for this year. For 2027, UNHCR is currently forecasting funding of less than $2.7 billion, which could be increased by the end of the year at the time of the donor conference.
Saleh is calling for funding that is provided earlier, is more predictable and is more flexible.
More
UNHCR cuts close to 5,000 jobs amid funding shortfall
In recent years, the UN agency has faced funding cuts from the US and other countries. Since 2024, nearly 8,000 people have left the organisation, reducing its staff from nearly 20,000 to just under 12,000.
Impact across 31 offices
Since taking up his post in early January, Saleh has commissioned an independent assessment of UNHCR’s operations. He wants a “more agile” and “more sustainable” organisation that collaborates more closely with other parts of the UN humanitarian system, particularly in terms of procurement.
Changes are to be implemented across 31 UNHCR sites. The aim is to avoid duplication at the Geneva headquarters and in regional offices, and to bring the UN agency even closer to the people it assists.
Structures are to be simplified and responsibilities more clearly defined. Another change is that the number of directors reporting directly to political posts will be reduced from 12 to 6.
Some 88% of staff work outside Geneva. And around 70% are local staff. Around 95% of resources are channelled into assistance in the various countries. Saleh also wants UNHCR to rely more heavily on artificial intelligence for its operations.

How Israel votes: A Guide to Knesset, political parties, and coalition governments - explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:58:22 UTC
16:58:22 KST

In Israel, voters do not directly elect their prime minister or individual members of parliament. Instead, each voter chooses a single list of candidates, usually representing a political party or an alliance of parties. The votes determine how the 120 seats in the Knesset, Israel’s parliament, are distributed.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
What happens after the election can be just as important as the vote itself. Parties negotiate alliances, agree on policies, and divide government responsibilities. The leader of the largest party does not automatically become prime minister, and a smaller party can sometimes determine who governs.
Israel uses a system called proportional representation, which helps explain its many political parties, complicated coalition negotiations, and frequent early elections.
Why does Israel have so many political parties?
Unlike the United States, where two major parties dominate national elections, Israel has a multiparty system. Its parties represent a broad range of political, religious, ethnic, and social interests.
Some focus on security, diplomacy, and economic policy. Others represent particular communities, including ultra-Orthodox Jews, religious Zionists, and Arab citizens of Israel. Parties also differ over relations with the Palestinians, religion’s role in public life, and the balance between government authority and judicial power.
The Knesset has 120 seats, a number inspired by the Great Assembly, a council of Jewish religious leaders and sages traditionally associated with the period following the return from the Babylonian exile in the fifth century BCE.
Unlike the US Congress, the Knesset has only one chamber. The entire country is treated as a single electoral district, meaning there are no separate parliamentary constituencies for Jerusalem, Tel Aviv, or other cities. Parties win seats according to their share of the nationwide vote, provided they receive enough votes to qualify.
How do Israelis vote?
Israeli citizens who are at least 18 years old are generally eligible to vote. Citizens can run for the Knesset beginning at age 21, although certain restrictions apply. The president, judges, the state comptroller, the military chief of staff, the two chief rabbis, and certain senior civil servants, military officers, police officers, and prison officials cannot run while holding their positions. Depending on their position, some must resign well before an election. Certain criminal convictions can also disqualify candidates.
Knesset terms are legally set at four years, but the interval between elections can be longer. Regular elections are scheduled for a Tuesday in the Hebrew month of Heshvan, which falls in October or November. The precise Tuesday depends on whether the preceding Hebrew year was a leap year. After an early election, the next regular election is scheduled for Heshvan four years later, though the interval may extend beyond four years. Early elections are also common, and the Knesset can postpone elections in exceptional circumstances with the support of at least 80 of its 120 members.
At polling stations, voters select a paper slip bearing the name and identifying letters of their preferred electoral list, printed in Hebrew and sometimes also in Arabic, place it in an official envelope, and deposit it in a ballot box.
Each voter chooses one list. There is no separate vote for prime minister, no vote for a local representative, and no ranking of individual candidates.
Every list presents its candidates in a predetermined order. If a list wins 15 seats, its first 15 candidates enter the Knesset. Parties use different methods to select and rank candidates, including primary elections, party committees, and decisions by party leaders.
A list can represent one party or several parties running together. Voters selecting a joint list vote for the combined slate, not its individual components.
What is the electoral threshold?
To enter the Knesset, an electoral list must receive at least 3.25% of all valid votes cast nationwide. This is known as the electoral threshold.
For example, if 4 million valid votes are cast, a list needs at least 130,000 votes to qualify. A list receiving 3.24% wins nothing, while one receiving 3.25% would ordinarily receive about four seats, depending on the overall results.
The threshold was originally 1%, rose to 1.5% before the 1992 election, to 2% in 2004, and to 3.25% in 2014. The increases were intended to reduce parliamentary fragmentation and encourage smaller parties to run together.
Votes cast for lists that fail to cross the threshold are excluded when distributing the 120 seats.
Suppose three parties each receive 3% of the vote. Together, they attract 9% of voters, but none enters the Knesset because each ran separately and fell below the threshold.
Their votes are not transferred to any other party. Instead, all 120 seats are divided among the qualifying lists, increasing those parties’ proportional shares.
This can alter the balance of power between political blocs and helps explain why parties with similar positions sometimes run on joint lists.
How are Knesset seats distributed?
After excluding votes for lists that fail to cross the threshold, election officials add the votes received by all qualifying lists and divide the total by 120. The result is an initial electoral quota representing the approximate number of votes needed for one seat.
Each list’s vote total is divided by this quota, with the whole-number result determining its initial allocation.
For example, if qualifying lists receive 3.6 million votes altogether, the quota is 30,000 votes per seat. A list with 310,000 votes initially receives 10 seats, with 10,000 votes left over.
Because this calculation normally leaves some seats unassigned, Israel uses a mathematical formula known as the Bader-Ofer method, named after former Knesset members Yohanan Bader and Avraham Ofer, to distribute the remaining seats.
Rather than simply awarding these seats to parties with the largest number of leftover votes, the formula divides each list’s vote total by the number of seats it has already received, plus one. The list with the highest resulting figure receives the next seat, and the calculation is repeated until all 120 seats have been assigned.
Suppose Party A receives 310,000 votes and has 10 seats. Its figure for an 11th seat is 310,000 divided by 11, or approximately 28,182.
Party B receives 205,000 votes and has six seats. Its figure for a seventh seat is 205,000 divided by seven, or approximately 29,286.
Party B would have priority for the next seat, despite receiving fewer votes overall.
The complete calculation also accounts for agreements between parties over their excess votes.
What are excess-vote agreements?
Before an election, two lists can sign an excess-vote agreement, sometimes called a surplus-vote agreement. This allows their votes to be combined when calculating eligibility for the remaining seats under the Bader-Ofer method.
If their combined votes qualify them for an additional seat, a further calculation determines which partner receives it.
The agreement can improve the chances of one partner gaining another seat, although it does not guarantee one.
Both lists must independently cross the 3.25% electoral threshold for the agreement to take effect. If either fails, the agreement cannot save its votes or transfer them to its partner.
These arrangements differ from joint electoral lists. Parties running together on one list combine their votes before the threshold is applied. Parties signing an excess-vote agreement remain separate, appear independently on the ballot, and receive their own Knesset seats.
An excess-vote agreement also does not require its participants to cooperate in forming a government. Its immediate purpose is mathematical, not political.
Why doesn’t the largest party automatically form the government?
Once the seats have been allocated, the next challenge is forming a government.
A party needs 61 of the Knesset’s 120 seats to hold an outright parliamentary majority. Because no single party has won such a majority in modern Israeli elections, governments generally depend on coalitions involving several parties.
A coalition is an agreement among parties to govern together, usually involving compromises over policy, government ministries, budgets, and legislation.
Consider an election in which Party A wins 35 seats, Party B wins 30, Party C wins 18, Party D wins 15, Party E wins 12, and Party F wins 10.
Although Party A is the largest, Parties B, C, and D could form a coalition with 63 seats, giving them a majority.
This also gives smaller parties considerable bargaining power. A party holding just five or six seats can sometimes determine whether a prospective coalition reaches the 61-seat mark. In exchange for joining, it may demand cabinet positions or commitments on policies important to its voters.
However, coalition partners must also make compromises, and disagreements can eventually threaten the government’s survival.
Relatively small shifts in voting can dramatically change the outcome of an Israeli election. The balance between right-wing and center-left blocs may come down to just a handful of Knesset seats. A party gaining or losing one or two seats, or narrowly crossing or missing the electoral threshold, can determine which bloc has enough support to form a government.
The outcome also depends on parties that do not fit neatly into either bloc. Some centrist, religious, or other parties may be willing to join coalitions led by different political camps, depending on their priorities and the agreements they can negotiate. As a result, even when the overall vote changes only slightly, the composition of the next government can be very different.
What does Israel’s president do after the election?
Israel’s president is the head of state, with mainly ceremonial and representative responsibilities, while the prime minister leads the government.
After an election, the president plays a central role in deciding who gets the first opportunity to form a government.
Once the official results are published, the president consults representatives of the newly elected parliamentary factions. Each can recommend a Knesset member to form a government.
The president considers these recommendations and assigns the task to a willing Knesset member, generally choosing someone who appears capable of assembling sufficient parliamentary support.
The president is not legally required to choose the leader of the largest party or even the candidate receiving the most recommendations.
The assignment must be made within seven days of the official publication of the election results.
How is a government formed?
The candidate selected by the president receives 28 days to negotiate a governing coalition. The president may grant extensions totaling up to 14 additional days, allowing a maximum of 42 days.
Negotiations typically cover coalition policies, government ministries, budgets, legislation, and arrangements for resolving disputes.
Once an agreement is reached, the candidate informs the president and the Knesset speaker that a government has been formed.
The proposed government is presented to the Knesset, including its policy guidelines, ministers, and their responsibilities. Lawmakers then vote on whether to express confidence in it.
Although a coalition normally seeks the support of at least 61 members, an initial confidence vote requires a majority of those voting, not necessarily 61 affirmative votes.
This means Israel can have a minority government if enough lawmakers outside the coalition support it or abstain. Such governments, however, can have difficulty passing budgets and legislation.
If the confidence vote succeeds, the new government takes office, and the person who formed it becomes prime minister.
What happens if the first candidate fails?
If the first candidate cannot form a government within the allotted time, or the proposed government fails to win the Knesset’s confidence, another election does not automatically follow.
Within three days, the president can assign the task to another willing Knesset member, who receives 28 days without an extension. Alternatively, the president can inform the Knesset speaker that there appears to be no possibility of forming a government.
If the second attempt fails, or the president has declared that no government appears possible, Knesset members have 21 days to propose their own solution.
During that period, at least 61 lawmakers can submit a written request asking the president to assign the task to a particular willing Knesset member. That candidate then receives 14 days to form a government.
If no candidate receives 61 signatures during the 21-day period, or the final candidate fails, the Knesset is considered dissolved, and new elections must be held within 90 days.
The outgoing government remains in office until a new one takes over.
Can a government fall before the next election?
Yes. Coalition partners can withdraw their support, a prime minister can resign, or the Knesset can dissolve itself and call early elections.
Israel also uses a system known as constructive no-confidence. Rather than simply voting to remove a government, at least 61 Knesset members must vote to express confidence in a specific alternative government that is ready to take office.
This prevents lawmakers from dismissing a government through a no-confidence vote without agreeing on its replacement.
A failure to pass the state budget within the legally required period can also trigger early elections.
Between April 2019 and November 2022, Israel held five general elections, largely because of repeated difficulties forming and maintaining governing coalitions.
The combination of proportional representation, multiple parties, and coalition politics means election night rarely settles every question about who will govern.
Voters determine which parties enter the Knesset and how many seats they receive. The government that emerges depends on which parties can assemble enough parliamentary support to take office and remain there.

An unidentified aerial object that prompted security alerts in northern Israel on Saturday night was most likely a balloon or a device kept aloft by hot air, rather than a drone, the IDF said on Tuesday following an extensive investigation into the incident.
The military said it could not conclusively determine the object's origin or purpose, but had ruled out the possibility that it was a drone or unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV).
According to the IDF, the object may have been entirely harmless and could have drifted into Israeli territory unintentionally.
The object was initially detected by surveillance personnel and Israel Air Force detection systems, which tracked its movement and directed troops on the ground as the incident unfolded.
The military said defensive measures were reinforced in nearby communities, including the deployment of local defense units, while checks were carried out to determine the nature of the potential threat.
Despite extensive searches, the object has not been located, and no changes have been made to Home Front Command guidelines.
The incident began on Saturday evening, when hostile aircraft infiltration alerts were activated in the Western Galilee, near the Lebanese border. Initial concerns centered on the possibility that a drone had entered Israeli airspace, prompting searches and additional security measures in the area.
IDF soldiers continued searching near the community of Arab el-Aramsha on Sunday, after surveillance systems detected the unidentified object. At the time, the military had not ruled out several possibilities regarding its identity.
IDF addresses recent false alarms and interceptions
The military explained that distinguishing between a small drone and a bird can be extremely difficult, requiring air defense personnel to respond rapidly whenever a potential threat is identified.
Separately, the IDF has been investigating recent interceptor launches against suspicious aerial targets near Israeli troops operating in southern Lebanon, as questions remain about the identity of several objects detected by military systems.
The IDF said it would continue searching on the ground and in the air while regularly reviewing its detection systems to improve identification capabilities and learn from operational incidents.

European commissioner outlines three key areas for EU enlargement preparations
The European Union must focus on three points as it prepares to accept new members: strengthening safeguards against backsliding on democratic norms, enabling more flexible decision-making, and expanding gradual integration for candidate states prior to full accession.
Source: European Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos speaking to journalists ahead of a meeting of the EU General Affairs Council in Luxembourg on 13 October, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Kos mentioned that the European Commission has presented its pre-enlargement policy review outlining the internal reforms the EU must undergo to be ready for future accessions.
Quote from Kos: "Three points are important to me. The first is that we make sure that once we get newcomers, they will follow the rules."
Details: Kos clarified that this refers to safeguards designed to protect democratic values and prohibit "backsliding".
Quote: "The next point is that we need a more flexible decision-making process. In these geopolitical, sometimes crazy times, we need to be more agile. That is why we suggest some steps how to use more QMV [qualified majority voting]."
Details: The third point is introducing enhanced gradual integration – "more Europe before membership".
Quote: "If a country will succeed to adopt everything necessary to be part of the sub-system or system of the European Union, we could get them on board even earlier [before formal accession – ed.]."
Background:
- On 6 October, the European Commission's College of Commissioners adopted a package of proposals on pre-enlargement policy reviews which will enable the EU to admit new members, including Ukraine.
- At the time, Marta Kos outlined five specific steps proposed by the Commission for future EU members.

Czech Mars 4×4 gets twin machine guns for drone defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:54:18 UTC
16:54:18 KST

- Czech 25th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment troops test-fired a Gladius Twin twin-machine-gun station on an SVOS Mars 4x4 against small drones at Boletice.
- The trials checked a Czech Ministry of Defence study; no order for the configuration has been announced.
Czech air defense troops have test-fired a remotely operated twin machine gun mounted on SVOS’s Mars 4×4 armored vehicle against small drones, as Czech industry offers the vehicle as a cheaper counter-drone option alongside the missile-armed version the Army of the Czech Republic has already ordered.
Soldiers from the 25th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment in Strakonice ran the trials at the Boletice military training area in southern Bohemia, using small, low-cost drones as targets. They first checked how well the electro-optical sensors on the Gladius Twin weapon station could detect and track the drones, and then fired live rounds at them. SVOS, which builds the Mars 4×4 in Přelouč, developed the configuration with EVPÚ Defence, the maker of the Gladius Twin, which carries two 7.62 mm machine guns and is mounted on the Mars 4×4 S-330 Hard Top variant. The companies did not say when the trials took place, how many drones were flown, at what ranges they were engaged or how many were hit.
The firing tests were meant to check in practice the conclusions of a Czech Ministry of Defence study on fitting the Gladius Twin to the Mars 4×4, which the state-owned Military Technical Institute and its aviation branch prepared for the army. According to the announcement, the trials showed that the weapon station worked effectively within the range of its ammunition and sensors, that it is suitable for integration on the Mars 4×4 for close-in air defense as part of force protection, and that cooperation with domestic industry pays off for the army.
The machine gun version is the second air defense configuration SVOS has shown on the Mars 4×4, following the vehicle armed with Saab’s RBS 70 NG laser-guided missiles. In July 2025, the Czech Ministry of Defence signed a contract worth about SEK 1.86 billion (about $195 million) with Saab for 24 Mars 4×4 vehicles carrying RBS 70 NG launchers, with SVOS as a subcontractor, plus eight tripod-mounted launchers and 80 missiles. Those vehicles are due to reach three batteries of the same 25th regiment between 2028 and 2030, replacing a mix of older RBS 70 and RBS 70 NG launchers that the unit currently operates in dismounted form, with crews exposed while firing.
Machine guns guided by a stabilized electro-optical sight give a much cheaper way to deal with small drones at short range than missiles, which can cost far more than the drones they shoot down. A weapon station like the Gladius Twin can also cover the final few hundred meters around a unit or base, where small reconnaissance and attack drones are most dangerous to troops on the ground.
SVOS says the Mars 4×4 already forms the basis of the Czech mobile short-range air defense system and has the technical features needed to carry other weapon systems.

Russian strike collapses a Kharkiv apartment stairwell and kills three, days after the US waived sanctions on Russia’s diesel
Unknown

2026-10-13
07:53:52 UTC
16:53:52 KST

Russian munitions brought down a stairwell of an apartment building in Kharkiv on the evening of 12 October, and rescuers recovered three bodies from the rubble overnight, local authorities reported. Survivors described fire, falling glass, and pets left behind. The strike came days after Washington waived sanctions on Russian diesel, as it expects Kyiv to stop hitting Russian refineries.
Russia hits Ukraine’s cities every day as it readies a winter campaign against Ukrainian infrastructure, and its oil exports keep bringing in the money that pays for the drones and missiles. A halt to Ukraine’s refinery strikes with no matching halt to Russia’s strikes would leave Moscow’s fuel income intact while Kharkiv digs through rubble. Estonia’s prime minister has already urged Europe to help Ukraine destroy those refineries instead.
A stairwell gone in Kholodnohirskyi district
Russian munitions hit Kharkiv’s Kholodnohirskyi district repeatedly from around 21:17, and Mayor Ihor Terekhov preliminarily identified them as Banderols. At 22:21, he said one strike had hit a residential building, possibly trapping people. He then added in a follow-up post: “Very serious destruction—an entire stairwell has collapsed.”
The strike destroyed an entrance of the four-story building, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) said. It counted 11 injured across the city’s evening strikes, and a rescuer was hospitalized, while Terekhov put the number at 10. By 06:56 on 13 October, rescuers had found a third body. Oblast head Oleh Syniehubov confirmed three dead and said the search continued. Experts will check whether the building is still fit to live in, he added.
Over 24 hours, Russian attacks killed three people in Kharkiv and injured 37, including two children treated for acute stress, Syniehubov reported.
“I realize I’m on fire”: two residents recall the strike
Larysa Maksimenko had just put her bedridden husband to sleep when the strike hit, she told Suspilne Kharkiv. She suffered a head wound and burns.
“I went to the kitchen to switch on the kettle for myself, to have some coffee. I realize I’m on fire. Then glass fell on me. I came to, and I’m buried under everything. All covered in blood,” she said.
The window bars were broken, and medics carried her husband out through the window. Rescuers later found a woman under the rubble in her apartment, likely a neighbor, Maksimenko said. All she wants now, she said, is to get to her husband in hospital.
Viacheslav Chibitko, who lives on the second floor next to the collapsed entrance, saw a flash, and then everything blew out. He got his three dogs out, but five cats are still inside. During the clearing, a concrete slab fell on a rescuer, Suspilne’s correspondent reported. Crews pulled him out and handed him to medics.
Kyiv’s toll rises, and strikes hit other cities overnight
The evening drone strike on a 25-story building in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district killed two people, Kyiv prosecutors reported. The second victim was found dead in a car near the building. Prosecutors counted at least seven injured, including a 17-year-old girl, while Mayor Vitali Klitschko counted 11 in the capital.
Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before sirens, gap that lands hard amid fears that Washington could cut data that warns of launches
From 18:00 on 12 October, Russia launched five ballistic missiles, nine loitering munitions, and 108 attack drones, Ukraine’s Air Force reported. Air defenses downed or suppressed 88 drones. A Russian drone attack injured four patients at a medical facility in Khmelnytskyi Oblast, oblast head Serhii Tiurin said. In Dnipro, a Russian attack injured a 64-year-old man, oblast head Oleksandr Hanzha reported. A downed Russian drone set two houses on fire in Murovane near Lviv, oblast head Maksym Kozytskyi said.
On 12 October, a Russian Smerch rocket with a cluster warhead hit a house in Cherkaske, Donetsk Oblast, killing three people, including a 13-year-old girl, oblast head Vadym Filashkin reported.
Russian attacks killed more than 150 people in the week to 11 October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Russian bombs killed at least 20 people in Zaporizhzhia on 10 October, by the oblast’s count. On 9 October, the US waived its sanctions on Russian diesel until April 2027. The White House expects Kyiv to halt refinery strikes under its proposed energy ceasefire.
