Russia's FSB Says Thwarted Kiev Attempt to Attack Baltimor Airfield in Voronezh With UAVs

====================================================================================================

Kyiv has learned to live between air raid alerts. After two months of relentless Russian attacks, there’s barely any time between them.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:53:37 UTC
16:53:37 KST

Kyiv has learned to live between air raid alerts. After two months of relentless Russian attacks, there’s barely any time between them.
Kyiv residents have lived under Russian drone and missile attacks since the start of the war, but this summer the attacks became a daily occurrence. Since late August, Russian forces have been attacking the city day and night, and air raid alerts constantly disrupt residents’ plans. Dozens of civilians have been killed in the capital over these months, and hundreds have been injured. As winter approaches, residents are preparing for power outages and heating problems. Meduza spoke with Ukrainian journalist Denys Trubetskyi, who writes for Die Zeit and other European outlets, about how doctors, business owners, and other Kyiv residents live and work under relentless attacks, and whether the coming winter could be much harder than previous ones.
‘Since last winter, Russia has focused on Kyiv. It’s the number one target behind the front lines’
— You were born in Sevastopol, but now you live in Kyiv and cover Ukraine for German-language outlets. When did you move?
— My career in German media came about pretty much by chance. I’ve never lived permanently in Germany or another German-speaking country, but at some point I started learning the language because I was interested in German sports and politics.
I got into journalism 14 or 15 years ago as a sportswriter, working for fairly big Ukrainian outlets like Football.ua. In 2012, Ukraine and Poland hosted the European soccer championship, and I met German colleagues while covering the German national team’s matches.
Then Ukraine entered a very interesting period politically: Maidan, the annexation of Crimea, which affected me directly because of where I’m from, and so on. I’d always thought about moving to Kyiv, and I’ve lived here since 2015. That’s also when I started working as a political correspondent for major German outlets — Die Zeit and Table.Media — as well as Swiss and Austrian publications.
— In late August, Russia began attacking Kyiv and the Kyiv region almost nonstop — at night and during the day. How is the city coping?
— To understand that, you have to look at Russia’s whole strategy of total war against Ukraine. I should explain why I call it total war. You can debate whether Russia is using all its resources for mobilization. When it comes to the war economy, it isn’t using all its resources yet.
But in the air war, Russia has been using every resource available since the fall of 2022. It’s sending pretty much everything it produces at Ukraine, including Kyiv. The jet-powered drones that have been pounding Kyiv since August are so new that some were built just two weeks ago. They sometimes stockpile ballistic missiles, but overall, attacks on the current scale wouldn’t be possible without using missiles fresh off the production line.
On September 11, 2022, Russia launched the first wave of attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. The strategy was meant to put as much pressure as possible on civilians. Since then, Russia has tried all kinds of ways to pressure Ukrainians — trying to knock out the country’s energy system, for example. But it’s come to realize that plunging half the country into a total blackout for a couple of weeks is very difficult.
So since last winter, Russia has focused on Kyiv. It’s the number one target for attacks behind the front lines. Kyiv and its metropolitan area account for roughly 15% of the population currently living in Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Last winter was the harshest in 20 years. Temperatures sometimes dropped to minus 25 degrees Celsius (minus 13 degrees Fahrenheit). Entire districts of Kyiv, especially on the left bank of the Dnipro, went weeks without electricity or heating. But this summer also turned out to be the hardest in the city’s history.
— What made it so hard?
— Two things coincided. First, [in winter] the genius U.S. president launched his “very successful” Operation Epic Fury, which caused a major weapons shortage. That had a serious impact on air defense. The PAC-3 MSE missile used in Patriot systems is the most effective against ballistic weapons. In July, Ukraine was receiving small batches of 15 to 20 missiles. We don’t know how things stand now, but those July figures are unlikely to have changed much.
Second, Russia increased production of its ballistic missiles. It used to produce up to about 60 standard ballistic missiles a month; now it’s up to 75. There are also missiles that follow a quasi-ballistic trajectory, like the Zircon. Roughly speaking, we’re talking about production of around 80 to 100 ballistic and quasi-ballistic missiles a month.
Ukraine has almost nothing to shoot them down with. And several Patriot systems are stationed in Kyiv — that’s an open secret. Obviously, once shortages developed here [in air defense], Russia started firing at Kyiv, because a new opportunity had opened up for its military.
Then there’s the situation with jet-powered drones — the Geran-4 and Geran-5. Ukraine had more or less been mentally prepared for attacks like these since the beginning of the year. Technically, there are ways to shoot them down, but it’s extremely difficult to find a solution that can be used on a large scale against drones flying at up to 650 kilometers per hour (about 400 miles per hour). And to make sure that solution doesn’t cost one and a half to two times as much as the Gerans themselves.
‘With everything flying so fast, you don’t even have time to do anything’
— How has this crisis affected everyday life in Kyiv?
— From May through the end of summer, ballistic missile strikes happened every third night on average. That’s really hard on your mental health and your day-to-day life.
Quite often, the strikes came before an air raid alert was even issued. But ballistic missiles fly so fast that many people barely have time to get down to a shelter, even after hearing the alert: A missile can hit one or two minutes after the alert. And if you’re outside at that moment, say, on your way to a shelter, that can be more dangerous than staying in the hallway.
You go to bed and you don’t know which night it’ll happen. In practice, a strike can come at any moment. When it happens every day, it’s hard to describe it without swearing.
— After the attacks intensified, The Guardian and The Washington Post described Kyiv as a frontline city. Do you agree?
— Things are different here. Kyiv is still a city behind the front lines, even if it’s the “number one target” behind them. FPV drones, artillery shells, and so on don’t reach us here. I wouldn’t use that particular term [“a frontline city”], although I understand it from a journalist’s perspective, and the situation [in Kyiv] is very difficult.
The problem with the endless launches of jet-powered drones is that it’s basically one endless attack that’s been going on since August. Without exaggeration, several people are killed and dozens are wounded every day. Of course, the chance of you personally getting hit is still small. But it’s increased considerably. There was a time when your risk of dying in a car crash in Kyiv was much higher than in an air attack. Now it’s the other way around.
I’m noticing that a lot of people around me are at their limit. They’re thinking about the coming winter. People who have the option of leaving for the winter are looking into whether they can afford it. I can’t do that: You can’t work as a Kyiv correspondent without being in Kyiv.
My friends were looking at apartments in Ivano-Frankivsk and Chernivtsi. Prices have naturally gone through the roof. You can describe Ukraine’s economic situation in one sentence: People have become much poorer. And we can say with certainty that food, internet, phone service, and so on will inevitably get much more expensive. Finding the money for an incredibly expensive apartment somewhere in western Ukraine is very difficult.
The economic side of this is very important right now. Many employers are suffering from the attacks — almost every industry has been affected. People’s wages are being cut while everything is getting more expensive. It leaves people feeling paralyzed.
Some people cope better than others in stressful situations like these. Among the people I know, the number taking sedatives or seeing a psychologist or psychiatrist has multiplied several times over.
— If you walk around Kyiv on a weekday now, what’s changed since the summer? What’s the first thing you notice?
— There’s a lot more destruction. Kyiv has 1,200 high-rise buildings, and I think about a third of them have been damaged over these four and a half years. Not always anything hugely dramatic, but at least a window blown out here or there.
There are fewer people in the city, though you might not notice it. The thing about Kyiv is that as some people leave, new people arrive — from Sumy or other cities [near the front lines].
There aren’t any official figures yet, but I’ve noticed it’s easier to park and fewer people are going to cafés and restaurants. You see fewer people on the streets, too, though that may be because so many are being switched to remote work.
And another thing you notice is that people are much more on edge.
— More and more people are working remotely?
— Yes, wherever that’s possible. Universities have been switching to remote learning on a fairly large scale. Schools haven’t been able to resume regular in-person teaching since September 1 — that’s very difficult with so many hours of air raid alerts every day.
— Which parts of the city are suffering the most from the attacks?
— Right now, all districts are suffering about equally. For example, Russia has recently been specifically targeting Kyiv’s gas stations. Literally any gas station could become a target, and you could happen to be nearby — stuck in traffic, for instance. Jet-powered drones can reach Kyiv from Russia’s Bryansk region in half an hour, depending on the model, and can fly around the entire city in three or four minutes. In that situation, there’s nothing you can do.
Russia has also been attacking Ukrainian data centers recently. Take the strike on the National Academy of Sciences [on September 28]: One of the offices of Ukrtelecom, a Ukrainian internet provider, is in the building next door. That same day, there was a strike on another Ukrtelecom office, which shares a building with the private clinic Dobrobut. Another strike [on September 25] hit a data center in Shuliavka, in an office building. There were terrible scenes there, too — bodies were literally lying in the street.
Russia isn’t holding back — I’m saying that without exaggeration. It’s not necessarily setting out to strike civilian facilities in these particular cases, but this is no longer collateral damage. It’s part of the military strategy. Russia can strike a gas station or a large office complex during the workday. It apparently intends to stick with this tactic. And with everything flying so fast, you don’t even have time to do anything.
— You’ve already said that internet and communications services in general could soon get more expensive in Ukraine. Are people already feeling the effects of attacks on data centers? Has internet service in Kyiv gotten worse?
— There are local disruptions, yes. At one point, roughly 100,000 subscribers in Kyiv and the Kyiv region lost internet access. But I still find it hard to understand exactly what this campaign is meant to achieve. The military’s internet infrastructure isn’t entirely independent of these data centers, but they [the Ukrainian armed forces] have their own infrastructure and networks, plus Starlink. These attacks seem more aimed at the civilian economy. Ukraine relies heavily on digital services.
How effective are they really? You might find yourself unable to pay for something by card, but there won’t be a total catastrophe. Ukraine may have one of the most decentralized networks of internet providers in Europe, or even the world — there are about a thousand operators in the country. Of course, there are big companies, but overall it’s a very extensive network.
‘We’ve been through all sorts of things in four and a half years. But never this level of anxiety. Now it’s constant’
— Are businesses managing to adapt to round-the-clock attacks and the changed conditions?
— It varies a lot. I’ve spoken with people running many large restaurants and food-service chains. They all have different views of the future, but they agree that restaurants in shopping malls won’t survive this winter: It’s dangerous to have employees come to work there during an air raid alert, even a yellow-level one.
There are reasons to believe Russia will strike shopping malls. So not only restaurants but probably all retail businesses in those malls will close down. And shopping malls are an important part of Ukraine’s economy. Kyiv has Respublika and Blockbuster Mall — they’re among the largest shopping malls in Ukraine and [Eastern] Europe.
Business owners — whether they sell clothing, run restaurants, or do something else — are trying to find solutions. But nobody can predict with complete certainty what things will look like in winter, so everyone’s improvising.
More generally, businesses are trying to adapt: A red alert means we don’t work; a yellow alert means we try to work somehow, because otherwise you could go crazy.
— Can a red alert last for hours?
— No, actually. That’s more likely with yellow alerts. This is a deliberate Russian tactic: launching small groups of jet-powered drones one after another. One arrives, gets shot down, then another is launched. It’s all done either to keep a yellow alert going almost indefinitely or to have another yellow alert issued 20 minutes later.
A red alert means either a truly massive drone attack or a specific missile threat.
— How much have Kyiv residents’ daily routines changed since attacks started happening during working hours?
— There is no routine — everyone’s improvising. Meetings are constantly being rescheduled and canceled, but businesses somehow manage to keep working. I’m amazed myself at how the cafés on my street manage to open on time. If you want to get a coffee at a café that opens at 8 a.m., somehow you can.
We’ve been through all sorts of things in four and a half years. But never this level of anxiety. Now it’s constant. People see it all happening. Very often, jet-powered Gerans fly right overhead. This will sound surprising, but that’s a good thing, because it means you won’t be directly hit. Most likely.
I’ve seen a lot over these years, but when this superfast thing that sounds like a quiet jet aircraft races over your head, it really gets to you.
— How has life changed for families with children?
— Everything’s become harder for them, because the children are effectively learning remotely all the time. Officially, it’s hybrid or in person, but the reality this school year is distance learning.
And this is another area where the internet situation matters. Because if attacks on energy infrastructure intensify, cell service and internet access could go down.
But the city has been through that before.
— The daily attacks must also have affected hospitals. How are they operating now?
— As a rule, surgery doesn’t stop during an alert — it all depends on the specific situation. During a red alert, hospitals try to move anyone they can to a shelter. During a yellow alert, they’re more likely to keep patients where they are, and 80% of Kyiv’s air raid alerts are yellow. Nobody moves intensive care patients anywhere. Ambulances and intensive care units keep working all the time.
As for strikes on hospitals, I wouldn’t say hospitals are being deliberately targeted at this point. But honestly, with the current strategy of terror — let’s call it that — we can’t rule out Russia moving on to that. Take the strike on the private clinic Dobrobut: The clinic wasn’t the specific target. Though perhaps Russia didn’t mind it getting hit, either.
There could be serious problems with medicines in the future. Some medications could be in short supply: There have been strikes on a facility in Kyiv belonging to Darnytsia, a major pharmaceutical company. This is primarily part of the economic war, but attacks like these show that Russia doesn’t care much about civilian lives. I don’t think that needs explaining anymore in 2026.
There’s also collateral damage. When warehouses are attacked, absolutely everyone gets hit — book publishers, manufacturers of all kinds of things. Quite a few warehouses storing medicines have also been destroyed. That doesn’t mean there’ll be a catastrophe, but shortages of certain medicines could develop.
You can support Ukrainian civilians facing these difficult conditions through Davayte, a project launched by Meduza, Helpdesk, and TV Rain in February 2024. We collect donations and work with our partners to help Ukrainians repair their homes and recover from injuries caused by Russian attacks, provide shelter for people who have lost their homes, and much more. Please follow this link to find out how to donate quickly and securely.
‘Shortages and major price increases are almost inevitable’
— You mentioned that Russia is heavily attacking warehouses in Ukraine. In late August, Agriculture and Food Minister Taras Vysotskyi said that about 90% of the country’s grocery-chain warehouses had been destroyed. Can you see that in the selection of products in stores?
— Yes, it’s changing. That’s especially true of perishables, because there are virtually no refrigerated warehouses left in the Kyiv region [because of Russian attacks].
I can’t say we’re facing an across-the-board shortage of fish, meat, or milk. But the selection has shrunk, and exactly what’s missing from stores depends directly on what was damaged two, three, or four days earlier. For example, right now you can barely find cola in Kyiv supermarkets, because the Coca-Cola plant in Brovary was hit very recently.
I don’t think there’s a risk of famine. Ukraine’s agricultural sector has enormous capacity, despite all the problems of 2022. But shortages and major price increases are almost inevitable. We can’t yet tell how severe they’ll be. But you’ll certainly be able to get through the winter eating, say, buckwheat.
There’s an effort now to reorganize logistics so that more goods go straight from suppliers to supermarkets. But the vehicle fleets that retail chains and suppliers needed and maintained in the 2000s no longer exist.
There’s still the option of importing food from the EU. We saw a similar situation in 2022 with gasoline and food. Back then, Russia was destroying Ukraine’s few oil refineries, and now Ukraine depends almost entirely on gasoline from Europe.
— In August, Ukrainian media reported that air raid alerts were bringing Kyiv’s transportation system to a standstill. The metro had effectively stopped carrying passengers, and buses and trolleybuses were overcrowded. Kyiv residents were flagging down cars in the street and asking drivers to give them a ride to the other bank. How is public transportation working now?
— That was actually one of the reasons for dividing alerts into yellow and red levels. All city-run surface transportation keeps operating during yellow alerts. That’s dangerous, of course, but otherwise the city simply can’t function.
Previously, though, large numbers of passengers on buses and trolleybuses would be made to get off at the nearest stop. If you can’t get to a shelter, that’s hardly safe, either.
The metro is a little different. Kyiv has three lines, two of which connect the left and right banks. During yellow alerts, one of those stops running, and the other becomes severely overcrowded.
— Has planning a route become harder?
— I’d strongly recommend avoiding trips from one bank to the other whenever possible. Especially from the left bank to the right. The city center is on the right bank, so large numbers of people travel there for work in the morning and return in the evening.
That’s another reason so many people are being switched to remote work. There’s the general safety concern, but also a very specific everyday problem: With constant traffic jams, people can easily be an hour late. There’s no point sitting in traffic.
— Since the beginning of October, the Russian military has struck bridges over the Dnipro several times, particularly the Northern and Southern bridges. What consequences could those attacks have for the city?
— Completely destroying bridges over the Dnipro is virtually impossible — we can see that from many other bridges in Ukraine. Despite continuing attacks and damage, the bridge over the Dniester estuary in Zatoka [in the Odesa region], the bridge over the Dnipro in Zaporizhzhia, and the Antonivskyi Bridge in Kherson are all still standing. Ukrainian forces struck the Antonivskyi Bridge during their counteroffensive in the fall of 2022, when Kherson was still occupied.
We’re talking about strategically important bridges, not small structures somewhere on the Siverskyi Donets, which really can be destroyed.
Still, if intensive attacks on Kyiv’s bridges continue, serious logistical problems will naturally develop. According to Ukraine’s Infrastructure Ministry, roughly 600,000 vehicles cross Kyiv’s main bridges every day.
The city is now considering setting up pontoon crossings and ferries, but as I understand it, the infrastructure needed for that isn’t ready yet. And it would be hard to replace the Southern Bridge fully that way, for example. It’s particularly important for transportation and logistics: A significant share of freight passing through the capital crosses it, and it also carries a metro line.
‘A friend of mine says she’s learned to fall asleep in the metro without worrying about what might happen’
— You regularly see headlines about air raid alerts lasting for hours. According to Ukrainska Pravda, Kyiv had one of its longest air raid alerts on September 28: It lasted more than nine hours. How does the city change during an air attack?
— It depends. If you walk around Kyiv during an ordinary attack, when there aren’t explosions right around you — whether you’re downtown or elsewhere — the city won’t look much different from normal. Life doesn’t stop. It’s an ordinary workday: People go about their business, drink coffee, and go places.
When there’s a confirmed threat of ballistic missile strikes, things are a little different. You can see people trying either to take cover with two walls between them and the outside or to get to a shelter. Again, it varies from person to person and depends on where you are.
What has really changed is that quite a few people, including people I know, are choosing to spend every night in a shelter — in the metro or an underground parking garage, for example. For many, that’s hard mentally, but a friend of mine, for instance, says she’s learned to fall asleep without worrying about what might happen.
Signs of a massive combined strike — an attack involving cruise missiles, ballistic missiles, and drones — usually appear several hours [before the strike itself]. You can tell whether an attack is coming from the movements of strategic bombers inside Russia.
At times like that, Kyiv’s metro is packed. The record for the number of people spending the night in the metro has been broken many times. The current record is 56,000. Realistically, that’s the maximum the metro can accommodate. Experts give higher figures, but after this summer’s combined attacks, you get the impression those are only possible on paper.
— Does Kyiv have enough shelters? Are they equipped for attacks lasting hours?
— The situation is pretty bad. Kyiv has about 4,500 shelters. It’s hard to say whether that’s a lot or a little. Not all of them are in good condition, and, let’s put it this way, not all of them are actually accessible.
During a jet-powered drone attack, conventional shelters — the metro, basements in schools and government buildings, and so on — aren’t all that helpful. They’re important, but Kyiv has almost none of what you see in Kharkiv and Odesa, for example. There, you can see portable concrete shelters on the streets that provide decent protection from drones.
Why are there almost none in Kyiv? That’s partly down to domestic politics. I don’t want to get too deep into it, but President Zelensky and Mayor Klitschko have been at odds for a long time. Different authorities block each other’s decisions to some extent.
I don’t want to take anyone’s side. But why almost nothing has been done about portable shelters in four years remains an open question. Kyiv’s mayor bears a great deal of responsibility here.
— What’s happening in Kyiv’s shelters during these hours-long alerts?
— Sometimes in the evenings, people try to get [into the stations] before the metro closes so they can lay out their mattresses and other things. Sometimes there’s a fight for spots.
Apart from these rather comical situations, I don’t think the atmosphere is that bad. It probably doesn’t compare anymore with the start of the war, when people held impromptu concerts in the stations. But even though everyone’s on edge, you can still feel people supporting each other. They share coffee and sandwiches, get to know each other, and so on.
Several times, I’ve gone down into the metro specifically as a journalist, to see how it all works and how people behave. And you really can still see some of that unity.
— In September, the Kyiv Post reported that Kyiv residents were increasingly ignoring air raid warnings. What do you think about that?
— You have to understand that it’s impossible to respond to every air raid alert for four and a half years. At some point, you could just go crazy. During yellow alerts, you could theoretically spend 18 hours in a shelter, but, as you can imagine, almost nobody does that.
But at night, when the chance of a ballistic missile strike is fairly high, people do go to shelters. I’d say that since May 2026, there’s actually been a noticeable increase in the number of Kyiv residents who don’t ignore air raid alerts.
‘People who wanted to prepare for winter have mostly been ready for a long time’
— You’ve already mentioned attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. Last year, some districts of Kyiv went without heating for weeks at a time, and temperatures often dropped below minus 20 degrees Celsius (minus 4 degrees Fahrenheit). What’s the outlook for this winter?
— It’s obvious there’ll be problems with energy supplies. Russia is trying to cut Kyiv off from the country’s power grid by striking both thermal power plants and power lines. Frequent repeat attacks make it harder to repair the damage. Kyiv could end up spending a week or two either with no electricity at all or with power for just a few hours a day. Hospitals, public and private, have long been ready for this. They largely prepared during the first winter of the war: They have generators and fuel reserves, so things are more or less okay on that front.
Air defense is also in worse shape now, for the reasons I mentioned at the beginning. But the weather is expected to be better this winter. Electricity consumption has also fallen. I think this winter will be more or less like the last one. It won’t be good, but I’m not expecting an outright apocalypse.
There could be problems with the sewer system — that’s very dangerous, and you can’t really prepare for it. If that happens, it’ll be a new experience for Kyiv residents.
— Last year, 600,000 people left Kyiv because of power and heating outages. Should we expect a similar mass exodus this winter?
— First, I want to point out that Klitschko’s figure of 600,000 was pulled out of thin air. People did leave, but there wasn’t a noticeable exodus. This winter will probably be different, since a whole range of factors will come into play.
Obviously, for people who have relatives [in other cities] or a house in some village where they can at least heat with firewood, that’s an option. But many people’s ability to travel is limited — primarily, I’m talking about military mobilization. There are checkpoints outside Kyiv, and if your paperwork isn’t all in order, you won’t get very far by car. So some people effectively won’t be able to leave Kyiv. And their girlfriends, wives, and children often stay with them.
And as I’ve already said, prices have risen so much that many people can’t afford to rent an apartment somewhere in western Ukraine.
— Can those who stay in the city prepare for winter?
— There’s nothing new here. Obviously, you can’t put a gasoline generator on the balcony of an apartment building, because your whole apartment could burn down. But people generally already have their power banks, EcoFlow portable power stations, and all that equipment ready.
I’m not saying everyone does, because there are people who don’t put much effort into it and just take things as they come. But people who wanted to prepare for winter have mostly been ready for a long time.

Türkiye posted a current account surplus of $4 billion in August, while the 12-month rolling deficit stood at $42.1 billion, according to central bank data.
The Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye announced that the current account excluding gold and energy indicated a net surplus of $8.2 billion during the month.
The country's goods deficit realized at $3.75 billion in August, the bank stated.
Net inflows from services recorded $9.7 billion in the same period.
Under the services item, travel revenues reached $7.28 billion and transportation revenues hit $3.26 billion.
Direct investment saw a net inflow of $141 million, as non-residents recorded a net inflow of $719 million.
Portfolio investments registered a net outflow of $1 billion in August.
The official reserves of the country increased by $7.14 billion during the same period.

Israel receives samples of Russian jet-powered drones from Ukraine for study
Israel is studying samples of Russian strike drones received from Ukraine, in particular new modifications of the Geran-type.
Source: Michael Brodsky, former Israeli Ambassador to Ukraine, during a media briefing at the Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs
Details: When asked by a journalist whether Israel had approached Ukraine for samples of the new Russian Geran-5 jet-powered drone, Michael Brodsky replied that such cooperation exists.
Quote: "Without going into details, such interaction is taking place. We have received weapons samples for study."
Details: Brodsky also confirmed that interaction between Ukraine and Israel exists regarding the study of weapons samples used in the war. He added that Israel has received certain samples from Ukraine, though the diplomat did not reveal details of this cooperation.
Brodsky explained that Israel's interest stems from the fact that similar technologies and weapons could end up in the hands of militant groups with which Israel is at war.
Quote: "Jet-powered drones are the number one problem for the entire world today. Whichever country finds an effective solution first will hold a major advantage, and others will begin adopting that solution."
Details: According to Brodsky, Israel is also actively working on countermeasures against such UAVs, including laser and other anti-drone technologies. Meanwhile, in his assessment, an effective universal solution does not yet exist.
Background: On Monday 12 October, crews from Lasar's Group used a new Ukrainian interceptor drone to bring down two Russian jet-powered Geran-5 drones flying towards Kyiv.

The additional cuts at the VRT are no longer open to negotiation Flemish Media Minister Cieltje Van Achter (Flemish nationalist N-VA) says. That means that flandersnews that over 21 years has played its role in putting Flanders on the international map will definitely close at the end of November.
Ms Van Achter was speaking following the trade unions’ announcement that they intended to visit her office, together with VRT management and representatives from the cultural sector, to put the cuts back on the table. The VRT must make additional savings of around 10 million euros in the coming years.
“I believe it is very important that the VRT continues to fulfil its public service remit effectively,” said the minister. “This involves independent journalism, analysis, high-quality programming for young people, Flemish stories, culture and sport. That core remit is essential.”
“Everyone must make tough choices”
The VRT is not among the most expensive public broadcasters in the European Union. The annual cost amounts to 44.58 euros per person in Flanders. Nevertheless, the Flemish Government wants the VRT to make tougher choices. The broadcaster will be required to make further savings in the coming years, on top of previous efforts.
The grant will be reduced by 3.4 million euros next year. That figure will rise to 7 million euros by 2029. On top of this, operating funds will not be index-linked, which, according to the VRT, brings the total additional savings to 10 million euros. These new cuts are in addition to the 16.6 million euros that the VRT was already required to save between 2026 and 2031.
The united trade union front at the VRT, which went on strike on Monday, announced that it intended to approach Van Achter’s office, together with the management and other affected parties in the cultural sector, to renegotiate the announced cuts.
Van Achter, however, emphasises that the figures are set in stone and are no longer open to negotiation. “I understand that the additional cuts are a heavy blow, but the Flemish Government must get the budget in order. You cannot ask the entire Flemish Government to make tough choices and then completely exempt one large public organisation from this.”
She now intends to work with the management and the board of directors to assess the implications for the broadcaster’s operations and how the cuts can be implemented in practice.

Wheel-powered drone makes the cut in U.S. Army trials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:48:39 UTC
16:48:39 KST

- AZAK said it was added as a seventh company to the U.S. Army’s Infantry Last Tactical Mile uncrewed resupply and casualty evacuation program.
- The Denver company builds vehicles around self-contained powered wheels and signed a fielding agreement with the Army’s G-TEAD in September.
Denver-based AZAK has been added as a seventh company to the U.S. Army’s Infantry Last Tactical Mile program, a competition for uncrewed ground vehicles that would carry supplies to front-line infantry, evacuate wounded soldiers and extend radio networks near the forward line of troops, the company said.
AZAK announced the news in a LinkedIn post on Oct. 12, saying the Army had originally capped the first group of finalists at six and brought AZAK in as a late addition after strong backing from the Army’s Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate, known as G-TEAD, and the 2nd Cavalry Regiment, the Stryker unit based in Vilseck, Germany. The company said it is now preparing for the next phase of evaluations and did not disclose which vehicle configuration it will enter or how many prototypes it will deliver.
The Army named its original six companies in August: Maren-Go, Overland AI, Forterra, Hendrick Motorsports, American Rheinmetall and HDT, which has since renamed itself BLADE and entered its six-wheeled Hunter WOLF, while Forterra has shown its MESA vehicle built on a Polaris Ranger. Each company is to deliver production-ready prototypes that can be controlled from beyond line of sight and switched between resupply and casualty evacuation, and the program is set to end with an operational assessment alongside an Army unit in early 2027 that will shape the production decision for the Army’s next generation of autonomous infantry vehicles.
AZAK takes a different route from most of its rivals, which start from a complete vehicle with a chassis, axles and a central engine. The company instead puts the motor, battery, gearbox, brakes and control electronics inside each wheel, so its S26 wheel module, first shown publicly at the DSEI exhibition in London in 2025, works as a self-contained drive unit that can be bolted onto different frames. AZAK says the 26-inch (66 cm) wheels can be combined into a small cargo carrier, a stretcher platform, a counter-drone mount or a drone launcher, with torque rising as more wheels are added, and that a damaged wheel can be swapped in the field instead of sending the whole vehicle for repair. Because the heavy components sit below the center of each wheel, the company says its vehicles have a low center of gravity that lets them climb over obstacles instead of driving around them.
The design also delivers a lot of pulling power for its size, according to the company. In a July demonstration, AZAK said a 227 kg (500-pound) vehicle built from its wheels towed a 24,040 kg (53,000-pound) Palletized Load System truck, the Army’s main heavy hauler for ammunition, along with about 454 kg (1,000 pounds) of ammunition, more than 100 times the vehicle’s own weight.
Most of AZAK’s progress has come through field trials with soldiers. The Army evaluated its platform during the 2025 xTech Overwatch competition and a rotation at the National Training Center at Fort Irwin, California, where Army photographs from October 2025 show soldiers testing the system, and the company brought a second-generation version to the AUSA Global Force Symposium in Huntsville, Alabama, in March. AZAK said soldiers also put its vehicles through Operation Overwatch, the xTech Edge Strike Ground competition and two Transformation in Contact rotations, in which the Army hands new equipment directly to operational units for feedback.
That record led to AZAK’s first Army deal in September, when the company signed an Other Transaction Agreement with G-TEAD to field its vehicles with Army units, becoming one of the first companies picked for the directorate directly by soldiers who had tested its equipment.

Gulf security and sovereignty are non-negotiable, Qatar's emir warns
Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani said on Tuesday that the security, sovereignty and stability of Gulf states were non-negotiable, calling for greater efforts to safeguard maritime navigation and critical infrastructure following the recent regional conflict.
Speaking at the opening of the Shura Council's regular session in Doha, Sheikh Tamim stressed the need to strengthen security in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, while protecting energy and water facilities and civilian infrastructure.
He said recent events had reinforced the importance of continued cooperation and coordination among Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states, warning that instability in one part of the world could not be isolated from the rest.
The emir recalled that Qatar had come under attack from Iran in what he described as a flagrant violation of its sovereignty, international law and the principles of good neighbourliness.
He praised the country's armed forces and security services for fulfilling their duty in defending Qatar, stressing that resilience was not born in moments of crisis but was the result of prior planning and preparation.
"Our commitment to dialogue and peaceful solutions does not mean compromising on the defence of our country," he said. "Our right to defend our sovereignty does not contradict our determination to prevent the war from expanding."
Qatar calls for diplomacy and secure waterways
Sheikh Tamim said Qatar had faced multiple responsibilities during the recent crisis, including protecting its sovereignty, fulfilling its role in global energy security and the international economy, and keeping diplomatic channels open.
He said Doha had worked to maintain essential services, supply chains and economic activity while contributing to efforts to secure a ceasefire and reopen waterways.
"We urge negotiations to reach peaceful solutions to the conflict," he said.
The emir also stressed that Qatar remained determined to protect its national achievements and would emerge from the crisis more resilient and better equipped to adapt to global changes.
"Our determination to build our nation and safeguard the achievements of our people is firm and unbreakable," he said.
Qatar emir condemns Gaza genocide
Turning to Gaza, Sheikh Tamim said Israel was carrying out a genocide against Palestinians and called for those responsible to be held accountable.
"What happened in the Gaza Strip was genocide, without question, and its perpetrators must not escape accountability," he said.
He reaffirmed that the Palestinian cause remained at the forefront of Qatar's priorities and warned of the dangers posed by Israel's continued aggression against Palestinians.
The emir also condemned Israeli settler attacks against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, saying they were being carried out under the protection of the Israeli military.
Addressing other regional conflicts, Sheikh Tamim called for comprehensive and equitable political settlements to the crises in Sudan, Libya, Yemen and Somalia, stressing the importance of preserving their territorial integrity and ensuring security and stability for their populations.
Hormuz closure disrupts Qatar's energy exports
On the economy, Sheikh Tamim said the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and damage to energy facilities in Ras Laffan had disrupted a significant portion of Qatar's exports.
He said the economic consequences of the crisis had been concentrated primarily in the energy sector, highlighting the vulnerability of global energy supplies to regional instability.
Despite the disruption, the emir said Qatar's economy had recorded real growth of 2.9% in 2025, while average inflation remained stable at 0.5%.
He warned that the country needed to remain prepared for further challenges and urged both institutions and citizens to take responsibility.
"We must be prepared for the worst-case scenarios, and everyone, institutions and citizens alike, must shoulder their responsibilities," he said.

India's statement at the UN on terrorism and crimes against humanity
NEW DELHI: India has called for terrorist acts that meet the requisite threshold to be recognised within the framework of crimes against humanity at the United Nations.It also stressed that states must take the lead in preventing, investigating and prosecuting such crimes through their national legal and judicial systems.
R Mythili, counsellor (legal adviser) at India's Permanent Mission to the UN, made the statement at the 81st session of the UN General Assembly's sixth committee during discussions on a proposed convention on the prevention and punishment of crimes against humanity.
India called for the primacy of national and territorial jurisdictions, with due respect for “State sovereignty and the principle of non-interference in internal affairs”.It also said a new convention must “complement, not duplicate, existing international legal mechanisms”, cautioning against simply transferring existing international legal regimes into the proposed framework.India further called for “broadly accepted principles of international law, stronger national capacities, and transparent and inclusive negotiations” to strengthen the international framework for preventing and punishing crimes against humanity.

A year after Gaza’s ceasefire, Israeli attacks persist as settler violence disrupts West Bank’s oil harvest.
The Gaza “ceasefire” marked its first anniversary on October 10, but more than 100 humanitarian and human rights organisations said it exists “in name only”.
Islamic Relief noted that Israeli forces have killed or wounded a Palestinian in Gaza on average every 90 minutes since the ceasefire took effect.
Gaza’s Health Ministry put the toll since the truce at 1,493 killed and 5,299 wounded as of October 12, up from 1,460 a week earlier; the cumulative death toll since October 2023 stood at 74,382.
Among the Palestinians killed in Gaza over the past week:
- Four Palestinians were killed in a drone strike near Panda Mall in western Gaza City on Saturday, which Israel said targeted members of Hamas’s Nukhba force.
- Also on Saturday, eight-year-old Shahd al-Najjar was killed by Israeli fire that struck her inside her tent in western Gaza City.
- Seven-year-old Jihad al-Ghandour died of wounds from a separate shooting near Jabalia camp north of Gaza City on Sunday.
- A child and his mother were killed Thursday when Israeli warplanes struck a home in Gaza City’s al-Sabra neighbourhood after an evacuation warning.
- A drone strike on a charging point west of Khan Younis killed four people on Sunday, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
- Two more men were killed in a strike near a mosque in al-Mawasi in the south on Monday.
In statements describing attacks, Israel’s military claimed several of those killed this week were Palestinian fighters.
The Israeli military said two men killed near the Jordanian Field Hospital were Islamic Jihad operatives; Wafa identified one as a recently released former prisoner.
It separately said a civil defence worker killed while responding to the wounded near Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza had been a Hamas sniper; Hamas rejected the claim, and it has not been independently verified.
Gaza’s health system continued its collapse:
- Gaza’s Ministry of Health said that 44 percent of essential medicines are completely out of stock.
- A Physicians for Human Rights Israel report found that a year into the ceasefire, not one of Gaza’s 36 hospitals is operating at full capacity.
- More than 18,500 patients need medical evacuation and more than 1,000 have died waiting, according to the joint NGO statement.
- The Health Ministry said this week that no patient had been permitted to leave through Rafah crossing in the last week.
Israeli forces have also continued pushing the so-called Yellow Line demarcating Israeli control further into residential Gaza City neighbourhoods this week, triggering fresh displacement.
One year into the ceasefire, the Board of Peace – Gaza’s transitional oversight body – has failed to meet most of its central commitments: no international stabilisation force has deployed, aid trucks are entering at roughly a third of the agreed rate, and Israel now controls nearly two thirds of the Strip — well above the roughly 50 percent it was supposed to retain before further withdrawal and a future handover of control to Palestinians.
Olive harvest under coordinated assault
The Palestinian olive harvest – traditionally a time of family and celebration – gathered pace as Israeli settlers and soldiers intensified efforts to disrupt it. Harvesters were killed, attacked and blocked, while isolated families faced dayslong settler sieges.
Pogrom attacks included:
- On October 7, Ali Hassan Yasser al-Bazzari, 44, was shot dead when settlers and soldiers opened fire on olive pickers on farmland between Burqa and Ramin, northwest of Nablus in the occupied West Bank. At least 16 others were wounded during the pogrom, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.
- The Palestine Red Crescent Society said Israeli forces assaulted ambulance crews trying to reach the wounded olive pickers and briefly detained three paramedics. Soldiers later raided the nearby village and made arrests, while the settlers who carried out the attack marched past unimpeded.
- The Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission recorded 19 settler attacks on Friday alone, another 12 on Saturday and 18 more on Sunday, according to Wafa.
- The Israeli rights group Yesh Din had already documented 109 harvest-related settler incidents across 75 Palestinian communities in a 10-day period between September 27 and October 6.
- The commission says settlers and soldiers have destroyed roughly 50,000 trees so far this year.
The attacks followed a familiar shape village to village, according to Wafa and field reports from local residents and activists:
- Settlers in Qusra stole a farmer’s olives before bulldozing more than 50 of his trees.
- In Birin, settlers from the recently established Adorim outpost set a dog on a 79-year-old woman harvesting nearby, hospitalizing her.
- Settlers from the same outpost cut power to roughly 20 homes repeatedly over the week.
- In al-Mughayyir, northeast of Ramallah, soldiers followed settlers into the village’s residential streets on Sunday, kicked an elderly woman trying to reach her home, and fired live rounds and tear gas into houses “without apparent reason,” according to Israeli field monitor Jonathan Pollack. The daily incursions are part of a monthslong campaign by settlers against villagers there.
- At Deir Abu Mash’al, a solidarity harvest organised by the Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission drew an attack by settlers in Area B that left eight people wounded, including a photojournalist shot in the thigh, Wafa reported.
Israeli forces frequently blocked the harvest, too. Soldiers used drone-mounted loudspeakers to drive farmers out of Wadi Abwein and turned pickers away in several locations elsewhere.
Israeli settlers’ own chat groups reveal how they frame such attacks in reverse — through a messianic lens, casting Palestinian harvesters reaching their own land in Deir Abu Mash’al as attempting to “seize” the land, and the olive harvest itself as cover for Palestinians gathering “intelligence” rather than picking olives that families have harvested there for generations. Settlers have been documented repeatedly stealing olives from Palestinians’ lands since harvesting unofficially started late last month.
Political jockeying ahead of elections
Once again, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas postponed Palestinian legislative elections – this time to September, citing Israeli restrictions on election materials and observers entering Gaza and East Jerusalem, and ongoing settler violence. Mustafa Barghouti, of the Palestinian National Initiative, said the decision reflects that “everything is concentrated in the hands of the executive authority”, with no parliament or independent judiciary to check it.
In Israel, with high-stakes parliamentary elections scheduled for October 27, Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen said his alliance – made up predominantly of Palestinian citizens of Israel – was prepared to support a coalition against current Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from outside government.
The support would be given in exchange for policy commitments, including a pathway to Palestinian statehood, The Times of Israel reported – a potential route to a majority that polls suggest neither bloc can reach without Arab party support.
Israeli authorities also began demolishing homes this week in al-Dahiya, an unrecognised Bedouin village in the Naqab, after a district court rejected a request to freeze the orders; roughly 60 homes face demolition.
In diplomatic news, the UK’s consulate in occupied East Jerusalem formally became a reduced “mission” after Israel’s deadline for its closure passed; it has long handled the UK’s relations with Palestinians.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Animal welfare groups submitted 12,000 petitions to the Central Election Commission Tuesday, calling for a referendum to ban wild boar snares.
The commission rejected a previous attempt in 2024, citing Indigenous hunting traditions and farmers’ concerns, per UDN. Campaigners argued that the traps catch animals indiscriminately, including protected species and pets.
The snares use spring-loaded metal wire to catch animals, sometimes mutilating them, the activists said. The referendum campaign includes demands for a complete ban on the use, possession, sale, exhibition, import, export, and manufacture of wild boar snares. A separate proposal requests amendments to the Animal Protection Act governing the manufacture and sale of the traps.
The activists said their current proposals differed from the rejected 2024 items because the new campaign specified metal traps, leaving traps made of natural materials such as bamboo and rattan out, UDN reported.
The campaigners suggested nets as an alternative for farmers looking to protect their livestock, while asking the government to set up a compensation system.

Microsoft president says milk faces more regulation than AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:45:00 UTC
16:45:00 KST

Microsoft president says milk faces more regulation than AI
- Microsoft president Brad Smith said AI needs urgent global rules, with independent checks, incident reports and an “emergency brake” for rogue systems.
- Smith said AI has fewer safety rules than milk or washing machines, and warned that companies should disclose breaches and harmful behaviour.
- He said Britain could lead regulation through its AI Security Institute, while the UK may tighten rules if the current voluntary system fails.
AI generated
LONDON – Artificial Intelligence needs urgent global regulation with independent evaluators able to vet new developments, the president of Microsoft said, warning that AI currently faces fewer safety requirements than milk.
In an interview with the BBC published on Oct 12, Brad Smith said a set of global safety rules needed to be in place, requiring a “victim” to be informed if their system is breached by a rogue AI agent and an “emergency brake” available.
He said there should also be a legal requirement for companies to write “incident reports”.
“We know how to do this for other products,” Smith said. “We should build on that knowledge and think about how to apply it to AI.”
“Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection.”
Tech companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI have started disclosing rogue or undesired behaviour by AI agents as part of a global debate about the fast-advancing technology that has included researchers’ warnings of an eventual existential threat to humanity.
Some companies have called for AI development to slow down, but that has sparked a debate as to whether executives have ulterior motives such as setting rules that preserve the lead of their firms, pre-empting a broader government backlash, or simply slowing breakneck spending.
Microsoft’s Smith said the one country that was well-placed to lead the way on regulation of AI was Britain, due to the AI Security Institute which was launched under former prime minister, Rishi Sunak.
Smith said officials in Washington viewed London very differently to how they viewed Brussels, which regulates AI based on the level of risk via its AI Act.
Britain’s institute receives pre-deployment access under voluntary agreements with the major AI models, allowing it to assess their capabilities and risks.
AI Minister Kanishka Narayan has told Reuters that Britain would consider regulating advanced models if the current system proved insufficient. REUTERS

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Army will launch its Lu Sheng 2 exercise on Wednesday, involving the 269th Combined Arms Brigade and the 564th Combined Arms Brigade.
The two brigades will face off in a 10-day, round-the-clock simulated combat exercise, per CNA.
This year’s drills will test the Army’s communications system and M1A2T tanks while incorporating command-and-control equipment and backup mechanisms, including the Taiwan Tactical Network and drone operations.
Major General Lin Shih-wei (林士偉), deputy commander of the Army Education, Training, and Doctrine Development Command, said the drills will focus on six areas: brigade- and battalion-level operational command, fire support coordination, defensive operations, integrated air-ground operations, drone deployment, and special operations. Each brigade will practice offensive and defensive missions, Lin said.
Shu Hsiao-huang (舒孝煌), a researcher at the Institute for National Defense and Security Research, said only full-scale exercises such as Lu Sheng can assess whether operational plans, tactics, and mobile logistics meet real-world requirements.
Such exercises can also expose potential weaknesses in fire support coordination and logistics, he said.
The military should also strengthen training with various types of drones and assess its ability to counter enemy reconnaissance and strike capabilities to identify existing gaps in combat readiness, Shu added.

IMF raises Taiwan's 2026 growth forecast to 10.7%, highest in Asia-Pacific
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:44:30 UTC
16:44:30 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has raised Taiwan's 2026 economic growth forecast to 10.7%, up from 5.2% in April. That would make Taiwan the fastest-growing economy in Asia-Pacific and one of only three economies worldwide forecast to post double-digit growth.
The fund released its latest World Economic Outlook report on Tuesday, forecasting global economic growth of 3.1% this year. Taiwan's projected growth is more than double Singapore's 5%, while Hong Kong is forecast to grow 3.8%, South Korea 3.3%, and Japan 0.7%.
Guyana's economy is forecast to grow 22.3% this year, while South Sudan's is projected to expand 10.5%, making them the only other economies expected to record double-digit growth. Taiwan's current account surplus is projected to reach 22% of GDP this year, among the highest of any major economy, reflecting strong export performance.
The fund forecasts Taiwan's consumer price index to rise 2% this year, up from its April estimate of 1.5%, while the unemployment rate is projected to remain at 3.4%. Taiwan's nominal GDP is projected to reach NT$32.59 trillion (US$1.02 trillion) this year, with GDP per capita at NT$1.40 million.
Among emerging Asian economies, Vietnam is forecast to grow 8.4%, India 7%, and Indonesia 5.1%. The IMF projects US economic growth of 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027, while the euro area is expected to expand 1.1% in 2026 and 1.2% in 2027.
China's economy is forecast to grow 4.5% this year and 4% next year. China's second-quarter growth fell short of expectations at 4.3% year over year, as weak consumption and investment partly offset robust exports, the report said.
The fund sharply downgraded its 2026 growth outlook for the Middle East and Central Asia, citing severe economic disruption from the ongoing Iran war. Saudi Arabia's economy is projected to contract 3.3% this year, although the fund expects a recovery next year if shipping through the Strait of Hormuz returns to normal.
The report also highlighted how AI-related technology exports and investment are helping offset geopolitical headwinds. Taiwan and South Korea are among the few economies producing advanced semiconductors at scale, and together account for 62% of net trade in AI-related computing hardware.

ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih has begun the process of placing its plant in cold shutdown following four Russian missile attacks, the company said on 10 October. The attacks killed six workers, injured more than 18 others, and forced the suspension of primary steel production.
ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih is Ukraine’s largest steelworks, so its shutdown adds to the pressure on an industry already hit by Russian attacks and disrupted exports.
ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih CEO Mauro Longobardo said the company’s priority was to protect workers and industrial assets. He said the ArcelorMittal Group would remain in Ukraine, but that its assessment was that safe operation was impossible while the war continued.
Workers and the city
As of July, ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih and its subsidiaries employed about 17,000 people, local outlet Pershyi Kryvorizkyi reported. On 29 September, the outlet reported that the company had not said how many workers could lose their jobs and was assessing its staffing needs after production stopped. It also said municipal water and heating utilities had about 1,000 vacancies and had been instructed to help ArcelorMittal workers find jobs. The outlet noted that it was unclear whether the vacancies were new and that the announcement did not specify the roles or salaries.
In late September, Kryvyi Rih defense council head Oleksandr Vilkul wrote on Telegram that the city would cut spending and stop a number of projects as tax revenues fell. He attributed the pressure to Russian attacks and the inability to export through seaports, and said several major industrial facilities were idle, including ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih and three mining and ore-processing plants.
September steel output down 4.7-fold
Ukraine’s steel production fell 4.7-fold year on year in September, to 131,000 tons, the steelmakers’ association Ukrmetalurhprom said, NV reported. Metinvest chief operating officer Oleksandr Myronenko told Forbes Ukraine on 15 September that the group would declare force majeure on some contracts after Zaporizhstal and Kametstal halted operations.
An expected $1 billion impairment
The ArcelorMittal Group said on 25 September that it expected to record a non-cash impairment of about $1 billion, mostly related to property, plant, and equipment. It also said it had provided more than $700 million in financial support to its Ukrainian business.

Taiwan to impose anti-dumping duties on Chinese polyamide film
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:44:23 UTC
16:44:23 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan will impose provisional anti-dumping duties on certain Chinese-made polyamide film for four months starting Oct. 19, the Customs Administration said Tuesday.
Polyamide film, also known as nylon film, is used in food packaging, industrial materials, and electronics because of its strength and resistance to heat and chemicals. The provisional rate will be 0% for three Yuncheng Group affiliates and 40.21% for all other manufacturers or exporters, per Tai Sounds.
The three companies assigned the 0% rate are Kunshan Yuncheng Plastic Industry Co., Ltd., Yuncheng Qilong New Material Co., Ltd., and Yuncheng Heshan New Materials Co., Ltd.
Yuncheng Group provided documents to show that it sets prices based on production costs and operates independently of the Chinese government, per CNA. Based on its calculations, investigators found no positive dumping margin for the group.
Exporters that did not cooperate with the investigation were assigned a 40.21% dumping margin, matching their provisional duty rate. The Customs Administration said the provisional duties are intended to prevent further harm to local producers while the investigation continues.
The Ministry of Finance must make a final determination on dumping within 60 days of the preliminary announcement. If dumping is confirmed, the Ministry of Economic Affairs will have 40 days to determine whether it injured the domestic industry.

KABUL, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- At least 679 people were killed and 1,634 others injured as seasonal flash floods and associated natural disasters swept across Afghanistan over the past year, authorities reported on Tuesday.
The disasters have also caused extensive destruction to infrastructure and rural livelihoods, Afghanistan National Disaster Management Authority spokesman Hafiz Mohammad Yusuf Hammad said.

Afghanistan remains one of the most disaster-vulnerable nations globally, where recurrent flash floods, landslides, prolonged droughts, and avalanches continue to claim lives, causing severe economic losses. ■

Christian tourists buy West Bank settlement goods in protest of European trade restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:41:11 UTC
16:41:11 KST

“This piece of legislation written by the Irish parliament shall not stand,” said Paul Coulter, national director of the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem (ICEJ) in Ireland, as he held up a copy of Ireland’s new law restricting imports from Israeli settlements. Then he tore the document apart in front of the camera.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The gesture came during an ICEJ visit to Israeli communities in the West Bank, also known as Judea and Samaria, where Christian visitors traveled through Samaria, Gush Etzion and Efrat and were encouraged to shop at local businesses. The tour, organized during ICEJ’s annual Feast of Tabernacles gathering in Jerusalem, was intended as a direct response to a growing set of European measures restricting trade in products from Israeli settlements. Some of those measures are already in force; others remain proposed legislation.
Ireland’s ban took effect on Sept. 15. The Netherlands followed with a broader restriction on Sept. 22 that reaches even goods carried in personal luggage. Norway, meanwhile, is considering legislation that would prohibit imports from and exports to Israeli settlements, along with certain property transactions and services. The Norwegian proposal remains under consideration after a public consultation that closed Sept. 19.
David Parsons, ICEJ senior vice president and spokesman, said the organization brought Christians attending the Feast of Tabernacles into the area specifically to support businesses affected by the measures.
“In recent weeks, several European countries and even Canada and others have announced that they’re going to pass sanctions against the Jewish communities in Judea and Samaria,” Parsons told The Media Line. “We brought them here to the Shomron, to Samaria, also down to Gush Etzion, Efrat, to go and show support by buying goods here.”
Christians protest European settlement boycotts
The governments imposing or considering the restrictions present them as measures directed at settlements they consider illegal under international law, rather than at Israel as a whole. Ireland says its law is part of an effort to comply with international legal obligations identified in the International Court of Justice’s 2024 advisory opinion. The Irish government argues that Israeli settlements in what it refers to as occupied Palestinian territory are unlawful and undermine prospects for a two-state solution. Its law prohibits imports originating in designated settlement postal codes and makes violations subject to existing customs law, including search, seizure and forfeiture powers.
Parsons rejected that reasoning and argued that the economic effect was precisely the point. “The real intent of these European countries is to dry up the settlements and their livelihoods, the way of life, so they’d have to leave here,” he said. That characterization is disputed by the governments behind the measures, which describe them as a legal and political distinction between Israel and territory captured in 1967.
The Irish measure, however, stops short of restricting what tourists bring home for themselves. Noncommercial goods in personal baggage are exempt when intended for the traveler’s own consumption or use. That distinction became part of Coulter’s message during the trip.
“Come and buy Israeli wine. It’s some of the best wine in the world,” he said. Later, addressing Irish visitors specifically, he added: “Break the boycott. If you can buy Israeli wine, buy it.” Coulter noted that Irish law does not prevent tourists from returning with those products for private consumption.
Coulter said opposition to ICEJ’s position has also followed the organization at home. He described venues receiving calls demanding that ICEJ events be canceled and demonstrations outside meetings that went ahead.
“We have our own hashtag, #BoycottApartheidICEJ,” he said. “Our venues are lobbied and phoned to cancel our meetings, and when the venues won’t cancel, we actually have protest mobs screaming and shouting at the gates of our meetings.”
Norway has not yet enacted its proposed trade ban. Its Foreign Ministry opened the proposal for public consultation in June, saying Norwegian citizens and companies should not contribute economically to maintaining settlements that the government considers unlawful. The proposal would prohibit importing goods from Israeli settlements and exporting goods to them. It would also restrict certain real estate purchases, construction and property-related services, and acquisitions of businesses based in the settlements. Violations would carry criminal liability.
Dag Øyvind Juliussen, national director of ICEJ Norway, said the prospect of criminal penalties has sharpened opposition among supporters of Israel in his country. “They want to pass a bill that would make it a crime to trade with the Jewish inhabitants in Judea and Samaria, the so-called settlements,” he told The Media Line, adding that the legislation must still go through the Norwegian parliament.
For Juliussen, joining the shopping tour was a way to turn that opposition into a physical act. “This is what we need to do,” he said. “This area has been the heartland of the Jewish people for 3,000 years.” He said Christians who share that view should make their position visible by supporting the people and businesses living there.
Christian groups challenge European trade bans on Israeli settlements
The Netherlands has taken a different approach. Since Sept. 22, travelers entering the country have also been barred from bringing in products that Dutch authorities identify as coming from Israeli settlements covered by the measure. That includes items bought for personal use, such as gifts or souvenirs.
Dutch customs officers can check luggage and ask where an item was made or purchased. Products found to fall under the ban may need to be surrendered or seized. The measure does not apply to Israeli goods generally, but specifically to products linked to the settlements covered by the Dutch restrictions. Customs authorities say inspections are selected on the basis of risk assessments and objective information rather than a traveler’s nationality, religion, ethnicity or appearance.
Parsons said the possible long-term consequences went beyond lost sales. He accused European governments of pursuing policies that could eventually pressure Jews to leave the communities. “Are you really willing to support ethnic cleansing of that nature through these sanctions and criminal laws against buying goods from this area?” he asked. His language went far beyond the stated position of the governments involved, which say their measures are aimed at settlements and at preserving the possibility of a negotiated two-state outcome.
ICEJ’s response during the tour was deliberately practical. “We’ve done that now by bringing dozens of Christians on several buses to these areas to shop,” Parsons said. His instruction to participants was straightforward: “Take out your plastic, take out your dollars, your shekels and buy goods from Judea and Samaria.”
That leaves people traveling together on the same ICEJ tour subject to different rules once they return home. An Irish visitor can bring a bottle of locally produced wine back for personal consumption under Ireland’s exemption. A Dutch traveler carrying the same bottle from a location covered by the Netherlands’ restrictions may have to surrender it at customs. The current policy was tightened after sexual violence cases involving US personnel emerged in 2024, restricting visits to establishments serving alcohol during early morning hours.
The latest talks follow renewed protests and demands for accountability. Okinawa’s prefectural assembly last Friday called for a fundamental review of the Japan-US Status of Forces Agreement, which governs American troops stationed in Japan.

MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Air defense systems intercepted and destroyed 604 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
A Ukrainian drone attack damaged a school, two private houses and a car in the Mosalsky District of Russia’s central Kaluga Region.
Damage from falling drone debris was recorded in the city of Nevinnomyssk in Russia’s North Caucasus Stavropol Region.
TASS has compiled key details about the aftermath.
Attack scale
- On-duty air defense systems intercepted and destroyed 604 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) over Russian regions between 8:00 p.m. Moscow time (5:00 p.m. GMT) on October 12 and 8:00 a.m. Moscow time (5:00 a.m. GMT) on October 13, the Defense Ministry reported.

- Air defenses intercepted most of the drones on the distant approaches, while 65 UAVs were brought down while approaching Moscow, Sobyanin said.

- According to the governor, drones were intercepted over the Babyninsky, Baryatinsky, Borovsky, Dzerzhinsky, Zhizdrinsky, Zhukovsky, Iznoskovsky, Kozelsky, Maloyaroslavetsky, Medynsky, Mosalsky, Peremyshlsky, Sukhinichsky, Khvastovichsky, Ferzikovsky and Yukhnovsky municipal districts and the outskirts of the cities of Kaluga and Obninsk.

- Air defense forces shot down 13 Ukrainian UAVs over the Voronezh Region overnight, Governor Alexander Gusev wrote on his Max channel.
Aftermath
- Air defenses repelled a large-scale aerial attack on the Stavropol Region, Governor Vladimir Vladimirov reported on Max.
- There have been no casualties reported so far.
- Damage from falling UAV debris was recorded in the industrial zone of the city of Nevinnomyssk.
- Inspection of the crash sites and assessment of the damage are underway.
- Emergency services began cleanup operations.

Ukrainian companies The Fourth Law and Odd Systems have announced signing a memorandum of understanding with U.S. defense technology company Performance Drone Works (PDW), under which the integration of Kurbas cameras into PDW drones will be assessed, with the possibility of localizing production in the U.S. later, the companies said.
"Ukraine is showing how fast technology can evolve when engineers and operators work closely together. We aim to combine proven technology with the U.S. engineering and production capacity needed to deploy it at scale," PDW CEO James Slider said, according to the release.
The Fourth Law and Odd Systems said in a joint release that the document was signed at the annual AUSA exhibition in Washington.

"Kurbas cameras were created and tested at the front. Together with PDW we can bring this technology to American platforms and, through Project Foundation, build a thermal sensor supply chain directly in the United States," The Fourth Law CEO and Odd Systems co-founder Yaroslav Azhniuk said in the release.
The release also said PDW is building capacity to integrate selected partner technologies and produce components for its platforms, and over time for the entire industry of unmanned systems in the U.S. and allied countries.
Performance Drone Works is a U.S. defense technology company specializing in the development of multipurpose aerial robotic systems, as well as software, communications, training systems and production capacity. It is headquartered in Huntsville, Alabama.
The Fourth Law and Odd Systems were founded in Kyiv in 2023 by entrepreneur Yaroslav Azhniuk. They operate in Ukraine, elsewhere in Europe and in the U.S.
The Fourth Law specializes in developing scalable autonomy for robotic systems, with a primary focus on defense.
Odd Systems develops and makes thermal and daytime cameras for drones and other robotic systems.
Last week The Fourth Law and Odd Systems announced the launch of a joint project, Project Foundation, to produce uncooled thermal sensors in Europe and the U.S.

U.S. Army names its new Korean-designed cannon XM1776
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:38:14 UTC
16:38:14 KST

- The U.S. Army and Hanwha Defense USA named the wheeled K9-based howitzer the XM1776 Mobile Tactical Cannon at AUSA 2026.
- The U.S. Army has ordered nine XM1776 prototypes with an option for nine more; the value of the change was not disclosed.
The U.S. Army has given its new wheeled howitzer an official name, the XM1776 Mobile Tactical Cannon, and has raised its prototype order from Hanwha Defense USA to nine systems, with an option for nine more.
The Army and Hanwha unveiled the designation at a naming ceremony at the company’s booth at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington on Oct. 12. The XM1776 is the American version of Hanwha’s K9 Mobile Howitzer, an eight-wheeled 155 mm self-propelled gun the U.S. Army is testing as a replacement for the towed M777 in some units. The number in the name points to 1776, the year of American independence, and Hanwha tied the unveiling to the country’s 250th anniversary this year.
When the U.S. Army picked Hanwha in August, the agreement called for six prototypes delivered on an accelerated schedule, with options for 12 more, worth up to about $263 million in total. Hanwha now says the U.S. Army has ordered nine prototypes with an option for nine more, keeping the possible total at 18. Neither the company nor the U.S. Army disclosed the value of the added systems, when they will be delivered, or how many have already been handed over. The first prototype arrived earlier this fall and was shown at a U.S. Army event on Capitol Hill this month.
“The XM-1776 Mobile Tactical Cannon represents the launch of the U.S. Army’s new long-range precision fires modernization effort and its powerful partnership with HDUSA to produce this system at speed and scale,” said Mike Smith, Hanwha Defense USA chief operating officer and president of land systems.
The XM1776 is built around the same 52-caliber gun used on Hanwha’s tracked K9, which serves with South Korea and about 10 other countries. Hanwha says more than 2,500 K9 howitzers have been fielded worldwide. A self-propelled gun can fire and drive off before enemy counter-battery fire arrives, something a towed M777 crew cannot do as quickly, and the K9’s longer barrel gives it more range than the M777.
Hanwha is setting up an integration and test site in Opelika, Alabama, as the first phase of U.S. production for the XM1776 and other K9 wheeled variants. Company leaders are meeting with more than 70 current and potential American suppliers this week as part of an effort to build what Hanwha calls an Artillery Industrial Base Coalition, aimed at moving more of the supply chain to the United States.
The U.S. Army plans to field the new cannon first to Stryker brigade combat teams, followed by mobile and infantry brigades, and wants a ready version in units by 2031. It has also opened a separate competition for a tracked Mobile Tactical Cannon.
