Minister: Iran's role in RAF Fairford incident affects Estonia's security
Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna says Iran's involvement in the RAF Fairford incident has implications for Estonia's security.
Fairford is used by US forces. Tsahkna said that matters to Estonia because NATO collective defense depends on allied infrastructure working and troops moving quickly across Europe in a crisis.
The UK has attributed the 27 September incident to Iran. Estonia is joining a joint statement by the foreign ministers of 28 nations condemning it.
"Estonia joins the joint statement by other foreign ministers, in which we acknowledge the United Kingdom's attribution and condemn Iran's violent attacks and other hybrid activity," Tsahkna said.
"European security threats are not limited to Russia's activities. According to the UK's assessment, what happened at Fairford shows the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps's continued readiness to operate through covert networks beyond Iran's borders. This means Iran's hostile activity must be treated as a European security question, not only a Middle East problem," he went on via a ministry press release.
I join my fellow foreign ministers in recognising the UK's attribution of Iranian involvement in the 27 September incident at RAF Fairford and condemning Iran's violent attacks and other hybrid activities. Threats to military facilities used by our Allies affect us all. We need closer coordination between Allies to expose hostile networks and prevent further attacks. We will not be intimidated. https://t.co/VaRvmwTZ7M

Five men, all UK nationals in their twenties, were arrested near the base in Gloucestershire in the early hours of 27 September after police were alerted to three suspicious vehicles. Drone attack sinks ship off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, PM says

Drone attack sinks ship off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, PM says
Two ships were hit in the attack, including the Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3, which sustained damage.
Two ships have been hit in drone attacks off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, with one of them sinking, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.
The Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3, which was sailing under a Maltese flag, was hit by three drones and damaged about 18 nautical miles (33km) off Bulgaria at about 1:30am on Tuesday (22:30 GMT on Monday), Radev said.
Radev said its 15-man crew, seven of them Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis, was rescued. Five crew members received medical assistance, and no one was seriously injured.
He added that one crew member from the ship that sank was also rescued.
Radev called the incident “absolutely unacceptable”.
“Another attack in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters,” he said in a televised address.
Radev also said there was no clear evidence of who carried out the attack, but “the outcome benefits” Russia and that the Russian ambassador would be summoned over the incident.
As a member of the NATO military alliance, Bulgaria holds a strategic position on the Black Sea, where Russia and Ukraine have vital ports.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned the attack on the ships.
“The Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine,” she said.
“This is unacceptable. I strongly condemn the drone attacks on merchant ships near Bulgaria’s coast. Putting the lives of the crew in grave danger and threatening security in the Black Sea,” she wrote on X.
“We stand with Bulgaria and thank its rescuers for their swift response. Those responsible should be held accountable,” von der Leyen added.
NATO chief Mark Rutte said the alliance would adjust its defences “as needed” following the incident.
“NATO will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea. We have already strengthened our posture along the eastern flank and will continue to monitor the security environment, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed,” Rutte said on X after talking to Radev.
The incident comes as concerns grow over hybrid attacks involving Russia.
Last week, drones hit two ships off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, causing one to sink. All 10 crew members from the ship that sank remain unaccounted for.

Hong Kong police arrest 20 over prostitution syndicate that trapped women in debt

Hong Kong police have arrested 20 people in connection with a cross-border prostitution syndicate that allegedly recruited women from Southeast Asia and required them to provide unpaid sexual services to repay travel debts.
Police said on Tuesday that the syndicate paid for the women’s travel and accommodation but required them to provide sexual services 30 to 45 times without payment before they could earn money from prostitution. The women then had to hand over half their earnings.
“This method left the women completely under the group’s control when they first arrived in Hong Kong, while allowing the syndicate to make huge profits,” Senior Inspector Lam Wa-yan of the special duties squad said.

Syria holds 19 hearings for war crimes suspects in Damascus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:35:03 UTC
16:35:03 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria holds 19 hearings for war crimes suspects in Damascus
A Damascus court held 19 hearings involving suspects accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity under the ousted Assad regime.
A Syrian court specialising in transitional justice held 19 hearings on Monday involving defendants accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity committed against civilians during the rule of ousted president Bashar al-Assad.
The hearings, held at Damascus's Fourth Criminal Court, form part of ongoing efforts to prosecute those responsible for abuses committed under the former regime.
Radif Mustafa, director of the Accountability Department at the National Commission for Transitional Justice, said late on Monday that the court had held 19 sessions, during which public trial proceedings continued, case files were read out, and evidence submissions and legal claims were presented.
The court also adjourned several cases to allow for the completion of legal procedures, including prosecution and defence submissions, the summoning of witnesses and the renewal of legal notifications.
Mustafa said the trials were continuing, adding that the number of cases and defendants reflected the scale of the judicial work required to address the legacy of serious violations committed under Assad's rule.
He stressed that accountability proceedings were moving forward in accordance with legal procedures, with defendants guaranteed the right to defend themselves, while responsibility for determining guilt and assigning criminal liability remained with the judiciary.
Mustafa also urged victims and their families, as well as anyone with complaints against the defendants or credible testimony, documents or information relating to abuses, to submit them to transitional justice courts through official channels.
He said documented complaints should not be overlooked and that relevant information must be brought into the legal verification process to help establish the truth and hold those responsible accountable based on evidence and the law.
The hearings follow a series of trials in Damascus in recent months targeting former security and military officials and other figures associated with Assad's government.
On 11 August, the Fourth Criminal Court sentenced Atef Najib, the former head of political security in Daraa, to death. It also handed down death sentences in absentia against Bashar al-Assad, his brother Maher al-Assad and several senior former officials.
Those sentenced included former defence minister Fahd Jassem al-Freij and former air force intelligence chief Jamil Hassan, following convictions for murder, torture and other violations classified as war crimes and crimes against humanity.
On 18 August, the court sentenced Wassim al-Assad, a relative of the ousted president, to death after convicting him of war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Six days later, on 24 August, it sentenced former Syrian grand mufti Ahmad Badr al-Din Hassoun to life imprisonment over crimes linked to the former regime.
The rulings form part of Syria's transitional justice process, which aims to hold those responsible for abuses against Syrians accountable following the collapse of Assad's regime in December 2024.

Former commander-in-chief Syrskyi explains why he sent troops to Kursk operation instead of defending Pokrovsk
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:31:00 EEST
16:31:00 KST

Former commander-in-chief Syrskyi explains why he sent troops to Kursk operation instead of defending Pokrovsk
Oleksandr Syrskyi, former commander-in-chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, considers the Kursk operation a successful manoeuvre and says that Russia had concentrated a force of nearly 100,000 troops near Pokrovsk at the time, meaning that redeploying Ukrainian units there would not have changed the situation.
Source: Syrskyi in an interview with BBC News Ukrainian
Quote from Syrskyi: "You have to understand that this operation was a necessity. If we recall 2024, after substantially increasing the pay of its military personnel and expanding the size of its forces, the enemy launched offensive operations in early summer 2024. This was effectively happening across all 13 operational sectors, with the enemy enjoying a 4½-fold advantage in some areas and, at times, even a sixfold advantage.
Under those conditions, with Russian aircraft dominating the skies, we were engaged in heavy defensive fighting, and we simply had to disrupt the enemy's plans, given the significant advantage it had."
Details: Syrskyi said the military leadership had studied the entire front line in detail and selected the Sumy front, where the Russians initially had 26,000 troops. During Russia's unsuccessful offensive on the Kharkiv front, however, it gradually redeployed all of its forces and assets from the Sumy front to Kharkiv. This failed to give the Russians any significant advantage, and they became bogged down in fighting along the border.
Syrskyi's decision to conduct an offensive operation on the Kursk front was approved by the Ukrainian president.
As a result, within a month, Ukraine's defence forces took control of 1,273 sq km of Russian territory, while the Russians were forced to halt their offensive on all operational-strategic fronts except the Pokrovsk front. Russia redeployed around 70,000 troops to the Kursk front, including airborne forces, marines and its best-trained motorised rifle units.
"This effectively gave us an opportunity to prepare reserves, give our troops some respite and restore the combat capability of units that had suffered losses in such heavy fighting. So the Kursk operation provided a major boost to the morale of our troops," Syrskyi said.
The interviewer pointed out that Russian forces had meanwhile been able to advance rapidly towards Pokrovsk and asked the general whether it would have been better to use the resources committed to the Kursk operation to defend the eastern front.
Quote from Syrskyi: "No, it would not. The point is that only three understrength air assault brigades and two assault battalions were used as part of the offensive force on the Kursk front.
Other units were involved in the second echelon as consolidation forces, but they too were only at 60-70% strength. They were effectively holding the front in this sector and only advancing behind the brigades. Their primary task was to consolidate their positions and hold the territory.
Two brigades spent a month preparing for the operation. The third, the 95th Brigade, was coming out of combat after heavy fighting on the Toretsk front and had very little time to restore its combat capability. So in practice, only one brigade attacked at full strength, while two brigades initially attacked with two battalions each, with their third battalions joining later once they had recovered.
So if they had been deployed on the Pokrovsk front – and we regard the Pokrovsk front as two separate sectors, Dobropillia and Pokrovsk – the Russians had concentrated a force of almost 100,000 troops there. Those two brigades, and later the third, would not have made any difference, given their technical condition.
On the Kursk front, however, the enemy had very weak defences and units covering the state border, consisting mainly of conscripts and stretched out thinly along the front. Some battalions covered 10 km, while others 12. So the defences there really were weak, and that was precisely why our forces achieved such enormous success.
When the enemy began redeploying its units, it was chaotic because there genuinely was a state of panic. I remember how much the Russian media were panicking at the time about the advance of our best brigades. The units being redeployed were thrown straight into battle and also suffered enormous losses.
According to the Russians' own figures, on some days during the fighting on the Kursk front, the casualty ratio for the enemy – which was hastily switching over to defence – was one to five. In other words, the enemy suffered five times as many casualties while defending as our troops did while attacking. I hope that answers your question."

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“A loud morning. The enemy attacked Dnipro with guided aerial bombs. A man was injured. Apartment buildings, transport infrastructure, and vehicles were damaged,” Lukashuk wrote.
Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration (OVA), said the injured man was 64. Medics provided him with the necessary care, but he declined hospitalization.
The type of weapon used in the attack has not been independently confirmed. If the use of guided aerial bombs is verified, the strike could mark a new escalation in Russian attacks on Dnipro.
Previous reports of guided bomb strikes on Dnipro
Reports of a Russian guided aerial bomb attack on Dnipro also emerged in early October last year. However, the weapon was later identified as a Hrom-1 missile, which had reached the city for the first time.
The Hrom-1 is a missile-bomb system that can be used as either a missile or a glide bomb. The two versions differ in their warheads and range: the missile carries a 315-kilogram warhead and has a range of up to 120 kilometers, while the bomb variant carries a 480-kilogram warhead and can travel up to 65 kilometers.

“The difference is due to the fact that the missile has a jet engine, while the bomb does not,” Ukrainian outlet NV reported.
Recent Russian attacks on Dnipro
In the morning on Oct. 12, Russian forces also attacked the city of Dnipro and the surrounding Dniprovskyi district. One person was killed in the city, while a fire broke out at a shopping center in the region’s suburbs.
In the early hours of Oct. 11, 2026, Russians attacked Dnipro with drones, damaging a high-rise building and setting warehouses ablaze. Several people were also injured.
On Oct. 10, Russia attacked the city three times throughout the day. The third strike sparked fires at food warehouses.

Albert Heijn and sister chains abroad hit by likely cyberattack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Albert Heijn and sister chains abroad hit by likely cyberattack
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Cybersecurity experts say it is very likely someone broke into Albert Heijn’s IT systems, as the outage at the Netherlands’ biggest supermarket chain leaves empty shelves in its stores.
Albert Heijn and its parent company Ahold Delhaize have kept systems switched off since Sunday afternoon and still describe the problem only as a “cybersecurity incident”. “An organisation that big doesn’t take measures like this lightly,” cybersecurity expert Joey Fennis told broadcaster NOS.
Fennis said that if attackers had got in, they may also have viewed or stolen data. Pim Takkenberg told current affairs programme Nieuwsuur it seemed “fairly clear” that someone malicious had been in the system. “An outage doesn’t usually last this long,” he said.
A third expert, Eward Driehuis, said the chain may instead have found a weakness it could not fix quickly, and shut its systems down as a precaution. Albert Heijn says its investigation is ongoing and has not said when services will be restored.
Supply chain
Albert Heijn has six distribution centres in the Netherlands. CEO Margaret Versteden-van Duijn told NOS on Monday that work at some of them had stopped completely, but she would not say which ones.
According to an email to suppliers seen by RTL Z, only the Zaandam centre is still operating, and suppliers have been asked to deliver there alone, in agreed time slots. Albert Heijn has not confirmed this.
The chain says fruit, vegetables and other fresh produce will be hardest to find, while frozen goods, bread and long-life products should remain more widely available. “Of course shelves will empty if this goes on longer,” Versteden-van Duijn told NOS. “That will vary from store to store.”
Beyond the Netherlands
Belgian supermarket chain Delhaize, also owned by Ahold Delhaize, has reported IT problems. Albert Heijn’s stores in Belgium, which are supplied from the Tilburg distribution centre, may run short of some products, broadcaster VRT reported, although the chain says the impact there is limited so far.
In the US, the websites of all five Ahold Delhaize supermarket chains, including Stop & Shop and Food Lion, were offline on Monday, according to trade publication Grocery Dive. Online ordering and deliveries were also suspended, Supermarket News reported.
The incident came on the same weekend as a separate cyberattack on hundreds of supermarkets in France. There, hackers remotely forced refrigeration systems to defrost, and chains including Intermarché and Coopérative U had to throw away fresh and frozen food. The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened an investigation.
The French attack targeted refrigeration equipment supplied by Danish firm Danfoss. Albert Heijn’s CEO told NOS she could not say whether the two incidents were linked, but an Ahold Delhaize spokesperson later told the news agency Reuters there was no reason to see a connection.

Fuel shortage in Bali: hours-long queues have formed at gas stations
Kyiv • UNN
At gas stations in Denpasar and southern Badung, drivers spend hours searching for Pertalite and Pertamax. Authorities say supplies are gradually being restored.
Drivers in various parts of the Indonesian island of Bali are facing long queues at gas stations, with some drivers spending hours trying to fill their tanks due to fuel shortages. UNN reports this, citing 7NEWS.
Details
Long queues have formed at gas stations across Denpasar and southern Badung, including Kuta, as Pertalite fuel—and, in some places, Pertamax—becomes increasingly difficult to find.
Some queues stretched beyond gas station entrances and onto surrounding roads, while drivers reported visiting several stations only to find that fuel supplies had run out. Traffic congestion has been reported, according to detikNews, affecting the flow of traffic.
One resident said the shortage had forced his wife to queue until dawn. "This morning, my wife joined the queue at 4:30 a.m. and waited for two and a half hours before she was finally able to refuel. This is crazy," he said.
The head of Bali's Manpower, Energy and Mineral Resources Agency, Ida Bagus Setiawan, said last week that the authorities were working with fuel supplier Pertamina and distributors to restore normal supplies.
"Technically, we were informed that the fuel flow was being redirected from the Pesanggaran depot to the Manggis transit terminal. The situation is gradually recovering," he said.
Setiawan said officials were still awaiting more detailed information about the cause of the distribution disruptions and their broader impact on fuel availability.
Badung Police Chief AKBP Joseph Edward Purba, as reported by detikNews, said that congestion at several gas stations in Badung had been caused by technical problems with fuel supplies from providers.
The shortage occurred after similar disruptions in late August, when fuel supply problems also led to long queues at gas stations in various parts of Bali.
Authorities say fuel distribution is gradually recovering, but its availability continues to vary depending on the location.

- Anthropic said new safeguards cut Claude distillation attacks by 90% to 99%, or “10 to 100 times lower” reasoning tokens extracted.
- The company said it blocked proxy networks and repeated probing, making large-scale copying of Claude’s protected reasoning much harder.
- Anthropic banned tens of thousands of accounts and warned that distillation, including by Z.ai, poses safety and national security risks.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – Anthropic said on Oct 12 that new measures designed to prevent rivals from copying the capabilities of its Claude AI models have reduced data harvested in so-called distillation attacks by about 90% to 99%.
Model distillation has emerged as a key concern for leading artificial intelligence companies due to intensifying US-China competition, with firms including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google arguing the practice enables rivals to reproduce advanced capabilities more quickly and at lower cost.
Anthropic said safeguards restricting access to Claude’s reasoning have sharply reduced extraction attempts, with “the number of reasoning tokens extracted by distillers” now “10 to 100 times lower than it was before”.
The California-headquartered company said it had made it harder to use proxy networks to repeatedly probe Claude’s protected reasoning, blocking extraction attempts and hindering large-scale distillation efforts.
Anthropic said its safety system is “roughly as robust as those that prevent Claude from helping build bioweapons” and has “a false positive rate of less than 0.1%”.
Anthropic banned tens of thousands of accounts linked to distillation campaigns and cited Chinese AI startup Z.ai, also known as Zhipu, as an example of a company that attempted to distil capabilities from Claude while developing its GLM-5.3 model, warning such practises pose safety and national security risks
Z.ai did not immediately respond to a request for comment. REUTERS

Fewer properties sold due to higher interest rates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:22:35 UTC
16:22:35 KST

Over the past three months, 2.2 per cent fewer homes have been sold in Belgium in comparison with the same period last year. This is clear from the latest information from the estate agents’ property barometer. The cause is the sharp rise in interest rates on mortgages. “You’re now paying 8.9 per cent more per month than a year ago,” calculates John Romain of independent mortgage advisers Immotheker Finotheker. House prices, too, continue to rise.
Sales of houses in Belgium have fallen particularly sharply, according to figures from the quarterly property barometer published by Fednot, the Federation of Notaries. Over the past three months, 2.8 per cent fewer houses were sold, whilst the decline in flat sales remained relatively limited at 0.4 per cent. Taken together, this means the overall Belgian housing market has contracted by 2.2 per cent.
In Flanders, the decline is smaller. Over the past quarter, 1.2 per cent fewer houses were sold and 0.7 per cent fewer flats. The number of property purchases has fallen in all Flemish provinces, with the exception of Flemish Brabant, where a slight increase of 1 per cent has been recorded.
Limburg, on the other hand, is the worst performer, with a fall of 5.1 per cent for flats and 2.4 per cent for houses.
Interest rates are to blame
The reason for this decline is the sharp rise in interest rates on mortgages, says notary Bart Van Opstal. “Interest rates have risen, which means that mortgages have also become more expensive.”
In August, interest rates reached their highest level in 12 years and have since risen even further. And that has a twofold effect, explains Van Opstal. “It is more expensive to take out a loan. If you take out a loan for an average house price and the interest rate rises by 1 per cent, you can easily end up paying hundreds of euros more per month.”
As a result, investors are also looking for alternatives to the property market: “They are now opting more for alternatives that offer higher returns, such as bonds. That is why they, too, are less active in the property market.”
Logically, a cooling of the market should be followed by price falls, but these have yet to materialise, Van Opstal observes. “We are in a prolonged period of price rises. House prices have risen by around 3 per cent since last year, whilst flat prices have risen by 2 per cent.”
A house in Flanders cost an average of 398,182 euros during the past three months. Last year, the figure was 384,781 euros, according to the notary barometer. Prices have risen by 3.5 per cent in the space of a year. Over the past five years, there has even been a price increase of 21.5 per cent. In 2021, a house in Flanders cost an average of 327,785 euros.

Ukraine Secures EU-Wide Agreement on Two More Accession Clusters Following Minority Rights Reform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:22:29 UTC
16:22:29 KST

- Category
- World
Ukraine Secures EU-Wide Agreement on Two More Accession Clusters Following Minority Rights Reform
All 27 European Union member states have agreed to open two additional accession negotiation clusters with Ukraine and Moldova, Irish Minister of State for European Affairs and Defense Thomas Byrne confirmed on October 12.
Byrne announced the agreement on X, outlining a series of EU enlargement decisions involving Ukraine, Moldova, Montenegro, and Albania.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“I can confirm that all EU member states have agreed to open clusters 2 and 3 for Ukraine and Moldova,” Byrne wrote.
The agreement covers two major areas of EU accession negotiations: Cluster 2, which addresses the internal market, and Cluster 3, which focuses on competitiveness and inclusive growth.
Cluster 2 covers the rules governing the EU's single market, including the free movement of goods, workers, services, and capital. It also addresses company law, intellectual property, competition policy, financial services, and consumer protection.
Cluster 3 focuses on economic and social development. Its eight negotiating chapters cover digital transformation and media, taxation, economic and monetary policy, employment, industrial policy, science and research, education and culture, and customs policy.
The EU accession framework divides negotiations into six thematic clusters, each covering specific areas of legislation that candidate countries must align with European standards.
Opening a cluster allows negotiations to proceed across its policy areas, but it does not mean the country has completed the required reforms. Individual chapters can be provisionally closed once the EU determines that the relevant conditions have been met.
Byrne also confirmed that EU member states had agreed to close three negotiating chapters with Montenegro: economic and monetary policy, statistics, and social policy and employment.
Albania will close Chapter 20, covering enterprise and industrial policy.
The Irish minister described the forthcoming developments as another "Super Tuesday" for EU enlargement, following what he called "Montenegro Monday."
The agreement follows Ukraine's adoption of legislation expanding educational rights for national minorities and indigenous peoples on October 12.
The amendments address an issue that had contributed to Hungary's objections to the advancement of Ukraine's EU accession negotiations.
The law allows greater use of eligible minority languages in schools while preserving Ukrainian's status as the state language. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had earlier indicated that Kyiv expected the EU to formally open the two clusters on October 13.
Ukraine's accession negotiations began in June 2024, and the EU subsequently opened Cluster 1, covering fundamental reforms, in June 2026. Cluster 6, covering external relations and foreign, security, and defense policy, opened on July 14, 2026. Under the EU's accession methodology, the Fundamentals cluster opens first and closes last, with progress in that area determining the overall pace of negotiations.

According to data from Marinetraffic, the tanker was sailing under Benin’s flag and was headed to the port of Cruz Grande in Chile. It wasn’t clear where the vessel had sailed from.
The magazine Maritime Executive writes that the tanker was built in 2006 and originally belonged to the company Sovcomflot, sailing under the name NS Captain. It was renamed Kaliningrad in 2024 and took its current name in 2025. Its operator is now a company based in Hong Kong.
Maritime Executive also says that Benin’s national registry, whose flag the tanker flies, was once “considered a haven for Russia-linked shadow fleet vessels.” The U.S. sanctioned the tanker in February 2024. The European Union, Switzerland, Canada, the U.K., and Ukraine followed with sanctions of their own.
France has detained tankers belonging to the “shadow fleet,” including some reportedly linked to Russia, several times since the start of 2026. In January, French authorities detained the tanker Grinch. In March, they detained the tanker Deyna, which was allowed to leave the port of Marseille a month later. In June, French authorities detained the tankers Tagor and Deliver. The politics of gratitude: The corruption no one sees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:21:59 UTC
16:21:59 KST

Not all political corruption begins with money. Sometimes, it begins with success. Public imagination has long been trained to look for corruption in suitcases of cash, shady contracts, and secret deals. Yet some of the most consequential distortions of political judgment emerge from a far subtler source: a politician’s emotional attachment to a project they helped create.
This hidden dynamic lay beneath the recent controversy surrounding Andy Burnham’s comments on Manchester City. After initially suggesting that the club deserved fair treatment before later reaffirming that no institution stands above the rules, Burnham found himself at the center of a debate that extended far beyond football.
At first glance, the story appeared to involve a politician defending a football club or perhaps its wealthy owners. In reality, something more interesting was taking place. Burnham was defending, consciously or otherwise, part of his own political story.
The transformation of Manchester over the past two decades has become one of Britain’s most celebrated urban success stories. Manchester City’s ownership was not solely responsible for that transformation, but it undeniably became part of it.
Investments around the Etihad complex and across large sections of East Manchester helped reinforce a narrative of renewal that politicians, civic leaders, and business interests collectively embraced. For Burnham, separating the success of modern Manchester from his own political identity has become increasingly difficult.
This is not primarily an ethical problem. It is a human one.
People instinctively defend the institutions, ideas, and projects that have given meaning to their lives. Politicians are especially vulnerable to this tendency because politics is ultimately a profession obsessed with legacy. Few enter public life merely to exercise power. Most hope to leave behind a lasting achievement. The moment that achievement comes under scrutiny, criticism of the project begins to feel like criticism of the self.
Britain has witnessed this phenomenon before.
Tony Blair spent years trapped within the narrative of “New Labour” and the promise of a modernised Britain. The project was initially so successful that its architect struggled to recognise its deeper flaws. This became most visible in the Iraq War.
Blair’s persistence was not simply a matter of defending a policy. Over time, the war became intertwined with his broader conception of leadership and international responsibility. Retreat no longer meant revising a political decision. It meant acknowledging that one of the defining chapters of his public life may have been built upon a profound misjudgement.
A similar pattern can be observed in Boris Johnson’s relationship with Brexit. Long after leaving office, Johnson has remained attached to the project not merely because he believes in its outcomes but because Brexit became inseparable from his political identity. It delivered power, fame, and a place in history. To distance himself from it would require a form of self-criticism that few politicians are willing to undertake.
Yet this phenomenon extends beyond individuals.
Governments fall in love with their achievements. Cities fall in love with their redevelopment schemes. Nations fall in love with the narratives they construct about themselves.
READ: UAE warns UK over potential fallout from Manchester City sanctions: Report
At a certain point, success ceases to be a project and becomes a creed.
And that is when the trouble begins.
The paradox is that failure often encourages self-examination, while success produces the illusion of infallibility. A failed policy invites scrutiny. A successful one tends to acquire defenders. The more celebrated an achievement becomes, the more difficult it is to assess honestly.
The true responsibility of a statesman is not to adore achievements but to question them. It is not to protect them from criticism but to subject them to it. A good engineer is not the person who loves a building most. It is the person who knows where it might collapse.
Modern politics, however, rewards precisely the opposite behaviour. It rewards the conversion of political accomplishments into heroic narratives. Eventually, the narrative becomes more valuable than reality itself. Protecting the legacy becomes more important than examining its weaknesses.
This is why one of the most dangerous forms of political corruption is not financial corruption but what might be called the corruption of gratitude.
A politician becomes indebted to a project, a business leader, an idea, a movement, or even an electorate that helped create their success. Once that bond is formed, impartial judgment begins to erode. Not because of bribery or coercion, but because emotional loyalty quietly replaces critical distance.
The politician who takes a bribe can be exposed.
The politician imprisoned by personal success is far more difficult to detect.
In many cases, such individuals sincerely believe they are acting in the public interest. They do not recognize their own bias because they are not protecting a benefactor. They are protecting a cherished part of themselves.
Nor is this tendency confined to politics. Revolutionaries often become prisoners of the narratives they once created. Writers become captives of their most celebrated books. Leaders cling to decisions that history has already judged harshly because they can no longer separate the truth from their own reflection in it.
This is what makes the Burnham episode more interesting than Manchester City itself.
The fundamental question is not whether the club’s owners are good or bad, nor whether the club is guilty or innocent. The deeper question is what happens when a politician can no longer distinguish between the interests of a city and the story they tell themselves about their role in its success.
That is where the quiet tragedy of politics begins.
And it is also where the most elusive form of corruption emerges.
Not from the pocket, but from the heart.
OPINION: Political failure, not economic shock, unmasks Iraq

Kaunas is phasing out paper tickets and cash payments in public transport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:21:00 UTC
16:21:00 KST

Kaunas will eliminate paper tickets and cash payments on public transportation starting in December, following a vote by the city council on Tuesday.
Twenty-seven council members voted in favour of the proposal, one opposed it and 10 abstained.
The city says eliminating cash payments will allow drivers to focus on operating vehicles instead of handling money and issuing tickets, helping public transportation run on schedule.
The proposal drew concerns from opposition politicians about access for senior citizens, tourists and passengers affected by banking or payment system disruptions.
Conservative council member Rasa Duobaitė-Bumbulienė asked whether the change would make it harder for older people traveling to Kaunas for medical appointments to use public transportation.
Martynas Matusevičius, head of the city’s Transport and Traffic Organisation Division, said older passengers receiving discounted fares accounted for a small share of those who currently pay drivers in cash.
Passengers can switch their discounted fares to bank cards, and Kaunas Public Transport’s information centre will provide assistance by phone and in person, he said.
The city is also considering installing ticket vending machines at planned public transportation transfer terminals, although their cost and maintenance requirements remain concerns, Matusevičius said.
He added that the contactless payment system had been tested and could continue operating even during internet disruptions, with payments processed later.
Under the new rules, passengers will still be able to use cash to buy or top up public transportation cards at designated sales points, including customer service offices, shopping centres and kiosks.
According to Kaunas Public Transport, tickets bought from drivers with cash accounted for just 4.5% of all fare payments during the first eight months of this year, about one-third fewer than in the same period last year.
About 60% of passengers use public transportation cards, while nearly 35% use the special mobile app, Žiogas. Bank cards and smart devices account for less than 1% of payments.
Contactless payments were introduced on Kaunas public transportation in August last year. Since September, passengers have also been able to buy discounted tickets using contactless validators.

AI models may soon self-replicate without access to data centres: Anthropic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:20:00 UTC
16:20:00 KST

AI models may soon self-replicate without access to data centres: Anthropic
- Anthropic warned that small AI models may soon self-replicate on insecure IoT devices, such as smart ovens and Android TV boxes, using only commercial internet-connected hardware.
- Its tests found models under 30 billion parameters could complete parts of the process, but many still could not finish full replication without help. GLM-5.2 and stronger models did so in simplified tests.
- Anthropic said self-replicating AI would be hard to stop, could target unfamiliar devices, and may be autonomous by the end of 2026 if progress continues. It urged stronger security.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – Anthropic said on Oct 12 that its experiments suggested small AI models may be months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial internet-of-things (IOT) devices, such as smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes.
In its experiments, Anthropic looked at whether artificial intelligence models could find vulnerable devices, copy themselves into those devices, and continue spreading without human help.
It found that small models under 30 billion parameters could complete the many steps needed for replication.
However, the firm found that such AI models also struggled to complete the entire sequence from start to finish.
In its simplified tests, where some security steps were removed, Anthropic found that GLM-5.2 and stronger models were capable of end-to-end replication.
Replicating models would be hard to shut down as there is no central switch-off point and, unlike non-AI malware, they could also figure out unfamiliar devices on their own, targeting data centre processors, Anthropic warned.
The firm focused on IOT devices like Android TVs, smart appliances and other internet-connected gadgets in its research as these are typically poorly secured.
It also warned that if small models improved at their historical rate, they would be able to autonomously replicate by the end of 2026, with small weight-based replicators following suit soon after.
Anthropic also said such autonomous AI systems were likely to replicate slowly and rely on widely available, relatively insecure computing resources. It added that systems should be strengthened to make it harder for such AI agents to spread. REUTERS

Dutch economy set to grow by 1.5% in 2026 as IMF raises forecast

Dutch economy set to grow by 1.5% in 2026 as IMF raises forecast
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has improved its forecast for the Dutch economy, but warned that high prices will continue to cause pain for consumers.
The Netherlands’ GDP is now expected to grow by 1.5% this year, up from 1% in the IMF’s last assessment in July. The trend is set to continue into 2027, when the IMF expects growth of 1.3%.
The organisation says the Dutch economy will benefit from stronger than expected growth in Germany, where it has revised its prediction from 0.7% to 1.3% for this year, as well as large global investments in AI technology.
Consumer prices will grow by 2.9% this year, reflecting the high cost of energy and fuel. The statistics agency CBS reported on Tuesday that inflation had risen to 3.4% in September, continuing an upward trend that started in July.
Fuel prices have risen by 27.2% in the last year, with a litre of diesel costing nearly €2.50 at the pumps. But prices for other commodities have fallen, such as food, which is down by 1.9%.
The IMF said the impact of the conflict in Iran on fuel prices had been tempered by countries finding alternative suppliers of oil and gas.

Banking watchdogs ramp up AI scrutiny as stability fears mount, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:15:00 UTC
16:15:00 KST

Banking watchdogs ramp up AI scrutiny as stability fears mount, say sources
- Banking regulators in the US and Europe are stepping up AI checks as fears grow that agentic AI could weaken cyber defences and threaten financial stability.
- US agencies, including the Fed, OCC and FDIC, are asking banks how they use advanced AI, especially foreign models, cyber defence agents and controls on autonomous systems.
- European supervisors want stronger recovery plans and better mapping of AI use across banks and providers, as experts warn a major attack could disrupt payments and lock customers out.
AI generated
NEW YORK/LONDON – Banking regulators are stepping up efforts to contain growing AI risks, six people familiar with the matter said, with some pointing to the potential for cyberattacks on banks or rogue agents undermining global financial stability.
The regulatory scrutiny, fresh details of which are reported here for the first time, reflects growing recognition that advances in frontier AI may require costly investments in cyber recovery, greater attention to dependencies on external technology providers and in some jurisdictions, more formal regulatory guidance, sources said.
Three top regulators in the US, including the Federal Reserve, are quizzing banks about their use of advanced AI models, two of the people told Reuters, adding to prior scrutiny.
Questions include whether they deploy Chinese-developed technology, use AI agents in cyberdefence and can control increasingly autonomous systems, three of the people said.
In Europe, supervisors, including the Bank of England (BOE) and the European Central Bank (ECB), are pressing banks to improve recovery plans, concerned that rapid advances in artificial intelligence could cause serious harm and disruption in financial markets sooner than previously feared, three people with knowledge of their thinking said.
A senior executive at a large European bank said they, too, are worried about potentially major damage to banking and financial markets “within six months”.
The debate over AI oversight has intensified amid warnings from the industry after recent incidents, with JPMorgan chief executive Jamie Dimon urging corporate leaders to join a US-focused industry group to address AI risks, Reuters reported.
US cybersecurity company CrowdStrike said in October that a person in China likely used a Chinese-developed AI agent and Anthropic’s Claude Code in a hack on South Korean banks. Rogue AI agents developed by OpenAI were meanwhile involved in a breach of the AI platform Hugging Face, Reuters reported.
Anthropic researchers have warned that increasingly powerful AI systems could eventually escape human control and even pose an existential threat, prompting calls for stricter regulation.
Banks are competing to adopt agentic AI, which can accomplish tasks with minimal human supervision, while also grappling with challenges in new models, including IT weaknesses flagged by Anthropic’s Mythos tool.
Michael Woodbridge, London-based cybersecurity partner at Grant Thornton, said: “The adoption of AI is often outpacing the ability to put the controls in place.”
US concerns aim at agentic AI
The US regulatory inquiries centre on how banks use agentic AI in areas such as cybersecurity, focusing on whether AI agents are being used to identify, prioritise and respond to threats.
Questions from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and the Fed focus on what limits are placed on systems, how their actions are monitored and approved and whether banks can clearly track and audit AI agent decisions, two of the people said.
They are also asking what safeguards exist to prevent agents from exceeding their authority, whether humans remain involved in key decisions and how banks can shut down autonomous systems.
The OCC, the Fed and the FDIC declined to comment.
Through their questions, regulators are probing more specific issues tied to advanced AI models, including the use of autonomous AI agents, foreign-developed models and new cyber risks, the three people with knowledge of their thinking said.
The written and verbal inquiries to large, mid-size and smaller banks show regulators are focusing on vulnerabilities from banks’ use of AI and their preparedness to act, they said.
Regulators are still gathering information and are not yet being prescriptive about what lenders should be doing, they added.
Europeans worry about recovery
Supervisors in Britain are separately encouraging the largest banks to examine so-called bare metal recovery plans, two of the people familiar with their thinking said. These systems are entirely independent of a bank’s main tech set-up and can kick in if primary operating systems are compromised.
But building and maintaining such state-of-the-art recovery is expensive, the people said.
Rather than introduce new requirements, the British authorities intend to work collaboratively with industry, they added.
The BOE declined to comment.
In July, the ECB gave lenders an end-of-October deadline to produce plans to counter AI-enabled cyberthreats, including improved backup and recovery.
Asked about its strategy for regulating AI, the ECB referred to its July letter and a June speech by board member Frank Elderson, who stressed the need to create a sense of urgency, not alarm, about the threats.
The need for supervisory action has taken on added urgency after European banks and regulators expressed frustration at getting limited access to Mythos in 2026, amid concerns that US banks will be given first sight to test frontier models.
Like their US counterparts, British supervisors are also asking banks to use frontier AI to identify vulnerabilities and accelerate patching, two people said, with one adding that lenders were so far doing a good job.
The third person said euro zone banks were also being asked to map how AI is being used across their businesses and third-party providers to understand key dependencies and ensure they can switch off and restart systems in a controlled manner.
Significant gaps remained at some firms, they added.
Sukand Ramachandran, managing director and senior partner at Boston Consulting Group, said: “To protect against attacks, rapid recovery matters as much as prevention.”
Without separately held clean, secure copies of critical data, “a serious attack could lock customers out of their accounts and disrupt payments across the wider economy”, he added. REUTERS

Second wave of early prison releases under way in England and Wales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:13:24 UTC
16:13:24 KST

The second wave of early prison releases has begun, with hundreds of offenders walking out across England and Wales under the government’s controversial plan to ease overcrowding.
About 2,000 criminals, including domestic abusers and violent offenders, are being freed this month, with another 3,000 to follow in stages over the next year. The total was reduced from 6,000 after an intervention by Andy Burnham.
Prisoners convicted of manslaughter are excluded, meaning the killers of PC Andrew Harper, who died in the line of duty in 2019, will not be eligible.
The second tranche of early releases comes as members of the probation union, Napo, hold a pre-ballot meeting on taking strike action over pay and workloads.
Pay negotiations with probation officers ended with a “best and final” conditional pay offer worth 5%, which the union’s negotiating committee rejected. Members will be asked to vote for industrial action on pay, along with a question on workloads, in a formal ballot on industrial action to launch on 19 October.
The union says probation officers have been required to take on large amounts of extra work since tens of thousands of prisoners began being released early from 2022.
The number of people in prison has jumped by more than 1,700 in the past three months. The prison population in England and Wales was at 87,499 on Monday, according to Ministry of Justice data, up from 85,761 on 29 June, a rise of 2%.
The MoJ said released offenders would be monitored under the “toughest supervision in British history”. New restriction zones designed to control the movements of the highest-risk sexual and violent offenders should confine released prisoners to areas a few miles wide, in an effort to reassure the victims of their crimes.
The MoJ said it had expanded electronic monitoring, with a new presumption that offenders will be tagged and monitored when they leave prison. Technology rolling out this year is said to give probation services near-live access to tagging data, helping staff spot breaches.
However, this month the victims’ commissioner, Claire Waxman, said the government’s confidence in the plan “is not yet matched by the reality on the ground”.

Global economy to grow 3.1% in 2026 amid severe Middle East contractions, IMF forecasts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:11:09 UTC
16:11:09 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) projected the global economy to expand 3.1% in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027, warning of severe downward revisions for the Middle East and China amid ongoing conflicts.
The Washington-based institution kept its near-term global forecast stable but warned of a deeply fractured economic outlook in its October 2026 World Economic Outlook report on Tuesday.
Eurozone economy is expected to grow by 1.1% this year, and the US economy is forecasted to see a growth rate of 2.1%.
The organization noted widespread downward revisions, with about 47% of economies seeing downgraded growth forecasts compared to April estimates.
The Middle East and Central Asia region suffered the most dramatic downward revisions, as its growth forecast for 2026 dropped 2.2 percentage points into negative territory at minus 0.3%.
The fund attributed this sharp decline directly to the dragging war in the region and a longer-than-expected closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Commodity producers most affected by disruptions to energy output and transport, including Bahrain, Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar, were projected to experience double-digit contractions in 2026.
Saudi Arabia's economy was also expected to shrink by 3.3% this year.
In Asia, the organization downgraded China's 2026 growth forecast to 4.5%.
Higher global oil prices, protracted uncertainty and structural headwinds were expected to weigh on the country's activity.
Sluggish domestic consumption and weakening investment amid continued property sector strains were anticipated to compound China's economic challenges.
The report highlighted a split global economy shaped by geopolitics and technology.
Energy-importing economies with little connection to the technology value chain were projected to face the most difficult configuration.
These nations would deal with higher import costs and exchange rate pressures, weaker real incomes, more constrained fiscal space and fewer offsetting demand impulses.
Many low-income and vulnerable countries fell into this category, threatening to widen income gaps globally.
Global headline inflation was forecast to pause its steady decline and rise to 4.7% in 2026, primarily driven by the war-induced negative supply shock impacting energy and food prices.

Germany's inflation hits 3.3% in September, highest since 2023
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:11:02 UTC
16:11:02 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Annual consumer inflation in Germany reached 3.3% in September, hitting its highest level since December 2023 as energy and motor fuel prices soared, official data showed on Tuesday.
The inflation rate in the country accelerated from 2.9% in August and 2.8% in July, according to Destatis data.
Ruth Brand, president of Destatis, said the rate exceeded the 3% mark to reach a new record high for the year and the highest level since December 2023.
Brand added that energy prices drove the increase, particularly mineral oil products at filling stations and heating oil.
Total consumer prices rose by 0.6% on a monthly basis in September.
Energy product prices jumped 14.9% in September compared to the same month last year, marking the third consecutive month of acceleration and the largest increase since February 2023.
Motor fuel prices surged 37.1% and heating oil soared 74.9% year-on-year in September, reflecting price increases on the crude oil market since the start of the Iran war.
Conversely, electricity, natural gas, and district heating prices fell by 5.5%, 2.8%, and 1%, respectively, partly due to government relief measures.
Food prices registered a below-average annual increase of 0.4% in September.
The core inflation rate, which excludes food and energy, stood at 2.4% in September, remaining below the overall inflation rate.
Prices of goods increased by 3.8% year-on-year, while services became 2.7% more expensive.

The award-winning documentary examines Israel’s use of artificial intelligence and automated surveillance systems in targeted killings and military operations during its genocidal war in Gaza.
The film’s title, "NAZA," refers to an acronym used by Israeli military intelligence to denote the number of civilians expected to be killed in an airstrike.

The fund expects unemployment to fall to 10.2% this year from 11.6% last year and to rise again to 11.3% next year.

Leading Ukrainian investment company Dragon Capital also cut its macro forecast significantly last week. It now expects GDP to fall 0.5% this year and 1.0% next year. Before the escalation of the war in July, it estimated possible growth of 1.5% this year and 0.5% next year.

airBaltic losses soar to 128.2 million euros despite rising revenue and passenger numbers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:06:17 UTC
16:06:17 KST

Latvia’s national airline airBaltic Group recorded losses of 128.2 million euros in the first half of 2026, compared with losses of just 1.7 million euros in the corresponding period of 2025, the airline’s representatives told LETA.
Meanwhile, the group’s revenue increased by 14.2% year-on-year, reaching 399.2 million euros in the first six months of 2026.
During the first half of the year, airBaltic carried a total of 4.4 million passengers, an increase of 15% compared with the same period last year.
Of these, 2.5 million passengers travelled on the airline’s own route network, representing growth of 3.9%.
The total number of flights operated, including aircraft, crew, maintenance and insurance (ACMI) leasing services, reached 42,300, an increase of 16.2%.
This included 24,000 flights operated on airBaltic’s own route network, up 5% year-on-year, and 18,300 ACMI flights, representing an increase of 35%.
The airline’s average passenger load factor in the first half of 2026 was 77.3%, one percentage point lower than in the corresponding period of 2025.
Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, amortisation and aircraft rental costs, as well as provisions for litigation (EBITDAR), amounted to 34 million euros, down 16.9 million euros compared with the first half of 2025.
According to airBaltic, revenue in the second quarter of 2026 reached 250.1 million euros, an increase of 15.3% compared with the same period last year.
However, the company recorded a loss of 58.1 million euros, compared with a profit of 27.6 million euros in the second quarter of 2025.
Passenger numbers increased by 17% to three million during the quarter.
Of these, 1.41 million passengers travelled on the airline’s own route network, representing growth of 3.2%.
The total number of flights operated in the second quarter, including ACMI leasing services, increased by 19.1% to 27,200.
The airline attributed its first-half revenue growth to a 7.4% increase in passenger transport revenue and a 36.5% rise in revenue from ACMI leasing services.
airBaltic emphasised that higher operating costs negatively affected profitability during the first half of 2026.
Foreign exchange fluctuations had a particularly significant impact on the company’s net financial results.
While currency movements generated a gain of 65.7 million euros in the first half of 2025, they resulted in a net loss of 21.2 million euros during the corresponding period of 2026.
Higher depreciation associated with fleet expansion and increased financing costs also contributed to the losses.
At the same time, airBaltic reported improvements in aircraft availability.
During the second quarter, the airline leased out an average of approximately 26 aircraft, compared with 19 aircraft a year earlier.
Fleet availability also improved significantly.
During the first half of 2026, airBaltic had no aircraft grounded due to Pratt & Whitney engine problems, compared with an average of 11 grounded aircraft in the first half of 2025.
According to the airline, the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East created a more challenging operating environment and affected profitability.
Fuel costs increased by 79.6% in the second quarter of 2026 compared with the same period last year, reaching 66.1 million euros.
Inflation also drove up personnel costs, carbon emission allowance expenses and other operating costs.
Airspace restrictions forced airBaltic to operate longer flight routes, while services to Tel Aviv and Dubai were suspended.
In response to higher fuel prices, the airline adjusted its summer capacity by cancelling approximately 5.7% of flights originally scheduled between March and October.
The total impact of higher aviation fuel prices on airBaltic’s financial results in the second quarter of 2026 was estimated at 29.3 million euros.
airBaltic President and CEO Erno Hildén stressed that the aviation industry continues to face significant pressure from external factors, including historically high aviation fuel prices affecting airlines across the sector.
“The current operating environment requires greater discipline and focus in managing the company.
“The airline’s priority is to strengthen airBaltic’s financial foundations and develop a more resilient operating model, with particular emphasis on efficiency, sustainable profitability and financial stability.
“The recently announced new business plan outlines a clear path towards achieving these objectives while maintaining airBaltic’s essential role in ensuring connectivity for Latvia and the wider Baltic region,” Hildén said.
Going forward, airBaltic will publish its operational performance figures in a Monthly Operating Report during the second half of each month, providing an overview of the airline’s key operating indicators for the preceding month.
In the first half of 2025, airBaltic Group reported revenue of 349.6 million euros and losses of 1.7 million euros.
For the full year 2025, the group’s revenue increased by 4.2% compared with 2024, reaching 779.344 million euros.
Meanwhile, its annual losses amounted to 44.337 million euros, approximately 2.7 times lower than in 2024.
The airline carried a total of 5.2 million passengers in 2025, an increase of 1% compared with the previous year.
As previously reported by LETA, airBaltic has initiated the restructuring of its financial obligations under the Chapter 11 procedure established by US law.
The airline has received binding commitments from lenders to provide up to 350 million euros in new debtor-in-possession (DIP) financing to support liquidity and operations during the Chapter 11 process.
airBaltic has already received the first financing tranche of 140 million euros.
Of this amount, 78.925 million euros will be used to purchase eight aircraft and seven engines.
The financing was arranged by Strategic Value Partners (SVP), with commitments from Barclays, Hayfin Capital Management, Morgan Stanley, Oaktree Capital Management and Strategic Value Partners.
The interest rate is SOFR plus 8%, currently equivalent to approximately 12%.
However, the financing arrangement also involves additional fees of up to 52.5 million euros.
As a result, the previous plan to raise up to 257 million euros from bondholders at an annual interest rate of 25% will not proceed.
Meanwhile, a bondholder group known as the Ad Hoc Group has filed objections in court concerning the terms of the DIP financing and its potential impact on bondholders’ collateral.
The Chapter 11 procedure protects airBaltic from creditor claims until the restructuring of its obligations is completed.
The airline has also stated that flights and customer services will continue as usual.
All flights will operate according to the planned schedule, existing tickets and reservations remain valid, and passengers can continue purchasing tickets and travelling with airBaltic as before.
The restructuring process is expected to result in a reorganisation plan that must be approved by the court.
The process is currently expected to conclude by mid-2027.
As previously reported, airBaltic bondholders approved the capitalisation of the next two bond interest payments in August, along with several other measures intended to provide the airline with additional flexibility in implementing its revised business plan.
Bondholders agreed that interest payments due on 14 August and 14 November 2026 would be added to the principal amount of the bonds rather than paid in cash.
They also approved a temporary waiver of minimum liquidity requirements until November 2026.
Germany’s national airline Lufthansa became an airBaltic shareholder in the summer of 2025.
Currently, the Latvian state owns 88.37% of airBaltic shares, while Lufthansa holds 10%.
Aircraft Leasing 1, a company owned by Danish businessman and financial investor Lars Thuesen, holds 1.62%, with the remaining 0.01% owned by other shareholders.
The company’s share capital amounts to 41.819 million euros.

Fewer hands for the harvest: Lithuania’s apple orchards face seasonal labour crunch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:06:00 UTC
16:06:00 KST

Seasonal apple picking, once a popular source of extra income for hundreds of residents in northern Lithuania, is becoming increasingly difficult to staff as fewer people are willing to take the short-term jobs.
At Naradava orchards in Pasvalys district, pickers can earn as much as 100 euros a day. But while the pay remains attractive to some, the number of people seeking seasonal work has steadily declined.
In previous years, employers sometimes had to select workers from a pool of applicants. This year, nearly everyone who applies is being hired.
Vytautas, who has been picking apples at the orchards for almost two decades, looks forward to the harvest every year. For him, the seasonal work is a valuable opportunity to earn money because finding employment in the countryside can be difficult.
“It’s possible, but it’s difficult at my age,” he told LRT TV. “Here, I can manage to earn some money.”
Some workers use the income to supplement their pensions, while others take vacation from their regular jobs specifically to work during the harvest.
For some, the extra income is earmarked for a particular purchase or a trip.
“I work and arrange my personal life – I buy something or go somewhere,” one worker said. “Maybe I’ll manage to go somewhere this weekend.”
The orchards are also facing another challenge this year. A cold winter destroyed about one-third of the company’s orchards, but Naradava still expects to harvest around 4,000 metric tons of apples.
Finding enough workers, however, is becoming increasingly difficult.
“We really need these pickers, and this year we are using various methods to find them – ads in newspapers, asking acquaintances, and social media,” said Džiugas Palionis, director of Naradava. “We have about 150 workers at the peak this year, whereas in better years we managed to have as many as 300.”
Dalia Radzivonienė, a forewoman at the company, said the change is particularly noticeable compared with previous years.
Residents of surrounding districts once began asking well in advance when they could start working and often wanted to reserve places for family members. Demand was so high that the company sometimes had to hold selections.
“Now we have to take whoever comes,” Radzivonienė said. “There aren’t as many people interested as there used to be. In some years, people couldn’t get in. Now we accept everyone who comes.”
Naradava recruits workers from nearby villages and towns and operates its own bus to transport them from Pasvalys, Biržai and surrounding areas, Palionis said.
“We manage to gather them somehow,” he said. “Every year, there are fewer workers.”
The apple harvest is expected to continue until the end of October.

Estonia's defense ministry allocates €250,000 for war movies
The MoD has announced a funding competition worth €250,000 to support the production of films and other audiovisual works aimed at strengthening the Estonian public's willingness to defend the country.
"I would like to impress upon everyone on the committee selecting these films at the Ministry of Defense that any film that is overly propagandistic or too polished and carefully packaged is actually less credible. When we talk about defending Estonia, my view, my belief, is that the truth ultimately works best," film director Ilmar Raag commented.
The Ministry of Defense is inviting submissions for feature films, documentaries, animated films, television series and narrative video games. The ministry has supported the production of Estonian war films for more than 20 years, including "Names in Marble," "1944" and "O2."
According to ministry representative Thomas Mell, different audiovisual formats make it possible to reach different generations.
"The willingness to defend the country is an important part of Estonia's national defense and strengthening it is one of our core responsibilities. Supporting films and other audiovisual works is one way to contribute to this. Film is a medium that reaches a wide audience, as do video games nowadays, for example, and they help communicate national defense issues in ways that resonate with different generations," Mell said.
Raag, who previously received funding through a Ministry of Defense competition to produce a documentary, believes that funding decisions must also take into account the potential for a backlash.
"Those who allocate funding at the ministry need to recognize that if a filmmaker takes an overly simplistic, propagandistic approach, it could actually backfire," Raag noted.
To qualify for Ministry of Defense funding, projects must align with national defense objectives. This raises the question of how much influence the state, as a funder, can exert over a film's content.
"As the Ministry of Defense, we do not interfere in any way with filmmakers' creative freedom. We do not dictate scripts, themes or how characters should be portrayed. Instead, filmmakers themselves are free to submit their proposals to us," Mell explained.
The Ministry of Defense is accepting applications until November 18. The funding can be used next year.

Latin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:00:18 UTC
16:00:18 KST

A four-month investigation by the Guardian has revealed that the surge in cocaine trafficking to Europe is directly linked to the expanding presence of Latin American criminal networks in Europe, where they have forged close ties with local mafia organisations.
The investigation, utilising databases, police and intelligence agencies, along with interviews with judges, prosecutors and experts from eight countries, shows that cartels and factions from Colombia, Brazil, Ecuador, Venezuela, Mexico and the US are active in at least 12 European countries. Between 2014 and 2024, there was a 471% rise in the quantity of cocaine seized and more local laboratories processing cocaine derivatives were dismantled.
The figure could be even higher, as it includes only groups officially identified in Europe through police operations, transnational investigations and ongoing court cases involving brokers, active members, cells or operational networks. It does not include gangs that lack a physical presence in Europe while working in “joint ventures” with European mafias.
The identified groups include Mexico’s Sinaloa cartel and the Jalisco New Generation cartel (CJNG); the Clan del Golfo mafia, and the guerrilla organisations ELN and dissident factions of Farc in Colombia; Brazil’s Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC, or First Capital Command) and Comando Vermelho (CV, or Red Command); Venezuela’s Tren de Aragua; and the US-originated Barrio 18 and MS-13 gangs, which are also prevalent in El Salvador, Honduras, Guatemala and, to a lesser degree, in Mexico.
These organisations have built a more prominent presence in Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands, Belgium and France, while their activities have also been noted in Germany, Romania, Croatia and Slovakia. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (Gi-Toc) also includes Bulgaria.
Daniel Brombacher, a political scientist and director of the Europe Observatory at Gi-Toc, said: “There is something new happening with a presence of Latin American groups in geographies where there’s no pre-existing infrastructure.
“This phenomenon is no longer limited to the traditional gateway countries,” he says. “Recent police operations have uncovered Mexican-run methamphetamine labs in southern France, north-eastern Poland and Brandenburg, south of Berlin. Latin American groups are also appearing in Romania and Bulgaria along the Balkan route.”
Latin American national authorities and experts suggest the list may be even longer. An unpublished report by the São Paulo public prosecutor’s office, partly based on data from the Brazilian intelligence agency (Abin) – which the Guardian reviewed – shows, for example, that the PCC, now Brazil’s biggest criminal group, operates in 16 European countries, including the UK, Ireland, Iceland, Serbia, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey.
The suspicion that Latin American cartels and factions are seeking to become established in Europe is not new. Since at least the 1980s, Colombian criminal organisations such as the Cali and Medellín cartels had footholds in regions of Spain such as Galicia. In 2013, a Europol report in 2103 warned of their rise. But what authorities are witnessing now is on an another level.
A Europol report this year states that “Latin American MTCNs [most threatening criminal networks] have also settled in the EU, from where they direct operations that affect the EU. This is particularly the case for mobile criminal networks involved in organised property crime.”
Interpol, led by the Brazilian federal police officer Valdecy Urquiza, has been approached, but has not commented.
The problem has become more visible over the past decade. Drug production in Latin America in that time has increased roughly fourfold to reach a record of about 4,100 tonnes in 2024. This comes after growth of up to 35% at the beginning of the decade. More cocaine is now produced in Colombia than during the era of the notorious drug lord Pablo Escobar. Nearly all the world’s cocaine and many related substances originate from Latin America, particularly Colombia.
Víctor Manuel Sánchez Valdés, an academic at the Autonomous University of Coahuila in Mexico who is an expert on organised crime, says: “The main ones are the Sinaloa cartel and the Jalisco cartel [CJNG] in Mexico; the Comando Vermelho and the PCC of Brazil; the Gulf Clan and different factions of the Colombian Farc; the Lobos and the Choneros of Ecuador; and Tren de Aragua of Venezuela.”
He believes that the Latin American presence in Europe is even more widespread than is generally recognised. “Sinaloa cartel and the CJNG have a presence in more than 20 European countries. Obviously, that does not mean they dominate or have large cells,” he says. “Rather, they are business emissaries.”
The UN Office on Drugs and Crime’s 2026 World Drug Report on illicit crimes states that global cocaine production in 2024 was between 3,800 and 4,700 tonnes – more than four times higher than it was in 2014. South America remains the main production hub, with coca cultivation covering a record 385,000 hectares over the past decade – three times the 2014 figure.
Europe has emerged as a key market because it offers organisations higher profit margins than the US. Since the beginning of the decade, European police have confiscated more drugs than American forces, and data indicates that Europe now represents about a quarter of global consumption.
Europol recently reported that out of 731 MTCNs operating across Europe, 149 are connected to Latin American organisations. Of these, 67 have Latin American members, and 22 mainly consist of Latin Americans.
