07:00:18 UTC
16:00:18 KST

While the merits of a so-called Britannia shield to protect Britain from missiles and drones are debatable, the Conservatives’ proposal did achieve one thing last week: the very idea of the shield was used to anoint a political leader.
In a significant development, little observed amid the hullaballoo of news events, Kemi Badenoch’s uncosted, pie-in-the-sky plans to build a £10bn anti-missile system were enthusiastically heralded by the rightwing press. It was not just a matter of the plans themselves being lauded, even by outlets that must know them to be ridiculous. More significant is what it said about the champion chosen by these media organisations in their offensive against the Labour government and Andy Burnham.
The Sun splashed a smiling Badenoch across its front page with a banner headline calling her the “Iron Dome Lady”; the Express paraded her in a power suit and a union jack. The Daily Mail, meanwhile, hailed the Tories for seeking to “protect the nation’s skies” and sealed the plans with its “Don’t Leave Britain Defenceless” campaign stamp. Even wartime leaders could not hope for better, unquestioning coverage from battle-aligned, nation-rallying propaganda sheets.
The slavish Badenoch coverage is significant so soon after Burnham’s first conference speech as prime minister. It marks the moment when much of the rightwing press has returned to its traditional Tory-supporting ways after years of flirting with – and outright eulogising – Nigel Farage and his now scandal-hit Reform UK party. It also suggests a back-to-basics return to the economy as the chief battleground for this fight, and not the madder excesses of the war on woke that has recently consumed them.
The praise for Badenoch, who was also recently treated to an all-expenses paid trip to Greece to meet Rupert Murdoch and executives from the Sun and Times-owning News Corp, suggests that she has cemented a position as the rightwing press’s best political hope of beating Burnham.
The search for a suitable champion has assumed a growing urgency because the prime minister has so far proved hard to leave a mark on. “Red Andy”, the early attack line, has not been widely used since the June byelection in Makerfield. The Mail may have dubbed Burnham’s first conference speech “the most Left-wing speech delivered by a modern British prime minister”, but in recent weeks only the Telegraph’s Allister Heath has fired the “Red Andy” missile in a column that called plans for pension reform, a social care system and all talk of a return to the European Union, “mad, nasty and shockingly extreme”.
This coverage reminds Alastair Campbell of his early years advising Tony Blair when he was depicted either as a “useless Bambi or Stalin”, he tells me. “They can’t decide if [Burnham] is a useless Paddington Bear or red in tooth and claw,” says Campbell. “They just can’t work him out yet.” A member of the loathed liberal elite or outright Trot?
There are a few factors that are making it difficult for the rightwing press to get the full measure of their enemy – including Burnham’s trajectory from New Labour luvvy to working-class champion, the King of the North. Labour advisers also cite the fact that Burnham’s inner circle, in contrast to his predecessors, has also been relatively leak- and conflict-free, leaving rightwing combatants with fewer vulnerabilities to exploit.
This is the calm before the storm, of course, with Burnham’s opponents gearing up for the budget and the inevitable controversies on 28 October. “The press are probing his defences,” Tom Baldwin, a former Labour party adviser, tells me. “They’ll keep trying, of course, and the chances are that one of their missiles will eventually hit a target.”
Amid rising fuel prices, geopolitical uncertainty and concerns over jobs, the back-to-the-future nature of this debate – indeed the back-to-the-Tory-future nature of it – is hardly surprising. Burnham has assaulted shibboleths. He has vowed to reverse “40 years of failure” with his pledge to repeal Margaret Thatcher’s ban on public ownership of water companies, to abolish the Tory version of the right-to-buy housing scheme, and to restore a sense of common good to Britain. To the right, this is unconscionable. Dan Hodges in the Mail, praising Badenoch’s “best speech yet”, wrote that the country faces a choice between Burnham’s “unashamed 1970s-style socialism” and the Tory leaders’ “bold attempt to reappropriate and recondition Margaret Thatcher’s radical conservatism”.
Although the rightwing outlets fight a similar battle against Labour, they do so for varying reasons. Some of those are ideological, but commercial imperatives also fuel their fervour. The 1970s and 80s marked a golden age for newspapers, when millions of loyal readers gave them heft and profits. With sales and readership figures now at a fraction of their peak in the late 80s, the Sun (which claimed sales of 3.8m per day in 1987) and several other titles no longer publish their numbers, focusing instead on online reach. In dwindling markets, the strategy is to stay competitive by aligning with, or perhaps exacerbating, the prevailing wave of political populism.
The Sun has struggled more than the Mail with the shift online. It has also struggled more with Burnham because of its coverage of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster, in which it falsely blamed Liverpool supporters for a crush that killed 97 people. According to Baldwin, citing well-placed sources, Burnham may become the first prime minister since the Labour leader Jim Callaghan to refuse requests for exclusive interviews and articles in Rupert Murdoch’s biggest tabloid.
The right’s battle-camp has the additional problem that Burnham himself is proving quite a wily opponent. The prime minister spends 10 minutes a day with his social media team before posting to his nearly 1m followers on Instagram and more than 700,000 on TikTok. His short-form videos on fuel prices and the triple lock don’t seem to target younger voters, but they are a way of bypassing a negative narrative – or what Campbell calls “the madness of the rightwing press”.
Burnham could opt to go his own way, to ignore the hostile rightwing outlets altogether. But in a democracy, that would be no more ethical for Labour than it is for Reform UK, which has barred press critics. David Yelland, the editor of the Sun when it put Tony Blair on its front page with the headline “Is THIS the most dangerous man in Britain?”, tells me it would also be unwise. The power of the rightwing press is diminished, he says; they are “toothless tigers in a jungle full of new dangers – dangers as lethal for them as the rest of us, by which I mean AI and what comes next”. But, “the truth is the Tory press still has influence over the political and media classes … it can still set the weather”. D
And as we know from famous battles past, the weather can be a decisive factor. The side that copes with it best usually wins.
- Jane Martinson is an academic and Guardian columnist. She is a board member of the Scott Trust, which owns the Guardian Media Group, and writes in a personal capacity

Nuisance or festive tradition? Swiss vote on fireworks ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Nuisance or festive tradition? Swiss vote on fireworks ban
At the end of November the Swiss will vote on a people’s initiative seeking to ban the sale and use of noisy fireworks. While supporters of the initiative want to reduce the noise pollution and environmental impact caused by fireworks, its opponents argue for the preservation of a popular tradition.
For a long time in Switzerland, no one could imagine Swiss National Day on August 1 without fireworks displays and other noisy firecrackers. In recent years, however, drought has regularly led to bans on them in several cantons. At the same time, fireworks are at the centre of a heated debate over their usefulness and the nuisance they cause. Their fate will be decided at the ballot boxExternal link on November 29.
What does the initiative call for?
It calls for a ban on the sale and use of noisy fireworks. Pyrotechnic devices that do not produce noise, such as Bengal lights or volcanoes, would remain permitted.
The initiative does, however, provide for exceptions. The cantons could grant special permits for events of supra-regional importance. Large fireworks displays could therefore still be organised for certain celebrations, such as August 1 or New Year’s Eve, provided a cantonal exemption is obtained.
It specifies, however, that these events should take place within a clearly defined timeframe and location, to allow a wide audience to enjoy them and to significantly reduce any negative effects.
Who is behind the initiative?
The initiative was launched by animal welfare organisations. A broad alliance of organisations from the fields of agriculture, health and nature conservation has formed in support of it. The initiators collected 137,429 signatures – more than the 100,000 required to trigger a popular vote.
What do supporters argue?
Supporters of the initiative claim they want to protect animals, people and nature by reducing the nuisance caused by fireworks. They argue that sudden loud bangs can trigger panic in animals and harm their welfare. Some animals run away and are never found by their owners.
They believe the public is also affected by this noise pollution. Children, the elderly and people with mental health conditions are said to be particularly sensitive to the loud bangs.
Supporters of the initiative also highlight the environmental impact of fireworks. According to them, these generate around 1,300 tonnes of waste each year, some of which ends up in public spaces or on agricultural land. They also point out that the burning of fireworks releases several hundred tonnes of fine particulate matter, metals and other pollutants into the air.
What do opponents argue?
In the eyes of its opponents, the initiative goes too far. First and foremost, they point out that the cantons and municipalities already have the right to restrict the sale and use of fireworks. Indeed, several of them have imposed restrictions this year due to the fire risks associated with the drought.
Opponents also emphasise that fireworks are only used for a few days a year. In their view, the nuisance they cause is therefore already limited in time and space.
They also believe that the initiative threatens a deeply rooted popular tradition, associated with the August 1 celebrations and, increasingly, with New Year’s Eve celebrations. Finally, they argue that a ban would infringe upon the economic freedom of businesses that manufacture, import, sell or use fireworks for professional purposes.
Who supports it, and who opposes it?
Parliament and the government recommend rejecting the initiative. In parliament, the left-wing Green Party and the left-wing Social Democratic Party supported the initiative, while the right-wing Swiss People’s Party, the centre-right Radical-Liberal Party and the Centre Party strongly opposed it.
How many fireworks does Switzerland use?
Annual fireworks consumption varies significantly from year to year in Switzerland. According to the Federal Office of Police, between 1,200 and 2,300 tonnes of fireworks have been sold in the country each year over the past decade. Around three-quarters of the pyrotechnic devices used are imported. China is by far the main supplier. Swiss production mainly consists of volcanoes, Bengal lights, sparklers, confetti cannons, table bombs and other table fireworks.
How do other countries regulate fireworks?
The debate on fireworks extends far beyond Switzerland’s borders. Several countries have already restricted or banned the use of fireworks.
In the Netherlands, where New Year’s Eve celebrations are regularly marred by accidents and violence, a ban on most fireworks intended for the public is set to come into force before the end of the year. The country would thus become the second European nation, after Ireland, to impose such strict limits on the use of fireworks by private individuals. Outside Europe, Australia and Singapore have also adopted highly restrictive regulations, with the use of fireworks largely restricted to authorised professionals.
Other countries have opted for a more nuanced approach. In Germany, for example, fireworks may generally only be set off around New Year’s Eve, and several cities have established zones where they are banned.

The Swiss voted for a pension hike. Now they must decide how to pay for it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

The Swiss voted for a pension hike. Now they must decide how to pay for it
On November 29, the Swiss will vote on funding a 13th monthly pension payment by increasing value-added tax (VAT) by 0.4 percentage points. If the proposal is rejected, payment of the 13th monthly pension will still go ahead from December 2026, but funding will yet have to be secured.
This December will be a special one for those receiving the Old Age and Survivors’ Insurance (OASI), the first pillar of the Swiss pension system. For the first time, retirees – whether living in Switzerland or abroad – will receive a 13th monthly pension payment. What is still unclear, however, is how this extra payment is to be funded. On November 29, Swiss voters will have their say on the solution proposed by parliament.
What exactly is the vote about?
The referendum does not threaten the 13th pension payment. This was approved by 58.2% of voters in March 2024. On November 29, the Swiss will be deciding on how to fund part of this new expenditure.
Single pensioners will now receive up to CHF2,520 ($3,031) more a year and married couples up to CHF3,780. This will cost a total of over CHF4 billion annually. As the number of retirees continues to grow and pensions are regularly adjusted to the cost of living, this figure is expected to rise, reaching CHF5 billion a year from 2035 onwards.
To cover part of these additional costs, parliament is proposing to increase VAT from 2028. The standard rate, which applies to most goods and services, would go up by 0.4 percentage points, from 8.1% to 8.5%. The special rate for the accommodation sector would rise from 3.8% to 4%. Meanwhile, the reduced rate of 2.6%, which applies in particular to food, medicines and books, would remain unchanged.
This VAT hike, which is expected to generate around CHF1.4 billion a year, would still not be enough to cover the full cost of the 13th pension payment. It would, however, ease the financial burden on the state old-age pension system. The Swiss government has already drawn up a scenario for additional funding for the 13th pension in its OASI 2030 reform proposal, which is currently under consultation. This could entail a further increase in VAT or a combination of VAT and social security contributions.
How is the state pension system funded?
The OASI is funded through a pay-as-you-go system. This means that the contributions from today’s active workforce directly finance current pensions. Worker and employer contributions account for around 70% of OASI revenue.
The federal government covers just over 20% of expenditure, mainly through its general funds, as well as taxes on tobacco and spirits. About 9% of revenue comes from VAT and the tax on casinos. Added to this are any returns generated by the investment of OASI reserves, which can vary significantly from one year to the next. In 2025, OASI revenue thus totalled just over CHF55 billion.
How are pension finances faring?
The state old-age pension system is currently in a relatively sound financial position. It closed the 2025 fiscal yearExternal link with a CHF4.4 billion surplus. This is largely thanks to the additional revenue generated by the Tax Reform and OASI Financing Act and the OASI 21 reform.
However, the retirement of the baby-boomers and the decrease in the active labour force are putting pressure on the social insurance system. On top of this now comes the cost of the 13th pension payment. From this year onwards, expenditure will exceed revenue by more than CHF1 billion. Without additional funds, annual deficits will hit nearly CHF5 billion by 2035, according to estimates by the Federal Social Insurance OfficeExternal link. With the VAT increase, the deficit is expected to drop to CHF3 billion.
Why is a nationwide vote necessary?
Increasing VAT requires an amendment to the Swiss Constitution. Voters must therefore decide whether to accept the Federal Decree on Additional Financing of the OASI through a VAT IncreaseExternal link. The bill will need to secure a majority of both the people and the cantons to be approved.
Who is for the reform and who against?
Parliament and the government support the VAT increase. The centre-right parties are against, while the left-wing and centrist parties are in favour. The major trade unions also support the reform, although there are dissenting voices within their ranks – in particular the public service union, which recommends rejecting the proposal.
Why vote for the reform?
The main argument is financial. The introduction of the 13th OASI pension payment was decided in a nationwide referendum. To respect the will of the people, funding must now be secured to prevent the OASI’s accounts from slipping into the red.
Supporters of the VAT hike believe this is the best way to finance the new pension payments quickly. In parliament, the left had advocated a mixed funding approach, combining an increase in payroll contributions and VAT. However, it regards the chosen solution as the best possible compromise given the current political dynamics. The left-wing supporters of the VAT increase also believe it will help reduce pressure to raise the retirement age, in particular from the political right.
The backers also point out that the 0.4 percentage points increase is modest and that essential goods are exempt. For the vast majority of retirees, they say, the gain from the 13th pension payment will outweigh the additional costs arising from higher VAT.
Why vote against?
The opponents of the reform do not challenge the payment of the 13th monthly pension, but rather the funding method. They believe that an increase in VAT will put too great a strain on households’ purchasing power, which is already squeezed by rising health insurance premiums, rents and day-to-day expenses.
They also criticise the fact that the reform would cover only part of the cost of the 13th pension. The focus should instead be on addressing the structural problems of the OASI, the Radical-Liberal Party (centre-right) argues.
On the left, the public service union regards VAT as an anti-social tax that hits low earners proportionally harder. It also points out that additional funding is not necessary in the immediate term, given the sound financial health of the state old-age pension system today.

Trump calls for energy truce; Moscow remains silent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:59:16 UTC
15:59:16 KST

On the 11th of October, US President Donald Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to observe an energy truce, refraining from strikes on energy infrastructure; Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reacted by saying this was news to him, while Moscow remains silent, the BBC reports.
When asked whether an agreement on an energy truce had been reached, Dmitry Peskov, the spokesman for Russian dictator Vladimir Putin, stated that communication is ongoing and the media will be informed as soon as there is something to say.
Peskov may not have much to say on the matter, but pro-Kremlin media certainly do. They have dubbed the energy truce a gift to Moscow. The pro-government outlet Moskovsky Komsomolets emphasized that Russia is, of course, the beneficiary of the truce. It implies only that Russia is prevented from destroying Ukraine's last remaining oil refinery—which is barely functioning anyway. Conversely, Kyiv would no longer be able to attack Russian oil refineries; thus, it is essentially an agreement that favors Moscow, which is why no one has rejected it. In other words, Moscow believes that Trump’s statement has tied Kyiv’s hands, not Moscow’s.
In recent months, Ukrainian strikes have caused serious damage to Russian oil refineries and triggered fuel shortages. If the strikes continue, Moscow can be expected to start arguing that Kyiv is harming US economic interests—and, by extension, Republican prospects in the midterm elections. Russian officials will seize the opportunity to claim that the strikes jeopardize Trump’s plans to purchase Russian diesel. Trump has indicated that a deal to buy diesel from Russia would benefit American consumers, though 
many remain skeptical that the volume offered by Russia could actually impact fuel prices in the US.
The Russians would be more than happy if Ukrainian strikes provoked anger in the White House. Moscow would rejoice if Washington stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv and halted arms sales to Europe intended for Ukraine. The Russians were already delighted when Trump began suggesting that Ukraine needed a new president.
Zelensky has called for a 60-day general ceasefire to allow presidential elections to be held in Ukraine. What does Moscow say about this? Peskov noted that the Kremlin and the dictator have repeatedly stated that Russians do not want a mere ceasefire but rather a lasting peace, and are ready to do everything possible to achieve it. However, "everything possible" does not include a 60-day ceasefire, a 30-day ceasefire, or anything of the sort. On the 12th of October, the Kremlin suggested a one-day ceasefire for the elections. Neither Ukraine nor Europe considers this a serious proposal. Putin has shown no interest in halting hostilities.
Recent statements, speeches, and directives from the Russian dictator indicate that, as winter approaches, Russia is relying on continued strikes to increase pressure on Ukraine. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov stated that Ukraine does not deserve the respite a ceasefire might provide. While the Kremlin speaks of lasting peace, it continues to wage war. On the 12th of October, Zelensky reported that Russia had launched strikes against several energy infrastructure facilities.
The Kremlin's goal has not changed; it seeks Ukraine's capitulation. It appears Moscow believes that a deal with Trump regarding diesel sales—combined with the American's growing impatience with Zelensky—will enable it to achieve its desired outcome.

Bulgaria to summon Russian ambassador over drone attacks on merchant vessels
Two merchant ships were attacked by drones on the night of 12-13 October off the Bulgarian coast, causing one of the vessels to sink. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has announced his intention to summon Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova for explanations, although the origin of the drones has not yet been established.
Source: European Pravda, citing Bulgarian media outlet BGNES
Details: Two merchant vessels came under attack during separate incidents in the Black Sea on the night of 12-13 October, according to information provided at an emergency meeting of the Security Council.
The Maltese-flagged cargo ship Chelsea 3 was attacked by three drones approximately 18 nautical miles east of the town of Byala. They hit the ship's deck and the side of its hull. All 15 crew members were evacuated and taken to Varna. Early reports indicate that five crew members received medical treatment for minor injuries.
The Chelsea 3 sails under the Maltese flag, is registered in Odesa and, according to the information provided, is Ukrainian-owned.
Another vessel sank approximately 17 nautical miles east of Krapets. For now, one crew member has been reported to have been rescued.
Rumen Radev announced that he would summon Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova and hold discussions with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.
"Another attack on merchant ships in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters is absolutely unacceptable," Radev stated.
The prime minister said that Bulgaria would demand explanations from Russian Ambassador Mitrofanova. He also specified that at this moment there is no conclusive evidence regarding the origin of the drones that would allow responsibility for the attacks to be attributed to a specific state. However, according to Radev, "the logic of what is happening suggests that the outcome of the attacks benefits the Russian Federation".
Radev noted that Bulgaria's permanent representatives to NATO and the European Union have been informed about these incidents.
Background:
- On 6 October drones attacked two commercial vessels – the Togo-flagged Alfa Watan and the Palau-flagged Able – in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the Ukrainian Navy had contacted its Bulgarian counterparts regarding the attack on two civilian vessels in Bulgarian waters. Zelenskyy stated that the attack had been carried out by Russia.
- Bulgaria has asked the EU and NATO for assistance in investigating the drone attacks in the Black Sea.

PM says government trying to stop 'abhorrent' US execution live stream
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13

Social platforms have 'responsibility' to block US execution live stream, Albanese says
In short:
Anthony Albanese says the government is doing "whatever it can" to prevent a live stream of an execution in the US from being viewed in Australia.
He says social media platforms have a "social responsibility" to do the right thing and not broadcast the execution.
What's next?
US President Donald Trump is yet to make the ultimate call about the December 3 execution.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says his government will do everything it can to stop the "abhorrent" live stream of a firing squad execution in the United States from being shown in Australia.
Last week US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at a military base in Texas in 2009, would be available for the public to watch, but Vice-President JD Vance cast doubt about whether that would occur.
The potential live stream has elicited a strong response in parliament, with federal members across the political divide urging the government to "pull every single lever" to block the broadcast.
On Tuesday Mr Albanese told Afternoon Briefing that the government would do whatever it could, but acknowledged it was not as simple as "turning off a light switch".
"Australia has had a bipartisan position of opposition to the death penalty and I find the idea of live streaming the death of anybody completely abhorrent," he told ABC.
"We should do whatever we can to stop that occurring."
He said the government was seeking advice on its options.
On Monday the eSafety Commission said it could not prevent Australians from seeing the execution.
"While eSafety does not have powers to proactively prevent a live stream from occurring online, online services have responsibilities under Australia's online safety regulatory framework to protect users from harmful material," a spokesperson told the ABC.
The prime minister said he would make it "very clear" to social media platforms that the content had no place in Australia.
"I think anybody broadcasting this will damage their own reputations as well. They have a social responsibility here to do the right thing," he said.
The ABC has contacted Google, Meta and TikTok to see if they plan to restrict the content, but has not received responses.
Asked whether he had made representations to Donald Trump on the issue, Mr Albanese said the US president had indicated in the media that he was weighing the matter.
"President Trump has already said he is giving consideration to this and I hope that there is a response in the United States as well," he said.
If the broadcast goes ahead, it will mark the first time an execution in the US has been live streamed.
Politicians express concern
Greens Leader David Shoebridge grilled Foreign Minister Penny Wong over the proposed live stream during Tuesday's Question Time and asked about the "shared values" between Australia and "a government that publicly broadcasts state-sanctioned snuff films".
Senator Wong said it would be "deeply distressing for any such vision to be live streamed".
"We don't believe anyone should be confronted with it, particularly younger Australians," she said.
Senator Wong said Australians had a right to expect such content would not appear on their screens.
"We believe that platforms do have a responsibility to meet these expectations," she said.
Shadow Foreign Affairs Minister Ted O'Brien said the government needed to ensure Australians could not view the execution.
"That concerns me deeply. We cannot have young Australians watching an execution," he told Afternoon Briefing.
"That would be appalling, repugnant, and that is why we need to be looking at every possible lever to ensure that is not live streamed, if indeed it goes ahead."

Australia beats South Africa by 214 runs to take 1-0 lead in Test series
Australia has taken a 1-0 lead in the three-Test series against South Africa after a dominant 214-run victory on day five at Kingsmead.
The Proteas lost their last four wickets for just five runs to be bowled out for 206, with Josh Hazlewood finishing with career-best figures of 6-49.
Matt Renshaw was named player-of-the-match for his knocks of 190 and 82, as well as his two second-innings wickets.
His spot in the team is now assured for the foreseeable future, but with Cameron Green still to return from injury, questions will be asked about where Renshaw is best suited in the line-up and he said after the match it was "pretty nice" to settle in the middle order.
"It's a bit different to opening the batting, but happy to do whatever the team needs me to do," he said during the post-match presentation.
Renshaw's batting set up the victory but his part-time off-spin became key to winning the game in the fourth innings after a dogged 69-run partnership between Aiden Markram (75 off 237) and Wiaan Mulder (29 off 110).
It finally came to an end after 34 overs when Mulder got a feather on a Hazlewood delivery down the leg side, where wicketkeeper Alex Carey completed a phenomenal one-handed grab.
Four balls later, Renshaw nicked off Kyle Verreynne for a duck to give Australia momentum heading into lunch.
Markram, the hero of South Africa's run chase in last year's World Test Championship final victory over Australia, continued his resistance alongside Marco Jansen (35) before Hazlewood clean bowled him with the second new ball.
Simon Harmer (0) gloved one through to Alex Carey later in the over and Markram's vigil finally ended when Australia successfully reviewed an appeal for caught behind, with DRS showing a faint inside edge.
When Anrich Nortje (4) lobbed Hazlewood to the leg side, South Africa had lost 4-5 in three overs and the match was over.

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,555,700 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:53:39 UTC
15:53:39 KST

Russia has lost 1,555,700 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 13.
The number includes 1,390 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,412 tanks, 25,534 armored combat vehicles, 162,418 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,141 artillery systems, 2,211 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,704 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,942 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

Ukraine's Air Force comments on delay of air-raid warning in Kyiv
Ukraine's Air Force has expressed hope that Ukraine and its international partners will establish why information regarding Russia's launch of ballistic missiles towards Kyiv on 12 October was not received in time, noting that such incidents have occurred before.
Source: Colonel Yurii Ihnat, spokesperson for the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the national joint 24/7 newscast
Details: Amid foreign media reports referencing sources that the US might halt intelligence sharing, the presenter asked: "Can you confirm the delay in notification and what specifically caused it?"
Ihnat confirmed that this time the air-raid warning indeed was issued only whilst the Russian ballistic attack was already underway but noted that this was not the first such instance. This has happened not only in Kyiv Oblast but also in frontline cities. In this case, the Air Force spokesperson expressed hope that Ukrainian intelligence together with foreign partners will determine the cause of the delay.
Quote: "The intelligence data that everyone is talking about now varies. There is intelligence utilising satellite communications that not only the US but also other NATO countries share with Ukraine. This covers the activity of enemy strategic aviation at their home airfields, ship movements in the Black or Caspian Seas and ballistic missile launches.
There are moments when this information fails to arrive. This is not the first case... If there were certain technical issues this time, I believe the experts can sort it out. And we will resolve this problem together with our partners."
Background:
- At 22:10 on 12 October, Russia struck the capital of Ukraine with five ballistic missiles. Radar systems detected the incoming missiles only once the attack on Kyiv was underway.
- Ukraine's Air Force reported that no information regarding launches from Russian territory had been received.

IMF lowers Türkiye’s growth forecast for 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:51:40 UTC
15:51:40 KST

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has lowered its 2026 growth forecast for Türkiye to 2.7 percent from 2.9 percent, while keeping its projection for next year unchanged at 3.6 percent.
The forecasts appeared in the October World Economic Outlook, released on Oct. 13 during the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok. The previous estimates were published in July.
The fund expects Türkiye’s annual-average consumer inflation to reach 31.2 percent in 2026 and 26.5 percent in 2027.
Its year-end inflation forecasts stand at 29.9 percent and 23.7 percent, respectively.
Türkiye’s current account deficit is projected at 2.9 percent of gross domestic product this year, narrowing to 2.4 percent in 2027.
The unemployment rate is forecast at 8.2 percent this year and 8.3 percent next year.
Globally, the IMF raised its 2026 growth forecast to 3.1 percent from 3 percent in July, while maintaining its 2027 estimate at 3.4 percent. It expects global inflation to reach 4.7 percent this year before easing to 4.1 percent next year.
The fund said growth was becoming increasingly uneven, with countries benefiting from investment in artificial intelligence performing better than many energy-importing and lower-income economies.
It warned that prolonged or escalating conflict in the Middle East could keep energy and food prices high, weakening growth and adding to inflation pressures.
Higher government borrowing costs and renewed trade tensions also posed risks.
The IMF urged governments to strengthen public finances and ensure that support for households facing higher food and energy costs remained temporary and targeted.

China Focus: China's key wine-producing base pioneers ecological transition models
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:51:38 CST
15:51:38 KST

YINCHUAN, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Since opening in August this year, a 22.77-kilometer avenue in northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region has been drawing a steady stream of visitors from both home and abroad.
"To the west is the majestic Helan Mountain, and to the east are endless vineyards. It is full of surprises and so much fun," Wang Xiaotong, a tourist from north China's Shanxi Province, said in describing the avenue flanked by vast vineyards.
She was unaware that, just decades ago, this place had been a barren stretch of desert. Through years of sustained effort, Ningxia has turned over 400,000 mu (about 26,667 hectares) of barren land at the eastern foot of Helan Mountain into a world-renowned ecological wine-producing base.
At a local winery, the owner Ding Jian boasts an underground wine cellar that she describes as able to "breathe." The cellar is designed with a naturally constant-temperature, constant-humidity structure, and a natural circulation system formed by ventilation holes in the walls.
Without any refrigeration or heating equipment, it maintains a stable environment suitable for wine aging and storage while consuming minimal energy, no matter how extreme the outdoor temperature is.
Another local winery has adopted an environmentally friendly layout at its production area, using dense windows to create a "chimney effect" that allows free air circulation and significantly reduces reliance on temperature control equipment.
The winery's manager, Zhang Xueyan, outlined a comprehensive ecological scheme. "Grape skins from the winery are supplied to cosmetics companies as raw materials, while discarded vines are provided to farmers free of charge to feed their cattle and sheep. The manure is then returned to the fields to nourish the organic vineyards," she said.
"Every step, from planting to brewing, is aimed at saving energy and cutting emissions, which is also the key to the sustainable and sound development of the industry," the manager concluded.
Ningxia has also explored "carbon asset" models since 2023, seeking to transform a vineyard's ability to absorb carbon dioxide into a tradable asset. In December 2025, the country's first wine vineyard carbon transaction was completed in Ningxia.
This transaction was of great significance as it verified that the "carbon asset" has a market-oriented foundation, while also providing a replicable and scalable practical model for the green transformation of the global wine industry, according to the management committee of the wine industrial park at the eastern foot of Helan Mountain.
In December 2025, the wine region at Ningxia's eastern foot of Helan Mountain was awarded the International Sustainable Development Award at the 20th Bettane & Desseauve Ministry of Foreign Affairs Celebration held in France, becoming the first Chinese wine region to receive this honor.
Sergio Cabrera, ambassador of Colombia to China, said Ningxia's wines not only excel in quality but also embody an outstanding environmental protection philosophy that puts ecology first in industrial development, an approach worthy of global reference.
The 47th World Congress of Vine and Wine, meanwhile, opened on Monday in Yinchuan, capital of Ningxia. This is the first time the congress, held alongside the 24th General Assembly of the International Organization of Vine and Wine (OIV), has been hosted in Asia since its launch in 1924.
Yvette van der Merwe, OIV's president, hailed China's important role and its growing contribution to the international vine and wine industry, highlighting Ningxia's significant development as a wine-producing region.
The eastern foot of Helan Mountain in Ningxia has become China's largest contiguous wine grape production area. This region has roughly 40,467 hectares dedicated to wine grape cultivation and development, accounting for nearly 42 percent of China's total planting area. ■

Across China: 5 years on, preservation efforts bear fruit in tropical rainforest park in south China's Hainan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:50:59 CST
15:50:59 KST

HAIKOU, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Streams babble through the forest. Birds chirp in clear and crisp notes. Dense vegetation thrives everywhere.
Hainan in south China is typically known for its coconut palms, beaches and sea breezes, but tucked away in the central part of this tropical island province is a different world.
The tropical rainforest in central Hainan is the most concentrated, best-preserved and largest contiguous continental-island-type tropical rainforest in China, and forms an important part of the world's tropical rainforest system.
In 2021, China formally established its first batch of five national parks, including the National Park of Hainan Tropical Rainforest. With a total area of 4,269 square kilometers, the park spans nine cities and counties and accounts for about one-eighth of Hainan Island's land area. Monday marked the fifth anniversary of its establishment.
Over the past five years, construction of the park has made solid progress. According to the latest figures from the Administration of Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park, 91 new wildlife and plant species have been discovered, and more than 95 percent of Hainan's primary forest and over 55 percent of its natural forest have been effectively protected.
Data from the National Forestry and Grassland Administration showed the population of Hainan's resident gibbons has increased to 44 in seven groups, making it the only gibbon species in the world with a continuously growing population.
During this year's Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holidays, the park's Yinggezui nature experience area opened to the public by reservation for the first time, with visitors from across the country coming in awe of the quietness and grandeur of this hidden rainforest realm. The experience area followed the principle of "ecological protection first, limited and orderly opening," offering free reservations with a daily cap of 800 visitors.
Fu Mingkai, a local staff member, said the area had been fully booked every day from Oct. 1 to 6.
"The area has not undergone excessive commercial transformation," Fu said, adding that visitors can get a close-up view of highly representative original rainforest landscapes, such as buttress roots and cauliflory, by slowly walking along a dedicated ecological route.
"This is a globally important gene pool of germplasm resources, and it is home to many plants and animals unique to Hainan," Fu said. "For example, the Hainan gibbon and the Hainan peacock-pheasant, which have very high requirements for their habitat, have both been found here."
The fact that the species appear here and that their populations have recovered shows the rainforest is healthy and full of vitality, he added.
"Thanks to strict protection in recent years, the vegetation has recovered and wildlife in the rainforest is improving," Fu said.
After the holidays, the Yinggezui experience area will continue to open by reservation on holidays, weekends and other periods to better meet public demand for ecological sightseeing and science education, he said.
Hainan has been sparing no effort in ecological protection.
Fu Cairui, another local staff member, has worked in rainforest protection for more than 20 years.
"More than 20 years ago, the surrounding mountains were full of life, but some local residents practiced slash-and-burn farming, and some primary forests were slowly eroded," he said. "Forests that once extended to low elevations could later only be seen at middle and high elevations."
Species such as the clouded leopard, Hainan peacock-pheasant and pangolin were common in his grandparents' time, but later became critically endangered, he said.
In his view, protecting the tropical rainforest is vitally important.
"Tropical rainforests have extremely high ecological value. They absorb carbon dioxide, release oxygen and slow climate change. They conserve water, purify water quality and maintain the regional water cycle. They also contain rich species resources and are a natural gene bank. To protect the tropical rainforest is to protect the habitats of rare plants and animals," he added.
Everyone is responsible for protecting the rainforest, Fu said.
"People can actively take part in environmental public welfare activities," he said. "We also go to schools and villages around communities to give lectures, and we hope the public will pay more attention to and support our work." ■

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Air Force has proposed allowing eligible pilots to serve until age 58, Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄) said Tuesday.
Under the existing system, lieutenant colonels face a service limit of 26 years, or approximately age 48, while colonels face a limit of 30 years, or approximately age 52. Pilots who leave the military lose their flight allowances, Koo said. The proposed extension would help the Air Force retain experienced officers, per Liberty Times.
Eligible lieutenant colonels and colonels could serve until age 58 regardless of those limits, per CNA. The plan would still require annual health checks and other regular reviews, the minister said. Officers who failed the tests could no longer continue flying.
Koo said he believed pilots loved flying and would be proud to continue serving. Maintaining their flight allowances until age 58 would also reduce the pressure to change careers in middle age and seek work in the private sector, he said.

Healey should ‘stay the course’ and repair UK finances, says top IMF economist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:49:39 UTC
15:49:39 KST

John Healey should “stay the course” and continue repairing the UK’s public finances, the International Monetary Fund’s top economist has said, after the fund lifted its growth forecast for Britain.
Little more than a fortnight before Healey’s first budget, Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s economic counsellor, said the UK “stands out” among G7 countries in having a plan to narrow its deficit.
“The UK has already started a consolidation process,” she said. “The message for the UK is simply, stay the course.”
Tenreyro, a former member of the Bank of England’s monetary policy committee, was speaking at the launch of the IMF’s twice-yearly World Economic Outlook (WEO) at the fund’s annual meetings in Bangkok.
Healey is under pressure to announce a generous energy support package in the budget, before the sharp rise in energy bills expected in January.
But in its WEO report, the IMF advises member governments against across-the-board subsidies, saying any support should be “temporary, targeted and non-distortionary”.
In a fillip for the chancellor, who is due to arrive in Bangkok later this week, the IMF has upgraded its growth forecast for the UK this year, but it expects a modest slowdown in 2027 as higher energy prices take their toll.
Responding, Healey said: “Conflict in the Middle East and Europe is hitting people in the UK and around the world. But Britain’s economy is showing strong international resilience in the face of these challenges.”
The IMF predicted GDP growth of 1.3% for the UK this year, up 0.3 percentage points from its most recent update in July.
UK GDP growth has been stronger than expected in early 2026, at 0.6% in the first quarter and 0.5% in the second quarter. The Office for National Statistics has pointed to the strong expansion of AI-related businesses as one factor behind the upside surprise.
However, the IMF warned that prolonged high oil prices and rising interest rates meant growth was likely to “edge down” in 2027 “as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”.
It cut its UK growth forecast for next year modestly to 1.2%, from 1.3%.
Markets have been revising up their expectations of future inflation and interest rates across big economies since the Middle East conflict re-escalated in the summer.
The Bank of England’s nine-member monetary policy committee is now widely expected to raise the policy rate at its November meeting, echoing similar moves by the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan.
Mortgage rates in the UK have already been rising in response to higher funding costs for banks in financial markets.
The BoE policymaker Megan Greene argued on Tuesday morning that the IMF’s growth upgrade was proof that UK interest rates should be higher.
Speaking to the Atlantic Council at the IMF meetings in Bangkok, Greene argued that interest rates were currently not very restrictive.
“There’s more recently been some labour market data that has also suggested that maybe slack in the labour market has peaked, so the labour market is loose,” Greene said.
The IMF singled out the UK as among the countries – also including Japan – where core inflation, which excludes volatile commodities such as energy, was not expected to return to the 2% target until late next year.
It expects average inflation in the UK to be 3.3% this year and to remain at 2.8% in 2027 – a challenge for Healey and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who are promising to offer voters a “breathing space” from rising costs.
Healey will spend little more than 24 hours in the Thai capital before flying home to put the finishing touches to his 28 October budget.
He is expected to focus on plans to devolve more tax revenues to mayoralties, alongside measures to help households cope with higher energy bills before the winter.
A string of other challenging decisions, including when the UK should be aiming to spend 3% of GDP on defence, is expected to be delayed until a big spending review at some point next year.
The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) warned this week that the budget would be a “work of fiction” unless Healey explained how he would deal with what it said were £35bn of future spending pressures.

Fuel prices: Sébastien Lecornu promises €10 cut per fill-up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:45:00 UTC
15:45:00 KST

In France, pump prices are among the highest in the European Union. The government has moved to cut the price per litre by 12 to 18 centimes, the Prime Minister said on Monday.
This is news that may go some way towards easing French anger. Thanks to the strategic reserves released by the government, diesel prices will fall by up to 18 cents per litre from Sunday 1 November. That means a cut "of around 10 euros for a full tank", the prime minister promises.
"Facing a crisis we did not choose, [...] the state is shouldering its responsibilities," Sébastien Lecornu said on X on Monday 12 October, after a meeting with fuel distributors. "This reduction will also feed through to the price of domestic heating oil, to diesel sold to transport professionals as well as to off-road diesel, used by farmers, fishers and construction workers," the resident of Matignon also stressed.
This measure, scheduled to run until the end of January, is made possible by "selling at cost price 10 million barrels of diesel from our strategic reserves" bought before the start of the war in Iran, at 0.28 euro per litre.
53 litres of diesel for one day’s wages
Government support seemed inevitable. France is currently one of the EU countries where pump prices are highest, with an average of 2.355 euros per litre of diesel as of 5 October, according to the comparison site fuel-price (source in French). That is well above the EU-27 average of 2.149 euros per litre. Only Finland (2.553 euros), the Netherlands (2.506 euros) and Denmark (2.488 euros) are more expensive.
However, the surge in prices at the pump is not limited to France. Among its European neighbours, prices are also reaching record levels. In Belgium, a litre sells for an average of 2.349 euros, compared with 2.254 euros in Germany and 2.273 euros in Italy.
Spain, meanwhile, is one of the countries with the lowest average price, with a litre selling for 1.918 euros.
But the price displayed at the pump is not enough to gauge how hard the bill hits motorists. Wage levels also play a decisive role. While Spain appears to be doing better, a worker on the country’s average wage can buy 54.2 litres of diesel with one day’s pay. In France, one working day buys 52.8 litres, compared with 47 litres in Italy and 62.3 litres in Germany.
And when it comes to filling up the tank, France sits around the European average, with a full tank equivalent to 4.4% of the average net monthly wage.
The situation is broadly similar for petrol. France is among the countries where a litre is most expensive, at an average of 2.212 euros on 5 October. Here too, the country’s average prices are much higher than those in the EU (2.006 euros), but below the average litre price in Denmark (2.605 euros, a figure that takes into account potential discounts), the Netherlands (2.432 euros) and Finland (2.370 euros).
However, France is also close to the European average when the petrol price per litre is set against the cost of living. One day’s work buys 56.2 litres, compared with an EU average of 57.4 litres.
Heating oil far pricier than the European average
Motorists are not the only ones bearing the brunt of soaring energy prices. As winter approaches, heating costs are also a source of concern for households that use heating oil. On 5 October, 1,000 litres of domestic heating oil were selling for 1,907.08 euros in France, 165.14 euros more than the EU average and 179.09 euros more than in the euro area, according to the European Commission’s figures.
In recent months, prices in France have followed the same trajectory as in Portugal and Italy, where 1,000 litres of domestic heating oil now sell for 2,204 euros and 2,063.10 euros respectively.
Other countries have nonetheless managed to keep prices more affordable. This is notably the case in Germany, where heating oil sells for 1,726.40 euros per 1,000 litres. In Belgium and Spain, heating oil is cheaper still, at 1,533.40 and 1,495.34 euros respectively, 19.6% and 21.6% less than in France.

====================================================================================================

Built-in Agility and the Architecture of the Infinite Lifecycle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:45:00 UTC
15:45:00 KST

While architecture often responds to a specific program of uses, taking into account areas, contexts, and various economic and technical conditions, buildings rarely remain the same throughout their lifespan. Programs, spatial dynamics, and users' needs change, as do environmental, economic, and technological conditions, requiring interventions that were likely not anticipated at the beginning of a project. Steel structures make it possible to envision architecture capable of growing, transforming, being disassembled, and reassembled. Their dimensional precision, industrialized components, and potential for mechanical connections enable the design of open systems prepared for future interventions.
Just as Mies van der Rohe designed the Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin and Richard Rogers and Renzo Piano designed the Centre Pompidou in Paris, steel was embraced by numerous architects throughout the 20th century, enabling them to create everything from large-span and high-rise structures to more flexible spaces with greater degrees of freedom. As its applications have evolved over time, steel has continued to support the development of adaptable architecture, even allowing future expansions to be planned from the earliest stages of a project.
Rather than understanding buildings as closed and definitive volumes, structural systems can establish growth strategies that anticipate future connections, reserve areas for extensions, or dimension certain elements to accommodate additions at a later stage. Planning for expansion thus becomes part of an architectural approach conceived as an ongoing process, in which a building can begin with a given floor area and later incorporate new modules, levels, or spaces without altering its existing structure. By working with standardized components and repetitive systems, steel supports this logic of incremental growth, allowing new elements to be integrated into preexisting structures.
When Steel Adapts to New Uses
However, adaptability also means responding to transformations that do not necessarily require more floor area, but instead accommodate new uses. An office can be converted into housing; an industrial building can host cultural activities; and a commercial structure can house educational or community programs. The capacity for adaptation depends on how much of the existing architecture can be retained while its interior components and building systems are modified. Steel supports this approach by allowing different components to be joined through mechanical connections, reducing reliance on permanent construction methods. Bolted connections, for example, make it possible to disassemble and reassemble certain elements, avoiding the need for extensive demolition.
At the heart of a historic village, "Laab Is More" reflects a model of community life rooted in mutual support and shared assistance. Blending modern and traditional elements, the house's aesthetic responds to the owner's appreciation for traditional ways of living, while the strategic use of steel reflects the spirit of northern craftsmanship and integrates with the community's simple, rural character. The layout draws on the region's traditional vernacular architecture and makes use of locally available materials, adapting them to new applications and a contemporary design.
The commission called for a shelter that would provide privacy and an inviting space for gathering while moving away from the traditional wooden structures of neighboring houses and minimizing the use of wood. The architecture tells a story about an emotional connection to the region's vernacular culture, where people traditionally sit on the floor and enjoy a staple dish called "Laab," as their ancestors did.
To ensure strength and durability, the foundations and structural system were built in concrete, supporting the steel columns, beams, and roof truss. Studio Sifah selected corrugated steel roofing sheets—made from BlueScope Zacs Cool steel in Asian White color with corrugated profile—to complement the zinc and fiber-cement roofs found throughout the surrounding area. The wall cladding echoes the dimensions and texture of the wooden panels traditionally used in rice barns, a familiar element of the northern region. The roof is separated from the walls, creating an intermediate space that visually lightens the structure. BlueScope Zacs Cool sheets in Asian White color were folded and finished with rubber strips, while concrete and steel were used to evoke the lightness of traditional vernacular wooden houses.
Steel as a Resilient and Functional Technology
Beyond the durability of steel and its ability to establish relationships with its surroundings, the material can also serve practical functions that extend beyond aesthetics. For example, designing for disassembly introduces a new perspective. A beam, column, or industrialized component can become a potential resource for recovery, allowing building components to be replaced, relocated, or reused once a program changes or an existing structure requires intervention. Partial disassembly can be useful for renovating specific parts of a building without affecting the entire structure, while a more comprehensive approach can allow recovered components to find new applications elsewhere.
Trinity House, clad in COLORBOND® steel in Gull Grey color, demonstrates how material selection can serve a practical function beyond aesthetics. From the roof to the walls, the building features a consistent palette and pattern defined by gray tones. But the material does more than establish a visual identity: COLORBOND® steel with THERMATECH® solar reflectance technology reduces heat absorption at the surface, helping maintain comfortable interior temperatures. In addition, CLEAN TECHNOLOGY, which uses a Super Polyester paint system, helps preserve the home's color over time. By combining aesthetics and performance, the use of COLORBOND® steel and advanced technologies demonstrates how material choices can contribute to attractive, comfortable, and adaptable environments.
Another example is FNI Office & Workshop, designed by architect Heru Mudito Prasetyo. The factory and office complex combines aesthetics and resilience through elevated structures, effective ventilation, optimized natural lighting, and minimal maintenance requirements. The project responds to a series of environmental and operational challenges. The client operates in the steel fabrication industry, where the production process relies on conveyor belts and rollers. The workshop was commissioned to accommodate and optimize these processes, which had become increasingly inefficient after years of use, limiting the production line. The building's volume responds to the project's requirements and challenges, seeking to accommodate the steel fabrication process, address the constraints of the site, and improve the quality of life of its users.
Designing adaptable architecture does not necessarily mean attempting to anticipate every transformation that may occur throughout a building's lifespan. It means creating structures flexible enough to accommodate different future scenarios. While the structural system establishes certain conditions—such as module dimensions, spans, load-bearing capacity, and connections—its components can be modified with greater freedom. From this perspective, a building's efficiency would depend not only on how much material or energy is required to construct it, but also on how many transformations it can accommodate without losing architectural or material value.
The potential of steel lies not only in its ability to achieve long spans, reduce construction time, or facilitate industrialized building processes. It also involves conceiving buildings as modifiable systems: structures capable of growing, adapting, being disassembled, and reconfigured. Rather than designing buildings that are intended to remain unchanged, this approach proposes creating buildings prepared to evolve, incorporating new needs without resorting to demolition and reconstruction. In a context where extending the lifespan of buildings and reducing material waste are becoming increasingly important, considering how buildings can transform becomes just as relevant as considering how they will be constructed in the first place.

IDF: mystery object that entered Israel from Lebanon was likely a balloon, not a drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:43:39 UTC
15:43:39 KST

An unidentified object that entered Israeli airspace Saturday night was most likely a balloon or another device kept airborne by hot air, rather than a drone, the IDF said Tuesday, following an extensive investigation into the incident.
According to the military, the object's origin and purpose remain unknown, and investigators cannot rule out the possibility that it was harmless and had simply drifted into Israeli territory.
"At this stage, it is not possible to determine with certainty its origin or purpose," the IDF said. "It can be established that it was not a drone or unmanned aerial vehicle, and it may have been an innocent object that drifted into Israeli territory."
The object was detected by Air Force observation personnel and detection systems, which tracked its movement and directed forces on the ground as they responded to the incident.
At the same time, security measures were reinforced in nearby communities, including the activation of local defense units, pending completion of the relevant checks.
The military said the object has still not been located despite continued searches. No changes have been made to Home Front Command instructions for civilians.
Addressing a recent increase in reports of false detections and interceptions, the IDF explained that distinguishing between a small drone and a bird can be extremely difficult for aerial detection systems.
Throughout the war, the Air Force has been responsible for detecting and intercepting threats across multiple fronts, with protecting civilians and deployed troops its primary priority.
"The difference between a drone and a bird is very small," the military said, explaining that it cannot afford to take risks when a potential threat is detected. Once a suspected threat is identified, forces must make rapid decisions that can lead to interception.
The IDF said it continues to search the area from the air and on the ground while reviewing its detection systems, with the aim of improving identification capabilities and applying lessons from recent operational incidents.

Sumykhimprom sale fails again for lack of bidders
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:42:59 EEST
15:42:59 KST

An auction to sell the state’s 99.9952% stake in Sumykhimprom, one of Ukraine’s largest chemical companies, did not take place because there were no buyers. It had been scheduled for October 13 in the Prozorro.Sale trading system with a starting price of UAH 1.005 billion.
“The asset is complex, with a heavy background, but for an investor in agrochemicals or building materials it is a ready site for building a national champion,” State Property Fund head Dmytro Natalukha said on Facebook on the eve of the auction.
A repeat online auction scheduled for January 13, 2026, with the price cut 9.3% to UAH 1.088 billion (excluding VAT), also failed for lack of participants, as did the previous auction on June 11, 2025.
On July 8 this year the government approved the terms and a starting price of UAH 1.005 billion for the stake.
Under the terms, the new owner had to keep the company’s main activities and invest at least UAH 150 million in technical re-equipment and modernization of production. The buyer also had to repay wage arrears, debts to the budget and overdue payables within six months, observe employees’ social guarantees under labor law and not lay anyone off for six months after the purchase.
The fund will offer several more big and interesting assets at auction next week, Natalukha said. First, the Odesa Portside Plant will go on sale on October 19.
“It is a pearl of Ukrainian industry, but also a monument to corruption that has survived five failed auctions and endless backroom games. It is the biggest and practically unique ammonia and urea transshipment hub on the Black Sea, with its own sea berths, terminals and direct access to deep water. It is a ready, world-class logistics and production hub,” he said, promoting it.
Two other assets, transferred to the state under the law on sanctions against Russians, are the Demurynsky Mining and Processing Plant and Motordetal-Konotop. Their auctions are scheduled for October 20.
Sumykhimprom is one of Ukraine’s largest producers of complex mineral fertilizers, titanium dioxide, sulfuric acid and other inorganic chemicals. It is one of the three biggest budget contributors in Sumy and the region, and it makes more than 30 grades of NPK fertilizers with different nutrient ratios for different soil and climate zones.
For more than 10 years the plant was managed by a group of companies linked to Group DF of entrepreneur Dmytro Firtash. In November 2023 the Sumy Region Commercial Court granted a motion by the State Property Fund and the Justice Ministry and closed the bankruptcy and rehabilitation proceedings against Sumykhimprom.
The fund planned to sell the company to a private investor even before the full-scale war, but privatization dragged on because of the position of Firtash, a minority shareholder who received 0.005% of the shares in 2010 and control of management. Sumykhimprom piled up debts, which made it possible to form a creditors’ committee and start rehabilitation proceedings.
The fund tried through the courts to end the bankruptcy proceedings from 2015 but succeeded only in 2023, which unblocked privatization.
Russian forces shelled the plant in March 2022, causing an ammonia leak. The plant stood idle for a year and resumed operations in spring 2023. As of June 2025 the front line was less than 30 km from Sumykhimprom.
According to its 2025 report, the company’s payables at the end of the year were UAH 4.135 billion, of which UAH 1.292 billion was debt in the bankruptcy case opened by the Sumy Region Commercial Court in October 2011, formed under the court-approved register of creditors.
“The lack of working capital, loss-making operations and plant downtime cause growth of payables,” the report said.
Sumykhimprom’s 2025 revenue was UAH 129.2 million (UAH 395.9 million a year earlier), gross profit UAH 53.3 million (UAH 9.9 million) and net loss UAH 405.7 million (UAH 600.2 million).
“The main reason for Sumykhimprom’s losses in 2025 is the forced downtime of production capacity from November 2024 to July 22, 2025 and the downtime of all structural units in the fourth quarter of 2025. In 2025, sulfuric acid shop No. 5 worked for only two months,” the report said.
Because of the worsening dangerous situation in the region, the regional military administration did not give permission to buy ammonia, which kept the company from launching its complex mineral fertilizer program as set out in the approved financial plan for 2025, the report said.

Malaysia’s Firefly cancels flights to Singapore over haze from Indonesia
Move comes as haze from Indonesian fires makes Singapore and Kuala Lumpur the world’s most polluted cities.
Firefly, a Malaysian low-cost airline, has extended the suspension of its flights between Kuala Lumpur and Singapore through Wednesday as smoke from fires in Indonesia continued to blanket the region.
The announcement came as IQAir, an air quality monitor, ranked Singapore and the Malaysian capital Kuala Lumpur as the world’s two most polluted cities on Tuesday.
Firefly said in a statement that flights between the Sultan Abdul Aziz Shah Airport (SZB) near Kuala Lumpur and the Seletar Airport in Singapore (XSP) have been cancelled up to Wednesday due to “weather and haze conditions”.
It called the action a “proactive safety measure”.
The fires, mostly on the Indonesian islands of Sumatra and Borneo, are the country’s most intense in 11 years. They have been spurred by El Nino, a weather pattern expected to be among the strongest in four decades.
IQAir, a Swiss air quality monitoring company, said Air Quality Index in Singapore stood at 199 on Tuesday and 183 in Kuala Lumpur. Readings above 150 are generally considered unhealthy, and those above 300 are classified as hazardous.
Firefly, a subsidiary of Malaysia Aviation Group, which includes Malaysia Airlines, first announced the flight cancellations on October 10, citing “low visibility” due to the haze conditions.
Firefly said that affected passengers were being rebooked on Malaysia Airlines flights between Kuala Lumpur International Airport and Singapore’s Changi Airport, subject to seat availability.
The Singapore government has reintroduced subsidised care for haze-related illnesses, as it last did in 2015, when smoke from Indonesian fires hung over the region for weeks.
In Malaysia, schools reopened in most states on Tuesday as air quality improved slightly, but they remain closed in three states, one federal territory and several districts.
Malaysia’s foreign minister, Mohamad Hasan, said on Monday that he would press for stronger regional mechanisms when foreign ministers of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) meet next month.
“We already have an ASEAN mechanism for natural disasters, but haze is not included or classified as a natural disaster,” he told reporters in Sepang, according to Bernama, Malaysia’s state news agency.
The Philippines, which chairs the bloc this year, confirmed that the issue would be on the agenda.
“It’s in the agenda,” Dominic Xavier Imperial, a spokesman for the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs, said of the November meeting, which will precede the 49th ASEAN summit in Manila.
Mohamad, the Malaysian minister, said Indonesia had deployed about 60,000 personnel to fight the fires, but thick smoke had grounded 34 aircraft, including planes and helicopters.
Remote terrain and limited water supplies have also hindered the effort, he said, and cloud seeding is not possible without suitable rain clouds. He acknowledged Indonesia’s efforts but urged more effective action, citing the toll on Malaysian communities.

Video: Why does Finland celebrate failure?
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:41:36 EEST
15:41:36 KST

Back in 2010, a student group at Aalto University in Helsinki came up with an idea: what if failure was something to be celebrated, instead of lamented?
Their initiative became 'Epäonnistumisen päivä', or 'Failure Day', and it was marked for the first time on 13 October that year.
Since then, the concept has been picked up by organisations and businesses in dozens of countries around the world — from 'failure panels' in the US to 'failure meetups' in Japan.
October 13 has now become the 'International Day for Failure', and it seeks to remove the social stigma around making mistakes as a means of encouraging open discussions about setbacks, reframing failure as a normal aspect of every day, and to encourage people to create and innovate.

How Ukrainians Can Process an Inheritance While Abroad – Explanation by the Ministry of Justice
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:41:29 EEST
15:41:29 KST

How Ukrainians Can Process an Inheritance While Abroad – Explanation by the Ministry of Justice
Kyiv • UNN
An inheritance can be accepted from abroad without traveling to Ukraine within six months. The application is submitted in person through a consulate or a notary.
Ukrainians residing abroad can accept an inheritance without personally traveling to Ukraine. This was reported by the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine, according to UNN.
It is not necessary to travel to Ukraine to accept an inheritance. If, at the time the inheritance was opened, you did not permanently reside with the deceased, you must submit an application to accept it. The general time limit is six months from the date the inheritance was opened. For those who permanently resided with the deceased at that time, a different rule applies: they are considered to have accepted the inheritance unless they rejected it within the established time limit
How to submit an application from abroad
According to the available information, to submit an application, the heir must have their signature certified at a Ukrainian consular office or by a foreign notary. If the document is оформed by a foreign notary, the requirements regarding an apostille or legalization and translation depend on the country and Ukraine’s international treaties.
Send the application by mail to a notary in Ukraine. It is advisable to first coordinate with the notary whether they can open or continue your inheritance case. Keep proof of dispatch: an application sent before the deadline for accepting the inheritance is considered timely, even if it reaches the notary later
The ministry emphasizes that the application to accept an inheritance must be submitted by the heir personally—a representative acting under a power of attorney cannot do this on their behalf. At the same time, the heir may authorize a representative in Ukraine to submit the documents required for the further processing of the inheritance and to obtain a certificate of the right to inherit.
Recall
All heirs under the law have equal shares in the inherited property unless otherwise provided by a will. However, the division of the inheritance may be changed by agreement among the heirs. What rules apply to inheritance and what should be taken into account.
