Ukraine strikes on Yandex data centers cut traffic to Estonian sites nearly 100%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:09:00 UTC
15:09:00 KST

Ukraine strikes on Yandex data centers cut traffic to Estonian sites nearly 100%
Traffic from Russia's Yandex network to Estonian websites has fallen nearly 100 percent following Ukrainian strikes on the internet company's data centers.
The Information System Authority (RIA) says average requests from Yandex fell roughly 420 times by October 13 compared with September's average, following strikes last week. RIA puts the overall drop in Yandex traffic to Estonian sites at 99.8 percent.
Ukraine struck three Yandex data centers last week — one near Moscow on Sunday, one in Sasovo on Thursday and one in Kaluga on Friday.
"The average number of queries coming from the Yandex network has decreased by 99.8 percent, or roughly 420 times, compared with the September average, as of October 13," said Simon Berner, an analyst at RIA's analysis and prevention department.
Yandex was forced to suspend operations at the data center near Moscow on Sunday after the facility was damaged in a Ukrainian drone strike.
Foreign media has reported that the strikes on Yandex also dealt a blow to the Kremlin's online influence operations, including via bot activity in English, which often takes a far-right perspective.
RIA says, however, that it is too early to assess possible changes in the activity of cyberattacks carried out by Russia.
"At the same time, there is no reason to assume that disruptions to Yandex data centers would have a significant effect on the frequency of cyberattacks directed against Estonia. Various infrastructures are used to carry out attacks, and these do not depend on the functioning of Yandex services," Berner said.
Monitoring Russia's influence activities, including the activity of social media bots and troll accounts, does not fall within RIA's competence, so the authority cannot confirm or refute claims that their activity has decreased.
Yandex also operates food delivery and taxi apps used by tens of millions of people; it has previously said its data centers are essential to the normal functioning of its services.
Yandex taxi services in Estonia were banned shortly after the start of the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

China has caused luxury giant LVMH’s sales to plunge
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:08:47 EEST
15:08:47 KST

China has caused luxury giant LVMH’s sales to plunge
Kyiv • UNN
LVMH’s sales on the mainland fell by a double-digit percentage, while Chinese consumers’ purchases abroad declined. In the United States, spending increased.
LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE this week provided a more detailed analysis of the deepening downturn in China’s luxury goods market, reporting that sales in mainland China fell by a double-digit percentage in the third quarter, while the group, which traditionally relies on big-spending consumers, also saw overseas sales decline. UNN reports this, citing Bloomberg.
Details
Weak spending contributed to a 5% decline in organic revenue in Asia, excluding Japan, the only region where the luxury giant recorded a year-on-year decrease. Purchases by Chinese shoppers abroad fell by several percentage points, while overall demand improved toward the end of the quarter ended September 30, Chief Financial Officer Cécile Cabanis told analysts during a conference call.
China’s slowing economic growth, long regarded as an indicator of the industry’s health, is raising doubts about the sustainability of the broader luxury market recovery and could be a warning sign for competitors, including Yves Saint Laurent owner Kering SA and Hermès International SCA, which are due to report their financial results, the publication writes. Less than a year ago, China was contributing to the industry’s recovery, but deteriorating economic sentiment is once again putting pressure on spending in the luxury goods segment.
"The news flow from China over the summer was not particularly good," Cabanis said. "So it really affected positive sentiment and created a short-term subdued environment in China."
Demand for luxury goods in China is declining across many categories. Consumer caution amid the broader economic downturn is restraining domestic spending and prompting some shoppers to turn to cheaper local brands. At the same time, the recent weakening of the stock market and tighter taxation of overseas assets are putting pressure on some of the country’s wealthiest consumers.
"It’s difficult for everyone right now," said Jacques Roizen, co-founder of Shanghai-based consulting firm Foresight Performance Partners. "LVMH’s portfolio, as a major company, is an industry index, and other publicly traded companies in the luxury goods segment will not be able to significantly outperform it."
The slowdown in demand in China contrasted with spending by American shoppers, which rose by several percentage points.
Louis Vuitton also faced a public backlash following a trademark dispute with local tea shop chain Molly Tea, which drew criticism in China during the quarter and added pressure on LVMH’s largest brand. Cabanis said that, although it was difficult to quantify the impact, consumer resistance hurt Louis Vuitton, at least at the beginning of the period.
Chinese tea chain ordered to pay Louis Vuitton $1.5 million over logo03.07.26, 15:00 • 64471 view
The downturn in China is occurring against the backdrop of an overall slowdown in the recovery of the luxury goods market, which is facing pressure from the conflict in the Middle East and cost-of-living concerns that are curbing spending on goods and services worldwide.
This pressure is already being felt in the luxury goods sector. Sales of the 25 largest luxury brands in China fell by more than 10% in July, Bloomberg previously reported. This threatens to derail the recovery that began less than a year ago, when an artificial intelligence-fueled stock market boom helped revive luxury spending.
LVMH’s renewed growth in revenue and earnings per share this year "has become unstable" as China’s slowdown deepened in the third quarter, Bloomberg Intelligence analysts Deborah Aitken and Karin Pitton wrote.
"There have been changes in China’s consumer environment, and this is prompting us to intensify our self-help efforts," CFO Cabanis said. "We need to do more, but we have not stopped investing in China."

NATO fund targets drone defence technologies as Ukraine reshapes priorities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:05:48 UTC
15:05:48 KST

NATO fund targets drone defence technologies as Ukraine reshapes priorities
Oct 13 - Russia's invasion of Ukraine is reshaping NATO's defence technology priorities, with counter-drone systems and space-based surveillance emerging as some of the alliance's most urgent capability gaps, the head of the NATO Innovation Fund told Reuters.
The 1 billion euro ($1.12 billion) fund, backed by 24 NATO nations, is expanding into Poland and looking for direct investments as it seeks to accelerate the development of dual-use technologies on NATO's eastern flank.
"We have seen drone incursions into countries here to an extent that is not being seen elsewhere," NIF President Ari Jonsson said.
"That really creates a different mindset when it comes to threats that you can actually see."
The most pressing needs on NATO's eastern flank are technologies that can detect, track and neutralise drones as well as space-based intelligence and reconnaissance capabilities, he said.
Lessons from the war in Ukraine had significantly influenced the fund's investment strategy, Jonsson said.
Poland's high defence spending, openness to new technologies and strong engineering base have made it an attractive destination for investment, he said.
Jonsson said the fund was deliberately looking beyond traditional defence contractors for the next generation of defence technologies.
To support that effort, the fund is opening a presence in Warsaw to speed up the identification and adoption of promising innovations.
"The NATO Innovation Fund is the first major fund, not originating from Poland, to establish a substantial presence in our country," Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domanski said in a statement. REUTERS

Meta challenges UK media regulator over fees, fines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:04:44 UTC
15:04:44 KST

Burak Bir
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
A UK High Court will hold a hearing Tuesday on a challenge brought by Meta, the tech giant that owns Facebook and Instagram, over fees and potential fines introduced under the country's Online Safety Act.
Meta is challenging Ofcom in the High Court, claiming that the UK media regulator acted unlawfully, specifically regarding their definition of "qualifying worldwide revenue," which is introduced under the act.
The law, which came into force last year, introduced protections against harmful online content, with Ofcom's operating costs for carrying out its online safety work funded by tech firms.
Under regulations introduced in September 2025, the fees are based on a company's qualifying worldwide revenue and apply to firms earning more than £250 million a year.
Meta explicitly argues that Ofcom's calculation methods are disproportionate and unlawful, while Ofcom said it would "robustly defend" its position.
The BBC reported in May that lawyers acting for Meta argued that the regulations should be reconsidered by the regulator.
Monica Carss-Frisk KC, for the tech giant, has said in court documents that Ofcom's approach is "troubling" and leads to "a handful of companies such as Meta bearing the vast majority of Ofcom's costs, despite the act making clear that it is concerned with a wide range of internet services offered in the UK.”
Under the Online Safety Act, firms found to have breached safety rules can face fines of up to 10% of qualifying worldwide revenue or £18 million ($23.7 million), whichever is greater.
Meanwhile, a senior director at the regulator told a committee in the House of Lords earlier this year that Ofcom was "operating in a highly litigious environment," including facing two actions by Meta and others from "a raft of services" bringing judicial reviews against the body for trying to collect data.
"We absolutely are looking to drive change in the best way we can," Oliver Griffiths, the Ofcom group director for online safety, told peers hearing evidence about the Online Safety Act.

Latest poll puts Eisenkot ahead of Netanyahu in Israel PM race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:43:00 UTC
19:43:00 KST

A poll published Sunday showed former army Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot is leading Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu 43% to 38% in suitability for office, while Netanyahu's bloc remained short of a parliamentary majority.
The survey, released by the Israeli public broadcaster KAN, projected 22 seats for Eisenkot's Yashar party in the 120-member Knesset compared with 20 for Netanyahu's Likud, down one seat from the previous week's poll, ahead of elections scheduled for Oct. 27.
Netanyahu's bloc gained two seats to reach 53, leaving it eight short of the 61-seat majority required to form a government.
Eisenkot's bloc was projected to secure 50 seats, with the remaining 17 going to parties classified by the poll as outside both camps.
Arab parties were projected to win a combined 13 seats, including eight for the Joint List and five for the United Arab List, known as Ra'am, led by Mansour Abbas.
Within Netanyahu's bloc, the poll gave nine seats to National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power party, eight to United Torah Judaism and seven to Shas. The Religious Zionism-Zehut alliance was projected to secure five seats.
Amcha Yisrael, led by former brigadier general Ofer Winter, was projected to win four seats, clearing the electoral threshold after failing to do so in the previous poll.
The survey also indicated substantial voter uncertainty, with 30% of respondents saying they had yet to decide which party to support and 21% saying they were considering not voting.
Meanwhile, 54% supported a televised debate between Netanyahu and Eisenkot before the election, including 38% of respondents who intended to vote for Likud.
The results suggest that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the Jewish opposition bloc would secure enough seats to form a government on its own.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s diplomatic allies Paraguay and Belize vowed Monday to maintain ties with Taipei after Beijing sanctioned two of their ministers for supporting Taiwan.
China’s foreign ministry on Monday announced sanctions against Paraguay’s Minister of Information and Communication Technologies Gustavo Emigdio Villate Samaniego and Belizean Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Francis Fonseca. The measures freeze their assets in China, prohibit Chinese organizations and individuals from conducting transactions or cooperating with them, and ban them from entering China, Hong Kong, and Macau.
Villate told ABC Color that the sanctions “were to be expected” given the major technology cooperation projects Paraguay is pursuing with Taiwan, including data centers and AI infrastructure. “We will continue working on all the projects we have, and we will push this even more strongly,” Villate said.
Villate said the initiatives that may have angered Beijing include the planned Binational Data Center in Chaco’i and an invitation to Taiwan-based Foxconn to join the Yguazu Digital AI hub. He described the sanctions as a “medal of honor” and said Paraguay would accelerate its joint technology development agenda with Taiwan at President Santiago Peña’s direction.
Paraguay’s foreign ministry also rejected the sanctions in a statement posted on X, saying they created “unnecessary friction” with the country. The ministry reaffirmed Paraguay’s firm support for Taiwan and its commitment to democratic values and principles.
Belize’s foreign ministry condemned China’s sanctions, saying the measures were unwarranted and would not change the country’s foreign policy. “Belize is a sovereign and independent state,” the ministry said, adding that every country has the right to conduct its foreign policy free from external pressure under the UN Charter.
The ministry said Belize established diplomatic relations with Taiwan through a sovereign decision and described the relationship as a partnership that has benefited Belizeans through cooperation in development, health, education, infrastructure, environmental protection, and agriculture. It added that Fonseca had acted in his official capacity and in Belize’s national interest, rejecting measures targeting him for carrying out his duties.
“These measures will not alter Belize’s foreign policy, nor will they deter the Government from carrying out its responsibilities,” the ministry said. It added that the government continued to “stand fully behind Minister Fonseca.”
“The Trump Administration opposes coercion and aggression by China against countries in our hemisphere for exercising their sovereign rights,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told Reuters.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taichung-based Thunder Tiger said Monday it would showcase drone technology at the 2026 Association of the United States Army exhibition in Washington, DC, CNA reported.
The three-day event runs from Oct. 12 to 14 and hosts defense contractors including Boeing, Lockheed Martin, and BAE Systems. Thunder Tiger said its exhibits include the Papadelta x Ultrabuggy unmanned ground vehicle, SeaShark 600 unmanned surface vessel, and Blue UAS-certified Overkill first-person-view drone, built using non-Chinese parts.
Thunder Tiger said its unmanned ground vehicle uses a pneumatic catapult to launch the drone while moving, without a runway or launch pad. The drone can be equipped with 175cc or 250cc piston engines, or the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology’s CS-80 microturbine jet engine, depending on mission requirements.
Thunder Tiger said its SeaShark 600 drone boat has a 6-meter aluminum alloy hull fitted with US-based Allen Control Systems’ Bullfrog precision aiming system and AeroVironment’s four-launcher Switchblade system. It can reach a top speed of 50 knots (92.6 kilometers per hour), travel more than 190 nautical miles (350 kilometers), and carry 300 to 600 kilograms for coastal patrols or assault missions.
Thunder Tiger said its Overkill drone has obtained US Department of Defense Blue UAS status. The series includes the complete drone as well as fiber-optic communications, motors, and other components. The drone can fly for up to 30 minutes at a top speed of 120 kph and carry a maximum payload of 3 kilograms.
Blue UAS certification supports the sale of unmanned systems for US defense use, though the US Department of Defense can also purchase systems without it. Green UAS certification applies to vendors seeking to sell to non-Defense Department agencies, such as the US Coast Guard and US Border Patrol.
Thunder Tiger also presented systems developed with US-based Auterion and Israeli and Taiwanese partners to reduce dependence on Chinese parts. It is pursuing rapid, modular, and standardized mass production to secure US defense contracts.

BT charged me for more than a year despite landline being dead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:00:18 UTC
15:00:18 KST

I’ve had no landline since May 2025 when BT switched it to Digital Voice. Weeks passed, and each call to BT involved at least an hour waiting on hold and answering security questions before being passed between departments.
Eventually, last December, two engineers were sent and discovered that a wire had been severed during the upgrade. They said they needed a cherry picker to reconnect it to its original location and would return. They did not.
Since then, I’ve called BT to no avail, and all the while I’ve been paying for a landline that doesn’t work.
I am on the priority register due to serious illness and am reduced to tears of helplessness.
HH, York
You have been paying £32.99 a month for a dead landline and broadband, which was unaffected. BT claims it was unaware of the problem until you complained last December. You insist you had reported it before then, but do not have records of when. It turns out the case was closed in December after the engineers’ abortive visit.
You next complained in January, but BT admits it again closed the case because, by then, your landline had been removed from your account, though you were still being charged.
It says it did not hear from you again until I intervened in July.
You said that you had believed promises that a fix was under way.
A complaints manager rang you after my contact, and you were offered an extraordinary £6.46 to “make up” for its failings. Your line was eventually activated in September.
The telecoms regulator Ofcom requires providers to pay £10.34 compensation a day if a reported fault is not corrected within two working days, which means you are, in theory, entitled to more than £4,600.
I’ve put this to BT, but it is digging in because, it claims, you waited months to report the problems. Since you can’t provide proof to contradict it, I can’t argue the toss.
You have the option of a complaint to the Communications Ombudsman but have now accepted £689 for the 60 days without service which BT acknowledges fall within the compensation rules, and for its mishandling of the two complaints it has on record.
Always keep a timeline of interactions with a company and follow up unaddressed complaints promptly and in writing.

‘A winning combination of culture and nature’: exploring Germany’s green heart by bus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:00:17 UTC
15:00:17 KST

It’s early morning in Erfurt, the capital of Germany’s Thuringia region, and Domplatz is abuzz with local growers setting out crates of vegetables and flowers beneath the soaring medieval cathedral towers. This 14th- and 15th-century engineering wonder holds the Gloriosa, the world’s largest medieval free-swinging bell, cast in 1497 and weighing 12 tonnes. Though the city and surrounding landscape are notably flat, its skyline is pierced by soaring church towers and steeples, the atmospheric old town hardly changed over the centuries.
Thuringia – often called the “green heart of Germany” – lies in the centre of the country, between Hesse, Saxony and Bavaria. It’s famous for its dense forests, intellectual heritage and hearty cuisine, and I’m here for four days to explore using public transport.
Leaving Frankfurt behind, my three-hour coach journey rolls through rising forested highlands before descending into the wide, agricultural basin that cradles Erfurt. After checking out Domplatz’s morning market, it’s just a short walk to one of the town’s other famous sights, the 120-metre-long Krämerbrücke – a 14th-century bridge lined with colourful half-timbered houses.
Erfurt was once at the crossroads of two major trade routes, and the wealth that built its impressive churches and merchants’ houses came partly from waid, or woad, a plant cultivated in the surrounding fields and processed for its blue dye. I stroll past the craft shops (some still sell the dye) to Petersberg Citadel, one of the largest and best-preserved fortresses in Europe, with a maze of underground tunnels. This is also the city where the Protestant Reformation took root – Martin Luther studied here and was a monk in the Augustinian monastery (you can join a guided tour or even stay overnight).
Dinner is in a suitably historic setting; Wirtshaus Christoffel, in the Haus zur weißen Lilie (House of the White Lily), dates back to the 12th century (the house-brewed beer and beef roulade with Thuringian dumplings are delicious).
Next morning, I head to Egapark (a seven-minute bus ride or a 30-minute walk from town). Spread across 36 hectares (89 acres), it was created for the 1961 international horticultural exhibition. The old Cyriaksburg fortress houses the German Horticultural Museum, which traces the history of gardening, while displays range from landscapes of cacti and succulents to tropical planting.
The city of Weimar, a 30-minute bus journey away, is next on my list. The birthplace of the artistic Bauhaus movement, and where Germany’s first democratic constitution was adopted, it’s full of interesting historic sites and design gems. I visit the Bauhaus museum, with its ceramics, textiles, metalwork and painting, and wander around town, passing the former art school buildings that now house the Bauhaus-Universität.
The next morning, I swap culture for chilling and take another bus to Bad Langensalza, a spa town of 10 parks and themed gardens, 40 miles (64km) away. My guide, Markus Fromm, explains that people come here to “cure, to relax, to refresh”.
Sulphur springs were discovered here in 1811, and today, the Friederiken Therme is the town’s main thermal spa, offering natural sulphur, brine and drinking mineral waters, alongside indoor and outdoor pools, saunas and treatments. Traces of the older spa history remain around the town: at Friederikenschlösschen, an 18th-century summer residence, a fountain still runs with sulphur water that has been used for healing since 1812.
But it’s the town’s gardens that really win me over. I wander Friederikenschlösschen’s restored baroque garden and visit the Klagetor, a gate tower dating from about 1365, where the old town gives way to the Japanese garden, Kofuku no Niwa (Garden of Happiness), with its koi ponds, clipped azaleas and sculpted pines.
For nature on an even grander scale, I take a bus to Hainich national park, 10 minutes away (you can easily rent a bike/e-bike and follow cycling paths to get there too). Spanning 7,500 hectares, Hainich offers more than 75 miles of signposted walking trails through its beech forests, part of a Unesco world heritage site. The wider Hainich is Germany’s largest unbroken deciduous woodland area. “Parts of this landscape have been left entirely untouched for decades, abandoned to their own devices without a shred of human meddling,” says park director Rüdiger Biehl.
Before hitting the trail, I stop at the park’s restaurant, Forsthaus Thiemsburg, for a regional lunch – roast pork in black beer and Thuringian dumplings, washed down with a cold Köstritzer pilsner. Then, into the trees. Deep in the beeches, the sun sporadically breaks through the branches and the leaves crunch loudly under my boots. Up in the canopy, it’s mostly just the birds making noise – chaffinches and wood warblers chatter, interrupted by the occasional sharp rattle of a middle spotted woodpecker drilling into a trunk.
The Baumkronenpfad, a wooden walkway through the treetops, rises to a 44-metre observation tower. Here, the canopy of an oak that is estimated to be 350 years old is almost at eye level. It’s a spectacular view, but the forest’s real engine is down below. Deadwood is left to decay where it falls, providing habitat for rare wood-boring insects and endangered Bechstein’s bats. Back in Erfurt that evening, I catch the final symphony concert of the season at Theaterplatz. It’s a reminder of the winning combination of culture and nature that I’ve enjoyed over my four days in Thuringia. I had come looking for a less familiar corner of Germany and found a region that offers plenty of variety – and all accessible with a few short bus rides.
The trip was provided by the German National Tourist Board. Dorint Hotel am Dom in Erfurt has doubles from £85. For journey planning, VMT has information on buses, trains and trams across central Thuringia, as well as a free app with live departure updates

Same-sex couple sue over Slovakia’s refusal to register marriage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:00:16 UTC
15:00:16 KST

A same-sex couple are suing authorities in Slovakia for refusing to register their Austrian marriage, testing whether a landmark EU court ruling can turn recognition abroad into legal security at home.
Their fight exposes a clash between European obligations and national restrictions – and what that means for LGBTQ+ people living under Robert Fico’s populist-nationalist government.
Ivan Novotný, 31, and Metod Špaček, 51, married in Austria in 2020, but six years on, their marital status at home remains unrecognised.
There is no same-sex marriage in Slovakia, a socially conservative, predominantly Catholic country; neither is there any form of civil partnership.
But Novotný and Špaček, who are both lawyers and former diplomats, are not asking for that. They want the Slovakian authorities to recognise a marriage that was concluded legally in another EU country – something the bloc’s top court has said is mandatory for all EU members.
“I’ve said this publicly several times, and [LGBTQ+] activists in Slovakia have criticised me for it: Metod and I are not discriminated against here. We have a lovely life here in Bratislava, in Slovakia,” Novotný said. “So, we don’t actually need [recognition of marriage] for our day-to-day lives.”
For example, said Novotný, when Špaček was hospitalised during the Covid pandemic he was treated by a “lovely” doctor who recognised Novotný’s official relationship to her patient.
He added: “She put me down on the report as ‘husband’ and gave me all your [Špaček] medical information. The problem is: that was because she was nice, not because she had to do it. If someone wanted to make trouble for us, they could do it.
“That’s not how the rule of law should work.”
The couple argue they are on solid legal ground after a ruling by the EU’s highest court in November 2025 in response to a case brought by a Polish same-sex couple who had married in Berlin.
Jakub Cupriak-Trojan and Mateusz Trojan had challenged the Mazovia provincial governor’s refusal to recognise their German marriage. The court ruled that member states must recognise such marriages where couples had exercised their right to move and reside in another EU country, and created or strengthened family life there.
The European court of justice ruling does not require member states to allow same-sex weddings at home.
The Slovakian authorities explained why Novotný and Špaček’s request to register their Austrian marriage had been turned down in a letter signed by the interior minister, Matúš Šutaj Eštok.
“[The letter] says that since the constitutional definition of marriage [in Slovakia] is a bond between a man and a woman, they lack the legal basis for formally recognising the marriage certificate. That’s essentially it,” said Špaček, who served as chief of staff to the country’s liberal former president Zuzana Čaputová.
Across town, in the house his grandparents built on a hill overlooking the Danube, Marián Žáry Kukelka, 44, recalled his wedding to his partner, Ondrej, in 2023. The couple married in Hainburg an der Donau, an Austrian town visible from their terrace.
Žáry Kukelka, a radio presenter for the public broadcaster STVR, is also suing Slovakian authorities. He uses his full married name on air (Žáry is Ondrej’s surname) and is supported by his colleagues. But his official documents refer to him as Marián Kukelka. He said: “It’s a court case for love. I don’t need that surname to live my life, but for me it’s a kind of tribute to my partner, that I can carry his surname too.”.
Žáry Kukelka lives behind Bratislava Castle, not far from Zámocká street – the scene of the homophobic attack in 2022 where two people were shot dead outside the LGBTQ+ bar Tepláreň.
The anti-LGBTQ+ rhetoric of many Slovakian politicians, especially in the government, was contributing to an atmosphere of increasing hostility, he said.
Last year, Fico’s government backed constitutional changes recognising only two sexes and tightening adoption restrictions. On Monday, the fourth anniversary of the deadly attack on Tepláreň, the prime minister attacked opposition MP Lucia Plaváková for marrying her female partner abroad, calling it a “flagrant provocation” and accusing her of violating Slovakia’s constitution.
Her party, the liberal opposition Progressive Slovakia, rejected the accusation, saying she had broken neither the law nor the constitution.
Žáry Kukelka told the Guardian that he himself had experienced little in the way of abuse as a gay man, although he admitted he thought carefully before using the words “my husband”, depending on whom he was talking to.
“Two weeks ago, we were in Switzerland, and there we held hands in public for the first time in a long time,” he said. “We felt it was different there.”
Slovakia’s interior ministry said it was bound by the country’s existing constitutional and legal framework, regardless of whether a marriage was valid abroad.
It acknowledged the primacy of EU law but argued that recognition for freedom of movement purposes did not require registration as a marriage. Its administrative work “cannot replace decisions by the legislature or the constitutional legislature,” the ministry told the Guardian.

Apple AirPods 5 review: the best open-fit earbuds yet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:00:15 UTC
15:00:15 KST

Apple’s latest AirPods set a new standard for open-fit buds with upgraded noise cancelling that now rivals many plugged-in designs of the same price.
The AirPods 5 have the same design the popular AirPods 4 offering an option for those that do not like silicone ear tips used by most noise cancelling earbuds. They come in two versions, with or without a wireless charging case and swipe controls, costing from £119 (€149/$129/A$219) – £10 cheaper than the launch price of their predecessors.
The earbuds and case are almost indistinguishable from the AirPods 4, which makes the case very small and easy to pocket, fitting in the watch pocket of a pair of jeans.
The buds are some of the most comfortable open-fit designs available and stayed put when commuting, running for the train and generally going about the day. But for those that didn’t get on with the previous design of the AirPods, these are unlikely to change that, and they have no stability wings or similar to keep them in place for vigorous exercise.
The stalk has a pressure-sensitive panel you squeeze once, twice or thrice for playback controls. A squeeze and hold changes the noise cancelling mode or activates Siri. On the more expensive versions with a wireless charging case, the panel is also touch-sensitive for swipe volume controls – the same system used in the AirPods Pro to great effect.
Specifications
- Connectivity: Bluetooth 5.3, SBC, AAC, H2 chip
- Battery life: four or five hours with ANC (22 hours with case)
- Water resistance: IP57 (up to 1 metre for 30 minutes)
- Earbud dimensions: 30.2 x 18.3 x 18.1mm
- Earbud weight: 4.3g each
- Charging case dimensions: 46.2 x 50.1 x 21.2mm
- Charging case weight: 32.3g/34.7g
- Case charging: USB-C or wireless (Qi or Watch)
Up to five hours of battery life
The cheapest AirPods 5 have up to four hours playback with noise cancelling and a case that can charge them four times for a total of 20 hours playback.
The AirPods 5 with wireless charging case have longer battery life lasting slightly more than five hours of playback with noise cancelling with a total of 22 hours playback using charges in the case. That’s long enough for a week of commuting, but far behind the best in the business. A compromise for the design and super-compact case.
Upgraded sound and noise cancelling
The new AirPods have noticeably improved noise cancelling and sound. They produce fairly detailed sound with good separation of tones and can handle complex and overlapping tracks very well. But it is the additional bass that helps them produce a fuller, more rounded sound that wipes the floor with most other open-fit rivals and compares well to many decent earbuds with silicone tips. They may not satisfy audiophiles but they are a great listen.
The noise cancelling is equally effective, managing to quiet busy roads, the drone of engines or fans, and dampen background chatter. It struggles with higher tones, such as loud keyboard clicks or the screeches from train wheels, but does as good a job as many similarly-priced noise cancelling earbuds with silicone tips and is miles ahead of the open-fit competition.
They suffer a little from wind noise and can’t rival the sound dampening of the best earbuds with tips from Sony, Bose or the AirPods Pro 3, but still do a solid job.
The transparency mode is first class, sounding almost exactly like not wearing them at all, which is great for awareness on the street. Call quality is equally good coming through loud and clear with only a hint of sudden background noise when passing something particularly loud.
The AirPods 5 support Apple’s various smart features with an iPhone, such as direct access to the new Siri, live translation, automatic volume adjustment, spatial audio, audio sharing, the ability to pause music when falling asleep and optimised battery charging to increase its longevity.
Sustainability
Batteries in earbuds typically maintain at least 80% of their original capacity for 500 charge cycles. Apple offers a battery service for £49 per earbud or case and replacements cost from £69. The specialists iFixit awarded the earbuds two out of 10 for repairability. The AirPods 5 are made with 40% recycled material, which the company breaks down in its environmental impact report. The company offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.
Price
The AirPods 5 cost £119 (€149/$129/A$219) or £139 (€169/$149/A$249) with a wireless charging case and touch controls.
For comparison, the AirPods Pro 3 cost £219, the AirPods Max 2 cost £499, the Google Pixel Buds 2a cost £129 and the Shokz OpenFit Air 2 cost £129.
Verdict
The AirPods 5 take the comfortable open-fit design of their predecessors and upgrade the sound and noise cancelling to rival many plugged-in earbuds with silicone tips, which is quite a feat.
They provide a good amount of bass for a full, detailed sound that’s a great general listen and a step above most open-fit rivals. The noise cancelling is capable of dampening unwanted sound to tolerable levels, comparing well with better than average silicone-equipped earbuds. It can’t match the best plugged-in earbuds, but it is certainly good enough. Apple’s transparency mode and call quality are top-notch, and it’s hard to fault the earbuds for daily use with a compact design that’s easy to pocket.
The battery life is a little short, and while they work with any Bluetooth device, I wouldn’t recommend them to people who don’t have at least one iPhone, iPad or Mac.
There are few great open-fit earbuds, but if you didn’t get on with other AirPods, these won’t tip the balance. The extra money for swipe volume controls and longer battery life is worth it, if you’re considering them.
The fifth-generation earbuds are marginally more repairable than their predecessors, which opens up the possibility of replacing the batteries down the line, but otherwise they are just as disposable as most other earbuds.
 Pros: comfortable open fit, good sound and noise cancelling, great case, great playback and volume controls, great connectivity, special features with Apple devices including spatial audio, great call quality.
Cons: battery life could be better, little passive noise isolation, lack of features when connected to non-Apple devices, no Bluetooth multipoint or higher quality audio format support, difficult to repair.

China is seeking public comments on draft rules that would streamline procedures for “low-risk” exports of aviation components such as engines and inertial navigation systems to give the industry a competitive boost.

China-US astronomy team may have found possible relic of a recent ‘gold factory’
Mystery glow seen in the Milky Way could be the result of a violent collision between two orbiting neutron stars, according to scientists
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Ling Xinin Ohio
A mysterious glow of high-energy light in our Milky Way galaxy could be the remains of an extremely rare cosmic “gold factory”, according to a new study by Chinese and US researchers.
The collision of two orbiting neutron stars – dead stars so dense that a teaspoon of their matter would weigh a billion tonnes – may have shone as brightly as Jupiter in the sky, they wrote in a paper posted last week on the preprint server arXiv, which has yet to be peer-reviewed.
The violent smash spewed out atoms and a flood of neutrons, which the atoms soaked up to form some of the universe’s heaviest elements, such as gold, platinum and uranium, while the wreckage collapsed into a black hole.
The blast probably happened less than 1,000 years ago, as the glowing cloud it left behind is still small and bright, signs of a young remnant, wrote the researchers from the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Beijing and the University of Notre Dame in Indiana.

US theme park operator Six Flags shuts nine roller coasters after man dies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
05:59:54 UTC
14:59:54 KST

Police are investigating after TV footage showed riders being evacuated from the 60-metre high Goliath ride.
One person has died and several others were injured in an incident on a roller coaster at a Six Flags park in the US state of Georgia, prompting the company to temporarily shut nine similar rides at six of its parks on Monday.
A Six Flags spokesperson said the attractions, which resemble the coaster involved at Six Flags Over Georgia, were closed “out of an abundance of caution.”
The park lies about 24 kilometres (15 miles) northwest of Atlanta. Officials have not said how the person died, how the others were hurt or what condition they are in. Detectives from the Cobb County Police Department’s major crimes unit are investigating.
The spokesperson said the park and local authorities had responded immediately, and that Six Flags was cooperating fully with the investigation.
“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” the spokesperson said, adding that the company was supporting the guests and staff affected.
Neither the authorities nor Six Flags named the ride, but local television stations broadcast footage of passengers being evacuated from the Goliath coaster.
According to the park’s website, Goliath opened in 2006 and reaches speeds of 70 mph (about 113 kph) and heights of 200 feet (61 metres). Over roughly three and a half minutes, riders “navigate through razor-sharp turns and soar over colossal hills,” the website says.
“I cannot imagine the horror the patrons and employees witnessed today, and my heart aches for the family who lost a loved one,” said Lisa Cupid, chairwoman of the Cobb County Board of Commissioners. She said the victim’s next of kin had been informed.
Cupid described the park as a major part of the county’s tourism industry, drawing visitors from across the south east of the US.
“We are all grappling with how something so devastating could happen at a place that has given generations of families such happy memories,” she said.
The death is at least the seventh at the Georgia park, according to the Doan Law Firm, which specialises in amusement park accidents. They include a 2006 case in which a man had a suspected heart attack on Goliath.

Middle East and Central Asia’s economy to shrink in 2026 amid war, IMF says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
05:59:48 UTC
14:59:48 KST

Middle East and Central Asia’s economy to shrink in 2026 amid war, IMF says
Iraq, Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar face double-digit declines in GDP amid the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran.
The economy of the Middle East and Central Asia is set to shrink in 2026 amid the fallout of the US-Israel war on Iran, with countries such as Kuwait and Qatar facing double-digit contractions, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
The region’s gross domestic product (GDP) is forecast to contract by 0.3 percent this year, a sharp downgrade from the 1.9 percent expansion projected in April, the IMF said in its latest economic outlook on Tuesday.
The IMF cited the prolonged disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a conduit for one-fifth of global oil supplies in peacetime, for the downgraded outlook.
Kuwait, Iraq and Qatar are forecast to have the most severe economic contractions, with their GDPs expected to shrink by 16.7 percent, 16 percent and 15.6 percent, respectively.
Bahrain’s GDP is forecast to contract by 11.3 percent, while Iran’s economy is projected to shrink by 7.6 percent.
Saudi Arabia, which has partially offset the hit to its energy sector by boosting oil exports through the East-West pipeline, is projected to record negative growth of 3.3 percent.
Kyrgyzstan is expected to have the strongest growth in the region, with GDP forecast to expand 9 percent.
The Middle East and Central Asia is the only region that is expected to experience negative growth in 2026.
Emerging and developing Asia’s GDP is forecast to grow 5.1 percent, while the economies of Sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America and the Caribbean are projected to expand 4.5 percent and 2.3 percent, respectively.
The United States and China, the world’s two largest economies, are forecast to register growth of 2.3 percent and 4.5 percent, respectively, while the eurozone’s GDP is estimated to grow 1.1 percent.
The IMF said it expected global GDP to grow 3.1 percent, up from 3 percent in its previous outlook.
The Washington, DC-based institution said while economic activity had proved resilient this year, the global economy faced multiple risks.
“Further escalation in conflicts, a reassessment of expectations surrounding artificial intelligence (AI), renewed trade tensions, and fiscal vulnerabilities could weaken growth,” it said.
“On the upside, stronger momentum in AI investment and productivity gains from AI or a sustained easing of geopolitical and trade tensions could strengthen growth.”

Australian emergency departments unprepared for aging population: report
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:57:20 CST
14:57:20 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Emergency departments at Australia's hospitals are unprepared for the country's aging population, a report has warned.
The report released on Tuesday from the Australasian College for Emergency Medicine (ACEM) said that almost 9 million people sought care at emergency departments nationwide in 2023-24, a quarter of whom were aged 65 and over.
Within that age group, it said more than half arrived at hospital by ambulance, almost 70 percent needed urgent care and 50 percent were admitted to a hospital bed compared to less than one quarter of younger patients.
It said that 53,510 older patients spent longer than 24 hours in emergency departments awaiting a hospital bed in 2023-24, up 254 percent from 15,084 who did so in 2018-19, while only 54 percent of older patients who needed admission left the emergency department within the eight-hour target.
A landmark intergenerational report released by the federal Treasury in September projected that the proportion of the Australian population aged 65 and over would grow from 17.8 percent currently to 24.8 percent by 2066.
The ACEM report projected that emergency department arrivals for people aged 85 and over will increase by 411 percent by 2050.
"Our health system and its workforce are just not equipped for this demographic change," ACEM President Peter Allely said in a media release.
"Unless these serious issues are addressed as a matter of urgency, emergency care will come too late for many Australians."
The report made several recommendations to federal, state and territory governments on how to address the issue, including improving integration between hospitals and aged care, increased funding and a rapid expansion of the residential aged care sector. ■

China unveils railway sci-tech innovation plan for 2026-2030
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:57:00 CST
14:57:00 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- China, which operates the world's largest high-speed rail network, has issued a railway science and technology innovation plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030).
This innovation plan outlines key tasks in basic research and frontier technologies, engineering construction, technical equipment, transport services, digital and intelligent railways, safety, and green and low-carbon development.
The plan, recently released by the National Railway Administration (NRA), proposes to basically establish, by 2030, a science and technology innovation system that leads railway modernization.
During the 2026-2030 period, China plans to build about 30 new railway industry science and technology innovation bases under the NRA, achieve breakthroughs in no fewer than 100 key core technologies, and produce no less than 500 major scientific and technological achievements.
It will also plan no fewer than 20 typical application scenarios or demonstration projects in areas such as the 400 km/h high-speed train operating system.
Regarding technical equipment, the plan proposes to steadily and orderly advance research on 600 km/h high-speed maglev technology as well as testing and verification of key technologies for domestic production.
In the case of transport services, the plan will promote upgrading the official 12306 ticketing platform from a single ticket-buying service to whole-journey intelligent services, providing one-stop intermodal travel solutions that precisely match passengers' "personalized, differentiated and diversified" needs.
China will accelerate the building of large models, datasets and computing power infrastructure in the railway industry, and will establish a minimum of 20 high-quality industry datasets and more than 20 typical artificial intelligence application scenarios, according to the plan.
Concerning green and low-carbon development, the plan calls for promoting demonstration operation of low-emission and low-fuel-consumption diesel locomotives as well as locomotives and rolling stock with multi-source power such as battery and hydrogen, establishing and improving a carbon management system, and helping total railway carbon emissions peak by 2030. ■

Traffic data points to patchy economic recovery in New Zealand
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:56:51 CST
14:56:51 KST

WELLINGTON, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Traffic volumes in New Zealand rebounded in September, but the recovery remained uneven as households faced higher fuel prices and rising interest rates, economic indices showed on Tuesday.
The Light Traffic Index, which tracks cars, vans and motorbikes and was released by ANZ, one of New Zealand's major commercial banks, rose 1.1 percent in September but remained 1.1 percent lower than a year earlier.
ANZ said the index could provide an early indication of consumer spending and economic demand, typically leading economic momentum by up to six months, with variations reflecting discretionary spending on outings and the movements of couriers and tradespeople.
Light traffic has been noticeably lower in recent months, likely reflecting people choosing to drive less due to higher fuel prices, according to an ANZ release.
Heavy traffic, mainly trucks and buses, increased 2.2 percent in September, reversing an equivalent decline in August and leaving the index 0.7 percent higher than a year earlier, the release said.
The bank's Heavy Traffic Index was commonly used to gauge production and wider economic activity because it captured freight movements linked to both wholesale and retail trade and exports, Radio New Zealand (RNZ) reported, citing the release.
The Heavy Traffic Index rebounded in September, supporting the bank's view that late-winter storms may have dampened activity in August, it said.
ANZ senior economist Matthew Galt said the figures showed an uneven economic picture, with export sectors such as agriculture performing strongly while households remained under pressure from higher fuel prices and rising interest rates, RNZ reported.
Businesses, however, were proving reasonably optimistic despite a recent surge in fuel prices, Galt said, adding the recovery was being supported by a low exchange rate and high export prices, while interest rates remained well below their peak two or three years earlier. ■

Column: Advancing global ocean governance to protect our blue planet
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:56:47 CST
14:56:47 KST

by Zheng Zongwen
After nearly two decades of discussions, including five years of negotiations, the High Seas Treaty, officially known as the Agreement under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ Agreement), entered into force in January this year. The agreement marks a new chapter in global ocean governance and the rule of law in international maritime affairs.
China, which participated in the full course of the BBNJ Agreement negotiations and signed it when it was first opened for signature, has ratified the agreement. Attaching great importance to the conservation and sustainable use of marine resources, China has been deeply engaged in global ocean governance, which dovetails with the objectives of the agreement.
STRONG CANDIDATE TO HOST SECRETARIAT
With a view to fulfilling the purpose and objectives of the agreement, China has submitted its bid to host the BBNJ Secretariat in Xiamen. Known as the "Garden on the Sea," Xiamen is a beautiful and livable city on the southeast coast of China and has been a gateway to international trade and cultural exchange for centuries.
Since 2005, Xiamen has hosted 20 sessions of the World Ocean Week, aiming to promote high-quality ocean development.
Boasting a rapidly growing blue economy and an enabling environment for innovation with more than 30 marine R&D platforms and over 5,000 researchers, Xiamen possesses robust strengths and great potential to advance global ocean governance.
It looks forward to providing the best working environment for the Secretariat and helping it better fulfill its founding missions.
CHAMPION OF MARINE BIODIVERSITY CONSERVATION
China has extensive coastal waters that are home to over 28,000 marine species, ranking among the world's richest in marine biodiversity.
In recent years, guided by the philosophy of harmonious coexistence between humanity and nature, China has worked tirelessly to develop marine resources through science-based marine spatial planning and better preservation of the ocean's regenerative capacity.
It has designated ecological red lines covering a coastal and marine area of 150,000 square km and established 353 marine protected areas. The area of mangrove forests, known as the cradle of marine life, grew to 31,700 hectares as of last year, making China one of the few countries with a net increase in mangrove coverage.
To maintain population stability, China has rolled out special action plans for flagship species, rescuing and conserving endangered marine wildlife such as the Chinese white dolphin and spotted seals.
More importantly, the outline of China's 15th Five-Year Plan(2026-2030) sets out comprehensive arrangements for strengthening marine development, utilization and conservation, which underpins China's commitment to ocean governance and marine biodiversity protection.
IMPORTANT CONTRIBUTOR TO GLOBAL BIODIVERSITY GOVERNANCE
Following the principle of extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits, China has stepped up policy coordination and pragmatic cooperation with other countries in advancing the building of a community of all life on Earth.
During its presidency of the 15th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity from 2021 to 2024, China championed the Kunming Declaration and facilitated the adoption of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. China also established the Kunming Biodiversity Fund, taking the lead by investing 1.5 billion yuan (224 million U.S. dollars), which has supported around 40 developing countries.
Furthermore, China has been the largest contributor to the core budget of the Convention and its protocols, as well as the largest developing country contributor to the Global Environment Facility since 2019.
To further strengthen global ocean governance, China has implemented voluntary fishing bans on the high seas, supported the establishment of Antarctic marine protected areas and engaged in developing green shipping corridors.
ACTIVE PROMOTER OF BLUE PARTNERSHIPS
As a frontrunner in implementing the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, China has actively promoted the building of equal, pragmatic and mutually beneficial blue partnerships.
It has established marine cooperation with over 90 countries and international organizations and jointly built more than 40 cooperative institutions, such as marine research centers. The Thematic Forum on Maritime Cooperation of the third Belt and Road Forum for International Cooperation held in 2023 gathered more than 200 officials and experts to discuss sustainable marine development.
In addition, China has launched the marine scholarship for foreign students and organized training courses on marine science, technology and management, benefiting tens of thousands of professionals from over 50 developing countries. Through these concrete efforts, China has contributed valuable insights and viable solutions to improving global ocean governance.
The full implementation of the BBNJ Agreement bears on the well-being of all humanity. As a responsible major country, China is ready to work with all parties to ensure the agreement delivers on the ground, and to make greater contributions to global ocean governance and the international maritime order.
Editor's note: Zheng Zongwen is a commentator on international affairs.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.

According to a Bertelsmann Foundation poll, 47% of EU citizens support Ukraine joining the European Union in the coming years, while 53% oppose its accession within that timeframe.
Source: European Pravda, citing ntv
Details: The results of the poll indicate that 83% of Ukrainians want their country to join the EU in the coming years, but only 47% of EU citizens share that view. The majority – 53% – are opposed to this.
Germany provides Ukraine with substantial military and financial support. However, among the EU's ten largest member states, German citizens are particularly sceptical about Ukraine joining the EU quickly, with only 41% supporting the idea. Only Romania has a lower figure, at 40%.
In Sweden, support for Ukraine's fast-track EU accession is the highest among the major EU member states, at 69%.
At the beginning of the full-scale invasion in 2022, 60% of people in Germany still supported Ukraine joining the EU quickly. The foundation has repeated this poll regularly, and support has since fallen both in Germany and across the EU as a whole.
In June, the foundation conducted a representative survey of 16,795 people across all EU member states using its Eupinions public opinion research tool.
Background:
- On 12 October, all EU member states agreed to open accession negotiating clusters 2 and 3 for Ukraine.
- On 12 October, the Ukrainian parliament approved amendments to the law on education. The changes were needed to secure Hungary's agreement to the opening of clusters 2 and 3 in Ukraine's EU accession negotiations. These are the Internal Market and Competitiveness and Inclusive Growth clusters.

The More Putin Escalates Attacks on Europe, the more Europe Should Support Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
05:46:00 UTC
14:46:00 KST

Vladimir Putin is escalating both his full-scale war against Ukraine and his shadow war against the rest of Europe. His main purpose in the shadow one is to break European support for Ukraine so he can subjugate that country, something he regards as existential for Russia’s future and his own.
While we in the rest of Europe must prepare as best we can to defend ourselves against every kind of hybrid attack, the central thrust of our response should be to redouble our support for Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukraine is his main target. It’s there, and only there, not in a contest of a thousand hybrid pinpricks, that Putin’s Russia can in a meaningful sense be defeated and deterred.
In a powerful new book, Warum Russland nicht aufhören wird (Why Russia Won’t Stop), the German historian Martin Schulze Wessel shows how Putin’s policy fits into a much older Russian tradition of territorial expansionism and striving for hegemony, combined with a religiously infused imperial ideology.
He reminds us that in 2016 Putin said, “Russia’s frontier ends nowhere” and in 2025, “wherever the boot of a Russian soldier steps, that is ours”.
West Europeans, fondly imagining that we have consigned such brute territorial imperialism to the dustbin of history, tend to think there must be some other explanation (e.g. something we did “wrong”, like the eastward expansion of Nato). Finns, Estonians and Poles know better. Despite Russia’s weaknesses, the author concludes, it is “the most dangerous country in the world”. Some in Asia might question that large claim, but certainly Russia is the most dangerous country for Europe.
Merz Calls on Russia to Accept Energy Ceasefire Following Talks With Zelensky
Schulze Wessel makes another simple but very pertinent point: Russia’s expansion was always facilitated by cooperation with other great powers and arrested when it faced equal and opposing powers. Since Donald Trump’s return to the White House last year, the United States has ceased to be the latter and has at times looked like the former.
So now it’s Europe that is shouldering the burden of being the equal and opposing power. Europe (including the UK) has now given more aid to Ukraine than the US. Its combined economies are 10 times larger than Russia’s; Germany’s economy alone is twice the size.
And it’s Germany that’s now central to this European effort. Cumulatively, since the beginning of the full-scale war in 2022, Germany has been the biggest individual country donor apart from the US. According to the Kiel Institute’s Ukraine support tracker, it has given twice as much as Britain or France.
As people in Kyiv and Odesa are daily pounded by Putin’s ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, it’s worth looking at the Kiel tracker’s figures for air defense systems. Germany has so far donated 19 of them, including five of the vital US-built Patriot air defense batteries – two more than the US itself has given.
In the first year of this war, I argued that Germany “has a unique historical responsibility to help defend a free and sovereign Ukraine”. At that time, I felt strongly that Germany was not yet doing what it should. Now, in the fifth year of a conflict that has already lasted longer than the first world war and shows no sign of ending, I can say without hesitation that it is.
This is not just a matter of the numerical scale of its support for Ukraine and its own increased defense spending, which, on the latest projections from the German finance ministry, will reach €154bn (£130bn) in 2028 (Roughly the same as Russia’s total estimated military expenditure for this year).
It’s also a matter of political will. Chancellor Friedrich Merz has shown that will, and courage, by taking the train from Germany to Ukraine on the evening of Oct. 3, the 36th anniversary of German unification, with a strong delegation including defense industry leaders.
The Russian bombardment of civilian targets in central Kyiv, including Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences and bridges across the Dnipro River, did not stop even though – or perhaps exactly because – Moscow knew the German leader would be there.
For a historian, there’s something very familiar here. Oh no, it’s Germany and Russia again! Yet each time is different. Historically, Germany is one of the powers that has done most to facilitate Russian expansion (just think of the 1939 Hitler-Stalin pact) but also most to threaten it.
In the first world war, and even at the margins in the second, some Ukrainian nationalists saw in a conflict between Germany and Russia a chance for their independence. Instead, they got imperial Germany’s colonialism (and then German defeat) in the first case and Hitler’s genocidal fascism (and then German defeat) in the second.
Another kind of German-Russian relationship. Has the former German Chancellor no shame? (Answer: no.) Gerhard Schröder and Vladimir Putin (from an official Kremlin social media post, 8 October)
Now, at last, Germany is genuinely engaged, at some cost and risk to itself, for the sovereignty of Ukraine. To anyone who knows this tangled history, there is something not just redemptive, but frankly inspiring in this sight: a democratic Germany playing a leading role in supporting an independent Ukraine’s bid to assume its proper place in a wider European community of free countries.
But for how long? And with how much support elsewhere in Europe? Precisely because Putin sees Germany’s centrality, it’s one of the main targets of his hybrid war, from explosive-laden drones at Leipzig airport that the German government has firmly attributed to Russia and assassination threats against defense industry bosses, all the way to covert political interference and disinformation.
While Ukraine faces its most difficult winter yet, three closely connected things will be put to the test: Germany’s will to stay committed on the right side of history; the capacity of democracies to sustain the fight against a dictatorship (a perennial concern); and Europe’s ability to remain united in this cause.
A sceptic can point to many grounds for pessimism. Merz is unpopular at home. Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), the party currently making the running in German politics, would abandon Ukraine to Russia. In France, the National Rally’s presidential candidate, Marine Le Pen, says her country can’t afford to go on giving so much to Ukraine.
Solidarity with Ukraine is also crumbling on the right in Poland, with two smaller parties sounding frankly anti-Ukrainian. In one Italian opinion poll last month, more than half those asked were opposed to continued weapons deliveries to Kyiv.
In Brussels recently, I found a large audience seemingly stalwart in support of Ukraine – until, right at the end, our discussion turned to the issue of using the Russian frozen assets held in Belgium. Ah now, that’s a different matter …
Yet with the terrible damage being inflicted on the Ukrainian economy, including its grain exports via the Black Sea, experts estimate that as much as €100bn of additional support for Kyiv may be needed in 2027 alone – and hard-pressed European taxpayers are in no mood to cough that up.
Putin believes that decadent European democracies will crumble before the iron determination of an imperialist strongman. Our job is to prove him wrong.
This op-ed, reprinted from the author’s blog History of the Present, first appeared in the Guardian. See the original here.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

Estonia to sound nationwide sirens in emergency alert test Wednesday
A nationwide EE-ALARM public warning test is to take place Wednesday, with sirens sounding between 3 p.m. and 3:10 p.m.
An SMS reminder will go out around midday. No action is needed during the test; in a real emergency residents should seek shelter.
The test, on Wednesday, October 14, will sound public sirens across the country and send notifications through the Eesti app and the "Ole valmis!" mobile application, as well as a ticker message on ERR's channels.
On 14 October, Estonia will conduct its third nationwide EE-ALARM public warning test of the year. An SMS reminder will be sent around midday. Between 15:00–15:10, sirens will sound, with alerts via the Eesti and Ole Valmis! apps and ERR channels. ⚠️ No action is needed during the test. In a real emergency, seek shelter!
— Estonian Defence Forces | Kaitsevägi (@Kaitsevagi) October 12, 2026
No notification will be sent sent when the test ends. The aim is to check the system's reliability, verify repairs and updates, and identify any shortfalls.
The Rescue Board asks residents to think in advance about where they would shelter at home, at work or at school. A recent survey found over two-thirds of Estonian residents would look for the safest place in their home, usually the basement, if told to shelter, but only about a quarter believe they already have such a feature in their home.
The test follows an accidental siren activation in Muuga on October 6 during routine maintenance work, ERR's Russian-language portal reported.
Wednesday's event the last of three nationwide tests in 2026. The others took place in March and June. Next year's tests are scheduled for February, June and October 2027.
More detailed information is here, and is also available from the kriis.ee site here and the Rescue Board here, while the Ole Valmis/Be Prepared app can be downloded here or from Google Play and Apple app stores.

South Korean President Lee Jae-myung rejected what he called “submissive” diplomacy, stressing that national interests must take precedence even as his country maintains its crucial alliance with the US.

South Korean intelligence officials have insisted that broader security cooperation remains intact.

Despite long history with Netanyahu, Trump hedges as Israel vote nears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
05:40:10 UTC
14:40:10 KST

Despite long history with Netanyahu, Trump hedges as Israel vote nears
US president has not endorsed Israeli prime minister ahead of October 27 election amid shifting public sentiment.
Washington, DC, United States – Since first entering the White House in 2017, US President Donald Trump has delivered on a right-wing Israeli wish list and pursued a foreign policy that has helped buoy Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s political fortunes.
The Israeli leader has, in turn, portrayed himself as the best steward of Israel’s most significant foreign relationship, weathering a handful of public criticisms and leaked discontents from Trump that have yielded little concrete policy change.
But despite the pair’s long history, Trump has so far taken a decidedly ho-hum approach to the October 27 Israeli election. The vote sees Netanyahu’s Likud party and the far-right coalition it leads under increasing threat from Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot and an opposition bloc he seeks to build.
It is an – at least public – ambivalence likely fuelled by shifting political winds in both the US and Israel, as well as the evolving relationship between Trump and Netanyahu, according to Yousef Munayyer, head of the Palestine/Israel programme at the Arab Center Washington DC.
“He seems to be keeping greater distance from it than you would think,” Munayyer told Al Jazeera, “given Trump’s past endorsements of right-wing allies, given the history of the Trump-Netanyahu relationship, and just how close Trump and Netanyahu have been”.
The US president thrice dodged a direct endorsement of Netanyahu in a recent Time magazine interview, even as he defended the Israeli prime minister’s leadership ahead of the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on southern Israel.
On Eisenkot, he conceded, “I don’t hear bad things.”
Shifting support?
To be sure, Trump’s actions towards Israel – and Netanyahu in particular – have often spoken far louder than his words.
During his first term from 2017 to 2021, Trump moved the US embassy to Jerusalem, recognised Israel’s annexation of the Golan Heights, withdrew from the 2015 Iran nuclear deal and spearheaded a series of normalisation agreements with Arab countries that sought to circumvent the Israel-Palestine issue.
During his second term that started in January 2025, he continued to surge even the most destructive US weapons to Israel amid its genocide in Gaza, escalated a crackdown on the International Criminal Court (ICC) and, as a crown jewel, entered a global economy-rattling war with Iran.
Trump has also called for Netanyahu to be pardoned in his ongoing corruption trial, while hosting the Israeli leader at least seven times since returning to the White House last year, far more than any other world leader.
Throughout their relationship, hints of discord over Netanyahu’s obstruction of Washington’s push for a more lasting peace in Gaza and an end to the war with Iran have never materialised into actual policy changes.
“It’s a relationship they’ve carefully choreographed for public consumption, and the few juicy bits that we’ve learned have been almost entirely of Trump’s choosing,” said Michael Omer-Man, Israel-Palestine director at the Washington, DC-based DAWN think tank, who did not rule out a sweeping US gesture to boost Netanyahu in the final stretch of the race.
“I don’t think that Trump’s abandoned Netanyahu,” he told Al Jazeera. “But he’s also a realist, and he’s seen a lot of his preferred candidates in various countries lose elections as well as win them.”
The stakes may just not be that high for Trump, Omer-Man assessed.
Eisenkot has promised a more moderate approach than Netanyahu’s, particularly when it comes to stemming rampant settler violence in the occupied West Bank. But those changes are largely aimed at boosting Israel’s standing among European governments and the global public, with little bearing on already permissive relations with the Trump administration.
“I don’t think we would see a whole lot of change vis-a-vis the US, because there doesn’t seem to be a whole lot of friction in the relationship,” he said.
“An Eisenkot government might stop taking over every single hilltop in the West Bank; they might allow more [aid] into Gaza,” he said, “but they’re not going to reverse any of the steps that have already been taken.”
‘Enemies versus friends’
Mairav Zonszein, a senior analyst on Israel at the International Crisis Group, also pointed to the shifting context surrounding Trump and Netanyahu’s relationship.
Trump’s reticence reflects, in part, a divide within the Trump administration over Netanyahu’s government, which reflects a wider Republican Party divide as US midterm elections approach.
“It’s probably a combination of the Iran war and the split in the Trump administration with people like [Vice President JD] Vance, who have come out very much against Netanyahu’s role in pushing for the US to strike Iran,” said Zonszein.
Public opinion polls have repeatedly suggested support for Israel remains high among Republicans, but has ticked down in recent years. Confidence in Netanyahu has also declined within the party.
At the same time, the perception of Trump’s influence has shifted in Israel, with Netanyahu’s critics seizing on the US role in constraining Israeli operations in Lebanon that threatened to derail a June memorandum of understanding that briefly paused the US-Israel war on Iran.
An Israeli Democracy Institute poll released in June found only 44 percent of Jewish Israelis thought Israel’s security was a top consideration for Trump, down from 61 percent in March, shortly after the US and Israel launched the war with Iran.
For his part, Netanyahu has avoided the billboards boasting his close relationship with Trump this election cycle, a departure from his approach in years past, Zonszein explained.
Instead, he has featured who he considers to be Israel’s top regional and international foes, including Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
Netanyahu, Zonszein said, is highlighting “his enemies versus his friends”.

Visa gets go-ahead to prepare for business in China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
05:39:37 UTC
14:39:37 KST

Visa, the global digital payments giant, said on Tuesday it has received approval from the People's Bank of China (PBOC) to begin formal preparations to establish a domestic bankcard clearing institution in the country.
The approval, announced by Visa in a statement, marks an important milestone towards the company serving China's domestic payments market.
“The approval of our application to prepare marks a significant step forward in Visa’s long-standing commitment to China," said chief executive Ryan McInerney.
"We greatly appreciate the important role of the leaders of the United States and China in pursuing a constructive and strategically stable relationship between the world’s largest economies,” he added.
Visa said China is one of the world's most advanced and dynamic digital payments markets and that it looks forward to bringing its innovation, security and reliability to Chinese consumers and businesses.
The PBOC said Visa must complete the preparatory work within one year before submitting a formal application to commence operations. 
The central bank and the National Financial Regulatory Administration will jointly review the application and, if approved, issue a bankcard clearing business licence.
Gary Ng, senior economist for Asia-Pacific at Natixis, said the move to introduce Visa showed China's willingness to further open up its financial sector. 
"Previously, we have seen some of the other competitors of Visa, such as Amex already has its own licence. MasterCard also can operate under joint venture. So, for Visa, it is really another step to put itself at the same level playing foot with the global competitors," he told RTHK. 
"But it really depends on whether Visa can compete with other cards at the same footing because there's obviously also UnionPay in the market. And let's not forget beyond cards, China is very reliant on other payment systems like Alipay and WeChat Pay.
"So it is a positive step, but it may not be fully big enough to change the overall picture."
Ng also said the move would facilitate cross-border transactions moving forward.

Armenia-China agreement to streamline freight transportation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
05:36:04 UTC
14:36:04 KST

Armenia-China agreement to streamline freight transportation
Armenia and China have signed an agreement on the facilitation of freight transportation, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing Armenpress.
The document was signed as part of a high-level meeting on the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route held in Beijing at the initiative of China’s Ministry of Transport.
According to Kristine Ghalechyan, a member of the Armenian delegation and Deputy Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure of the Republic of Armenia, freight carriers will now obtain the relevant permits through a specially introduced system, which will be recognized by both countries and will make it possible to carry out freight transportation under more streamlined procedures. The permits will be issued at two levels: for general freight transportation and for special cargo.
She also said that carriers will be exempt from a number of road taxes and fees. In particular, the agreement provides for transportation on a reciprocal basis that will be exempt from taxes or fees established for the use of public roads, as well as special charges and duties stipulated by the national legislation of the respective party.
“This exemption will not apply to taxes, duties and fees levied under the legislation of each party to compensate for damage caused on roads by vehicles. This is the exception,” Kristine Ghalechyan said.
She emphasized that the agreement would help enhance Armenia’s transit and logistics role, expand trade turnover between Armenia and China, and deepen strategic cooperation. The agreement also provides for the possibility of organizing both regular and non-regular international passenger bus transportation, along agreed routes and through agreed border crossing points.

Trump doesn't believe China and Russia are helping Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
05:33:35 UTC
14:33:35 KST

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that he does not believe China and Russia are helping Iran, arguing that both countries have too much to lose by doing so.
Responding to comments that Beijing and Moscow are assisting Tehran, Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform: “If they are, it’s at a very low level, but I don’t believe they are at all.”
“They have too much to lose, and we would know about it, and know about it very fast!” he added.
His remarks echo a July Truth Social post in which he said that Chinese President Xi Jinping had told him during their meeting in China in May that Beijing would not “under any circumstances” sell weapons to Iran, including through Chinese companies, and that Russian President Vladimir Putin had also told him that he would not sell weapons to Iran.
At the time, Trump warned that if they did get involved, “it would be very bad for them.”
In May, the Trump administration sanctioned several Chinese companies accused of supporting Iran’s military procurement network and providing satellite imagery that allegedly enabled Tehran to target US forces.
Beijing denies the allegations that Chinese entities aided Iran’s military.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28, prompting Tehran to respond with missile and drone attacks in the region and effectively close the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies.

Saudi capital's airport to remain shut this week as airlines cancel services
