Over 90 percent of people in China can reach their nearest medical service facilities within 15 minutes. Its basic medical insurance covers around 95 percent of the population. China's approach to promoting people's health epitomizes the country's people-centered development philosophy. Through consistent efforts in medical and healthcare system reforms, capacity-building, legislation and health promotion, among others, China has blazed a path of inclusive and balanced health development to ensure health for all -- a solemn promise of the CPC and the Chinese government.
Undoubtedly, China's all-round progress in its medical and health sector marks an important contribution to the sustainable development of humanity. As the world faces various health challenges, China has actively engaged in global health governance.
China has deepened cooperation with other countries in the medical and health sector, worked together to address cross-border public health risks, solidly advanced the building of a community of health for all, contributing China's strength to the global health cause. Traditional Chinese medicine has been introduced to more than 190 countries and regions. Since late 2012, China has dispatched medical aid teams to 59 countries and regions. During the COVID-19 pandemic, China supplied a multitude of anti-epidemic products to the world.
People's health is an important indicator of socialist modernization. With clear goals and intensified efforts, China will unswervingly follow the path of health development with Chinese characteristics and advance the Healthy China Initiative to secure greater progress in enhancing people's health. As a major country, China will also further participate in global health cooperation and governance to contribute more to the wellbeing of humanity. ■

Beijing forum eyes new paths for modern urban governance
China
Unknown Publisher

Georgios K. Giannaros, first deputy mayor of Athens, Greece, addresses the opening ceremony of the 2026 Beijing Forum on Swift Response to Public Complaints in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Xie Han)
BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese and international experts gathered in Beijing to explore new paths for modernizing urban governance, as the 2026 Beijing Forum on Swift Response to Public Complaints began Monday.
The two-day event, themed "Digital Intelligence Era and People's City," drew more than 3,200 participants from over 70 countries and regions.
In 2019, Beijing, home to over 20 million residents, launched a "swift response to public complaints" initiative aimed at addressing public concerns promptly and resolving everyday challenges efficiently. It has integrated more than 60 hotline services into the single hotline number 12345, which serves as the primary channel for residents to voice their concerns.
Official data shows the Chinese capital has handled about 200 million public appeals in just over seven years, with resolution and satisfaction rates both exceeding 97 percent.
Beijing's "swift response to public complaints" reform began with a single hotline and platform and has since evolved into an urban governance system integrating big data and AI, one that has tackled a range of pressing public concerns, Gao Xiang, president of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, said in his opening address.
"Digital empowerment of people-centered urban governance is the prevailing trend in urban governance worldwide," he said.
This year's forum unveiled a batch of research outcomes on urban governance, including theoretical studies of the reform itself, an evaluation of global city hotline services, and case studies of governance innovation worldwide.
It also rolled out two English-language publications on the reform -- the monograph "How Urban Governance Works: the Case of Swift Response to Public Complaints in Beijing," and a special issue with the "Journal of Comparative Policy Analysis: Research and Practice." Both signal a move from lessons learned to theoretical exposition, and from Chinese practice to international comparison.
"The experience of Beijing's citizen service system offered valuable lessons for Athens in advancing people-centered urban governance and building a city that listens to its citizens and responds to their concerns," said Georgios K. Giannaros, first deputy mayor of Athens, Greece.
Held every two years, this year's Beijing Forum on Swift Response to Public Complaints featured six parallel sub-forums, where participants noted that the reform has driven changes in mega-city governance, offering the world a window into China's approach to governance. ■

Feature: Beyond music, Chinese, U.S. youth build lasting friendships

by Xinhua writer Shi Chun
NEW YORK, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- At the conclusion of a concert in New York, young singers from China and the United States were embracing, exchanging farewells and posing for photos.
For them, Thursday evening's concert at the Chinese Consulate General was not just a musical performance, but a reunion of friends brought together by years of cultural exchange.
Under the theme "Youth, Dialogue, Future," the event was attended by more than 100 performers from Young People's Chorus of New York City, Guangdong Experimental High School Choir and Lang Lang International Music Foundation.
The concert presented a series of renowned vocal and instrumental works from both countries, including the Circle of Life, Bridge Over Troubled Water and As Wished.
Young performers captivated the audience with their spirited singing and energetic dance moves, drawing rounds of applause and cheers.
For 17-year-old Sylvie, a member of the New York chorus, the evening's most meaningful moments came from reconnecting with friends she had made in China.
Sylvie began learning Chinese six years ago. In 2024, she traveled to Guangzhou, Shenzhen and Zhuhai with her chorus, where she made Chinese friends.
"I'm so happy that we've met again. We've kept in touch on WeChat and talked in both Chinese and English," she told Xinhua.
Now Sylvie has added Beijing, Shanghai and Chengdu to her wish list for the next trip. "I really like China and wanna go back soon. It's definitely a different experience," she said.
The reunion reflected a relationship that has grown for more than two decades between the two choirs. Their story began with an international choral competition in Japan and has since expanded through online collaborations, student exchanges and reciprocal visits.
In autumn 2024, Francisco J. Nunez, founder and artistic director of Young People's Chorus of New York City, led the U.S. choral ensemble to China at the invitation of Guangdong Experimental High School Choir. This year, he welcomed the Chinese singers to New York.
"This is like ping-pong," Nunez said with a smile. "It's not a tour. It's a relationship."
"Each time in these steps, our relationship has grown stronger, with more singing, more families and more friendship," he said.
Quan Hanyan, chairman and principal of Guangdong Experimental High School Group, said continued cultural exchanges offered young people in both countries valuable opportunities to foster mutual understanding and a deeper bond.
"In a world with so much noise, these young people have chosen to listen to each other. That is how a bridge is built across the Pacific," Nunez said.
Chinese Consul General in New York Chen Li praised the sister choirs' longstanding partnership as an example of friendship between Chinese and U.S. youth.
He encouraged young people from both countries to learn from one another and grow together, and use their youthful voices to write a new chapter in China-U.S. friendship.
As the Chinese singers prepared to head home, Nunez offered once again his best wishes.
"Tomorrow, you'll get on an airplane," he told them. "But it's not goodbye. It's until we sing again." ■

Cambodian PM urges stronger action against rising climate threats
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:06:41 CST
13:06:41 KST

PHNOM PENH, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet has urged relevant authorities to treat disaster management as a core priority, calling for a significant strengthening of human and material resources to combat rising climate change risks.
In an official message marking National Disaster Management Day on Tuesday, which coincides with both the ASEAN Day for Disaster Management and the International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction, Hun Manet warned that the world faces increasingly complex and fast-evolving disaster risks driven by environmental, social, and economic factors.
"Climate change, rapid urbanization, and environmental degradation pose serious threats to sustainable social and economic development," he said.
Hun Manet said that Cambodia continues to face extreme weather conditions, including rising temperatures during the rainy season, erratic rainfall patterns, strong winds, lightning strikes, riverbank collapses, infectious diseases, and fires -- all of which threaten human lives and community property.
To mitigate these impacts, Hun Manet directed authorities at all levels to prioritize flood and drought management, emphasizing the need to upgrade local water infrastructure and closely monitor vulnerable households to build stronger climate resilience across the country.
Furthermore, the prime minister called on citizens to actively strengthen their own household resilience. He urged families to develop "safety and preparedness plans," which include assembling home emergency kits stocked with clean water, dry food, medicine, a radio, and vital documents.
He advised citizens to inspect and reinforce their homes against wind and lightning, while paying close attention to the safety of children, the elderly, people with disabilities, and pregnant women in times of emergency.
Hun Manet also advocated for increased public investment in housing resilience for vulnerable families, saying that establishing robust social safety nets, providing adequate and safe shelter, and ensuring timely community access to risk information are critical steps to sustaining the nation's economic growth.
According to data from the National Committee for Disaster Management (NCDM), Cambodia has recently been dealing with severe weather impacts. Last month, heavy rainfall triggered widespread flooding across portions of 10 provinces, directly affecting nearly 60,000 families and forcing approximately 5,000 families to evacuate to designated safe areas.
The rising waters also inundated roughly 52,000 homes and damaged more than 72,000 hectares of rice paddies. ■

IMF upgrades 2026 global growth forecast but war and debt threaten outlook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
03:57:42 UTC
12:57:42 KST

IMF upgrades 2026 global growth forecast but war and debt threaten outlook
The IMF has raised its 2026 global growth forecast slightly to 3.1%, citing the resilience of advanced economies despite rising energy prices caused by the Iran war. But it warned that poorer countries that are not benefiting from the AI boom remain particularly vulnerable to energy shocks, economic uncertainty and mounting debt.
The International Monetary Fund on Tuesday forecast global growth in 2026 would slow less than previously expected because of advanced economies' "resilience" in the face of war-fuelled energy prices, but warned low-income countries remained vulnerable to the supply shock.
In its World Economic Outlook (WEO) released at the organisation's Annual Meetings in Bangkok, the IMF raised its 2026 global growth forecast by 0.1 percentage points to 3.1 percent, compared with 3.5 percent growth in 2025.
It warned that while many advanced economies have been buoyed by rising investment in artificial intelligence (AI) technology, poorer countries that are not benefiting from that boom face stark choices as they deal with high energy prices caused by the Iran war.
"The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is under strain, with risks tilted to the downside," Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF's chief economist, told journalists in Bangkok.
Watch moreCan AI play a role in reducing inequality?
With global debt-to-GDP ratios at sky-high levels, including in advanced economies, the IMF has called on governments to cut spending and manage borrowing – a difficult task for those in the developing world struggling with the Iran war shock.
"What we are advocating for is for policymakers to balance the near-term needs of inflation, and that involves food security, that involves energy security ... while also keeping in mind the medium-term stability," said Deniz Igan, chief of the IMF's World Economic Studies division.
'Bifurcated outlook'
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said at a panel discussion: "We have to recognise that the world that used to value only one thing, economic efficiency ... now is a world in which security considerations have to be factored in."
The United States' war on Iran, launched in February, has plunged the Middle East into violence and seen global energy prices skyrocket as a result of Tehran's retaliation.
Prices of refined petroleum products remain between 70 and 95 percent above pre-war levels, putting pressure on countries dependent on energy imports for economic activity.
On Monday night, blasts resounded across Saudi Arabia's capital as the war's impact widens into that country, with Iran-backed Yemeni Houthi forces hitting oil facilities, tankers and transport hubs.
Energy-importing countries not exposed to the AI boom remain the most vulnerable, creating what the IMF termed a "bifurcated outlook" in its WEO report.
The report detailed that the twin economic forces of the war in Iran and the AI technology boom had created a "fragmented" world economy.
"Headwinds from a prolonged war and persistent geopolitical tensions could revive inflationary pressures, strain fiscal and external positions, and hit energy-importing and low-income countries hardest," it said.
"At the same time, the current technology tailwind could stop abruptly if expectations about AI-related profits and productivity gains are reassessed, weakening investment and tightening financial conditions."
Responding to AFP, Tenreyro said AI had been a major factor driving the world economy, accounting for almost half of the increase in global trade from 2023 to 2025.
Contraction here, growth there
The IMF's split view of the world economy was evident in its specific projections.
The Middle East and Central Asia region – exposed directly to the Iran war – is expected to suffer a 0.3 percent contraction in 2026.
Saudi Arabia's is one of the worst affected, with its economy projected to shrink 3.3 percent – representing a 5.0 percentage point cut in the Fund's forecast.
The IMF said the region is expected to bounce back quickly once the war is over, but there remains high uncertainty as to when that will be.
Read moreHow is the EU responding to record fuel prices?
In advanced economies, growth fuelled by the AI boom and other factors remained strong.
The world's advanced economies were forecast to grow 2.1 percent in 2026, with those in the AI supply chain such as Taiwan and South Korea posting significantly higher figures.
Growth in China, the world's second-largest economy, was expected to slow, the IMF said, mainly because of weak domestic demand.
Global inflation remained set to accelerate to 4.7 percent in 2026, with effects spread across advanced and developing economies.
Call for action
Tenreyro warned that urgent action was required by all countries in the face of downside risks, and called on governments to only use temporary, targeted measures to help ease the burden on the public of high energy and other costs.
In lockstep, "monetary policy should remain firmly focused on price stability", she added, indicating that interest rate hikes to curb high inflation were appropriate.
Georgieva told audience members: "Macroeconomic and financial stability is your first line of defence. It is a source of security."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Trump insists energy ceasefire holds as Ukraine reports new Russian strikes
US president urges Zelenskyy, Putin to end ‘ridiculous war’ and insists the two nations have agreed to stop attacks on energy infrastructure.
United States President Donald Trump has insisted that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to stop striking each other’s energy infrastructure, as he called on both sides to end the “ridiculous” war.
Trump’s comments on Monday came even as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian forces had struck at least six Ukrainian energy facilities since the US president declared the truce on Sunday.
“Well, they agreed,” Trump told reporters, referring to Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin. “Because I said, ‘You agree’. That’s why they agreed, because I said they agree.”
When pressed about the Russian strikes, Trump said, “Well, I’d have to look at it and see, because there’s been violations on both sides.”
The US president called the war, which began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, a “disaster” and claimed, without offering evidence, that at least 32,000 people had been killed this month alone.
“All I know is that Zelenskyy and Putin have to get together and end that ridiculous war,” he said.
Kyiv blindsided
Trump had blindsided Kyiv and its European allies when he announced the purported energy ceasefire on Sunday. The announcement came two days after he temporarily eased US sanctions on Russian diesel, a move that drew outrage in Europe and Ukraine.
Zelenskyy said it reversed years of Western efforts to isolate Russia’s economy and would only embolden Putin.
Lawmakers from both major parties in the United States have also said the diesel decision appears to violate US law. Several Republicans have objected that it undercuts a law Trump himself signed to tighten restrictions on Moscow.
Zelenskyy said on Monday that Ukraine supported an energy ceasefire and had carried out no attacks on Russian refineries overnight. He said Kyiv was prepared to sign “guarantees to make sure they can be trusted”.
But he said it was “increasingly evident” that Moscow would not comply.
“Today alone, the Russians have attacked 6 energy facilities in Ukraine. 33 people were wounded across the country,” Zelenskyy wrote on social media. “This is what happens when Russia sees the prospect of higher revenues for its war machine.”
Russia, however, has rejected any pause in fighting, with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov promising to press ahead with the military campaign.
“I do not think he deserves a respite,” he said of Zelenskyy. “I don’t think we’ll be buying into assurances and promises again.” Russia, he added, would continue to pursue the goals of what it calls its “special military operation” in Ukraine.
US midterms
Trump, meanwhile, has portrayed Ukraine, rather than Russia, as the main obstacle to peace. He has said that Putin is more eager on a deal than Zelenskyy, and has called on Ukrainians to vote their president out of office – an unusually harsh turn in a relationship that has been strained since Trump returned to the White House in 2025.
Al Jazeera’s Alan Fisher, reporting from Washington, DC, said Trump has previously announced agreements between Russia and Ukraine that never materialised.
“He says he wants to protect industries in the US like farmers and ranchers, and to do that he needs the price to go down. But it seems that he thinks there’s a deal, but no one else is sure that there actually is one,” Fisher said.
The latest announcement, according to our correspondent, appeared to be driven by Trump’s desire to bring down diesel prices before the US midterm elections on November 3.
Most polls predict that Republicans will lose control of Congress as voters grow frustrated with rising prices, particularly for petrol.
An opinion survey published on October 1 by the Associated Press news agency and the University of Chicago suggested that 65 percent of US adults blame the White House for the high cost of living, especially Trump’s tariff policies and his new war against Iran.
Ukraine’s European allies, meanwhile, voiced scepticism about the energy ceasefire and approved the largest set of European Union sanctions since Russia’s 2022 invasion.
The bloc’s foreign ministers added some 1,569 people and businesses to the bloc’s sanctions list to maintain the pressure on Moscow.
“Russia will only negotiate seriously under pressure, which is why we are sticking to our sanctions against Russia,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in Berlin.

The 46,000 sq ft facility “will manufacture, repair and maintain key parts for virtually all new and existing submarines”.
The decision follows a memorandum Trump signed in August that called for Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to submit a plan to establish such a repair centre “to receive new and refurbish old components and parts as required by the submarine repair industrial base” within 90 days of the directive.
Trump announced this at an Oct 12 rally in Youngstown, Ohio, as he barnstorms the country to boost Republican candidates with roughly three weeks until the Nov 3 midterm elections.
The President has touted private investments and government-backed projects in a bid to win over voters who are giving his handling of the economy and the war in Iran poor marks.
The election is expected to hinge largely on high costs of living squeezing households.
While Trump has touted new projects in key states – many of which voted for him for president – voters appear more focused on pocketbook issues.
Stubborn inflation led the Federal Reserve in September to raise interest rates, and Trump has sought to lower energy costs that have soared because of the wars in Ukraine and Iran.
Mortgage rates above 7% have sent pending US home sales plummeting to a 12-year low.
Meanwhile, retail petrol – below US$3 before Trump and Israel launched a war against Iran earlier in 2026 – has now risen to more than US$4.35 this week.
Republicans face a tough path to retain control of Congress, and Ohio is a crucial battleground in that fight.
Trump’s rally follows one earlier in October near Dayton, Ohio.
While the President won the state in all three of his presidential campaigns, Republicans find themselves on the defensive across the map in this election cycle.
Republican Senator Jon Husted is trying to fend off a competitive challenge from former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown.
The RealClearPolitics average of polls had Brown with a roughly 3 percentage point edge on Oct 12.
The Senate Majority PAC – a top Democratic super political action committee – plans to spend US$7 million (S$9 million) in Ohio, redirecting resources from a North Carolina Senate race, where the party’s candidate is now the clear favourite to win and pick up a GOP-held seat.
Ohio also hosts a competitive gubernatorial race as Republican Vivek Ramaswamy – a one-time 2024 presidential rival-turned-ally of Trump’s – is in a tight race with Democrat Amy Acton to succeed incumbent GOP governor Mike DeWine.
The RealClearPolitics polling average earlier on Oct 12 showed Acton leading Ramaswamy by nearly 4 percentage points.
Even though the President is suffering from approval ratings at historic lows, he is banking on being able to reinvigorate and turn out enough of his base in reliably Republican states to blunt Democratic momentum and avoid a wave election that could sweep his political opponents into power. Lukewarm Liberal response to Josh Frydenberg's potential return
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
03:14:09 UTC
12:14:09 KST

Lukewarm Liberal response to Josh Frydenberg's potential return to politics
In short:
Federal Liberals have given a lukewarm response to news former treasurer Josh Frydenberg is considering a return to politics.
Mr Frydenberg lost his seat of Kooyong nearly five years ago to independent Monique Ryan.
What's next?
One Liberal MP has warned the party cannot afford to wait for Mr Frydenberg to "save us".
Federal Liberals have given a lukewarm response to former treasurer Josh Frydenberg's mooted return to politics, with one colleague saying the party cannot afford to wait for him to "save us", and One Nation's Barnaby Joyce urging him to "cut the BS" over his ambitions.
Promoting his memoir with a media blitz during a parliamentary sitting week, Mr Frydenberg insisted he had been "very content" after losing his seat of Kooyong but stopped short of ruling out a comeback.
"I think everyone misses the cut and thrust of politics once they leave," he told Radio National Breakfast.
Mr Frydenberg lost the blue-ribbon Melbourne seat nearly five years ago as part of the teal wave which also claimed seats like Goldstein from the Liberals.
Asked if he would recontest Kooyong, now held by independent Monique Ryan, Mr Frydenberg said he had not "made any decision about my political future" but admitted he had maintained "many very close relationships" with local Liberal members.
Mr Joyce, a One Nation MP who was elected on a Nationals ticket, said it was clear his former colleague was angling for a future anointment as leader of the opposition.
"Let's cut the BS, mate. We can all see through this," he said.
Deputy Liberal Leader Jane Hume said she would welcome Mr Frydenberg back but made it clear his position would be "behind Angus Taylor".
"We'd like to see our A team line up on the front bench," she said.
"I think he'd make a terrific addition to Angus Taylor's team."
Reaction within the wider Liberal cohort was mixed, with Queensland MP Garth Hamilton arguing the focus should be on rebuilding rather than speculation about a Frydenberg comeback.
"The only comeback I'm interested in seeing at the moment is Powderfinger," he told Afternoon Briefing.
MP Simon Kennedy welcomed Mr Frydenberg's contribution but warned the opposition could not wait for him to "save us".
"We have to hold this Labor government to account now," he said.
Nationals MP and former party leader David Littleproud said Ms Ryan was "finished" if Mr Frydenberg decided to put his name on the ballot in Kooyong.
"I think Josh has a huge contribution to make, and I hope that he runs," he said.
Frydenberg says he supports Angus Taylor
In excerpts from Mr Frydenberg's book, he urged the Liberal Party to "reclaim" the centre of politics, arguing there was a lack of political courage in Canberra.
But Mr Frydenberg said on Tuesday he supported Angus Taylor and his frontbench, despite litigating the "need for us to change".
"I support Angus and the team, it's a tough job", he said.
Mr Frydenberg writes in the book that the Liberal Party had become "obsessed with who is leading it, rather than who could be voting for it".
"We as a party hold very few of the metropolitan seats which dominate the political landscape in Australia and that's what we need to win back is part of a broader strategy to get back to government," he said.
GST policy pitch falls flat
He also pitched several policy changes, which included having a "national debate about lifting the GST".
That idea has found few friends with Mr Taylor and even Jess Wilson, a former staffer to Mr Frydenberg and now the Liberal leader in Victoria, ruling it out.
"The last thing Victorians need is to see the price of everything go up, so I don't support it," Ms Wilson said.
Ms Wilson is about six weeks away from a hotly contested state election in which cost of living has been a central element.
Victorian Labor Premier Ben Carroll also rejected the idea of a GST rise, labelling it a "ridiculous proposition".
New South Wales Liberal leader Kellie Sloane would not rule out a change to GST but said she would fight to get a fair deal for her state, while WA Liberal leader Basil Zempilas indicated he would not support a change.
Federal Liberal frontbencher Dan Tehan said it was wrong to consider hiking taxes during a cost-of-living crisis.
"What you need to be doing [is] reducing taxes and reducing spending," he said.

IMF lowers China growth forecast to 4.5% amid global escalates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
03:13:29 UTC
12:13:29 KST

The International Monetary Fund has lowered its forecast for China's economic growth this year to 4.5 percent, warning that elevated energy prices triggered by conflict in the Middle East and a sluggish domestic consumer market are dragging on output.
The revised projection, detailed in the Fund's latest IMF World Economic Outlook report, marks a 0.1 percentage point reduction from its previous estimates published in July.
Growth across the world's second-largest economy is projected to decelerate further to 4.0 percent in 2027, also down by one-tenth of a percentage point.
"Higher global oil prices, together with protracted uncertainty and structural headwinds, are expected to weigh on activity," the report stated, adding that targeted "policy support is expected to prevent a sharper slowdown".
The forecast hovers along the lower margin of Beijing's official target range of 4.5 percent to 5.0 percent.
A prolonged slump across China's property sector continues to deter domestic consumer confidence, muting retail activity despite resilient manufacturing exports and expanding high-tech industries, including artificial intelligence and electric vehicles.
Regional divergence
The IMF raised growth forecasts for key regional semiconductor exporters, lifting South Korea to 3.3 percent and Taiwan to 10.7 percent, driven by soaring international demand for advanced computing hardware.
Together, Taiwan and South Korea account for 62 percent of net global trade in AI computing components.
Conversely, the Fund noted that while parts of Southeast Asia benefit from data-centre investments, smaller developing island nations face subdued growth due to heightened fuel costs and declining tourism receipts.
In Japan, growth is projected at 0.7 percent, up 0.1 percentage points, assisted by fiscal measures introduced by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.

Australian inquiry calls for independent safety checks of AI companies
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:12:20 CST
12:12:20 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- A parliamentary inquiry has recommended that the Australian government subject AI companies to independent safety checks following a breach of the nation's healthcare system by an OpenAI agent.
The bipartisan committee established by the federal parliament in August wrote on Monday night to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to present its early advice, recommending that the government should position independent experts within leading AI companies to report safety findings and incidents.
The letter said that June's OpenAI breach of a web portal linked to the healthcare system, which was not disclosed until September, demonstrated the need for appropriate and robust safeguards to protect Australian data.
It said that security agencies should receive early access to new models as a condition of allowing companies to train them in Australia and that the government should immediately review protections used across its data repositories.
Addressing the inquiry earlier in October, OpenAI chief strategy officer Jason Kwon reiterated the company's apology for the June incident and said it has imposed additional monitoring allowing staff to stop training if a model accesses the internet in a way it is not supposed to.
Kwon said that OpenAI would support Australia imposing a mandatory reporting framework for similar incidents.
In addition to the security reforms, the inquiry also recommended that the government review copyright settings, noting that the work of Australian content is being used to train AI models overseas without compensation for creators.
"Australian copyright holders need to have control over how their material is used, and of course be compensated for that," Senator Jonno Duniam, co-chair of the inquiry from the opposition Liberal Party, told reporters at Parliament House on Tuesday.
The committee said that the government should establish an ongoing parliamentary inquiry to monitor AI and conduct rapid reviews of new regulation when required. ■

ISTANBUL, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese companies have been expanding their presence in Türkiye's consumer electronics, smart pet care and security markets, leveraging technological innovation, local partnerships and tailored services to meet local demand and explore broader international opportunities.
At the 12th International Pet Products, Materials and Accessories Suppliers Exhibition, Chinese smart pet care brand Petkit presented smart litter boxes, water fountains and dual-compartment feeders. The devices can identify individual pets and track their drinking and toileting habits, helping owners monitor their pets' health.
Petkit, which entered the Turkish market nearly five years ago, has expanded its retail presence through local partnerships. Gao Xiaoqun, the company's overseas business manager, said its products had entered MediaMarkt stores with help from its Turkish partner, providing a valuable reference for the company's expansion into other European retail markets.
Chinese consumer electronics brands are also gaining traction as Turkish consumers increasingly value products that combine functionality, design and reliability.
Mustafa Can Akbas, brand marketing director at Huawei's consumer business group in Türkiye, told Xinhua that consumers were looking beyond traditional technical specifications toward products that offer practical benefits in everyday life.
Huawei ranked third in Türkiye's premium tablet market in the first half of this year, with an 11 percent market share, according to a report cited in the original Chinese-language report. Its smart wearables and wireless earphones have repeatedly topped sales rankings.
Chinese companies are also strengthening their presence in Türkiye's security industry. At a recent security and fire safety exhibition in the country, Chinese video surveillance provider Hikvision showcased its latest products.
Lu Ran, general manager of Hikvision's Turkish subsidiary, said localized services were key to the company's growth. Having served Turkish customers since around 2005, Hikvision has established offices in Istanbul, Ankara and other major cities, building a local service network with its partners.
Türkiye's location at the crossroads of Europe and the Middle East also offers opportunities for further expansion, Lu said, noting that overseas projects undertaken by Turkish businesses could help the company reach additional markets.
According to Yesim Akgun Savas, sales director at Marmara Fair Organization, more than 50 of the 126 exhibitors at the security and fire safety exhibition were from China, showcasing products ranging from biometric identification systems and smart locks to alarm systems and video surveillance equipment.
The exhibitions highlighted how Chinese companies are combining product innovation, local partnerships and tailored services to strengthen their foothold in Türkiye and explore opportunities in wider international markets. ■

Invasive fire ants detected at western Sydney freight facility
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:12:17 CST
12:12:17 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- A biosecurity response has been activated after authorities detected a nest of invasive red imported fire ants at a major freight facility in Sydney's inner west.
The state government of New South Wales (NSW) said on Tuesday that authorities from the federal Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry discovered a fire ant nest at a key logistics and warehousing facility for the freight industry located 11 km west of central Sydney.
It said that entomologists confirmed the ants to be red imported fire ants, but that specialist detection dogs located no other nests at the facility or in the immediate vicinity.
Red imported fire ants are considered a major biosecurity threat to Australia. The species was first detected in Australia at the Port of Brisbane in the northeastern state of Queensland in 2001, prompting the federal government to establish the National Fire Ant Eradication Program (NFAEP).
The NSW government said on Tuesday that testing by the NFAEP confirmed that the ants found in Sydney likely originated from overseas via a container rather than Queensland.
The state government said it established an incident management team in response to the detection to undertake surveillance within a 2 km radius of the freight facility, with a priority focus on local businesses that deal in soil, turf, building materials or vegetation.
A report published by independent think tank the Australia Institute in June warned that red imported fire ants could cause significant environmental, social and economic damage if allowed to spread across the country.
It estimated that fire ants would sting 8.3 million people in Australia every year if the species spreads, causing 33 deaths annually from anaphylaxis.
NGO the Invasive Species Council estimates that more than 95 percent of Australia is suitable for fire ants and infestation. ■

China Focus: Global mayors explore revitalized historical attractions at China's Luoyang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:12:03 CST
12:12:03 KST

ZHENGZHOU, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Standing before the Longmen Grottoes, a UNESCO World Heritage Site in central China, Aimilia Tziva, deputy mayor of Irakleio, Attica, Greece, was amazed by the Ionic-style capitals that reminded her of Greek architectural traditions.
"We can see now how the cultures are connected," she said.
Tziva was among more than 90 mayors, municipal officials, international organization representatives and experts from over 10 countries who gathered in Luoyang, central China's Henan Province, from Oct. 9 to 11 for the 2026 Global Mayors Dialogue, where participants exchanged views on cultural heritage preservation, industrial upgrading and urban renewal.
During the event, guests visited landmarks including the Sui-Tang Luoyang City National Archaeological Site Park, the Luoyang Museum, and the Longmen Grottoes. Together, these sites offer a glimpse of how Luoyang, a historic capital of 13 ancient Chinese dynasties, is preserving its cultural legacy while integrating it into contemporary urban life.
Luoyang boasts a civilization history of more than 5,000 years, with cultural heritage sites densely distributed across the city and blended into its modern landscape, Yu Jie, secretary of the Party committee of the Longmen Grottoes Academy, said.
The city has long prioritized heritage protection while balancing the preservation of archaeological sites with urban expansion. It has also applied innovative technologies and developed public cultural spaces to make heritage more accessible, fostering closer ties between historic sites and its urban residents, Yu said.
The Sui-Tang Luoyang City National Archaeological Site Park illustrates this approach. At night, reconstructed city gates and palaces are illuminated, offering visitors a glimpse of the ancient capital's grandeur during the Tang Dynasty (618-907).
"It's good, and obviously lots of people want to see it," said Robbie Rodiss, chairman of Durham County Council in Britain. The reconstruction of historic buildings makes scenes from the past tangible, and provides an excellent way to showcase the character of the ancient city, he said.
Tziva particularly appreciated how the city has transformed its ancient history into economic momentum.
At Luoyi Ancient City, a performance depicting a celestial maiden scattering flowers draws dazzling camera flashes from visitors, while tourists in traditional Chinese attire stroll through the historic lanes, creating the impression of traveling back in time.
The integrated cultural tourism district, which combines sightseeing, entertainment, dining, accommodation and shopping, received more than 730,000 visits during China's recent National Day holiday, with daily visitor numbers peaking at 145,000.
This is exactly how to preserve the old-time glamour in modern life, Tziva said.
John Mahu Macharia, director of trade, investment and industrialization of Nakuru County, Kenya, shared Tziva's view.
"Once you preserve such culture, you can imagine the number of tourists that will visit, the number of jobs you are going to create," he said, adding that the trip has shed light on the development of cultures in Kenya.
Julio Cesar Zamora, mayor of Tigre, Argentina, said Luoyang's efforts to preserve historic sites while putting them to contemporary use offer valuable lessons for cities seeking to integrate their cultural legacy into modern development.
During the event, a consensus paper on urban civilization was released, highlighting the core values of sustained preservation and development of traditional cultures. It calls for cities to strengthen their appeal as places to live, work and visit, while fostering innovation and cooperation through dialogue.
Roberto Di Stefano, mayor of Sesto San Giovanni, Italy, said he hoped the event would deepen cooperation among cities in cultural heritage preservation, cultural communication and urban renewal.
Beyond the cultural attractions of Luoyang, China is working to foster innovation in traditional cultural industries while preserving heritage and unlocking its economic potential.
China's cultural industry generated 20.8 trillion yuan (about 3.09 trillion U.S. dollars) in revenue, averaging 8.4 percent annual growth from 2021 to 2025, national data showed.
China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), released in March this year, calls for improving the cultural industry and market systems, upgrading traditional cultural business models, expanding the supply of high-quality tourism products, and promoting deeper integration between culture and tourism. ■

TOKYO, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- A fire that broke out at a plastics factory warehouse in Tochigi Prefecture, north of Tokyo, early Monday was still burning more than 24 hours later, according to local media. No injuries have been reported.

A total of 38 fire engines and emergency vehicles had been deployed, but the blaze had yet to be extinguished as of 7 a.m. Tuesday, public broadcaster NHK reported, citing police and firefighters.
The flames had weakened, but plastic products stored in the roughly 800-square-meter warehouse were still burning. The building had also collapsed, leaving debris scattered across the site and making it difficult to pinpoint the source of the fire. Firefighters were continuing to battle the blaze, the report said.
Although the factory operates around the clock, no employees were inside the warehouse when the fire broke out, and all workers were safely evacuated. ■

Economic Watch: Jasmine's journey from teacup to multi-billion-yuan industry
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:11:39 CST
12:11:39 KST

FUZHOU, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- In Fuzhou's Shangxiahang historic district, teahouses are hard to miss, with jasmine tea steaming in cup after cup. Jasmine-themed cultural and creative products spill out of gift shops, filling the district with a lingering floral scent.
For more than 2,000 years, this tiny white flower has been woven into the identity of Fuzhou, capital of east China's Fujian Province. Today, as the city flower, it has become a bridge connecting China's time-honored industries with modern consumers, digital agriculture and rural revitalization.
"In this district, historical memory meets modern commerce. We use jasmine as a cultural starting point," said Zeng Xiang, manager of a teahouse in the district.
"Beyond traditional tea, we are exploring modern jasmine beverages and cold-brew tea, bridging the city's culture with younger consumers," said Zeng, noting that the store alone draws 300 to 500 visitors daily, with sales reaching up to 50,000 yuan (about 7,428 U.S. dollars).
Just steps away, a jasmine aesthetics hall brings the craft to life. Visitors watch artisans blend, rest and sieve tea leaves with fresh blossoms until the fragrance is fully absorbed -- a process recognized as intangible cultural heritage.
"Many tourists, both domestic and foreign, are fascinated by Fujian's tea culture and enjoy trying jasmine tea scenting themselves," said Yan Jinhua, an inheritor of the craft. "It gives them a glimpse into the artisans' dedication and the city's daily life."
Yet the story of jasmine does not end in the teacup. Behind the bustling shops lies a broader rural economy. In Lianhua Village in Fuzhou, farmers pick around 10 kilograms of jasmine flowers a day during the harvest season, earning nearly 200 yuan daily.
To help local growers, for example, Minrong Tea Industry Co., Ltd., a company rooted in a multi-generational Fuzhou jasmine tea family, has linked farmers, processing bases and agricultural technicians.
"With guidance from technical specialists, farmers have raised yields by about 65 kilograms per mu, adding several thousand yuan to their annual income," said Wang Dexing, chairman of the company.
By 2025, Fuzhou's jasmine tea industry supported 26,000 flower-growing households and 42,000 tea-growing households, raising their average annual income by 12,000 yuan and 30,000 yuan respectively. The output value of the city's jasmine tea industrial chain reached about 11.8 billion yuan by the end of 2025.
Fuzhou is not the only place where jasmine is thriving. Farther south, Hengzhou in the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, a core production area accounting for 80 percent of China's total output, has also transformed its jasmine industry.
Once reliant on traditional practices and weather, with most flowers used only for scented tea, the city now benefits from a diversified system spanning jasmine foods, wellness tourism and potted-plant cultural products, alongside widespread smart farming.
"AI-assisted service has extended the flowering period by a month and increased yield by 250 kilograms per mu," said local farmer Lei Shuiping as she scanned jasmine leaves with a mobile app that identifies pests, recommends precise pesticide ratios and provides field management plans.
This digital shift is spreading across the region. A local "Digital Jasmine" platform, with over 125,000 users so far, offers full-chain services from planting to sourcing. It integrates environmental monitoring, smart irrigation and fertigation, and AI-based pest identification.
As production becomes smarter, the flower itself is reaching new markets. Fuzhou tea companies supply more than 30 percent of the jasmine tea base used by leading domestic new-style tea brands, with annual consumption reaching 40,000 tonnes. Jasmine-scented hand cream, soap and essential oils are expanding the flower's reach beyond beverages.
Fuzhou has also turned jasmine into a city IP. In March, the public consumption brand "Fuzhou Youli" introduced "Mo Xiaoli," a cartoon jasmine character that appears on dolls, fridge magnets and other merchandise.
"We hope the character helps remind people of Fuzhou," said Bao Jingshan, a staff member of the brand, noting that with over 40 products launched, it accounts for more than 20 percent of store sales.
This transformation aligns with China's first national guideline, issued this year, on boosting the high-quality development of time-honored industries. It encourages heritage industries such as silk, tea and porcelain to integrate with culture, tourism and rural revitalization, while building smarter factories and stronger consumer brands.
This comes as Chinese consumers are shifting from "buying more goods" to "seeking better services and experiences." "Jasmine is a city memory," said Bao. "When people take these products home, they carry a piece of Fuzhou memory with them." ■

IMF edges up 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1 pct as Mideast conflict, AI boom split world economy
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:11:37 CST
12:11:37 KST

A press briefing on the World Economic Outlook of International Monetary Fund (IMF) is held in Bangkok, Thailand on Oct. 13, 2026. IMF on Tuesday nudged its 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1 percent, up 0.1 percentage point from its July projection, as economies lifted by the artificial intelligence (AI) investment boom offset those hurt by the Middle East conflict. (Xinhua/Rachen Sageamsak)
BANGKOK, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- The International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Tuesday nudged its 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1 percent, up 0.1 percentage point from its July projection, as economies lifted by the artificial intelligence (AI) investment boom offset those hurt by the Middle East conflict.
In its latest World Economic Outlook, titled "Resilience Under Strain, Urgent Choices," the IMF projected global growth slowing from 3.5 percent in 2025 to 3.1 percent in 2026 before recovering to 3.4 percent in 2027. The 2027 figure is unchanged from the July forecast and 0.2 percentage points higher than the April forecast.
The IMF said growth is becoming more concentrated. Just 32 economies now account for 95 percent of global growth, down from 54 in April. Roughly 47 percent of economies had their forecasts downgraded.
The fund described the world economy as neither simply slowing nor accelerating but having growth reallocated according to each country's exposure to the war-driven energy shock and to AI-related demand.
The strongest performers combine limited energy vulnerability with deep ties to the AI hardware supply chain. By contrast, energy importers with little connection to the technology cycle, including many low-income countries, face the hardest mix of higher import bills, weaker currencies, and falling real incomes.
The IMF's baseline assumes the Strait of Hormuz reopens in March 2027, with conditions broadly returning to prewar levels by October 2027. Before the war, the strait carried about a quarter of the world's seaborne oil trade.
The fund estimated that closing the strait would have cut global growth by 0.9 percentage points this year without offsetting supply responses. Rerouted Gulf output, higher production elsewhere, inventory drawdowns, and a lower oil intensity of the world economy reduced the net hit to about 0.3 percentage points.
Saudi Arabia's 2026 outlook was cut by 5 percentage points from July to a 3.3 percent contraction. Meanwhile, Bahrain, Iraq, Kuwait, and Qatar, commodity producers most affected by disruptions to energy output and transport, are expected to shrink by double digits this year.
The IMF warned that inventories are being depleted toward stress levels that could trigger sharp price jumps. Oil prices are assumed to average 95.74 U.S. dollars a barrel in 2026, up about 41 percent from 2025, and 87.39 dollars in 2027.
Global headline inflation is now forecast to rise from 4.1 percent in 2025 to 4.7 percent in 2026 before easing back to 4.1 percent in 2027.
Compared with its April projections, the fund raised its inflation forecasts by 0.3 percentage points for 2026 and 0.4 percentage points for 2027.
Core inflation is not expected to return to 2 percent until the end of 2027 in Japan and Britain and mid-2028 in the euro area and United States.
Among major economies, U.S. growth is forecast at 2.3 percent in both 2026 and 2027, supported by consumption, fiscal policy, and technology investment. The euro area is seen growing 1.1 percent this year and 1.2 percent next, reflecting the continued drag of high energy prices and weak consumer confidence.
India's growth is projected at 7.0 percent in both years. Japan is forecast at 0.7 percent and Britain at 1.3 percent for 2026. ■

Calls show how confusion delayed emergency response for death row inmate Christa Pike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
02:50:00 UTC
11:50:00 KST

Calls show how confusion delayed emergency response for death row inmate Christa Pike
Emily Cochrane
- Confusion over a 911 call delayed help by about 30 minutes during Christa Pike’s botched execution at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Tennessee.
- Dispatchers and prison staff struggled to confirm the call was real, and officials first said it was false before later confirming an ambulance was needed.
- The case has renewed criticism of Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol, after Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital and her lawyers said she was still breathing and needed urgent care.
AI generated
NASHVILLE, Tennessee – The emergency response to Christa Pike’s botched execution in September was delayed by about half an hour, because of confusion over the authenticity of the 911 call, according to dispatch and radio calls released on Oct 12.
The first 911 call for an ambulance was made by someone inside the US’ Riverbend Maximum Security Institution at 8.40pm local time on Sept 30, about an hour after the lethal injections there began, according to a redacted transcript of the phone call.
But confirming the legitimacy of that call took several minutes of back and forth between Nashville emergency services and officials at the prison, according to audio from eight other calls and radio traffic, which was released as part of a public records request by several news organisations, including The New York Times.
The confusion seemed widespread.
The initial 911 call did not come, as it might normally, from central control at the Tennessee Department of Correction, and the caller did not have the right security verification.
In response, dispatch workers repeatedly tried to verify the call by reaching out to prison staff and other officials at the prison during the execution.
“We are trying to find out if that is an actual thing that is happening and we need to send an ambulance,” one caller said. Or, she added, “if this is someone that is just basically prank-calling”.
It appeared from the phone calls that the Department of Correction’s central control was not immediately aware of the request for help.
One person at central control, who was not identified, told Nashville emergency services that the department “would have been the one to call you guys – we didn’t call anyone”.
In another call, at 9.03pm, someone told responders that supervisors have said “it is a false call” and that “there is no medical assistance needed”.
But at 9.07pm, an emergency responder said as part of radio traffic that “some sort of state official” is “outside the gate at the prison telling us that it’s real and demanding us to go in”.
Minutes later, they got word that prison officials had formally confirmed by phone that the request was legitimate.
The Tennessee Department of Correction did not immediately respond to a request for a comment about the apparent breakdown in communication.
Previously, the agency said that every step of the protocol had been followed and the process did “not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out”.
Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol has come under renewed scrutiny after the failed attempt to carry out the execution of Pike, 50, who had been on death row for the torture and murder of Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old classmate in Knoxville.
Lawyers for Pike, the first person to survive receiving two doses of the drug pentobarbital during an execution, said on Oct 10 that she had been discharged from a Nashville hospital and returned to prison.
The confusion captured on the calls appear to emphasise how the execution protocol, criticised by state defence lawyers and lawmakers in both parties for its vagueness, does not appear to account for problems during an execution.
Tennessee has had two botched executions in 2026, including Pike’s.
The protocol really did not consider that the execution may not succeed, said Joel Zivot, an anaesthesiologist and intensive care physician who consulted for Pike’s defence team before the failed execution.
Prison officials, he added, “had no idea that it could fail”.
Zivot was among the medical experts who warned that Pike’s underlying medical conditions, including small veins, could complicate the execution. Those warnings were ignored, her lawyers said.
“Considering, of course, what everyone said to them – that it could fail – they certainly did not seem to react,” Zivot said.
It was not clear from the recordings whether oxygen and other resuscitative gear were on hand in the execution chamber, or if Pike received medical care before an ambulance arrived more than an hour after the drugs were injected.
The transcript of the initial 911 call and some of the audio recordings were redacted, in part because Tennessee law prohibits the identification of anyone connected with execution procedures.
But the person who made the initial 911 call appeared unfamiliar with the steps needed to verify the legitimacy of an emergency call from the prison, leading to the effort to authenticate the call.
“Is nobody there that knows the process?” someone asked on a call between the Nashville Fire Department and emergency services.
“I have no idea,” someone else responded. “I guess because this is a special case, they may not know.”
The calls also showed that Kelly Gleason, one of Pike’s lawyers, called 911 at 9.08pm, after a colleague who had witnessed the botched injections told her that Pike was still breathing.
“She is still alive and breathing and needs immediate life-saving care,” Gleason said on her call for help. The ambulance drove through the gates a few minutes later. NYTIMES

Is Australia prepared to cope with its 'modern-day success story'?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
02:49:53 UTC
11:49:53 KST

IN BRIEF:
- Emergency departments will increasingly struggle to cope with an influx of elderly patients, a new report has found.
- Experts say that older people are falling through the cracks at every level of the health and aged care systems.
Australians are living longer and the healthcare system is increasingly unable to cope, according to a new national report on the state of emergency departments (EDs).
The Australasian College of Emergency Medicine's (ACEM) third annual report notes that while Australia's ageing population is a "modern-day success story", the nation is not sufficiently prepared for the influx of elderly people into EDs.
From 2019 to 2024, the number of older people attending EDs increased by 16 per cent, compared with a 4 per cent increase among younger people, with half of all elderly presentations to an ED resulting in a hospital admission.
The group also found disparities in hospital care requirements between groups of older people.
While all non-Indigenous people aged 65 years and over were significantly more likely than younger people to be classified in higher urgency categories, arrive by ambulance and be admitted into hospital, that also holds for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people aged 50 years and over.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
ACEM president Dr Peter Allely said EDs were "far from ideal" environments to treat elderly patients, due to their "harsh lighting, loud noises and constant interruptions".
"We see too many frail people made afraid, confused and unwell by an unfamiliar environment, far away from their loved ones, familiar faces, supports and home comforts."
He said that, despite the "scale and predictability of demographic trends", governments across Australia had done little to prepare for the "volume and complexity of care needs" for the ageing population.
As a result, significant pressure was now being felt at "all levels" of the health system, including hospitals, primary and aged care facilities, and in-home support programs, he added.
ACEM is the organisation responsible for training emergency medicine specialists and setting standards for emergency care in Australia and New Zealand.
Across-the-board lack of preparedness
University of New South Wales professor in ageing health Lee-Fay Low agreed, saying she didn't think Australia had been doing anything long-term to prepare the health system for Australia's ageing population.
Similarly to Allely, Low said this lack of preparedness wasn't unique to hospitals, but could also be seen in primary care clinics, aged care facilities, and even among families.
Low, who is also leader of the Ageing and Health Research Group at the University of Sydney, said the ongoing aged care crisis was affecting people's ability to receive preventative care.
"Right now, because you have to wait for aged care, those things that might help might prevent you from going to emergency, like poor nutrition, ending up with an infection because your hygiene's not looked after."
Even since the Royal Commission into Aged Care handed down its final report in 2021, lengthy waitlists for aged care providers have seen many people go without crucial care, Low said.
"After the Aged Care Royal Commission, the government released more home care packages, allowing people to age in place without going into nursing homes. But that waitlist is a year long again now.
"The problem is that with the aged care reforms, things are worse now ... I mean, waiting a year is ridiculous.
"People living in their homes aren't really getting that aged care in a timely way, and that precedes these emergency visits."
New health department data released yesterday found an average of 17 older Australians died while waiting to receive support at home care each day last year — an increase of more than a third on the previous year.
As of June 30, more than 106,000 Australians were on the official waiting list for a place in the Commonwealth-funded Support at Home program, while the ABC's Four Corners reported in August that the true number of people waiting was almost 154,000.
'Urgent action' needed
Older Australians made up only 17 per cent of the population in 2024 but accounted for almost a quarter of all ED presentations.
The ACEM report said that, without "urgent action", increased ED presentations by older people would disproportionately impact the healthcare system.
Using population growth modelling from the Australian Bureau of Statistics, the report projected a 177 per cent increase in total ED presentations between 2010 and 2050, noting projected increases of 242 per cent for people aged 65 to 84, and 411 per cent for people aged 85 and over.
ACEM is calling for federal, state and territory governments to urgently improve the quality of care older people receive across the health system, reduce ED demand, lift hospital capacity and provide sustainable hospital care for all Australians.
The government's latest Intergenerational Report projected rapid population ageing and falling fertility rates would fundamentally reshape the economy and budget out to 2065–66. By 2030, nearly one in five Australians will be aged 65 and over.
"The ratio of working people to older people is going to change substantively," Low said.
Allely warned that "Australia's health system and its health workforce are just not equipped for this demographic change."
More funding not the only remedy
Low said preparing for an ageing future required more than a funding boost.
"We always say we should have more funding, but I think where the funding is focused is important."
She also said proper reform would also require "an adjustment in presumptions and expectations Australians have for care as they get older".
"I think the presumption and the expectation in Australia is that when you get older, if you need care, you've paid taxes your whole life and the government will look after you. And that's already untrue, right? Aged care doesn't look after you straight away."
Low said a "national conversation" was needed to identify where the responsibility for care lies — whether it is with the government, or a co-contribution arrangement through which "as part of saving for retirement and super, that we also put aside some money, if we need help and we can pay for care".
Reforms also need to ensure the aged-care sector has a sufficient workforce, one-third of which is currently made up of migrants. Australia needs to reconsider decisions made around cutting migration, Low said.
She also suggested more families needed to start conversations about the "expectation that maybe mum and dad will need some help, and at that stage we might have to work less or chip in somehow to support the care".
But beyond families, she said, "this is not a conversation that we've had nationally".

Man rescued after being trapped in Sardinian cave for 26 hours
- Published
A man has been rescued from a cave in Sardinia, Italy, after being trapped about 32ft (10 metres) underground for about 26 hours following a rockfall.
The 31-year-old, Luca Olmetto, was inside Gorropeddu cave at Urzulei, a town on the Italian island, when he became stuck on Sunday, according to ANSA, a local news agency.
Following a major rescue operation, involving more than 100 emergency personnel working meticulously over 24 hours, Olmetto was found alive and freed on Monday afternoon, the National Alpine and Speleological Rescue Corps said.
Olmetto, who studies caves, was then airlifted to hospital for further medical checks and treatment, local media said.
He had been exploring the cave, which is situated along a mountain range in central-eastern Sardinia, when rock suddenly collapsed on Sunday afternoon.
A rescue operation then followed, led by the National Alpine and Speleological Rescue Corps and the local fire department.
It was a "particularly complex operation", the National Alpine and Speleological Rescue Corps said in a statement shared on social media along with pictures of the team working in what they described as "extremely confined" spaces.
After gently and manually removing debris to access the cavity of the cave, the man was brought to the surface, the statement said.
The speleologist was then stabilised and transferred by helicopter to the hospital, it said.
In a post shared on social media, the council of Codrongianos, a town in north-west Sardinia where Olmetto is from, said: "After hours of great anxiety, the news that the entire Codrongianos was waiting for has finally arrived: Luca is out of the cave!
"It has been a difficult hour, during which the entire community has been on edge following the rescue operations," the post continued.
The council of Codrongianos thanked the rescuers "who worked tirelessly to reach him".

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The National Chung Shan Institute of Science and Technology announced on Monday that it has passed two international certifications.
NCSIST said its propellant mixing and casting production line has obtained Level 2 certification under the US Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification program, per Liberty Times. The achievement demonstrates the institute’s ability to meet cybersecurity requirements for the US defense industrial supply chain, NCSIST said.
The NCSIST Research and Development Center for Missile and Rocket Systems operates the production line, which mass-produces rocket propellants and explores opportunities to join US supply chains, Liberty Times reported.
NCSIST said a CMMC Third-Party Assessment Organization conducted the assessment.
The institute also obtained ISO 42001 certification for its AI management system. ISO 42001 is the world’s first AI management standard designed for third-party certification.
To prepare for the assessment, NCSIST established a cross-departmental AI management system committee and implemented training, according to Liberty Times. It also formed an AI policy and a risk-management framework.
NCSIST said it will integrate its ISO 27001 and CMMC cybersecurity frameworks to strengthen protections for AI-enabled systems. The institute added that it plans to expand AI in areas including autonomous navigation for unmanned vehicles, automated target recognition, and decision-support systems, according to Liberty Times.
It emphasized that as autonomous decision-making and battlefield intelligence analysis become increasingly important technologies in asymmetric warfare, AI system resilience against enemy attacks and algorithm reliability have become critical national security concerns.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s three major container shipping lines reported strong revenue growth in September, with analysts expecting favorable market conditions to continue through the fourth quarter, CTEE reported Monday.
Evergreen Marine Corp. reported consolidated revenue of NT$49.7 billion (US$1.6 billion) in September, up 63.75% from the same month a year earlier. The figure was the company’s highest monthly revenue in 25 months.
Yang Ming Marine Transport Corp. posted revenue of NT$21.7 billion, an annual increase of 69.94%. This extended its year-on-year growth streak to seven consecutive months.
Wan Hai Lines Ltd. reported revenue of NT$21.8 billion, up 97.63% from a year earlier. Its monthly revenue exceeded NT$20 billion for the first time since July 2024.
Evergreen President Wu Kuang-hui (吳光輝) said at an investor conference last week that the peak shipping season had lasted longer than expected. Favorable market conditions were likely to persist through the first quarter of next year. Booking trends remained encouraging, with cargo volumes expected to stay strong through November before a restocking wave in December, according to LTN.
Institutional investors said several factors could support fourth-quarter earnings despite the seasonally slower period. These include pre-Lunar New Year restocking in North America, rising cargo volumes on European routes, and seasonal shipping activity across regional Asian markets.
Looking ahead to 2027, analysts expect more new vessels to enter service, expanding the global fleet. The additional tonnage could put downward pressure on freight rates.
However, the impact could be partly offset by port congestion and continued vessel diversions around the Red Sea due to geopolitical tensions. Analysts also expect long-term contract rates on North American and European routes to exceed this year's levels, providing additional support for earnings.

WASHINGTON – US Senate candidate James Talarico, who is eyeing an historic Democratic midterm win in Texas, pushed back against an online conspiracy theory that he had secretly checked into an Ohio mental health facility, calling it “the craziest thing I’ve ever heard”.
The upstart candidate told MS Now on Oct 11 that a bout with the flu had caused him to step away for over a week from the campaign trail in his close race with Republican Ken Paxton, President Donald Trump’s pick to represent deeply red Texas.
“I had the flu,” Talarico told the news network. “This is the craziest thing I’ve ever heard.”
Talarico added in an interview with NBC Dallas-Fort Worth that the episode was “a good reminder that you can’t believe everything you read on the internet”.
The false narrative that Talarico was lying about the flu to conceal a mental health crisis took off on X as prominent right-wing users circulated a dubious recording that supposedly showed an employee at Ohio’s Lindner Centre of Hope confirming that he had been a patient.
Billionaire X owner Elon Musk, who has poured money into supporting Paxton, repeatedly boosted the posts, writing in one reply that “the Talarico campaign is hiding something big”.
The facility said in a statement on Oct 11 on X that Talarico “has never received treatment from Lindner Centre of Hope”.
Talarico reshared the centre’s post and quipped that he had “never even been to Ohio”, while his press secretary blasted the claims as “a pathetic conspiracy theory”.
The saga, which underscores how rapidly unverified rumours can race across the internet, is the latest case of misinformation to ruffle the hotly contested Texas race.
Talarico has already faced artificial intelligence-generated advertisements and baseless claims that he is vegan, an apparently disqualifying dietary choice in the barbecue-heavy southern state.
Questions about his whereabouts intensified over the previous week as Paxton and Trump mocked his absence in the final stretch before the Nov 3 election.
The questions morphed into conspiracy theories when pro-Trump influencers released a snippet of a call that self-described “right-wing provocateur” Rhein Amacher said he placed Oct 10 to the Ohio facility, in which an employee seemed to say Talarico had just been discharged.
Observers quickly pointed out inconsistencies in the timeline: Talarico attended a Dallas concert for country artist Kacey Musgraves that same day – and campaigned in Austin the day before.
He had also held virtual campaign events while battling influenza.
Several conservative commentators have since walked back their posts pushing the narrative about Talarico seeking treatment in Ohio, but Amacher told AFP he stands by his allegations.
A longer recording of the call published online, however, reveals that the operator Amacher spoke to repeatedly said she was finding no record of Talarico in their system.
Amacher got through after giving his name as “Tim”, saying he was trying to send a care package to a cousin and providing a four-digit patient code, the full recording shows.
AFP has not independently verified the authenticity of the call.
Federal medical privacy laws generally prohibit institutions from sharing patient information, and the centre’s website says it requires callers to provide a code determined by the patient.
Amacher admitted on X that when asked for the code, he “simply made one up”. AFP

====================================================================================================

Feature: Two photos, 84 years apart, witness special bond between Chinese, American people
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:19:33 CST
11:19:33 KST

NANCHANG, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Gazing at a black-and-white photograph, 94-year-old Guan Dongxiang drifted back to a wartime encounter that unfolded 84 years ago.
The photo shows a little girl with short hair standing behind an American pilot in a flight jacket, her mouth round and eyes wide with surprise.
"That's me," Guan murmured. The pilot in the frame was one of the Doolittle Raiders, whom Guan's family risked their lives to help decades before.
On Sunday, in the Yangcun Village committee office in Shangrao, east China's Jiangxi Province, Guan was waiting for the raiders' descendants, who had traveled all the way from across the Pacific.
Footsteps approached from the doorway, and the descendants walked in. Among them was Thomas Macia, whose father, James Macia, had served as navigator and bombardier for Crew No. 14 of the Doolittle Raid.
"There she is," Thomas said excitedly. "I knew she existed. I had not met her before. So I think the greatest thing is that she is a direct connection to 1942."
Thomas stepped forward quickly. Guan immediately reached out. When their hands clasped, the elderly woman smiled and her eyes lit up.
Thomas bent down to study the photograph alongside Guan, gesturing and saying that he had known this picture since he was this age.
The image had left a deep impression on him since childhood. When Thomas was 9, he first saw it in his father's album: a young Chinese girl standing beside co-pilot Jack Sims.
The story behind the photo traces back to April 18, 1942, when a group of 16 U.S. bombers took off from the USS Hornet and bombed Japan in retaliation for the attack on Pearl Harbor.
After the raid, 15 planes heading for an airport in Quzhou in east China's Zhejiang Province ran out of fuel and crashed in various localities in east China, including Jiangxi.
Chinese villagers risked their lives to rescue the parachuting airmen and helped them evacuate to safety. Of the 75 airmen aboard the planes, 64 were rescued by the Chinese people.
Their rescue, however, came at a tremendous cost. Many locals were suspected of sheltering the Americans, and some were tortured or even killed by Japanese soldiers.
In China, the Doolittle story has long been regarded as a symbol of the friendship forged between the Chinese and American peoples during their joint fight against fascism.
The history has left a deep mark not only on Thomas, but also on Guan. Though age has blurred many of Guan's daily memories, the spring of 1942 remains sharp.
"It was the morning of April 19, 1942," she recalled. She was nine and grazing cattle by a field while her father, Guan Wenqing, the village head, worked nearby.
Sims parachuted onto the mountainside, soaked and wrapped in his parachute. He slept until morning before Guan Wenqing and the villagers found him and brought him down the mountain.
"We cooked hot noodles, but he couldn't use chopsticks and wasn't used to them," Guan said. Sims pulled out candy and shared it with the children watching.
None had seen such foreign snacks before, and none dared try. "I was bold, so I took a bite. It was sweet and delicious," she recalled.
Together with Chinese soldiers, Guan Wenqing then escorted Sims to the county seat. Nine days later, Sims returned to Miliang'ao Village with a camera and took the image.
The photograph was carried back to the United States and kept in James Macia's album.
James Macia had also been saved by locals after bailing out of his plane. He once pointed to a spot on a map and told Thomas that his life had been saved by the Chinese villagers, officials and soldiers there -- people he remembered until he died in 2009.
Unable to return to China in his lifetime, James Macia carefully kept the photograph. Thomas later made it his mission to revisit the site and meet the descendants of those who had helped.
In 2018, Thomas traveled to China for the first time and met Luo Shiping, a researcher with the Shangrao Anti-Japanese War Culture Research Association. Over the following years, they exchanged nearly 1,000 emails.
Thomas combed through U.S. archives and provided clues, while Luo trekked through the mountains of northeastern Jiangxi, interviewing witnesses. Guided by the old photo, researchers searched several places and finally found Guan Dongxiang, who was by then 90 years old.
In the postwar years, Doolittle Raiders and their descendants established organizations such as the Children of the Doolittle Raiders. They hold annual commemorations, seminars and photo exhibitions to honor the Chinese who took part in the rescue.
Researchers in Shangrao have continued to collect scattered documents and oral testimonies, working with their American counterparts to preserve this transnational memory.
Before leaving, Thomas posed for a new photograph with Guan and her family. The descendants of Crew No. 14 promised to return.
"One old photograph captured a chance encounter and life-and-death aid in wartime, while one new photograph continues the story of cross-ocean friendship in peacetime," said Luo, noting that together, they bear witness to a friendship forged in blood and fire that has not dimmed in 84 years. ■
