====================================================================================================

Global study projects annual new dementia cases to reach 24.7 mln by 2050
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:19:17 CST
11:19:17 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- An estimated 11.4 million people worldwide developed dementia in 2023, with the number of new cases projected to rise to 24.7 million annually by 2050, according to an Australian-led international study.
The study, led by researchers at the Center for Healthy Brain Ageing (CHeBA) at Australia's University of New South Wales, analyzed data from 38,418 people across 22 population-based studies in 18 countries and territories, according to a center statement on Tuesday.
The research, published in JAMA Neurology, provides a new global benchmark for understanding how frequently new dementia cases occur across different populations and helps explain the changing global dementia landscape.
It found that dementia incidence was higher among women than men, at 10.6 cases per 1,000 person-years compared with 8.6 among men. The rate was also substantially higher in low- and middle-income countries, at 13.6 cases per 1,000 person-years, compared with 8.3 in high-income countries.
Dementia currently affects more than 57 million people worldwide, with previous research projecting the number of people living with the condition to reach about 150 million by 2050, according to the study.
"The higher incidence we observed in low- and middle-income countries is particularly concerning because these regions are experiencing rapid population ageing while often having the fewest resources for prevention, diagnosis and care," said senior author and CHeBA Co-Director Prof. Perminder Sachdev.
The study did not establish the reasons for the differences by sex or income level, which may reflect a combination of health, social, economic, educational and environmental factors, the researchers said. ■

Trade deal with U.S., Canada still in effect: Mexican president
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:19:10 CST
11:19:10 KST

MEXICO CITY, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- The United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) remains valid and in effect, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Monday, emphasizing that reviewing the trade pact does not mean ending or dismantling it.
In response to U.S. President Donald Trump's repeated suggestions that the deal could be scrapped or replaced, Sheinbaum explained that the agreement is undergoing a periodic review as required by the USMCA.
Under the USMCA, a review six years after the agreement took effect assesses its operation, considers any changes that may be needed, and determines whether all three parties agree to extend it for another 16 years.
Sheinbaum said that Mexico and Canada had requested a 16-year extension, while the United States had proposed maintaining a 10-year framework with annual reviews.
Discussions are continuing on matters of mutual interest covered by the trade agreement, but no agreement has yet been reached, she said.
The priority is to lower U.S. tariffs on Mexican exports of automobiles, steel and aluminum to the United States and avoid new tariffs while the review is underway, she said.
The USMCA review process began on July 1, after the United States opted not to automatically extend the agreement, and instead proposed annual reviews over the coming decade. ■

Brushstrokes bring Red Army martyrs' portraits for families

This photo shows the studio of a volunteer team focusing on painting portraits of martyrs, at the Academy of Fine Arts of Anhui Normal University in Wuhu, east China's Anhui Province, Sept. 25, 2026. During this year's Mid-Autumn Festival holiday, a volunteer team from the Academy of Fine Arts of Anhui Normal University was busy in Jinzhai County of Lu'an City in east China's Anhui Province, drawing portraits of Red Army martyrs who participated in the Long March, the historic military maneuver in modern Chinese history, and presented them to the families of the martyrs.
Since November 2021, the Academy of Fine Arts of Anhui Normal University has formed a team to carry out a series of volunteer services focused on drawing portraits of martyrs. Up to now, hundreds of students have participated in these activities, jointly drawing more than 600 portraits of martyrs, which have become an important way for their families to express feelings of longing.
Across time and space, the youthful faces of those who had fallen on the battlefield were finally seen again by their families back home.
Tucked in the Dabie Mountains, Jinzhai county contributed tens of thousands of people to the Communist Party of China (CPC)-led revolution in the first half of the 20th century. A total of 12 main units of the Red Army originated from here.
Now, the Anhui Normal University project to paint portraits of Red Army martyrs is giving some families a long-awaited face to go with the stories passed down for generations. Usually the volunteer team would first contact the relatives of martyrs and then study photographs of the martyrs' descendants to determine basic facial contours. They would then revise the portraits repeatedly, drawing on family descriptions of the martyrs' eyes, expressions and habitual looks, until these relatives feel the likeness is right.
For teachers and students of the team, painting portraits of martyrs is not merely a simple sketch creation but also an immersive study tour of revolutionary history. The brows and eyes rendered by the artists' brushes have captured the youthful appearance of the martyrs and also provided a place for the remembrance to rest. The past events recounted by the relatives of the martyrs are a testament to the enduring revolutionary legacy of the Dabie Mountains from generation to generation. (Xinhua/Zhang Duan)

Feature: China's "Auntie Basketball" scores cultural connections on U.S. tour
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:18:48 CST
11:18:48 KST

GUIYANG, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- A basketball game born in the villages of southwest China has found a new audience thousands of miles away, turning a grassroots sporting exchange into a celebration of friendship, culture and shared joy.
A 21-member "Auntie Basketball" delegation returned to China's Guizhou Province on October 9 after completing its first overseas cultural and sports exchange tour in the United States, bringing home memories of new friendships forged across the Pacific.
Unlike conventional basketball, "Auntie Basketball" is a community-based sport rooted in the traditions of Qiandongnan Miao and Dong Autonomous Prefecture in Guizhou.
The game takes its name from a local custom in which married women return to their home villages to visit their families. Known locally as "aunties," the women play a relaxed version of basketball that allows participants to run while holding the ball and features flexible substitutions, placing enjoyment and participation above strict competition.
From September 28 to October 6, the delegation visited schools and communities in California, Nevada, Utah and Washington state, playing friendly matches and showcasing Guizhou's ethnic traditions.
"For this exchange, the seeds were planted two years ago. It is a reunion among old friends," said Yang Guoxiang, deputy director-general of the Qiandongnan Prefecture Bureau of Culture, Sports, Radio, Television and Tourism.
The reunion had its origins in 2024, when a U.S. youth delegation visited Taipan Township in Taijiang County, the birthplace of China's popular "Village BA" basketball tournament.
During that visit, American teenagers played alongside local Auntie Basketball players, experiencing the game's relaxed atmosphere and distinctive rules.
Two years later, the players met again at the Tulalip Tribes Sports Community Center in Washington state.
"When we stepped onto the court, several American girls recognized us right away and came over to greet us. We were surprised and excited," said 41-year-old player Yu Ping.
She recalled how the American visitors had initially struggled to adapt to the unconventional rules during their first encounter in Guizhou.
"At the beginning, they were not familiar with our rules and felt a little shy. But after playing for a while, they quickly adapted and learned to run while holding the ball," Yu said.
For many members of the Chinese delegation, the tour marked their first journey overseas.
Of the 21 participants, 16 were players drawn from local communities, including teachers, forest rangers, nurses, bus drivers and company employees. Most were around 35 years old and came from the Miao, Dong and other ethnic groups.
For Li Damei, a player from Nangong Town in Taijiang County, basketball has been a lifelong passion.
"There were not many entertainment options when I was young, so I started playing basketball in fifth or sixth grade. Sometimes I became so absorbed in the game that I forgot the time and even burned meals in the kitchen," she recalled.
Now in her 50s and a grandmother, Li has lost none of her enthusiasm for the sport.
Before the trip, however, she worried that American audiences might struggle to appreciate their unconventional style of play.
"I was nervous at first, wondering whether people there would accept our way of playing. But they embraced it wholeheartedly. Seeing them enjoy the game made me very happy," she said.
The delegation played four friendly matches during its U.S. tour, attracting enthusiastic participation from local communities. Some spectators asked to join the games, while children took to the court to try Auntie Basketball for themselves.
But the exchange extended well beyond the basketball court.
At halftime and after matches, the players changed into traditional costumes to perform Miao Flying Songs, the Fanpai Wooden Drum Dance and the Golden Pheasant Dance, introducing American audiences to Guizhou's intangible cultural heritage.
Though not professional performers, the women brought the same confidence and enthusiasm to their cultural displays as they did to the games.
Yang said the delegation had adapted its traditional clothing for the overseas tour, preserving distinctive cultural elements such as Miao hairstyles, embroidery and silver ornaments while allowing greater freedom of movement on the court.
Visitors also had opportunities to explore Guizhou specialties, including Roxburgh rose fruit products, spicy potato snacks, Miao embroidery, batik handicrafts, silver ornaments and traditional Yao bath-care products from Congjiang County.
The combination of sport and cultural activities proved popular with local audiences.
"I think the whole event was wonderful. It was a great cultural exchange," said Deyamonta Diaz, director of the Youth Exchange Center of the Tulalip Tribes.
"We got to share some of our culture, and we loved experiencing your culture as well. It was like the Village BA - full of energy, passion, smiles and laughter."
The Chinese players also visited American campus basketball training sessions, sports facilities and youth development programs, gaining new perspectives on how the sport is organized and promoted.
Following the tour, Qiandongnan plans to expand the international reach of its rural sports and cultural activities, including Shibing County's light volleyball competitions and village folk song performances.
For the basketball-playing aunties, however, the most lasting memories may be the friendships formed on the court, where different languages and backgrounds proved no barrier to sharing the joy of sport. ■

Australian man charged after elderly driver seriously injured in collision during police chase
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:18:36 CST
11:18:36 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- A man from Western Australia (WA) has been charged after an elderly man was seriously injured in a high-speed collision during a police chase on Monday morning.
The 80-year-old man was taken to hospital with serious injuries sustained when an unmarked police car collided with his vehicle in the southern suburbs of Perth around 10:45 a.m. on Monday.
Two officers who were in the unmarked car, a man in his 40s and a woman in her 30s, were also hospitalized as a precaution.
The WA police force said on Tuesday that the officers were pursuing an allegedly stolen vehicle when the crash occurred.
The driver, a 27-year-old man, was arrested after crashing into a civilian vehicle and attempting to flee on foot. ■

four pitched-roof volumes build timber-clad coastal house in belgium
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
02:10:12 UTC
11:10:12 KST

four pitched-roof volumes build timber-clad coastal house in belgium
house of cards by vantieghem talebi follows the asymmetrical cruciform geometry of an existing foundation and draws on the steeply pitched roofs of traditional beach houses along the belgian coast.
[ADVERTISEMENT]
Four triangular timber volumes shape coastal ‘house of cards’
House of Cards is a coastal residence in Koksijde, Belgium, designed by Vantieghem Talebi around the structural and zoning constraints of an existing foundation. The new house follows the foundation’s asymmetrical cruciform geometry, with each triangular bay forming a distinct volume resembling a house of cards. The design is limited to the maximum permitted height and draws on the steep rooflines of traditional beach houses in the area.
The exterior is clad in a timber rainscreen made from chemically seasoned Douglas fir battens, which continue across the steeply pitched roofs to create a consistent envelope. Prefabricated battens conceal fixings, while gutters and drainage systems sit behind the cladding. Each of the four triangular volumes is constructed from prefabricated cross-laminated timber (CLT) panels, assembled on-site over three days and joined through an off-center arrangement. This configuration leaves the main living level column-free, with each volume defining a separate room.
Exposed CLT panels and a floating staircase define the interior
The design team at Vantieghem Talebi utilizes the CLT structure as the interior finish. Four floor panels define the structural bays across the living area ceiling, while exposed timber panels follow the pitched roofs above the bedrooms and central hall. A floating staircase sits within a wood floor grid spanning the structural bays, making use of the open interior.
The house incorporates a Type D mechanical ventilation system with heat recovery, along with rainwater collection and reuse. Outside, the dune landscape has been restored, while low concrete retaining walls provide pedestrian and vehicle access to the subterranean level. The existing foundation, site conditions, and planning restrictions inform both the building’s structure and its architectural form.
project info:

architect: Vantieghem Talebi | @vantieghem_talebi

Can Singapore engineer love on dating apps? From public service to private romance
FirstDate is being piloted among government employees aged 21 to 35 amid Singapore’s efforts to raise its fertility rate
For Singaporean civil servant Clare*, finding a suitable lifelong partner has been an uphill battle. Swiping on dating apps soon became a chore after multiple unsuccessful first dates, so when the government launched its own platform, the 32-year-old was all for it.
“It’s like: ‘Why not?’, and I think it does have a few screening procedures so it might save you some trouble like having to deal with impersonators or people who do not match with their advertised profiles,” she said.
FirstDate is being piloted among government employees aged 21 to 35 by GovTech, which told local media there was no decision yet to expand the initiative beyond the public sector. The government agency has not provided figures on how many users in the sector meet its present criteria for the app.

Trump takes out political frustrations on Zelensky, Ukraine

Unknown Publisher

Trump takes out political frustrations on Zelensky, Ukraine
- Trump is under pressure from a weak midterm campaign and high prices. He is trying to ease fuel costs and win back voters.
- He lifted some sanctions to allow Russian diesel imports. Critics say the move is small and will not change energy prices much.
- Trump has sharply attacked Zelensky, blaming him for blocking peace and urging him to hold elections. He has stayed silent on Russia’s growing attacks on Ukraine.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – With the US president Donald Trump’s surprise deal on Russian diesel and his call for Volodymyr Zelensky to step down, Trump appears to be redirecting the frustrations of his increasingly difficult midterm campaign.
It would not be the first time Trump has heaped criticism on his Ukrainian counterpart, who endured a memorably stormy on-camera meeting in the Oval Office in February 2025.
But back then, the US President was riding the momentum of a thunderous return to power. Now, he faces a much more uncertain political position.
The vast majority of polls predict Trump’s Republicans will lose control of Congress in the midterm legislative elections on Nov 3, as Americans grow more dissatisfied with rising prices, particularly at the petrol pump.
In an opinion survey published Oct 1, the Associated Press and University of Chicago found that 65 per cent of US adults blame the White House for the high cost of living, especially Trump’s tariff policies and his new war against Iran.
The threat of Americans voting with their pocketbook helps explain Trump’s Oct 9 announcement that he will lift certain sanctions to allow Russian diesel imports, supposedly to ease prices.
Trump has said his goal is to reduce pressure on the sectors that backed him in large numbers in 2024, such as agriculture, livestock farming and road transport.
“President Trump, despite his claim to the contrary, I think, is acutely aware that the American public is holding him responsible for the significant rise in prices, including for diesel,” Garret Martin, a professor of international relations at American University, told AFP.
“He knows that he only has a few weeks to try and change the narrative about these rising costs. So I think that’s the main factor for this timing.”
That aligns with British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting’s assessment during an Oct 11 interview with Sky News.
“Let’s be candid about this, midterms are coming up. Cost of living is an issue. And no doubt President Trump is feeling the same pressure that lots of leaders are facing in terms of wanting to ease cost of living pressures, energy prices,” Streeting said.
‘Shift the blame’
Members of the President’s own party have protested the Russia move, which backtracks on a law that Trump himself signed to tighten restrictions against Moscow.
The 80-year-old Republican has also repeatedly condemned Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, snapping at reporters on Oct 10 that Zelensky “better damn well stop” the strikes.
By contrast, Trump has not commented on the intensification in recent months of Russian strikes against Ukrainian territory, which have caused a surge in civilian casualties.
Again Capital analyst John Kilduff told AFP that Trump’s strategy is in part “to shift the blame and responsibility for the high prices for diesel fuel at the pump to the attacks by Ukraine and Russia, rather than the fact that there’s little refined products getting out of the Strait of Hormuz right now”.
Like many experts, Kilduff doubts the latest deal with Moscow will fundamentally change the energy situation.
“The amount of oil that Russia has promised to release in October is a very small amount compared with world demand,” Andy Lipow, an analyst at Lipow Oil Associates, told AFP.
The United States consumes 3.9 million barrels of diesel per day.
The deal with Moscow initially covers 2.22 million barrels total – barely more than half a day of American consumption.
Trump, who has recently fumed over not being chosen for the Nobel Peace Prize, has blamed Zelensky for being the main obstacle for peaceful resolution of the conflict.
“Russia would like to make a deal... but for whatever reason, Zelensky does not want to make a deal,” Trump said on Oct 10.
He also criticised the Ukrainian President for not holding an election since Russia first invaded Ukraine in 2022.
“I think he should have an election and he could have settled this thing many times,” Trump said, in one of his sharpest attacks against the Ukrainian head of state, who was elected in 2019.
Trump insisted that Russian leader Vladimir Putin, who has been in power since 1999, “strongly” wants to see a settlement to the conflict. AFP

“We enter upon a stage which we did not design and we find ourselves part of an action that was not of our making. Each of us being a main character in his own drama plays subordinate parts in the dramas of others, and each drama constrains the others. In my drama, perhaps, I am Hamlet or Iago or at least the swineherd who may yet become a prince, but to you I am only A Gentleman or at best Second Murderer, while you are my Polonius or my Gravedigger, but your own hero. Each of our dramas exerts constraints on each other’s, making the whole different from the parts, but still dramatic.”

Advertisement
Thailand’s deepening labour shortage roils harvest as unpicked fruits rot
‘We have to choose which fruit to harvest and leave the lower-priced fruit to rot on the trees,’ a farmer says
2-MIN READ2-MIN
Ripe mangosteen and rambutan hang unpicked from trees in eastern Thailand, where a shortage of migrant workers is forcing growers to decide which crops are valuable enough to harvest and which will be left to rot.
For Jomsak Putirattana, who also grows durian in Chanthaburi province, the departure of his five Cambodian workers after a border dispute disrupted crossings has intensified competition for labour.
Daily wages have more than doubled in some cases, from about 350 baht to 400 baht (US$10 to US$12) to as much as 800 baht to 1,000 baht, he said, making some lower-value crops too costly to harvest.

Scientists just gave the powerhouses of our cells a high-tech upgrade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
01:33:58 UTC
10:33:58 KST

Scientists just gave the powerhouses of our cells a high-tech upgrade
A remarkable new way to coat cells’ tiny powerhouses without disrupting their function has been developed, potentially paving the way for new treatments for mitochondrial diseases.
- Date:
- October 12, 2026
- Source:
- Politecnico di Milano
- Summary:
- Scientists have created a new coating for mitochondria that preserves their ability to produce energy, potentially opening the door to new treatments for diseases involving these tiny cellular powerhouses. The technology could one day help transfer healthy mitochondria into damaged cells, although its effectiveness in transplantation remains unproven.
- Share:
Scientists have developed a way to coat mitochondria, the tiny structures that produce energy inside our cells, with advanced materials without interfering with their function. The achievement could eventually help researchers develop new approaches to treating diseases caused by malfunctioning mitochondria.
The research was conducted by IRCCS Fondazione Istituto Neurologico Carlo Besta (FINCB) and Politecnico di Milano through their joint BraiNs laboratory, established in 2023. The collaboration combines the mitochondrial biology expertise of Dr. Valeria Tiranti (FINCB), a researcher in the Medical Genetics and Neurogenetics Complex Unit (SC) and head of the Fondazione Mariani Centre for Paediatric Mitochondrial Diseases, with the chemistry and materials engineering expertise of Professor Pierangelo Metrangolo (Politecnico di Milano).
The findings were published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society (JACS).
A New Way to Coat the Powerhouses of Our Cells
Mitochondria generate the energy that cells need to carry out their essential activities. When these structures malfunction, they can contribute to several diseases, many of them rare. Mitochondrial diseases are particularly harmful to organs and tissues that require large amounts of energy, including the brain and muscles. Effective treatment options for these conditions remain limited.
To explore new possibilities, the researchers turned to Metal-Organic Frameworks (MOF), a class of advanced materials whose properties can be tailored for different applications. The importance of these materials was highlighted by the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, awarded to Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson, and Omar Yaghi for their work in this field.
Applying these materials to mitochondria presents a major challenge because the structures are extremely delicate and can easily lose their ability to function properly.
The research team overcame this obstacle by developing a technique that applies tiny amounts of MOF material directly to the mitochondrial surface. Crucially, tests showed that the coated mitochondria continued producing energy, demonstrating that the process could modify their surfaces without compromising this essential function.
Potential for Future Mitochondrial Treatments
One of the most promising aspects of the discovery is the ability to customize the coating for different purposes.
"The possibility of modifying the coating now opens up new research prospects: in the future, it will be possible to develop MOF with different characteristics depending on the objective, creating coatings capable of performing specific functions," observes Prof. Metrangolo.
A potential application is mitochondrial transplantation, an experimental technique intended to introduce healthy mitochondria into cells whose existing mitochondria are not functioning correctly. Researchers believe that specially engineered coatings might eventually make it easier to deliver healthy mitochondria and help them interact with the cells receiving them.
"A specifically designed coating could, in the future, facilitate this transfer and the interaction between mitochondria and cells," emphasizes Dr. Tiranti.
However, this possibility remains unproven. Additional research will be necessary to establish whether coated mitochondria perform better during transplantation than mitochondria without a coating.
The study was completed as part of a research project led by PhD candidate Marco D'Amato. Funding was provided through the "CALabria HUB per Ricerca Innovativa ed Avanzata (Cal.Hub.Ria)" project, supported under the Ministry of Health's Health Operational Plan (Piano Operativo Salute, POS).
Story Source:
Materials provided by Politecnico di Milano. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Marco D’Amato, Ivano Di Meo, Maria Nicol Colombo, Chiara Santanatoglia, Francesca Baldelli Bombelli, Valeria Tiranti, Pierangelo Metrangolo. Engineered Metal-OrganicFrameworks Preserve MitochondrialBioenergetics at Micromolar Concentrations. Journal of the AmericanChemical Society, 2026; DOI: 10.1021/jacs.6c11154

- Published
The Brexit debate is back.
For years, it felt like the only thing Westminster talked about.
I have had a ringside seat at it all, from the Conservative election victory in 2015, with the party's promise in its manifesto that year to offer "a straight in-out referendum on our membership of the European Union by the end of 2017."
Then there was the then Prime Minister David Cameron's negotiation with the European Union to try to secure what he saw as a better deal and then the referendum itself on Thursday, 23 June 2016.
And that, you will remember, was merely the start, as years of wrangling began. Two general elections came and went in 2017 and 2019 and it took the two prime ministers after David Cameron, first Theresa May and then Boris Johnson, before the UK left the European Union at 23:00 on Friday, 31 January 2020.
Little wonder perhaps that by that point, almost irrespective of someone's views on the topic, there was an appetite to talk about something else. Anything else. Political parties picked up that vibe and while their long standing instincts on the EU were there to see if you scratched the surface, there was minimal desire to extemporise about them any time soon.
With the arrival of Andy Burnham as prime minister, that has changed, despite what he said just a few months before he arrived in Downing Street.
He has been happy to repeatedly lean into an argument claiming that it is time to "face up to the reality that Brexit has done more harm than good" and "the status quo is not good enough for Britain." First he made this case at the Labour Party Conference last month and now he has made it again in the House of Commons.
Burnham is attempting to make a two-pronged case.
First, in the short term, he wants to "deepen" the UK's relationship with the EU at a summit in Brussels at the end of next month. He insists such a deepening would be within the promise made by Labour at the last general election that the UK would say no to the customs union, the single market and freedom of movement.
Which brings us onto the second element of his case, in the medium term. What might Labour promise in its next general election manifesto? The prime minister told me a fortnight ago the manifesto could promise an in-out referendum.
In the Commons, he sought to reassure you, whatever your view on Brexit.
"This country in the next decade needs to know where it's going. There are no assumptions here, and as I said, the British public will be the boss of whatever is decided," he said.
Hang on, say critics, it was decided by voters a decade ago.
"They weighed the arguments and made a decision. The least they are owed is politicians willing to defend it," argues Lord Frost, external, a former Brexit minister and chief Brexit negotiator in the Telegraph.
The focus of the next five weeks, ahead of a UK-EU Summit in Brussels on Friday 20 November, is what Downing Street sees as short term wins on youth mobility, food and drink, and energy.
Andy Burnham hopes to make an argument that what he will portray as a sensible, pragmatic deepening of the relationship with Brussels can help cut illegal immigration and boost economic growth.
He sought to goad the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch for seeking to oppose a plan he thinks can contribute to growth. She argued it risked regurgitating yesterday's arguments with little prospect of success.
And, strikingly, his attempt at goading his opponents went further still. He told The Rest Is Politics podcast that upon arriving in Downing Street, he had asked if there was Russian interference in the Brexit referendum.
"I've had a clear answer that, yes, there was," he claimed, without saying who provided that clear answer or what the evidence for that suggested clarity was.
In the Commons, his language appeared a little softer. He told MPs it was "inconceivable" to think that Russia did not try to interfere. A double negative deployed this time, about alleged attempts at interference.
His political opponents were already pouncing. The Reform UK leader Nigel Farage was blunt – calling the prime minister "a liar."
The former Prime Minister Boris Johnson added that he had asked the same question as Andy Burnham did when he became Foreign Secretary, external "and they replied that there was no evidence of any successful interference in the 2016 referendum, by Russia or any other power".
And so a debate resumes about the difference between attempted interference, interference and successful interference.
But the key point is this: for the first time since the UK left the European Union, we now have a prime minister who is willing to unflinchingly debate Brexit: whether it is working, how it is working, how to improve it, and if it's proved to be a failure.
In so doing he hopes he can tap into public sentiment. Opinion polls suggest a perception among a majority that leaving the European Union has not turned out how many might have hoped.
On top of this, he hopes to lure pro Europeans broadly on the Left who may recently have supported the Liberal Democrats, the Green parties of both England and Wales and Scotland, the Scottish National Party and Plaid Cymru towards Labour. That is the political logic from the government's point of view, for now at least.
And as for where all of this leads – well, good question. In the coming weeks, months and perhaps years, there may be a Back to the Future vibe to our political debate. A splash of familiarity, as a conversation about the relationship we have with our nearest neighbours resumes.

Authorities reported that the brief storm brought down trees onto roads, powerlines and roofs in the Northern Territory (NT) city of Alice Springs and nearby, causing blackouts that affected around 9,000 properties.

He said in a statement with the NT's Chief Minister, Lia Finocchiaro, that emergency crews would be deployed from the capital of Darwin to help clean up and restore power.
Residents in the affected area have been urged to show caution around fallen powerlines, trees and damaged infrastructure.
"The damage is significant but thank goodness there are no injuries reported," Yan said.
"We want to keep it that way. We need people to stay safe with powerlines and trees down all over town."
The weather bureau warned that similar storm cells could develop on Tuesday afternoon and evening. ■

CAIRO, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Czech shooter Jiri Privratsky scored 251.3 points to win the men's 10m air rifle gold medal at the International Shooting Sport Federation (ISSF) World Cup in Cairo on Monday.
Sweden's Marcus Madsen took silver with 250.2 points, while France's Dimitri Dutendas claimed bronze with 229.9.
Privratsky trailed Madsen by 0.3 points after 22 shots, but overtook the Swede on the penultimate shot, scoring 10.6 to Madsen's 9.8 to take a 0.5-point lead. The Czech then sealed victory with a final shot of 10.7, compared with Madsen's 10.1, extending his winning margin to 1.1 points.
Asked whether he had expected to win the gold medal, Privratsky said, "Not at all. Absolutely not."
"This was one of the toughest finals for me in a while because the scores were incredibly tight and very similar," he said. "Even just one shot could change everything, and that was extremely difficult."
In earlier World Cup events this season, Privratsky finished fourth in the 10m air rifle in Munich, fourth in the 50m rifle three positions in Hangzhou, and ninth in the same 50m event in Granada.
"It actually means quite a lot because this season wasn't very good for me in World Cups, as I didn't win any medals," he said. "So this one, especially in air rifle, is very valuable."
Earlier on Monday, Singapore's Teh Xiu Yi won the women's 25m pistol gold with 38 hits, ahead of France's Heloise Fourre with 37 and Bulgaria's Miroslava Mincheva with 32.
On Sunday, India's Udhayveer Sidhu won the men's 10m air pistol gold, followed by Germany's Christian Reitz and Italy's Paolo Monna.
In earlier finals, France's Camille Jedrzejewski and Theo Moczko won the 10m air pistol mixed team gold, with Latvia's Agate Rasmane and Emils Vasermanis taking silver and Ukraine's Olena Kostevych and Pavlo Korostylov bronze.
In the 10m air rifle mixed team, Japan's Nobata Misaki and Hanakawa Naoki won gold, followed by Croatia's Anamarija Turk and Miran Maricic, and Germany's Anna Janssen and Maximilian Ulbrich.
The ISSF World Cup in Cairo is the final Rifle/Pistol World Cup of the season ahead of the World Cup Final, which will be held in Rome from December 3 to 8. ■

'Super pest' fire ant nest found in logistics warehouse in Sydney
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
01:21:15 UTC
10:21:15 KST

In brief
- Surveillance and treatment will be expanded to a 2km radius of Sydney suburbs in the coming weeks.
- The Invasive Species Council warned the spread of fire ants could cost the Australian economy up to $2 billion a year.
Fire ants likely imported from overseas in a shipping container have landed at a critical logistics site, with measures underway to rapidly wipe them out.
A biosecurity team at the federal agriculture department detected the fire ant nest at the Enfield Intermodal Logistics Centre in Sydney's inner-west.
The nest was quickly treated at the centre, a facility for the freight industry, to prevent an infestation from taking hold.
Genetic analysis by the National Fire Ant Eradication Program confirmed the species as red imported fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) likely to have arrived from overseas via a container.
NSW Agriculture Minister Tara Moriarty said properties within a 500m radius of the freight facility would be inspected to keep to assure the community the fire ants were being eradicated.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"It's important to note that no further ants have been found, but we are focused on making sure any potential spread is identified and eradicated quickly," she said on Tuesday.
"While fire ants are one of the world's most invasive species, they can and have been successfully eradicated in NSW."
Why are fire ants a problem?
The Invasive Species Council warned the spread of the "super pest" could cost the Australian economy up to $2 billion a year.
The council's website says the ants, which first arrived at a Brisbane port in 2001, are one of the "world's worst invasive species" and their stings can kill people and livestock and "wipe out entire native ecosystems".
The federal department's entomologists confirmed the red and brown ants — two to six millimetres in length — are not related to the only other fire ant-impacted site in the country in south-east Queensland.
Further surveillance and treatment will be expanded to a 2km radius of Sydney suburbs in the coming weeks.
Fire ants were detected at Port Botany in 2014 and were successfully eradicated.
The council's advocacy director Reece Pianta warned the risk of fire ants spreading beyond Queensland's borders was still alive.
''This detection is a reminder of why we need to keep investing in strong border biosecurity and surveillance," he said.
"Fire ants are widespread among many of Australia's trading partners, so finding new incursions quickly is critical to stopping them becoming established."

"Diplomacy is the only way to reach agreement on security arrangements, consistent with international law," said Cordone.
Counterterrorism and refugee returns

AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – Fortnite-maker Epic Games is making a “huge pivot” towards using AI to boost video game development, chief executive Tim Sweeney said on Oct 12.
The American gaming giant is “moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration,” Sweeney wrote on X.
“The aim isn’t to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal,” he continued, referring to the company’s Unreal Engine which provides game development software to third-party users.

It also lands about six months after Epic said it would lay off more than 1,000 employees, though the company attributed the decision to broader issues like slower growth, rather than AI.
Ramping up its use of AI internally now will increase Epic’s ability “to survive the AI revolution, help other developers do the same, and come out on the other end making better code and content faster,” Sweeney wrote on Oct 12.

“Our job, as the provider of tools and technology to much of the industry, is to design for the present that is and the future that will soon be. Personally I’m optimistic about it and see it as empowering for creators,” Sweeney wrote in response.

Trump signals possible face-to-face meeting with North Korea's Kim during Asia tour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
00:31:34 UTC
09:31:34 KST

US President Donald Trump has said that he may meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his planned trip to Asia.
“I may, yeah. That'll be exciting, won't it? But I get along with him,” he said, speaking to reporters at the White House on Monday.
A meeting would mark a potential new chapter in Trump’s efforts to engage directly with Kim, with whom he held several historic meetings during his first term as president as the two leaders sought to address North Korea’s nuclear weapons program.
Trump will travel to the Philippines for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit on November 16, then head to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit from November 17–19.
Trump and Kim Jong-un first met on June 12, 2018, at the Singapore Summit.
The historic encounter took place at the Capella Hotel on Sentosa Island, marking the first-ever meeting between a sitting US president and a North Korean leader.
The two leaders shook hands, held private talks, and signed a joint statement committing to work toward complete denuclearisation of the Korean Peninsula, establish new US-DPRK relations, and pursue a lasting peace regime.
The summit followed months of heightened tensions, missile tests, and public threats in 2017, before both sides agreed to direct talks earlier in 2018.
It produced no binding denuclearisation deal but was widely described as a breakthrough in personal diplomacy that led to two more meetings in 2019.
In February 2019, Trump and Kim held their second summit in Hanoi, Vietnam, but the talks collapsed abruptly after the two leaders failed to bridge gaps over sanctions relief and North Korea’s nuclear programme.
Four months later, on June 30, 2019, they met for a third time at the DMZ in Panmunjom, where Trump briefly stepped onto North Korean soil — the first sitting US president to do so — and the pair agreed to restart stalled negotiations.
Trump’s latest statement comes a day after North Korea's launch of multiple ballistic missiles towards the East Sea.
The South Korean military confirmed the launch appeared to respond to South Korea's successful test of a hypersonic glide vehicle last week.
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) detected the launches originating from the Pyongyang region.

AI generated
WASHINGTON – Reddit has asked a federal judge to block its former law firm Proskauer Rose from defending Perplexity AI in a lawsuit alleging the AI search start-up company stole Reddit content, arguing it was dropped like a “hot potato” by lawyers who owed it client loyalties.
In a court filing on Oct 9 in Manhattan federal court, Reddit said Proskauer has a conflict of interest due to its past work for Reddit in a whistleblower case. Reddit also said Proskauer earlier vowed it would not represent Perplexity.
“Proskauer cannot drop Reddit like a hot potato in favour of Perplexity,” Reddit said in its filing.
Proskauer contends Reddit has no basis to disqualify the firm. In a court filing on Oct 9, the firm said its work for Reddit in the whistleblower matter did not create a conflict of interest that should bar the firm from representing Perplexity now. It also denied it ever agreed not to represent Perplexity.
Reddit declined to comment other than to refer to its court filings. Perplexity and Proskauer did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The case is part of a wave of copyright cases targeting AI companies over their alleged use of protected content for AI training. Proskauer argues Perplexity should be able to rely on its chosen counsel in a case exposing it to large potential damages.
Reddit filed the lawsuit in 2025, alleging Perplexity illegally scraped its online forums for data it needs for its online “answer engine” system. Perplexity has denied Reddit’s copyright infringement claims. Reddit has content licensing deals with Google and others for AI training. REUTERS

60% of 33 lakh who received SIR notices in Delhi are now verified
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
00:14:09 UTC
09:14:09 KST

NEW DELHI: Over 60% of the 33 lakh voters who got SIR notices in Delhi have been verified after the Election Commission eased the verification process late last month.BLOs are now visiting homes to collect documents, instead of requiring people to appear for hearings at govt offices. Also, BLO have been empowered to make corrections for minor issues, such as spelling mistakes, without seeking extensive documentation.About 33 lakh voters, including chief minister Rekha Gupta, AAP national convener Arvind Kejriwal, external affairs minister S Jaishankar and BJP veteran LK Advani got notices in Sept.
While over 19 lakh voters were flagged for "logical discrepancies", including mismatches in names and age-related inconsistencies, nearly 14 lakh were classified as "unmapped" because their records could not be linked to the 2002 SIR. The notices sought clarification and supporting documents to verify eligibility for inclusion in the final SIR roll, scheduled for Dec 4.Disposal of SIR notices expedited after mid-SeptemberThe office of the chief electoral officer of Delhi, in a post on X Monday, said: "We had started a proactive campaign to resolve these issues (discrepancies). By now around 20 lakh cases out of 33 lakh have been resolved. If any person has any grievance, please feel free to contact any of the 14,947 BLOs, 902 AEROs, 70 EROs, 13 DEOs or the CEO.
No eligible voter will be excluded from the voter list."An official told TOI, "The disposal of SIR notices was very slow until the third week of Sept but picked up after we introduced new measures. Nearly 15,000 BLOs have been asked to clear at least 10 notices daily. In cases involving logical discrepancies, they have been instructed to verify the voter's age, Indian citizenship and ordinary residence in the constituency. Eligible voters will not be removed merely because of logical inconsistencies in their records."A few BLOs told TOI they are using BLO declarations to verify voters with minor discrepancies, such as a missing letter in the name, after checking documents and getting the voter's signature on the declarations. Some BLOs said they had been using such declarations for quite some time now.AEROs, meanwhile, have been asked to upload details of resolved cases without delay. "We found that some AEROs were not uploading the cases they had already verified, partly because the deadline for completing the exercise was still weeks away. They have been instructed to ensure that resolved cases are uploaded promptly," said the official.
In cases where voters could not be mapped to the previous electoral rolls, BLOs have been asked to clear the cases promptly after taking and checking prescribed documents, such as a voter's date of birth and other documents.Delhi's electoral roll listed 1.56 crore voters in January 2025, days before the assembly elections. In June, when the SIR began, this number had shrunk to 1.45 crore. The draft electoral roll published on Aug 31 had 97.5 lakh voters, with around 47.6 lakh names deleted.EC said a majority of these people had shifted homes and failed to submit enumeration forms. Those who have received SIR notices are among the 97.5 lakh voters. The disposal of SIR notices and completion of verification will continue until Nov 30.
Alok K N Mishra is a New Delhi–based journalist with the Times of India, where he covers politics, governance and public policy. He follows the forces that shape national political behaviour, elections and policy making, and spends much of his time analysing the ever-changing Indian politics and governance dynamics. Before moving to the national capital, he reported extensively for years from Bihar and Jharkhand, gaining insights and experiences that continue to shape his understanding of politics, governance, administration, and public affairs and communication.

Pope Leo to enter hospital on Oct 13 for surgery on lung nodule
Unknown

Pope Leo to enter hospital on Oct 13 for surgery on lung nodule
- Pope Leo XIV will enter Rome’s Gemelli hospital on Oct 13 for surgery to remove a small lung nodule.
- The Vatican said the growth was found early and is “well-contained”, with recovery expected to take about a week and public events cancelled until Oct 20.
- Doctors said lung nodule surgery is usually minimally invasive and has a very low complication rate. Leo still plans an 11-day South America trip in November.
AI generated
VATICAN CITY – Pope Leo XIV was due to be hospitalised in Rome on Oct 13 ahead of surgery to remove a small growth on one of his lungs, in the first major health issue of his 17-month tenure.
Leo, 71, said on Oct 11 that a small nodule had been found on a check-up, was “well-contained” and had been spotted early.
He was expected to leave the Vatican for Rome’s Gemelli hospital late morning, the Vatican press office said, without specifying when the actual operation would take place.
Leo, elected by the world’s cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to have had health issues previously.
The Vatican has said his recovery is expected to take about a week. All his public events have been cancelled until Oct 20.
A nodule on the lung is a small, localised lesion that can be benign. The American Thoracic Society says fewer than 5% of lung nodules overall prove cancerous, although risk rises with age, size, and other factors such as smoking.
Dr Federico Venuto, chief of thoracic surgery at Rome’s Policlinico Umberto I hospital, said procedures to remove lung nodules are usually minimally invasive, and can sometimes involve use of a thin camera tube called a thoracoscope.
“The complication rate is extremely low,” he told Reuters.
The late Pope Francis, Leo’s predecessor, died at age 88 in April 2025 and was hospitalised several times as he grew frail in his later years.
Leo, who spoke in a firm, clear voice at his only public event on Oct 12, keeps a very busy schedule. He is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from Nov 6 to 17.
In the same address on Oct 11, when the Pope announced his need for surgery, Leo pledged he would go forward with the trip. REUTERS

Trump says Kimberly Guilfoyle could be fired as Greece envoy after alleged misconduct

Trump says Kimberly Guilfoyle could be fired as Greece envoy after alleged misconduct
- Published
President Donald Trump is weighing firing the US ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, following reports of her alleged improper behaviour in Athens, which she has denied.
Asked if he was considering sacking her, Trump told reporters at the White House: "We're looking at it. Yeah, we're not happy." She is the ex-fiancée of the president's son, Donald Trump Jr.
The Wall Street Journal reported Guilfoyle allegedly asked a Trump donor to pay her hefty credit card bill in exchange for access to his administration.
Her lawyers denied any wrongdoing by Guilfoyle and said she was owed the money for speaking engagements and consulting work for the donor.
Guilfoyle, 57, a former Fox News host and ex-wife of California Governor Gavin Newsom, was appointed as envoy to Athens in December 2024, a month before Trump returned to the White House as president.
At the time, Trump said "her extensive experience and leadership in law, media and politics, along with her sharp intellect make her supremely qualified" to represent the US abroad.
A series of text messages seen by the BBC - and first reported by the Wall Street Journal - appear to show Guilfoyle asking for the money from Eric Deters, a long-time Trump ally.
"It won't show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express," she wrote in one Signal message.
In another message - dated just days before her US Senate confirmation hearing last July - Guilfoyle wrote: "Honey please I need you to get this done for me today."
Deters never sent the money. Guilfoyle's lawyers have disputed the authenticity of the messages.
They said in a two-page statement on 12 October that Deters owed Guilfoyle about $150,000 for speeches and consulting work that she performed for him long before her ambassadorship.
"Asking a client to pay for work already done is not corruption. It is the opposite of corruption," they said.
Audio recordings obtained by the Wall Street Journal reportedly include Guilfoyle boasting of her connections to prominent Greek business tycoons who she said bankrolled luxury travel and flights on private jets.
According to the newspaper, she also boasted to an official in Athens that the US could topple the Greek government.
Democrats on the Senate and House foreign affairs committees have been calling on the state department to investigate her conduct in Greece.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was pictured with Guilfoyle last week during his trip to Athens, was also reported to be unhappy with her in light of the allegations.
A former prosecutor in San Francisco and Los Angeles, she joined Fox News in 2006.
After leaving broadcasting in 2018, she joined the Trump campaign. The same year, she began a relationship with Donald Jr, and the couple eventually became engaged.
The pair reportedly parted ways in 2024, around the time she was appointed to the position in Greece.
Donald Jr wed socialite and model Bettina Anderson last year in Florida.

NYT, Economist among publishers joining coalition to curb unpaid AI use
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
00:06:47 UTC
09:06:47 KST

NYT, Economist among publishers joining coalition to curb unpaid AI use
- The New York Times, AFP and The Economist joined the SPUR coalition to stop AI firms using publisher content without permission.
- SPUR now has more than 80 members in over 20 countries and is building standards to track AI use and support licensing deals.
- Publishers are also suing AI firms and losing traffic as AI search answers reduce clicks, with Google referrals down 33% globally, Reuters Institute said.
AI generated
NEW YORK- The New York Times, Agence France-Presse and The Economist on Oct 12 joined more than 40 publishers in a coalition aimed at preventing artificial intelligence firms from using or profiting from their content without permission.
The Standards for Publisher Usage Rights (SPUR) coalition, launched in February, now has more than 80 members across over 20 countries.
New members include The Atlantic and Brazil’s National Association of Newspapers, joining founding members such as the Financial Times, BBC and Associated Press.
Publishers are stepping up legal efforts to prevent AI companies from using their content without permission to train large language models.
Earlier in October, USA Today and several newspapers it owns sued OpenAI, alleging copyright infringement.
OpenAI and its backer, Microsoft, also face similar copyright claims from prominent authors and news organisations, including the New York Times.
SPUR, which is funded entirely by its members, is developing industry-wide standards and technical systems to help publishers track and control how AI companies use their content and facilitate licensing agreements, according to its website.
“Intellectual property protection and technological advancement can and must co-exist,” Rebecca Grossman-Cohen, the New York Times’ head of strategic partnerships and chief of staff, said in a statement.
Publishers are also grappling with declining referral traffic as search engines roll out AI-generated answers that allow users to consume information without clicking through to websites.
Google organic-search referrals to more than 2,500 websites fell 33% globally between November 2024 and November 2025, according to a Reuters Institute report, citing data from Chartbeat.
SPUR said it recently introduced its Content Telemetry Standard, designed to standardise how AI agents record and report their use of media content, as part of efforts to ensure creators are compensated for their work. REUTERS

Live: The manosphere unpacked. Our experts answer your questions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
00:00:53 UTC
09:00:53 KST

Experts weigh in on whether the manosphere is a 'passing wave' or 'tectonic shift'
If you're worried about the rise of the manosphere and the messages it's sending teenage boys and men about masculinity, relationships and their place in the world, you're not alone.
It's a complex topic with no easy solution, so we asked a panel of experts to answer your questions.
One early question from Stuart was whether what we're seeing now could be a "passing wave of online misogyny" or was it something bigger?
Clinical psychologist Zac Seidler from Movember said it would take more time to see exactly how the manosphere differs from other gender reckonings.
"It would be remiss of me not to say that this is in no way a 'passing wave',"
he said.
Dr Seidler said the "volume and ferocity" of online misogyny was being fuelled by tech platforms.
"The underpinning themes have not changed, their reach has."
How to start conversations
Many people also asked how parents can begin and approach conversations with their children about the topic.
Developmental paediatrician Billy Garvey said the reality was while these conversations might be scary, it's better we're involved to help guide our kids.
"Our best chance is to start with low pressure, when our kids feel safe," he said.
"Like during a walk around the block with just us or while playing together with no-one else around."
Dr Garvey said body language, tone of voice and lack of judgement were almost as important as what we say.
Genevieve Sheppard from Our Watch added that it's important to remember that content and the message of the manosphere are "harmful for everyone", boys and men included.
"The manosphere tells boys there's only one way to be a man and if they don't live up to that, they're considered a failure,"
she said.
"Boys need opportunities to build confidence, connection and belonging."
The experts also answered questions on when to intervene with someone in a manosphere spiral, how to spot that and how to help neurodivergent boys who might engage with that kind of content.
It's a topic that can be difficult, so if you or someone you know needs help, you'll find resources in the pinned post below.
You can catch up on the full Q&A below and stream The State of Man now on ABC iview.

Thank you for joining us
What a thoughtful bunch you are! Thank you for joining us and submitting such varied, nuanced and considered questions. We hope you found this blog interesting and useful.

Key Event
'No boy is really lost forever'
What gives experts hope that this trend can be reversed?
- Katie
Zac says:
Honestly, Katie, it's the everyday interactions I have with boys and men in the flesh. They give me hope. That's because the crap you see online has become so divorced from reality that we need to find a way to heal alongside each other, not be afraid of connecting and bridging our differences.
I'm worried we are getting to a place where our lived experiences are believed to be so radically different that we can't even sit across from someone and curiously, openly, respectfully disagree with them. Young men and women must coexist and find a way to do so safely. This should be our goal.
Billy says:
I've had the privilege of meeting so many boys who everyone else had given up on including clinicians. I've seen them journey from mental illness, substance abuse, aggression and violence to a place where they are strong because they connect with their emotions, develop healthy ways to express them and ask for help when it's too much. Then they learn to do that for others too.
I was a lost boy constantly told I would never amount to anything. Meeting these boys and being a small part of their healing has been one of the greatest experiences of my life and in my darkest days, including the last couple of weeks on social media, they still give me hope that no boy is really lost forever.
Genevieve says:
Great question!
Young people tell us they want to have positive, respectful relationships. They are already challenging sexist comments and supporting friends who have been harmed. Their parents are also doing a good job of opening up and seeking out thoughtful conversations — like many of the parents asking questions here today! Here's a link for parents looking for further guidance.
We are also seeing attitudes shift in the right direction, broadly speaking. ANROWS data shows that the understanding and attitudes of Australian adults towards violence against women and gender equality have significantly improved over time.
This shows that attitudes aren't fixed and can be influenced through effective prevention and education. What gives me hope is that these attitudes are learned, which means they can also be questioned and changed. The manosphere may be loud, but it doesn't speak for all boys and men.
How do I have a tricky conversation with a parent?
Any advice for how to navigate social situations with parents whose approach you don't agree with or foster unhealthy gender norms? e.g. A friend who tells his son he's being a 'wuss' if he cries. How do I protect my son from absorbing that information without making things awkward? Or should I just rip the bandaid off and say something?
- Amy
Billy says:
Often we feel stuck between remaining silent or unhealthy conflict, but there is a middle path. Our kids watch what we do more than what we say, so going towards the boy who is hurt or scared and saying something like, "That was scary. I'd be really upset if that happened to me. I'm sorry mate and I'm here for you."
Later on, we can chat with the other parent in a way that is positive and avoids shame, seomthing like:
"I've been learning about emotional development in boys from this awesome podcast and it says that if we help boys understand and express their feelings, they can develop strong mental health that will help them into their adult life when we aren't around as much. You're such a great role model for our boys, so I wonder if you could help me with it too as the boys really look up to you?"
What about tradwives?
Alongside the rise of the manosphere, there has been a rise in women's groups that reject aspects of modern feminism. Isn't this simply evidence that some young men and women want a return to traditional gender roles?
- Clement
Genevieve says:
There's always a broad spectrum of attitudes across any issue, that's completely normal. We know that this is a minority perspective; per Australian government research, nine in ten people believe gender equality is important.
The harms of traditional gender roles are well-documented. These dynamics tend to limit women's decision-making and autonomy, which can reinforce inequality. They also impact men's health, wellbeing and opportunities, restricting the ways they can express themselves and build emotionally open connections.
Conversations in the manosphere about traditional gender roles centre around dominance, ownership and possession.
In their view, these are not mutually respectful relationships built on equal footing, but a deliberate way to put men above women. That's harmful messaging for young people to be receiving as they begin to develop relationships and build romantic connections.
When to speak up
What should we do if we witness young boys discussing/professing manosphere ideology in public? Does respectfully confronting them create further division? Should we attempt to contact their schools if they’re in uniform?
- Cyrus
Zac replies:
As a stranger, a public confrontation rarely changes a young person's mind. Boys in a group are often performing for each other, and being challenged by an adult they don't know usually makes them double down so they don't lose face. It can confirm the story they've been sold, that adults and society are against them.
That doesn't mean saying nothing. If it feels safe, a light, calm comment can land better than a lecture. Something like "come on lads, you don't really believe that" gently signals that it's not OK without humiliating anyone. Sometimes just being an adult who isn't impressed is enough. And if someone nearby, especially a girl or woman, is being targeted, your first priority is supporting her.
When it comes to contacting schools, I'd be thoughtful. If it's harassment, threats or something that raises a safety concern, then yes, let the school know. If it's kids repeating things they've seen online, a calm, non-punitive heads-up can help the school understand what's going on with their students. But the aim should be to support the boys, not get them in trouble. Punishment alone tends to push this stuff underground.
Why now?
Why now? The manosphere movement has been a thing in various forms for over a decade. It's not like it hasn't been a problem until now. You could even argue that Movember as a movement owes some of its origins and early success to the Men's Rights Activists of the late 2000s-2010s.
- Matthew.
Zac says:
You're right that this isn't new. Pick-up artist forums, men's rights groups. and incel spaces have been around for well over a decade. What's changed is reach, speed and who they're speaking to.
A few things are different now:
- You used to have to go looking for these forums. Now short-form videos serve this content to 13-year-olds who never searched for it. We're seeing it in primary and early high school, not just among aggrieved adult men.
- Influencers have worked out that outrage and grievance pay, through courses, subscriptions and affiliate schemes. That's a strong incentive to keep pushing.
- Ideas that once lived on fringe forums now show up in podcasts with millions of listeners, in politics, and in schoolyard slang.
- The pandemic left a lot of young men isolated, anxious and online at exactly the moment this content was booming.
On Movember, I'd gently disagree. Movember started in Melbourne in 2003 as a group of mates bringing back the moustache. It grew into a men's health cause, starting with prostate cancer, and has had nothing to do with the men's rights movement (if anything, we actively challenge these narratives each day).
But there's a fair point underneath your question. Both grew out of the same reality: men's health, suicide and loneliness were being badly neglected. The difference is what you do with that. One path says, "men are struggling, so let's help them and the people around them." The other says, "men are struggling, and it's women's fault."
You can either zero-sum it and take it out on others, breeding division, or create a global movement that aims to bring people together (our movement has a huge female contingent!).

Neurodiversity and the manosphere

- Angus
Billy says:
I'm fortunate to have learnt so much from neurodivergent boys over the last 26 years. In the clinic, I'm increasingly seeing more who are falling victim to the manosphere, but it's not because of their neurodivergence but because of their experience of the world around them. They are more likely to experience exclusion, bullying, and loneliness which are exactly the wounds that these influencers target.
The key is to understand how each child learns about and engages with the world, especially neurodivergent children. We can harness those preferences to help them develop emotional and social beliefs and behaviours that build connections and friendships.
Autistic boys often thrive on detail, so we can help them understand algorithms and what might be behind this messaging. We can practise conversations where skills in perspective-taking, consent and conflict resolution are built in so that they are less likely to be isolated and lonely.
Overall, we must keep working towards building environments that harness the strengths within these boys so they feel celebrated within them. Often, neurodivergent children have a huge capacity for justice, empathy and shared enjoyment of specific interests. Instead of these experiences overwhelming them, we want to give them healthy outlets where they feel seen and supported. That way the part of the manosphere that harms them are less likely to find a place to land.
Why aren't men standing up?
Why is the gender violence towards women not outraging men and why aren't they showing their outrage by organising public demonstrations and demanding action to protect women and girls? Why the victim blaming?
- Rose
Zac says:
Thanks for this Rose. It's a really timely question and one that lots of men on my feed are thinking about and trying to tackle (this has to be men's work).
I'll try to explain the barriers as best I can, but these are by no means exhaustive, nor do they condone the lack of action we are seeing from men in the community.
- Many men are taught from boyhood that speaking up about anything emotional, or going against the group, is risky. Staying quiet feels safer than standing out, even when they disagree.
- When men hear "men's violence", many hear "you" and get defensive instead of engaged. That defensiveness isn't an excuse, but it does shut the conversation down before it starts.
- Psychologically, blaming the victim is a way of distancing: "that wouldn't happen to someone I know" or "a man like me wouldn't do that". It protects people from an uncomfortable truth that this is happening in their own circles.
- Many men still see violence against women as a women's issue, rather than something men cause and men can help stop.
Healthy manhood as we see it at Movember is about looking after yourself so you can also look after others. It means being active not passive when it comes to the health and wellbeing of those you love.
Speaking up and calling out certain behaviours in everyday moments is the key to making meaningful change in our communities.
Practical steps for supporting women
As a young woman who's passionate about gender equality and female health and safety, what are practical steps we can do to support our fellow females who are nervous to speak up?
- Jasmine
Genevieve says:
Thank you for being an ally! Your commitment and dedication to gender equality is deeply appreciated!
The data show that most people support gender equality and the safety of women and girls. Often, people feel like the issue is so big that they don't know what to do to help.
Supporting each other doesn't always mean confronting someone in the moment. Sometimes, it means checking in on someone privately, documenting a concern, or seeking support together.
The important thing is that women aren't left to manage sexism alone, that men don't believe the bar for being a good bloke is as simple as "not using violence", and that everyone's safety and choices are respected.
Some practical steps that everyone can take:
- Back each other up. Challenge sexist comments when it's safe to do so, or follow up privately.
- Check in. Ask what support someone needs without pressuring them to speak up.
- Stand alongside them. Offer to help raise concerns or approach a trusted person together.
- Amplify women's voices. Acknowledge their ideas and make sure they are heard.
- Respect their safety. Don't judge someone for staying silent or taking a different approach.
- Share the responsibility. Challenge sexism so women aren't left to manage it alone.
- Follow up. Check in after difficult situations and offer ongoing support.

Many adults across different roles in a child's life can have a positive impact, but some organisations have created resources specifically for dads and sons to discuss issues relating to the manosphere.

How can I reach my 15-year-old?
My son and his friends are naturally moving towards values from the 80s and 90s as they are tired of being told it is bad to be a man and men are always wrong. He is 15 and his generation has turned against woke culture. What are your thoughts?
- Matt
Genevieve says:
As The State of Man illustrates, a lot of the momentum pushing young men towards problematic attitudes isn't as natural as it might appear. Algorithms curated by billion-dollar tech companies and the well-financed manosphere movement are hugely impacting what young people see and believe.
The manosphere playbook relies on creating fear and division. It's important to remind your son that there's nothing wrong with being a boy or taking pride in being a man. It's when masculinity is restrictive and rigid, telling you there's only one way to be a man, that it becomes harmful.
Research shows that when boys grow up with flexible expectations of how to be a man, they are more likely to be happy and healthy, with greater freedom to express themselves, seek support and build positive relationships.
Many boys are already challenging ideas of what it means to be a man and finding positive ways to express who they are. Even if some online rhetoric says otherwise, there are some great positive examples pushing on the manosphere's fear-based messaging. The fact you're having these conversations with your son is a sign that he trusts you, and that's already really encouraging.
Manosphere vs masculinity content
Do we need to be careful to delineate between manosphere content and masculinity content? My view would be that there is value to some masculinity content that pushes the ideas of responsibility and confidence. Clearly though, it can become toxic when hijacked by some influencers.
- Patrick
Zac says:
Patrick, I completely agree, and this distinction matters a lot.
"Manosphere" has become shorthand for anything aimed at men online, and that's a problem. When we lump it all together, young men hear "everything you watch is bad", and we lose them. Plenty of content encourages men to look after their bodies, take responsibility, build discipline and back themselves. That's good for men's health.
At Movember, our research led by Dr Krista Fisher on masculinity influencers found exactly this complexity. Young men are engaging with this content in big numbers, and it's not all harmful. Some of it does help. But we also found that the more young men trusted certain influencers, the more likely they were to hold harmful attitudes towards women, and some were doing worse on mental health measures.
So where's the line? A few questions I'd ask of any content:
- Does it build you up or tear others down? Confidence is great. Confidence that depends on women or "weaker" men being beneath you isn't.
- Does it make room for struggle? Healthy content lets men be human. Toxic content treats vulnerability as weakness.
- Is it about growth or grievance? "Take responsibility for your life" is very different from "the world's against you, and here's who to blame".
- What's it selling? Be wary when the answer to every problem is a paid course.
The goal isn't to take masculinity content away from young men. It's to help them tell the difference, and to make sure the good stuff is louder than the bad. The Movember Young Men's Media Collective is one of the ways we're trying to do that: pumping out some more of the good stuff to young guys' algorithms with content creators who get it.
A dad worried about the future
I'm raising a wonderful little dude (3 years old), and worry about the language used to describe men and masculinity as he grows up. I personally ditched social media after COVID and so haven't been subjected to the manosphere or the algorithm quicksand, but am aware that he will likely encounter it or versions of it over the next 15 years. Billy says:
What a beautiful hope, and I share your worry too, as a dad to my own son. Too often, masculinity is only brought up as a negative thing that we should be ashamed of. Masculinity isn't the problem, though. It's the rigid, shallow and narrow version that we must comply with that harms us and others too.
We can work together to create versions of masculinity that are different to that though, we can role model true emotional vulnerability, caregiving, creative expressions and healthy intimacy. We can show boys that anger is OK, but aggression, intimidation and violence have no place as ways of dealing with it.
Instead, they learn to see anger as an internal signal that something is wrong and if they can't handle it alone they ask for help instead of burying it or letting it explode. That alone would change the world for the better.

Combatting normalised misogyny

- Thea
Genevieve says:
The unfortunate reality is misogyny is already normalised. That shouldn't be a cause of pessimism, but it adds to the urgency of acting to combat it. The good news is, evidence tells us young people want to help and are asking for help developing the skills to be part of the solution.
To get there, schools, parents and online spaces need to work hand-in-hand to be as effective as possible.
At schools, this looks like a committed approach to Respectful Relationships Education. That goes beyond a one-off lesson or guest speaker at school.
It also looks like school leadership taking gender equality seriously and making it a part of day-to-day life: having zero tolerance for disrespect towards women and girls, having an inclusive uniform policy and creating a learning environment that supports young people in challenging rigid gender stereotypes.
But this work goes beyond schools. Parents need to engage in open and safe conversations and create space for young people to be vulnerable. Parents should show curiosity and avoid judgement. Creating this space isn't about knowing all of the answers or having one big chat, it's about regular everyday small conversations.
Our Watch research shows that young people (in particular young men) want to have these conversations with their parents, but it also shows that parents lack confidence. Our Watch has developed guidance to help parents start having those conversations.
When should we intervene?

Billy says:
There is no one thing that builds any aspect of child development such as self-esteem, emotional regulation or resilience.
The beautiful thing is there are opportunities all through the life course to build healthy beliefs and behaviours about masculinity. Secure attachment for boys in their early years is essential and the research shows that sensitive and responsive parenting, especially from fathers to sons, helps to build healthy emotional and social development in children.
Schools are best placed to support children when they prioritise safety and belonging for all children, and true inclusion means that every single child makes us stronger through the unique strengths they bring to the group. They should have more independence and autonomy from us as parents, but we should still be a part of that journey as a safe harbor they can come to for advice and emotional support.

Can the government fix this?
Given the eSafety Commissioner currently does not have the power to stop the live stream of the death by firing squad sentence in the USA in December, how can we be confident that the Australian government can stop or even help reduce the influence online platforms have and how they exacerbate issues around gender and the manosphere?
