====================================================================================================

Musicians are less prone to the ventriloquism illusion, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
22:00:30 UTC
07:00:30 KST

An experiment comparing musicians and nonmusicians found that musicians tend to be less susceptible to the ventriloquism effect. When a sound came from one location and a visual flash from another, musicians’ judgments of where the sound came from were pulled less toward the flash than nonmusicians’ judgments were. The paper was published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance.
The ventriloquism effect is a multisensory illusion in which a sound is perceived as coming from the location of a nearby visual stimulus rather than from its true source. It occurs because the brain normally combines information from different senses and gives greater weight to vision when judging where something is located.
This ability to integrate sights and sounds is essential in everyday life, but the brain must also recognize when sensory signals come from different sources and should remain separate. Musical training may be especially relevant to this process because musicians spend years learning to coordinate highly precise auditory, visual, and motor information. Previous studies have found that musicians are better than nonmusicians at detecting mismatches between simple sounds and visual events, and two earlier experiments by the same team found that musicians showed less ventriloquism when asked to locate only the sound.
Study author Matthew Paul O’Donohue of Queensland University of Technology in Australia and his colleagues wanted to understand why. Musicians might be less susceptible to the illusion because they perceive sounds or sights more precisely, or because they have a weaker built-in expectation that a sound and a flash come from the same source. Based on their earlier work, the researchers predicted, in a plan registered before data collection, that the second explanation would hold.
Study participants were 35 musicians and 35 nonmusicians, most of them first-year psychology students. The musicians averaged 22 years of age and the nonmusicians 20, and each group included 26 women. Musicians were defined as people with at least 7 years of experience playing an instrument who had played for an average of 1 hour a week over the past 12 months; on average, they had played their main instrument for about 12 years. Nonmusicians had no more than 12 months of experience playing an instrument outside school and no more than 2 years of compulsory music lessons in school.
Participants sat in a dark room facing a screen that hid five speakers. On each trial, a brief flash, a burst of noise, or both appeared from one of five positions along a horizontal line, and participants used a mouse to mark where each stimulus had come from. When both appeared, participants located each one separately, which required them to divide their attention between hearing and vision. On these combined trials, the flash and the sound came from the same position only 20% of the time.
Participants completed the full set of 420 trials twice. Before the second run, they were told that the flash and the sound came from the same location only 20% of the time, and they were reminded of this at the start of each block. This allowed the researchers to test whether a simple instruction could change people’s expectations, and whether musicians’ advantage stemmed from assumptions formed during the experiment itself, in which case the instruction should have erased the difference between the groups.
Musicians and nonmusicians were equally precise at locating the flash or the sound when only one was presented. For both groups, flashes were located less consistently the farther they appeared from straight ahead.
When both stimuli were presented, musicians’ sound judgments were pulled about 1.6 degrees less toward the flash than nonmusicians’ were, on average. This difference was modest; it held up in one of the two statistical approaches the researchers used but fell just short in the other. After participants learned the 20% figure, the ventriloquism effect shrank overall, but musicians still showed less of it than nonmusicians.
To explain these results, the researchers used a mathematical model of how the brain decides whether to combine information from two senses. The model attributed the group difference to musicians’ lower prior expectation that the sound and the flash came from the same place, rather than to differences in how precisely they could hear or see. The instruction lowered this expectation overall, but nearly all participants who had started out with an expectation below 20% raised it, suggesting that people adjusted their expectations to match the information they were given.
“Our results suggest that musicians tend to exhibit less spatial ventriloquism than nonmusicians even when distributing their attention across audition and vision. … Finally, we have shown that this prior expectation changes when participants are informed of the true probability of a common location for the stimuli, demonstrating that top–down factors can exert a strong influence on this Bayesian prior,” the study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of the ventriloquism effect. However, because the researchers compared existing musicians with nonmusicians rather than assigning people to musical training, the study cannot show that musical training itself reduces the illusion, as opposed to other traits that differ between the groups. The difference between musicians and nonmusicians was also small, and numerically much smaller than in the team’s earlier experiments, in which participants only had to locate the sound.
The authors also note that the musicians played a wide range of instruments, and that some subgroups, such as orchestral musicians, might show stronger auditory spatial skills or combine visual cues differently. In addition, it is not yet known whether the instruction changed what participants perceived or simply changed how they chose to respond.
The paper, “A Multisensory Causal Inference Prior is Attenuated in Musicians and is Further Attenuated Following Instruction,” was authored by Matthew Paul O’Donohue, Naohide Yamamoto, Brian Odegaard, and Philippe Lacherez.

Tyeb Mehta's 'Rickshaw Puller' fetches record 69 crore
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
21:55:44 UTC
06:55:44 KST

In 2002, a Tyeb Mehta triptych aptly titled Celebration, from The Times of India collection, set off quite a party in the Indian art market when it became the first Indian painting to cross the crore mark at auction. Though it came in the winter of his life, it was a remarkable milestone for an artist who had spent much of his life in a cramped one-room Bombay apartment that doubled as a studio by day and a bedroom at night. Since that landmark sale, prices for Mehta's paintings, including those featuring his signature bulls, have bull-dozed many old records. The latest is Rickshaw Puller, which fetched Rs 69.1 crore at Volte Una's inaugural auction, setting a world auction record for the artist. The sale surpassed Mehta's earlier personal high of Rs 61.8 crore, set by Trussed Bull in April 2025. Rickshaw Puller is now the fourth-most expensive Indian work of art ever sold at auction. The top spot belongs to Raja Ravi Varma (Rs 167 crore), followed by M F Husain in both second and third.Mehta first encountered rickshaw pullers as a young boy during summer holidays spent with his grandmother in Kolkata and they became a recurring theme.
In his early works, the rickshaw puller was a sombre figure rendered in greys and deep reds. In the 2002 painting that set the record on Sunday, man and machine seem almost fused into one, yet one can feel the physical exhaustion of hauling passengers through the city's sweltering streets.
The record is particularly striking for an artist known for his exacting standards, who routinely destroyed works he considered unworthy. It also marks a significant debut for Volte Una, a new auction house built around an unusual premise: offering one major work at a time rather than multiple lots in a single sale. The format is designed to give collectors time to engage closely with each artwork before bidding, with an emphasis on privacy."Why should a masterpiece be lost in a crowd? This way, we could expose Tyeb Mehta's painting to the most serious and discreet collectors globally in private settings," said Tushar Jiwarajka, founder of Volte Una. "We have introduced a business model that allows traditional buyer's premium to be significantly reduced, cutting transaction costs for both buyers and sellers."

Scientists uncover the 2.3-billion-year-old secret that helped keep Earth habitable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
21:27:10 UTC
06:27:10 KST

Scientists uncover the 2.3-billion-year-old secret that helped keep Earth habitable
Researchers may have solved a 2.3-billion-year-old mystery about how Earth's oceans helped keep the planet oxygen-rich and habitable.
- Date:
- October 12, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Riverside
- Summary:
- Scientists may have solved a 2.3-billion-year-old mystery about how Earth maintained enough oxygen to support life. Ancient rocks reveal that phosphorus recycling in the oceans created a self-sustaining cycle that helped keep oxygen levels high, even as the planet underwent dramatic environmental changes. The discovery challenges assumptions about Earth's early atmosphere and raises new questions about why complex life took so long to emerge.
- Share:
More than 2 billion years ago, Earth underwent a dramatic transformation as oxygen began building up in its atmosphere. But that change left scientists with a major mystery: How did the planet maintain enough oxygen to remain habitable over millions of years?
Researchers have now uncovered evidence that the answer may lie in an ancient recycling system within Earth's oceans. By studying rocks from South Africa, they found that changes in ocean chemistry helped create a natural cycle in which biological activity supported the continued accumulation of atmospheric oxygen.
The research, published in Nature Communications, involved scientists including University of California, Riverside geologist Andrey Bekker. Their findings suggest that phosphorus, a nutrient essential for life, played a central role in sustaining the oxygen levels that would eventually help make more complex organisms possible.
How Ancient Oceans Helped Sustain Earth's Oxygen
About 2.3 billion years ago, Earth experienced the Great Oxidation Event, a major turning point when oxygen became a lasting component of the atmosphere. Scientists have understood this transition for decades, but explaining how oxygen remained sufficiently abundant afterward has been much more difficult.
The researchers identified a feedback loop that may help explain what happened. As oxygen spread into the oceans, it altered the chemistry of seawater and increased concentrations of sulfate, a compound containing sulfur and oxygen.
Certain microbes used this sulfate to break down organic material more efficiently. In the process, they released phosphorus back into the water, making this vital nutrient available to other organisms.
With more phosphorus available, biological productivity increased. That meant more organic carbon could eventually become buried in seafloor sediments rather than being broken down. Because the decomposition of organic matter can consume oxygen, burying more carbon helped favor the continued buildup of oxygen in the atmosphere.
This created a reinforcing cycle in which rising oxygen levels encouraged chemical changes that supported biological growth, which in turn helped maintain atmospheric oxygen.
"Living things cannot grow or function properly without phosphorus," Bekker said. "Once more of it became available in the oceans, it allowed more organic carbon to be buried. A side effect of that process is that more oxygen continued to be released into the atmosphere."
Ancient Rocks Reveal a Hidden Phosphorus Cycle
To investigate this process, the scientists examined ancient rock samples from South Africa using a technique that provides a more detailed picture of phosphorus availability in prehistoric oceans.
Earlier research could determine how much phosphorus was present in ancient rocks, but those measurements revealed little about whether organisms could actually use it. Some phosphorus becomes trapped in minerals, making it effectively inaccessible to living things.
The researchers addressed this limitation by separating phosphorus according to the minerals that contained it. They accomplished this by dissolving different mineral components one at a time, allowing them to distinguish phosphorus that had been available for biological activity from phosphorus locked away in mineral structures.
This distinction is crucial because the total amount of phosphorus in an ocean does not necessarily indicate how much is available to sustain life. The new approach provides a clearer way to reconstruct ancient nutrient cycles and understand how they influenced atmospheric oxygen.
"We can now separate the phosphorus that was available to organisms from phosphorus that was essentially locked away," Bekker said. "That gives us a much clearer picture of nutrient levels in ancient oceans than we had before."
Earth's Oxygen History May Have Been More Turbulent Than Expected
The findings also point to a more complicated history of Earth's atmosphere than scientists previously recognized.
Rather than remaining relatively steady after the Great Oxidation Event, oxygen levels may have risen and fallen much more dramatically. These fluctuations likely continued to influence ocean chemistry and the movement of essential nutrients through marine environments over tens of millions of years.
The results could also change how scientists interpret the evolution of early life.
One longstanding question is why complex organisms took so long to appear after oxygen first became a significant part of Earth's atmosphere. Limited oxygen has often been considered a possible explanation for this delay.
However, if oxygen remained relatively abundant during extended periods of Earth's early history, it raises the possibility that other environmental conditions or biological limitations played a greater role in slowing the emergence of complex life.
What Earth's Ancient Oxygen Cycle Means for the Future
Although the research focuses on events billions of years in the past, its implications extend to the oceans we depend on today.
Climate change is already contributing to declining oxygen levels in parts of the world's oceans. If oxygen loss continues, it could disrupt phosphorus recycling and reduce the amount of this essential nutrient available to marine organisms.
Such changes could limit biological productivity and make ocean ecosystems less resilient to environmental stress.
The findings may also help scientists search for signs of life beyond Earth. Worlds with oceans are considered promising places to investigate potential habitability, but the presence of water alone does not guarantee that conditions can support life over long periods.
Understanding how oxygen, nutrients, and biological processes interacted throughout Earth's history could help researchers identify similar chemical relationships on distant planets and other ocean-bearing worlds.
"Earth's history shows that oxygen, nutrients, and life evolved together," Bekker said. "Understanding those connections gives us a more nuanced perspective on our own planet's future and what we might look for on other planets."
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of California - Riverside. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Lewis J. Alcott, Benjamin J. W. Mills, Andrey Bekker, Zidong Peng, Simon W. Poulton. A nutrient control on oxygenation dynamics during Earth’s Great Oxidation Episode. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-76597-y

"In our view, a sharper tightening would do little to prevent the imminent energy-driven inflation peak but would weaken growth and employment," the report said. "In a high energy price scenario, we expect bank rate rises to as high as 4.75 percent next year."
The report acknowledged that investment and productivity improvements offer a route to stronger medium-term growth, but noted the outcome is highly uncertain.
Recent strength in business investment, particularly in information and communications technology and artificial intelligence-related activity, is encouraging, but if investment raises demand without broad productivity benefits, it would fuel more inflation and higher interest rates, the report said. ■

"They also reported sharp increases in commodity prices and growing fuel shortages, threatening the continuity of essential health and water services."
OCHA said that inadequate shelter, unsafe sanitation facilities, food insecurity and limited access to health care are exposing displaced women and girls to heightened risks of violence, exploitation and abuse. Across Yemen, funding cuts mean that 72 percent of women and girls' safe spaces have closed. In addition, 73,000 dignity kits are urgently needed to support displaced women and girls.
Civilian casualties continue to rise. According to figures from the UN Human Rights Office, OCHA said that since the start of August, at least 54 civilians have been killed, half of them children. A further 171 civilians have been injured, including 107 women and children.
OCHA said it continues to work with partners to monitor displacement, assess emerging needs and coordinate the response. GOMA, DR Congo, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Former President of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) Joseph Kabila was named head of a newly formed political-military alliance on Monday, bringing the political and military leaders of the March 23 Movement (M23) rebellion under his leadership.
The new alliance, known as the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), was unveiled at an event attended by Kabila and senior M23 officials in Goma, the capital of North Kivu Province.
Under the new leadership structure, Corneille Nangaa, a leading figure in the rebel coalition, Bertrand Bisimwa, a senior M23 leader, and Sultani Makenga, the M23's military commander, were appointed the FRN's three vice presidents.
The FRN replaces the Congo River Alliance, the political coalition allied with the M23 rebels. It also brings together several other armed groups.
The announcement came three days after Kabila, who ruled the DRC from 2001 to 2019, delivered an address to the nation on Friday, calling for an inclusive national dialogue to solve the country's crisis.
On Sept. 30, 2025, the DRC's High Military Court sentenced Kabila to death in absentia on charges including treason and crimes against humanity.
According to the verdict, Kabila was found guilty of multiple offenses, including participation in an insurrectional movement, intentional homicide, torture and rape, in a case linked to his alleged involvement with the M23 rebellion in eastern DRC.
Since January 2025, the security situation in eastern DRC has sharply deteriorated, with renewed fighting involving the M23, which has seized control of several strategic areas, including Goma. ■

Shanghai wins 1st WIPO City of Innovation award
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
05:24:24 CST
06:24:24 KST

WIPO Director General Daren Tang (L) presents an award to Chinese city Shanghai during the Inaugural Award Ceremony for the first WIPO City of Innovation award at the headquarters of the WIPO in Geneva, Switzerland, Oct. 12, 2026. Chinese city Shanghai, Britain's Liverpool and Belgium's Charleroi were announced Monday by the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) as winners of the first WIPO City of Innovation award. (Xinhua/Lian Yi)
GENEVA, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Chinese city Shanghai, Britain's Liverpool and Belgium's Charleroi were announced Monday by the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) as winners of the first WIPO City of Innovation award.
Launched for the first time in 2026, the WIPO City of Innovation award is open to cities across all 194 WIPO member states and is bestowed on visionary cities for their bold pledges to foster innovation and creativity over the coming year. The three winners were chosen from 15 finalist cities.
According to WIPO, Shanghai's vision is to strengthen its position as an international hub for science, technology and intellectual property (IP), while fostering a broader culture of innovation and creativity. Its pledges include expanding IP education and services, opening innovation infrastructure and data, supporting cultural and creative industries, and strengthening connections between research, industry, entrepreneurs and investors.
Zhou Yaming, Deputy Secretary-General of the Shanghai Municipal People's Government, said the award represents WIPO's strong recognition of Shanghai's innovative developments and its efforts in building a thriving IP ecosystem.
"It also reflects the international community's endorsement of China's commitment to open innovation, mutual benefits and shared success," He said.
Winners were selected by an independent international jury of high-profile experts in the cultural and creative sectors, urban planning, community development, and innovation-driven growth.
Andrea Dempster Chung, member of the International Jury Panel and Co-Founder & Executive Director for Kingston Creative, said Shanghai's application was extremely impressive, not just because of its strong research and development base that the city already had, but for the sheer scale of its ambitions and the strength of pledges.
"This would be pivotal in shifting the city's future and this is one of the reasons why Shanghai was selected," she said. ■

JERUSALEM, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Israeli human rights group Yesh Din said Monday it had documented 377 incidents of Israeli settler and soldier violence across 162 Palestinian communities in the West Bank over a two-week period ending Saturday.
In a statement, the group said the incidents included 58 cases of violence and physical assaults against olive harvesters, 57 cases in which Palestinians were prevented from harvesting, 100 incidents of crop theft and 34 cases of damage to or destruction of olive trees.
Israeli soldiers were present in at least 44 of the olive harvest-related incidents, representing 25 percent of the total, the group said.
It noted that the findings demonstrate a systematic pattern of violence aimed at preventing Palestinians from harvesting olives, damaging their livelihoods and forcing them off their land.
It also accused Israeli authorities of failing to enforce the law against violent settlers and soldiers, arguing that the lack of accountability enables continued attacks and restrictions on Palestinian farmers. ■

Explainer: What pay raises, ice cream prices reveal about 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
05:24:12 CST
06:24:12 KST

STOCKHOLM, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Imagine receiving an extra 1,000 U.S. dollars this month, would you spend it differently if it were a one-time bonus rather than a permanent monthly pay raise?
The distinction may seem simple, but it lies at the heart of research that earned Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences on Monday "for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization," according to the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.
Behind the technical wording is a simple idea: to understand how an entire economy works, economists must first understand how households decide what to spend and businesses decide what to charge.
WHAT DID THE LAUREATES DISCOVER?
Hall helped explain why the relationship between income and consumption is more complicated than traditional economic models have assumed.
People generally prefer to maintain relatively stable spending over time, rather than dramatically changing their consumption whenever income rises or falls. Their decisions therefore depend partly on what they expect to earn in the future.
That helps explain why a one-time bonus and a permanent pay raise may lead to different spending decisions. Whether the extra income was expected also matters.
In a 1978 study, Hall argued that if households already incorporate all available information into their spending plans, changes in consumption should largely depend on new, unexpected information.
For example, a long-anticipated pay raise may already have influenced someone's spending decisions before the money arrives. An unexpected job loss, however, could force an immediate reassessment.
The distinction matters for policymakers: the impact of tax cuts or government payments depends not only on how much money households receive, but also on their expectations and financial circumstances.
Woodford, meanwhile, helped explain how businesses' pricing decisions, together with household consumption, shape the broader economy.
At Monday's Nobel announcement, an ice cream price illustrated the point. An ice cream seller may set prices for an entire season because changing them repeatedly costs time and money, such as printing new menus.
Economists call this phenomenon "sticky prices," meaning that prices do not immediately adjust to changes in demand or production costs.
Because prices may remain unchanged for some time, businesses must also consider future costs and competitors' prices when setting them. When demand weakens and prices remain fixed, businesses may respond by reducing production and employment.
Woodford's 2003 book presented a New Keynesian macroeconomic model built on microeconomic foundations, bringing together household decisions based on expectations about the future, sticky prices and interest rate policy.
WHY DO THEIR DISCOVERIES MATTER?
Traditional Keynesian models had long guided economic stabilization policies, such as lowering interest rates and increasing government spending during recessions.
However, the oil crises of the 1970s exposed their limitations, as inflation rose alongside unemployment and challenged previously assumed relationships between key economic variables.
Hall and Woodford's research helped lay the foundation for a new generation of models showing how government and central bank policies can influence household and business decisions.
By incorporating expectations about the future, these models also showed why communicating policy intentions can be an important tool for economic stabilization.
Speaking to reporters after winning the prize, Woodford pointed to the 2008 global financial crisis, when conventional interest-rate cuts proved insufficient to restore economic activity.
One alternative was "forward guidance," through which central banks communicate how they expect interest rates to evolve.
Such announcements can influence households' spending and businesses' investment decisions even before interest rates change.
The models have also helped policymakers better understand economic shocks, including sudden increases in energy prices that can push inflation higher while slowing growth.
"The laureates' work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world," John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said.
For policymakers, understanding decisions about household budgets and business prices can help them respond to economic shocks and soften the economy's ups and downs. ■

LONDON, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Two Iranian nationals have been sanctioned by Britain for their "hostile activity" on behalf of Iran, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said in a statement on Monday.
They are now "subject to an immediate asset freeze, travel ban and director disqualification," Miliband said.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday that it was "highly likely" that Iran was involved in last month's incident at Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford, the BBC reported Monday.
"We recognize the United Kingdom's attribution of Iran's involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford on 27 September," according to a joint statement released on Monday by the foreign ministers of 29 countries, including Britain and the United States.
On Sept. 27, British police evacuated homes near RAF Fairford. Seven people have since been arrested on suspicion of explosives offenses and preparing an act of terror. The seven suspects, all in their 20s, have been released on bail.
Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi rejected on Sept. 30 the British government's claim that Iran has "played a part" in a recent incident near the RAF Fairford, a base hosting the U.S. Air Force in southwest England. ■

Unknown Publisher

MADRID, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- High-speed rail services between Madrid and Barcelona were suspended in both directions on Monday after a fire broke out on an AVE train in northeastern Spain, forcing the evacuation of 283 passengers, rail operator Renfe said.
The fire was detected in the train's rear driving cab at around 4:05 p.m. (1405 GMT) near Ricla in Zaragoza province. The train had departed Madrid's Puerta de Atocha station, bound for Figueres near the French border.
All passengers were evacuated under safety protocols with no injuries reported. Firefighters from Zaragoza's provincial fire service responded to the incident.
Renfe warned that the suspension could last throughout Monday and offered free ticket changes and refunds for affected services. No timetable for restoring services was immediately available. ■

SANAA/RIYADH, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Monday evening that it had launched a new ballistic missile strike on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, while Tehran reiterated its readiness to facilitate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a statement that the group targeted the Riyadh airport with a ballistic missile, claiming the missile "accurately hit" the target.
He said the group also launched a drone attack on King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait, southwestern Saudi Arabia, claiming a direct hit.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition said in a statement that its forces had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile fired toward Riyadh on Monday evening.
Explosions were heard in the Saudi capital around the time of the reported attack, and residents received alerts via mobile apps.
The Houthi group has intensified strikes on the Riyadh airport in recent days.
Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said Monday that a Pakistani resident was killed and 11 others injured in a strike targeting the airport Sunday afternoon.
The authority said it had extended the suspension of operations at the airport.
A Saturday Houthi strike on the airport killed 12 people and injured 309 others, according to the authority.
Also on Monday, the Houthis said Saudi Arabia had carried out 119 strikes on several Houthi-held areas over the past 24 hours.
Houthi-run al-Masirah TV reported that at least nine people were killed and seven others injured in airstrikes on Al-Jawf, a province near the border with Saudi Arabia.
Yemeni military spokesperson Majid al-Nuzaili said in the day that government forces had carried out 1,879 attacks on Houthi military targets in recent hours, claiming that about 950 Houthi fighters had been "neutralized."
The escalation has sparked mounting regional and international concern.
At a weekly press conference on Monday, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran has "repeatedly expressed readiness to use our good offices to facilitate dialogue between the (warring) parties."
His remarks came a day after Iran's Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi, in a phone conversation with his Saudi counterpart Prince Faisal bin Farhan bin Abdullah Al Saud on Sunday, voiced Iran's readiness to provide "any kind of assistance" to help initiate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the Yemeni government. The renewed fighting marked a major escalation after a UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted major hostilities. ■

News Analysis: Türkiye likely to offer Riyadh defense tech, not combat troops under Mecca pact
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
05:23:59 CST
06:23:59 KST

ISTANBUL, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement signed by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye is facing its first major test following a deadly attack by Yemen's Houthi group on Riyadh's international airport, raising questions about how far Türkiye is willing and able to go in defending its partner.
Analysts say Ankara is more likely to provide Saudi Arabia with defense technology than combat troops, as Türkiye seeks to avoid direct involvement in the conflict.
The Mecca alliance announced on Oct. 5 that it would deploy forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia in response to intensified Houthi strikes on the kingdom. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan later emphasized that the pact, signed in Mecca on Aug. 7, is purely defensive in nature and does not authorize offensive military operations.
As the proposed deployment of forces to Saudi Arabia moves closer to parliamentary approval in Türkiye, public debate has emerged over the risks of the country being drawn into the conflict.
Rather than taking on a direct combat role, Türkiye is likely to contribute to the pact through diplomatic initiatives, defense technology and intelligence cooperation, with unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), air defense systems and cyber capabilities serving as key assets, Canan Tercan, a foreign policy expert at Istanbul Aydin University, told Xinhua.
Mustafa Enes Esen, a former Turkish diplomat, echoed this assessment, saying Türkiye's contribution would remain largely technical.
Türkiye is preparing to provide equipment, intelligence and drone operators, Esen said, adding that Ankara intends to use the pact to advance its defense ties with Saudi Arabia rather than fight Riyadh's war.
This approach builds on recent momentum in bilateral relations, he noted. In 2023, Türkiye and Saudi Arabia signed the largest defense export contract in Turkish history, centered on the sale of Akinci combat drones.
By limiting its role to defending Saudi facilities rather than targeting Houthi forces in Yemen, Ankara, Esen said, could expand its regional influence without inviting a backlash.
Under Article 92 of the Turkish Constitution, the deployment of Turkish armed forces abroad requires authorization from the Grand National Assembly.
Analysts note that Ankara could focus on providing technical and intelligence support, including drone operators and air defense specialists, rather than deploying combat troops, thereby avoiding a potentially contentious debate over direct military involvement.
Taking a cautious view of the Mecca pact's role in collective defense, Baris Doster, an international relations scholar at Marmara University, said that unless the three parties face a common threat, the agreement is more likely to serve as a symbolic diplomatic gesture than as an operational military alliance. ■

WASHINGTON, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- U.S. Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar's home in Washington, D.C., was searched early Monday by Immigration and Customs Enforcement investigators, the latest high-profile incident involving immigration as midterm elections draw closer.
Omar represents Minnesota's 5th Congressional District in the U.S. House of Representatives, which includes Minneapolis and surrounding suburbs. She was the first African refugee to become a member of Congress, the first woman of color to represent Minnesota, and one of the first two Muslim-American women elected to Congress.
CBS News quoted sources as saying that the investigation reportedly concerns her immigration paperwork.
NBC News, meanwhile, reported that the search is part of a years-long criminal investigation by Homeland Security Investigations, the U.S. attorney in Minneapolis and the Department of Justice, and "deals partly with immigration and fraud," citing a source familiar with the investigation.
The search took place roughly three weeks before the midterm elections, with Omar seeking re-election to her seat in Minnesota.
The Democratic representative said on social media that she was fine and called this a targeted operation.
"Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation," Omar wrote on X. "I will not be silenced."
Trump has repeatedly lashed out at Omar, a member of Congress's progressive wing, criticizing her political positions and telling her to "go back" to where she came from.
Born in Somalia, Omar and her family fled the country's civil war when she was eight years old. The family spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya before moving to the United States in the 1990s. ■

Steve Smith is being assessed by the Australian team after being hit on the helmet while batting on day four of the first Test against South Africa.
Smith continued batting, but did not take the field when Australia fielded late on day four in Durban.
What's next?
Smith is expected to be tested again on Tuesday morning in Durban, and will continue to be assessed for as long as Australia sees fit.
Australia will continue to test Steve Smith for a delayed concussion, after the vice-captain's blow to the head added further questions around the side for the second Test.
Smith did not take the field on day four in Durban, after being struck on the side of the helmet by a short ball from South African speedster Anrich Nortje while batting in the morning session.
The 37-year-old was assessed on the field and passed a test, appearing unfazed as he reached 27 in Australia's pursuit of quick runs.
However, Australia opted to keep him off the field in case there had been a concussion, and conduct further tests. As of stumps, Smith had not failed any.
He is expected to be tested again on Tuesday morning in Durban, and will continue to be assessed for as long as Australia sees fit.
Smith has previously battled concussions, most famously when he was struck in the head by Jofra Archer during the 2019 Ashes.
While the early signs are good, any concussion would leave Smith in serious doubt for Sunday's second Test in Gqeberha given the tiered-return protocols.
It would also add to the quandary around the make-up of Australia's side for that match.
Josh Inglis is back in South Africa after his fractured finger, batting in the nets wearing a splint on Monday and offering every sign he will be available for Sunday.
Cameron Green is also recovering from an abdominal strain, and not yet ruled out of the second Test.
Either of the pair would likely have batted at number five in this Test if fit, but Matt Renshaw's scores of 190 and 82 have made the case for him to stay there.

CBA to give workers a payrise, union says
Commonwealth Bank workers will give their lowest paid workers a 13 per cent payrise over the next three years, according to the Finance Sector Union. The union says this came after months of "relentless pressure" from them and staff and that the bank made this gesture as it didn't want protests at its AGM tomorrow.
The offer still requires a formal vote of all CBA workers but it is significantly better than previous proposals, which would have seen wage rises eaten by inflation, the FSU said.
The FSU says the bank will also provide five days paid reproductive leave, a two-week increase to paid parental leave, greater consultation when setting KPIs and the introduction of an artificial intelligence committee.
Thousands of workers signed a petition addressed to CEO Matt Comyn and shared their stories about fears of homelessness, having to take second jobs and turning off their heating to make ends meet, the FSU said.

Australia’s winter harvest forecast ‘large but lower’, says Rabobank
Rabobank forecasts 62.9m tonnes of produce will be harvested this winter in Australia. That's almost 8% lower on last season but still about 2.5% above the five-year average. RaboResearch's Vitor Pistoia says it's a mixed picture across geographies:
“Production is more concentrated in southern and western regions of the country this year. Below-average rainfall across the northern east coast is expected to reduce output in Queensland and New South Wales. By contrast though, favourable moisture levels and strong yields are supporting production increases in South Australia and Victoria."
By commodity, wheat, barley and pulse production are all forecast to come in lower than last year, while canola volumes are set to increase.
Analysis: Is the RBA one and done or are there more rate rises to come?
There is no doubt that the minutes from the Reserve Bank's September board meeting reveal a very "hawkish" stance — that is they very much skew to the risk of further rate rises.
"Members agreed that financial conditions were restrictive but that some indicators could imply that the extent of restriction was only modest," the board minutes noted.
And the implication from the minutes was that a "modest" restriction on economic activity might not be enough given the economy was "a little stronger" than the RBA had expected and inflation was also higher than forecast.
"Members acknowledged that waiting for further confirmation of the outlook for inflation could be costly, given that inflation had already been above target for an extended period and there were concerning indications from surveys and liaison of a growing risk that medium-term inflation expectations in the business community may be rising," the board members observed.
The RBA staff also cast doubt on the recent rise in the unemployment rate as being representative of the state of the jobs market due to methodological changes in the survey.
They believe the jobs market is still a bit "tight".
The RBA's economists also downplayed the risks from the housing market slowdown feeding through into the economy.
"Scenario analysis suggested that even relatively large falls in housing prices would have only modest direct effects on activity and spending," the minutes noted.
At best, you could read this as the September rate hike getting in ahead of time, obviating the need for further hikes later.
This appears to be how the market interpreted it, with the chance of a November hike virtually unchanged at 33%, with a 50% chance of a hike before the end of this year.
However, you could also interpret these minutes as reflecting an RBA economics department that is blasé about the risks of a sudden, rate-driven economic downturn and may stumble into causing one with a further hike or hikes later this year and early next.

IMF upgrades global growth forecast
The IMF has upgraded its global growth forecast to 3.1% for 2026. That's up ever so slightly from the 3% it forecast in July. It says strong investment in AI is a major reason for its better outlook, but downside risks are mounting, including rising debt loads and the Middle East conflict.
At its meeting in Bangkok, the IMF noted a growing divergence between countries benefiting from AI and those bypassed by it. Just 32 countries now account for 95% of global growth, compared to 54 countries in April.
Downward growth revisions have become more widespread, with the IMF downgrading 47% of economies since the April forecasts were issued, including several energy importers outside AI value chains.
Hardest hit by downgrades were the Gulf countries directly impacted by the US-Israeli war against Iran, with Saudi Arabia's GDP now forecast to contract 3.3% this year compared with the 1.7% growth predicted in July.
With Reuters
IMF cites AI slowdown, spiking yields as looming global market risks
The International Monetary Fund warned on Tuesday against "complacency" in global financial markets, citing risks from an artificial intelligence-driven selloff, rising government bond yields, or cyberattacks as potential threats facing still- resilient markets.
The body cautioned in its latest Global Financial Stability Report that should AI profits or investments wane, it could trigger a correction in related asset prices that could spill into broader markets. Such a selloff, as well as a spike in sovereign bond yields or a major cyberattack, were among "plausible near-term catalysts" that policymakers should monitor, the group wrote.
"These risks by themselves do not necessarily threaten financial stability but could become systemic...if they areamplified by underlying vulnerabilities," the group said in the semiannual report, adding that financial stability risks remain elevated.
The IMF said AI investments have so far helped offset economic drags from war in the Middle East and overall policy uncertainty. But it noted "growing evidence" that AI capabilities may not require as much investment, or the potential economic gains may not be as large as expected.
Should the momentum slow, the IMF noted growing leverage in the AI sector could exacerbate any shock by triggering forced selling and higher volatility. For example, hyperscalers now represent 10% of global investment-grade bond issuance, up from less than 1% in 2024.
"The consequences of an AI correction could be global," the IMF warned, as it called on policymakers to curb leverage use, including derivatives and margin loans, where it is "excessive."
Reuters
Firm RBA September rate hike, but what's next?
There's no question the Reserve Bank was committed to hiking interest rates at its September meeting.
It flagged an increase in the cash rate in the weeks leading up to the meeting.
Governor Michele Bullock, and deputy governor Andrew Hauser, both spoke publicly about the risks of higher inflation.
One week before the interest rate hike Ms Bullock suggested the unemployment rate may need to rise in order to get inflation back down within the target range of between 2 and 3 per cent.
The release of the minutes to that meeting, published today, made reference to that idea saying, "members acknowledged that the trade-off between inflation and full employment had deteriorated because of global cost pressures."
"They confirmed that their strategy was still to return inflation to target in a timely manner, while preserving as many of the gains in employment as possible.
"However, executing this strategy in an environment of more persistent adverse supply shocks would require accepting slower growth in demand and employment than would otherwise be the case," the minutes said.
And, looking ahead, assuming the economy keeps pushing up against a supply shortage, or "capacity constraints", there's a risk interest rates may need to rise further.
"They noted that the outlook for inflation would depend, among other things, on developments in the Middle East, the path of external demand, the extent of domestic capacity pressures and on how that influenced the pass-through of cost shocks and the evolution of inflation expectations," the minutes said.
"Members noted that it was possible these factors could continue to place upward pressure on inflation."
AI boom bolstered growth in global trade, benefiting China and India, IMF says
The strong demand for AI has bolstered growth in China, India and other Asian countries, outpacing the overall growth in global trade, IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro said on Tuesday.
Global trade would have grown at a far slower rate without the AI boost, Tenreyro told reporters at the annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok.
Tenreyro said the IMF remained concerned about high debt levels, urging countries to start cutting budgets to reduce deficits. She said central bankers should pursue more restrictive policies, including raising interest rates to get inflation rates back to target.
Reuters
RBA minutes highlight risk of continued high inflation
The Reserve Bank has published the minutes of its September meeting, and the vibe won't be welcome news for homeowners struggling with their mortgage rates.
Some of the top lines were:
- The Middle East crisis, price of agricultural commodities an AI-hype are all international factors driving inflation.
- At home, domestic capacity pressures were higher than previously thought.
- These factors mean the central bank didn't feel it could wait to hike.
- The desire is still to return inflation to target (2-3%) while not generating too much unemployment. This trade-off has gotten trickier.
This is what NAB's Chief Economist Sally Auld deduced from the minutes:
"We do not have any further tightening in our forecast for the RBA. However, risks remain biased to a modest tightening of monetary policy in coming months if the Monetary Policy Board further revises higher its estimation of the upside risks to inflation, or if global influences on the broader stance of domestic monetary policy are more powerful than markets expect."

Former DRC president Joseph Kabila forms alliance with M23 rebels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
21:12:01 UTC
06:12:01 KST

Former Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) President Joseph Kabila has formed a new political-military movement, allied with the M23 armed group, formalising a partnership that unites the former head of state with the rebel movement controlling large swathes of the country's violence-plagued eastern provinces.
The Kabila-M23 tie-up was officially announced at a joint press conference at Kabila's personal residence in Goma, the provincial capital in eastern DRC that M23 rebels have controlled since January 2025.
The 55-year-old former leader, who governed the nation from 2001 to 2019, was condemned to death in absentia a year ago by a military court for "complicity" with the M23 rebels.
Authorities in Kinshasa accuse Kabila of serving as a key founder of the Congo River Alliance (AFC), the now-dissolved political front of the rebel group.
Collapsed peace pacts
The launch of the alliance unfolds against an increasingly unstable political environment in Kinshasa.
Kabila's successor, 63, President Felix Tshisekedi, will reach the end of his second and final five-year presidential mandate in 2028.
While the Congolese Constitution establishes a strict ceiling of two five-year terms, the governing majority has spent recent months priming public opinion to support constitutional amendments that could permit an extension.
Eastern DRC has remained engulfed in chronic armed violence for more than 30 years, during which successive regional and international peace initiatives have failed to stem the bloodshed.
A diplomatic accord signed in December by Kinshasa and Kigali under Washington's auspices has delivered no tangible stability on the ground.

Russia says its diesel exports may exceed volumes announced by Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
21:00:36 UTC
06:00:36 KST

Russia says its diesel exports may exceed volumes announced by Trump
MOSCOW – Russia will be able to return diesel exports to levels above those US President Donald Trump has outlined under a deal with Moscow which has been criticised by Ukraine and some US lawmakers, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Oct 12.
Trump announced on Oct 9 that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel designed to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war in Ukraine.
“We will see how the situation develops further, but Russia has the capacity to increase diesel fuel exports,” Novak, President Vladimir Putin’s point man on oil, said on Rossiya-24 state TV channel.
“By the end of the year, exports could reach 3.0-3.5 million tonnes per month, returning to the levels seen before the crisis,” he said.
Russia’s diesel exports have collapsed due to Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries and self-imposed overseas sales restrictions. Russia has frequently attacked Ukrainian energy infrastructure since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Before Ukraine launched a barrage of drone attacks on Russian oil refineries in 2024-2025, Russian diesel exports amounted to more than 3 million tonnes per month.
Despite a self-imposed export ban, Moscow has continued to supply diesel to countries, mostly in Central Asia, under government deals. Russian diesel exports to Central Asia in September amounted to 427,000 tonnes, according to industry sources.
Soaring US diesel prices are hurting US truckers and farmers, and are a concern for voters and political parties ahead of US midterm elections on Nov 3.
Trump’s envoys told Ukrainian officials on Oct 9 that the Russian diesel deal was part of an effort to draw Russia back to negotiations after the failure of previous efforts to launch sustained talks to end the war, three people familiar with the meeting told Reuters.
The deal has triggered a backlash from some US lawmakers, who say it will give Moscow cash to pursue its war without forcing Putin to make concessions.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has criticised the deal as a reversal of years of Western policy aimed at isolating Russia’s economy.
Zelenskiy said on Oct 12 that Russian strikes against at least six energy targets during its latest wave of deadly air strikes across Ukraine showed Moscow had no interest in an energy ceasefire.
Balancing global supply and demand
Novak also said that under the deal with Trump, Russian diesel supplies will partially balance global supply and demand.
“We are already seeing this effect, including in global diesel markets, where prices have fallen by around 5% to 6%,” Novak said.
In his comments, Novak also said that US figures putting at US$250 billion (S$320.2 billion) the value of Russian resources sold to Europe were “significantly” understated.
“The figure for the period from 2022 to the present day is US$320.7 billion,” Novak told Rossiya-24. “This is the volume of energy resources supplied to European Union countries.”
Trump said on Oct 9 that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes (2.25 million barrels) of diesel to US and global markets.
That is less than a day’s supply for the US transport sector alone, according to US Energy Information Administration data, which shows daily use of around 2.94 million barrels.
Trump also said Russia would supply another 500,000 tonnes in November and a further 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter”. REUTERS

Housing Foundation announces allocation of 70,000 rural land plots to applicants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
20:54:14 UTC
05:54:14 KST

Housing Foundation announces allocation of 70,000 rural land plots to applicants
TEHRAN- The head of the Housing Foundation of the Islamic Revolution said: Under the Housing Foundation’s legal mandate in the Seventh Plan, 70,300 land plots in villages have been allocated, and information on 320,000 units has also been uploaded to the relevant system.
According to an ISNA report, Manouchehr Khajeh-Dalouei, during the signing of a memorandum of understanding with Resalat Bank to finance “Home of Hope” housing, stated: Under the Housing Foundation’s legal duty to provide land and rural housing in the Seventh Development Plan, so far 70,300 land plots in villages have been allocated, and information on 320,000 units has also been uploaded to the relevant system.
Stating that in some villages we face restrictions in providing land, he added: In a significant portion of villages, sufficient land is not available from natural resources, and to provide the land needed by applicants, action must be taken through agreements with owners.
The head of the Housing Foundation, stating that the foundation had drafted a directive for reaching agreements with owners, said: The Court of Administrative Justice has raised ambiguities about this directive, and as a result, implementation of this part has been suspended.
Khajeh-Dalouei continued: Follow-ups are underway to resolve these ambiguities and redraft the legal framework so that it becomes possible to reach agreements with owners and allocate the residential share of the agreed lands to rural applicants.
He expressed hope that with the drafting of a new legal framework, it will be possible to provide land for housing applicants in the vast majority of villages.
In another part of his remarks, the head of the Housing Foundation of the Islamic Revolution, while explaining the details of the Home of Hope plan, said: Under this plan, construction of 200,000 residential units for disadvantaged groups has been envisaged, and so far executive operations for about 105,000 units have begun.
Referring to the conditions for benefiting from the Home of Hope plan, he stated: Applicants must belong to disadvantaged groups and must not have previously used government housing facilities; meaning their Form “J” must be green.
According to the head of the Housing Foundation, eligible applicants across the country can use the capacities of this plan, and the Ministry of Transport and Urban Development is responsible for providing land in existing cities and new cities. The required land is also provided to applicants free of charge.
Khajeh-Dalouei, referring to the planning carried out for the construction of 200,000 units under Home of Hope, added: Based on the report received up to Saturday, executive operations for about 105,000 units have begun, and the plan is progressing at an appropriate pace.
Regarding measures taken to provide the land needed for the plan, he said: The Housing Foundation has concluded a memorandum of understanding with the National Land and Housing Organization to provide land for 50,000 residential units, of which 25,000 units will be built in new cities. Land provision and allocation are being carried out under these memoranda.
The head of the Housing Foundation considered the direct participation of applicants in the construction process to be one of the main features of Home of Hope and explained: In this plan, unlike some centralized housing projects, the people themselves participate in the process of constructing residential units, and the Housing Foundation has taken responsibility for following up on matters related to permit issuance and other executive stages.
Khajeh-Dalouei continued: In the design and technical matters, measures have also been taken in cooperation with the Construction Engineering Organization, and specific structural systems have been designed for the construction of the units so that applicants can use these models if they wish.
In another part of his speech, the head of the Housing Foundation referred to support for households covered by support institutions and said: For eligible applicants covered by the Imam Khomeini Relief Committee or the State Welfare Organization, a 400 million toman non-repayable grant for housing construction has been envisaged.
He stated: In this regard, agreements have been concluded with the Relief Committee and the State Welfare Organization. According to him, for the current year, agreements have been made regarding the provision of housing for 52,000 units, and under the agreement with the Relief Committee, the provision of housing for 44,000 units has been considered.

‘Using petrochemical capacities to strengthen national economy required’
TEHRAN- The acting minister of oil, emphasizing the need to strengthen the governance role of the National Petrochemical Company, said: The capacities of the petrochemical industry must be used to create employment, increase production, generate income, and strengthen the country’s economy.
According to Shana, Hamid Bovard, in a meeting with the CEO and senior managers of the National Petrochemical Company, emphasized the importance and significant position of the petrochemical industry in the country’s economy and stated: This industry has considerable capacities for creating added value and generating income.
Referring to the need to strengthen the regulatory and governance role of the National Petrochemical Company in the petrochemical industry, he stressed: This issue must be pursued seriously in various dimensions and clarified, and in this path, I support you in every way.
The acting minister of oil, stating that with cooperation from various sectors, the market situation, product prices, and supply mechanism must be carefully reviewed and managed, emphasized: This approach provides the ground for proper use of the industry’s capacities.
Bovard, recalling that petrochemical products play a role in producing various goods for people’s lives, said: Therefore, the petrochemical industry’s activity is not limited to the production and export of base products; it also supplies an important part of the needs of the country’s downstream industries.
Emphasizing the need for greater attention to the petrochemical industry’s capacities, he added: Existing capacities must be used to create employment, increase production, generate income, and strengthen the country’s economy. The development of the petrochemical industry can bring significant economic and social effects, and from this perspective, attention to its development is very important.
The acting minister of oil, referring to solutions for ensuring sustainable feedstock for petrochemical industries, stressed: The petrochemical industry’s entry into the development of the country’s oil and gas fields with the aim of ensuring sustainable feedstock must be on the agenda and pursued seriously.
Bovard, emphasizing the need to take fundamental measures to maintain the continuity of petrochemical product exports and foreign currency generation for the country, said: Efforts must be made, by strengthening exports, to return the foreign currency from petrochemical exports to the country’s economic cycle.
He emphasized the importance of pursuing reconstruction programs for petrochemical units damaged in the third imposed war and added: The issue of reconstruction must be pursued seriously, and all existing capacities must be used to accelerate it.
The acting minister of oil, appreciating the efforts of managers and colleagues in the petrochemical industry, stated: In this industry, a collection of experiences and expertise has come together, and all actors are expected to work with doubled motivation to advance the country’s goals.

Exports continue through alternative routes: TPO head
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
20:48:17 UTC
05:48:17 KST

Exports continue through alternative routes: TPO head
TEHRAN- The head of the Trade Promotion Organization (TPO), referring to the effects of trade restrictions and a 34 percent drop in the weight of the country’s foreign trade in the first six months of this year, said: At the same time, part of exports is still being carried out by sea, and another part through corridors and land and rail routes. He also called rumors about the closure of some of the country’s borders incorrect.
According to ISNA, Mohammad Ali Dehghan Dehnavi, head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, at a press conference on the 30th National Export Day ceremony and honoring national exemplary exporters, which will be held on October 21, stated: Given the importance of economic and trade diplomacy in the current situation, appropriate cooperation has been established with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in the field of trade diplomacy, because to resolve the problems caused by restrictions and blockade, we need this area to be highly active. Talks with neighboring countries, important trade partners, and friendly countries are essential so that we can make greater use of our communication capacities and partially replace the capacities that have been lost. Good measures have been taken in trade diplomacy, and major steps have been taken that have largely improved the problems.
The head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, referring to the effects of trade restrictions and the maritime blockade on the country’s foreign trade, said: Despite the decline in trade weight, the use of alternative transport routes and import management has kept a significant part of foreign trade going. Given the country’s special conditions, public release of the details of trade statistics comes with considerations, but reviewing the available statistics can provide a picture of the foreign trade situation.
He said that about 75 percent of the weight of the country’s foreign trade last year was carried out by sea, adding: The bulk of these exchanges took place through the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman; therefore, maritime restrictions affected a large part of the country’s exports and imports.
Dehghan Dehnavi, referring to foreign trade statistics in the first half of this year, said: Estimates show that the weight of the country’s foreign trade has decreased by about 34 percent. However, part of exports is still carried out by sea, and another part through corridors and land and rail routes.
He continued: The use of alternative routes has increased transport costs, because land and rail transport are more expensive than sea transport even under normal conditions. In addition, increased demand for road and rail routes has led to congestion at some borders.
The head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, referring to the difference between the decline in export weight and value, stated: While the weight of foreign trade has decreased by about 34 percent, the drop in export value has been about 20 percent. This difference shows that goods with higher unit value have been able to bear higher transport costs and their exports have continued.
He explained: Paying $50 in transport costs per ton may make the export of low-value goods uneconomical, but for goods worth several thousand dollars, bearing such a cost is more feasible. For this reason, part of the goods whose exports have stopped have lost their economic justification due to increased costs.
Dehghan Dehnavi also spoke about the import situation, saying: The weight of the country’s imports has decreased by about 20 percent. A significant part of imports consists of essential goods, which, despite their lower unit value, account for a large share of import volume. A review of the statistics shows that essential goods have been supplied well. At the same time, the value of imports has decreased by about 35 percent, which indicates a greater decline in import value than in weight.
The head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, referring to the policies of the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade in import management, stated: From the beginning of this year, restrictions were imposed on the import of some goods, and for some other goods, including production machinery, demand management was put on the agenda so that foreign exchange resources would be allocated to essential needs and raw materials. This approach caused the decline in import value to be greater than the decline in weight; meaning less foreign exchange was consumed, while imports of essential goods and raw materials continued.
Dehghan Dehnavi, stating that the country’s foreign trade has been managed under current conditions, said: This does not mean the situation is desirable; a decline in exports and imports imposes costs on the economy and can affect economic activities and production.
Referring to the fact that about 85 percent of the country’s imports consist of raw materials and intermediate goods, including machinery, he added: A decline in imports of these goods affects production; therefore, we are trying to continue supplying them by using alternative resources and routes. We hope that with facilitating measures and greater support for exports, part of the declines created will be compensated in the rest of the year and the sustainability of the country’s foreign trade will be maintained.
In another part of his remarks, the head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization referred to the importance of developing non-oil exports and stated: The 29th of Mehr every year is designated as National Export Day so that, while honoring exemplary exporters, an opportunity is provided to express their issues, problems, and solutions, as well as to create national consensus among government bodies and the private sector for the development of non-oil exports.
He said that the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, as the main custodian of this event, has tried in recent years to hold the National Export Day ceremony in the best possible way, adding: The purpose of holding this ceremony is to declare support for the country’s exporters and provide a basis for expressing problems and finding solutions for export development.
Dehghan Dehnavi, referring to the initiative of holding National Export Week since last year, said: Since export development is a diverse issue and various bodies influence it, all relevant sectors must participate to achieve this goal. Accordingly, this year, from today until Tuesday next week, seven working days have been dedicated to the issue of exports, and programs have been planned for each day.
The head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, referring to the dedication of the first day of these programs to the issue of infrastructure and trade corridors, stated: Trade corridors have always been important, but this year, due to the conditions that have arisen for the country and the issue of the maritime blockade, they have become more important.
He continued: In recent months, much has been done to make corridors that can compensate for restrictions created in other sectors more active. The Ministry of Roads and Urban Development and other responsible bodies have made great efforts in this regard. The program related to infrastructure and trade corridors will be held with the presence of the Minister of Roads and Urban Development at the Islamic Republic of Iran Railways, and a memorandum of understanding will also be introduced in this program to make the continuation of the path, especially in the rail sector, smoother.
Referring to the programs of the coming days, he said: On Tuesday, the issue of value-creating trade with the export of knowledge-based goods and services will be pursued, and the Vice Presidency for Science, Technology and Knowledge-Based Economy has been invited to this program. This year, we have tried to hold more programs in partner agencies so that, while appreciating their actions, the message is conveyed that all agencies have come to support the development of non-oil exports. On Wednesday, the issue of exporting technical and engineering services will be pursued with the presence of companies exporting these services and representatives of the Ministry of Roads and Urban Development and the Ministry of Energy.
He said that export management companies are among the important tools for the country’s export development, stating: For Saturday next week, a program has been planned with the cooperation of the Tehran Chamber of Commerce so that the issue of export management companies and their capacities is given attention. On the same day, the issue of legislation and an export leap will also be raised, and with the presence of the heads of some parliamentary commissions, legislative issues in the field of exports will be examined so that the parliament’s support for export development is also considered.
Referring to the program for Sunday next week, he said: On this day, the issue of facilitation in exports will be pursued, and exporters who have fulfilled their foreign exchange obligations on time will be honored. Exports play an important role in the country’s economy due to their impact on GDP and employment. Fulfilling foreign exchange obligations and repatriating export earnings, alongside export activity, is a worthy action, and on this occasion, with the presence of regulatory officials, companies that have had exemplary performance in fulfilling their foreign exchange obligations will be appreciated.
He continued: On Monday, the issue of associations and trade events in the field of exports will be pursued with the cooperation of the Iran Chamber of Commerce and with the presence of associations and the Export Confederation, so that the ground is provided for greater activity by private sector associations in exports. Tuesday is dedicated to trade diplomacy, and this program will be held with the participation and presence of representatives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. During these seven days, a diverse range of executive bodies, peer organizations, public sector institutions, and representatives of the private sector and chambers of commerce will participate in holding the National Export Day programs.
According to him, the message of these programs is that, given the country’s special need for foreign exchange generation this year, all agencies will cooperate to help the private sector, remove obstacles, and grow the country’s exports so that the losses caused by war and blockade are compensated to a large extent. The main ceremony of National Export Day will be held on Wednesday next week, the 29th of Mehr, and we will try to hold this ceremony with the presence of the president and according to the procedure of previous years.
The head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization then presented a report on the process of selecting exemplary exporters and said: This process began several months ago in the Trade Promotion Organization, and after the call was announced, companies that applied to be selected as exemplary exporters participated in this process. The selection of exemplary exporters is carried out based on specific guidelines; in total, 365 companies registered in this process, and after reviews, 275 files were finalized because some applicants did not complete their files or did not meet the necessary conditions to obtain the required points.
Dehghan Dehnavi continued: One of the positive actions this year was making the process of selecting exemplary exporters systematic, such that the selection was carried out without the interference or personal taste of individuals and based on scored criteria. Finally, 43 individuals or legal entities were selected as national exemplary exporters, and 13 companies were selected as national distinguished exporters.
The head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, explaining the criteria for selecting distinguished exporters, said: Distinguished exporters are exporters who have been selected as exemplary exporters in five consecutive periods. Medal-winning exporters are also companies that have obtained the distinguished title for three consecutive periods; however, this year no company qualified for this category. Alongside exemplary and distinguished exporters, in other sections, including export management companies, cooperative companies, free zones, provinces, and the printing and packaging field, selected parties will be introduced as exporters worthy of appreciation, and a government organization will be introduced as an exemplary export-supporting organization for the first time; an organization that has had the greatest role and help in the field of exports in its area of activity will be introduced in this section.
In another part of his remarks, the head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization emphasized the role of the media in promoting export culture and stated: We ask media figures and journalists to participate in informing about National Export Day and the programs planned during these seven days so that the concept of exports, its role, and its position in the country are elevated more than before and the private sector becomes more interested in this field.
He said that exporters enjoy a distinct position among private sector activists, adding: A producer who supplies their product inside the country performs a valuable activity; but a producer who can offer their product to global markets shows that their product has the necessary quality to be sold outside the country and that they have the knowledge, information, and technology needed to be present in global markets. Therefore, a producer who has export capability gains a higher position from this perspective compared with other producers.
Comparing the position of exporters and importers, he stated: If a trader or businessman is an exporter, they have a different position in terms of value creation for the country’s economy compared with an importer. Buying goods, despite its importance, is not difficult by itself, because there are many sellers in the world who offer goods, but selling goods in global markets requires marketing and trade skill. Imports also have their own importance and position in terms of supplying the country’s needed goods, consumer goods, and raw materials, but they cannot have the position of exports.
He said that exports must be considered as the driving engine of the economic sector and a factor for directing and advancing production, adding: Greater support must be provided for exports, and conditions must be created so that exporters can develop their activities in global markets.
