British tanker completes fourteen missions in Saudi deployment
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
20:15:48 BST
04:15:48 KST

A Royal Air Force Voyager sent to Saudi Arabia to provide air-to-air refuelling has already flown fourteen operational missions, alongside air defence also deployed by Britain, the Prime Minister told the House of Commons.
Andy Burnham set out the deployment in a statement on the United Nations General Assembly and the international meetings that followed it, describing the Middle East as one of the subjects he had discussed with President Trump in New York.
He said: “I confirmed Britain’s decision to send air defence and a Voyager aircraft to Saudi Arabia to provide air to air refuelling support. I can confirm today it has already completed 14 operational missions. This support is needed to protect civilians. I condemn the appalling attacks on the King Khalid International Airport. We will continue to stand with Saudi Arabia against the Houthis.”
The deployment was agreed in late September in response to a Saudi request, with the Prime Minister acting on the advice of the Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, and the Foreign Secretary, Ed Miliband. Mr Burnham said then that Britain was acting to secure the interests of this country and the wider region, and that pathways needed to be kept open. Saudi Arabia was reported to be running low on interceptor stocks as Houthi ballistic missile and drone attacks, which began on 8 September, continued.
The attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh came on 8 October, when a Houthi ballistic missile killed three people, among them a Saudia pilot, Captain Hamoud Ali Alkalthami, and wounded dozens more, several of them foreign nationals. A Saudia aircraft was damaged. Operations at the airport have since resumed.
Attacks on Abha and King Khalid airports in early October killed three civilians and injured thirty-six, according to the Saudi civil aviation authority, and strikes on Jazan and Najran airports wounded at least three. The coalition said on 18 September that it had intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at King Khalid, and an explosion was heard near the airport the following day with smoke rising from a fuel storage area.
Pakistan and Turkey have agreed to deploy forces under mutual defence arrangements signed with Saudi Arabia earlier this year, and a Pakistani foreign ministry spokesman has said his country now has a substantial number of forces and resources in Riyadh, acting in defence of Saudi territory without crossing into Houthi-held areas.
Voyager is the Royal Air Force’s only air-to-air refuelling aircraft and also carries the strategic air transport role, flying in two configurations, the KC Mk 2 with two underwing pods for fast jets and the KC Mk 3 with an additional centreline hose for larger aircraft.

====================================================================================================

Wolf Warriors in Sheep’s Clothing: China’s New Subnational Diplomacy in Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:15:00 UTC
04:15:00 KST

For the government of China, diplomacy is more than simply a means of cultivating international relationships and advancing national interests. It is also an instrument of regime maintenance. In this capacity it can take the form of coercive interventions in the domestic affairs of other states with the aim of suppressing conduct or critique considered hostile to the ruling Chinese Communist Party (CCP). Deploying diplomatic agents to secure compliance with CCP objectives is in fact a significant feature of China’s subnational relations with local governments and communities in Australia.
During Xi Jinping’s first decade as CCP general secretary and chairman of state, Beijing’s approach to Australia grew increasingly blunt and confrontational, a style known as “wolf warrior diplomacy.” More recently, Chinese diplomats have shifted to a quieter, more self-assured form of subnational diplomacy. In contrast to the bluster of the wolf warrior era, this approach is largely conducted behind closed doors and has become more evident since Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s July 2025 visit to China.
The election of the Albanese government in 2022 early signaled a thaw in what had been an icy bilateral relationship between Australia and China under the preceding Coalition governments of Malcolm Turnbull (2015-18) and Scott Morrison (2018-22). On his second visit to China as prime minister, Albanese spent a week “stabilizing” relations through renewed business, trade, educational, cultural, and inter-governmental initiatives.
Among the knock-on effects in Australia was a flurry of Chinese diplomatic initiatives at the local level. Consular staff in Brisbane, Sydney, Melbourne, Adelaide, and Perth now plainly assumed they were licensed by Albanese and his business entourage to press for local Australian compliance with their own demands on a range of issues. In meetings with local governments and peak community bodies, they carried a message: tolerating comments or events that displeased or offended the Chinese state or CCP would embarrass not just China or its ruling party, but the government of Australia.
This was new. Rather than howling into the void, China’s diplomats were framing their demands in the Australian government’s own idiom. Wolf warrior diplomacy was giving way to “wolf warrior in sheep’s clothing diplomacy.” China’s officials were adopting the language of their hosts to press their demands upon local governments and communities. On evidence, to date the new approach is relatively effective but it carries risks for all parties.
The Evidence
A consular initiative in Melbourne undertaken shortly after the conclusion of Albanese’s trip to China shows the strategy in action. In August 2025, China’s consul general in Melbourne requested a meeting with an independent non-profit organization that will remain unnamed. Its board welcomed the approach. This was not a low-key visit. The cluster of consular colleagues accompanying the consul general almost outnumbered the hosts around the table.
During the formal presentation, the consul general reviewed Australia-China ties since 1972 and Melbourne’s consular opening in 1986. Past difficulties were behind us, he said. The Albanese government had corrected the errors of its Coalition predecessor. Canberra was restoring stability through trade, regional development, and people-to-people partnerships while recognizing China’s core interests – code for CCP rule and China’s claims over Taiwan, Tibet, Xinjiang, and the South China Sea, among other claims.
The consul general then urged the board to read a recent article by iron-ore tycoon Andrew (Twiggy) Forrest, who predicted a bright future if everyone came on board the China boat. But, Forrest also warned: “Treat a friend like an enemy, and one day they may well become one.”
A few locals around the table recalled hearing a similar warning five years earlier, when a Chinese diplomat presented a Canberra journalist with a list of 14 grievances, accompanied by the statement: “If you make China the enemy, China will be the enemy.” Most of those grievances presented in November 2020 concerned Canberra’s efforts to limit Chinese government engagement with subnational entities, on the one hand, and its failure to restrict independent Australian institutions critical of China and the CCP on the other. China’s representatives in Australia appeared to be agitated not so much by the Coalition government’s external relations as by its domestic political arrangements governing the states and its failure to suppress commentary on China and its ruling party in Australia’s media, think tanks, and civil society.
The public backlash to the “14 grievances” prompted China’s local representatives to park their threat for the time being. Events proved that they could afford to wait because the same warning would be reiterated by Forrest, one of Australia’s leading businessmen, in wake of Albanese’s visit.
Having invoked Forrest, consular officials came up with a pointed request for the Melbourne board to cancel an event it was hosting with Australian journalist Cheng Lei. Cheng had been recently repatriated following three years in a Chinese jail for alleged spying activities. Giving her a platform to discuss her imprisonment, the Chinese diplomats implied, would undo all the good work of Albanese and his business team.
Despite the consul general’s request, Cheng’s talk went ahead. Nonetheless, China’s coercive interventions around her activities continued. Six months later, her play “1154 Days,” which recounted her solitary confinement and imprisonment in China, was dropped from Melbourne’s premier arts festival. “I feel like I’m back in China,” Cheng Lei told The Age.
Her concern was justified. The play had received a provisional place on the arts festival program, normally a routine step toward inclusion, but the board – not the festival’s creative staff – ruled against it. The RISING arts festival is funded through Creative Victoria and managed through the City of Melbourne’s Arts House, placing the festival program in a classic pincer movement between state and city governments known for their habit of surrender under consular pressure.
Chinese government meddling in Victoria’s school textbooks, community organizations, Chinese-language media, and local government deliberations had been thought things of the past following the introduction of new federal laws around foreign interference in 2018 and legislation limiting state government overreach in foreign relations in 2020. Not so.
Interviewed for this article, Cheng said that City of Melbourne officials received several consular calls and a personal visit urging them to avoid her play. More curious still, Arts House paid the artists the agreed performance fee, even though the performance was disallowed. The problem was not costs but the risks to the city and state governments’ relations with the local consulate.
Cheng’s play was performed off-festival with support from a venue outside the City of Melbourne’s jurisdiction. There is a curious historical parallel here. In 1936 an anti-Nazi play was banned from city theaters in Sydney and Melbourne following representations from the German consulate, then under the direction of the Nazi Party. To their credit, the players found a way around the ban by performing on the back of a truck.
For the fleet of Chinese consuls sailing in the wake of Albanese’s China visit, Melbourne was just one port of call. The Victorian consular team sought meetings with civic institutions and officials in Bendigo, Ballarat, Frankston, Geelong, and also Hobart in Tasmania, as well as with university executives and cultural institutions, including Melbourne’s Museum of Chinese Australian History. Consular officials based in Western Australia met up with local government officers in Perth, Joondalup, Cockburn, Gosnells, Geraldton, and Swan; Queensland-based ones visited Brisbane, Rockhampton, Mackay, Toowoomba, the Sunshine Coast, Gold Coast, and Southern Downs. The South Australian consulate paid visits to the local governments of Adelaide, Murray Bridge, and Clare Valley. In each state, consular officials also met with civic and community bodies.
In contrast to earlier consular tours, the nationwide consular outreach following Albanese’s visit drew little public attention. Not long beforehand, the Sydney consular team suffered public embarrassment when local newspapers reported on the consul general’s meeting with the mayor of Newcastle. At that meeting, the consul warned the mayor against the possibility of an AUKUS nuclear-submarine squadron possibly being based nearby, saying that this would harm China’s strategic interests. The mayor was reportedly taken aback to have been challenged on Taiwan, Tibet, and nuclear submarines – topics well outside the scope of Australian local government diplomacy – during a routine meet-and-greet with Chinese consular officials.
On Albanese’s return, consular teams adopted a quieter subnational style aligned with Canberra’s own “calm and measured” international diplomacy, which was explicitly contrasted with the former Coalition’s “bellicose megaphone diplomacy.” Albanese’s approach, while helping to restore bilateral commercial, ministerial, and people-to-people ties at the national level, raised expectations on the part of China’s representatives in Australia that their demands for local discretion on sensitive matters would yield willing compliance. Canberra’s restraint was being repurposed to serve Beijing’s coercive subnational diplomacy.
Backfire?
It is doubtless clear to China’s diplomats in Australia that the Albanese government’s measured diplomacy has not altered Australia’s broader strategy in the region. This geopolitical strategy was inherited intact from the Coalition government and is aligned with regional partners’ understanding of the challenges and threats China presents.
That does not inhibit consular officials from cajoling local governments and community organizations to silence talk of those threats in the interests of stabilizing bilateral relations. In May 2026, Melbourne’s consul general told a local city newspaper that claims of “so-called” threats would “backfire” and rebound “just like a boomerang” on any making them.
Backfire on whom? Most consular interventions have remained below Canberra’s threshold of awareness, but this is changing. In July 2026, Melbourne’s Museum of Chinese Australian History appeared to breach a federal funding agreement by hosting a consular speaker at its annual high-achievers program without notifying the government funding body. The rotating host for the 2026 Chinese Australian Achievers Awards was Lord Mayor Rees’ City of Melbourne, which customarily invites China’s consular officials to speak at community events. By withdrawing funding, Canberra signaled its concern about consular officials piggybacking at federal expense on local events.
A more serious threshold was crossed later that month when the Museum first invited then disinvited Foreign Minister Penny Wong to launch journalist Emilia Tagaza’s book “Behind a Million Faces,” described by the Museum as “a seminal book on the history of Chinese Australians.” Wong accepted the invitation. Her office nominated September 1, 2026 for the launch, and it requested an advance copy of the book to be forwarded ahead of that date.
In July, however, according to emails reviewed by the author, members of the Museum board reviewed their own advance copies and objected to its contents on several grounds. These included the author allegedly underplaying the U.S. factor in Australia’s deteriorating relations with China and overemphasizing communism, exaggerating China’s “assertiveness,” and incorrectly suggesting that Chinese migrants to Australia sought to escape CCP control. It directed the CEO to forward the author 17 pages of corrections, none of a factual nature, most entailing reframing the agreed facts to minimize offense to the government of China. When Tagaza rejected the board’s amendments, the CEO was directed to cancel the launch and withdraw the invitation to the foreign minister.
That was not the end of it. The CEO reinstated the launch and Wong’s invitation after receiving advice that the board decision may have infringed the author’s free speech. Just weeks before the event, however, the board again reversed course and canceled the event and the invitation. September passed without the Museum book launch, and with the foreign minister wondering what on earth was happening in Melbourne.
She had more than one reason to wonder. In 2024 a former Museum board member had become the first Australian to be jailed for planning foreign interference on behalf of the CCP – although not in his role on the board. But in fact nothing out of the ordinary was happening in Melbourne. Conspicuous displays of anticipatory obedience toward the local consulate are the default position among state and city governments, elite cultural institutions, and peak organizations in the city. Given sufficient haranguing and inducement, institutions adapt their behavior to what they imagine local consuls want, in many cases without receiving specific requests. Self-censorship is commonplace.
The Museum too has a record of silencing voices and histories that could annoy China’s local officials. A small everyday instance of anticipatory obedience can be found in the Museum’s display on the recent history of immigration from China. A Museum volunteer told me that a draft text linked the 1989 Beijing/Tiananmen Massacre to Prime Minister Bob Hawke’s memorable offer of permanent residence after the massacre to tens of thousands of resident Chinese students. Were it not for the Chinese military’s slaughter of students and workers in Beijing, the 40,000 students would not have been invited to stay. The text on display elides this “offensive” context: “40,000 students arrived and studied whilst many stayed in Australia.”
More seriously, the Museum promotes certain histories while silencing others. The board raised no concerns before or after the launch in August 2026 of a book on the history of the Victorian branch of the Australia-China Friendship Society (ACFS), held at the Museum in association with events marking the 75th anniversary of that Society’s founding. The ACFS’s relationship with China is mediated by the Chinese People’s Association for Friendship with Foreign Countries under the direction of the CCP’s United Front Work Department. The consul general spoke at the historical commemoration along with Lord Mayor Nicholas Reece.
What was novel in the case of Tagaza’s aborted book launch was not the selective censorship but censorship undertaken in full gaze of the Australian foreign minister. The board’s customary deference to China’s official perspectives on Australian history, immigration, and bilateral relations is not normally acted out in front of federal ministers. And this time the coercive influence over local government and community affairs wielded by China’s consulate in Melbourne embarrassed a senior member of Albanese’s Cabinet.
Three considerations appear to have shaped the Museum’s decision to cancel the launch and the foreign minister’s invitation – not once but twice. First, as noted, there were concerns that parts of the text may prove problematic for sections of the “Chinese community.” Second, the Museum faced growing community opposition on unrelated matters. Third – and, in my view, most importantly – the Museum anticipated the local consul general’s likely response to a high-profile ministerial launch of a book that did not reflect the Chinese Communist Party’s perspectives on Australian history, immigration, and bilateral relations.
If invited to speak, the consul general would have been obliged to challenge the book’s shortcomings in the minister’s presence; if the Museum failed to invite him, it risked damaging its relations with the consulate. Faced with a choice between embarrassing Australia’s foreign minister and disappointing the local consulate, the Museum board chose to embarrass the minister.
Being Stabilized
Beijing’s diplomacy is directed at advancing China’s national interests and first among those national interests is securing the ruling party in power. The conventional separation of domestic and foreign policy collapses under this obligation because the top national security priority applies equally in both domains: preserving the status and power of the CCP is just as important outside China as it is within it.
The same goes for managing security risks. Domestically in China, a nationwide “stability maintenance” (weiwen) system anticipates and suppresses perceived threats to CCP rule before they arise. Outside China, this task falls to locally stationed consular officials. Those silenced by the weiwen system in China say that they have been “stabilized.” The same could be said of Australia.
Under the banner of stabilizing bilateral relations, Chinese consular staff apply their stability maintenance techniques to undermine initiatives and silence dissent across Australia’s local governments and communities. As they interpret it, Canberra’s softly-softly diplomacy gives China’s consulates the license and leverage to pressure cultural, arts, community, and government bodies to comply with their wishes by framing them as consistent with Australia’s policy of stabilization. As Cheng Lei told the Melbourne Age, Australia is starting to feel like China.
For now, the domestic risks of being stabilized bear on freedoms of expression, association, and religion that underpin the Australian way of life. International risks entail states such as Victoria missing out on Taiwan’s extraordinary growth spurt for fear of offending a local PRC consul. The broader geopolitical risk for Australia is that China’s diplomats could apply their new wolf-in-sheep’s-clothing strategy to Pacific Island communities at Australia’s expense. After all, if Australia can be shown to be compliant with China, how would it advantage smaller Pacific nations to do otherwise? There is a danger that Australia’s massive Pacific investment, made to counter the China threat, could serve CCP interests via the canny invocation of Australian words and actions on the part of Beijing’s representatives in the region.
Beyond the Pacific region, the wider lesson is that all countries seeking “strategic stability” in relations with China will, if they let down their guard, find China’s diplomats practicing stability maintenance in their own backyards – using the host country’s commitment to stability to keep the CCP secure and in command, everywhere.

AI inquiry urges independent safety watchdogs inside companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:10:27 UTC
04:10:27 KST

Labor and Coalition deny interference in AI inquiry after David Pocock raises 'stitch-up' concerns
In short:
Labor and the Coalition have rejected concerns about undue interference in a parliamentary AI inquiry after the prime minister's office reviewed draft recommendations.
The bipartisan proposals include independent safety checks on AI companies, greater access for security agencies and a review of copyright laws.
What's next?
The committee will deliver its final report in November.
Labor and the Coalition have denied there was "interference" in a raft of recommendations from an artificial intelligence inquiry after accusations of a major party "stitch-up".
A joint committee on AI has recommended Australia require AI companies to submit to independent safety checks, reserve computing power for local use and give security agencies early access to new models.
The committee has endorsed investment in data centres, backed by national standards covering resource use, additional electricity generation and community consultation.
It has also urged a review of Australia's copyright settings, which would be at odds with creative groups seeking stronger enforcement of existing protections rather than changes to accommodate the AI industry.
The federal government has signalled it hopes to introduce legislation outlining national standards for data centres and frontier AI models by the end of this year and pass the laws through parliament in early 2027.
Pocock warns of 'major party stitch-ups'
ACT independent Senator David Pocock has raised concerns an adviser to Anthony Albanese "pre-vetted" the committee's "early advice" letter before it was sent to the prime minister.
Senator Pocock said he respected the committee process and the need to work in a "multi-partisan way" but was unhappy to discover there were "mark-ups" from Mr Albanese's office on a draft of the document.
"We've seen enough major party stitch ups,"
he said.
"Regaining the community's trust, especially on the issue of AI, requires robust debate and committee work."
Labor MP Jo Briskey, who is the committee chair, said she had engaged with the prime minister's office ahead of finalising the early advice.
"It's been a process by which we are seeking advice and making sure that this is working across the board," she said.
"This is an indication to the government on where the committee is heading, where we think there is some really important [consensus] to just get on with the job."
Ms Briskey said the inquiry's final report, due in November, was not predetermined and there was "more work to do".
Duniam says 'no interference' in committee work
Liberal Senator Jonno Duniam, who also consulted with the Coalition on the letter, is the deputy chair and said the collaborative approach of the committee was an example of parliament "working well".
"There has been no guidance, no interference, there has been a lot of discussion, a lot of consultation," he said.
Senator Duniam said Australia had a "very small" window to make the most of AI.
"If we wait, if we dither, if we do nothing, then of course that opportunity will sail by our country and our adversaries will be taking advantage of that opportunity at our expense."
Regarding copyright, Senator Duniam said the committee wanted the issue resolved in the "interests" of creatives and rights holders.
"At the moment you've got a situation where data, copyright, intellectual property, whatever form it comes in is currently being used by offshore models. It's being harvested to train models offshore," he said.
"And do you know how much our copyright holders are getting as a result? One hundred per cent of nothing."
Push for independent experts inside AI companies
The committee has recommended the government put independent experts inside leading AI companies that would have access to their systems and a duty to report safety findings and incidents to government.
Security agencies like the Australian Signals Directorate should receive early access to new models as a condition of arrangements allowing frontier AI labs to train them in Australia.
The government has been urged to immediately review protections used across its data repositories, particularly those holding sensitive and national security information.
It has also been advised to monitor the risk of AI helping to develop biological weapons.
Alongside those safeguards, the committee has questioned whether existing copyright rules were delivering for Australian creators or supporting local AI development.
Copyright rules under scrutiny
The committee noted current copyright arrangements were "not facilitating" licensing deals for Australian culture and content.
"The status quo sees the work of Australian artists, musicians and media outlets used overseas without adequate control or payment," the letter said.
They also acknowledged frontier AI labs had indicated existing copyright settings were a "barrier" to undertaking training in Australia.
The committee recommended the government "examine" current copyright settings and prioritise ensuring that Australian creators "retain control over how their works are used, that they are paid, and that AI systems reflect Australian values and culture".
But Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) chief executive Annabelle Herd told the inquiry last week that existing licensing systems could support AI training without rewriting copyright protections to suit foreign companies.
"They should come to the negotiating table, not to the prime minister's office," she said.
OpenAI breach drives calls for oversight
Last month it was revealed OpenAI's experimental models accessed government websites without authorisation during training, including a Services Australia portal hosting Medicare statistics.
The letter from the committee said the OpenAI breach demonstrated the need for "appropriate and robust safeguards" to protect Australian data and those who own and use it.
It was recommended the safeguards apply to frontier AI developers deploying models and agents in Australia, ensuring there was "proper and transparent accountability and oversight mechanisms" along with "well-established practices to deal with incidents that may occur in the future".
Frontier labs should also be required to monitor and report incidents to the government in a "timely manner".
OpenAI chief strategy officer Jason Kwon last week said the company would "support a framework on mandatory disclosures".
Australia cannot simply be 'consumer' of foreign AI
It was recommended the government establish an ongoing parliamentary joint standing committee to monitor AI, which could conduct "rapid reviews" of new regulation when required.
This committee would also be reported to at "regular intervals" on serious events and incidents, including cyber incidents involving AI, unintended actions of agents and models as well as "misuse" of the technology.
The letter recommended reserving a share of computing capacity for national security and university research, with health and social services also among the potential beneficiaries.
"The overarching objective should be to ensure that Australia is not merely a consumer of AI technologies developed elsewhere, but a trusted, competitive and strategically capable participant in the global AI industry," the letter said.

Billions in the bin as economy struggles with true cost of food waste
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:07:35 UTC
04:07:35 KST

Food waste costing Australian businesses and the economy billions
In short:
Australia wastes about 7.6 million tonnes of food each year, costing the economy more than $36 billion.
Less than a quarter of businesses regularly inspect their food waste, and operational methods mean it can go unnoticed.
The federal government has committed to halving food waste by 2030, but some experts are concerned about progress.
When Karl Riseborough realised how much food went to waste each week at his Sydney pub and brewery, he was shocked.
Grain left over from the beer-making process was thrown out, as well as food waste from the kitchen.
What surprised him most was the volume of waste on top of the spent grain.
"The food scraps coming back, the plate waste, the kitchen prep waste … you don't really notice when it was all going straight into the bin," Mr Riseborough said.
Food waste expert Belinda Chellingworth said many traders had no idea how much waste they were generating, or how much it was affecting their bottom line.
Every year about 7.6 million tonnes of food is wasted in Australia at a cost of more than $36 billion to the economy.
Of that wasted food, 70 per cent is edible and there are critical knock-on effects for landfill management, food security and the climate.
With the support of Ms Chellingworth, who happily calls herself a "garbologist", Mr Riseborough has stopped throwing away 50 kilograms of spent grain from each batch of beer he brews.
"Now I have regular users who come and collect it once I've brewed and use it for the benefit of their gardens or their animals," Mr Riseborough said.
"We had two 240-litre bins that were getting collected each week. We're now down to one bin collected each fortnight."
He said that saved him about $5,000 a year.
Cumulative effect not realised
Australia's hospitality sector wastes 1.2 million tonnes of food each year, according to the Sustainable Restaurant Association.
The economic impact of food waste in the food service sector is about $6.4 billion, averaging about $66,000 annually per business.
Ms Chellingworth said less than a quarter of businesses regularly inspected their food waste.
"Typically, many businesses, if they've got food left over at the end of their operations or the end of the day, then it will be landfilled," she said.
"For many businesses, and particularly large businesses, the cost of food waste across their operations isn't fully realised because they incur it multiple times, but it's not obvious."
For example, over-ordering food is a cost to the kitchen. If it is not sold, that is a revenue cost, and then whatever goes into the bin also involves a cost for collection.
"So they're paying for it multiple times, but they're different departments, different cost centres, and it's often not added together, so they don't understand the full cost across the whole business," Ms Chellingworth said.
She said landfill capacity was reaching critical levels in many areas.
Some tips in Perth are set to run out of space in two years and sites in New South Wales are set to reach capacity in four years.
Victoria's capacity is expected to be reached in the next 10 years.
Government target 'unachievable'
To combat the economic and environmental impacts of food waste, the federal government has committed to halving food waste by 2030.
But UNSW food and health professor Johannes le Coutre does not believe the plan is on track.
"I'm not sure if that's attainable or achievable with the current landscape," he said.
"In Australia we have a unique situation in that we are dealing with a big distance and that even in the food industry a lot of value-added manufacturing occurs overseas."
In a statement to the ABC, a spokesperson for the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water said: "The Australian Government is working with jurisdictions and industry to drive behaviour change and expand organics recycling capacity.
"This includes investing $37 million into new and upgraded organics recycling infrastructure, $30 million to set up the End Food Waste Cooperative Research Centre to research food waste interventions, [and] $10 million on the Great Unwaste Campaign to help Australians reduce food waste at home."
Alongside food waste, Professor le Coutre said about 3.5 million households were experiencing food shortages.
"If we address the food waste problem, we might be able to help that," he said.
"We are a modern country, a modern economy … we need to raise awareness, we need to improve technology, and we need to improve policy."
Ms Chellingworth said some businesses were reluctant to donate excess food due to common misunderstandings.
"It's not widely understood or well-known, but every Australian state and territory has laws in place to protect food donors, provided that certain conditions are met when the food exchanges hands," she said.
"The food needs to be edible when it's donated, any instructions on how to refrigerate it or prepare it afterwards need to be provided, it must be free … and it needs to go to a registered organisation."
Food waste a global issue
Excessive food waste is a global concern and will be a focus at the United Nations Climate Change Conference, COP31, in Türkiye next month.
Professor le Coutre said the impact of food waste on the climate could not be underestimated.
"A lot of greenhouse gas emissions are based on agricultural, industrialised activities on our planet — that is something which needs to be improved," he said.
"Livestock management can be improved in order to lower greenhouse gas emissions and, if we work on that end, we will have a chance as well to improve food security, improve food systems, and lower food waste."
Ms Chellingworth said there were examples abroad that Australia could take inspiration from.
"France has laws that mean that supermarkets over a certain size must donate edible food," she said.
"In the Netherlands, they've had a long-running food waste campaign for all of their citizens to help them understand how they can reduce food waste at home, as well.
"Stronger mandates for food rescue and food donation … would start to help alleviate the pressure that a lot of households are feeling with cost of living and food insecurity as well."

Britain calls in industry for fleet of drone submarines
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
20:03:56 BST
04:03:56 KST

The Royal Navy has opened preliminary market engagement for the Type 93 extra-large uncrewed underwater vehicle and the AUKUS Signature Payload Programme, inviting companies to register interest before any requirement is set, according to a notice published on Find a Tender at ten past twelve on Monday.
“The Royal Navy seeks to improve its understanding of the market and wider ecosystem for Extra-Large Uncrewed Underwater Vehicle (XLUUV) platforms, associated payloads, and enabling functions,” it says. “This activity supports the development of the Type 93 capability and the Royal Navy’s commitments under the AUKUS Pillar II Signature Project.”
Registrations are sought from “XLUUV platform providers, payload providers, relevant technology and software suppliers including Autonomy, AI and Mission Management Systems, integrators, through-life support providers, and other relevant suppliers.” Those who come forward may be invited to collaborative workshops, one to one meetings, industry days and written requests for information, and small and medium-sized enterprises are flagged as particularly suitable.
“The Royal Navy is initially considering platforms approximately 2 metres in diameter and 12 metres in length, however organisations offering platforms of other dimensions are also encouraged to register,” the notice says, adding that it “should not be considered as a commitment from the Royal Navy to progress with any future procurement activities.”
XV Excalibur, the uncrewed submarine Britain already operates, is twelve metres long, two metres across and displaces nineteen tonnes. It was unveiled at Devonport in May last year, as this publication reported at the time, having been built by MSubs of Plymouth under the three-year Project Cetus, for which the Ministry of Defence awarded a £15.4 million contract in December 2022. It joined the Fleet Experimentation Squadron as a demonstrator with no operational role.
The Royal Navy controlled Excalibur in home waters from an operating centre in Australia during Talisman Sabre in July 2025, the first British and Australian demonstration of XLUUV interoperability under AUKUS Pillar II. It carried out the first underwater operation of a quantum optical atomic clock that November and transferred to Royal Navy ownership in December. In June the Submarine Delivery Agency awarded MSubs a further £6.7 million for trials and evaluation running to May 2028, work intended to move the programme towards functional payloads.
On 13 September, Excalibur fired an American Mark 48 exercise torpedo at the British Underwater Test and Evaluation Centre in Scotland. Britain and the United States described it as the first time either country had launched a heavyweight torpedo from an uncrewed vessel, carried out under Project Broadsword and Trial Iron, both part of AUKUS Pillar II.
The Type 93 designation first appeared in February last year, in Project CABOT documents setting out a persistent wide area anti-submarine search capability built around the Type 92 Sloop, an uncrewed surface vessel, and the Type 93 Chariot, described then as a drone submarine. Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, confirmed in July that the Defence Investment Plan had announced Type 92 uncrewed underwater sensing platforms and Type 93 extra-large uncrewed underwater vessels as part of the Atlantic Bastion programme, adding that the number of platforms to be procured and their construction schedules had not yet been determined.
He has also told Parliament that the Hybrid Navy will take at least £1.5 billion over four years, and that by 2030 the aim is to have the first large autonomous vessels in service, among them a prototype uncrewed missile platform and extra-large uncrewed underwater vessels carrying payloads developed through AUKUS.
The notice states that the programme “directly aligns with the Strategic Defence Review (SDR), Defence Investment Plan (DIP) and AUKUS Pillar II priorities, supporting the transition to a Hybrid Navy through the integration of autonomous and uncrewed maritime capabilities.”

Australian engineer speaks after being freed from Baghdad jail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
18:54:37 UTC
03:54:37 KST

Australian engineer Robert Pether speaks after being freed from Baghdad jail
In short:
Robert Pether has spoken for the first time since being allowed to leave Iraq, ending a five-year ordeal including time in a Baghdad prison.
The Australian engineer paid tribute to his family's efforts to free him.
Mr Pether was arrested in 2021 and later found guilty of what his family says were trumped-up fraud charges.
Australian engineer Robert Pether has paid an emotional tribute to his family for maintaining their fight for his freedom, moments after touching down in the Irish capital Dublin.
Mr Pether was finally allowed to leave Iraq on Monday, after an ordeal lasting more than five years, most of which was behind bars in a Baghdad jail.
He was arrested in 2021 along with an Egyptian colleague, and later found guilty by an Iraqi court of what his family long argued were trumped-up fraud charges relating to his involvement as a contractor working on the massive Central Bank of Iraq headquarters construction project.
His jail sentence came with a massive fine, worth $16 million.
Mr Pether, 51, was released from jail in June last year, but was banned from leaving Iraq until this week.
Speaking to the media at Dublin Airport, and fighting back tears shortly after his reunion with his family, who are based in Ireland, Mr Pether said his wife and children had "lived this every single day with me".
"Our children lost years with their dad. They watched their mum fight every day to try and bring me home," he said.
"They grew up with uncertainty, fear and circumstances that no child should ever have to carry.
"I am so thankful for my wife Desree, for always fighting for me, while at the same time holding our family together, all while dealing with a situation that took an enormous toll on her too."
Mr Pether said his focus was on his family, even though he appreciated there would be many questions about his circumstances.
"There will be time to talk about what happened, why it happened, who was responsible and why nobody should ever be allowed to do this to another person or another family again," Mr Pether said.
"But today, more than anything, I want to talk about the people who carried us through it."
'We were innocent'
Mr Pether's wife Desree had been his most vocal advocate, campaigning for years for his release.
She had repeatedly raised concerns about his physical and mental health behind bars, and flagged serious flaws in his prosecution — particularly arguing he was forced to sign a confession, written in Arabic, without knowing what the document said.
In 2021, the United Nations investigated the situation facing Mr Pether and his Egyptian colleague, Khalid Zaghloul, and said the pair had been subjected to "acts of torture and ill treatment".
"Today I don't want to spend too much time talking about courts or governments or everything that was done to us," Mr Pether said in Dublin.
"I do need to say something about the injustice of what happened, because coming home today should never be mistaken for that injustice somehow having been corrected.
"It wasn't. Not even close."
He said the convictions against him and Mr Zaghloul had not be overturned, and neither man "has been exonerated".
"We were innocent when we were taken on 7th April 2021, and we remain innocent today," Mr Pether said.
"I was released from prison hours away from death, my body shutting down, after months of critical illness and excruciating pain, but I remained trapped in Iraq.
"I didn't have my passport, visa or identity documents, and I had no ability to move around freely or safely, leave the country or even go to a hospital."
'Thank you seems completely inadequate'
Australia's Foreign Minister Penny Wong had welcomed Mr Pether's release earlier in the day, and said she spoke to him before he left Baghdad.
"I know this has taken a real toll on him and his family," she said in Canberra.
Ireland's Taoiseach, or prime minister, Micheál Martin posted on social media Mr Pether's release would "come as a great relief" and said he appreciated "the Iraqi Government responding to the calls for his release from both Ireland and Australia".
Ms Pether had accused the Australian government, under prime ministers Scott Morrison and Anthony Albanese, of dragging their feet in pushing for his release, saying at times the family felt abandoned by their home country.
She turned to the Irish government for help, despite the fact Mr Pether does not share the Irish citizenship his wife and children have.
"One of the things this experience has taught me is that governments are ultimately made up of people," Mr Pether said.
"And sometimes an individual deciding to care, to pick up a telephone, to keep asking a question or simply refusing to give up can change the course of somebody else's life.
"There are some people who went so far beyond anything we could ever have asked of them that saying thank you seems completely inadequate."

Roundup: European leaders question Trump's Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
02:52:47 CST
03:52:47 KST

BRUSSELS, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- European leaders on Monday questioned whether Russia would honor an "energy ceasefire" announced by U.S. President Donald Trump, while saying a real halt to attacks on energy infrastructure could offer relief if implemented.
The announcement, which Moscow has yet to confirm, came amid growing concerns in Europe over Washington's recent diesel supply agreement with Russia and its implications for Western sanctions and transatlantic relations.
European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc would welcome an energy ceasefire if it was observed, but questioned whether Russia would comply.
"We welcome the energy ceasefire when it holds. We have not yet seen that also Russia will stick to it," Kallas told reporters ahead of a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Luxembourg.
She said a ceasefire limited to oil refineries would disproportionately benefit Russia, which has far more refining facilities than Ukraine.
"If we want to end this war, the only way we can do this is by putting more pressure on Russia," Kallas said, calling on the United States to impose sanctions on Moscow.
LEADERS QUESTION RUSSIA'S COMMITMENT
French President Emmanuel Macron said Monday that he had seen no sign of an energy ceasefire on the Russian side, pointing to continued strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also expressed skepticism about the prospects for a ceasefire. At the Warsaw Security Forum, he said Russia had repeatedly rejected proposals for de-escalation.
"Russia is not interested in a ceasefire, or in de-escalation or peace," Tusk said, adding that European countries should have no illusions about Moscow's intentions.
Tusk also called for further strengthening sanctions against Russia.
Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics said that there were currently no signs Russia was ready to end the conflict, as Russian President Vladimir Putin remained convinced he could achieve victory.
Nevertheless, Rinkevics said that a U.S.-brokered energy ceasefire, if successfully implemented, would benefit all sides. Europe should continue providing military and financial assistance to Ukraine and help the country prepare for the coming winter, he added.
Bosnian Serb leader Milorad Dodik, however, welcomed the ceasefire. He described the announcement as an opportunity to restore dialogue and move toward peace, while accusing European officials of prolonging the conflict through continued military assistance to Ukraine.
DIESEL AGREEMENT DRAWS CRITICISM
European criticism also focused on Washington's agreement with Moscow on diesel supplies.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Monday that the U.S.-Russia diesel agreement was "out of the question" for Germany and Europe.
Russia would only negotiate seriously under pressure, he said. Germany would maintain its sanctions against Moscow, and he called for tougher measures following continued Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Hanna Notte, director of the Eurasia Nonproliferation Program at the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies and a non-resident senior associate at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said the latest developments were creating new tensions between Washington and Kyiv and further straining transatlantic relations.
"Politically, Russia is really the beneficiary here," Notte said.
She said the diesel agreement set a precedent allowing Moscow to conclude bilateral economic deals with Washington without first reaching a settlement on the Ukraine conflict. It could also undermine the credibility of Western sanctions, particularly after years of efforts to discourage other countries from purchasing Russian energy, she argued.
Felix Klauser, head of German public broadcaster ZDF's Moscow bureau, said the diesel agreement represented a political gain for the Kremlin, which could portray the easing of sanctions as a symbolic breakthrough at home and abroad.
He said the agreement meanwhile increased pressure on Ukraine to halt attacks on Russian oil infrastructure. Its political symbolism appeared to matter more to Trump than the actual volume of Russian diesel reaching global markets before the U.S. midterm elections, Klauser said.
QUESTIONS OVER CEASEFIRE TERMS
Finnish national broadcaster Yle also raised questions about whether the proposed energy ceasefire would impose equal obligations on Russia and Ukraine.
Markku Kangaspuro, a professor at the University of Helsinki, told Yle that Russia could benefit from the arrangement without even agreeing to a ceasefire.
Tyyne Karjalainen, a researcher at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs, said that Ukraine could face more severe consequences if the ceasefire broke down, including the risk of Washington withdrawing security support.
A commentary published Monday in The Irish Times argued that Trump's proposed energy ceasefire was heavily tilted in Russia's favor, potentially depriving Ukraine of one of its most effective means of exerting pressure on Moscow.
Nevertheless, the commentary noted that expanding the ceasefire from oil refineries to all energy infrastructure could help ease Ukrainian civilians' suffering during the approaching winter.
Such a move could pave the way for a broader ceasefire, it suggested, although a negotiated settlement to the conflict remained a distant prospect. ■

ESafety says it can't prevent Australians from seeing execution live stream

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
18:48:57 UTC

eSafety office says it cannot prevent Australians seeing execution live stream
In short:
The office of eSafety says it does not have the power to proactively block the live streaming of a US execution from being available in Australia.
It says online services have the responsibility to protect users from harmful material.
What's next?
There are calls for the Australian government to make representations to the Trump administration opposing the death penalty.
Australia's online safety regulator eSafety says it does not have the power to "proactively prevent" the live stream of a firing squad execution in the United States from being shown in Australia, but argues platforms have a responsibility to protect users from harmful content.
Last week, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at a military base in Texas in 2009, would be available for the public to watch.
Across the political divide in Canberra there has been widespread concern about Australians seeing the December 3 live stream.
Loading...
The eSafety office said there were limits to its powers.
"While eSafety does not have powers to proactively prevent a live stream from occurring online, online services have responsibilities under Australia's online safety regulatory framework to protect users from harmful material," a spokesperson said.
"As the regulator responsible for enforcing these obligations, eSafety is in regular contact with online platforms and will continue to monitor the situation, considering any action as appropriate."
Experts agreed eSafety's power was more geared towards being able to take down content rather than pre-emptively blocking it.
Government says Australians 'rightly expect' to not see live stream
The ABC has contacted Google, Meta and TikTok to see if they have plans to restrict the content, but has not received responses.
The federal government said Australians "rightly expect" the content would not appear on their screens, and platforms have a responsibility to meet those expectations.
"Vision of an execution being live streamed here would be deeply distressing to many Australians," a government spokesperson said.
"No-one should be confronted with it, particularly younger Australians."
The government's response followed Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young writing to the communications minister and eSafety commissioner, demanding they "take whatever action is necessary" to block the "barbaric" event from being shown in Australia.
One Nation's Barnaby Joyce said it was "Roman amphitheatre stuff" that he did not want anyone to witness, while Liberal Tim Wilson said it was "enormously problematic" and Australia "shouldn't be promoting that sort of violence".
Expert says it highlights need for Digital Duty of Care
Swinburne University media lecturer Belinda Barnet believed the most the eSafety commissioner could do was issue take down notices, as was done in the case of a Sydney church stabbing in 2024.
"I don't see how they can take pre-emptive action," she said.
However, Dr Barnet acknowledged that take down powers were limited because content could run away as soon as it existed online.
"It's just a Band-Aid solution but we don't have a lot else in our armoury,"
she said.
Dr Barnet said it highlighted the need for the government's Digital Duty of Care Bill, which is being introduced into parliament this week, as it will require platforms to take steps to reduce the risk of harm to users on their sites.
"At the moment there is no onus on the platforms to protect all of us in Australia from what you could call harmful content," Dr Barnet said.
Government facing calls to make representations to US over death penalty
It is Australian policy to oppose the death penalty in all circumstances for all people, which includes supporting the universal abolition of the death penalty.
Monash University lecturer and vice president of the Capital Punishment Justice Project, Sara Kowal, said Australian officials should be telling the United States, whether it is publicly or privately, that they oppose the death penalty.
"This would be a perfect example of a case where the Australian government should be making strong representations to the Trump administration," she said.
Iran and Afghanistan are among the few countries that still carry out public executions.
"It's really abhorrent to see the United States trying to join this club,"
Ms Kowal said.
At the weekend, US President Donald Trump said he had not yet made a final decision about live streaming the execution.

Loophole allowing new coal and gas to avoid stricter climate laws
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
18:46:30 UTC
03:46:30 KST

Coal and gas avoiding stricter laws by expanding existing mines, Climate Council warns
In short:
Coal and gas mines have to follow less strict emissions laws when they are expanded compared to outright new mines.
The Climate Council says that amounts to a "loophole" being used by the industry to add new emissions without having to follow "best-practice" limits.
What's next?
The Safeguard Mechanism, which sets emissions laws for heavy industry, is under review.
Coal and gas mines are using what the Climate Council warns is a "loophole" to expand operations and add new emissions while avoiding stricter laws imposed on new coal and gas projects.
The Climate Council says unless emissions from mine expansions are treated the same as emissions from new mines, it will cause an additional 4.5 million tonnes of CO2 a year by 2035.
Coal and gas mines are among the roughly 200 facilities covered by the Safeguard Mechanism — climate laws that require Australia's biggest polluters to cut or offset emissions by about 5 per cent a year or else face heavy penalties.
Under the laws, which are currently being reviewed, new coal and gas facilities are required to follow more strict, "best-practice" limits that take into account the most efficient technologies available for mines.
But existing facilities are not required to meet that higher standard when expanding or extending the life of an existing mine.
Modelling by Reputex has estimated that across 22 planned coal and gas expansions and extensions over the next decade, which will be treated as existing facilities, they will be able to emit 11 times more than if they were treated as new facilities.
The Climate Council says expansions are being used widely across the industry, taking advantage of that favourable treatment and leading to more emissions.
"Companies have an incentive to characterise everything as an expansion rather than a new facility," chief executive Amanda McKenzie said.
"We're arguing that is one of the loopholes that needs to be shut."
The Safeguard Mechanism is under review and due to be revisited next year, when the government will decide whether to set a steeper trajectory towards net zero emissions by 2050.
The Climate Council says when that time comes, "best-practice" CO2 limits should be applied to all new coal and gas emissions, regardless of whether they come from a new mine or an expanded one.
It says fossil fuel facilities are not doing enough to transition to net zero, and those covered by the Safeguard Mechanism actually increased emissions in the most recent year.
Most new coal and gas emissions from expansions
The council says since the Safeguard Mechanism laws were amended in 2022, more than three quarters of all new coal development have been expansions or extensions to projects.
It pointed to last month's approval for an open-cut coalmine in the Hunter Valley, which owners Yancoal and Glencore applied to extend by more than a decade.
Its life extension into the 2040s, which includes the mining of deeper coal seams, represents an additional $2.7 billion capital investment and will add an extra 809 megatonnes of CO2 emissions — or a bit less than two years' worth of Australia's annual emissions.
Because the Yancoal-Glencore owned coalmine was already covered by the Safeguard Mechanism, the extension will be treated under rules for existing projects, which the Climate Council estimates will result in emissions 60 per cent higher than if it was treated as a new project.
The NSW Independent Planning Commission, which approved the life extension, said while it would contribute to climate change and add to Australia's emissions, that was outweighed by its benefits, including supporting up to 1,400 local jobs and ongoing tax revenue from the mine.
"Despite these new investments being significant enough to require a new environmental approval, the vast majority of their pollution will not be considered 'new' by the Safeguard Mechanism," the council said.
Mining sector rebuffs Coalition promise to scrap Safeguard Mechanism
The Coalition has vowed to "take a chainsaw" to the Safeguard Mechanism, saying they would scrap the laws claiming they are driving up costs for heavy industry and manufacturing.
But after more than a decade of policy instability, the mining sector has urged not to up-end climate laws again.
On Friday the Minerals Council of Australia said the Safeguard Mechanism should be retained, saying it was working as intended to reduce emissions.
"The industry seeks change that is manageable, orderly, and establishes an appropriate regulatory framework for industry and the nation to achieve medium- and long-term emissions targets," MCA chief executive Tania Constable wrote on Friday.
The Minerals Council also urged the government not to push big polluters to cut emissions even harder after 2030, when requirements to cut emissions by about 5 per cent a year will soften to 3.3 per cent a year.
The industry argues existing projects should not be asked to meet "best-practice" emissions requirements since expansions and extensions are still using existing infrastructure, whereas new facilities are able to invest in more efficient technologies.
The Climate Council says if mining operations cannot be expanded under "best-practice" rules, then they should not seek to do so.
"We have to have laws that are genuinely getting us out of coal and oil and gas, so finding ways to enable the companies to continue to expand is nonsensical," Ms McKenzie said.
A spokesperson for Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen said the government's reforms to the Safeguard Mechanism were "working well".
"The focus of the review set out in the consultation paper is ensuring they continue to deliver," the spokesperson said in a statement.
"No decisions have been made to change current settings and our department is engaging with stakeholders to hear their views."

They moved to Australia. Years later, they developed an unexpected condition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
18:43:22 UTC
03:43:22 KST

In brief
- Nearly one in four Australians experience hay fever, according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.
- For some migrants, hay fever doesn't appear until years after they move to Australia.
Zoe had never experienced hay fever before moving to Australia.
But a few years after arriving, she began experiencing red and itchy eyes. At first, she assumed they were a reaction to her contact lenses.
When the symptoms worsened and returned year after year, she started looking for another explanation.
Along with itchy eyes, she said she developed severe nasal congestion and an urge to sneeze. After seeking medical advice, she was told she had hay fever.
"It took me years to realise," Zoe, who asked for her last name to be withheld for privacy reasons, told SBS Thai.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Allergic rhinitis, commonly known as hay fever, occurs when the immune system reacts to airborne allergens. Common triggers include pollen, dust mites, mould and animal dander (flakes of skin in fur, hair or feathers).
Nearly one in four Australians experience hay fever, according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.
For some migrants, the condition only emerges after several years of living in the country, with research suggesting exposure to new environmental allergens may play a role.
Why allergies can emerge years after migration
Dr Jason Yu, a Sydney-based general practitioner and clinical allergist, became interested in allergy medicine after moving between countries. He had not experienced allergies as a child but developed them years later.
He said allergies can develop at any stage of life, although they often first appear in childhood.
"We don't know the exact reasons why people develop allergies," Yu told SBS Thai.
One possible explanation for developing new allergies after migration is exposure to a novel environment, which can introduce people to allergens they hadn't previously encountered.
Yu said dust mite allergies are common in Sydney and other coastal areas, while grass pollen, including ryegrass pollen, was another prominent trigger in Australia.
"Pollen can be blown kilometres away," he said.
Yu said there isn't yet a definitive explanation for why some people develop allergies and others don't.
Genetics and the development of the immune system may also play a role. Infections can also influence immune responses, although their relationship with allergy development is complex.
Research has previously documented the development of allergic conditions among people who migrate to Australia.
A 1996 study found up to 60 per cent of people who moved from South-East Asian countries to Australia developed hay fever, while 15 per cent developed asthma within their first 10 years in Australia.
A 2015 study from Curtin University also reported similar findings, suggesting people who migrated from China were more prone to allergies after moving to Australia.
For Hansa, whose last name has been withheld for privacy reasons, the first signs of hay fever were easy to mistake for a cold.
"One day, all of a sudden, my nose wouldn't stop running, my eyes were watering, and I kept sneezing," she told SBS Thai.
While living in Thailand, Hansa occasionally reacted to construction dust, but she hadn't experienced the same symptoms after moving to Australia.
About three years after her arrival, the symptoms began.
She had assumed that if she was allergic to something, the reaction would appear straight away, rather than emerge several years after the move.
Antihistamines are commonly used to manage hay fever, but Yu said the ideal form of treatment depends on a person's symptoms.
For those whose main symptom is nasal congestion, corticosteroid nasal sprays may be more effective than antihistamines alone, he said.
For persistent or more severe allergies, allergen immunotherapy may also be an option.
When hay fever becomes more serious
Hay fever and asthma are different but closely related conditions.
Hay fever primarily affects the eyes and upper airways, while asthma affects the lower airways and causes symptoms such as wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath.
"If you feel short of breath, you feel like heaviness on your chest, you definitely should see someone about it," Yu said.
He said this was particularly important because, in rare circumstances, exposure to grass pollen can trigger a potentially life-threatening event known as thunderstorm asthma.
Under certain weather conditions, storm outflows can concentrate grass pollen into smaller particles. When inhaled, those particles can penetrate deeper into the lungs, triggering inflammation and narrowing airways.
"It doesn't happen often, but if it does happen, it has really deadly consequences," Yu said.
Melbourne experienced what's considered the world's largest recorded epidemic of thunderstorm asthma in November 2016. Thousands of people developed breathing difficulties, placing significant pressure on the city's emergency services and hospitals.
The event also highlighted the disproportionate impact thunderstorm asthma can have on some migrant communities.
A study published by The Lancet in 2018 found people of Asian or Indian ethnicity were disproportionately impacted, representing 39 per cent of people who attended hospital. Six of the 10 who died were of South or Southeast Asian ethnicity.
Hay fever and asthma can also occur together, and Yu said some people may not realise they have both conditions.
"I've had a few patients come in; they didn't realise they had asthma as well; they thought they just had hay fever.
"But because I checked, I could actually identify they actually have asthma."

The country coming for a $20-billion Australian export market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
18:43:14 UTC
03:43:14 KST

IN BRIEF:
- Brazil is the world's leading beef exporter and producer.
- Commentators warn that shifts in global markets could see the country absorb Australia's markets.
Australian beef could face its toughest competition yet, as the world's leading producer encroaches on its traditional export markets.
Since the early 2000s, Brazil has consistently ranked as the world's leading beef producer, with an enormous 230 million-strong herd in 2024, more than the country's estimated population. The South American country is also the world's leading exporter, sending its beef to 130 different countries.
Australia has long prided itself on its beef exports: in 2025, 1.5 million tonnes of beef were sent to 83 countries. In 2025, the value of Australian beef exports was $19.6 billion, according to Australia's red meat research and marketing body, Meat and Livestock Australia (MLA).
But commentators are suggesting South American exporters are expanding in Australia's most important export markets — South Korea and Japan — which could have significant impacts on price competition over the coming months.
Speaking on a recent agribusiness podcast, Angus Gidley-Baird, senior animal proteins analyst at food and agribusiness bank Rabobank, said Australia’s beef sector should closely monitor developments in Brazil.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"Over the past few years, we’ve seen Brazil increase its presence in several of Australia’s export markets," Gidley-Baird said.
"Combined with changing trade dynamics involving China, the United States and Europe, it is becoming increasingly important for Australian producers and exporters to understand what is happening in the Brazilian beef sector."
Brazil already has a big presence in the Australian meat industry, through worldwide giant JBS. It's the biggest meat processing company in Australia, owning a series of foodlots and abattoirs, as well as the smallgoods company Primo Foods.
More than half of Brazil's beef exports are to China, and it hit its annual quota of 1.1 million tonnes for shipments to the country last month.
China's commerce ministry said it would start collecting an additional 55 per cent tariff on Brazil's beef shipments on 1 October after the South American country reached its annual quota of 1.1 million tonnes.
Rabobank Brazil animal protein analyst Wagner Yanaguizawa said that new quota restrictions significantly reduced Brazilian shipments during the second half of 2025, creating surplus volumes that would need to be redirected elsewhere, and could translate into greater competition for Australia in alternative destination markets.
Yanaguizawa said the United States was likely to absorb some of the displaced volume, while the Middle East, Indonesia, Vietnam, Chile and the United Kingdom also presented opportunities. Those markets would not be sufficient to offset reduced Chinese demand, though, he said.
Yanaguizawa said the potential opening of Japan and South Korea to Brazilian beef also warrants close attention from Australian industry participants.
"Japanese and South Korean inspections of Brazilian processing plants had been completed, and final reports were pending before market access decisions could be finalised. Industry expectations are that access could be granted later this year," Yanaguizawa said.
"These two markets are very important for Australia, and soon Australia may have a new competitor," he said.
The MLA is aware of the shift. On an August 2026 podcast, the corporation's regional manager for Southeast Asia, Valeska, said that as global trade patterns shifted, Australian beef volumes had been redirected from China into Southeast Asia.
At the same time, competition across Southeast Asia was intensifying, as exporters from South America actively pursued new opportunities across the region.
"The South Americans are really active and quite aggressive. At the [World Food Expo in the Philippines] yesterday, we spoke with Brazilian packers who indicated they're looking at alternative markets."
Valeska said she believed Australia's long-term investment in Southeast Asia positioned the industry well.
"We're not resting on our laurels. Australian beef is definitely ramping up activities across Southeast Asia, and I think it's an opportunity to really secure the premium segment while continuing to grow demand through other channels."

Carrie gets a bloody 2026 remake just in time for Halloween
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

What to watch in October, from classic horror reboots to shocking docs
Welcome to what to watch, where we take you through what's on the box in October.
This month brings a heartbreaking story of charity betrayal from the UK and an Australian horror-comedy about killer gnomes. Plus, Mike Flanagan has a go at rebooting Carrie and Catherine Zeta Jones gets to pull out her Welsh accent for Kill Jackie.
Here's what we're watching this month.
Believe In Magic: The Mother of All Cons
What's it about? A mother and daughter in the midst of a nightmare, or a cruel scam? Believe in Magic tells the story of Megan Bhari and her mother Jean O'Brien, founders of a UK charity supporting seriously ill children and their families.
The organisation, built in 2012 around the story of Megan's own battle with a brain tumour, raised hundreds of thousands of pounds and was praised for its work. Megan was dogged in her efforts to promote the organisation.There were tea parties at Buckingham Palace and a princess ball hosted by One Direction’s Louis Tomlinson and his mother.
In 2015, Jean reported that Megan’s condition had worsened. Pleading for funds as part of a Save Meg appeal, she gave little detail on Megan’s care and treating doctors. It prompted suspicion from members of the charity’s community who said they “smelled a rat”.
One mother’s doubts led her to dig deeper into the charity, as well as Megan and Jean’s claims. What she and other parents found was explosive. The charity was investigated and ultimately shut down.
But there’s a bigger twist in this new three-part investigative series by the BBC. No spoilers here, other than to say, at times it's hard to keep your jaw off the floor at what is an unbelievable and ultimately tragic story.
Perfect for: Lovers of true-crime stories like Inventing Anna, Catfish or Apple Cider Vinegar.
Where to watch: The first episode premieres on ABC TV and iview on Tuesday, October 13.
Carrie
What's it about? There are few stories in the modern horror canon that are more revered than Carrie. First as Stephen King's groundbreaking debut 1974 novel and then Brian De Palma's landmark 1976 film adaptation.
Modern adaptations of the girl with telekinesis haven't fared ,as well, with the 1999 sequel, The Rage, the 2002 TV movie and 2013's modern reboot all being resoundingly poo-pooed, but if there is one thing Hollywood will do it's capitalise on established IP. Which is how we arrive at Carrie (2026) an extended miniseries helmed by Mike Flanagan, who has proved himself very handy at adaptations with The Haunting of Hill House and The Haunting of Bly Manor.
All the familiar beats are here, just transported to high school in 2026. Carrie (Summer H Howell) is now not just an outcast, but a complete recluse kept prisoner in her home with her overly religious mother (Samantha Sloyan, a Flanagan fave who is born for this role). They're both exposed to the world after the untimely death of Carrie's construction worker father, who is a new addition to the story. So the timid teen is even more raw when she's pushed into the cruel world of bullies with smartphones.
King's original story is pretty tight, so Flanagan pads the eight-episode run time by expanding on some overlooked details about a coven of similarly gifted girls, which gives off the hint that the director is sniffing out a season two. Carrie purists might revolt, but Mike Flanagan fans remain fed.
Perfect for: those who like a very expanded horror universe.
Where to watch: Carrie is streaming on Prime Video now.
Dustfall
What's it about? This gritty mystery drama follows detective Antigone "Tig" Pollard (Anna Torv, The Newsreader) as she tries to solve a brutal sexual assault on a schoolgirl, revealing small-town secrets and dredging up her own past in her pursuit of the truth.
Given the subject matter, Dustfall makes for uncomfortable viewing at times, but it dares you to not look away. It's also punctuated by charming lighter moments which will likely feel distinctly familiar for anyone who grew up in regional Australia.
Dustfall spotlights layered female characters through Tig's often-complicated relationships, with her lifelong friend Shayna (Alice Ansara), her force of nature mother Olivia (Juliet Stevenson); and victim-survivors Edie (Zoe Phillips) and Maya (Gemma Chua-Tran).
Tig's also navigating a blossoming romance with local Mitch (Ben Knight), learning the ways of her detective partner Remi (Bert La Bonte), and can't escape Andy (Peter Fenton), the much older local rock star who has held an unsettling power over her since her teenage years.
Each episode leaves you wanting more, with a genuinely gripping storyline that builds in intensity until the very end, delivering a shocking but satisfying twist.
Based on Vikki Petraitis's novel The Unbelieved, Dustfall features stellar performances from a cast of established and up-and-coming actors and is bound to open doors.
Perfect for: Those who want their next bingeworthy series with a side of sharp social commentary that will stay with you long after the credits roll.
Where to watch: All episodes of Dustfall are streaming now on ABC iview.
Gnomes
What's it about? If you like your Australian comedy zany and silly, then you might have just been handed your favourite show of the year in Gnomes.
Senior Sergeant Arnold Kipps (Asa Butterfield) is perfectly happy acting as the big dog top cop in the tiny regional town of Nompton. His peaceful, if not a bit under-respected, life is interrupted when his ex-partner and old flame Ellie McKay (Megan Smart) comes down from the city to announce that Arnold's station is to be shut down due to lack of activity and they're only keeping one local police officer on.
And this is before an evil gnome queen is unleashed during prep for the annual gnome festival and animates all the garden gnomes in town into vicious killers.
Written by wife and husband duo Tegan Higginbotham and Paul F Verhoeven, the laughs are so smooth and fast it's easy to forget that Gnomes is a horror — that is until one of the titular terrors slices a man's face off with DVDs.
While UK import Butterfield is very much at home with the frustrated nerd slapstick he perfected on Sex Education, ditzy police duo consisting of Higginbotham and Matt O'Kine nearly steal the show (do we see a spin off on the horizon?).
Perfect for: Some smooth brain, halloweeny laughs.
Where to watch: Gnomes is streaming on Stan now.
Kill Jackie
What's it about? For the first time in her 40-year career, Welsh actor Catherine Zeta-Jones is using her real accent on screen. It's to play the titular Jackie in revenge thriller Kill Jackie, about a one-time "rich, sexy dealer of cocaine" turned art dealer who is trying to evade the seven assassins on her tail.
Except she's not really that interested in evading them, even though the so-called Seven Demons are psychopaths, hell-bent on killing not only her but the people she loves and even those with whom she has only a mildly inappropriate professional relationship, like her tax accountant (Daniel Ings; Lovesick).
Instead, Jackie is going to destroy them herself. And considering the assassins have torched her apartment and art collection, and stolen a lot of her money, she doesn't have much to lose.
It's fun to watch Zeta-Jones return to a Chicago-style role as a woman scorned, although Jackie is much happier to fly under the radar than the fame-hungry Velma Kelly, who she played when she was just 32.
Described by one assassin as "more resourceful than expected", Jackie has more friends and well-wishers than you would expect from someone who boasts "the most important thing about me [is] I don't give a f***".
Now 56, Zeta-Jones seemingly doesn't give a f*** either.
Perfect for: Fans of the spate of recent woman-assassin-slash-badass TV, from Furious to The Assassin and Killing Eve.
Where to watch: Kill Jackie is streaming on Stan now.
