The incident at RAF Fairford is assessed as highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran and almost certainly directed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the Prime Minister told the House of Commons.
Andy Burnham made the attribution in a statement covering the United Nations General Assembly and the international meetings that followed, turning to protective security at bases shared with the United States.
He said: “Since Unga, Mr Speaker, we have been in close contact with the US about protective security at our shared bases. I want to thank our police and military personnel for their swift response to the incidents at RAF Fairford and RAF Molesworth. My right hon. Friend the Home Secretary will update the House regarding the incident at RAF Fairford, but I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard. We will not tolerate these threats on our soil. We will crack down on Iran’s use of criminal networks using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams.
“And we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm.”
Iran’s embassy in London called the claims unfounded and malicious speculation, and the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said Britain was barking up the wrong tree.
Police were called at about a quarter to one in the morning of 27 September to reports of suspicious vehicles heading towards the Gloucestershire base. Armed officers from Gloucestershire Constabulary arrested five men near Whelford, initially on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act 1875 and then on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act under section five of the Terrorism Act 2006. A major incident was declared, a cordon went up and homes nearby were evacuated while Army bomb disposal teams examined three vehicles.
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said on 29 September that no improvised explosive devices had been found and that a quantity of petrol had been recovered. Engaging Raz: Themes in Normative Philosophy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
18:14:00 UTC
03:14:00 KST

Engaging Raz: Themes in Normative Philosophy is a posthumous Festschrift for Joseph Raz (1939–2022), collects papers from “two highly selective, international conferences held in Raz’s honor after his passing.” It is a splendid volume: an entirely fitting tribute to, as its editors aptly write, a “towering figure in late twentieth century and early twenty-first century analytical philosophy”, whose work “profoundly influenced the discipline”.
The range of topics covered alone is a testament to the reach and significance of Raz’s contributions. There are essays, to give an incomplete list, on the relation between reasons and values, the nature of practical reason and action, exclusionary reasons, autonomy, the rule of law, the interest theory of rights, multiculturalism, and authority. It is also a striking, indirect testament to the reach and significance of Raz’s work how much, through no fault of the editors or contributors, the book leaves out. Two highly selective, international conferences and over 500 pages were not enough to allow for coverage of such topics as normative powers as such (although there are two excellent papers on promises and contracts), skepticism about the moral, criticism of the ideal of equality, the myth of instrumental reason, and incommensurability, among much else.
Many of the papers offer close readings of Raz’s work, most assess and develop Razian theses, and all engage with Razian themes. The result is a surprisingly cohesive volume; nothing feels shoehorned in. Each of the essays is of exceptionally high quality, from some of most distinguished thinkers in moral, political, and legal philosophy, as well as the philosophy of action, along with a few newer voices who, to judge from the strength of their contributions, will have much to teach us in coming years. None of the papers reads as dashed off or opportunistically unloaded. All are digestibly clear and concise. The joint effort and self-discipline of editors and contributors are remarkable; anyone who has edited or contributed to a collection of essays must marvel at how quickly the talks materialized on the shelf.
Many of the essays develop and advance, in conversation with Raz, their authors’ own ongoing work. Anyone interested in, for instance, T.M. Scanlon’s “buck-passing” account of goodness and value, Ralph Wedgwood’s attempts to reconcile ethics and decision theory, Elinor Mason’s notion of taking responsibility, Andrei Marmor’s elevation of accountability to philosophical attention, David Owens’s rethinking of the significance of commands, Massimo Renzo’s theory of alienated action, David Enoch’s distinction between “sovereignty” and “nonalienation”, or Daniel Viehoff’s fiduciary reading of the relation of state and citizen—and the list could go on—will want to read their essays.
Many of the essays, including some of those just listed, provide, directly or indirectly, opinionated surveys of the state of the art on Razian themes, along the lines of the most helpful handbook or encyclopedia entries. If someone with passing familiarity with Raz’s discussions of, say, exclusionary reasons, the rule of law, the interest theory of rights, multiculturalism, or the “adequacy” of an option set were to wonder, “Where has the debate gone since?” they could not do better than to read the papers on those subjects by Ulrike Heuer, Michael S. Moore, Emad H. Atiq, Kimberley Brownlee, Daniel Weinstock, and Steven Wall, respectively.
The wide-ranging nature of the collection would frustrate any attempt to engage with its content as a whole. So, I will confine myself to a question provoked by Enoch’s and Wall’s revisiting of Raz’s account of autonomy, presented in his seminal The Morality of Freedom. It is whether autonomy, as Raz articulates it, is really something of value, in the way that he suggests it is.
In Raz’s own words, the
ruling ideal behind the ideal of personal autonomy is that people should make their own lives. The autonomous person is a (part) author of his own life. The ideal of personal autonomy is the vision of people controlling, to some degree, their own destiny, fashioning it through successive decisions throughout their lives. (The Morality of Freedom, 369)
An autonomous life thus contrasts with “a life of no choices, or of drifting through life without ever exercising one’s capacity to choose” (The Morality of Freedom, 371). Enoch derives a natural methodology from this ideal, so described. In matters of autonomy, he suggests,
Whenever questions come up, whenever it is necessary to adjudicate between competing ways of filling in details, we should return to the underlying ideal, even if somewhat metaphorically put, and ask which way of filling in the details is more loyal to that underlying ideal. (247)
Let that be our methodology too.
There can be little debate that there is such an ideal, of an autonomous life. My question is whether one’s life necessarily goes worse for one insofar as one’s life does not realize that ideal. Of course, we need an “other things equal” qualification. And we might need to restrict our attention to life in cultural settings such as those of “western industrial societies” (The Morality of Freedom, 369). So, let us ask: other things equal and within such cultural settings, does one’s life go worse for one if and because one does not lead it autonomously, independently (as Wall clarifies, 273) of one’s attitudes toward living an autonomous life?
This is what I wonder. Imagine that someone leads the life that is otherwise best for them. It makes them happier, in a hedonic sense, than any other life would, and it is perfectly matched to their talents, so that they succeed in what they set out to do, more than they would in any other life. They willingly endorse it. But still this person has drifted into the life, or left it to chance, or was reared into it. To illustrate the last possibility, suppose that, from childhood, the siblings worked at the family business. As they reached adulthood, the others left the business for other things, something the parents wholeheartedly welcomed. But one sibling, content with the life they had, just continued in the business, doing each day what they had done the day before. While perfectly aware of alternatives—after all, the other siblings were pursuing them—this sibling, happy with what they had, never deliberated about whether to pursue such an alternative, never so much as to reject it.
Let us imagine further that this contented sibling enjoys the conditions for an autonomous life, even if, by hypothesis, they do not do anything further to make use of those conditions to lead an autonomous life. Those conditions, as Enoch lists them, are “appropriate mental abilities, an adequate range of options, and independence from coercion and manipulation” (248). Enoch and Wall do a real service in elaborating and amending these conditions. Enoch and Wall part ways with Raz in suggesting that the availability of even bad options can contribute to the autonomy of a life (253; 290), and Enoch goes so far as to suggest that the pursuit of a bad option can do so (258).
The last condition, of independence, that one is not coerced or manipulated into the life that one leads, reflects the fact that, as both Enoch and Wall note, leading an autonomous life is, at least in part, an interpersonal or, as Enoch puts it, a “relational”, matter. To lead an autonomous life is to lead it not subject to the will of another. Enoch and Wall observe (260; 293) that the adequacy of a range of options is itself in part a relational matter. Suppose that one is not coerced or manipulated into leading the life that one leads. To that extent, one is independent. Nevertheless, suppose, options have been removed from one’s menu (or, one might add, their costs increased) “intentionally” (Enoch) or by “unjustified interference” (Wall) (although perhaps without coercion). This seems more compromising to the autonomy of the life that we choose from the menu than if the same options were removed (or made more costly) by, say, natural forces or the uncoordinated, market choices of others. (Parenthetically, though, I’m a bit puzzled by Wall’s suggestion that this effect on our autonomy occurs only through interference that is unjustified on other grounds. One might have thought that the reason why such interference is unjustified is precisely that it had this effect on our autonomy.)
To these three conditions—capacities, options, and independence—Enoch adds a possible fourth, concerning “the conditions under which the preferences guiding the choice were shaped” (248). This references his paper “False Consciousness for Liberals, Part I: Consent, Autonomy, and Adaptive Preferences”, in which he argues, roughly, that when the preferences guiding the choice were shaped by injustice, the resulting life suffers from an autonomy deficit. This is another way in which one might live a life subject to the will of another.
So, in sum, there is a great deal of complexity and nuance in the conditions for autonomy. But imagine that these conditions are met. One is “living one’s best life”, as they say, one is not, in doing so, subject to the will of another, and one has an adequate range of options. Still, one has drifted into the life, or left it to chance, or was brought up into it. So, one is not living an autonomous life. While one “willingly endorses” one’s pursuits, this is not enough for autonomy, the ideal of which “transcends the conceptual point that personal well‐being is partly determined by success in willingly endorsed pursuits and holds the free choice of goals and relations as an essential ingredient of individual well‐being” (The Morality of Freedom, 369, reading this passage perhaps differently from Enoch at 249–250).
Recall that, following Enoch, our methodological lodestar in articulating the relevant value is the metaphor of authoring one’s life. And as we are imagining things, the metaphor does not fit. One is not the author of one’s life. One has simply let stand the text that one has found oneself with, as a biographical subject might let stand the offerings of a ghostwriter, rather than composing it oneself. As Wall writes, “they will not realize autonomy, even if they are very successful in realizing these other goods, if they do not pursue these other goods in certain ways and under the right conditions” (273), and while one has pursued these other goods “under the right conditions”, one has not pursued them in the “certain ways” that distinguish an autonomous life.
To be sure, there might be a kind of ideal that one does not realize, an achievement one has not achieved. But such is life. No one can realize all ideals or achieve all things. The question is whether one leads a worse life than they would if they stopped, deliberated, and chosen it. Is there reason to pity one for not doing so? Does someone else have reason to see to it that one chooses the life: to say, “Yes, I realize that this is the best life you could lead, but you really need to stop, deliberate about other options, and choose it, for its own sake—your well-being depends on it”? To insist on this, I worry, may be to betray a kind of fetish for planning or predilection for a studied way through life, which may not suit everyone. It is important that people live their lives under conditions of autonomy: with options and without being subject to the wills of others. But this is not because their lives are necessarily better if they are autonomously lived. Or so I speculate. In any event, if this collection leads us to return to Raz’s ideas with fresh eyes and new questions, then it is surely a success.

Definition and Essence from Aristotle to Kant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
18:13:00 UTC
03:13:00 KST

For all the effort that philosophers have put into defining things, there is surprisingly little modern attention paid to the question of what a definition is. Over the centuries, however, there has been a great deal said about what definitions are and what purpose they serve. From an historical point of view, such discussions have opened up rich avenues of inquiry into foundational issues in metaphysics and epistemology. We historians, taking our lead from contemporary concerns, have not taken much notice of these long-running disputes. The topic is ripe for exploration.
Peter Anstey and David Bronstein have assembled an admirable collection of papers that seeks to do just this, based on a conference held in Sydney in 2019. As one might expect, Aussies are well represented, but overall the contributors are an impressively international group. The volume exemplifies all the virtues of an edited collection. First, it offers an awesomely wide scope, not just chronologically but also topically, inasmuch as the chapters range variously over science, mathematics, logic, language, and core questions of M&E. Second, it achieves this range without sacrificing expertise: chapter by chapter, we are delivered into the hands of first one expert and then another. To be sure, the volume also exhibits the constraints of the genre. The historical coverage is full of gaps, the specific topics discussed are a haphazard mix, and—in keeping with the unfortunate convention of this genre—none of the chapters engages with any of the others. Still, the quality of each individual chapter makes the volume as a whole a tremendous success.
The chapters are roughly equally split among ancient, medieval, and early modern material (all European), and nine of the twelve are focused squarely on definition. On the face of things, it is an oddity that the volume begins with Aristotle, and so omits what one might take to be the most historically important treatments of definition in the whole canon, those of Socrates and Plato. But this turns out to be a good-making feature, because it allows the volume to focus more squarely on the Aristotelian theory and reactions against it, which is how conversations about definition mostly take shape in the philosophical traditions that emerge from ancient Greece.
Although the notion of essence appears in the title, essences generally play a secondary role in the volume. That role is important, however, because one of the hallmarks of the Aristotelian approach is that the object of a definition is an essence. (P. 14 of Bronstein’s opening chapter quotes Topics 101b38 on a definition as “an account [logos] signifying the what it is to be [to ti ēn einai].”) Accordingly, one of the overarching themes of the volume is the way in which philosophers variously seek to respect or reject the relationship between definitions and essences. One mark of philosophy’s gradual drift away from Aristotle is the growing number of authors who abandon the goal of defining essences. Calvin Normore explains that, by the time of the nominalists of the fourteenth century, the object of a definition is always a word (151). Some definitions nevertheless are real, expressing the quid rei, which is to say that they define a word in such a way as to capture the essences of things. A nominal definition, in contrast, yields only the quid nominis, which is to say that it offers merely an expression that can be used synonymously with the term being defined. By the time of Hobbes, the very notion of an essence falls into doubt: an essence is simply “that accident for which we give a certain name to any body” (as quoted by Normore, 156).
According to the volume’s introduction, “Aristotle is the first figure in the Western intellectual tradition to articulate a theory of definition” (2). No doubt, Aristotle has no earlier rival in setting out a theory in such explicit and systematic detail. Crucial to that project is the role definitions play in science (i.e., epistēmē). According to Posterior Analytics 99a21, “all the sciences come about through definition”. Bronstein quotes that remark (37) and works out in careful detail what it means. Definitions are of special importance to Aristotle because of the crucial role they play in demonstration. Some definitions are the indemonstrable starting points of a demonstration, whereas others fall out as the conclusion of a demonstration (Bronstein, 19–21). The Posterior Analytics offers a handful of familiar toy examples of how this goes but, across Aristotle’s corpus, one famously finds few developed examples of the method being put to work.
That lacuna gives extra value to James Franklin’s chapter on definition in Euclid. Definitions are of course a crucial feature in the Elements, and Franklin offers examples of what work they do there. Against those who suppose that all definitions are nominal, Franklin argues that the case of mathematics, in antiquity and in modern times, makes a case for the significance of the search for real definitions. Interestingly, though, he argues that what makes this search tractable in the mathematical case is that such definitions pursue objects in the category of Quantity. Outside of mathematics and allied fields, those who have sought to advance their accounts more geometrico have involved themselves in “wild goose chases”, producing work that is “close to useless” (52). Franklin goes on to assess why these projects can succeed in quantitative domains but not when we seek to define the essences of substances.
The many and varied lights that the volume shines on the Aristotelian tradition make clear that the dream of a demonstrative science founded in real definitions had its critics from the start. Katja Vogt shows that the Stoics reject the very idea of a single privileged definition, and regularly deploy multiple non-exclusive definitions for the same thing. This is of a piece with their rejection of the very idea of forms or essences. If we jump ahead to Thomas Aquinas, as discussed by Gabriele Galluzzo, we find a view that embraces the Aristotelian methodology of demonstration grounded in definition. But even Aquinas thinks that our definitions fail to grasp the essences of things. When we seek to frame a real definition in terms of genus plus differentia, we in practice can do no better than offer accidental differentiae that serve as signs of the unknown essential differentia (Galluzzo, 143). So, yes, human beings can be defined as rational animals, but that complex expression merely points at the unified thing that is the substantial form of a human being, whose true nature we are largely ignorant of. Aquinas, to be sure, is quite different from Hobbes, in that for Aquinas it is crucially important that human beings have a substantial form, which is their immortal soul. But in terms of their scientific methodologies, the difference is less than one might expect, since Hobbes too thinks, as Anstey puts it in his chapter, that “all scientific knowledge is demonstrated from definitions” (196).
There is, however, something deeper that divides the camp of Aquinas and his nominalist critics from the camp of Hobbes and his contemporaries. For when medieval Aristotelians endorse essences, they commit themselves not just to the idea that every substance within a species shares a cluster of properties that are necessary and jointly sufficient for membership within that species. More than that, they endorse the causal thesis that substances have an inner explanatory principle that accounts for all of the intrinsic features of the thing. (Anstey and Bronstein, in their introduction on p. 2, refer to this as the explanation condition.) For Aristotelians, the object of definitions is that inner principle, and definitions are meaningful within science precisely insofar as they capture these explanatory structures. Aquinas may not have thought that we can succeed in fully understanding the essences of things, but he did think we could frame definitions that track these structures well enough to be useful. In contrast, once the project of real definition falls entirely out of favor, the whole Aristotelian theory of demonstration starts to look misguided.
The volume’s later chapters offer various illustrations of this transformation. For Descartes, as Deborah Brown understands him, definitions play a role “that is more pedagogical than epistemic’ (171). For Arnauld and Nicole, in the Port-Royal Logic, only nominal definitions can serve as principles in demonstrations, with the result, as Anstey puts it, that “real definitions have little or no role in the discovery of scientific knowledge” (205). Laura Kotevska’s chapter on the Port-Royal Logic shows that its focus on nominal definitions comes with a deemphasis of the syllogism, and a concern for using definitions to make sure of the connection between words and ideas. John Locke, similarly, takes the role of definitions to be “making another understand by Words, what Idea, the term defined stands for” (Essay III.3.10). Anstey quotes this passage, remarking that Locke “does not accept the view that definitions function as principles in demonstrative sciences” (209). These developments are put most vividly on display in Kirsten Walsh’s chapter on “proof by experiments in Newton’s Opticks”. In a sense, this chapter has little to do with the other chapters in the volume, but that is part of the point. Walsh shows that Newton’s famous series of experiments with a prism offers a “proof” that relies only marginally on definitions and axioms, and instead attempts to construct “a new kind of proof” (245), one based not on indemonstrable premises but instead on experiment. With this, we have left the domain of Aristotelian definition entirely.
I hope the preceding remarks provide a sense of how much there is to be learned from this volume. Let me close with two brief remarks on the book’s production. First, as one expects from Routledge, each chapter has its own bibliography, and endnotes rather than footnotes. The former practice makes good sense in an era where these chapters will circulate mainly as separate files. Perhaps Routledge regards the latter practice as expressing a distinctive style, but to the reader, it comes off simply as cheap. Second, an impressive amount of attention has been given to copy editing and proofreading. I could find only three minor blemishes of this kind across the whole volume. In an era where publishers have largely stopped caring about such matters, the participants here are to be congratulated for taking the time to get this right.
ACKNOWLEDGMENTS
Thanks for their advice to Jacob Calhoun and Matthew Wennemann.

sculptures made of timber and steel occupy raw concrete shell in seoul before demolition
ghost barstairs: temporary hypotheses brings experimental furniture, sculpture, and plywood structures into a vacant concrete building in seoul, using its exposed frame to explore the possibilities of a space between demolition and renewal.
[ADVERTISEMENT]
GHOST BARSTAIRS explores traces left in an empty building in Seoul
Design studio Sukchulmok and artist Kangyeon Lee present GHOST BARSTAIRS: Temporary Hypotheses in a vacant reinforced-concrete building in Sinsa-dong, Seoul, shortly before its demolition is completed. With accumulated finishes removed, the building’s exposed structural frame becomes the setting for an exhibition exploring the space between its former use and an undefined future.
The title outlines three elements of the project: GHOST, referring to traces of what has disappeared; BAR, describing rigid lines that establish new structures and boundaries; and STAIRS, suggesting layers and movement through vertical space. Light entering the building from the basement to the rooftop illuminates the exposed frame, where Sukchulmok’s experimental furniture intersects with Lee’s sculptural works. Set within an unfinished spatial canvas, these installations serve as a ‘temporary hypothesis (假設),’ a moment caught in transience and a sculptural query cast into the realm of undefined potential.
Timber and steel form new structures within the concrete shell
Studio Sukchulmok explores numerical proportions through the physical properties of stone, steel, and wood. On the first floor, a central booth combining semicircular timber and a steel cone anchors the space. Artist Kangyeon Lee draws on a past labor experience placing ham on pizza dough on a production line. He translates the resulting sense of alienation into works that evoke anonymous figures obscured by cycles of consumption and forgetting. Using materials such as metal and plastic, his sculptures introduce contrasting forms within the raw concrete structure.
A further spatial intervention by BRBB design practice occupies the basement, where plywood panels meet, curved, and leaned against one another to form self-supporting structures. These elements operate independently of conventional partitions or circulation routes, treating the arrangement of materials as a way to define space. Installed shortly before the building’s next phase, GHOST BARSTAIRS uses furniture, sculpture, and temporary structures to examine the possibilities of an unfinished architectural setting. The exhibition documents a brief interval in which the building’s former identity had receded and its future remained open.

EU accession negotiations typically take years to conclude, and the opening of negotiations does not guarantee membership. ■

News Analysis: Europe faces four major challenges in pursuit of AI sovereignty
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
02:06:13 CST
03:06:13 KST

by Xinhua writer Shao Haijun
ZAANDAM, THE NETHERLANDS, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Europe's ambition to strengthen its artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities faces challenges, from dependence on foreign technology providers and limited investment in domestic companies to emerging safety risks and regulatory uncertainty.
At the recent World Summit AI 2026 in Zaandam, the Netherlands, participants said Europe needed to expand its computing infrastructure, channel more capital into domestic technology companies and build a competitive ecosystem giving governments and businesses greater control over the AI systems they use.
TECHNOLOGICAL DEPENDENCE LIMITS EUROPE'S CONTROL
A fundamental challenge for Europe is reducing its dependence on foreign technology providers without sacrificing the benefits of international cooperation and open markets.
Mark Papermaster, chief technology officer of U.S. semiconductor company AMD, said on the opening day of the summit on Oct. 7 that AI sovereignty meant having control over computing infrastructure and the freedom to choose among different technologies, combine components and use both open-weight and proprietary models.
For European governments and businesses, dependence on a limited number of suppliers can constrain their choices in developing, deploying and securing AI systems.
Nigel Shadbolt, a member of the British government's Council for Science and Technology, stressed the importance of that choice. "When we talk about sovereignty in Europe, it's about having the ability to make a choice," he said. "You haven't locked yourself into a particular dependency."
Sovereignty, however, does not necessarily mean producing every component domestically.
Papermaster said an open ecosystem could allow European governments and businesses to combine different hardware and software components and models, provided appropriate security measures and safeguards were built into the systems.
LIMITED FINANCING THREATENS AI COMPANIES' GROWTH
Financing remains another major obstacle to turning Europe's strengths in research, talent and computing initiatives into global competitiveness.
"I think one of Europe's biggest weaknesses is on the finance side," said Olivier Debeugny, CEO of OVHai LLM, a French company specializing in resource-efficient AI models and architectures.
Debeugny said Europe had a strong foundation in education and the human capital needed for AI development, but it needs more financial support to turn those advantages into competitive businesses.
He argued that substantial spending on digital services in Europe ultimately benefited U.S. companies. "Every year, a huge amount of money is spent on digital services in Europe. A very large share of that money ultimately goes to companies in the United States," he said.
European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde highlighted a similar pattern in a speech in Vienna on Sept. 14, 2026. "European savers are again financing the transformative technology of the age: artificial intelligence. Again, most of the money is flowing to the United States," Lagarde said, noting that euro area households held about 440 billion euros (492 billion U.S. dollars) in U.S. technology firms.
The challenge is not simply a shortage of capital, but also how existing investment is allocated. Cristina Caffarra, co-founder and chair of the Eurostack Initiative Foundation, said European institutional investors managed trillions of euros, much of which remained invested in traditional assets.
"We need to find ways to channel more of this capital into European technology," Caffarra said.
AI SAFETY RISKS DEMAND STRONGER SAFEGUARDS
The third challenge is ensuring that increasingly capable AI systems remain secure and operate within appropriate boundaries.
Recent incidents involving advanced AI agents have highlighted this concern. In June, an AI agent developed by OpenAI reportedly breached a data portal linked to Australia's universal healthcare system.
"Highly capable systems could, for example, cheat, hack into systems or obtain credentials in ways their developers had not anticipated," Shadbolt said.
Papermaster said addressing these risks required more than improvements to individual AI models. Safeguards also needed to extend across computing infrastructure and the applications built on it.
"Security and safety are fundamental and need to be architected into every facet of AI applications," he said.
As AI systems become more capable of carrying out tasks autonomously, ensuring their security will become increasingly important to maintaining public trust and enabling wider adoption.
REGULATORY UNCERTAINTY MAY WEAKEN EUROPE'S COMPETITIVENESS
Europe also must maintain its influence over global AI governance while creating conditions for domestic companies to innovate and compete.
Sasha Rubel, head of generative AI policy for Europe, the Middle East and Africa at Amazon Web Services (AWS), highlighted the compliance burden facing European businesses and the need to make regulatory requirements clearer and easier to implement.
"The fundamental question is: how do we simplify the rules?" Rubel said. "This is not about whether we should regulate. It is about making the rules clear enough that they can actually be applied and that innovators understand how to comply."
Her remarks reflect industry concerns that regulatory complexity and uncertainty can divert resources from innovation and make it harder for companies to bring new technologies to market.
Daniel Friedlaender, senior vice president and head of office at the Computer & Communications Industry Association Europe, pointed to a related gap between technological innovation and AI adoption.
Europe has considerable innovation in research laboratories and businesses, he said, but uptake has been slower. Regulatory predictability, clarity over compliance and access to capital were among the factors affecting companies' ability to scale up and expand their markets.
Ultimately, AI sovereignty will depend not only on the technologies Europe develops and the rules it establishes, but also on whether it can finance, secure and scale those technologies while retaining the freedom to choose among global suppliers. ■

====================================================================================================

Researchers identify a factor linked to how much happier couples are than singles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
18:00:55 UTC
03:00:55 KST

People in romantic relationships typically report higher life satisfaction than single people, but a new study of more than 380,000 adults in Great Britain suggests that the size of this gap varies depending on where people live. The gap tended to be wider in areas where romantic partnerships were more common, mostly because partnered people in those areas reported higher satisfaction. The research was published in Psychological Science.
Relationship status simply refers to whether a person is currently in an intimate partnership or is single. Life satisfaction is an evaluation of how positive or fulfilling a person finds their overall life circumstances. In social psychology, the idea of person-culture match suggests that people experience higher well-being when their individual traits, beliefs, or lifestyle match the prevailing norms of their immediate community.
Prior studies suggest that the size of the life-satisfaction gap between partnered and single people is not the same everywhere. Married people tend to report higher life satisfaction than unmarried people, but the size of that difference varies across countries and U.S. states, and one U.S. analysis found that marriage was more strongly tied to life satisfaction in states where more residents were married.
Not every study has found a strong role for social norms, though: a 2012 study of 45 European countries found that a country’s family values had little bearing on the well-being gaps between partnership statuses, apart from a wider gap between divorced and married women in more family-oriented societies.
Other research suggests that community-level norms can shape how individual life circumstances affect personal well-being. For example, earlier work by some of the same researchers, covered by PsyPost in 2024, found that in regions with higher obesity prevalence, individuals with obesity experienced less severe relationship and health disadvantages compared to low-prevalence regions.
The current study aimed to bridge these lines of research to test whether local relationship rates relate to the well-being gap between singles and couples. “Many studies find that partnered people are happier than single people and such findings often read as evidence that romantic relationships are good for us,” lead researcher Tita Gonzalez Avilés of the Institute of Psychology at the University of Bamberg told PsyPost. “But the reasons behind this life satisfaction gap are not entirely clear. We wanted to shift the focus from the relationship itself to the regional contexts in which partnered and single people’s lives unfold.”
The research team reasoned that in areas with high relationship rates, couples might feel more supported and aligned with local relationship norms. Single individuals, on the other hand, might feel more excluded or experience greater social pressure in environments where couplehood is the dominant pattern.
To examine this question, the scientists analyzed data from the BBC Big Personality Test. The sample included 382,078 adults living across 379 local authority districts in Great Britain, administrative areas similar in size to counties in the United States. Participants answered questions about whether they were currently in an intimate relationship and rated their life satisfaction on a scale from one to seven.
The researchers calculated regional relationship rates by determining the percentage of participants in each district who reported being in an intimate relationship. District relationship rates ranged from about 55 percent in one London borough to 80 percent in the district of Bolsover. To isolate the role of local relationship rates, the authors controlled for individual characteristics including age, gender, education, employment, income, health, and personality traits, as well as district-level factors such as population density, median income, birth rates, median age, political leanings, and religious affiliation.
Across Great Britain as a whole, partnered individuals reported higher life satisfaction than single individuals. Partnered people scored about half a standard deviation higher on life satisfaction, a difference the authors noted is comparable to differences tied to employment status or health. These findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that people in intimate relationships report higher emotional well-being and life satisfaction compared to singles.
The results also align with research covered by PsyPost in 2025 that examined lifelong singlehood among primarily older adults and found lower life satisfaction among singles compared to partnered individuals.
“Although life satisfaction varied across regions, partnered individuals consistently reported higher life satisfaction compared to single individuals on average,” Gonzalez Avilés noted. “So, while regional context contributes to people’s life satisfaction, it cannot fully account for the gap between these two groups.”
When the researchers looked across regions, they found that the size of the gap varied based on the local relationship rate. In districts with the lowest relationship rates, the gap was 0.49 standard deviations; in districts with the highest rates, it was 0.63, an increase of nearly 29 percent. This widening gap was primarily driven by partnered individuals, who reported higher life satisfaction in high-relationship districts, while life satisfaction among single individuals remained relatively constant regardless of the local relationship rate.
The district-level pattern held across several robustness checks. The association remained consistent when using official census marriage and cohabitation rates instead of survey-derived relationship rates, when applying broader regional controls, and when using stricter minimum thresholds for district sample sizes.
In additional analyses that were not planned in advance, the researchers found that the gap was also larger in districts with lower median incomes, a higher share of votes to leave the European Union in the 2016 Brexit referendum, and more residents reporting a religious affiliation. In the more politically conservative and religious districts, the wider gap mainly reflected lower life satisfaction among single people. The authors note that they did not directly measure attitudes toward singlehood and describe their explanations for these patterns as speculative.
“We expected single people to be less satisfied where many others are partnered but found no evidence for this,” Gonzalez Avilés said. “What seemed to be more important for the single people was not how many people are partnered but the prevailing regional attitudes toward singlehood (i.e., single people being less satisfied in more conservative and religious regions).”
“Regional relationship norms and societal expectations can affect how partnered and single people evaluate their own life,” Gonzalez Avilés added.
In an exploratory analysis that was not registered in advance, the researchers evaluated whether the pattern held at a neighborhood scale across 52,836 participants in 218 postal districts in London. In postal districts with the lowest relationship rates, the gap was 0.41 standard deviations, compared to 0.62 in districts with the highest rates, reflecting an increase of about 51 percent. As in the national sample, this difference was mainly driven by partnered residents reporting greater satisfaction in neighborhoods where relationships were common.
The authors also examined whether people in high-relationship areas placed more importance on having a relationship. They found no evidence that couples or singles placed higher importance on being partnered in those areas. Single people in high-relationship areas actually placed slightly less importance on having a relationship, which the researchers speculate could reflect singles shifting their focus toward other life goals.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The sample consisted of online volunteers who chose to take a personality test between 2009 and 2011, and roughly 64 percent of the respondents were women. The data are also more than 15 years old. The authors did find that regional marriage rates in the survey closely mirrored 2011 census figures, which supports the accuracy of the geographic estimates.
The overall regional effect was modest, and partnered people reported higher life satisfaction than singles even in districts with the lowest relationship rates. Because the data were correlational, the study cannot establish cause and effect. Happier couples might simply be more inclined to move to communities where relationships are more prevalent.
“We did not test why partnered individuals were more satisfied in regions where romantic relationships were more common,” Gonzalez Avilés explained. “It may be that they have more positive experiences when living among many other couples, but it is also possible that happily coupled people are more likely to move to such regions.”
The researchers tested this possibility by repeating their analysis using only individuals who still resided in the region where they grew up, which reduces the likelihood that migration explains the pattern. Future studies tracking people over time could provide better insight into whether moving or changing relationship status shifts life satisfaction. Scientists could also investigate whether specific mechanisms, such as tax, housing, or other policy advantages for couples, help explain why partnered people fare better in these environments.
The findings are also based solely on Great Britain. Testing these relationships in other countries could help researchers determine whether similar regional patterns exist in different cultural and institutional settings.
The study, “Ties That Bind, Places That Matter: The Life-Satisfaction Gap Between Partnered and Single Individuals Varies Across Regions,” was authored by Tita Gonzalez Avilés, Franz J. Neyer, Peter J. Rentfrow, and Tobias Ebert.

Military homes pilot tests new technology at Pirbright
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:00:03 BST
03:00:03 KST

Six refurbished homes at Pirbright are being used to test technologies intended to make service family accommodation warmer and cheaper to run, in a trial the Ministry of Defence describes as the first of its kind for military housing, according to the department.
Each of the six carries a different combination of equipment, including solar panels, battery storage, electric heated skirting boards, hot water systems and zero-emission boilers, so the department can work out which combinations deliver the most benefit. All six have also been given modern kitchens, bathrooms, fencing and doors.
Feedback from the families living in them will shape investment decisions across the estate. The trial follows a research and development day held earlier this year at which businesses showed technology that might be used in military housing.
Sebastian O’Hara, operations director for accommodation at the Defence Infrastructure Organisation, said: “Service families deserve homes that are warm, safe and fit for modern living.
“This pilot is the first of its kind for military housing giving us the opportunity to test new technologies in real homes and understand directly from families what makes the biggest difference to their day-to-day lives. The feedback we get from our families will be used to inform investment decisions, shape the future of military housing and ensure we focus on solutions delivering better outcomes for families.
“This is about learning what works, listening to our customers and building a better housing service for the future. Through the new Defence Housing Service, we’re driving change across military housing, delivering better homes, raising service standards and putting the needs of Service personnel and their families at the heart of everything we do.”
The work forms part of the Defence Housing Strategy, backed by £9.2 billion and intended to see 40,000 military homes modernised, refurbished or rebuilt over the next decade, delivered through the new Defence Housing Service.
Separately, 3D scanning is being used to create digital versions of military homes, with around 2,000 properties due to be scanned and digitised over a two-year trial. The intention is to plan repairs and upgrades more efficiently, keep better records across a property’s lifetime and carry out some inspections remotely.
A pilot will give families a greater role in signing off repairs and maintenance before jobs are closed, and a code of conduct will set expectations for how staff and contractors treat families.

Smart glasses 'life-changing' for blind and deaf people, despite concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Smart glasses are giving blind and deaf people more independence
In short:
Disability advocates want to highlight the benefits of smart glasses.
They fear the "pervert glasses" rhetoric could lead to stigma against people using the glasses for essential daily tasks.
What's next?
The Greens are expected to introduce a bill for an import ban in the Senate this week as the government reviews feedback on draft privacy laws.
When Chris Edwards pops on his smart glasses, his world opens up.
With them, he can read a recipe, check the settings on his washing machine and get street directions as he walks with his guide dog.
Mr Edwards, who is blind and is also the chief mission officer at Vision Australia, says the technology is "life-changing" for people like him.
"The ability for smart glasses to help [give] a new level of independence for someone who's blind and low vision, on things that they would normally rely on other sighted people to do, is outstanding," he said.
But he is concerned by the public debate around smart glasses.
They have been branded as "pervert glasses" in the media after they were used to secretly film people without their consent.
Cheap smart glasses have also attracted negative headlines over their vulnerability to hacking, prompting the Australian privacy commissioner to launch an investigation, while Kmart appears to have pulled them from the shelves.
Mr Edwards said it was unhelpful for smart glasses to be continually labelled in negative terms, as the emerging technology had become a positive tool to help people in the broader disability community to navigate daily life.
For Matt Henderson, a town planner from Adelaide, his smart glasses have helped him participate more in the workplace.
Mr Henderson has been deaf since birth, uses hearing aids and lip-reading to communicate. He said his glasses provided live captions during conversations and meetings.
"They've definitely increased my confidence massively.
"I'm not reliant on as many people for things, so it's independence as well."
Fractious political debate
There have been widespread calls for restrictions on smart glasses, with new Greens leader David Shoebridge planning to introduce a bill for a 12-month import ban on the devices in the Senate this week.
"It is urgent. We need to act before the genie entirely escapes out of the bottle," Mr Shoebridge told the ABC.
But Senator Shoebridge added there was a carve-out in the draft legislation that would allow for an importer to be permitted to bring in the devices to sell as disability aids.
Several local councils have imposed bans at swimming pools and childcare centres, while Western Australia placed a comprehensive ban on the devices in the state's schools.
"Smart glasses may look cool but there's absolutely no place in our schools or classrooms for them," WA Education Minister Sabine Winton said last month.
While she and local councils said there would be exemptions for those with special needs, many in the disability community feared that nuance was getting lost in the heat of the debate.
Last month, Finance Minister Katy Gallagher also sought advice about whether smart glasses should be "prohibited" in public service workplaces and, if so, what exemptions might be appropriate.
Announcing the draft privacy laws in late August, Attorney-General Michelle Rowland said she acknowledged the community's "deep concerns" about the products.
"I think that every decent-minded Australian would like to ensure that these devices are not being used for nefarious purposes," Ms Rowland said.
"I'd also just finally point out that disability advocates, and groups, people who are directly impacted in a positive way by this technology, also need to have their voices heard in this debate."
Last month the government closed submissions on its proposed privacy reforms, inviting feedback on smart glasses.
Health Minister Mark Butler previously spoke about the public's "horror" over the devices.
"They are a huge bad step in the infringement on our privacy," he said at the time.
"I think they serve no useful purpose. They are a terrible development in our society, just for the profit of big tech."
The ABC approached Mr Butler's office but he declined to comment further.
What can smart glasses do?
Both Mr Edwards and Mr Henderson feared terms like "pervert glasses" would make people uncomfortable or deter them from tapping into the potentially life-changing technology.
"The last thing that I probably need … is for this tool to suddenly be caught up in this whole conversation of smart glasses being something that we don't really want in our society," Mr Henderson said.
Mr Henderson's glasses don't have video-recording capacity but can be used for live captions, as well as translation and navigation, among other things.
"Essentially, imagine it's projecting the words in front of your vision," he said.
For Mr Edwards, the artificial intelligence (AI) aspect was crucial; while some apps served similar functions to smart glasses, he said, one of the key benefits of the wearable technology for blind people was the hands-free aspect.
"One of the challenges with a blind person is that whether they're a cane user or a seeing-eye dog user, that automatically eliminates one hand," he said.
"So if you're trying to navigate somewhere and there's a set of stairs, that means if you're holding a phone and a seeing-eye dog in the other hand, you can't hold a handrail. You can't grab a cup of coffee."
Mr Edwards said he could use voice commands to direct the glasses to describe things in front of him, such as taking a picture of a menu and asking what the vegetarian options are.
Previous versions of smart glasses as disability aids cost thousands of dollars, but newer models are more financially accessible, costing about $600.
Some in the Deaf community have said there are limits to the glasses and they can not replace the sign language Auslan, which has its own grammar and syntax and does not translate directly to written English.

The European Union adopted its largest-ever single set of sanctions against Russia to date on Monday, blacklisting 1,569 individuals and companies within the country's military-industrial complex.
The measures blacklist 826 Russian companies and 743 chief executives, bringing the total number of listings under the EU sanctions regime protecting Ukraine’s territorial integrity to nearly 4,600. The designated entities face immediate asset freezes and funding blocks, while the targeted individuals are now barred from entering the bloc.

Further commenting on the latest EU sanctions, Kallas, however, stressed: "This is not the time to ease pressure on Moscow but to increase it."
The new listings follow the European Council's June 2026 directive to intensify pressure on Moscow in response to an escalating military campaign that has deliberately targeted civilian infrastructure and, according to the Council, aims to undermineUkraine's resilience.

Five Ukrainian minehunters have completed seven days of intensive training off the south coast of England, closing with a run in close formation around the Type 45 destroyer HMS Dauntless in the eastern Solent, according to the Royal Navy.
The ships are based in Portsmouth as part of British support to Ukraine, and the training ranged across the Dorset, Hampshire and Isle of Wight coastlines, taking in gunnery, the destruction of dummy mines and formation sailing with a major warship.
UNS Henichesk, Mariupol, Melitopol, Chernihiv and Cherkasy made up the quintet. Under the supervision of British military personnel they first demonstrated their ability to defend themselves with gunnery shoots off Portland, then moved on to locating, identifying and where necessary destroying underwater explosive devices.
That work used Seafox, the remotely operated submersible that has been a mainstay of Royal Navy mine countermeasures for a couple of decades. Chernihiv and Cherkasy both carried out live firings of the system, which ended in controlled explosions neutralising the mine threats they had been set.
The seven days formed the final chapter of Exercise Lion Protector, a Joint Expeditionary Force exercise running from August until the weekend and intended to refine how member nations respond militarily to protect Europe’s northern flank. Its fifth and last phase shifted the emphasis onto the ability of JEF navies to protect maritime infrastructure and guarantee the security of sea lanes.
Earlier phases took the UK Commando Force to the Faroe Islands to work on safeguarding the Greenland, Iceland and United Kingdom gap, the first time Royal Marines have operated in the Atlantic chain since the Second World War. The Royal Navy rates Lion Protector second only to Sea Breeze, the Ukrainian Navy’s premier annual exercise, in scope and complexity. Sea Breeze itself was held off the south coast of England over the summer.
Dauntless played the part of the major warship in the closing serial, with the Ukrainian ships manoeuvring around her as a small task group. The destroyer is preparing to escort the fleet flagship HMS Prince of Wales when she resumes her Firecrest 2026 deployment to the High North. Mine countermeasures have become one of the more practical forms of British help to Ukraine, since the Black Sea remains heavily mined and the Ukrainian Navy has had to rebuild capability.

Hackers turn up the heat in refrigerators at hundreds of supermarkets in France, sparking fires and food losses
Major French supermarket chains on Monday said they were hit by a cyberattack that caused their refrigerators to shoot up in temperature in hundreds of stores, forcing spoiled food to be thrown away and raising concerns about food security.
Top retailers E. Leclerc, Intermarché and Cooperative U confirmed to AFP they suffered a cyberattack that Cooperative U's chief executive described as "unprecedented."
"Food security requires more attention at all levels," said the EU's food and agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen on X, condemning the attack and saying such "exploitation of food" was now a "reality."
At least 300 shops of Intermarché or its Netto brand were targeted, along with over 100 Cooperative U outlets, and several E. Leclerc stores, the retailers told AFP in separate statements.
"Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented," Cooperative U CEO Dominique Schelcher wrote on X.
Paris prosecutors confirmed the attack, which reportedly also hit other major chains, and also indicated it had sparked fires.
BFM TV said hackers "managed to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores."
The affected branches will have to "throw away all of the products" that are fresh and frozen, Intermarché told AFP.
Carrefour said 80 of its supermarkets were attacked but that the vast majority of its 6,000 stores were not affected, according to the Reuters news agency.
E. Leclerc confirmed to AFP "that a cyberattack affected one of its refrigeration equipment suppliers," resulting in "repercussions on the operation of refrigeration systems in several stores."
A source close to the issue said refrigeration control systems from Danish manufacturer Danfoss were targeted.
Danfoss told AFP in a statement that most of the affected equipment was "legacy" products which "no longer receive software or security updates."
It said its AK-SM800 and AK-SC355 fridge regulator systems were notably affected, with a version of the former using "outdated firmware." It added that it had long advised supermarkets to update from those models. Danfoss gave no figures on how many systems were affected.
Dutch supermarket operator Ahold Delhaize, which also has operations in the United States, said it was also dealing with a "security issue" in its network, Reuters reported. A phone app for the retailer told clients that due to a "cybersecurity incident" it was unable to deliver groceries.
"Large-scale cyberattack"
A person close to French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said France's cybersecurity agency had already identified "a vulnerability in software supplied by a Danish company and has contacted the vendor."
"It is liaising with its European counterparts, as other countries may be affected," and is seeking "to identify other French companies involved in order to alert them" and "prevent the spread," the source added.
The office of the Paris prosecutor confirmed to AFP that an investigation has been opened into "the large-scale cyberattack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France."
The probe will help "identify the victims and establish the link with the damage they reported in terms of foodstuff losses and the outbreak of fires," the prosecutor's office said.
Intermarché condemned the food waste and financial losses resulting from the attack, without providing figures.
BFM TV said temperatures were "altered remotely, resulting in the destruction of stocks of fresh and frozen products."
Rising fears of hybrid attacks
The incident comes against the background of growing concern over the potential havoc that can be caused in Europe in all sectors by malicious actors carrying out cyberattacks.
President Emmanuel Macron, a strong supporter of Ukraine in its fight against the Russian invasion, last month ordered measures to protect France's critical infrastructure from Russian "hybrid attacks."
Industrial equipment such as refrigeration units, long isolated from the internet, is now connected via sensors or remote monitoring systems, Antoine Hautin of cybersecurity consultancy Almond told AFP.
By likely affecting hundreds of units simultaneously, the attack demonstrated "a certain level of sophistication," he added.

Austria says Ukrainian journalist's arrest on suspicion of spying was unrelated to his job
VIENNA, Oct 12 - The arrest of a Ukrainian journalist in Vienna last week was ordered because he was seen watching a location that two men suspected of spying had also surveilled, not because of his profession, the Vienna prosecutors' office said on Monday.
Austrian police arrested two Ukrainians on Monday last week on suspicion of spying. The following Thursday they arrested two more: investigative journalist Mykhailo Tkach and cameraman Yaroslav Bondarenko.
While the first two have been remanded in investigative custody, Tkach and Bondarenko were released without charge.
The Vienna prosecutors' office said in a statement that in the course of the investigation into the first two men, suspicions emerged about a third, apparently referring to Tkach but without mentioning any names.
"These suspicions were based in particular on witness statements indicating three men had been seen observing one location, as well as on the fact the observation took place during the same period and was carried out in the same manner," the statement said.
That led prosecutors to believe the three Ukrainians were part of the same group and the third man's arrest was ordered, it added. A fourth man - apparently Bondarenko - happened to be in the same car when police found him, and both were arrested.
"At the time of the arrests, it was not known that the suspects were a Ukrainian investigative journalist and a cameraman," the statement said, adding: "The arrests were in no way related to the two men's professional activities."
Bondarenko was injured by shards of glass from a car window during the arrest.
Tkach, Bondarenko and their employer, Ukrainian newspaper Ukrainska Pravda, have criticised the Austrian authorities for the arrest, saying they could simply have summoned them.
The Austrian authorities have not provided details on the two Ukrainians still in custody. Austrian media have reported they are suspected of working for a Ukrainian intelligence service. REUTERS

ICMR sets up high-altitude research centre in Keylong to study health risks in Himalayas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

JP Nadda said the centre would help build a strong institutional foundation for research into the health challenges faced by people in the Himalayan region and personnel deployed in high-altitude areas.
NEW DELHI: From how soldiers acclimatise to thin air at extreme altitudes to how low oxygen levels and harsh winters affect the health of Himalayan communities, a new research centre in Himachal Pradesh will study the distinctive medical challenges of living and working in the mountains.Union health minister Jagat Prakash Nadda on Monday performed the bhumi pujan and laid the foundation stone of the Indian Council of Medical Research's (ICMR) Centre for High Altitude Medicine and Public Health Research at Keylong, Himachal Pradesh.Built on an ICMR field station established at Keylong nearly a decade ago, the centre will function as a permanent, year-round institution with specialised personnel and state-of-the-art laboratories. It will generate evidence on the health effects of low oxygen levels, extreme cold and changing climatic conditions, with research spanning both military personnel and civilian populations.The research will focus on altitude-related health risks, acclimatisation, maternal and newborn health, child nutrition and disease patterns in Himalayan communities. It will also explore drone-based medicine delivery, digital health and artificial intelligence to improve healthcare access in remote areas.
ICMR will combine its research expertise with AFMS’s field experience, with AIIMS Bilaspur studying the effects of high-altitude conditions on patients visiting the region.Nadda said the centre would help build a strong institutional foundation for research into the health challenges faced by people in the Himalayan region and personnel deployed in high-altitude areas. He stressed the need for systematic studies to identify risks and develop appropriate preventive healthcare interventions.
Air Marshal Sandeep Thareja, Director General of the Armed Forces Medical Services, said the research would help develop protocols for acclimatisation, early detection and treatment of altitude-related illnesses. ICMR director general Rajiv Bahl said the centre would involve local communities in research aimed at improving health. The findings are expected to benefit Himalayan and border regions. Defence minister of state Sanjay Seth, Jai Ram Thakur and Kangana Ranaut attended the event. Nadda also inaugurated a student science exhibition and launched the centre’s website and video, besides releasing a commemorative postal cover.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

Rep. Ilhan Omar Says She Will ‘Not Be Silenced’ After Federal Agents Raid Her Home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
17:41:53 UTC
02:41:53 KST

Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota on Monday afternoon called the federal agents’ search of her Washington, D.C. home an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” The Somali-born lawmaker is a vocal critic of President Donald Trump and has previously been subjected to his insults.
“For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” said Omar in a social media post. “I will not be silenced.”
A spokesperson for the Department of Justice told TIME: “Today in the Washington, D.C, area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice. This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation.” No further details were provided.
The U.S. Congress is currently not in session and it is unclear if Omar was home at the time of the search.
Omar's office denounced the raid as "an outrageous abuse of power" and said the "Congresswoman has done nothing wrong."
According to Reuters, a person familiar with the investigation said it is related to alleged immigration fraud and part of the probe concerns the Somali-born lawmaker's immigration paperwork that was filled out by her late father when she was a child.
TIME has reached out to the White House and Omar’s office for further information.
While the reason behind the criminal investigation remains unclear, it is not the first time Omar’s immigration records have become a focal point. Earlier this year, Republican Rep. Nancy Mace of South Carolina unsuccessfully filed a subpoena of records pertaining to Omar, who gained her U.S. citizenship in 2000, when she was 17.
In a podcast interview in March, Vice President J.D. Vance, without offering evidence, said "we actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud against" the United States. Omar’s office at the time dismissed Vance’s claims as fabricated and defamatory.
Last month, White House border czar Tom Homan told Fox News that Omar was the subject of an "ongoing criminal investigation," but declined to offer specific details.
Trump says he had "nothing to do with" raid
Hours after the search, Trump suggested he was not involved in the investigation and referred to Omar as "crooked" and "terrible."
“Well, I understand they’re looking at her very carefully,” he told reporters outside the White House. “I’ve always found her to be totally crooked, personally, but that has nothing to do with me.”
He added: “I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ [Department of Justice]. I have nothing to do with it.”
Democrats condemn raid on Omar’s home
The raid was carried out just over three weeks before the midterm elections, in which the Republicans will grapple to maintain control of the House and Senate. Omar is seeking a fifth two-year term in the House of Representatives.
Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz led Democrats in denouncing the raid, saying “Americans see this for what it is—President Trump is abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election.”
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries referred to the raid as “deeply disturbing” and argued that it raises “serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government” against Trump’s adversaries.
"Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family," he said in a statement, which was co-signed by House minority whip Rep. Katherine Clark and Rep. Pete Aguilar, chair of the House Democratic Caucus.
The Justice Department has historically avoided federal prosecutors indicting a candidate or federal law enforcement taking "overt" investigative steps regarding a candidate—such as executing a search warrant—within 60 days of a primary or general election.
Rep. Ro Khanna of California referred to the raid as a "disturbing" development and implored "any decent American" to "stand up and speak out."
Rep. Robert Garcia, also of California and the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, said the search is an "outrageous escalation in the President's continued weaponization of our government against anyone who dares to stand up to him."
He added: "Searching a Representative's home over a decades-old immigration filing by her father is an authoritarian abuse of power. No family deserves these continued attacks."
Trump has previously been accused of targeting his political opponents.
Last year, he called on former Attorney General Pam Bondi to begin prosecuting California Sen. Adam Schiff, a Democrat, former FBI Director James Comey, and New York Attorney General Letitia James, all of whom led investigations into Trump, political or criminal.
James was charged with mortgage fraud by the Justice Department last year, but a federal judge dismissed the case. James denied the allegations.
In April, a federal grand jury indicted Comey over a social media post that the Trump Administration characterized as a threat against the President. Comey said he was "innocent" and vowed to fight the case, which has been delayed until early 2027.
Omar has accused Trump of having a “weird” obsession with her
Trump has long targeted Omar and her birthplace Somalia during his anti-immigration speeches and remarks. He has repeatedly pointed to well-documented instances of “fraud” in Minnesota involving people of Somali ancestry and welfare programs, seemingly blaming the community as a whole rather than the individuals involved.
Last December, while delivering an address in Pennsylvania, Trump referenced Omar during an anti-immigration tirade, claiming she does “nothing but b-tch” and arguing that she comes from a county considered to be “the worst” in the world. “We ought to get her the hell out,” the President said, pausing as members of the crowd chanted “send her back.”
Omar at the time responded by saying Trump’s “obsession” with her is “beyond weird.”
“Since he has no economic policies to tout, he’s resorting to regurgitating bigoted lies instead,” said Omar via social media, reacting to a clip of the President’s speech. “He continues to be a national embarrassment.”
In January, Omar was approached by a man with a syringe during a Town Hall meeting in Minneapolis. The man sprayed her with a substance before being restrained by on-site security. Lab analysis later determined the liquid contained acetic acid and identified it as a mixture of water and apple cider vinegar. Last month, a 56-year-old man named Anthony James Kazmierczak was sentenced to 14 months in prison for the assault.
Shortly after the Town Hall incident, Omar called out Trump’s use of “hateful rhetoric” against her and suggested he had made her a target.
“What the facts have shown, since I’ve gotten into elected office, is that every time the President of the United States has chosen to use hateful rhetoric to talk about me and the community that I represent, my death threats skyrocket,” she said. “I wouldn’t be where I am at today, having to pay for security, having the government to think about providing me security, if Donald Trump wasn’t in office and if he wasn’t so obsessed with me."

Tehran theater to host reading performance of “The Star-Spangled Girl”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
17:40:28 UTC
02:40:28 KST

Tehran theater to host reading performance of “The Star-Spangled Girl”
TEHRAN- On Saturday, the Simorgh Theater Hall in Tehran will be hosting a reading performance of the acclaimed American playwright Neil Simon’s comedy “The Star-Spangled Girl”.
The reading performance will be directed by Mehrshad Moradi, based on a Persian translation by Shahram Zargar.
The play will be read by a cast composed of Erfan Sepehr and Reyhaneh Keyhan.
“The Star-Spangled Girl” is a romantic comedy, set in San Francisco during the 1960s. Blending romance, political disagreement and situational humor, the play follows two young men whose radical ideals and unconventional lifestyle are challenged by the arrival of a patriotic woman.
Andy Hobart and Norman Cornell are roommates and political activists who run a small magazine called “Fallout” from their apartment. Dedicated to challenging the American establishment, the publication reflects their opposition to the prevailing political and social order. However, their commitment to the cause has brought little financial success. Struggling to keep the magazine afloat, they face unpaid bills, pressure from their printer and overdue rent. Andy, the more practical of the two, tries to manage their financial difficulties while finding ways to keep their landlady from demanding payment.
Their lives change when Sophie Rauschmeyer, a friendly young woman from the American South and a former Olympic swimmer, moves into the apartment next door. Her charm immediately captivates Norman, who falls head over heels for her. His feelings, however, are not returned. As Norman's infatuation grows, Andy decides to hire Sophie to help with the magazine, partly to please his lovesick roommate and partly to support their struggling publication.
Sophie initially suspects that the magazine's activities are dangerously subversive, reflecting her patriotic outlook and sharply contrasting with the men's radical politics. Yet the situation takes an unexpected turn when she develops feelings for Andy instead of Norman. Andy, who shares her attraction, finds himself caught between his growing affection for Sophie and his political convictions.
The emerging romance threatens to undermine the partnership between the two friends. Norman must confront his unrequited love, while Andy faces a conflict between his personal desires and ideological commitments. As romantic misunderstandings and political disagreements collide, the three characters become entangled in a comic struggle that tests their friendship, loyalties and beliefs.
Simon reportedly drew inspiration from a lively political exchange he witnessed between writer Paddy Chayefsky and René Carpenter, the wife of astronaut Scott Carpenter. The encounter explored the humorous possibilities of political disagreement between people whose apparent identities and convictions seemed incompatible.
Although the play featured Simon's characteristic witty dialogue and comic situations, its reception was mixed. Some critics found its humor entertaining, while others considered the story comparatively lightweight and less effective than his earlier successes, including “Barefoot in the Park” and “The Odd Couple”. Simon himself later expressed reservations about the play, suggesting that it lacked the substance of his stronger comedies.
In 1971, the play was adapted into a film directed by Jerry Paris, with Tony Roberts as Andy, Todd Susman as Norman and Sandy Duncan as Amy, the character renamed from Sophie. The film retained the central romantic conflict and political contrasts but received largely unfavorable reviews.

President Pezeshkian joins children at “Smile of the Homeland” ceremony
