President Pezeshkian joins children at “Smile of the Homeland” ceremony
TEHRAN- Iran’s “Smile of the Homeland” ceremony was held in Tehran on Sunday, bringing together President Masoud Pezeshkian, Education Minister Alireza Kazemi and more than 600 children and teenagers, including children with special needs, to mark National Children’s Week.
Organized by the Institute for the Intellectual Development of Children and Young Adults (IIDCYA), the event featured a variety of cultural and artistic programs aimed at promoting friendship, solidarity and a sense of belonging among young participants.
The program included poetry recitals, a choir performance, a dramatic patriotic chant, video presentations and a ceremony honoring educators working in the institute’s mobile libraries.
Addressing the children, Pezeshkian used the example of several sticks tied together to illustrate the strength that comes from unity. He said that when family members, neighbors, and people in a city or country stand together, they become stronger and are less likely to be divided.
The president encouraged the children and teenagers to build friendships, help one another and remain supportive of their peers, saying that cooperation among them could contribute to building a strong and progressive Iran.
Kazemi, meanwhile, highlighted the theme of this year’s National Children’s Week, “Children’s Smiles, the Alphabet of the Homeland,” emphasizing the need to protect children’s rights and provide equal opportunities for their growth and development.
He said no child should be deprived of the opportunity to develop their abilities because of poverty, individual differences or family circumstances. The minister stressed that efforts should be made to ensure that every child’s talent is recognized and that no child feels overlooked or unheard.
Kazemi also underscored the roles of families, schools and cultural institutions in children’s upbringing, describing the IIDCYA as an important national resource for identifying and nurturing the talents of children and teenagers.
The artistic program included a poetry recital by Sara Goudarzi, a member of the institute’s Qaf youth poetry and literature club. The institute’s choir performed the song “We Must Rise” in the presence of the president and education minister.
Sarina Seifi, a member of the institute, also presented a patriotic chant as part of the event. In another segment, Pezeshkian met with 10 children with special needs from the institute’s Inclusive Center No. 40 in Tehran Province.
Video presentations focusing on children’s smiles, a meeting with the martyred Leader, Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei, and a promotional clip for National Children’s Week were also screened during the festival.
A special segment was devoted to recognizing the work of educators serving in the institute’s mobile libraries. Ali Nadi, representing the mobile-library educators, received a certificate of honor and a commemorative statuette from the president.
The institute’s mobile libraries travel to different areas to provide children and teenagers with access to books and cultural activities. They also help promote reading and engage young audiences in underserved communities where access to cultural resources may be limited.
The festival concluded with children and teenagers gathering for a commemorative photograph with Pezeshkian and Kazemi at the Behnam Hall of the institute’s Cultural and Artistic Center.
In Iran, National Children’s Week is an annual observance held in early October to highlight children’s rights, well-being, education and creative development. The week features cultural, artistic and educational programs organized by schools, cultural institutions and organizations such as the Institute for the Intellectual Development of Children and Young Adults (IIDCYA).
Activities often include book-reading sessions, art workshops, performances and events promoting children’s participation in social and cultural life. The observance also provides an opportunity to raise awareness of the need to protect children, nurture their talents and ensure equal opportunities for all, including those living in disadvantaged circumstances and children with disabilities.

Majidi dedicates Busan premiere of “Midday Meal” to martyred children of Minab, brave people of Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
17:39:21 UTC
02:39:21 KST

Majidi dedicates Busan premiere of “Midday Meal” to martyred children of Minab, brave people of Iran
TEHRAN – Majid Majidi’s latest film “Midday Meal” premiered at the 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF), and the director dedicated it to the brave people of Iran and the martyred children of Minab.
Prior to the screening of the film in the festival’s main competition section on October 9, the director said in brief remarks: “I would like to dedicate the screening of this film, on my own behalf, to the brave and courageous people of Iran and the martyred children of Minab. As you have heard, 168 children were massacred on the first day of the war (the US and Israel imposed on Iran), yet the people continue to stand firm and resist”.
“We salute these courageous people who have not bowed their heads and will not. We will rebuild all that has been destroyed. The Iranian people are resilient; they stand against oppression and maintain their independence. The only crime of the Iranian people is that they wish to be independent,” he emphasized.
A production of 2026, the 133-minute family social drama, which deals with children and human rights, marks Majidi’s first visit to the festival, Honaronline reported.
Funded by the Institute for the Intellectual Development of Children and Young Adults, the film was shot exclusively in southern Iran and features an entirely local cast, with no established stars, including Mohammad Rahimi, Kheyri Zakeri, Rahim Bakhsh Pira, and Heybatmorad Damani.
A rural schoolteacher loses sight of his own morality and sanity as he questions the divergent needs of his young (and old) charges in “Midday Meal,” Majidi’s 11th feature film. A slow-burning bonfire of moral vanities unfolding in a land beset by poverty and bureaucracy, the Iranian auteur’s moving drama bows in competition in Busan, where he and lead actor Mohammad Rahimi can expect to take home awards.
In a parched badland village that looks like the end of the world, Solan is the only teacher. After years of enduring the poorly paid temporary job, he holds one modest dream - to become a full-time teacher and to live in a proper house with his mother. But everything begins to unravel with the death of the benefactor who had funded the school’s meal program. If the meals stop, most of the students will stop coming, and the school’s closure becomes inevitable. The education office offers no real help, only an order to keep the classes running. Desperate, Solan withdraws his rental deposit, moves into the school, and begins a precarious double life as a teacher by day and oil smuggler by night. And through it all, his mother stays by his side, quietly trusting him.
In “Midday Meal,” master filmmaker Majidi shows this world with unflinching rawness, and his direction reveals a gift for capturing layered emotions that resist easy words. His camera runs close to the characters’ emotions, then falls still at key moments, heightening the drama through that very stillness. Do Solan’s ends justify the means? Are choices driven by pure goodwill, or are they nothing more than self-interest masquerading as virtue?
Within its own running time, the film can only project a single facet of reality, but how far today’s conscience might take root for generations to come is left to the audience.
With “Midday Meal,” Majid Majidi doesn't seek to replicate the success of the films that made him famous. He returns to the concerns that have spanned his career, but places them within a more mature, grittier, and complex narrative. Poor children are still present, injustice still subtly permeates lives, but this time, we witness the tragedy through the eyes of an adult - one who understands what is right but cannot always do what is right.
This year's edition of BIFF is the first since the International Federation of Film Producers Associations designated Busan as one of its 17 A-list festivals. The winner of the Busan Award for best film now also qualifies for submission to the Oscars for best international feature. The distinction puts Busan alongside the five other Oscar-qualifying festivals: Cannes, Berlin, Venice, Sundance and Toronto.
Now in its second year, the best film competition brings together 14 Asian films, 12 of them world premieres. Four are from first-time directors, and four are by women filmmakers.
In addition to “Midday Meal,” the lineup includes “Beach Fictions” by Korean newcomer Lim Hayeon, “Between Two Lovers,” from Hirokazu Kore-eda protégé Hirose Nanako, and “The First Taste of Loneliness,” by Chinese director Gu You. Also included in the line-up are entries from Uzbekistan, Indonesia, and Taiwan.
Majid Majidi, 67, is an Iranian filmmaker and producer. His films often feature child or adolescent protagonists, explore themes such as childhood innocence, family bonds, poverty, social issues, and solidarity, and are characterized by a humanistic sensibility.
His important films include “Children of Heaven” (1997), “The Color of Paradise” (1999), “Baran” (2001), and “The Song of Sparrows” (2008). “Children of Heaven” was nominated for the Academy Award for Best International Feature Film.
More recently, Majidi directed “Muhammad: The Messenger of God” (2015), an epic film dealing with the childhood of the Islamic prophet Muhammad (PBUH).
The Busan International Film Festival, held annually in Haeundae District, Busan, South Korea, is one of the most significant film festivals in Asia.
The main focus of the BIFF is to introduce new films and first-time directors, especially those from Asian countries. Another notable feature is the appeal of the festival to young people, both in terms of the large youthful audience it attracts and through its efforts to develop and promote young talent.
The 31st Busan International Film Festival will run until October 15.

Meta debuted its latest artificial intelligence model, Muse Wonder, and says it's the most advanced option for powering digital assistants. But it doesn't come for free.
To access the model, users of the Muse personal agent app will need to sign up for a monthly subscription of $20 or $100. The release underscores Meta's efforts to create new AI-derived revenue sources outside of its core online ad business.
Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said in an interview on Monday that the company developed Muse Wonder, codenamed Watermelon, to improve the capabilities of "personal and professional agents" so they don't stumble on tasks like booking dinner reservations and checking for availabilities.
"When you do real-world tasks, you're going to get roadblocks and you're going to get things that come up or various setbacks," Wang said. "We specifically tried to train the model to be able to try other approaches instead of stalling and then checking back in with the user at any time."
Meta said in a blog post that the latest model "offers our strongest safeguards to date" against "cyber misuse." Those protections only come with the paid model for now.
Muse shot up to the top of Apple's App Store after Meta introduced the AI agent app last month. The app is free, with subscription plans available for more usage.
Wang said Meta's AI team has been monitoring for agent-related "incidents or issues" with Muse in order to understand problems and resolve them. Some users have complained on social media that the agent accessed personal messages without authorization, which the company has disputed.
Meta is trying to better inform people of how to use the app to avoid certain problems, Wang said.
"I think there are certainly instances users have authorized various communications or whatnot earlier in a conversation, and then may have forgotten about that," Wang said. He added that the company is educating users on such matters "to ensure that consumers can trust the product going forward."
Muse Wonder will also be available to coders who pay to access the company's related Meta Model API. Wang said that offering will cost more than the standard subscriptions because it is a "much larger model and at frontier level." He said it will still be priced "meaningfully below" leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic.
An even more powerful variant of Meta's latest model, dubbed Muse Wonder Full, will only be available to developers who sign up to the company's software engineering focused Muse Code AI agent under a $50 or $200 a month subscription plan.

The figure comes from The Putin Tax, a report published this month by Mr Downie with Dr Dominic Reed, which puts the annual cost of Russian hostile activity against Britain at between £2 billion and £2.5 billion and describes itself as the first attempt to measure that burden. Feature: Kenyan pastoralists turn to fish farming amid climate shocks, banditry threats
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
01:13:10 CST
02:13:10 KST

SAMBURU, Kenya, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- For six decades, Leshan Saitoti, a pastoralist from Samburu County in northern Kenya, relied entirely on cattle rearing to support his family.
Like generations before him, Saitoti depended on his herd for milk, meat and blood, traditional staples of the Samburu people.
However, five years ago, a severe drought wiped out 33 of Saitoti's cows and 1,200 goats almost overnight.
The devastating losses plunged his family into poverty, a challenge faced by many households across Kenya's arid and semi-arid regions.
Undeterred by the setback, Saitoti and his four sons turned to an unlikely alternative -- fish farming.
Along with a growing number of pastoralists in Samburu, they have embraced aquaculture in pursuit of more reliable food supplies and income.
"Fish farming has not only improved the diet in our homes but also transformed our lives by providing better income from a lucrative market," Saitoti said.
To support the transition, the Samburu County Government has been distributing tilapia and catfish fingerlings to local pastoralists to promote aquaculture across the region.
The initiative is providing an alternative source of income for pastoralist communities while helping strengthen food security, said Moses Leluata, county executive committee member for agriculture, livestock, fisheries and veterinary services.
"We have distributed over 28,000 tilapia and catfish fingerlings to help pastoralists embrace fish farming. We are building resilience to threats posed by insecurity and climate change," Leluata said.
For a community whose language has a dozen distinct words for a cow's coat patterns but no word for fish, the transition has entailed a steep learning curve.
Like many elders in his village, Saitoti initially knew little about fish, including how they tasted or how to prepare them.
Today, however, fish has become a popular and nutritious addition to his family's meals.
A local youth group of 20 former cattle-rustling trackers has shifted its focus from monitoring grazing corridors to managing fish ponds.
Equipped with nets and pond liners and trained by the Samburu County Government and the World Food Program, the young men now oversee daily fish-farming operations.
They feed the fingerlings twice a day, guard communal waterpans against overfishing and carefully record fish growth in exercise books.
"We were trained in fish farming, from feeding the fish to harvesting them, and we have followed the instructions," said James Ole Lekina, the group's youth leader.
"Fish has become a booming business in our major towns, and we have no regrets about taking up aquaculture," Ole Lekina added.
A mature tilapia sells for around 390 Kenyan shillings (about 3 U.S. dollars) in local markets, offering fish farmers a potential source of income.
The locally produced fish is also reshaping regional supply chains.
Grace Maina, who runs a popular fish eatery in Maralal, the administrative capital of Samburu County, once relied on supplies transported from Lake Naivasha, more than 350 km away.
The long journey drove up transportation costs. Today, she buys fresh fish directly from local dams and community ponds.
"Fish consumption is increasing day by day. Pastoralists are increasingly eating fish instead of red meat," Maina said.
Tilapia can reach market size in about six months, compared with the roughly three years it takes for cattle to mature, said Sostine Wanjala, a fisheries officer with the Samburu County Government.
"There are greater benefits from fish farming. It requires a shared pond, which can be restocked, unlike cattle, which take years to mature and can be wiped out in a single drought season," Wanjala said.
For women in Samburu, the shift toward aquaculture has also opened up new economic opportunities. In a culture where men have traditionally held livestock ownership, women are now raising and owning fish.
Small self-help groups, many comprising widows who lost their family's livestock to severe droughts and cattle rustling, have received pond liners to establish fish farms in their backyards.
"Many locals engaged in fish farming have regained the dignity they lost when the loss of their cattle intensified hunger, poverty and social tensions," said Rebecca Leitimalo, a fish farmer in Samburu County. ■

The event also featured interactive booths offering Chinese calligraphy, paper-cutting, traditional costumes, tea ceremonies and Chinese cuisine, attracting enthusiastic participation from Egyptian students. ■

Military confrontations have escalated in recent weeks in the East African country's northernmost Tigray region, pitting the Ethiopian National Defense Force and its allied forces against troops loyal to the Tigray People's Liberation Front and its allied armed groups.
The escalation unfolds against the backdrop of the devastating two-year war from November 2020 to November 2022, which caused a massive humanitarian crisis before being formally halted by the Pretoria peace accord in South Africa.
Meanwhile, Tilahun said that a significant number of armed combatants in Tigray are currently showing a "strong desire" to abandon conflict and return to peaceful civilian life by joining the demobilization centers in large numbers.

"Türkiye stands with Saudi Arabia and our Saudi brothers and sisters in the face of these attacks that violate law and humanity," he added.

"Mutual respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity is our fundamental principle. In our view, division and fragmentation only serve the interests of malign forces seeking to turn our region into a sea of blood," he said.
Mecca pact
The president also announced that work is underway to submit the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement – a pact signed on Aug. 7 between Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan – to parliament in the coming days to complete domestic approval procedures.
Erdogan said the three countries are continuing efforts to establish the institutional framework for the agreement, adding that defence cooperation is progressing along two main tracks: collective defence and regional cooperation, and the development of a permanent, functioning institutional structure.

German silence on Gaza and the West Bank ‘has been loud’: Philippe Sands

German silence on Gaza and the West Bank ‘has been loud’: Philippe Sands
Winner of German Book Trade's Peace Prize insists on ‘excavating matters that some wish to hide’
TEHRAN — Philippe Sands, a professor of law at University College London and human rights lawyer at the International Court of Justice in The Hague, has criticized Germany’s “silence on crimes committed on the territory of Palestine, in Gaza and in the West Bank.”
Writing an article on Voxeurop published on October 12, he said Germany’s silence about Israel’s crimes in Gaza and the West Bank “has been loud.”
The Franco-British lawyer who was awarded the German Book Trade's Peace Prize on Sunday also said Germany’s restrictions on those who speak out loudly against crimes committed against Gazans are “troubling”.
 
“To silence those who seek to call out the crimes is indecent,” he wrote.
On Sunday, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier praised him as a humanist "who, despite growing resistance, fights tirelessly for human rights, justice and mutual understanding."
"Inappropriate silence"
In his acceptance speech while receiving the award, Sands criticized Germany’s "inappropriate silence" regarding Israel’s actions in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank.
On November 21, 2024, the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
Some argue that the war on Gaza is a clear example of genocide but some others disagree.
“Whatever the rulings, the debate about labels is, I fear, an unhelpful distraction. There is no hierarchy among the various international crimes. To kill as a war crime or a crime against humanity is not less grave than a genocide. These are all terrible crimes,” he wrote.
Sands said those who “demand accountability” for crimes “should not be silenced or excluded or punished, merely for exercising a freedom of expression.” He suggested that “writers and journalists, songsters and poets, filmmakers and others must be able to tell their stories.”
“Germany has called out and acted on many horrors, from the Yazidis to the Uighurs, from Syria to Sudan and Ukraine, but it has been silent about the crimes committed against Palestinians in Israel since October 7, 2023,” he explained.
“On Gaza and the West Bank, the German silence has been loud. Relatedly, the restrictions on debate are troubling. This is all the more so after the ICJ’s clear advisory opinion of 2024, on the Palestinian right of self-determination. Britain, Canada, France and others have since recognized a Palestinian state. In recent days they have imposed sanctions. The British Foreign Secretary has characterized conduct in the occupied territories as ethnic cleansing.”
He stated that Germany “knows about ethnic cleansing” in Gaza but why it is silent is a matter of question.
However, he said, some German officials have taken a departure from Berlin’s policy and began strongly criticizing Israel for its behavior toward Palestinians.
“Some German leaders have begun to speak more sharply in their criticism of Israel’s actions. That is right, even if so tentative and limited. It is not anti-Semitic. It is not ‘anti-Israel’. It is truth.”
Sands suggested that the Berlin government must break its silence about the crimes that Israel has been committing against Palestinians.
“Eighty years after Nuremberg, (Germany) must surely be to break silences about international crimes, wherever they occur and by whomsoever they are committed, even friends, especially friends.”
He said, “Silence is not the way. Not for a family. Not for a community. Not for a country.”
Sands insisted on “bringing truth to power, confronting prejudice and double standards, excavating matters that some wish to hide.”
While the U.S. has imposed sanctions on the ICC and threatened its judges, Sands said, “Let us protect the writers and the jurists, so they may be free from threat, attack or sanction.”
Sands concluded his remarks by citing a poem from his favorite Canadian poet who says:
 
Let us run no more, with the lawless crowds, whoever they may be. 
Let us hold to account the killers in high places, even as they say their prayers aloud.
Let us ring the bells, that still can ring.
Let us not forget there is a crack, a crack in everything, that’s how the light gets in

Yemen Leaves Riyadh Grounded
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
17:04:46 UTC
02:04:46 KST

Yemen Leaves Riyadh Grounded
Repeated strikes close Riyadh airport and shatter Saudi air defenses as Ansarallah enforces its 'blockade for blockade' doctrine
TEHRAN — Riyadh’s airport has been hit five times since Tuesday, October 6, by Saudi authorities’ own count, and the government cannot promise a sixth will not come. On Saturday, a missile struck King Khalid International Airport, killing at least 13 people and wounding more than 300, according to the kingdom. On Sunday, another projectile set Terminal 4 on fire. On Monday, the Saudi civil aviation authority extended the shutdown.
A wealthy kingdom that spent a decade selling itself as the Persian Gulf’s safe harbor cannot keep its capital’s runway open.
Cirium reported that 99.7 percent of scheduled flights at King Khalid were canceled on Sunday. Flightradar24 showed no aircraft over a city of roughly eight million. Lufthansa Group grounded its Riyadh service through October 16, Air France-KLM through the end of the month, and Etihad stretched its Saudi cancellations again.
The FAA warned American carriers about Saudi airspace, and Washington, London, Berlin, and Madrid told their citizens to stay away from the airport. Riyadh’s schools moved online. The metro stopped serving two airport stations.
The defenses are thin. Saudi officials have told the Wall Street Journal they are running low on interceptors.
The kingdom is shuffling air defense batteries between palaces and increasingly vulnerable energy sites and desperately searching the world for more.
Sanaa’s equation
Brigadier General Yahya Saree laid out the terms in his October 11 statement. Yemeni forces, he said, carried out four operations in 24 hours: three waves against King Khalid, a direct hit on King Fahd Airport in Dammam, and fires at Aramco’s Shedgum and Tanajib facilities in the Eastern Province.
He told airlines, airport staff, and travelers that Saudi airports and airspace are unsafe, exempting only Mecca and Medina, and put responsibility for any failed interception on Riyadh.
Sanaa’s rule is “airport for airport, blockade for blockade, and escalation for escalation.”
Ansarallah did not invent this logic out of a vacuum. There were documented Saudi strikes on Sanaa airport on July 13, with three munitions landing on its only working runway. That airport is the front door for aid to the area where most Yemenis live.
Saree said Saudi jets flew 124 raids in a single day, bringing the total of this escalation to 2,058. The World Food Programme says three-quarters of families in parts of Yemen are going hungry.
Eleven years of bombing and port restrictions taught Yemenis what a closed airport means. Riyadh is learning it now. Ansarallah’s warnings were repeated and ignored.
Washington stays out
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman asked for urgent American help, according to multiple news reports in American media outlets.
He pledged around $1 trillion in U.S. “investment” this year and was embraced at the White House. What he has received in his war on Yemen so far is intelligence, targeting support, and military advisers.
Trump called the airport attack “very bad” and said of joining Saudi strikes: “We may. We’re going to look at it.” Secretary of State Marco Rubio offered “condolences.” Condolences do not intercept missiles.
The reasons for restraint are plain. The war on Iran has already consumed American munitions and attention, closed and disrupted the Strait of Hormuz, and pushed fuel prices high. Midterm elections arrive on November 3, and a Republican Party facing angry drivers has no appetite for another unwinnable quagmire.
Trump himself has said that the Yemenis contacted Washington to say they do not want to fight the United States. The American president certainly remembers the high costs of “Operation Rough Rider” from March to May 2025, when a massive multi-week air assault spectacularly failed to blunt Sanaa’s strategic capabilities.
Ansarallah announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia in July and has the range to successfully strike American ships in the Red Sea. It has not fired on one.
So far it has held back, as Riyadh realizes that Washington dreads the cost of a wider regional war far more than it dreads a weakened Saudi ally.
The bill for Vision 2030
The World Petroleum Council Energy Congress opened in Riyadh under security, but BP pulled out, and the chief executives of ExxonMobil, TotalEnergies, Shell and Chevron vanished from the program.
The Finance Ministry expects the economy to shrink 3.6 percent this year. Foreign investment fell in each of the first two quarters.
Riyadh dropped the 2029 Asian Winter Games in January, and Neom and other showpieces sit stalled or under review. An effective attack on the East-West pipeline in September cut the kingdom’s route around Hormuz.
Vision 2030 asks visitors and investors to believe Riyadh is safe. A shuttered airport answers that question for them.
Expo 2030 and the 2034 World Cup now carry a plain logistical doubt, and so do the data centers meant to make Saudi Arabia an “AI hub.” Billions spent on golf, football, and festivals sought to buy an image, and Yemen's punishing strikes have thoroughly damaged it.
Furthermore, as the kingdom prepares to host the 2027 AFC Asian Cup across venues in Riyadh, Jeddah, and Khobar, the unfolding security crisis and shuttered transport infrastructure cast an immediate shadow over the tournament, turning what was intended as a grand showcase of soft power into a stark reminder of Saudi Arabia’s extreme vulnerability.
MBS’ war
Mohammed bin Salman launched the war on Yemen in 2015 expecting victory after mere weeks. He got a stalemate, a 2022 truce and, this summer, a resumed war he is losing.
When Ansarallah pushed down the Red Sea coast in August, Riyadh held back its air power, and Mokha fell. The coalition’s “Dawn of Yemen” counteroffensive, with 100 jets in its opening phase, has not stopped missiles reaching Riyadh, Dammam, Abha, Jazan and Najran. Sanaa has released footage of Saudi-backed fighters surrendering.
The crown prince now moves between bunkered palaces under a handpicked guard, the WSJ reports. His last public appearance was October 6, when he gave blood for a donation drive.
Saudi officials are quietly weighing a diplomatic exit. Sanaa has already named its price: stop the aggression and lift the siege.

US claims do not match what we see on the ground: Baqaei
TEHRAN— Iran has dismissed US assertions that maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has returned to normal, saying Washington’s continued naval blockade and economic sanctions are incompatible with restoring security to the strategic waterway.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei made the remarks at his weekly press conference in Tehran on Monday, addressing the situation in the strait, the latest exchanges between Tehran and Washington through mediators, US sanctions, regional tensions and remarks by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio invoking ancient Greek and Persian history.
Baqaei said the situation in the Strait of Hormuz was a direct consequence of the US-Israeli war against Iran, which began on February 28, and rejected assertions that Iran had lost its strategic leverage.
“The Americans’ claims do not match what we see on the ground,” he said. “They can continue to claim that the Strait of Hormuz no longer matters and that Iran has lost its leverage, but we will continue to do our job.”
He added that developments in international markets and efforts by countries to secure fuel supplies demonstrated the continuing importance of the waterway.
Hormuz security linked to an end to US pressure
Baqaei stressed that Iran had not introduced maritime controls to gain leverage over other countries, arguing that the measures taken in the strait were a response to the security circumstances created by the US-Israeli attacks.
“What we have been witnessing in this waterway since February 28 is the direct result of actions by the US and the Zionist regime in attacking Iran,” he said. The waterway, he added, had been used to launch attacks against Iran, prompting Tehran to adopt measures that it considers consistent with international law.
The spokesperson said security would not be restored while Washington continued its naval blockade and economic pressure against Iran. He described these measures as acts of aggression that had consequences extending beyond Iran to the wider region and international markets.
“We are not pleased with this situation, as the security of the Strait of Hormuz is necessary for us more than anything else,” Baqaei said. “However, the United States’ aggressive actions have caused trouble for itself, the region, and the world.”
The remarks also addressed Washington’s claims that the waterway was under US control. Baqaei said such assertions bore little resemblance to the situation on the ground and questioned why the United States would seek assistance from Russia to address its oil supply needs if, as Washington maintained, the situation in Hormuz had been resolved.
Responding to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s stated readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to international markets, including the United States, Baqaei said each country was entitled to make decisions according to its national interests. He nevertheless described Washington’s reported interest in Russian supplies as significant in light of its assertions about the strait.
Iran reviewing US response to seven-point proposal
Baqaei said Iran was still examining Washington’s response to Tehran’s seven-point proposal, with communications between the two sides continuing through intermediaries.
He said the proposal, discussed on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, addressed Iran’s demands, including the lifting of the naval blockade, an end to the war on all fronts and the release of Iranian assets. According to the spokesperson, these issues were also covered by a memorandum of understanding previously agreed upon.
Iran would convey its position to the mediators once the review was complete, he said, adding that the new US sanctions imposed during the process must also be lifted.
Pakistan and Qatar, he said, remained the principal mediators between Tehran and Washington. Iran also welcomed the good offices of friendly countries, including Russia.
Addressing remarks that the US response had fallen short of Iran’s expectations, Baqaei indicated that Tehran was still assessing the points raised by Washington before communicating its position through the intermediaries.
Baqaei also addressed the nuclear issue, questioning Washington’s continued emphasis on Iran’s nuclear program after US officials had repeatedly asserted that it had been destroyed. He argued that attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities and the lack of an effective international response had prompted debate inside Iran about the benefits of continued membership in the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT).
He said the international non-proliferation framework faced challenges in all three of its principal areas: nuclear disarmament, preventing the spread of nuclear weapons and ensuring countries’ access to peaceful nuclear technology.
Iran seeks dialogue to ease regional tensions
Turning to regional developments, Baqaei said Iran remained deeply concerned about escalating tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen and was ready to use its good offices to facilitate dialogue.
He said Tehran opposed continued conflict between two Muslim countries, arguing that further escalation would undermine regional stability and create opportunities for Israel to exploit divisions.
Iran had repeatedly supported the implementation of understandings previously reached between the parties, he said, urging them to return to dialogue and prevent further deterioration.
Baqaei also welcomed the prospect of stronger relations between Iraq and Saudi Arabia, reiterating Iran’s support for greater cooperation among regional countries. Tehran had previously proposed meetings involving Persian Gulf littoral states, including Iran and Iraq, and continued to support initiatives aimed at strengthening regional trust.
“Strengthening relations and trust among regional countries is the foundation and prerequisite for creating a secure region, free from the destructive interference of foreign actors,” he said.
On reports alleging that the United Arab Emirates was providing intelligence, financial or logistical support to terrorist groups operating in eastern Iran, Baqaei said Iranian security, military and law-enforcement agencies were monitoring such activities.
He described efforts to destabilize Iran’s borders as part of a US-Israeli plan, while emphasizing that Tehran was in continuous consultation with its land and maritime neighbors to prevent terrorist groups from exploiting the regional situation. He did not identify a specific neighboring country as responsible for supporting the groups.

'Advance injustice': Allahabad HC flags POCSO Act's rigid application in minor couple cases

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
17:03:25 UTC
02:03:25 KST

The Allahabad high court has urged the law commission to recommend amendments to the POCSO Act.
The Allahabad high court has called on the law commission to consider recommending changes to the protection of children from sexual offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, to address cases involving minor couples while taking India's prevailing social realities into account.A two-judge bench comprising justice Atul Sreedharan and Justice Achal Sachdev said that the strict enforcement of the legislation could, in certain exceptional circumstances, lead to outcomes that “advance injustice rather than justice”, especially when a relationship has resulted in the birth of a child.The comment was made during the court's consideration of Rakesh Yadav's habeas corpus petition, which sought an order to produce his wife.The bench observed that the law appeared not to have adequately considered India's social conditions, where a substantial section of the population remains illiterate or semi-literate and may have limited awareness of their legal and constitutional rights, along with the responsibilities and consequences associated with them.The girl's father told the court that she had studied up to class 5 but could not read a newspaper and was able only to sign her name.
He said he had never attended school.The court allowed the man's habeas corpus petition. The couple had eloped, and the girl subsequently gave birth to their child, following which a case was registered against him under the POCSO Act.Court calls for flexibility in exceptional cases"It is definitely not an excuse to be ignorant of the law. The bench noted that the POCSO Act's execution may, in some factual circumstances, lead to outcomes that seem to promote injustice rather than justice if this concept is implemented in a purely pedantic manner."According to the news agency PTI, the court suggested that the law commission consider amendments allowing special judges greater flexibility in exceptional cases to take the specific circumstances into account while deciding an appropriate sentence.It also recommended examining alternative penalties, including community service, in situations where applying the POCSO Act could lead to the unnecessary disruption of a family formed amid a lack of awareness of the law.The bench observed that the existing legislation appeared to have insufficiently considered India's prevailing social realities.Describing the matter as a conflict between human development and the strict application of the law, the court noted that adolescents around the age of 15 may develop emotional and physical maturity that can lead to attraction towards another person.
However, the bench stressed that the state must ensure minors continue their education until they reach the age of majority. It also underlined the need to provide them with adequate opportunities to acquire vocational skills and become self-reliant.According to the case records, the couple had eloped and signed an affidavit on September 1, 2025, declaring themselves husband and wife.The state government and the girl's father stated that her date of birth was July 25, 2010.After being separated from her husband, the girl was placed in a Balika Griha, where she subsequently gave birth to a child.The court noted that the case records did not contain a date-of-birth certificate issued by a school or a birth certificate from a municipal authority or panchayat.

Finnart mine hunting date revealed but costs withheld
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
18:00:29 BST
02:00:29 KST

Mine hunting equipment, autonomous systems and support vessels will begin moving to the former Finnart Oil Terminal in 2028, though the MOD will not say what the site will cost to run, how many jobs it will create or when it will be fully operational, according to answers given in Parliament.
When the purchase of the terminal on Loch Long was announced in July, the department presented it as a naval fuel depot, to be operated by the Oil and Pipelines Agency and intended to expand sovereign fuel holding capacity. General Sir Gwyn Jenkins, the First Sea Lord, said afterwards that the site “will also become a new mine hunting base for the Hybrid Navy”.
Dave Doogan, the Scottish National Party member for Angus and Perthshire Glens, asked for the planned timetable for establishing mine hunting operations at Finnart, and separately what estimate had been made of the facilities required there and of the autonomous mine countermeasures systems and support vessels to be based at it.
Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, gave the same answer to each: “The Ministry of Defence has purchased the Finnart Oil Terminal on Scotland’s west coast, marking a multi-million-pound investment to strengthen the United Kingdom’s national security and defence resilience. There will be a phased relocation of equipment, autonomous systems and support vessels to support mine hunting operations from 2028. This approach allows investment and capability growth to be matched to emerging operational requirements, ensuring continuity of mine countermeasures capability while supporting the longer-term transformation of the HMNB Clyde estate and MHC operating model.”
James Cartlidge, the Conservative member for South Suffolk, asked how many additional jobs the acquisition would create and over what timeframe. Mr Pollard said: “This acquisition and subsequent investment into the current Finnart Oil Terminal site will help create new opportunities and strengthen the local supply chain, supporting long-term economic growth in the West of Scotland. Specific numbers cannot be confirmed at this early stage within the project, but an increase in head count is anticipated to support the engineering, construction, and commissioning phases over the coming years.”
Asked in two further questions for an estimate of annual operating costs, and for the timetable for the terminal to become fully operational, the minister gave the same reply to both: “This project is in the planning stage, and detailed work is now underway to deliver the next phase. Given this, and commercial sensitivities, it is not currently possible to provide further details regarding estimates of operating costs or when the site will be operational.”
The five answers between them yield one firm date, the 2028 start for the phased relocation, while the running costs, the headcount, the date of full operation and the scale of what will be based there all remain undisclosed.

Muse Wonder Puts Meta Back at the AI Frontier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
17:00:27 UTC
02:00:27 KST

When Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg rebooted his company’s artificial intelligence efforts last year, it seemed to be a very expensive gamble. Meta’s latest AI models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, seem to show that the bet is finally paying off by putting the company back at the frontier of AI development.
Muse Wonder Full boasts frontier capabilities, Meta says, meaning that it is among the most capable AI models in the world. “Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” the company said in a blog post today.
The Muse Wonder models will be available through an API and through Muse Code, a tool for writing software with AI. Meta says the best version of the model will power features across its platforms, including its Muse personal agent.
Zuckerberg overhauled his company’s AI research last year by sinking billions into the recently formed Meta Superintelligence Labs, and hiring the former Scale AI CEO Alexandr Wang to lead it. This effort has sometimes been rocky, with some researchers not sticking around for long.
Meta was once a trailblazer in AI. Its Llama series of models were the first frontier open-weight offerings from a big lab. Llama, which could be downloaded and run on one’s own hardware, was widely adopted by researchers and startups.
But the company fell behind after delivering several disappointing versions of the model, and as Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google rapidly introduced more capable models.
Meta announced the first model from its new lab, Muse Spark, in April of this year. The company has also released a small open-weight model called Muse Glimmer, and says it plans to release larger open-weight models in the future. It did not disclose details of how new Muse Wonder models were built or trained.
Muse Wonder was built to compete with the very best, however. Meta says the largest version of the new model outperforms Anthropic’s second-best model, Claude Fable 5.1, and ranks just below its best, Claude Opus 5.5, on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, a widely used aggregated score of model capabilities.
Meta says the model outperforms OpenAI’s best model, GPT-6 Astra, and both Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 on some specialized benchmarks, including ones that measure a model’s ability to work with legal documents and to build software. Benchmarks are not always a reliable measure of real-world performance, but this is still a significant step forward for Meta’s models.
Muse Wonder also includes two novel features designed to help make agents more effective and less inclined to misbehave. The new features, called Active Memory and Active Focus, are designed to keep the model locked into a stated goal and prevent it from becoming confused. This can be a challenge when AI performs complex research or builds a large software project, for example, and can lead to expensive mistakes or compounded errors.
Meta says it has put significant effort into training Muse Wonder to refuse to generate dangerous outputs, such as recipes for building bioweapons or help with hacking. It says the company scores well on several benchmarks designed to measure how resilient models are to those prompts.
A series of recent incidents involving rogue AI agents from Anthropic, OpenAI, and others also shows how easily powerful AI models can stray when given open-ended commands. Meta did not disclose whether it has seen agents powered by Muse Wonder misbehave in testing or what it has done to mitigate this issue specifically.
Zuckerberg said in a post on X last month that the company had delayed the release of its Muse models to work on safety. Meta also revealed a framework designed to ensure that it scales its models’ capabilities safely in a blog post earlier this month.
Muse Wonder may add more fuel to an already furious race to develop more capable AI, however. It certainly suggests that Meta is once again competitive in the increasingly high-stakes AI race.

Saudi capital’s airport to remain shut this week as airlines cancel services

Unknown Publisher

Saudi capital’s airport to remain shut this week as airlines cancel services
RIYADH - The authorities have extended the closure of Riyadh’s international airport until Oct 17 and airlines scrapped flights after continuing attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis emptied the skies over Saudi Arabia’s capital.
Operations at King Khalid International Airport, Saudi Arabia’s second-busiest airport after Jeddah, were suspended to “allow for the completion of procedures to ensure the safety and operational readiness of the airport’s facilities”, the Saudi civil aviation authority said in a statement.
Late on Oct 12, the Houthis said they had attacked the airport with a ballistic missile, shortly after Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the group towards Riyadh.
The Houthis also said in a statement that they targeted an airbase in Khamis Mushait in the kingdom’s south-west with a drone. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation.
A Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) issued later in the day showed that the airport will stay closed until 9pm GMT on Oct 17 (5am on Oct 18, Singapore time).
The airport has been shut since an attack on Oct 10 that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. On Sunday, another attack killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others.
The attacks marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi aviation in years, adding to pressures on an industry already grappling with conflict across the Middle East and with higher jet fuel prices that are eating into profits.
They have also raised worries over civil aviation becoming a target in armed conflict.
“This level of sustained intense attack on civil aviation is unprecedented,” said Mark Zee, founder of OPSGROUP, a membership-based organisation that provides aviation safety advice.
“I think this requires us to rethink how we view the current risk picture, and tread very carefully,” he said.
Air traffic tracker Flightradar24 showed planes avoiding the city on Oct 12, though jets were crossing Saudi airspace and landing at top hub Jeddah on the country’s west coast.
Cancellations across all Saudi airports reached 46.4%, aviation analytics firm Cirium said.
Crisis overshadows Saudi business outlook
The disruption has forced airlines across Europe and Asia to suspend services, while the Federal Aviation Administration advised US carriers on Oct 11 to exercise caution when flying to or over Saudi Arabia.
EU aviation body EASA widened a Saudi airspace warning on Oct 9, citing missile and drone attacks.
“The impact goes beyond Saudi Arabia to the wider region and to its global connections,” said aviation analyst John Strickland.
OPSGROUP advised airlines to avoid the southern aviation corridor over the Middle East altogether, and take a route from Europe to Asia over central Asia.
That adds “extensive distance” for some routes and “closes off options for getting into Dubai, Abu Dhabi for most western carriers,” Zee said.
On Oct 13, Etihad Airways said it had cancelled flights between Abu Dhabi and Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam due to “regional disruption”. 
All flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh have been cancelled until Oct 19, it said.
Lufthansa Group has cancelled all flights to Riyadh until Oct 16, while Air France-KLM has extended a suspension to and from Riyadh until the end of the month. Abu Dhabi’s Etihad Airways also extended cancellations.
Delta Air Lines said it was delaying planned services from Atlanta to Riyadh, initially due to start on Oct 23, until March 2027.
The escalation with the Houthis has raised concerns over the broader economic impact. Saudi Arabia’s real GDP is projected to contract by 3.6% in 2026, reflecting a combination of factors including lower oil activity.
The attacks have put events scheduled in Riyadh in October under pressure, including the kingdom’s flagship investment conference and the WPC Energy Congress, where several top oil executives were dropped from the programme. REUTERS

Fatal tank blast could pause Japan’s Type 10 orders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:49:21 UTC
01:49:21 KST

- Japan’s defense ministry is considering leaving the Type 10 tank out of its fiscal 2027 budget request after an April shell explosion killed three soldiers.
- Firing training with the Type 10 remains suspended until an accident investigation is completed; its findings have not been released.
Japan’s Ministry of Defense is considering leaving the Type 10 main battle tank out of its fiscal 2027 budget request, after a shell exploded inside one of the tanks in April and killed three soldiers, according to Japanese defense newspaper Asagumo.
Gen. Masayoshi Arai, chief of staff of the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force, disclosed the plan at a regular press conference on Sept. 15, the newspaper reported, adding that Arai will make the final call based on the findings of the accident investigation, which have not yet been released. The ministry has not said how many Type 10 tanks it had planned to request funding for, how much money is involved, or whether purchases would resume once the investigation is complete.
The accident happened at about 8:40 a.m. on April 21 at the Hijudai Training Area in Oita Prefecture on the southern island of Kyushu, when a 120 mm high-explosive anti-tank round detonated inside the turret of a Type 10 during a live-fire exercise. The blast killed the tank commander, the gunner and a safety officer riding in the tank, and seriously injured the driver. The tank normally carries a crew of three, but four soldiers were aboard because of the safety officer.
The Japan Ground Self-Defense Force halted all firing training with the Type 10, including blank rounds, the same day, and stopped live-fire training on the older Type 90 tank with the same type of ammunition. An accident investigation committee was set up at Western Army headquarters in Kumamoto, and Arai has said Type 10 firing will not resume until it finishes. Investigators have been examining radio logs, the vehicle and the ammunition, with Japanese media reporting that the electrical firing circuit that sets off the round is a key focus. In June, the Type 10 took part in the Fuji Firepower Review near Mount Fuji, Japan’s largest annual live-fire demonstration, but did not fire its main gun.
Built by Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, the Type 10 is Japan’s newest tank and entered service in 2012. It weighs about 44 metric tons (48.5 tons), lighter than the Type 90 so it can move more easily on Japan’s roads and bridges, and carries a 120 mm smoothbore gun fed by an autoloader that can fire NATO-standard ammunition. Explosions of a round inside a Japanese tank’s turret are extremely rare, and the last comparable case in Japan dates back to the late 1970s.
The Ministry of Defense submitted its fiscal 2027 budget request at the end of August, and Asagumo did not say whether the Type 10 was already left out of that document or whether the ministry is still weighing a later change.

The weapon shifting Yemen’s frontlines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:48:59 UTC
01:48:59 KST

The weapon shifting Yemen’s frontlines
By Ali Minabi
TEHRAN – While Yemeni missile attacks on Riyadh airport capture global headlines, another tactical weapon has shifted the frontlines near Bab al-Mandab.
Recent military developments on Yemen’s southwestern fronts have introduced a new and significant tactical shift in the course of the confrontation between Sanaa and Riyadh. This came after the Yemeni Armed Forces (YAF) announced that the Shawaz drone had entered operational service for the first time.
The drone was used to target Saudi-backed forces advancing from the direction of Lahij governorate toward the areas of Al-Wazi’iyah district (Taiz governorate) and Kahbub (strategic high ground), both adjacent to the international shipping lane at Bab al-Mandab.
Over the past week, the YAF’s War Media division has released footage documenting operations to repel and pursue Saudi-backed forces and their vehicles using this type of drone. The footage shows substantial losses among those fighters at their field positions, creating an obstacle to attempts to break through in this strategically vital sector.
The YAF has succeeded tactically in turning attempted breakthroughs into mobile killing zones that consume Saudi manpower and equipment. This type of weapon, the Shawaz drone, along with preemptive operations, may have played a decisive role in that success. As a tactical weapon, the Shawaz drone has transformed both the battlefield equation and the battle of competing narratives.
Characteristics and capabilities
Shawaz drones represent a model of low-cost, highly maneuverable tactical weaponry. They are remotely operated and provide live video feeds of the battlefield. Their significance extends beyond carrying out offensive strikes; they also provide real-time reconnaissance and intelligence on enemy deployments and the scale of their movements. This gives field commanders the ability to manage engagements according to the principle of proportionality while minimizing human losses along the front lines.
The footage released by the War Media division shows that Shawaz operations should not be dismissed as another set of battlefield images. By analyzing the footage, several functions of this tactical weapon can be identified.
Direct pursuit and attack
The Shawaz drone’s role is not limited to pursuing and targeting military vehicles, armored vehicles, fortified positions, and barricades. The footage has also demonstrated its ability to pursue individual personnel on the battlefield, as seen in the recent operations in Kahbub and Al-Wazi’iyah.
Dual offensive and intelligence-gathering
The Shawaz performs two military functions: offensive operations and intelligence-oriented reconnaissance. It enables the YAF to monitor enemy mobilizations, deployments, numbers, weapons, and other relevant details. This allows the Sanaa government to apply the principle of proportionality in accordance with the demands of the battlefield.
Remote observation and engagement
The drone provides the ability to observe and engage targets remotely, thereby reducing the potential human losses among YAF personnel in direct confrontations.
Psychological impact and the changing battlefield equation
Psychologically and perceptually, the documented footage has created an atmosphere of fear and deterrence among the YAF’s foes on the ground. Its effects have extended beyond the immediate battlefield, influencing the wider environment surrounding Saudi-backed forces.
These drones have established a new battlefield reality, forcing Riyadh’s forces to abandon their customary displays of strength through large military convoys and adopt dispersed positions and defensive concealment out of fear of this weapon.
Yet these measures have neither protected them nor prevented them from being targeted. This is evident in the footage of the Kahbub and Al-Wazi’iyah operations, in which Shawaz drones pursued individual personnel and military vehicles in multiple directions, while those targeted were gripped by fear and panic.
The recent footage of Shawaz drones and their operations also brings to mind the attack drones used by Hezbollah against the Israeli Occupation Forces (IOF) in southern Lebanon. Those drones became a source of terror and an enduring nightmare for the regime’s occupying troops. Their impact was not confined to those on the battlefield; their psychological effects extended to political and military decision-making circles, as well as field commanders.
There is little doubt that Yemeni drones exert a similar psychological impact on Saudi-backed forces operating on the Yemeni battlefield.
Battlefield implications and the battle of competing narratives
An examination of recent developments suggests that the latest offensive operations have inflicted substantial attrition on Saudi-backed forces between Lahij governorate and Bab al-Mandab. These operations have come alongside earlier missile and aerial strikes that inflicted extensive losses on Saudi forces, their vehicles, and their modern armored equipment, whether American-made or Saudi-made.
The footage recorded by Shawaz drones, together with material documented by Yemen’s War Media division, has made a significant difference in the media battle over competing narratives. The visual evidence, captured by both the Shawaz drones and War Media cameras, has refuted claims promoted by Saudi news outlets and some Arab television channels that Saudi-backed forces had “established full control over Bab al-Mandab” or were “advancing toward Al-Mokha.”
The Shawaz footage, by contrast, showed that these forces are suffering military attrition, including casualties and equipment losses, while operating under severe psychological pressure. It also showed these forces retreating rather than occupying positions from which they could launch an offensive and establish control.
In the battle of narratives and competing accounts, the YAF’s documented operations, filmed both from the air and on the ground, have demonstrated a consistency between the battlefield situation and the account presented to the public. When the YAF or military sources announce an operation or achievement and substantiate their claims with footage, their account becomes more convincing.
This visual documentation has played a central role in dismantling opposing media narratives and has reinforced the YAF’s claimed operational and psychological advantage in managing the battlefield.
The opposing side, by contrast, has gone beyond propaganda. It now lies more often on the falsification of facts and the construction of reality through crude, repetitive, and theatrical claims unsupported by any visual evidence.
This was evident last week when Saudi outlets claimed to have “secured control over Bab al-Mandab and advanced toward Al-Mokha.” Within hours, however, those claims, and those promoting them, had been discredited because they lacked elements of credibility, as well as tangible evidence from the battlefield.

2026 Elections: Man given deferred prosecution over post of fake Puma Shen photo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:45 UTC
01:42:45 KST

A man who admitted he reposted a defamatory image of Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) has been granted deferred prosecution for two years, on condition that he attends legal education classes, prosecutors said yesterday.
The man, surnamed Wu (吳), on June 7 reposted a fabricated image on Facebook, purporting to show Shen with a nude woman near a table littered with drug paraphernalia, the Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office said.
The image was first posted on X by a user named “Hsueh Ting-ting Returns” (薛丁丁歸來), whose Internet protocol address has been traced to China.
Photo: Chien Li-chung, Taipei Times
In Wu’s repost of the image, he wrote: “This photo looks like someone. Can anyone recognize who it is?”
He also drew attention to a nearby table, on which there was white powder and what appeared to be drug paraphernalia.
Under the image, Wu posted a genuine photograph of Shen speaking to reporters at the legislature, with the caption: “Does it look like him?”
Shen filed a complaint with the Ministry of Justice Investigation Bureau, saying the fabricated image was defamatory because it falsely implied that he frequented disreputable places, used drugs and engaged in sexual activity with unidentified women.
During the investigation, software tools such as Reality Defender, Resemble AI and Media Integrity AI were used to analyze the image, and confirmed it was fabricated, said the bureau, which referred the case to prosecutors for further investigation.
When questioned by investigators, Wu admitted that he had posted the image knowing that it was fake, and later issued a public apology to Shen, prosecutors said.
While Wu, who is in his 60s, had committed aggravated defamation, they granted him a two-year deferred prosecution, because he showed remorse and had no prior criminal record, prosecutors said.
Shen agreed with the decision, they said.
As part of the deferred prosecution arrangement, Wu must attend 10 sessions of legal education during the two-year period, prosecutors said.
Meanwhile, a separate investigation is being conducted into the creation of the fabricated image first posted by “Hsueh Ting-ting Returns,” they said.
Shen is challenging incumbent Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) in the local government elections scheduled for Nov. 28.

France’s Thales to build Japan base, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:41 UTC
01:42:41 KST

French defence contractor Thales will establish a maintenance and operational support base in Japan in what is seen as the first such move by a foreign firm in the country, a report said yesterday.
Thales chairman and CEO Patrice Caine told the Nikkei business daily that the base “will mark a milestone toward Thales’ long-term engagement in Japan.”
It is believed to be the first time a foreign defense company has established a dedicated base in Japan for the maintenance and operation of Japanese defense equipment, the Nikkei said.
Photo: Reuters
It added that Thales might also expand its Japan-based business to civilian use. The report comes as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi boosts defense spending in the face of China’s rapid military expansion and an unpredictable North Korea, moving away from the traditional pacifist stance that limited the use of force to self-defense.
Thales already supplies equipment to the Japanese Self-Defense Forces, the Nikkei said.

Taipower head wants power sector at the table in tech decisions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:41 UTC
01:42:41 KST

The electricity industry should be included in technology-sector decisionmaking as soon as possible, Taiwan Power Co (Taipower, 台電) chairman Tseng Wen-sheng (曾文生) said yesterday.
Energy would become increasingly important to the technology industry because computing power depends on electricity, Tseng told a news conference ahead of the Net-Zero Taiwan and Energy Taiwan exhibitions, which open tomorrow.
Electricity would also become a critical part of the semiconductor and technology industries’ supply chains, he said.
Photo: Lin Jing-hua, Taipei Times
As industrial power supply and demand patterns evolve, Taipower should play a greater role in industrial decisionmaking rather than simply providing electricity, Tseng said.
Parts of Taipower’s operations should take a more industry-oriented approach, enabling the company to better understand the technology sector’s operating models, business challenges, financial arrangements and supply chain partnerships, he said.
As businesses’ demand for renewable energy grows, electricity suppliers and consumers should jointly discuss energy procurement, the acquisition of renewable energy certificates and energy storage, Tseng said.
Because the industry sector changes rapidly, the time frame for electricity investment decisions has shortened from about 10 years to five years, or even three, he said.
Tseng said he hopes to hold more talks with the technology and renewable energy industries, as well as others, to discuss electricity market rules and ways to cooperate.
Taiwan’s electricity supply is sufficient and Tapower can meet the country’s industrial development needs, Tseng said.
He cited Taiwan’s global ranking in investment in natural gas-fired power generation, third in 2024 and sixth last year, as evidence of the rapid pace of investment in power generation.
However, he said that electricity demand from artificial intelligence applications could grow exponentially.
If companies build their own data centers or keep computing operations on-site to protect trade secrets, demand for computing power in Taiwan could also become more difficult to predict, he said.
Taipower is closely monitoring electricity distribution and the growth in demand for high-voltage power, Tseng said.
Meeting the rapidly growing demand for computing power would require not only enough electricity generation, but also a grid that can deliver power where and when it is needed, while coordinating with renewable energy sources and energy storage systems, he said.

NZ bank in free speech row over sheep memes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:38 UTC
01:42:38 KST

A bank in New Zealand has found itself at the center of an unlikely free speech row after an attempt to remove “explicit” memes about its sheep mascot from social media.
Kiwibank unveiled the mascot “Buck” this year in an ad campaign urging consumers to “bank Kiwi.”
However, the cute sheep with green wool quickly drew some unwanted attention online, with viral posts on social media alluding to Buck’s good looks — and uncharitable references to stereotypes about New Zealanders.
Photo: AFP
The state-owned bank responded by sending takedown requests, removing the image of Buck in the offending posts and leaving only the phrase: “this media has been disabled in response to a report by the copyright owner.”
Users responded by barraging the platform with dozens more in its place, and the original post has now garnered more than 4 million views.
A social media user said: “what if we ALL say the kiwibank sheep is sexy. They can’t get us all.”
Commentators described it as a classic example of the so-called “Streisand effect” — in which an attempt to hide something draws even greater attention to it.
Kiwibank spokesman Ben Mabon said the company had been responding to “explicit and harmful content being shared using Buck’s image.”
“Our concern was a serious one, and we believed it was important to address it,” he said in a statement. “We recognise that the response became part of a conversation. We felt doing nothing wasn’t the right thing to do because of the harmful content.”
In an open letter to Kiwibank, New Zealand’s Free Speech Union accused the company of censorship.
“Copyright protects creative work from being copied. It does not protect a brand from being laughed at, even by people who like it a bit too much,” the letter read. “Using copyright to remove speech a company dislikes is censorship, even when the subject is a sheep.”
New Zealand has long been known for having more sheep than people, with a ratio of 4.5 sheep to every person as of last year.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:42:38 UTC

The Philadelphia Eagles kicked a go-ahead field goal with 8 seconds left in London.
And they lost.
That is how things have been going for the Eagles these days.
Photo: AP
The Jaguars pulled off an improbable 19-17 victory on Cam Little’s 57-yard field goal as time expired at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Sunday.
The Eagles have lost three in a row and are 2-3 for the first time since 2021.
Jalen Hurts had led a late-game drive to set up Jake Elliott’s 48-yard field goal, giving the Eagles a 17-16 lead.
All they had to do was finish off the final 8 seconds, but the ensuing kickoff was kept inbounds and Ameer Abdullah returned it 53 yards, leaving 1 second on the clock.
Enough time for Little to send it through the uprights.
Eagles coach Nick Sirianni did not sugarcoat it.
“I didn’t make the right decision, and it cost us the game,” he said. “There’s no other way around it. There’s nothing really else to say about that. It’s just I didn’t do my job good enough in that situation.”
Sirianni fielded several questions about the fateful kickoff, owning the loss.
“There’s really nothing else to say. I didn’t make the decision — the right decision in that situation,” he said. “They returned it to where they returned it, and then they made a kick. You know, credit to them on that. Again, bad job by me.”
In some ways, Sunday’s game had seemed a tough task for the Eagles. They only arrived in London on Saturday and were undermanned.
They played without injured leading rusher Saquon Barkley and his backup, Tank Bigsby, who was placed on injured reserve this past week. They were missing wide receiver DeVonta Smith and had a patchwork offensive line after the retirement of Lane Johnson and the trade of Cam Jurgens.
The Eagles rushed for only 22 yards but Hurts kept them in contention by spreading the ball around to multiple receivers and converting on 6 of 15 third down attempts — a week after going 0 for 12 on third down.
Hurts completed 21 of 40 passes for 220 yards and one touchdown. His 62-yard touchdown pass to Darius Cooper gave Philly a 14-7 lead in the second quarter.
However, he missed open receivers.
“We didn’t perform well enough. I didn’t perform well enough, and that obviously starts with me,” Hurts said. “I’ll be thinking about all the different things that ultimately I could have done. I always use them as learning lessons, so I think that’s what’s great. We’ve got to learn from it.”

Man City defeat Liverpool amid future uncertainty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:42:37 UTC
01:42:37 KST

Manchester City survived a hostile reception at Anfield in their first match since a guilty verdict on widespread financial impropriety, but a 3-0 win over Liverpool highlighted the uncertainty that surrounds the Premier League season.
Enzo Maresca’s men are sitting pretty at the top of the table with six consecutive wins, including away victories at their two biggest rivals after also beating Manchester United last month.
Yet those points could count for nothing unless City successfully appeal the findings of an independent commission that found them guilty of more than 100 Premier League charges.
Photo: AP
No sanction has yet been decided. However, if City’s appeal fails, a severe points deduction that could lead to relegation or even expulsion from the English top-flight is on the table.
There is even the prospect of three Premier League titles City won between 2009 and 2018, the period to which the charges relate, being stripped.
For a league that frequently boasts of its huge global audience, the prospect of an appeal process dragging on for months, leaving a question mark over every City result and what it means for other Premier League clubs, is a damaging one.
“This is not good for the Premier League right now. That’s what I’ve just recognized today,” former Manchester United captain turned pundit Gary Neville told Sky Sports. “This is really bad for the Premier League and it’s going to continue for a few months.”
Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola said that “the uncertainty is not good for anyone”.
Defeat leaves the Reds nine points behind City, down in ninth in the table.
Even if Liverpool turn out to be not strong enough to challenge for the title, the three points lost on Sunday could be vital in the battle for a place in the Champions League.
Sanctions against City could have an impact on the battle for relegation.
“That today, what does it mean going forward?” Former Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher told Sky Sports. “This has to be done before the end of the season. There’s no way this can carry on to the end of the season because we’re all getting kidded.”
Liverpool feel scorned by the revelations of City’s wrongdoing more than most, having finished second to them three times in the past 12 years.
City’s rivals say that the illegal spending during that 2009-2018 period built the foundations for a golden era that continues to bear fruit.
Liverpool were toothless without the injured Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo on Sunday, forcing Andoni Iraola to give 21-year-old Lewis Koumas his Premier League debut up front.
By contrast, Maresca had the luxury of bringing Jeremy Doku off the bench early in the second half in a substitution that transformed the game.
Moments later the Belgian winger provoked a second yellow card for Ryan Gravenberch and Liverpool never recovered.
Doku had a hand in the first and third City goals, scored by Erling Haaland and Rayan Cherki, either side of his own sumptuous strike into the top corner.
That strength in depth has been fundamental in City’s rise to becoming the dominant force in English soccer since an Abu Dhabi-backed takeover in 2008.
As chants, banners, flags and scarves at Anfield showed, City stand accused of cheating their way to the top.
But the investigation has left the rest of the Premier League stuck in stasis, waiting for a case that began eight years ago to finally be over.

翻譯 Translation
Huahua: Lately, I’ve seen lots of friends sharing camping photos on Instagram. The beautiful starry sky and warm campfire make the whole scene look amazing.
Qingqing: Camping has become more and more popular in recent years, especially “glamping.” You don’t have to set up your own tent, so it’s great for beginners.
Huahua: Really? I’ve always thought camping was a lot of trouble. There’s nothing I hate more than a hassle.
Qingqing: These days, many campsites have beds and air conditioning, and some even have cafes.
Huahua: That doesn’t sound much different from staying at a hotel.
Qingqing: The best thing about camping is that you can get close to nature, and at night you can enjoy a sky full of stars.
Huahua: That sounds really appealing. I’d like to give it a try too.
Qingqing: Autumn weather is perfect for camping. Whether you want to camp in the mountains or on flat ground, campsites are in high demand. If you want to go there, you have to book early.

6. 吸引 (xīyǐn) attract; appeal to
7. 體驗 (tǐyàn) experience; try out
8. 搶手 (qiǎngshǒu) in high demand; highly sought-after
