Uncrewed truck with anti-drone laser shown at AUSA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:22:20 UTC
01:22:20 KST

- Harbinger’s uncrewed Praesidia hybrid truck is powering an AeroVironment LOCUST X3 30-kW counter-drone laser at American Rheinmetall’s AUSA 2026 booth.
- The companies have not said whether the laser-armed configuration is tied to any U.S. Army contract or test.
An uncrewed hybrid truck built by California’s Harbinger is powering a 30-kilowatt AeroVironment counter-drone laser at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington this week, shown at American Rheinmetall’s booth.
Harbinger CEO John Henry Harris said in a LinkedIn post on Oct. 12 that the company’s Praesidia vehicle is supplying power to an AeroVironment LOCUST X3 laser weapon mounted on the truck, with autonomy software from Forterra.
The display is at Rheinmetall’s booth, No. 2285. Harris pitched the combination as cheap, mass-producible equipment with “unlimited magazine depth,” a reference to the fact that a laser keeps firing as long as it has electrical power rather than running out of missiles or rounds. He did not say whether the system has been tested together in the field, whether any U.S. Army unit plans to use it, or what it would cost.
The Praesidia is a militarized version of the plug-in hybrid chassis Harbinger builds for commercial delivery trucks. It has no cab, is driven by wire so autonomy kits can control steering, braking and acceleration, and combines a large battery pack with a gasoline engine that acts as a generator. Harbinger says the vehicle can travel more than 800 km (500 miles) on a full tank and full battery, or about 170 km (105 miles) on electric power alone, and can export up to 350 kW of power to equipment it carries. That power is what a laser weapon needs: a high-energy laser draws electricity continuously while firing, and the vehicle carrying it has to supply it.
AeroVironment’s LOCUST laser family came from BlueHalo, which AeroVironment acquired in 2025. The U.S. Army has tested earlier LOCUST lasers mounted on Joint Light Tactical Vehicles as part of its effort to shoot down small drones without spending missiles. AeroVironment has not published detailed specifications for the X3 version beyond the 30 kW power level Harris cited.
The truck at AUSA comes from a program already under contract. In August, the U.S. Army gave American Rheinmetall an 18-month deal to build autonomous supply vehicles under Project Sustainment, using Harbinger’s chassis, Forterra’s autonomy software and Primordial Labs’ Anura control interface. Those vehicles are meant to haul supplies to company-sized units without a driver. Harbinger has also said it is configuring the Praesidia for battlefield communications, troop transport, perimeter security and counter-drone missions, and the CIA-backed venture firm In-Q-Tel invested in the company in June.

Greenland lawmakers signal support for Trump security deal
COPENHAGEN, Oct 12 - A majority of Greenlandic lawmakers signalled support for the Arctic island's recent security agreement with US President Donald Trump in a debate on Monday, although some opposition party members questioned the deal's economic value.
The United States, Denmark and Greenland last month signed the agreement, aimed at ending tensions after Trump's repeated threats to take control of the strategically located and mineral-rich island.
The agreement is subject to a second reading in parliament before being put to a vote, with lawmakers expected to pass the legislation.
The deal expands the US military's role in Greenland, paving the way for two new military bases and Trump's "Golden Dome" missile defence system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination.
The chair of opposition party Naleraq, Pele Broberg, said many details still remained unclear on how the agreement would work in practice.
"The US is granted extensive rights in our country. The people of Greenland are not guaranteed any fixed payment for those rights," Broberg said in the parliamentary debate in Greenland's capital Nuuk.
The government parties, which have a majority of seats, defended the deal.
Former Foreign Minister Vivian Motzfeldt of the governing coalition's Demokraatit said Greenland had secured "massive" protection without having to pay for it, while winning recognition as an autonomous nation.
Foreign Minister Mute Egede said the deal was "a huge step forward" that could not be measured in terms of money.
Erik Jensen, chair of the Siumut party, said his party backed the deal.
"For several years, Siumut has been campaigning to ensure that agreements concerning Greenland are no longer concluded without Greenlandic participation... That is why we are satisfied," Jensen said. REUTERS

A view of Ramlila Maidan, designated as a protest site along with two new venues,. (PTI photo)
NEW DELHI: Ramlila Maidan, newly designated as one of the capital's three protest sites, is already booked for most of the next two-and-a-half months, leaving just three days available for reservations this year.Additionally, while a small section of the ground can be used for protests free of charge, booking the larger venue, which spans 12 acres and can accommodate up to 50,000 people, involves a daily fee and a refundable security deposit.
Revealing that only December 29, 30 and 31 as the availiable dates, an official quoted by PTI said, "The booking rate for the ground is Rs 50,000 per day, plus a Rs 55,000 security deposit that is refundable. The initial outlay including taxes comes to Rs 1.21 lakh for a day's booking."However, officials clarified that a small portion of the ground, with space for around 150 people, remains available for protests and gatherings free of charge.Permission to use the larger ground must be obtained from the Municipal Corporation of Delhi's horticulture department, which processes bookings after applicants secure a no-objection certificate from Delhi Police.
The arrangement has drawn criticism from opposition leaders and protesters, who argue that the limited availability and high booking costs could make demonstrations difficult to organise.AAP Delhi president Saurabh Bharadwaj questioned the decision, pointing to events already scheduled at the venue. Govt. played another fraud with its citizens. The Ramleela Maidan is occupied with two Ramleelas," Bharadwaj wrote on X."How can one hold a protest here? Do they want to create chaos?" he asked.Protesters also highlighted the financial burden, noting that demonstrations at Jantar Mantar did not require comparable payments.Civic officials, however, pointed to the revenue implications of allowing unrestricted use of the ground. "If given up for protest without any fees, the civic body will stand to lose at least Rs 50,000 plus per day," an official said, quoted by PTI.The ground is frequently reserved for public events and religious festivities, particularly around Dussehra and Diwali, contributing to the shortage of available dates.Apart from booking constraints, the venue presents traffic-management challenges. Located in a busy commercial area near three hospitals and municipal offices, Ramlila Maidan has witnessed major congestion during political rallies and other large gatherings.Officials said police often have to introduce one-way traffic restrictions on Asaf Ali Road and divert vehicles towards Jawaharlal Nehru Marg. A BJP rally in 2014 reportedly caused traffic jams extending nearly four kilometres to ITO, despite being held on a Sunday.
The venue has been central to Delhi's political history for decades. Once a pond, the site was filled and levelled around 1930 to accommodate Ramlila performances, which began there in 1932. It subsequently hosted major political gatherings addressed by leaders including Jawaharlal Nehru, Indira Gandhi, Jayaprakash Narayan and Atal Bihari Vajpayee.On June 25, 1975, the day the Emergency was declared, Jayaprakash Narayan and Vajpayee addressed a rally at the ground. Relatively recently, Arvind Kejriwal took oath as Delhi chief minister there in 2013.The controversy follows an standing order issued by Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar, which removed Jantar Mantar from the list of designated protest venues and identified Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and CBD Ground in East Delhi as the three new locations for demonstrations. Police said a detailed, revised standard operating procedure for protests at these sites would be issued separately.

AEVEX is showing a full-size model of Specter, its new jet-powered one-way attack drone, at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington this week, along with a maritime drone line built from its recent purchase of BlackSea Technologies.
The California-based company announced Specter on Sept. 23 as a high-speed, turbojet-powered autonomous strike platform under development with Divergent Technologies, a Los Angeles company that builds structures through additive manufacturing. AEVEX says Specter will come in ground-launched and air-launched versions and has a swappable nose section that can carry explosive warheads, electronic warfare equipment or surveillance sensors without redesigning the airframe.
The drone uses AEVEX’s CompassX autonomy software, which the company says is built to keep working when GPS and communications are jammed. AEVEX has not released Specter’s speed, range, size, payload weight, price or flight test schedule, and has not named a customer.
Divergent’s role is to make the drone easier to build in large numbers. Its DAPS production system designs and prints complex structural parts digitally, which AEVEX says lets it change the design quickly and plan for high-rate production from the start of engineering. The model at AUSA is the first time the company has shown Specter at full size.
AEVEX is best known for the Phoenix Ghost loitering munition, which the United States sent to Ukraine starting in 2022, and for larger Group 3 drones such as Disruptor. The company went public on the New York Stock Exchange this year. It also buys rocket-assisted takeoff motors for its drones from X-Bow Systems, which has delivered hundreds of them under a $12 million contract.
The company used AUSA to introduce AEVEX Maritime Systems, a new unit formed after it acquired BlackSea Technologies, a Baltimore-area maker of uncrewed surface and underwater vessels that supplies the U.S. Navy and other U.S. forces. The acquisition was valued at about $650 million. AEVEX says its portfolio now covers air, surface and subsurface drones, aimed at an army expecting to fight with jammed navigation, cut communications and supply lines under attack.

Musk has spent $366 million to help Republicans retain control of Congress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:10:32 UTC
01:10:32 KST

Inside Elon Musk’s US$276 million US midterm rescue mission for Republicans
Theodore Schleifer
NEW YORK - Elon Musk has quietly funnelled more than US$276 million (S$353 million) into Republican groups and his super political action committee since the start of July, building a huge turnout operation to help the party battle headwinds in the midterm elections.
The staggering amount of money makes Musk, the richest person in the world, by far the largest known donor in the midterms. Representatives for Musk supplied the previously unreported figures on his political giving to The New York Times before a federal filing deadline on Oct 8.
In an effort to save Republicans’ Senate majority, Musk gave a total of US$158 million this summer to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing the party’s candidates for the chamber, according to his team.
In sum, that is one of the largest political donations in American history, and more than the group’s Democratic rival raised from all of its donors that quarter.
Musk has also built a major Republican turnout operation through a super PAC he founded in 2024, America PAC. He donated over US$76 million this summer to the group, which in turn spent that much on building a sprawling canvassing programme to try to turn out hard-to-reach Republican voters.
The group is active in seven Senate battlegrounds and nearly three dozen House races.
Musk has already given far more money, about US$366 million, to federal committees during the 2025-26 election cycle than he did during the 2024 election, when he laid out roughly US$290 million to help return President Donald Trump and Republicans to power.
He has given even more in undisclosed donations during both elections, according to people briefed on the giving.
The latest torrent of spending has helped give the Republican Party a financial advantage in the midterms, as well-funded outside groups like Trump’s powerful super PAC flood the airwaves with advertising in the final weeks.
No Democratic billionaire is spending nearly as much as Musk, and money remains a central worry for the party in an otherwise favourable political environment.
The donations also clear up the mystery of how much staying power Musk wants to have in American politics.
“In terms of political spending, I’m going to do a lot less in the future,” he said in May 2025.
Musk, who oversees a vast business empire that has benefited from enormous federal contracts, is famously unpredictable and often jumps from one project to another.
He has been far quieter about his political work since his dramatic blowup with Trump last year.
After months of wielding vast influence inside the White House and overseeing Trump’s government cost-cutting project, he raged against the president’s major domestic policy Bill and floated threats to start a third party.
But the two men have warmed back up, appearing together at three events in the last two weeks and praising each other.
Now Musk has donated more than a quarter-billion dollars to help Trump and Republicans in the midterms. The money signals his commitment to the right and sets him up as a potential player in the 2028 presidential election, when his super PAC says it intends to remain active – the first time it has confirmed such plans.
Beyond Musk’s donations to his super PAC and the Senate Leadership Fund, his representatives said that from July through September, he had given smaller but still substantial amounts to other conservative groups:
- US$20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the main super PAC for House Republicans
- US$10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, a group supporting Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee for Senate in Texas
- US$10 million to the Republican Governors Association
- US$2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association
“If Democrats take control of Washington and win key gubernatorial and attorney general races this November, then America risks becoming a socialist, woke and borderless country,” said Andrew Romeo, a spokesperson for America PAC.
“These robust investments have allowed the GOP apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history.”
Pushing for Paxton
On voters’ doors across Texas, the campaign literature carries a stark warning: “Radical Democrat socialists are winning elections all across America. Could Texas be next?”
The hanging door cards are the work of Musk’s voter-turnout operation, which deployed nearly 3,000 paid canvassers last week around the country, according to America PAC officials.
The group has devoted most of its more than US$76 million in midterm spending so far to this canvassing programme, shelling out smaller amounts on advertising, mail, phone calls and text messages. Much of the messaging targets Democrats, sometimes in misleading or overheated ways.
This spring, Trump’s political advisers asked Musk to reprise America PAC’s 2024 field programme, a person familiar with the conversation said. Despite the challenging environment for Republicans, some party strategists believe that a field programme can make the difference in particularly tight races.
America PAC relies on a few voter-canvassing firms that compete aggressively with one another for work and for staffing, according to people briefed on the operation.
Turnover in the canvassing industry is high. One canvasser who worked for America PAC told the Times that he was paid between US$1.50 and US$3.00 for each door he knocked on across Texas in the heat. America PAC says it has knocked on about 6.5 million doors across the country so far.
Musk and his operation, people close to them say, have been particularly focused on the Texas Senate race.
The group has unloaded over a third of its disclosed spending in that expensive race, more than in any other. It is uncommon to run an extensive field campaign in large states like Texas, where television ads are more often used to reach voters.
Musk, a resident of Austin, has extensive business interests and property holdings in Texas. Paxton, the state attorney-general, has investigated Musk’s opponents, including Media Matters, a liberal group.
Musk’s US$10 million donation to Paxton’s super PAC came at a critical time, when the Republican candidate was being badly outspent.
And Musk’s US$158 million in donations to the Senate Leadership Fund, the most the super PAC has ever received from a single donor in a quarter, may have made it possible for that group to suddenly spend big for Paxton after months of reluctance.
That is because Musk’s donations preceded the decision in late August by the super PAC, led by allies of Senator John Thune of South Dakota, the majority leader, to start what has become a US$149 million pro-Paxton ad campaign.
A focus on transgender issues
As it did in 2024, Musk’s operation is focused not on persuading swing voters, but on registering and turning out voters with conservative beliefs – especially “low-propensity” ones who are less likely to cast a ballot.
This is a lot harder for Republicans in a midterm election, without Trump at the top of the ballot.
To do it, Musk’s super PAC is leaning hard into the culture wars, especially transgender issues. (Musk’s daughter, who is transgender, has spoken about their clashes over her identity, and he has suggested that this led to his increased political engagement.)
At voters’ doors in Texas, canvassers are told to target Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic candidate for governor, over her record on transgender issues, according to parts of a script reviewed by the Times.
Similarly, the Musk operation is leaving literature on doors that claims that James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas, has a “radical trans agenda.” And America PAC’s top ad in the state, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact, denounces Talarico over his past comments suggesting that “God is nonbinary.”
The Musk group is also targeting other Democratic Senate candidates over transgender issues, including Josh Turek, the party’s nominee in Iowa. Nationally, one of the super PAC’s most visible ads on Facebook features a man in makeup and reads: “He made his plan to vote. Did you? Don’t stay home while crazies elect radicals.”
The group is running ads and sending mail on a broad range of topics, but socialism is a core theme.
The Musk super PAC regularly attacks Democrats as socialist and ties them to figures such as New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, according to 48 pieces of direct mail shared by Mintt, a mail-tracking firm.
Online, it is even running personalised messaging that invokes a voter’s first name. For example, in a video showing smiling Democrats: “Why are they smiling? Because Christopher hasn’t made a plan to vote yet.”
Much of this outreach points voters to an America PAC website where conservatives can learn how to register to vote. The super PAC is pushing what it calls an “America Pass,” a digital card on Apple or Google wallets on voters’ phones that lists their registration information, along with election dates and deadlines in their home state.
A big spender with a backseat role
While Musk is spending big again and using some tactics that are similar to those he deployed two years ago, this is not 2024 anymore.
He is in a different place politically. While he and Trump appear to be on good terms again – “our modern-day Thomas Edison,” the president called him on Oct 8 – Musk is taking a hands-off approach this election and does not appear as personally passionate.
He has not brought up the midterm elections or the Trump presidency much in private conversations with friends, according to people who have spoken to him in recent months.
He is focused on his businesses, these people say, and he and his business lieutenants have taken a less active role in America PAC’s operations, entrusting major decisions to Chris Young, his top adviser.
And on the social platform X, a semi-reliable indicator of where the billionaire’s mind is, Musk has written just seven direct posts in 2026 about candidates in competitive midterm races, according to a Times review, a far cry from his relentless calls throughout 2024 to elect Trump.
Five of those posts focused on Talarico – and one appeared critical of Senator Susan Collins, a vulnerable Republican in Maine.
Gone, too, are Musk’s barnstorming campaign stops, such as the ones he did in Pennsylvania in October 2024 or a Wisconsin judicial election in the spring of 2025.
There are no more sweepstakes where he personally hands an oversize check of US$1 million to those who register voters or sign a petition, a gambit that drew legal challenges.
Musk has not evidently grown infatuated with candidates this time around, as he did with Trump.
The closest he came was a US$10 million donation for a long-shot Republican running for the US Senate in Kentucky – an investment that went poorly.
The US$276 million figure is, of course, just what is publicly known. Musk has also made some seven-figure donations to support midterm candidates through groups that are not required to disclose their donors, according to a person with knowledge of the matter. NYTIMES

Lockheed unveils longer-range Patriot missile, PAC-3 Edge

- Lockheed Martin unveiled PAC-3 Edge, a longer-range, higher-altitude Patriot interceptor, as its entry in the U.S. Army’s Future Interceptor competition.
- Lockheed says the U.S. Army advanced it to the next stage and it is working toward an early operational capability by 2031.
Lockheed Martin has unveiled PAC-3 Edge, a new Patriot interceptor designed to reach higher, fly farther and maneuver harder than the PAC-3 MSE now in service. It is the company’s entry in the U.S. Army’s Future Interceptor competition.
The company debuted the missile on Oct. 12 at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington. Lockheed says the U.S. Army has moved it into the next stage of the competition and that it is working toward what the service calls a residual operational capability by 2031, meaning a small number of missiles ready for emergency use before full fielding. The company did not release range, altitude, speed or cost figures, and did not name the other competitors.
PAC-3 Edge builds on the PAC-3 MSE, the hit-to-kill missile that destroys targets by striking them directly and has been used heavily against Russian missiles in Ukraine and Iranian missiles in the Middle East. Lockheed says the new version adds a new seeker, an upgraded propulsion system and improved flight controls. The seeker was designed by the company’s Strigo Product Center, which Lockheed says it funded with $250 million of its own money.
The company says the missile is meant to counter a wide range of aircraft, missiles and hypersonic weapons at higher altitudes and longer ranges than current Patriot interceptors. In the U.S. Army’s layered missile defense, it would sit between the PAC-3 MSE and the THAAD system, which intercepts ballistic missiles at much higher altitudes.
The U.S. Army has tried before to field a next-generation Patriot interceptor. It ran a Lower-Tier Future Interceptor competition between Lockheed and Raytheon, then announced in 2024 that it would cancel the effort before reviving the idea as the Future Interceptor program. The U.S. Army has not published the program’s budget, the number of missiles it plans to buy or when it will pick a winner.
PAC-3 Edge becomes the fourth missile in Lockheed’s Patriot family, alongside the older PAC-3 CRI, the PAC-3 MSE and the lower-cost PAC-3 ACE the company announced in July for European customers.

General Dynamics shows Wolf XM30 at AUSA 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:05:38 UTC
01:05:38 KST

- General Dynamics Land Systems displayed only a one-eighth-scale model of its Wolf XM30 at AUSA 2026, while its prototype undergoes U.S. Army testing.
- The U.S. Army expects to choose between the Wolf and American Rheinmetall’s Lynx in 2027 to replace the M2 Bradley.
General Dynamics Land Systems has brought its Wolf XM30 infantry fighting vehicle to the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, but only as a one-eighth-scale model, leaving the full-size vehicle out of public view while it undergoes U.S. Army testing.
The company is offering the Wolf as a replacement for the M2 Bradley Fighting Vehicle in the U.S. Army’s XM30 Mechanized Infantry Combat Vehicle competition.
In a social media post on Oct. 12, General Dynamics said the vehicle was designed from the start around the U.S. Army’s Modular Open Systems Approach, which uses common hardware and software interfaces so new sensors, weapons and electronics can be added without redesigning the vehicle. The company also said the Wolf was “born digital,” meaning its digital engineering model is used in testing, production and maintenance as well as design. It did not release new specifications, photos of the full-size vehicle or any test results.
General Dynamics delivered its first Wolf prototype to the U.S. Army at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, on Aug. 21. The only public photo since then has shown the vehicle wrapped in a black tarp on a flatbed trailer. The company has said seven more prototypes will go to the 1st Armored Brigade Combat Team, 1st Cavalry Division, at Fort Hood, Texas, where soldiers will put them through field trials. The Wolf is based on the company’s Griffin III demonstrator, itself derived from the ASCOD 2 infantry fighting vehicle, and its team includes GM Defense, AeroVironment and General Dynamics Mission Systems.
The other finalist, American Rheinmetall, is not showing its Lynx XM30 at AUSA at all. The company said its prototypes have gone straight to the U.S. Army for soldier evaluation. American Rheinmetall delivered the first of eight Lynx prototypes days after General Dynamics’ delivery in August.
The U.S. Army’s requirements for the XM30 call for an uncrewed turret armed with the XM913 50 mm cannon, a hybrid-electric drivetrain and room for six dismounted infantry soldiers. The vehicle would carry infantry squads and cavalry scouts into combat and support them with fire once they dismount, the same job the Bradley has done since the early 1980s.
The U.S. Army picked General Dynamics and American Rheinmetall as finalists in June 2023, with the design and prototype phase valued at about $1.6 billion between them. The U.S. Army expects to choose a winner in 2027, and its budget plans call for buying 108 vehicles by fiscal 2031 ahead of larger production later.

Scientists uncover a possible trade-off in how the hippocampus replays new memories
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:00:43 UTC
01:00:43 KST

When the brain rests after learning something new, it actively replays the recent experience to lock it into memory. A recent small study published in the Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience reveals that this mental replay involves a trade-off, where the brain prioritizes the general meaning of an event while weakening the memory of specific details. These biological adjustments suggest that false memories are a natural byproduct of how the mind extracts useful themes from the world.
Memory involves balancing two competing tasks. The brain must hold onto the specific details of a single event, but it also needs to find patterns across multiple events to predict what might happen in the future. If a person only remembers exact details, they might struggle to apply lessons from the past to new situations.
In traditional models of brain function, the hippocampus acts as a fast-acting recorder for new experiences. Over days and weeks, it slowly teaches these memories to the neocortex, the outer layer of the brain, which extracts statistical rules and overarching concepts. However, recent computational models suggest that this division of labor might also exist entirely within the hippocampus itself.
If the hippocampus manages both rapid recording and slow generalization, it must have a mechanism to edit memories shortly after they form. The biological principle of competitive plasticity suggests a possible method. When a person learns related concepts, the neural pathways sharing common features activate together and become stronger. Unique, isolated details that do not reactivate as often are competitively weakened.
To understand how the brain handles this balance, researchers Nicholas C. Hindy, Ryan Coleman, and Surya Rajan Meenakshi Selvam focused on specific sub-regions of the hippocampus. After a person experiences something, the hippocampus spontaneously reactivates the neural patterns associated with that event. The research team wanted to see if this reactivation process transforms a memory rather than just making a perfect copy of it.
They specifically looked at a sub-region called CA1. This area acts as a primary output hub, sending information to other parts of the brain. The structural position of CA1 allows it to resolve competition between specific episodic details and broader generalizations.
The experimental design aimed to see this competitive editing in action. The researchers conducted a small study with 24 adult participants using a classic psychological test known for reliably producing false memories. Participants heard word lists designed around a missing target concept. For example, a list might include the words bed, rest, and awake, but leave out the central theme word, sleep.
The words were read aloud by artificial voices, splitting the incoming information into two distinct channels. The semantic channel was the meaning of the words and their shared theme. The episodic channel was the specific sensory experience of hearing a male or female voice.
The research team used high-resolution functional magnetic resonance imaging to scan the participants. Standard brain scans often blur the tiny sub-regions of the hippocampus together. By using high-resolution techniques, the team could isolate the CA1 area, as well as neighboring regions known as CA3 and the dentate gyrus.
After listening to the words, participants spent 90 seconds performing a simple math task. This kept them distracted but allowed their brains to rest from active memorization. During this short rest period, the researchers used the brain scans to measure how often the hippocampus spontaneously replayed the neural patterns associated with the word lists.
Finally, the participants completed a memory test while still inside the brain scanner. They had to indicate whether they recognized words from the lists, and whether they falsely recognized lure words that fit the theme but were never actually played. They also had to recall which voice spoke the recognized words.
The researchers found that spontaneous brain reactivation during the rest period had opposing effects on the two types of memory. When the CA1 region replayed a memory more frequently, participants were more likely to confidently claim they had heard the lure words. At the same time, this increased reactivation predicted worse accuracy when participants tried to remember whether a male or female voice spoke a specific word.
This means the mental replay strengthened the overarching concept of the word list but weakened the memory of the exact sensory experience. The memory of the actual words that had been played remained unchanged by the reactivation process. The effect only influenced the broad themes and the specific voice details.
While the CA1 region showed the strongest evidence for a bidirectional trade-off, the other sub-regions displayed specialized roles. Reactivation in the CA3 area was linked exclusively to a higher rate of false memories for the overarching themes. Neuroscientists believe CA3 helps with pattern completion, a process where the brain rebuilds a full memory from a partial cue, which may naturally strengthen the broader concept.
Conversely, activity in the dentate gyrus was linked only to worse memory for the specific voices. The dentate gyrus is typically associated with pattern separation, the ability to tell similar experiences apart. When this region is forced to process overlapping themes, its ability to hold onto precise episodic details might be compromised.
The research team also noticed a spatial pattern along the length of the hippocampus. The front and middle sections of the structure were primarily linked to extracting general themes and falsely recognizing the related lure words. The rear section of the hippocampus was linked to the loss of specific source details, such as the voice of the speaker.
The study relies on correlational data, meaning the results show a relationship between brain activity and memory performance but cannot prove that the reactivation directly caused the memory changes. People might have processed the words differently while listening, which could influence both the brain replay and the later memory errors. The rest period was also very short, only capturing the earliest moments of memory formation.
The brain scans tracked activity linked to entire word lists rather than individual words. The researchers could not separate the replay of a single word from the general activity of the whole list. Future research will need to separate individual events with greater precision and track memories over longer periods to see how these trade-offs evolve.
The study, “Hippocampal Reactivation Trades Episodic Detail for Semantic Gist in Human Memory,” was authored by Nicholas C. Hindy, Ryan Coleman, and Surya Rajan Meenakshi Selvam.

Defence Readiness Bill to give government reserve powers
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
17:00:36 BST
01:00:36 KST

Legislation being developed to give ministers powers in reserve for escalation towards war will cover the Defence Nuclear Enterprise, and the government has committed to bring it forward within this Parliament, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what progress had been made on recommendation 33 of the 2025 Strategic Defence Review, which covers legislative reform that could direct industry to prioritise defence nuclear requirements in the sovereign supply chain, or enable compulsory acquisition of assets where necessary to protect national security.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State at the Ministry of Defence, said: “The Government has accepted the SDR recommendation to develop a ‘Defence Readiness Bill’ to ensure ‘the Government has powers in reserve to respond effectively in the event of escalation towards a war involving the UK or its allies’. Defence is working closely with the rest of government to develop detailed policy requirements, including for the Defence Nuclear Enterprise, and to establish what new legislation is required as part of the Government’s wider Home Defence programme.
“Defence Readiness legislation is being developed to ensure the Government has the powers it needs to keep the UK safe, both now and in times of heightened crisis or escalation towards war.”
The minister listed the measures under development as improving the ability to defend against sub-threshold threats; increasing industry preparedness, agility and resilience; expanding the supply of privately owned services to defence and access to and protection of critical national infrastructure; and strengthening the mobilisation of defence’s people, including the Reserves and civil servants.
Mr Pollard added: “The Government has committed to deliver this legislation within this Parliament. As is standard with the legislative process, any future legislation will be brought forward when parliamentary time allows.”
The answer does not say whether the powers to direct industry or compulsorily acquire assets that Mr Obese-Jecty asked about will appear in the Bill, and no date was given for its introduction.
A second question from the same member asked about progress on recommendation 30, which seeks to strengthen NATO and British led training and exercises addressing escalation and conflict scenarios with nuclear-armed states.
Louise Sandher-Jones, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “The Government is implementing the recommendations of the Strategic Defence Review 2025, including Recommendation 30, which seeks to strengthen coherence between the conventional and nuclear elements of NATO’s deterrence and defence posture.
“The Ministry of Defence continues to strengthen UK and NATO-led training and exercises through a programme of national and multinational activity that improves readiness, interoperability and the ability of Allied forces to operate across the full spectrum of conflict. This includes participation in NATO’s exercise programme, including the Alliance’s flagship STEADFAST exercise series, which tests collective defence plans and strengthens Allied deterrence and defence.
“Through these activities, we are working closely with Allies to ensure NATO is better prepared to deter, defend against and, if necessary, respond to threats from capable and nuclear-armed adversaries.”
The latest instalment of that series, the annual nuclear deterrence exercise Steadfast Noon, begins in Italy on Tuesday with seventeen nations taking part.

Scarred blood vessels may be one clue to APOE4’s Alzheimer’s risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

Scarred blood vessels may be one clue to APOE4’s Alzheimer’s risk
The gene variant may alter cells that support the brain’s blood vessels
The gene APOE4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease. But it’s still something of a mystery to researchers.
Now, new work suggests one way the gene variant does its dirty work. It influences the production of scar tissue throughout vital vascular connections carrying blood to and from the brain, researchers report September 24 in Cell. This process may also contribute to the buildup of the protein amyloid-beta, which is thought to be one of the first signs of Alzheimer’s disease in the brain.
APOE4 is an allele, one of three slightly different, common forms of the APOE gene, which makes a protein that helps carry fats in the bloodstream. The variant is common among people who have Alzheimer’s disease. “If you had a room of 10 people with Alzheimer’s disease, and you asked how many of those people have the APOE4 allele, six of them would,” says neuroscientist Joel Blanchard of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City. Yet many people who carry APOE4 never develop the dementia-causing disease, leaving researchers trying to understand what the gene variant actually does to make the brain more vulnerable.
One clue came from people who seemed unusually resilient to that risk. In 2024, researchers examined more than 3,500 people, including some who carried two copies of APOE4 but had not developed Alzheimer’s. Genetic analysis showed that they had a mutation in their DNA that meant their blood vessels had far lower levels of a protein called fibronectin, a kind of cellular superglue that assists wound healing. The reserachers suggested that too much fibronectin could make it harder for the brain to clear amyloid-beta from the brain. A buildup of those plaques is a hallmark of the disease.
That result pushed Blanchard and his colleagues to look more closely at blood vessels. “The prevailing thought in the field is basically that the Alzheimer’s disease is so bad that the blood vessels break down,” Blanchard says. ”But we wanted to ask the question: Is it the other way around?”
Blanchard and his colleagues built an atlas that mapped gene expression — how DNA is read and converted into proteins — across the human brain vasculature at a cellular level. Stitching together data from three existing brainwide maps, their atlas represented 66,000 cells from 220 people. They team examined how this map differed in people with two copies of APOE4 compared with those with less harmful gene variants.
APOE4 carriers had fewer pericytes, starfish-shaped cells that wrap around and stabilize blood vessels. They also had higher numbers of myofibroblasts, cells normally formed during tissue injury that pump out fibronectin, the team found.
The map offered a snapshot, but it couldn’t show whether the missing pericytes were actually transforming into myofibroblasts. The researchers turned to 3-D models of human brain tissue grown from stem cells. In models carrying two copies of APOE4, pericytes began taking on the characteristics of scar-producing myofibroblasts. The transformation also offered a possible explanation for the earlier clue from resilient APOE4 carriers: Myofibroblasts produce large amounts of fibronectin. And when the researchers prevented cells in their models from producing fibronectin, amyloid accumulation dropped.
The researchers also found a possible trigger for the cellular switch. In the APOE4 models, signaling through the immune molecule TGF-beta helped drive pericytes toward the scar-producing state. Blocking that signaling in cell models and aged mice restored the proportion of blood vessels wrapped up by pericytes.
The TGF-beta data are “particularly interesting,” because inhibiting the protein reversed some of APOE4’s effects on pericytes, says Abdel Ali Belaidi, a neuroscientist at the Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health in Parkville, Australia. But TGF-beta performs many jobs throughout the body, he says, making it a difficult molecule to target safely with a drug.
And damage to the brain’s blood vessels is only one of the many ways APOE4 has been linked to Alzheimer’s. Other studies have shown that the gene variant alters inflammation and interacts with another Alzheimer’s-linked protein, tau. How all these changes lock together to link APOE4 so strongly to Alzheimer’s disease is a greater mystery than one study can solve. ”As a field, we’re all progressing toward an answer,” Blanchard says.

Pakistan: Declaration of emergency must not be pretext to crackdown on human rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:53:34 UTC
00:53:34 KST

Responding to the declaration of a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, as well as the imposition of governor rule and the deployment of armed forces in the province, Babu Ram Pant, Amnesty International’s Deputy Director for South Asia, said:
“Reports of arbitrary detentions of key leaders – including the provincial chief minister – and internet disruptions across the province raise concerns about the proportionality of these emergency measures. While states may, in strictly limited circumstances, derogate from their human rights obligations to respond to a public emergency that threatens the existence of the nation, emergency measures are not a blank cheque to crack down on human rights, silence dissent, or concentrate power.
“Given the history of enforced disappearances and extrajudicial executions in counterterrorism operations by the armed forces, the deployment of the army further militarizes the province and could create conditions for unlawful use of force. Pakistani authorities must avoid using military personnel for ordinary policing tasks and ensure that military forces remain accountable and comply with international human rights law and standards.
Emergency measures are not a blank cheque to crack down on human rights, silence dissent, or concentrate power
Babu Ram Pant, Amnesty International’s Deputy Director for South Asia
“At this critical juncture, the federal authorities must ensure independent oversight of all actions taken under the emergency framework, and guarantee that any emergency measure is strictly necessary and proportionate to the situation.”
Background
President Asif Ali Zardari approved recommendations by the federal cabinet to impose a state of emergency and governor rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province under Articles 232 and 234 of Pakistan’s constitution respectively, citing an “unprecedented level of violent intensity of terrorist attacks” and a “breakdown of constitutional machinery” in the province on 11 October. A state of emergency allows the federal legislature (national assembly and senate) to pass laws regarding the province and allows the federal government to suspend fundamental rights such as the freedoms of assembly, association and expression.
The notification by the president stated that the powers of the provincial assembly will be exercised by the federal parliament and it was stated that the chief minister along with the provincial ministers, advisors, special assistants and advocate general would cease to hold office. Separately, the federal government deployed the Pakistan military “in aid of civil powers” in the province under article 245 of the constitution.
Former Prime Minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party has been in power in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province since 2013. PTI formed its latest government with a two-thirds majority after the 2024 general election.

Hackers heat French supermarket fridges, sparking fires and food losses
PARIS, Oct 12 - Hackers forced the temperature of many French supermarket fridges up to 50 degrees Celsius (122°F) overnight, causing fires and food losses at several hundred stores across the country in a major cyberattack.
The Paris prosecutor's office said a "large-scale" attack was "affecting connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France" and reported damage included "food losses and fires".
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu instructed France's National Cybersecurity Agency ANSSI to investigate, a person in his office said.
They said France "was coordinating with its European counterparts, as other countries may also be affected," while also investigating whether any other French firms were at risk.
Les Mousquetaires, which owns retailer Intermarche, said around 150 of its stores had been hit, with fridges heated up to 50 degrees Celsius for six hours. It had thrown all the food away to avoid any sanitary risks, a spokesperson said.
And Cooperative U CEO Dominique Schelcher said his supermarket had also been hit by the attack.
"Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented," he wrote on X.
Carrefour said 80 of its supermarkets had been hit but that the vast majority of its 6,000 stores had not been affected.
Several other supermarket chains, including Monoprix, E.Leclerc and Auchan, did not respond to requests for comment.
DUTCH SECURITY ISSUE
Dutch supermarket operator Ahold Delhaize, which operates the Netherlands' largest supermarket chain Albert Heijn and has substantial operations in the United States, said it was also dealing with a "security issue" in its network, and had taken several systems offline to protect them.
A smartphone app for the retailer told clients that due to a "cybersecurity incident" it was unable to deliver groceries.
Online orders represent around 10% of sales for Albert Heijn. Physical stores remained open and Dutch news agency ANP reported that rivals had seen an influx of delivery orders.
It was not clear if there was any link between the French supermarket attack and the problems flagged by Ahold Delhaize.
Ahold is the fourth-largest grocery retailer in the US, where websites for its Stop & Shop, Giant, Hannaford and Food Lion stores all had notices saying "site temporarily down".
It was unclear if other operations were affected.
The source close to Lecornu said ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in software supplied by Danish company Danfoss.
Danfoss said it was "aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems".
The affected units "were running outdated firmware", Danfoss said, adding that it had "long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions". REUTERS

According to the minister, a Thrissur-based agency received the contract to construct the wards at an estimated cost of Rs 1.38 crore per facility. However, he claimed that none of the 55 completed facilities was suitable for admitting or treating patients.The minister also pointed to several alleged deficiencies in the buildings, including the absence of air-conditioning and toilets, unfinished civil works and ceilings that could not accommodate fans.Despite an expenditure of around Rs 1.83 crore per ward, the completed facilities were not fit to house patients, he said.In view of the alleged shortcomings, the government has constituted an expert committee headed by the principal secretary, health, to investigate the matter, Muraleedharan added.

South Africa to release 2.5 mln hectares of state land to black farmers: president
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
23:30:21 CST
00:30:21 KST

JOHANNESBURG, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- South Africa is releasing about 2.5 million hectares of state-owned land to black farmers, with title deeds, as part of efforts to address racial inequalities in agriculture and expand their participation in commercial farming, President Cyril Ramaphosa said Monday.
In his weekly newsletter, Ramaphosa said that despite significant growth in the agricultural sector since the end of apartheid, its benefits had not been shared equally.
South Africa's agricultural exports reached a record 270 billion rand (about 16.3 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, but commercial farming remains dominated by white-owned farms, while black farmers account for only around 10 percent of commercial farming output.
Ramaphosa stressed that transforming the sector is essential to addressing historical inequalities and strengthening food security. "The first step in building a new generation of South African farmers is providing them with titled access to land," he said.
Through the Proactive Land Acquisition Strategy, the government is releasing the land with title deeds to black farmers, Ramaphosa said, adding that secure access to land needs to be accompanied by affordable financing, practical training, mentorship and access to technology and other resources.
"Far too often, emerging farmers are kept trapped at subsistence level because they cannot get the financing they need for farming inputs, infrastructure and additional land," he said.
The president noted the Land Bank and the Department of Agriculture have introduced a blended finance scheme combining government grants with loans, encouraging more commercial banks and agribusinesses to join the program and develop additional funding mechanisms.
"We can bring more land under cultivation, create a new generation of black commercial farmers and ensure that we grow enough not only to feed all our people, but to sell to markets across the world," Ramaphosa said. ■

Austrian judges, prosecutors go on strike over staff shortages

Unknown Publisher

00:30:14 KST

Austrian judges, prosecutors go on strike over staff shortages
VIENNA, Oct 12 - Austria's judges and prosecutors went on strike on Monday over staff shortages among their ranks, demanding that the state fill the gap despite government efforts to shrink the budget deficit back to within the European Union's limit.
As in many European countries, Austria's judiciary is plagued by delays and backlogs as it struggles to cope with an ever growing number of cases. To draw attention to the problem, judges and prosecutors across the country have stopped handling non-urgent matters this week.
"Stop! We simply can't take this anymore," Anna-Maria Wukovits, vice president of the Austrian Prosecutors' Association, told a press conference marking the start of the protest week.
"Prosecutors cannot go on like this. We are at our limit," she added.
Austria's national judges' association estimates there is currently a shortage of more than 250 judges nationally, while Wukowits told national broadcaster ORF that for prosecutors the figure is around 70.
Workloads for prosecutors and judges have increased for various reasons, including ever more complex cases such as those involving cyber crimes, and many criminal complaints are now written using artificial intelligence but must then be reviewed manually by prosecutors, Wukowits said.
"Those often involve reams of pages that have to be read. One cannot ignore that," she said.
While the justice ministry has expressed sympathy with the prosecutors and judges, it has said the government's current priority is reducing the budget deficit, which came in last year at 4.1% of economic output, well beyond the EU limit of 3%.
"The rule of law cannot be maintained in the long term only because judges work unpaid overtime. For years, our colleagues have been making up for structural staff shortages by working on evenings, weekends and even on holiday," Austrian Judges' Association President Gerhard Karmuth said in a statement. HARBIN, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Harbin Ice-Snow World in northeast China -- the world's largest ice-and-snow theme park -- will set a new record this winter by expanding its site to 1.25 million square meters, with a total of 400,000 cubic meters of ice and snow used.
The announcement was made on Monday at the opening ceremony of the 2026-2027 ice-and-snow season promotion event, held by the Heilongjiang provincial ice-and-snow tourism development promotion association.
In February this year, the globally renowned winter attraction in Harbin, Heilongjiang's provincial capital, received more than 120,000 visitors in a single day, a historic high, winning praise from domestic and international tourists.
The park is expected to feature more than 1,000 ice-and-snow structures this winter, with six major sections covering ice-and-snow landscapes, amusement experiences, performances, ice-and-snow competitions, themed IP and supporting services, offering an immersive winter experience. Core landmarks such as the park gate and main tower will be upgraded.
The visitor experience and performances will also be improved. "Key landscapes will be renewed, and there will be more interactive experiences," said Sun Zemin, a promoter of Harbin Ice-Snow World.
In deepening the integration of sports and tourism, Harbin Ice-Snow World will work with Harbin municipal sports bureau to host a series of ice-and-snow sports events, covering curling and ice hockey among others, to promote winter sports.
The theme park is now in full preparation for the 2026-2027 ice-and-snow season.
China has unveiled an ambitious plan to develop its ice and snow economy as a new economic driver, targeting a total market size of 1.2 trillion yuan (about 178.3 billion U.S. dollars) by 2027 and 1.5 trillion yuan by 2030, according to a guideline released by the State Council in 2024.
Leveraging the opportunity, Harbin is implementing a slew of market regulation and tourist guidance measures to continue optimizing its tourism experience, adding greater economic momentum through the use of its ice and snow resources. ■

Roundup: Bound by resolve, China and Lesotho mark national milestones, look to shared future
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
23:30:08 CST
00:30:08 KST

by Silence Charumbira
MASERU, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Two distant nations, vastly different in geography, size and historical trajectory, reached major national milestones within days of each other this month.
On Oct. 1, the People's Republic of China marked its 77th anniversary. Three days later, the Kingdom of Lesotho celebrated 60 years of independence.
Despite their physical distance and different sizes, a common thread runs through both anniversaries: an unyielding resolve to chart an independent path toward development and modernization.
"Our two countries have different national circumstances," Chinese Ambassador to Lesotho Yang Xiaokun said at a cultural event in Maseru on Friday. "But these anniversaries remind us of the determination of our peoples to shape our own future, pursue development, and build a better life."
Both nations embarked on modern state-building from arduous beginnings. In 1949, the New China emerged as a war-torn, agrarian society. In 1966, Lesotho gained independence as a poor, landlocked kingdom surrounded by apartheid South Africa.
Since independence, Lesotho has sought a development path suited to its own conditions, working to strengthen economic resilience and governance. China's own transformation into the world's second-largest economy has likewise rested on a path tailored to national realities, built on self-reliance and long-term planning.
"Modernization does not equate to Westernization, and there is no single model for development," Yang emphasized, affirming the right of African nations to chart their own course.
Lesotho's recent experience underscores why economic self-determination matters. The kingdom's vital garment industry has faced severe disruptions due to shifting global trade environments, leaving factories vulnerable.
Having navigated similar uncertainties during its own growth, China has consistently offered stability to its African partners. Under the frameworks of the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation, China has extended zero-tariff treatment to all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic ties, including Lesotho.
Practical cooperation between the two nations continues to yield tangible results, ranging from debt relief and streamlined trade in agricultural exports like wool and mohair, to human resource development initiatives that sent over 270 Basotho professionals to China for training this year alone.
Progress extends beyond economics into cultural exchanges and global governance, where China advocates equal rights, equal opportunities and equal rules for all nations regardless of size. On Friday, a Chinese artistic troupe performed traditional Wu Opera in Maseru to mark Lesotho's diamond jubilee, celebrating mutual learning between distinct civilizations.
"Sixty years is not only a milestone; it is a new starting point," Ambassador Yang said, closing his address with Lesotho's national motto: "Khotso, Pula, Nala" (Peace, Rain, Prosperity).
Standing at this historic juncture, China and Lesotho are moving forward as equal partners, bound by a shared resolve to turn bilateral cooperation into lasting prosperity for both peoples. ■

Thailand's intellectual property filings rise nearly 9.6 pct in first 9 months
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
23:30:02 CST
00:30:02 KST

BANGKOK, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Applications for intellectual property (IP) protection in Thailand rose 9.59 percent year on year to 61,288 in the first nine months of 2026, official data showed on Monday, reflecting the growing use of IP by Thai and foreign businesses to gain a competitive edge.
According to the Commerce Ministry's Department of Intellectual Property (DIP), registrations granted across trademarks, invention patents, petty patents, and design patents rose 6.34 percent from a year earlier to 43,379 during January-September.
Trademark applications, the largest category, climbed 10.76 percent to 45,696. Retail and marketing services, health and herbal products, and cleaning and beauty products led the filings. Thai applicants made up 56 percent of trademark filings.
Invention patent applications rose 3.98 percent to 6,483, and foreign firms filed 87 percent of them.
Petty patent applications jumped 18.16 percent to 4,313, with Thai applicants accounting for 94 percent, led by universities and state research agencies. Design patent applications were nearly flat at 4,796.
Voluntary copyright notifications surged 63.71 percent to 17,176 works, most notably literary works, including computer programs.
DIP Director-General Jittima Srithaporn said the department aims to make IP protection more effective and better suited to trade and investment needs, build confidence among applicants, and support the commercial use of IP.
The department will also keep improving its IP protection and services, using digital technology and artificial intelligence to raise efficiency, link up data, and make the system easier for the public and businesses to use, Jittima said in a statement. ■

Some 24,000 families affected by C. Philippine volcano eruption
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
23:30:01 CST
00:30:01 KST

MANILA, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- The eruption of Kanlaon Volcano on Saturday in the central Philippines has affected around 24,000 families, the country's Office of Civil Defense (OCD) said Monday.
According to OCD, about 94,000 individuals have been affected by ash emissions from the "moderately explosive eruption" of Mount Kanlaon Volcano in Negros Island. The event generated a plume that rose 5 km to 6 km above the crater.
Eight separate ash emission episodes at Kanlaon were observed on Sunday, while at least five episodes have been reported on Monday, according to the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS).
As of Monday, Kanlaon remains under Alert Level 2, with Level 5 as the highest on the scale, and PHIVOLCS said another explosive eruption is possible. Communities near Mount Kanlaon remain at risk of ashfall, volcanic gases, pyroclastic density currents, and ballistic projectiles should explosive eruptions recur.
PHIVOLCS suggested that the 4-kilometer permanent danger zone must remain evacuated, and communities within 6 km of the summit should stay vigilant and prepared in case the volcano is raised to Alert Level 3. ■

ULAN BATOR, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Facing oil supply constraints and fuel shortages, Mongolia is accelerating its transition to new energy vehicles (NEVs), as affordable, reliable Chinese NEVs rapidly gain popularity.
Mongolia is advancing its transition to electric mobility by incorporating the promotion of NEVs and the development of charging networks into its medium- and long-term national development plans. The country plans to establish around 500 electric vehicle charging stations, known as "green stations," in the capital, Ulan Bator, and other parts of the country over the next two years.
In the past, many local consumers had reservations about NEVs, with some concerned about their performance in Mongolia's harsh winter climate. However, as fuel supplies tighten and the cost of running conventional gasoline- and diesel-powered vehicles rises, Chinese NEVs have attracted growing interest.
Otgonbayar is among the early adopters of Chinese NEVs in Ulan Bator. "I bought a Chinese NEV in 2024, and after using it for more than two years, my perception of these vehicles has changed completely," he said.
Otgonbayar noted that a full charge costs just 20,000 Mongolian tugriks (about 5.6 U.S. dollars), more than sufficient for his daily commute, while offering a smoother driving experience.
Like Otgonbayar, an increasing number of local vehicle owners are recommending Chinese NEVs to their friends and family after experiencing their benefits firsthand. Choosing Chinese NEVs and embracing greener mobility are becoming increasingly popular among Ulan Bator residents.
At a Chinese NEV dealership in Ulan Bator, customers are regularly seen enquiring about vehicles, placing orders and collecting their purchases. Sales staff said sales had risen significantly in recent months, reflecting strong market interest.
In recent years, several Chinese companies have stepped up cooperation with Mongolia in the new energy sector. Zheng Dongdong, vice president of Zero Carbon Engine Technology Group Co., Ltd., said the company was working with relevant local authorities to develop supporting measures to facilitate the introduction and wider adoption of NEVs. ■

Federal authorities raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar on Monday morning as part of a criminal investigation of the Minnesota Democrat.
Omar, who has not been charged with a crime, said she was being targeted for political purposes because of her opposition to President Donald Trump.
A person familiar with the situation, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the nonpublic investigation, told CNBC that the probe of the 44-year-old congresswoman is complex and has been going on for years.
MS NOW reported that a law enforcement source with direct knowledge of the raid — which comes weeks before November's midterm election — said the investigation into Omar is based on allegations of fraud.
Fox News, which first reported the raid, cited a source familiar with the probe as saying it is focused on her immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her father when she emigrated to the U.S. with him from Somalia as a child.
Homeland Security Investigations, a division of the Department of Homeland Security, conducted the raid. HSI investigators were seen outside Omar's home in the Northeast quadrant of Washington throughout the morning.
Omar, who is seeking reelection, has been a target of criticism by Trump for years. She heckled the president during his State of the Union address to Congress on Feb. 24, which came on the heels of aggressive immigration enforcement actions in Minneapolis by federal authorities.
Omar, who is deputy chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, blasted the raid and the investigation in a post on X on Monday.
"I'm ok," Omar wrote.
"Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation," she wrote.
"I will not be silenced."
Omar became a U.S. citizen in 2000 at 17. She was elected to Congress in November 2018 to represent Minnesota's 5th District, which includes all of Minneapolis.
She and Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., became the first two Muslim women elected to Congress.
The Department of Justice, in a statement to CNBC when asked about the raid, said, "Today in the Washington, D.C., area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice."
"This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation," the DOJ said.
Omar's spokeswoman, Jacklyn Rogers, in a statement said, "This raid by Trump's DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies."
"For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," Rogers said. "Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies."
In September, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin told right-wing commentator Benny Johnson at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas that DHS was investigating issues around Omar and her family's immigration to the United States.
"There may be more to this, the whole family migration and possibly some illegal activity for them to come to the United States to begin with," said Mullin. He said the investigation could end with deportations.
The DOJ, for years, has had a policy regarding the announcement and initiation of federal investigations and prosecutions close to elections. The policy discourages beginning an investigation, taking investigative steps, bringing criminal charges, or making public statements for the purpose of affecting an election or to give a candidate an advantage or disadvantage.
The person familiar with the raid on Omar's home told CNBC on Monday that the DOJ does not consider that action to violate the policy because the raid was not meant to be public.
Republican John Nagel is running against Omar in a race the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates "solid Democrat." The general election is just over three weeks away on Nov. 3.
The Democratic leadership of the House of Representatives blasted the Trump administration for the raid.
"The Trump administration's raid on Congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home is deeply disturbing and raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump's adversaries," said House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Minority Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., and Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, the Democratic Caucus chair, in a statement.
"For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations," the statement said. "Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family."
"The American people deserve transparency, and we will deliver full accountability for the rogue abuse of power from the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Justice."

Delta delays debut of Saudi Arabia service until March after Riyadh airport attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:13:17 UTC
00:13:17 KST

Delta Air Lines said it will delay the launch of its nonstop service between Atlanta and the Saudi capital Riyadh until March after several deadly attacks hit the city's airport there.
Delta planned to begin the route on Oct. 23, with an Airbus A350-900 wide-body plane, in what would have marked the first nonstop commercial flight between the U.S. and Saudi Arabia operated by a U.S. airline.
Since Thursday, more than 2,000 flights have been canceled to and from King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, according to FlightAware. The deadly attacks, claimed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, escalated Saturday, when a projectile struck a passenger terminal at the airport, officials said, killing at least 12 people and wounding more than 300.
King Khalid International Airport remains closed as of Monday.
"We remain in close contact with relevant government and aviation partners, including Saudia and Riyadh Air, as we monitor the situation," Delta said in a statement. "Saudi Arabia remains an important market for Delta, and we are committed to serving the Kingdom for the long-term."
Delta CEO Ed Bastian had told CNBC on Thursday that the airline hadn't yet decided whether to postpone the debut.
"Obviously, we were disappointed to see the news this week," he said. "Safety is going to make the call."
Delta's decision came after the Federal Aviation Administration on Sunday issued a warning for U.S. airlines.
The FAA said pilots should "exercise caution" in or around Saudi Arabia "due to safety-of-flight risks associated with ongoing military activities" and navigation systems. In the warning, which is in effect until Dec. 10, the agency said the threats could be a potential risk "to aircraft at all altitudes."
Airlines suspended flights to the airport, some for the rest of the week, while countries including the U.S. and Australia advised citizens against travel to the region.
— CNBC's Michele Luhn contributed to this report.

UK says recent air base indicent 'almost certainly directed' by IRGC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:04:00 UTC
00:04:00 KST

A recent alleged plot targeting the RAF Fairford air base in Britain was "highly likely" to have been coordinated in Iran, and "almost certainly directed" by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday.
The incident near RAF Fairford began in the early hours of Sept. 27 when five British men in their 20s were arrested near the base on suspected terrorism and explosive offences.
They were later released without charge on police bail "under stringent conditions," and police said they were considering whether a foreign state had been involved.
Last week, U.S. President Donald Trump said a threat linked to Iran had prompted the removal of American B-1 bombers from the air base, and U.S. officials have told Reuters that there had been a suspected plot involving Iran to launch a drone attack.
"We will not tolerate these threats on our soil," Burnham told parliament.
"We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm."
Later on Monday, Iran denied any involvement in the incident at the air base, which has been used by the U.S. in its war with the Islamic republic.
"The Iranian ambassador in London, Ali Moussavi, has again categorically rejected the accusations concerning Tehran's role in the incident at the Fairford military base," state news agency IRNA reported, adding that he "called on the British government to present evidence supporting its allegations if it possesses any."

Dog shelter worker awarded HK$89,000 over canine attack despite volunteer claim

A Hong Kong court has awarded more than HK$89,000 (US$11,340) to a worker at a dog shelter who was seriously injured in a canine attack, rejecting her employer’s argument that she was a volunteer.

She sustained multiple injuries and was taken to Tin Shui Wai Hospital’s accident and emergency department.

Croatia Expands Probe Into Alleged Multi-Million-Euro Toxic Waste Scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:02:00 UTC
00:02:00 KST

Reported by
Croatia's anti-corruption office, USKOK, expanded its investigation into an alleged international illegal waste dumping ring, arresting and questioning five new suspects and three companies over the suspected criminal disposal of hazardous materials near the town of Benkovac and inside the Velebit Nature Park near Senj.
The suspects were released after questioning, as USKOK stated there were no legal grounds to request pre-trial detention. Friday's action marks the third expansion of the sweeping environmental crime probe, which now targets a total of 14 individuals and four companies suspected of severe environmental crimes and falsifying official documents within a criminal enterprise.
The investigation, supported by Europol and law enforcement from Italy and Slovenia, became public in February 2025 with the initial arrest of 13 people. Authorities dismantled an alleged criminal network that is accused of orchestrating the illegal import of hazardous waste from Germany, Italy, and Slovenia into Croatia.
According to Europol, instead of properly treating the materials, the network allegedly buried or dumped at least 35,000 tonnes of waste across at least three locations, generating an estimated 4 million euros ($4.5 million) in illicit profits. To execute the scheme, suspects allegedly generated hundreds of falsified waste tracking sheets and fake construction diaries to disguise hazardous materials as municipal waste cover or legitimate building materials.
The severe environmental toll of the scheme became clear in early August, when USKOK released an expert report from the University of Zagreb's Faculty of Geotechnical Engineering, which concluded the local habitat was "partially irreversibly destroyed." Testing at an illegal landfill in Gospić revealed critical levels of heavy metals—including copper, zinc, lead, and antimony—and "forever chemicals," synthetic compounds that do not easily break down in the environment or the human body.
The report noted that downstream water samples showed high concentrations of the chemicals while upstream samples were clear, proving the landfill was the source. Experts warned there is a "high probability of further deterioration" if the waste is not immediately removed.
The latest USKOK findings reveal the destruction extends further. Between 2020 and 2024, the network allegedly dumped nearly 2,900 tonnes of hazardous plastic and industrial waste at the Senj site, and almost 6,500 tonnes of waste laced with heavy metals and microplastics into an inactive mineral field in Benkovac. Prosecutors warned the microplastics serve as a permanent pollution source that could easily leach into groundwater and the local food chain.
The revelations of widespread contamination and potential long-term health impacts sparked mass outrage. In September, tens of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets of Zagreb to demand stronger environmental protections, while local communities demanded strict sanctions against those responsible for the ecological damage.
Seeking to manage the ongoing political fallout and reassure the public, Prime Minister Andrej Plenković announced following a meeting with a scientific council that the government is initiating urgent remediation efforts in Gospić. Plenković stated Monday on X that surface waste will be removed in large bags and buried toxins temporarily covered, insisting that recent air and water tests show no deviations from permitted limits and that the public water supply remains completely safe.
