'Scary' dementia modelling shows how cases will surge by 2050
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
15:01:28 UTC
00:01:28 KST

Dementia cases to soar to 'scary' highs and women will face more risk, study reveals
By 2050 an estimated 24.7 million people will be diagnosed with dementia each year and women will be disproportionately affected, according to a landmark study.
The research found approximately 11.4 million people developed dementia globally in 2023 and that by 2050 that figure will double and demand for care will explode.
The study's authors said women's brain health needed to be prioritised and risk factors like hormonal changes and unequal education or job opportunities needed investigating.
"Understanding these differences is critical if we are to develop dementia prevention, diagnosis and care strategies that respond to the populations facing the greatest future risk," lead author Dr Ashleigh Vella said.
The research from the Centre for Healthy Brain Ageing (CHeBA) at the University of NSW analysed 38,418 people through population-based studies from 18 countries and territories.
It is one of the most comprehensive studies looking at the incidence rate of dementia. The study found cases were highest among women and people living in low income and middle income countries.
Nearly two thirds of dementia diagnoses in Australia are women and this has long been considered a symptom of their longer life expectancy but researchers said there may be more at play.
The paper, published in the Journal of the American Medical Association Neurology, suggested the higher prevalence could be caused by other factors such as:
- Menopause
- Disproportionate educational and occupational opportunities
- Cardiometabolic factors such as body mass index and physical activity
Co-director of the CHeBA and Senior Australia of the Year Professor, Henry Brodaty, said historically women had less access to education and fewer career opportunities which could lead to poorer cognitive resilience.
"[Studies have shown] people who are in more complex occupations, particularly where they have complexity in managing people, they have a lower rate of cognitive decline and dementia," he said.
"Education has its most benefit in childhood and early development through to young adulthood but you can still build up your cognitive reserve or buffer against pathology building up in the brain throughout your life."
Higher rates of depression, anxiety and obesity among women could also be contributing factors, Professor Brodaty said, and more research was needed on the role menopause might play.
"Perhaps stopping oestrogen production may play a role but it's not established … and there's been conflicting results about whether hormone replacement therapy makes a difference."
Leading dementia researcher Matthew Pase at Monash University said the research was ambitious and provided important comparisons on dementia rates between low income and high income countries.
He described the figures as "scary".
"To see what rates are projected to be in low-income countries is alarming because they are less equipped to deal with this … so any solutions need to be scalable and not just be available for people who can pay to see an academic at a medical centre in Sydney or Melbourne."
Reducing dementia risk
Professor Brodaty, whose father passed away with Alzheimer's at just 52, said having a clear idea of what was coming meant there must be more investment in diagnosis, care and prevention.
Almost half of dementia cases could be prevented or delayed by addressing 14 risk factors.
Professor Brodaty urged Australians to "embrace" brain health by:
- Engaging in at least half an hour of physical activity five days a week
- Staying socially connected and "stretching the brain" by learning new things
- Eating a diet rich in vegetables, legumes and extra olive oil aka the Mediterranean diet
- Talking to their GP about brain health when they have their subsidised health check between the ages of 45 and 49
Professor Pase said given the high cost of the two dementia drug therapies approved in Australia, which are not subsidised through the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, prevention was still key.

Three outdated band facilities at Wellington Barracks in Westminster are being demolished to clear the way for purpose-built accommodation for the Army musicians of the Foot Guards Bands, according to the Defence Infrastructure Organisation.

Completion is scheduled for 2028, and the department says the work will allow personnel at the barracks to carry on fulfilling their ceremonial and operational roles in the heart of London.

As part of its “Vast Ocean Plan” for global expansion, one of China’s largest automotive companies recently announced its sponsorship of Portugal’s national football team.
“Europe stands as a strategic priority,” Changan Automobile said in a press release in May, adding that its partnership with the Portuguese Football Federation offered a new opportunity for “brand engagement across the region.”
In an earlier phase of a global push by the state-owned company, Changan moved into Russia. According to the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a U.S. think tank, Russia acquired the original design for the Geran from Iran and has innovated it over the past few years. Today, the Geran is one of the main weapons deployed by Russia, targeting both Ukrainian military and civilians.
In July, a Changan Hunter appeared in a video published by Russian propagandist Vladimir Solovyov. The video shows Russian soldiers in camouflage and masks assembling several drones, including a Geran, and arming it with an explosive device. At least four residents of Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoJK) were killed in a blast caused by a suspected improvised explosive device (IED) across the Line of Control (LoC), adjacent to the Krishna Ghati sector in Poonch district, on Monday.The incident prompted heightened security on the Indian side, PTI reported, citing officials.The powerful blast reportedly took place in the Satwal-Naki area of Hajira tehsil of PoK, when a group of people were reportedly laying water pipes along the Pakistan side of the LoC.According to preliminary information received from across the border, cited by officials, the deceased were identified as Faizan Sagheer, Ishtiaq, Waqas Sharief, and Asim Rafiq of Battal Mandhol village of PoK.The deceased were reportedly cousins.According to officials, the involvement of any of the deceased in terror activities was not known immediately.Following the blast, security forces sounded an alert across the sector and stepped up vigilance along the LoC to assess the situation and prevent any potential security breach, officials said.
In a separate incident, Indian Army troops detected two rusted landmines near the border fence in the Basoni area of the Mendhar sector on Monday.
The landmines were spotted during track construction at 8.25 am and 12.10 pm, respectively, officials said. Both devices were subsequently destroyed by Army experts in controlled explosions.Around a dozen landmines have been detected and defused by the Army in the area over the past week.

Ramlila Maidan: The ground where protests dealt a blow to Congress government, twice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:46:04 UTC
23:46:04 KST

Ramlila Maidan is best known as a venue for the annual staging of Ramlila, the traditional enactment of the Ramayana.
NEW DELHI: Delhi has a new map for protest, with Jantar Mantar losing its status as a designated venue for demonstrations on Monday. Delhi Police has named three alternative sites, including Ramlila Maidan in central Delhi, a ground that has witnessed political movements with far-reaching consequences for the Congress.The other two designated venues are Burari Ground in north Delhi and CBD Ground in east Delhi. The move comes amid protests against the Election Commission over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. While Jantar Mantar's removal marks a significant shift in the capital's protest landscape, Ramlila Maidan brings its own political history to the fore.
A view of Ramlila Maidan, designated as a protest site along with two news venues,. (PTI photo)
The venue has a political legacy of its own: two major mass movements held there, decades apart, that became defining moments in the Congress’s political history.
Two protests that changed Congress's fortunes
Ramlila Maidan has been the stage for two major mass movements that challenged the Congress at crucial moments in its political history, decades apart.The first came on June 25, 1975, when socialist leader Jayaprakash Narayan addressed a massive rally at Ramlila Maidan against then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi's government, calling for resistance to the establishment.
Jayaprakash Narayan addressed a massive rally at Ramlila Maidan.
That night, Gandhi imposed the Emergency, suspending civil liberties and triggering a crackdown on the Opposition.
The Congress lost the 1977 Lok Sabha election, its first defeat at the Centre, as the Janata Party came to power.More than three decades later, the ground witnessed another movement that put the Congress-led government under pressure. In 2011, anti-corruption activist Anna Hazare launched a nationwide agitation demanding a strong Lokpal law. The protest began at Jantar Mantar before moving to Ramlila Maidan, where Hazare staged a high-profile hunger strike that drew widespread public attention.
Anna Hazare during the India Against Corruption (IAC) movement in 2011.
The agitation intensified the political pressure on the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance (UPA), already facing a series of corruption allegations. It also helped create the momentum for the emergence of the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), which went on to challenge both the Congress and the BJP in Delhi and fundamentally alter the capital's political contest.Separated by 36 years, the two movements cemented Ramlila Maidan's place in India's protest history, with each marking a significant challenge to a Congress-led establishment.
History of Ramlila Maidan
Ramlila Maidan is best known as a venue for the annual staging of Ramlila, the traditional enactment of the Ramayana. According to historian Narayani Gupta, Ramlila was held on land near Ajmeri Gate as early as the 19th century. Historian Sohail Hashmi has said the early celebrations were supported by the Khatri community.The ground acquired a wider public role after Independence, hosting large gatherings and events involving national and international leaders.Soviet leaders Nikita Khrushchev and Nikolai Bulganin visited in 1955, US President Dwight Eisenhower addressed a gathering there in 1959, and Queen Elizabeth II spoke at a public event in 1961.Over time, the ground became a venue for political rallies, mass meetings and demonstrations, cementing its place in the capital’s public life.
How the protest site has shifted
Jantar Mantar was not always the designated site. The Boat Club lawns near Rajpath were used earlier, until a week-long farmers’ protest led by Mahendra Singh Tikait in 1988 raised security concerns. By 1993, protests had moved to Jantar Mantar, which was close to Parliament but easier to police.In 2017, the National Green Tribunal banned protests at Jantar Mantar, citing environmental and civic issues, and named Ramlila Maidan, nearly four kilometres away, as the official venue for sit-ins.However, the Supreme Court, while setting aside a blanket ban on protests at Jantar Mantar in a 2018 ruling, had held that the right to peaceful protest could not be completely extinguished and that the competing rights of protesters and residents had to be balanced through regulation.The Court had accordingly directed authorities to permit limited and regulated use of the area.With the Delhi Police now de-notifying Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site and shifting demonstrations to three other venues, the question is whether the decision is legally sustainable in light of the Supreme Court’s ruling.
The Supreme Court, in Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India, was dealing with a 2017 order of the National Green Tribunal (NGT) which had directed authorities to immediately stop dharnas, protests, agitations, public speeches and other such activities at Jantar Mantar Road and shift protesters to an alternative site.Protest groups have since argued that greater distance from Parliament reduces the visibility of their demands. Farmers who were denied permission even at Ramlila Maidan in 2020-21 camped instead at Delhi’s borders at Singhu, Tikri and Ghazipur.The latest order formalises a shift away from the central site, though it remains to be seen how the revised rules will affect where and how protests are held.
Rajeev Singh is a Digital Content Producer with The Times of India. He covers politics, policies, defence, and conflicts for readers curious to know their implications. He loves digging into legal maxims and political trivia. On off days, when not turning pages or learning русский, he lives in the reverie of “what ifs” and “how abouts.”

What the US and China Should Discuss at APEC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:45:00 UTC
23:45:00 KST

On September 24, the presidents of the United States and China met in Washington and agreed to build what their joint language calls a “constructive relationship of strategic stability.” On November 18-19, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to meet again, on the sidelines of the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen. Two summits in three months is a rare occurrence in China-U.S. relations.
In the September summit, already their second of 2026, one key area stood out as the focus: artificial intelligence. The risks of AI now have a dedicated channel for discussion. There’s not yet a corresponding China-U.S. platform for talking about the economics of the AI race.
During Trump’s state visit to Beijing in May, the two leaders agreed to restart government-to-government AI dialogue. In September, at the eighth round of economic consultations in New York and Washington, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng held the first AI dialogue within that framework. They agreed to establish a channel for communications on AI incidents, and scheduled a second round of talks before the end of November.
Shortly thereafter, at the presidential summit, Xi described China and the United States as two AI powers that should “draw on each other’s strengths, not guard against each other.” He added, “The two sides can continue their dialogue on AI, exchange views on its risks and benefits, and jointly prevent the misuse and abuse of AI.” Trump noted that discussions on “pressing issues” related to (among other topics) AI, which he calls “superintelligence,” could “promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come.” Both leaders thus offered the new dialogue platform political cover.
That is genuine progress, with a revealing limit. All the steps thus far – the exchanges on risks and benefits, the incident channel, the push for lab self-regulation – concern the dangers AI might create. Nothing yet addresses the looming economic problem of the AI sector.
The Growing AI Bubble
In the United States, recent developments are rather worrying. The business model for U.S. frontier AI businesses assumes that compute demand will keep growing exponentially, model capability will convert reliably into revenue, and capital will stay patient. All three assumptions are looking increasingly risky.
The capex needed to remain at the frontier is heavier, relative to the industry’s age, than anything technology has carried before. Utilities are signing power contracts for gigawatts of capacity that do not exist.
Meanwhile, Wall Street has started asking a question it ignored a year ago: where, exactly, is the return? In July, efficient Chinese open-weight models showed that frontier-level performance could be reached with a fraction of the compute. AI-linked U.S. equities sold off hard; analysts stepped back from price targets built on the assumption of permanent scarcity.
China has the mirror-image problem. Chinese companies are trying to close the frontier gap under foreign constraints while having to produce returns large enough to justify the spending at home. In a September study, the Rhodium Group calculated that the combined free cash flow of Chinese tech giants Alibaba, Tencent, and Baidu swung from positive 170 billion yuan in 2025 to negative 16 billion yuan in the first half of 2026.
The five American hyperscalers saw their own fall from $191 billion to $14 billion and raised $163 billion in long-term debt in six months to keep building.
Clearly, neither the U.S. nor the Chinese AI sector can fund this race from operations anymore. Both countries’ capital markets are tired of narratives without actual returns. Patience on both sides is wearing thin.
The China-U.S. competition exacerbates these economic dynamics. Each new round of U.S. export controls accelerates the Chinese substitution process, which shrinks the market available for American firms. At the same time, deeper substitution raises the investment China must absorb, which worsens China’s return-on-capital problem.
In other words, further escalation in the AI race might drain away the capital both systems depends on. This is not a moral argument, but a real financial dilemma.
Washington and Beijing have already conceded, in their September dialogue, that they face some common risks from AI risks. What’s not clear is whether the economic problem is included on that agenda.
The Chance at Shenzhen
The November APEC summit offers an unusually practical setting for addressing this issue. The APEC CEO Summit will bring about 1,000 business leaders to Shenzhen with AI on the formal agenda and a Shenzhen Initiative to be released. The host city itself, long nicknamed the Silicon Valley of the East, holds China’s densest cluster of AI and robotics firms.
Unofficial channels are also in place. Tsinghua’s Center for International Security and Strategy and the Brookings Institution have hosted 14 rounds of China-U.S. AI dialogue since 2019, with Microsoft’s former chief research and strategy officer Craig Mundie serving as a co-chair.
Three deliverables should be on the agenda for the APEC meeting.
First, China and the United States should add the missing piece of the puzzle in Shenzhen. The official AI dialogue will be held in November; at the APEC summit, both sides can start a standing China-U.S. AI economics dialogue mechanism supported by think tanks and industry associations, the “track two” format long used in China-U.S. exchanges.
Every official AI conversation so far lacks the people who control the money: finance officials, stock market regulators, and executives. The first such dialogue could take place on the margins of the APEC meeting, convened by think tanks and industry associations rather than ministries.
In Shenzhen, the Guangdong Artificial Intelligence Industry Association – which operates the Guangdong AI & Robotics Overseas Service Center, the province’s platform for firms going global – could co-convene, alongside established think tanks, a working session between U.S. investors, analysts, and executives and their Guangdong counterparts, on the industry’s own ground.
Why start with the “track two” format? Because the U.S. and Chinese governments would find it hard to host this conversation. No U.S. administration can openly entertain the thought that its AI boom may be overextended; no Chinese ministry can candidly compare burn rates with a foreign power. Finance officials can talk to economists, and economists can talk to each other. An unofficial venue is the only why this particular talk can happen.
Second, China and the United States should set a floor under export controls and market access in Shenzhen. Neither side can afford to be seen conducting negotiations over such fundamental issues, but they can quietly exchange red lines in a private setting. Misjudgment, not malice, triggers most crises. The cheapest deterrent is a sentence spoken early.
Third, it’s time to increase collaborations on the periphery. Standards for AI deployment in third countries – things like data governance, safety evaluation, labor displacement – don’t always pit U.S. and Chinese interests against each other. In fact, that happens far less often than either side assumes. Shenzhen has already hosted APEC-track discussions on responsible AI under the Policy Partnership on Science, Technology and Innovation framework. A joint signal from Washington and Beijing supporting shared regional norms would cost little, match the CEO Summit’s own agenda, and keep third parties from profiting from dueling standards.
Time Is Short
By greenlighting discussions on the economic side of AI, Washington would be shifting a burden, not making a concession. Industry leaders and academic would be the interlocutors, meaning the administration does not need to make more promises even while the Treasury gains more insight into AI’s financial stability.
For its part, Beijing would reinforce its longstanding claim that Chinese AI is an economic project rather than a military one. The talks would also give China’s capital-hungry sector a forum to argue against escalation using commercial – not diplomatic – logic.
The dialogue wouldn’t release a communiqué or joint statement. This would be a recurring conversation that, over time, builds a shared vocabulary for what sustainable AI competition could look like.
The capital markets are not waiting; they are repricing both countries’ AI sectors now. There’s still a chance for China and the U.S. to get ahead of the bubble, but the window is closing. After the U.S. midterms, coalition politics in Washington will harden, and every unmanaged month afterwards would strengthen the case for constraint in Beijing.

Iran offers to mediate between its Houthi allies and Saudi Arabia

Iran offers to mediate between its Houthi allies and Saudi Arabia
Erika Solomon
- Iran offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militia, saying there is no military solution to conflicts in the Middle East.
- A Houthi strike on Riyadh airport killed at least 12 people and injured hundreds, followed by reported strikes on Sanaa and more drone and missile threats.
- The conflict has widened across Yemen and the Gulf, raising fears of fresh regional fighting as Iran warns it could target digital infrastructure if war resumes.
AI generated
TEHRAN – Iran has offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen, after a string of deadly attacks on the kingdom, warning that overlapping conflicts in the region have no military solution.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi made the offer to his Saudi counterpart, Faisal bin Farhan, during a telephone call on Oct 11, according to a statement posted on social media by the Iranian minister’s office.
“Insisting on a military approach and ignoring a political solution will further complicate the current situation,” the statement, posted on Araghchi’s Telegram channel, said.
Araghchi said Iran stood “ready to provide any assistance to help initiate a dialogue” between the two sides.
The Saudi government said the two ministers spoke, though it made no reference to any mediation offer from Iran. The call was a day after the deadliest attack on a Persian Gulf country since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran.
On Oct 10, a Houthi strike on an airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, killed at least 12 people, with hundreds injured.
That sparked an exchange of strikes with Saudi-led forces targeting the airport in Sanaa, Yemen’s Houthi-controlled capital, according to reports on Oct 11 in local news media affiliated with the group.
The Houthi-run health ministry said a child was also killed in a strike on a residential building in Sanaa.
Saudi authorities have not commented on those assertions, but reported another deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh’s airport on Oct 11.
On Oct 12, a state-owned Saudi television channel, Al Ekhbariya, warned that the Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen was fending off drones and cruise missiles headed toward Saudi Arabia. The Saudi authorities have not commented publicly.
Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis rapidly escalated in September when Houthi forces seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast, taking territory that sits alongside a strategic waterway for global trade and a key export route for Saudi oil.
The militia has been fighting the internationally recognised government of Yemen, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, since 2014. A fragile truce agreed in 2022 has unravelled in recent months.
The conflict has stoked further upheaval in the oil-rich Persian Gulf region, which was already reeling from the economic fallout of the US-Iran war.
US and Iranian officials appear braced for the possibility that their stalemated regional conflict could spill back into the open, with the Pentagon drawing up new plans for strikes.
Iran’s national security adviser, Mohsen Rezaei, threatened on Oct 11 that if fighting were to resume, Iranian forces would target digital infrastructure in the Gulf, including data centres, cables, and artificial intelligence facilities.
The Houthis are one of several militant groups that Iran is allied with across the region, and part of what the Islamic republic calls its “Axis of Resistance”.
Though the Houthis have benefited from years of military and financial support from Iran, regional experts have long described them as among the most independent of these allied forces, with ambitions distinct from Iran’s. NYTIMES

NEW DELHI: A Rahul Gandhi-led INDIA bloc march to the Supreme Court against alleged electoral irregularities encountered police barricades in central Delhi on Monday before the opposition leaders eventually reached the court and filed a joint petition against the Election Commission of India (EC).The march, dubbed "March for Democracy", brought together opposition leaders, MPs, party workers and activists, with Rahul Gandhi, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, Congress leader Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav among those who joined the procession.The march was initially halted at Bhagwan Dass Road, where police had erected barricades to prevent the procession from proceeding towards the Supreme Court. As the crowd swelled and the standoff continued, several leaders, including Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, Akhilesh Yadav and Tejashwi Yadav, climbed atop a vehicle as supporters raised slogans against the government and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
As per Supreme Court website, their legal team had filed the petition against the EC as the leaders failed to reach on time.Subsequently they reached the Supreme Court premises and filed the petition in a show of strenght.
Visuals released by the news agency showed Rahul Gandhi, Kharge and other INDIA bloc leaders filing the plea.The march came after the Chief Justice of India refused to meet the opposition leaders who had sought an appointment to submit a memorandum over alleged electoral irregularities. CJI Surya Kant had said the matter was already before the court and advised the leaders to pursue the judicial route by filing a petition.ALSO READ: 'Ready to contest on ballot paper': Himanta lobs dare at Cong but with a big rider
11 leaders named in the petition
The petition names Rahul Gandhi as the lead petitioner, along with 10 other opposition leaders from INDIA bloc parties. The petitioners are:
Rahul Gandhi, Congress
Mallikarjun Kharge, Congress
Saugata Roy, Mamata-TMC
Akhilesh Yadav, Samajwadi Party
Tejashwi Prasad Yadav, Rashtriya Janata Dal
Sanjay Raut, Shiv Sena (UBT)
MA Baby, CPM
D Raja, CPI
Mahua Majhi, Jharkhand Mukti Morcha
Supriya Sule, NCP (Sharadchandra Pawar)
ET Mohammed Basheer, Indian Union Muslim League leader
The Election Commission of India has been named as a respondent. Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the other two Election Commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, have also been named as respondents, according to the Supreme Court website.
What does the petition seek
The petition filed by Rahul Gandhi and 10 other opposition leaders in the Supreme Court has challenged the manner in which the Election Commission has taken decisions relating to the SIR of electoral rolls, news agency ANI reported.It seeks disclosure of the EC’s complete files, agendas, minutes, notings and objections concerning the disputed decisions, including the June 24, 2025 decision to commence the SIR, as well as ECINET and ERONET access logs.It also seeks a judicial examination of whether these decisions were taken in accordance with Article 324 of the Constitution, the 2023 law governing the Election Commission and the Supreme Court’s ruling in TN Seshan vs Union of India.The petition seeks several safeguards against voter deletions during the SIR, including a direction that no elector be removed from the electoral roll without prior notice and a reasonable opportunity to be heard.
It also seeks the booth-wise publication of deleted electors, along with the reasons for their deletion and demographic details.The petition further calls for an independent committee headed by a retired Supreme Court judge to audit deletions and modifications in electoral-roll databases, including ECINET and ERONET. It also seeks an interim suspension of the ongoing SIR until the court adjudicates the matter.Additionally, the plea asks the court to direct the Election Commission to ensure that “every decision of the Election Commission relating to the Special Intensive Revision is taken and duly minuted” in accordance with the 2023 Act.

Pope Leo to go to hospital Tuesday for lung nodule surgery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:36:52 UTC
23:36:52 KST

Pope Leo heads to hospital Tuesday for lung nodule surgery
Pope Leo XIV is being admitted the hospital on Tuesday, days after he shared he would undergo surgery to remove a lung nodule discovered during recent medical tests, the Vatican announced.
The Holy See press office didn't say when the operation itself would take place, but said it will require a weeklong recovery in the hospital.
The U.S.-born pontiff revealed the discovery of the nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and said he was following doctors' advice to have it removed.
He said it was found in an early stage and was "circumscribed."
"The doctors believe it's best to take action, so, following their advice, I've decided to have surgery to remove it," Leo, 71, said Sunday. "Thank you for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers."
He will be treated at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, which has a special apartment for the pope.
The Vatican press office said Monday that no particular issue precipitated the tests, denying Italian media reports suggesting an inflammation had prompted Leo to undergo the checkup.
The pope's surgery marks the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. It was significant because the pope himself revealed the news, in perhaps the most public way possible: at the end of his Sunday noon blessing with thousands of people in St. Peter's Square.
The Vatican has for centuries zealously guarded the pope's health and has often sent out confusing information, or none at all, about papal illnesses. Pope Francis tried to change that by being upfront about his frailties and musing on his eventual death. But even during his pontificate, information was tightly controlled.
Leo's decision and reveal suggested an unusual level of transparency by the American pope.
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 1 inch that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen, according to the American Cancer Society. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening.
On Monday, it was business as usual at the Vatican. Leo presided over an audience with members of a Rome-based charity, the Circolo San Pietro, and received a donation from them. He spoke in a strong, clear voice, praising their service and sacrifice. The crowd gave him a rousing round of applause afterward.
He had six other private audiences, made three appointments and the Vatican released a letter he had penned to the outgoing dean of the College of Cardinals, thanking him for his service. The letter was signed on Sunday.
In the afternoon, he was expected to continue his audiences and, if time, rejoin a weeklong conference he convened on ministering to families.
The pope has a major trip planned Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It's unclear whether the planned surgery and recovery would affect the itinerary.

FAA warns U.S. airlines of safety risks over Saudi Arabia after attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:31:32 UTC
23:31:32 KST

The Federal Aviation Administration told U.S. airlines to exercise caution when flying in or around Saudi Arabia after deadly attacks claimed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, which have shut down the airport in the Saudi capital.
King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, remains closed as of Monday after strikes that started last week. The attacks escalated Saturday, when a projectile struck a passenger terminal at the airport, officials said, killing at least 12 people and wounding more than 300.
Airlines suspended flights to the airport, some for the rest of the week.
The U.S., Australia and other countries advised citizens against travel to the region.
The FAA late Sunday said pilots should "exercise caution" in or around Saudi Arabia "due to safety-of-flight risks associated with ongoing military activities" and navigation systems. It said the threats could be a potential risk "to aircraft at all altitudes." The FAA's warning is in effect until Dec. 10.
Most U.S. airlines don't fly to Saudi Arabia, but the country's flights and passenger counts had climbed in recent years. The route between Riyadh to Jeddah in the country's west was the fifth-busiest in the world last year, according to aviation-data firm OAG.
Delta Air Lines had been scheduled to launch its first nonstop flight from Atlanta to Riyadh on Oct. 23 but the carrier on Monday said it would delay that service until March.

US federal agents search home of Rep. Ilhan Omar as part of probe

U.S. federal agents searched on Monday the home of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar, a Muslim lawmaker for the state of Minnesota and frequent target of Trump administration criticism, as part of a criminal investigation, media reports said.
Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents conducted the search, said the sources, who were not authorized to publicly discuss an ongoing investigation and spoke to The Associated Press (AP) on the condition of anonymity.
More details about the investigation were not immediately clear, although Vice President JD Vance has in the past accused Omar of committing immigration fraud – an allegation she has denied – and has said he and a top White House official were trying to figure out how to investigate the Minnesota congresswoman.
The Justice Department said in a statement Monday that HSI agents executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the department in the Washington, D.C., area, but provided no other details. The street was blocked off on Monday morning as HSI agents remained near the home.
"This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation," the department said.
The raid followed a criminal fraud investigation into the Somali-born lawmaker's immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her late father when she was a child, Fox News Digital reported, citing unidentified sources.
A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, of which Homeland Security Investigations is part, referred questions about the search to the Justice Department.
Omar represents Minnesota’s 5th District, including Minneapolis. She was first elected to the House in 2018 and has been a member of what's called The Squad of female lawmakers known for their progressive views and pointed opposition to President Donald Trump, a Republican.
Republicans have raised questions about Omar's past since before she was even elected, including asserting that she had married her brother and committed immigration fraud. Omar has broadly denied the allegations as "disgusting lies."
"It certainly seems like something fishy is there, but everybody's entitled to equal justice under the laws," Vance told reporters in May.
"So we're going to investigate it. We're going to take a look at it. If we think there's a crime, we're going to prosecute that crime."
In a separate interview with conservative podcaster Benny Johnson, Vance said without offering evidence that "we actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud against the United States of America."
He said that he and deputy White House chief of staff Stephen Miller had been discussing it and "trying to look at what the remedies are."
"That’s the thing that we’re trying to figure out," he said. "What are the legal remedies now that we know that she’s committed immigration fraud. How do you go after her? How do you investigate her? How do you actually do the thing? How do you build the case necessary to get some, some, some justice for the American people?”
Omar’s office in March dismissed Vance’s claims as fabricated and defamatory.
"This is rich coming from someone who literally said they were willing to ‘create stories’ to redirect the media,” Omar’s chief of staff, Connor McNutt, said in a statement.
"This is a ridiculous lie and desperate attempt to distract from the pedophile protection party’s unpopular war of choice, increasing gas prices, and rapidly dropping polling numbers," McNutt said of the vice president’s allegations and comments.
Omar, an outspoken critic of Trump, has called his focus on her an "unhealthy and creepy obsession."
Last week, Trump also criticized the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate from Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, who is Muslim, while offering support for the Republican candidate, Mike Rogers.
Civil rights advocates have criticized the Republican president's rhetoric towards minorities and immigrants, including when he previously called Somalis "garbage."
Trump in February said that Omar and Democratic Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, who is also Muslim, should be "institutionalized" and sent back to "where they came from."
Both lawmakers had criticized Trump during his State of the Union address as he touted his administration's hard-line immigration crackdown and its immigration enforcement actions.
There was no immediate public response from Omar to Monday's search.
No charges were announced in connection with the search.

Same cause, separate protests: Why Congress and CJP are keeping their distance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:21:24 UTC
23:21:24 KST

Protests by INDIA bloc and CJP over alleged voter-list manipulation and the Election Commission
NEW DELHI: "All the protests are one protest," Rahul Gandhi said when asked about the parallel demonstrations against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Yet, despite their common demands, the Congress leader and the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leadership have not shared a stage.Congress and other INDIA bloc leaders on Monday marched towards the Supreme Court over alleged electoral irregularities, while CJP continued its own campaign against the Election Commission.The two groups had also followed separate courses during the October 10 protests. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, TMC chief Mamata Banerjee, AAP leader Arvind Kejriwal and Left leaders were among those detained by Delhi Police. Rahul Gandhi, meanwhile, was in Chennai, though he condemned the police action.
Rahul Gandhi made "vote chori" a central political slogan of the opposition. CJP has also adopted it in its street demonstrations. But despite their overlapping demands, the two sides have largely pursued separate protest programmes.This has raised a political question: Why is Congress maintaining a distance from a movement that shares one of its biggest political demands?
Neha Bora joins Congress protest march to Supreme Court
A fight for political space?
CJP's agitation against the Election Commission fits into a larger political battle that Congress has already made central to its opposition strategy.
Rahul Gandhi's "vote chori" campaign has targeted alleged electoral irregularities in Karnataka, Haryana, Maharashtra and Bihar.The slogan "Vote Chor, Gaddi Chhod", frequently heard at CJP protests, also draws on the political language popularised by Rahul Gandhi.Former Congress national spokesperson Sanjay Jha, however, rejects the suggestion that the two sides are competing for political space."I don't think the battle is between the CJP and the Congress. All members of civil society, students, political parties, intellectuals, authors, activists, NGOs, everyone who's concerned about Indian democracy, are fighting both independently and collectively," he said.Describing CJP as a successful student movement, Jha credited it with bringing the issue to the forefront after investigations by The Indian Express.
Anti-CEC protest on two different days (left) Rahul, Priyanka getting detained on October 7; (right) CJP's Dipke, Das and Ranka getting detained on October 10
"To say that there is any competition between the two is BJP propaganda, and we should not fall for that," he said.His argument is that the two groups can pursue the same demands without necessarily working together.However, their separate mobilisation has also brought attention to differences in their political approach and relationships with other opposition parties.The BJP and Election Commission, meanwhile, have rejected allegations of electoral manipulation, with the poll body maintaining that revisions are intended to identify ineligible entries and ensure the accuracy of electoral rolls.ALSO READ: 'Can't beat us, threaten us': Rahul thanks protesters after INDIA bloc march to SC
NEET protests showed similar pattern
The relationship between Congress and CJP is not simply one of competing claims. Their responses to the NEET-UG controversy in 2026 showed that they could support the same cause while maintaining separate political programmes.CJP emerged as a youth-led citizens' movement amid the controversy over alleged examination irregularities. It demanded accountability, education-system reforms and the resignation of then education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.On July 20, CJP organised a "Chalo Sansad" march from Jantar Mantar towards Parliament. Delhi Police stopped the march, citing violations of prohibitory orders and violence, while CJP alleged that police used excessive force against peaceful demonstrators.
(Left) NEET protest on July 20 by CJP; (right) anti-paper leak protest by Congress July 21
The following day, Congress organised a separate protest outside Prime Minister Narendra Modi's residence, led by Rahul Gandhi, Mallikarjun Kharge and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra.The party demanded Pradhan's resignation, a parliamentary discussion on paper leaks and education reforms, and an apology to students over the police action.Congress had been raising concerns over examination irregularities before CJP's march. Rahul Gandhi had met students in Kota and Dehradun, while he and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra visited injured students at Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital after the police action.The two sides supported similar demands but organised their programmes independently.That pattern is now visible again in the demonstrations against Gyanesh Kumar.
Rahul Gandhi said there are 'no parallel protests'
Assam episode brings differences into focus
The differences became more visible after CJP's recent outreach in Assam.Congress spokesperson Reetam Singh alleged that CJP co-convenor Ashutosh Ranka had refused a courtesy meeting with Congress leaders, including Assam Congress president Gaurav Gogoi, despite Congress workers helping secure the release of detained CJP members.Singh claimed Ranka had declined to engage because the outreach was considered an AAP initiative."Aam Aadmi Party is known for piggy riding and hijacking issues of others," Singh alleged, accusing AAP of attempting to associate itself with movements led by others.These are Congress's allegations, and do not independently establish why CJP representatives declined the meeting.CJP co-convenor Saurav Das had also criticised what he described as a "self-declared liberal" ecosystem that believed "saving India" and the "Constitution" was its exclusive responsibility.The reference was politically significant because "Save the Constitution" has been a prominent part of Rahul Gandhi's campaign.Ranka also accused sections of that ecosystem of targeting CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke as the movement gained traction.Neither named Congress directly in the posts cited, but the subsequent exchange with Singh brought differences between the two sides into focus.Singh, however, argued that CJP should not be treated as any party's property."Let us keep it civil and issue centric. The cause is bigger than a political party," he said.The exchange suggested disagreements over political associations and coordination, even as both sides continued to raise similar demands.ALSO READ: 'Disclose EC files, set up audit panel': Key points from INDIA bloc's plea in SC
Why did the Left, TMC and AAP join?
The October 10 protest made the difference in political positioning more visible. Mamata Banerjee publicly backed CJP before the demonstration, saying, “We are fully supporting the Cockroach (Janta) Party and all the young generation and students. And my humble request, please stop these atrocities.”She later joined the protest in Delhi, pasting a band-aid over her mouth before being detained alongside TMC leaders. Kejriwal announced that he would attend with his family, while senior Left leaders backed the agitation and challenged restrictions imposed ahead of the demonstration.
Pinarayi Vijayan, Mamata Banerjee, Arvind Kejriwal getting detained during October 10 protest
Congress had not announced participation in the same manner. But Rahul Gandhi's absence from Jantar Mantar did not mean silence on the police action. He condemned the mass detentions, accusing Delhi Police of “thuggery” and alleging that the government was encouraging violence against women and young protesters. He also announced plans for Congress and INDIA bloc leaders to meet the Chief Justice of India.Congress, therefore, continued to challenge the government while pursuing its own political mobilisation and institutional interventions. The distinction is between supporting a cause and joining a particular protest platform.CJP legal head Ratna Singh said the invitation remained open to all parties.“If the Congress is willing to come forward and join the protests, it is most welcome. Not just the Congress, but other parties too. Everyone should come together,” she said.“This is not the time to look at different groups protesting separately. We must see this as a unit, as a team effort, with people raising their voices against the wrongs happening in this country,” she added.Her appeal raises a question that extends beyond Congress: What does solidarity mean when parties agree on an issue but differ over how a protest should be organised, represented and politically sustained?
The Anna Hazare lesson
The tensions around CJP have echoes of the 2011 India Against Corruption movement. The BJP publicly backed Anna Hazare's anti-corruption agitation against the Congress-led UPA government. Congress later accused the BJP and RSS of exploiting the movement to undermine its government.
The movement's political afterlife was significant. Arvind Kejriwal, one of its prominent figures, went on to form the Aam Aadmi Party in 2012.
Anna Hazare, Arvind Kejriwal, Kiran Bedi during India Against Andolan movement, 2011
The parallel is relevant to the present Congress-CJP friction. Congress spokesperson Reetam Singh has alleged that CJP's Assam outreach was viewed as an AAP initiative, accusing the party of “piggy riding and hijacking issues of others”.The allegation raises a question about whether Congress sees CJP not simply as a citizens' movement, but as a platform whose political associations and future trajectory matter.

Dozens of possible dinosaur footprints emerge in Iran, researcher urges urgent documentation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:12:51 UTC

Dozens of possible dinosaur footprints emerge in Iran, researcher urges urgent documentation
TEHRAN – A rock surface bearing dozens of possible dinosaur footprints has been exposed in Iran following a landslide, prompting a paleontologist to call for urgent scientific investigation and documentation to protect the traces from weathering and erosion.
Erfan Khosravi, a paleontologist and zoologist, announced the discovery in a post on his personal account on the social media platform X, the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA) reported on Sunday.
Khosravi said the footprints had emerged from beneath sediment deposits after a section of a mountain collapsed. He warned that exposure to the elements could damage or destroy the traces if they were not documented promptly.
The proposed research program includes surveying and investigating the site, making casts of the footprints and recording their three-dimensional structures. These measures could help preserve fine details and provide researchers with material for more detailed scientific analysis.
Khosravi, a graduate of the University of Tehran, said the work was being pursued independently, without government funding. The scope and methods of the documentation would depend on available resources, with different practical approaches considered as the project progresses.
He emphasized that the footprints’ three-dimensional features could provide important clues about how the animals’ feet contacted the ground and how they moved. Preserving these details could help researchers investigate the traces beyond their visible outlines.
Khosravi invited people interested in paleontology and natural heritage documentation to contact him through direct messages on X for further information.
He said the findings would be compiled into a scientific paper and submitted to specialist journals for publication. Financial supporters would be acknowledged in the relevant section of the paper in accordance with journal requirements and agreements with the sponsors.
Dinosaur footprints are known as trace fossils, geological records of animal activity rather than preserved body parts. They form when animals walk across soft sediment that later hardens and is buried, preserving impressions that may survive for millions of years. Their shapes, depth and spacing can help researchers investigate the animals’ movement, foot structure and interactions with their environment.
Iran has a documented record of dinosaur tracks, although such discoveries remain relatively limited. A scientific study published in 2022 described a dinosaur tracksite in the Farrokhi Formation near Khur in central Iran, dating to about 70 million years ago. The researchers said the site added to knowledge of dinosaur activity in Iran and the wider West Asia. The newly reported footprints will require their own geological and paleontological assessment to establish their authenticity, age and scientific significance.

tarek atoui turns tate modern’s turbine hall into a giant experimental orchestra
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:12:03 UTC
23:12:03 KST

tarek atoui turns tate modern’s turbine hall into a giant experimental orchestra
the lebanese sound artist brings sculptural instruments and multisensory installations to london's turbine hall for the 2026 hyundai commission.
[ADVERTISEMENT]
TAREK ATOUI TRANSFORMS TATE MODERN’S TURBINE HALL
The vast industrial interior of Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall is about to find its own voice. Lebanese artist and composer Tarek Atoui takes over the London museum’s iconic space with a large-scale sound installation opening on October 13th, 2026. Created for the 11th Hyundai Commission, the site-specific work brings together experimental musical instruments, sculptural structures, and acoustic experiences that extend beyond conventional listening. Rather than simply filling the hall with music, Atoui approaches the architecture itself as an instrument, exploring how sound can travel through space, materials, and the human body.
Born in Beirut in 1980 and currently based in Paris, Atoui has spent more than two decades challenging the boundaries between music, sculpture, and performance. His practice revolves around the invention and reinvention of musical instruments, often developed alongside craftspeople, engineers, composers, and fellow artists. Glass, water, ceramics, and unconventional mechanical systems frequently appear in his work, producing sounds through touch, movement, breath, or vibration. The resulting installations invite audiences to experience music as something physical and spatial, rather than something that simply reaches the ears.
INSTRUMENTS RESPOND TO THE TURBINE HALL’S ARCHITECTURE
For his latest commission, Atoui has developed four families of instruments selected for their relationship with the Turbine Hall’s monumental proportions and reverberating acoustics. Among them are traditional Asian sheng instruments, activated through computer-controlled air systems, and oversized versions of Central Asian karnai horns produced using 3D printing. Large Korean drums introduce another acoustic dimension, while specially developed textiles function as experimental sound-generating devices. Together, these instruments combine centuries-old musical traditions with contemporary fabrication techniques, forming an unconventional orchestra in which the distinction between sculpture and sound equipment becomes increasingly difficult to maintain.
Particularly intriguing are the large fabric elements developed in collaboration with Satoshi Kondo and Issey Miyake. Coated with conductive graphite paint, the textiles act as oscillators, producing sounds through their movement within the hall. Elsewhere, stone slabs containing speakers transmit vibrations directly through their surfaces, allowing visitors to physically feel sonic frequencies. These elements reflect Atoui’s longstanding interest in listening beyond hearing, informed in part by his collaborations with deaf and hard-of-hearing communities. In this orchestra, the body becomes another way of listening.
TAREK ATOUI EXPLORES LISTENING AS A COLLECTIVE EXPERIENCE
The installation also challenges the relationship between the artwork and its surroundings. Rather than treating the Turbine Hall as a neutral container, Atoui draws on its height, reverberation, and atmospheric conditions to shape the composition itself. Acoustic and electronic sounds interact with the building’s industrial character, while the instruments’ physical presence establishes a visual landscape of pipes, drums, textiles, and resonating surfaces. Catherine Wood, Interim Director of Tate Modern, notes that architectural space plays an important role in Atoui’s investigation of sound and vibration, making the museum’s vast public interior a particularly compelling setting for his work.
Performance and collaboration are equally central to the commission. More than 40 musicians are expected to engage with the installation throughout its six-month run, introducing improvisation and new sonic arrangements into the space. Their contributions will allow the work to evolve rather than remain a fixed composition. This open-ended approach reflects Atoui’s understanding of music as a shared activity, in which the relationships between instruments, performers, architecture, and audiences matter as much as the sounds themselves. A museum installation with no definitive soundtrack, then.
CURATED BY NABILA ABDEL NABI AND DINA AKHMADEEVA
Atoui’s project marks the 11th edition of the Hyundai Commission, an annual initiative inviting international artists to create site-specific works for Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall. Since its launch, the series has welcomed more than 19 million visitors, providing a platform for ambitious artistic experiments within one of London’s most recognizable cultural spaces. The partnership between Tate and Hyundai Motor, established in 2014 and recently extended until 2036, continues to support installations that challenge conventional approaches to contemporary art and public participation.
Curated by Nabila Abdel Nabi and Dina Akhmadeeva, Hyundai Commission: Tarek Atoui will be open to the public from October 13th, 2026, through April 11th, 2027, with free admission. Through an evolving arrangement of instruments, materials, and live performances, the artist proposes a different way of navigating the museum: one in which sound can be seen, felt, and experienced collectively. For a space accustomed to monumental visual gestures, Atoui’s intervention suggests that some of the most interesting things happening in the Turbine Hall may not need to be seen at all.

NATO general sets out tough military response to any ‘foolish’ Russian attack
BRUSSELS/WARSAW – NATO’s top commander warned Russia on Oct 12 that his forces would destroy “anything and everything” involved in any attack if Moscow was “foolish enough” to launch an assault on alliance territory.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, US Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich stressed that NATO was a defensive alliance. But he outlined a three-pronged approach of blocking, blunting and breaking enemy forces to make any attack “utterly futile”.
His remarks come amid heightened tensions between Europe and Russia and lingering concerns among European allies over US President Donald Trump’s commitment to NATO’s mutual defence pact.
Trump recently announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin allowing Russia to supply diesel to global markets and renewed his criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
European governments accuse Moscow of stepping up a campaign of sabotage, drone incursions and cyberattacks against them, while Russia warned last month it could use nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off its Kaliningrad exclave.
Grynkewich did not mention Russia by name but much of his message was clearly directed at Moscow. NATO’s 2022 Strategic Concept describes Russia as the alliance’s most significant security threat.
“If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight,” he said. “We will, in short, ensure any attack, against any ally, proves utterly futile.”
NATO would strike beyond front lines
Grynkewich said NATO’s response would not be limited to forces involved in an initial attack.
“Should the adversary choose to press the attack or commit his reserves, we will break the warfighting system engaged against us,” he said.
“This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains and controls that force.”
Putin said in October that Russia had no plans to attack any European country and wanted to co-exist peacefully. Such declarations have not reassured European leaders, given that Russia made similar statements before the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
Russia has also repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage and other hybrid operations.
Commander seeks to reassure allies
Grynkewich said he had decided to talk publicly about NATO’s plans because recent acts of sabotage and arson had made people around the alliance nervous.
“What I want to do is assure the one billion citizens of our alliance that we’ve got this. We know what we need to do. We know how we would do it,” he said.
He said he also wanted to send a message to anyone considering harming NATO members.
Grynkewich sought to downplay concerns about Washington’s commitment to the alliance, recalling that Trump spoke of “love” at a NATO summit in Ankara in July.
“I was in the room and I felt the love,” he said. REUTERS

South Africa, India share common vision for medicinal plant conservation: Minister

India and South Africa are joining forces to protect medicinal plants and ensure future biodiversity. (https://en.wikipedia.org/)
India and South Africa have similar views on the need to protect medicinal plants and preserve biodiversity, South African deputy minister of forestry, fisheries and the environment Narend Singh said at a symposium in Durban.Organised by the Indian consulate in Durban, the event brought together experts in AYUSH — Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homeopathy — from both countries to explore opportunities for stronger collaboration in traditional and alternative medicine.Addressing the gathering as the keynote speaker on Saturday, Singh said the two nations had worked together to promote systems that uphold rights, ensure fairness and facilitate the equitable sharing of benefits derived from genetic resources and traditional knowledge.He stressed that the current generation has a responsibility to safeguard biodiversity so that future generations can continue to benefit from it.According to the South African National Biodiversity Institute, 262 indigenous plant species are used in traditional medicine in the country, accounting for approximately one-tenth of its total plant species.Singh warned that rising demand for medicinal plants in urban areas, coupled with unsustainable harvesting, climate change, drought, poverty and illegal trade, was putting growing pressure on these natural resources.
“Town and city demand for these plants has outpaced what the wild can supply. Harvesting has become increasingly difficult and, at times, irresponsible. Drought and climate change are worsening the situation, while poverty encourages people to collect whatever they can sell. Some of this trade is also illegal,” he said, referring to the findings of South Africa’s 2024 red list of endangered plants.
Highlighting the risks of excessive harvesting, Singh said 154 medicinal plant species commonly used in traditional practices were facing the threat of extinction, putting their distinctive genetic resources at risk, according to the news agency PTI.He emphasised that the loss of medicinal plants would also endanger the traditional remedies and knowledge associated with them. Singh called for greater efforts to cultivate medicinal species, replenish depleted resources and ensure their sustainable use.He said traditional knowledge could not be genuinely protected while the natural resources supporting it continued to be depleted. Responsible management of genetic resources and gene pools, he added, was essential to preserving medicinal plants for future generations.India’s Deputy high commissioner to South Africa, Banu Prakash, noted that South Africa possessed a rich legacy of traditional knowledge linked to medicinal and aromatic plants.“We were surprised to see the number of herbal products that are popular and being used here,” she said.
While appreciating the South african government’s efforts to plant millions of trees in recent years, Prakash called for greater emphasis on planting species associated with Ayurvedic medicine.
Another speaker, Shobhit Kumar, research officer (ayurveda) in the health and family Welfare vertical at NITI Aayog, said India did not view traditional medicine and modern medicine as competing approaches.Instead, he said, the focus was on finding ways for the two systems to complement each other for the wider public good.Kumar said traditional medicine could work alongside allopathic treatment to help advance the goal of universal health coverage.

Microsoft to rely more on homegrown AI chips, reducing dependence on Nvidia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:04:16 UTC
23:04:16 KST

Microsoft will ramp up use of its homegrown artificial intelligence chips after years of reliance on Nvidia's graphics processing units, as the software giant attempts to bolster its AI stack.
Starting with its third-generation Maia AI accelerator, unveiled on Monday, Microsoft said it will mainly rely on its own silicon to handle incoming requests.
Microsoft's greatest strength in AI has been its Azure cloud, which runs a series of models for clients. Its Microsoft 365 Copilot and GitHub Copilot offer AI-powered services to software engineers and other office workers. And the company develops in-house models, though they've yet to make a big splash in a market dominated by OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.
The emerging opportunity in chips stems from unrelenting demand for advanced processors and a desire in the market for choice. Nvidia's GPUs have been the standard for AI workloads and models, and they fill Microsoft's existing data centers, while also serving to train models from OpenAI and Anthropic.
But as demand keeps growing, the model leaders have embraced a variety of silicon from companies including Amazon, Advanced Micro Devices, Cerebras, Google and, in recent months, Microsoft.
For general-purpose use, Microsoft already taps its own central processing units as well as silicon from Intel and AMD. Finance chief Amy Hood said at a Goldman Sachs conference last month that use of its own chips has helped with "margin improvement over the course of a decade."
Microsoft introduced its inaugural AI chip, the Maia 100, in 2023. It touted the Maia 200 this past January, and CEO Satya Nadella told analysts in July that Maia 200 "delivers 30% better performance per dollar than the latest generation hardware in our fleet" and said it was handling OpenAI models.
Production of the Maia 300 starts in 2027. Microsoft is targeting multi-gigawatt deployments of chips in the Maia family, according to a blog post from Executive Vice President Scott Guthrie. But Alistair Speirs, a general manager, declined to provide a timeline.
"We reserve a little bit of optionality there, because this is an industry that's changing very fast, and we want to deploy the right silicon for the right models that we're using at the right time as well," Speirs said.
Microsoft expects to pack 96 Maia 300 chips into each data center rack, double the number for the Maia 200. The new version can run through up to seven times more AI tokens per rack, with 40% more tokens per megawatt when compared with GPUs.
"We need new architectures that will give us essentially better performance, better use of the power that we have," Speirs said. "You can think of power translating pretty directly into operational cost for something like a data center as well."
Parts of Microsoft 365 Copilot should speed up with Maia 300, said Jim Kleewein, a technical fellow at the company.
In a note distributed to clients on Wednesday, Evercore ISI analysts estimated that Maia will represent about 10% of Microsoft's spending on AI chips by the first quarter of 2027. The analysts recommend buying Microsoft shares.
Nvidia will still be a big part of the equation. CEO Jensen Huang spoke at an event last week where Microsoft announced a Surface laptop containing an Nvidia processor. And when it comes to training models, Microsoft partners with Nvidia and AMD, Speirs said.
Unlike Google's tensor processing units or Amazon's Inferentia and Trainium, Microsoft's accelerators can't be rented by the hour to other companies.
"Nobody has tested them outside of Microsoft yet," said Patrick Moorhead, CEO of advisory firm Moor Insights and Strategy.

Is fatness a feminist issue?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
14:00:42 UTC
23:00:42 KST

Recent research published in Sex Roles suggests that while many fat women identify as feminists, they do not consistently view their body size as a feminist issue. The study highlights a divide in how women understand their bodies, with some pointing to gendered double standards and societal discrimination, while others view their weight as a matter of personal responsibility.
Anti-fatness refers to the systemic and interpersonal prejudice directed at people with larger bodies. Feminist scholars have often linked this anti-fat stigma to traditional gender roles and patriarchal beauty norms. This perspective argues that societal pressure to be thin falls especially hard on women, creating toxic environments that negatively impact their body image, mental health, and social standing.
“American society is often fixated on how women look,” lead author Breanne Fahs, a professor of women and gender studies at Arizona State University and author of Fat and Furious: Igniting Radical Fat Resistance, told PsyPost. “Women are often told to be young, pretty, and skinny by their parents, partners, classmates, and strangers. Psychological research has often shown the problems with ‘thin idealization’ and living for a male gaze. In particular, women are criticized about having defective bodies, and they consequently fear gaining weight, try dangerous diets, and/or loathe their own bodies.”
“In the 1970s, second wave feminists warned that the fixation on slender bodies seriously hurt women and the slogan of ‘fat is a feminist issue’ was born,” Fahs added. “In the last twenty years there has been a growth of social movements that challenged the sexist assumptions of fat stigma, with the group called National Association to Advance Fat Acceptance (NAAFA) leading the way.”
Research has shown that fat women generally face harsher social and economic consequences for their body size than fat men. In one study, fat women were 16 times more likely than fat men to report weight-related job discrimination, and other studies have found that fat women receive harsher judgments of their parenting and are more often denied loans, promotions, or apartments. Fat men, on the other hand, tend to face less stigma and fewer everyday indignities for similar body sizes.
Despite these documented disparities, it has remained an open question whether fat women themselves view their physical experiences through a political or feminist lens. Fahs and her colleague Eric Swank, a professor of social and cultural analysis at Arizona State University, sought to understand how fat women talk about this connection and whether they recognize the gendered dimensions of weight stigma that academics often discuss.
“Lots of research has looked at the causes and consequences of fat hatred among women of all body sizes,” Fahs explained. “Some studies have even looked at the reasons for being a fat activist, but the way fat women view feminism has mostly been overlooked.”
Fahs’s own work helped motivate the project. She has written about women’s dread of gaining weight, anti-fat bias in health care, and the relationships between fat therapists and fat patients. Her experience as both a professor and a practicing clinical psychologist left her curious about whether fat women see anti-fat stigma through a feminist lens.
To investigate this, the researchers interviewed 20 women living in the United States who self-identified as fat or overweight. The participants were recruited through local classified advertisements on Craigslist, allowing the research team to reach a geographically diverse group. The women ranged in age from 27 to 66, with an average age of 40. Half were women of color, 40 percent identified as bisexual or lesbian, and their body weights ranged from under 200 to over 300 pounds.
All 20 interviews were conducted by Fahs over video calls and lasted about 90 minutes each. She asked the women questions about their bodies, their social experiences, and their political perspectives. Two key questions guided the core of the analysis: whether the participants considered themselves feminists, and whether they believed fatness was a feminist issue. The researchers did not provide a definition of feminism, allowing each participant to respond according to her own understanding.
The participants’ responses pointed to a complex divide between personal identification and political frameworks. Thirteen women explicitly identified as feminists, three said they might use the label for certain issues, and four rejected it entirely. When asked if fatness was a feminist issue, the group was evenly split: eight said yes, four said maybe, and eight said no. Several self-identified feminists insisted that fatness was not a feminist issue, while one woman, identified in the study as Marge, firmly rejected the feminist label but still stated that it was.
The researchers identified six distinct themes in how the participants evaluated the issue. Three of the themes supported a connection between weight and feminism. Four women highlighted gendered double standards, observing that society readily accepts fat men as funny or relatable, while fat women face intense social disapproval for the same size. Three women described fatness as a central way women are judged, explaining that a woman’s social worth remains tied to physical appearance.
Overt discrimination, tied for the most common theme linking the two concepts, was raised by four participants. These women cited institutional obstacles in hiring, healthcare, and media representation as evidence of a broader feminist problem. When discussing these barriers, Fahs noted that participants “elaborated how workplaces, hospitals, schools, and families discriminate against women who are fat.”
The remaining three themes rejected the connection between body size and feminism. Three women stated that fatness has nothing to do with feminism, arguing that body weight is an individual matter of personal responsibility and lifestyle rather than gender politics. Two women maintained that fatness has nothing to do with gender, arguing that weight stigma affects people of all genders equally and should not be framed as a women’s issue.
In the final theme, three participants argued that fat women deserve ridicule, framing teasing as a natural consequence of body size or a motivator to lose weight.
Describing these women, Fahs said, “They thought fat women were supposed to be ‘made fun of by someone who is not fat’ and fat people ‘should lose weight’ if they do not want to be teased. This diversity of perspectives shows how fat resistance and feminist fat liberation perspectives still diverge from narratives of self-blame and ridicule.”
The findings point to an uneven alignment between feminist theory and the everyday perspectives of fat women. While some participants expressed an awareness of gender inequality, others expressed anti-fat attitudes, which the authors say could reflect internalized stigma or a form of anti-feminism, or viewed their struggles as entirely personal. The researchers noted that framing fatness through a political lens rather than individual failure could help people challenge anti-fat bias and reduce feelings of personal self-blame.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study relied on a small group of 20 women recruited through Craigslist during the COVID-19 pandemic, so the sample does not reflect the full population of fat women in the United States. In addition, the questions about feminism came after about an hour of discussion focused on fatness, which may have influenced the way participants answered.
The study also asked participants whether they identified as feminists rather than measuring specific feminist beliefs, and several women appeared to associate feminism primarily with the #MeToo movement or perceived extremes. Both researchers identify as fat feminists, and Fahs conducted all 20 interviews herself, which could have shaped how participants discussed sensitive topics. Future research using standardized surveys could help clarify how widespread these viewpoints are across the broader population.
The study, “Does Fatness Politicize Women? Fat Women’s Narratives on Whether Fatness is a Feminist Issue,” was authored by Breanne Fahs and Eric Swank.

Europe still divided on buying locally for defence, MBDA CEO says
Oct 12 - The head of European missile maker MBDA said on Monday that efforts to steer more defence spending towards European suppliers faced political hurdles, with EU governments still divided over how much to rely on US security guarantees.
Washington has been pressing European NATO allies to increase defence spending, while France has led calls to buy more European-made weapons amid questions over the US commitment to Europe's security.
"Do we want as Europeans to really take our own fate in our hands and then bring our European capabilities to the NATO alliance, or are we simply increasing our capabilities by buying outside?" MBDA CEO Eric Beranger asked the Warsaw Security Forum.
"There are some different attitudes between the various governments. I think the jury is still out," Beranger said, adding: "There is still some way to go".
DETERRENCE
Beranger, who steps down next month, was among several speakers debating European strategic autonomy at the forum, which is taking place amid heightened tensions over the war in Ukraine.
Several European countries, including conference host Poland, Germany and the Netherlands, have turned to US suppliers for equipment such as F-35 fighter jets.
"Limiting American defense industry in European procurement programs threatens that partnership and weakens our mutual security", the US mission to the European Union said in February.
Nuclear deterrence was also a focus of the discussion, with Russia recently renewing warnings that it could use nuclear weapons to defend itself.
"Of all the events at this conference that the Russians will be most interested in hearing ... it will be this one", former British defence minister Ben Wallace said, referring to Europe's ability to strengthen its nuclear and conventional deterrence.
"Deterrence is not only capabilities; deterrence is also perceptions. Do we believe our American allies will come? Does Russia believe our American allies will come?" said Claudia Major, senior vice president for transatlantic security at the German Marshall Fund.
"I don't say give up on the US. I just say don't blind ourselves", Major added, citing recent friction with the US over Greenland, Russia and Ukraine.
NATO members, including the US, reaffirmed their commitment to collective defence in the Ankara Summit Declaration in July, repeating that "an attack on one is an attack on all".
Stressing that credibility is central to deterrence, Beranger said Europe already had the industrial base it needed to strengthen its defences. REUTERS
