How diesel became the new geopolitical battleground, and what it means for the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
12:22:54 UTC
21:22:54 KST

Access to diesel, the fuel that powers global economic activity, has become the latest geopolitical battleground amid two raging wars, setting off a domino effect across nations and hitting the Global South hardest.
Diesel prices are going through the roof in most of the world. Even in the US, which retains the capacity to subsidise retail consumers as the world’s richest country, the diesel price has gone up 70 percent since it attacked Iran on February 28.
But the diesel crisis is far worse in the Global South, where poorer countries lack emergency stockpiles or massive cash reserves to protect consumers from an existential threat to basic food supply chains, transport, and critical infrastructure.
Some countries, like the Philippines, have declared national energy emergencies, while others, such as Sri Lanka, have rationed fuel supplies. In some African countries, fuel prices have surged by up to 150 percent.
In Pakistan, the government has adopted a daily price revision mechanism for diesel, which is now 40 percent more expensive than it was at the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran.
Analysts point out that unlike previous price shocks driven mainly by crude constraints, the current upswing in diesel prices is partly due to a deficit in refinery capacity.
Drone and missile attacks by Iran and its allies have targeted large crude processing plants in Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Bahrain.
Russian refineries have also come under a spate of attacks by Ukraine in what is being described as the ‘energy war’; Russian refineries are now operating at 60 percent of capacity.
The price of diesel has increased more than the price of petrol — used mostly by passenger cars — for two main reasons. One, diesel supplies were already tighter than those of gasoline, even before the start of the Iran war.
And two, refineries in the Gulf countries that came under fire produced more diesel than petrol. No other countries had the idle capacity that could be tapped immediately to make up for the production loss.
As a result, millions of barrels of Middle Eastern and Russian diesel have disappeared from the global market.
To counter the shortage, the US has struck a deal with Russia to buy diesel, even though heavy sanctions otherwise restrict Moscow's ability to sell energy worldwide.
Separately, US President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine on October 11, even though Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was still waiting to see the deal's details.
Resource nationalism rears its head
Analysts say the global diesel crisis has unleashed a wave of ‘resource nationalism’ in which top producers limit supplies, driving global ‘crack spreads’, or refining margins, to historic highs.
Last month, Moscow extended a strict ban on diesel exports through the summer and autumn, stating shipments would not fully return until Western sanctions were lifted.
Likewise, Beijing temporarily paused fuel exports to prioritise its domestic inventory.
Before striking a diesel import deal with Russia, the US aggressively pressured European allies to release strategic reserves or face a US diesel export ban, setting off a global alarm.
Baris Alpaslan, an economist and chief adviser at IC Holding – a Turkish conglomerate with energy production and distribution businesses – makes a distinction between resource sovereignty and resource nationalism.
“I think we need to distinguish between the legitimate exercise of resource sovereignty and the broader consequences of resource nationalism,” he tells TRT World.
Protecting domestic supply is a real duty, particularly during a major crisis, he says.
But the problem arises when many countries do it all at once.
“(Export bans) may shift part of the economic cost of a geopolitical crisis onto countries that had little or no role in causing it, particularly poorer, fuel-importing economies in Africa, Asia and Latin America,” he says.
Higher diesel prices quickly feed into transport costs, food prices, and broader inflation, he says.
“The frustration in the Global South is understandable. Many of these countries are price takers in global energy markets, with limited fiscal capacity to cushion their populations against external price shocks,” he says.
The collective result can be a deeper global shortage, with the poorest and most import-dependent economies often bearing a disproportionate share of the cost, he says.
New battle lines
Yasar Sari, director of the Haydar Aliyev Centre for Eurasian Studies at Ibn Haldun University, tells TRT World that access to diesel is already pushing countries to “form alliances around fuel supplies, rather than ideology”.
He points to India’s import dependence – more than 80 percent of its crude requirement – and the strain of balancing outside diplomacy with negotiations inside BRICS, a group of emerging economies mostly from the Global South.
The May BRICS summit produced no joint statement and referred only to “differing views among some members” of the bloc, which includes both Iran and the UAE as full members.
The absence of a joint statement indicated that energy security issues are eroding regional cohesion, he notes.
China’s heavy inventories, estimated to be 1.49 billion barrels and described as mostly crude, still give Beijing leverage to hold product at home, he adds.
European countries hold the largest emergency diesel reserves, with France and Germany together accounting for more than a third of the EU’s strategic stocks, he says.
American public stocks provide a regional cushion at best, not a global store, he notes.
This is the reason the US has pressed France and Germany to draw those stocks down, with restrictions on US diesel exports held out as leverage ahead of the US midterms planned for the first week of November.
Sari refers to the 1973 Arab oil embargo, when producers from the Gulf cut supply to states that had backed Israel.
But he highlights the difference between then and now: “(Fuel) weaponisation is less about producers withholding supply and more about importers hoarding it – a reverse embargo in which vulnerable nations scramble to secure what remains,” he says.
According to Alpaslan, energy access is increasingly becoming a source of geopolitical leverage.
A government short of diesel for farms, freight or power may be more receptive to a supplier that can offer reliable deliveries or favourable financing, he says.
His concern is that energy insecurity can narrow the foreign-policy choices available to poorer countries.
“The real test is whether access to essential fuel remains governed primarily by reliable trade and commercial considerations, or increasingly becomes an instrument of political pressure,” he says.
Survival beyond wars
Sari says China and South Korea can shield home markets and limit exports. Indonesia, the Philippines, Bangladesh and Ethiopia cannot.
“Fuel access isn’t causing a clean geopolitical split, but it is accelerating fragmentation, with each nation’s survival strategy shaped by its reserves and ability to pay,” he says.
How long can that be managed?
Sari says the window to manage the crisis without triggering catastrophic damage to the global economy is narrow – likely measured in weeks, not months.
Even a political settlement would not quickly restore normalcy, he notes.
He describes the G7’s 100-million-barrel release as a gesture that only buys time.
Ending both wars today will end the war premium almost at once, he says.
“But physical supply recovery would take months to years because of damaged refineries, disrupted shipping, and structural changes in trade flows,” he says.

12:21:58 UTC
21:21:58 KST

A Turkish court on Oct. 12 acquitted 44 people who faced legal proceedings over protests that erupted following the March 2025 arrest of Istanbul Mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu.
The ruling came in the case, which was brought against young protesters who took to the streets after İmamoğlu was detained on March 19, 2025, as part of a corruption investigation involving the Istanbul Municipality.
The court acquitted 44 of the 45 defendants standing trial over the demonstrations in Saraçhane, the area outside Istanbul City Hall that became a focal point of the protests.
The remaining defendant was sentenced to seven months and 15 days in prison on charges of inciting the commission of a crime over a social media post.
The court, however, ruled to defer the announcement of the verdict, a measure under Turkish law that can allow a conviction to be annulled if the defendant meets certain conditions during a specified period.
Mass demonstrations broke out across Türkiye following İmamoğlu’s arrest on corruption allegations last year, with hundreds of people detained in connection with the protests.
İmamoğlu, a prominent opposition figure, went on trial on March 9, nearly a year after his imprisonment. The proceedings remain ongoing, and no final verdict has yet been delivered in his case.

'We won't let the truth be buried': October 7 survivors demand Netanyahu release records
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:11:35 UTC
21:11:35 KST

Dozens of survivors and relatives of victims of the October 7 massacre are demanding that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu release complete transcripts, recordings and logs documenting security discussions held in the period leading up to the Hamas attack and on the morning of the massacre.
In a letter sent to the prime minister Tuesday, they wrote: "We will not accept that the truth about this grave failure remains locked in a safe, buried, concealed, distorted and replaced by a version designed to serve those whose responsibility is under scrutiny. We demand that you immediately order the safes in the Prime Minister's Office to be opened and the materials submitted for review by the military censor and released to the public, in accordance with the law."
The signatories include former hostages, bereaved family members and others affected by the October 7 attack. Among them are Yocheved Lifshitz, who was abducted to Gaza and whose husband, Oded, was murdered in captivity; former hostage Ditza Heiman; Dikla Shamriz, whose son Alon was abducted and later mistakenly killed by IDF troops in the Gaza Strip; and Carmit Palty Katzir, whose father, Rami, was murdered in the massacre and whose mother, Hanna, was abducted.
Other signatories include Einav Zangauker, Hadas Kalderon, Danny Elgart, Maayan Sherman, Rani and Ayala Metzger and Vicky and Yehuda Cohen.
The appeal follows a series of investigative reports published in recent weeks. Over the weekend, Ronen Bergman and Yuval Rubovitch reported in Yedioth Ahronoth and ynet on what they described as Netanyahu's selective presentation of events in a 55-page account he submitted to the state comptroller.
In addition, Avi Gil, Netanyahu's former military secretary, described an alleged attempt by the prime minister's chief of staff, Tzachi Braverman, to change the recorded time of a phone call in an official transcript from the morning of the massacre. The allegation was first reported by journalist Nadav Eyal in July 2024.
"The recent investigations raise serious suspicions of falsification of official documents and tampering with evidence," the letter said.
"These are compounded by reports that approximately 30 classified transcripts were removed from the Prime Minister's Office and that the original records of security discussions were concentrated in safes at the Prime Minister's Office.
"These original materials, which could disappear or be tampered with at any moment, are essential for establishing firsthand what was said in real time and determining the reliability and completeness of the published records and transcripts."
The signatories are demanding that Netanyahu immediately order the safes opened, allow an independent examination of the original records and submit the materials to the military censor for review before their release to the public.
"We cannot bring back those who were murdered, nor can we erase the massacre and the abduction of our loved ones," they concluded. "But we will not accept that the truth is buried as well. Open the safes. Release the original transcripts and recordings. Let the truth speak before it is lost."
According to Bergman and Rubovitch's investigation, senior officials in the Prime Minister's Office took a series of steps during the opening days of the war to ensure that records of security and war Cabinet discussions would be prepared by the prime minister's staff, with only a single copy kept in secure safes in Jerusalem.
The report linked those measures to several other developments, including the alleged falsification of the transcript of Netanyahu's second phone call with Gil on the morning of October 7.
It also described how officials in the Prime Minister's Office, other than the military secretary, recruited female soldiers and officers who had previously served in the office to help prepare what the investigation characterized as Netanyahu's carefully constructed version of events.
Under the direction of senior officials in the Prime Minister's Office, a 55-page document was prepared and presented by Netanyahu as his complete account of events. He subsequently submitted it to the state comptroller.
A series of investigations published by ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth in recent weeks found that the document, which Netanyahu presented as part of his effort to establish the truth and provide transparency, contained what the reports described as extensive attempts to cover up events, manipulate facts, distort the record and, in some cases, make outright false claims.
Separately, retired Maj. Gen. Gil, who served as Netanyahu's military secretary both before and after the October 7 massacre, publicly alleged for the first time in an interview with Channel 12 on Thursday that at least one official record from the morning of the attack had been altered by the Prime Minister's Office.
Gil identified chief of staff Tzachi Braverman as the person behind the alleged alteration.
The matter remains under investigation and is awaiting a decision, which is not expected before the elections.

“Il faut qu’on se réveille” : pour Edouard Philippe, le retard européen dans l’IA n’est pas une fatalité
Le candidat Horizons à l’élection présidentielle souhaite mobiliser l’épargne des Européens pour investir dans les entreprises numériques, a-t-il déclaré au sommet sur la compétitivité de POLITICO.
PARIS — "Le monde de l’IA fait du capital américain avec de l’épargne et des données européennes, et ça m’agace, parce que c’est une question de souveraineté", a lancé Edouard Philippe ce mardi, à l'occasion du sommet sur la compétitivité de POLITICO.
Le candidat à la présidentielle a insisté sur la nécessité pour la France, et l'Europe, de ne pas abandonner la course à l'intelligence artificielle face aux Etats-Unis et à la Chine.
"Il y a une telle souveraineté qui s'attache à ces données et leur traitement, qu'on ne peut pas se dire 'tant pis, on bénéficiera des bienfaits' : il faut qu'on se réveille".
Advertisement
Philippe souhaite ainsi mobiliser l'épargne des Européens et "consacrer beaucoup de moyens pour essayer de limiter le retard pris", en appuyant sur nos quelques points forts, comme la start-up française Mistral. Et ce, quand bien même ils ne seraient pas 100% souverains côté investisseurs.
L'ancien Premier ministre a également moqué la décision du moteur de recherche allemand Ecosia d'abandonner Mistral. "Qu'on nous dise que Mistral n'est pas complètement souverain, je peux l'entendre, car on est jamais totalement autonome. Mais si c'est pour se tourner vers des modèles chinois, ça ne me paraît pas un progrès considérable".
Il ne s'étonne pas non plus que les Allemands aient envie de développer leurs propres modèles d'IA, mais cela ne doit pas empêcher les deux pays de mener des "projets communs" dans des "marchés et domaines stratégiques".
Enfin, Edouard Philippe s'est dit contre le "chacun pour soi" et favorable à une régulation mondiale de l'IA pour "voir comment on gère la recherche, le développement et les usages" de cette technologie.

Impact of artificial intelligence on the administration of justice and the protection of human rights were the topics of the 17th Warsaw Human Rights Seminar. The event attended by MFA Undersecretary of State Artur Harazim was held in Warsaw on 12 October 2026.
Advances in artificial intelligence improve the efficiency of the administration of justice and facilitate access to legal information. At the same time, however, they give rise to significant challenges in terms of algorithmic transparency, data protection, non-discrimination, accountability, and the protection of procedural rights.
During the Seminar, experts sought answers to the question of how to reconcile the use of new technologies with the standards of the European Convention of Human Rights and the principles of the rule of law.
The Seminar was inaugurated by the deputy head of Polish diplomacy, Artur Harazim, who underlined that:
The central question is not whether AI will become part of our justice system. In many respects, that process has already begun. Our objective should be to ensure that innovation serves justice.
The keynote address entitled “Artificial intelligence and the future of human rights protection” was delivered by former President of the European Court of Human Rights Robert Spano. Then, President of the Supreme Administrative Court Jacek Chlebny spoke on the use of emerging technologies in administrative courts.
Later on, Poland’s Commissioner for Human Rights Sylwia Gregorczyk-Abram and a European Court of Human Rights judge Úna Ní Raifeartaigh discussed the future of human rights protection in the digital age. The Court’s role in the protection of human rights in the era of artificial intelligence was also addressed, as well as the impact of technology on legal practice and representation before the courts.
The Seminar was attended by judges and representatives of the European Court of Human Rights, the Council of Europe, and the Court of Justice the European Union, as well as the representatives of national human rights institutions, the judiciary, public administration, the legal profession, and academia.
The event concluded with a session on the future of human rights and justice in the era of artificial intelligence, featuring the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Michael O'Flaherty.

What a looming Ethiopia-Eritrea war could mean for Egypt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:11:48 UTC
21:11:48 KST

Breadcrumb
As war looms between Ethiopia and Eritrea, what's at stake for Egypt?
Cairo, Egypt - As fighting in Ethiopia threatens to reignite a full-scale war, Egypt has repeatedly denied accusations that it is backing the rebels.
But Cairo has good geostrategic reasons to watch the crisis closely.
In late September, seven armed groups in northern Ethiopia, several of them former enemies, formed an alliance united by a single aim: to topple the government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.
The alliance has raised fears that the peace deal that ended Ethiopia’s two-year war in 2022 may unravel. That conflict killed an estimated 600,000 people, making it one of the deadliest of the 21st century, and drove tens of thousands from their homes across the country’s borders.
Egypt denies Addis Ababa’s allegations that it is supplying arms to the new alliance. Yet its interest in Ethiopia extends well beyond the latest fighting.
In recent years, Cairo has worked to expand its influence across the Horn of Africa, deepening political, military, and economic ties with Somalia, Eritrea, and Djibouti, while maintaining longstanding relationships with Sudan and South Sudan.
Military-cooperation agreements and mutual-defence pacts have helped cement this presence. Egypt is also preparing to deploy troops to Somalia as part of the African Union’s Support and Stabilisation Mission.
For Cairo, instability in Ethiopia is not simply a neighbouring country’s problem: it is a potential threat to its wider regional interests and national security.
Containing Ethiopia
Egypt’s strategy in the Horn of Africa has centred on strengthening ties with countries surrounding Ethiopia, partly to counter what Cairo perceives as Addis Ababa’s ambitions for regional dominance.
A central source of friction is the Nile, Egypt’s principal source of freshwater. Over the past decade, Ethiopia has built the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) on the Blue Nile, giving it greater control over the timing of water flows downstream.
Addis Ababa is also planning at least three further dams that could affect water supplies to Egypt and Sudan.
The Ethiopian government argues that such projects are essential to economic development, electricity generation and lifting tens of millions of people out of poverty.
Egyptian analysts, however, see a broader strategic calculation. They argue that Ethiopia’s growing control over the Nile could give it economic and political leverage over downstream countries.
“My belief is that Ethiopia doesn't need all these dams to economically develop or generate electricity for its people,” Egyptian water resources expert Nader Nour-Eddin told The New Arab.
The GERD stalemate
Egypt is totally dependent on the Nile for the needs of its population of 120 million, as well as its agricultural and industrial activities.
The fallout from the GERD has forced Cairo into an expensive adaptation strategy that has so far cost it billions of dollars, including through the construction of a series of seawater desalination plants and others for sewage treatment.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has repeatedly described the Nile as an "existential issue" for his country.
Earlier this month, he described the Nile as his country's "lifeline" and said that Egypt would continue to defend its Nile water rights through all measures enshrined in international law.
The stalemate over the GERD, following a decade of failed negotiations between the Egyptians and the Ethiopians, is also part of an evolving struggle between the two sides over the Red Sea.
Landlocked Ethiopia's Red Sea quest is causing concern in Egypt, where it is viewed as part of Ethiopia's desire to control a crucial maritime chokepoint that leads up to an indispensable economic artery for the Egyptians, namely the Suez Canal.
Ethiopia says that Red Sea access is indispensable for its economic development and trade with the outside world.
The risk of a regional war
A war between Ethiopia and Eritrea might have seemed unlikely only a few months ago. Now, however, the two countries are edging towards confrontation, raising questions about how Egypt might respond.
Tensions between the two countries have been piling up for several months, especially as Ethiopia has escalated its rhetoric on access to the Red Sea, with the Eritrean Port of Assab at the centre of its plans.
Ethiopia talks about this port within the context of its historical right to ownership, with Ethiopian officials and commentators framing Eritrea's 1993 independence from Ethiopia and Ethiopia's loss of sea access as a "conspiracy".
Ethiopian political analyst Jemal Beshir Ahmed said the loss of his country's coastline in 1993 was the result of political decisions, the Eritrean armed struggle, and external geopolitical involvement that left Ethiopia landlocked.
"This is an Ethiopian political interpretation, rather than an undisputed historical fact," he told The New Arab.
Ethiopia views Assab as the "most natural option", he added, given its proximity to the Ethiopian border, its existing infrastructure, and its long history as an important outlet for Ethiopian trade.
The civil war raging in northern Ethiopia is now drawing in multiple outside parties, opening the door for them to settle old scores, achieve geostrategic gains, or vanquish their rivals.
Eritrea, reportedly supporting the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), has deployed troops in northern Ethiopia, in what is seen as an attempt by Asmara to create a buffer against Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) advances towards the Eritrean border and consequently into Assab, which is located only a few kilometres away from the Ethiopian border.
It probably views the war as a good chance to create an advance base in this area to prevent – or at least slow down – any attempt by the ENDF to march towards the joint border.
Ethiopia may use the same deployment of Eritrean troops as an excuse to move its forces into the neighbouring country and recapture Assab, thus killing two birds with one stone: regain a territory historically believed to be its own and settle old scores with Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, a figure loathed by many in Addis Ababa.
In any war between Eritrea and Ethiopia, Egypt may exploit an opportunity to kill Addis Ababa's regional ambitions and undermine the Horn of Africa state for many years to come, preventing it from becoming the potential Red Sea threat or Nile Basin hegemon that Cairo fears.
It can do this by offering support to the Eritrean army in its expected showdown with the ENDF.
Those closely following these serious developments believe a war erupting in the Horn of Africa would become a magnet for all types of external forces.
Independent Eritrean Horn of Africa specialist Azeez Hagos said a war between the two countries would be difficult to contain as a purely bilateral conflict.
"This war would erupt in an already interconnected regional environment," he told The New Arab.
Northern Ethiopia is unstable, Sudan is emerging from a devastating war, in which Addis Ababa has faced accusations of supporting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), and tensions involving Egypt, Somalia, and the Red Sea are already overlapping.
"If the balance in Sudan continues to shift, some of that political and security pressure could also rebound towards Ethiopia," Hagos said.
He noted that the danger becomes even greater if the conflict reaches southern Eritrea or Assab.
At that point, he said, it would no longer be only a land war between two neighbouring states.
"It would directly involve Red Sea security, ports, maritime routes and the interests of littoral states and other regional powers," Hagos said. "I would not see such a war as simply another Eritrean-Ethiopian confrontation."
A quadrilateral Egyptian-Eritrean-Somali-Sudanese summit in the Egyptian Mediterranean city of Alamein earlier this month offered insights into the anti-Ethiopia alliance forming on the margins of the Ethiopian civil war.
Calls for support for Addis Ababa are also pouring in, including from Israel, whose foreign minister in early October expressed backing for Ethiopia's unity and stability.
A war with Eritrea would complicate Ethiopia's situation, forcing it to fight a foreign enemy, while at the same time battling a host of internal adversaries.
The growing involvement of outside powers, alongside the flow of weapons to competing parties, illustrates how the conflict could become a proxy battleground in a wider struggle over maritime chokepoints and the distribution of political and military influence across the Horn of Africa.
Unless diplomacy prevails, the confrontation risks developing into a prolonged war of attrition, destabilising both the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea region as rival powers compete to shape their future.
Saleh Salem is an Egyptian journalist

11 infants treated for suspected food poisoning at West Bank settlement day care
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:25:09 UTC
21:25:09 KST

Eleven Israeli infants at a day care center in the West Bank settlement of Beitar Illit were treated Tuesday after showing symptoms of suspected food poisoning, police and emergency services said.
Police said the symptoms followed exposure to food, after firefighters and rescue personnel ruled out the presence of hazardous substances at the scene. The day care center was closed and the incident was reported to the Health Ministry.
According to Magen David Adom, five infants were taken to Hadassah Ein Kerem Hospital in Jerusalem. The hospital said one was in moderate condition, while the other four were undergoing further examinations.
The infants arrived with "flushed faces and showing signs of distress," the hospital said.
Four women who accompanied the infants were also being treated at the hospital, all in mild condition.
In January, two infants died at a private, unlicensed day care in an ultra-Orthodox neighborhood in Jerusalem. Another 53 infants were evacuated from the building, many suffering from coughing.
Medical examinations indicated that the two infants may have suffered from heatstroke. Emergency responders said they had been inside a stroller in a closed room heated by an air conditioner running at full power. The infants were sweating and had red spots on their skin, symptoms that can indicate heatstroke.
Initial emergency service reports said the infants had been harmed by toxic fumes, but firefighters later ruled out the presence of hazardous substances or toxic gas.
"The findings are that there are no findings," Prof. Yaniv Sherer, director of Hadassah Ein Kerem Hospital, said at the time. "We have not located or isolated any material in the infants' blood that explains what happened."
Sherer said heat or overcrowding may have contributed, but that the hospital could not determine the cause.
